senses.ex: The reviewer dismissed the self-help book as arrant nonsense dressed up in scientific jargon.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "arraier", to put in order, a word related to "ready" and the idea of preparation.

senses.def: a varied or orderly collection of things
senses.ex: The market displayed an array of spices, from smoky paprika to bright yellow turmeric.

senses.def: arrange people or things in a deliberate order
senses.ex: The curator arrayed the artifacts by century so visitors could trace changes in the pottery.

senses.def: dress someone in elaborate or distinctive clothing
senses.ex: The performers were arrayed in embroidered jackets and tall boots for the parade.

origin: From Anglo-French "arere", meaning "behind", ultimately from Latin "ad", toward, and "retro", backward.

senses.def: overdue money that remains unpaid
senses.ex: After missing three rent payments, the tenant faced arrears that grew with every late fee.

senses.def: the state of being behind with scheduled payments or work
senses.ex: The clinic was in arrears with its patient reports after the computer outage.

syn: overdue payments, back payments, unpaid debt

origin: From Old French "arester", to stop, from Latin "ad", to, plus "restare", to stay back or stop.

senses.def: seize someone by legal authority and take them into custody
senses.ex: Police arrested the driver after a breath test showed he was well over the legal limit.

senses.def: stop or check the progress of something
senses.ex: Doctors hoped the new medication would arrest the spread of the infection.

senses.def: catch and hold someone's attention
senses.ex: A huge mural of a whale arrested the attention of everyone who walked into the lobby.

senses.def: the act of taking someone into legal custody
senses.ex: The arrest of the mayor on bribery charges shocked the small town.

syn: detain, apprehend, seize, capture, take into custody

origin: From the verb "arrest" in its sense "to stop", so an arresting sight stops you in your tracks.

senses.def: striking and immediately attention-grabbing
senses.ex: The photographer's most arresting image showed a lone child standing in a field of burned sunflowers.

origin: Borrowed from French "arriviste", from "arriver", to arrive, so an arriviste is someone who has only just arrived among the rich or powerful.

senses.def: ambitious newcomer to wealth or status, often seen as pushy or lacking refinement
senses.ex: The old families of the resort town sneered at the tech arriviste who bought the largest mansion on the bay.

syn: upstart, parvenu, social climber, nouveau riche, newcomer

origin: From Middle French "arrogance", from Latin "arrogantia", meaning presumption or an overbearing claim to superiority.

senses.def: an exaggerated belief in one's own importance or superiority
senses.ex: His arrogance made him dismiss the lab assistant's warning without checking the faulty instrument.

origin: From Latin "arrogare", to claim for oneself, from "ad", to, plus "rogare", to ask; "arrogant" comes from the same verb.

senses.def: take or claim something for oneself without having the right to it
senses.ex: The committee chair arrogated the power to approve all spending, though the bylaws gave it to the full board.

origin: Borrowed from Spanish "arroyo", meaning "stream" or "brook", a name often applied to dry channels in the American Southwest.

senses.def: a dry streambed that carries water after heavy rain
senses.ex: Flash rain filled the arroyo overnight, forcing hikers to wait above its steep banks.

origin: From "art", in its older sense of skill or cunning, plus "-ful".

senses.def: clever or skillful in a sly or crafty way
senses.ex: The artful negotiator let the other side believe they had won while quietly securing every point she wanted.

senses.def: showing creative skill and taste
senses.ex: The chef's artful arrangement of herbs and edible flowers made the salad look like a painting.

origin: From Latin "articulatus", jointed or distinct, from "articulus", a small joint, so articulate speech is divided into clear, separate parts.

senses.def: able to express ideas clearly, fluently, and effectively
senses.ex: The most articulate member of the debate team was chosen to deliver the closing argument.

senses.def: express an idea or feeling clearly in words
senses.ex: The counselor helped the frightened boy articulate why he no longer wanted to go to school.

senses.def: pronounce words or sounds clearly and distinctly
senses.ex: The voice coach made the actors articulate every consonant so the back row could follow the dialogue.

origin: From Italian "artefatto", from Latin "arte", by skill, plus "factum", a thing made.

senses.def: object made by human beings, especially one of historical or cultural interest
senses.ex: Divers recovered pottery, coins, and other artifacts from the Roman shipwreck.

senses.def: misleading feature or result produced by the method of observation rather than the thing observed
senses.ex: The strange streak in the photograph turned out to be an artifact of the camera's cheap lens.

origin: From French, from Latin "artificium", craftsmanship, from "artifex", craftsman, from "ars", skill, plus "facere", to make.

senses.def: clever trickery or deception used to achieve something
senses.ex: The spy relied on artifice rather than force, charming her way past guards with forged invitations.

senses.def: skill and ingenuity in making or doing something
senses.ex: The garden looked wild and natural, but in fact it was the product of great artifice.

origin: Borrowed from French "artisan", ultimately from Latin "ars", meaning "skill" or "craft".

senses.def: a skilled maker of goods, especially by hand
senses.ex: The artisan shaped each clay cup by hand, leaving a small thumbprint beneath the glaze.

senses.def: made with skilled handwork, often by traditional methods
senses.ex: The bakery sold artisan loaves with crackling crusts and sourdough starters maintained for decades.

origin: From "art", in its older sense of skill or cunning, plus "-less", without.

senses.def: natural and sincere, without deceit or pretense
senses.ex: The child's artless question about why the guest wore a wig left the whole table red-faced.

senses.def: lacking skill or refinement; crude
senses.ex: The artless translation turned the poet's elegant verses into clumsy, flat prose.

origin: From "artless", without cunning, plus "-ness", from "art", in its older sense of skill or craft.

senses.def: simple naturalness and sincerity, free of deceit or pretense
senses.ex: Voters warmed to the candidate's artlessness, which made her seem refreshingly different from polished career politicians.

origin: From "ascendant", rising, from Latin "ascendere", to climb up, from "ad", to, plus "scandere", to climb.

senses.def: position of dominant power or influence
senses.ex: By the end of the decade, the reform faction had gained ascendancy within the party.

origin: From Latin "ascendere", to climb upward, built from "ad", toward, and "scandere", to climb.

senses.def: gaining power, influence, or prominence
senses.ex: The younger coalition was ascendant after winning several districts once held by established parties.

senses.def: a position of growing power or influence
senses.ex: With three victories in a row, the chess club was clearly in the ascendant.

origin: From Old French "acertener", to make certain, from "a-", to, plus "certain", from Latin "certus", sure.

senses.def: find out something for certain
senses.ex: Investigators are still trying to ascertain how the fire started in the empty warehouse.

syn: determine, establish, discover, verify, find out

origin: From Greek "askesis", meaning "exercise" or "training", through Late Latin. The discipline later took a spiritual sense.

senses.def: rigorous self-discipline, especially for spiritual or moral growth
senses.ex: Her month of silence was an ascesis intended to strengthen attention and loosen old habits.

origin: From Greek "askētikos", from "askētēs", one who practices or trains, from "askein", to exercise, a word used first of athletes and later of hermits.

senses.def: practicing strict self-denial and avoiding comfort or pleasure
senses.ex: The monks lived an ascetic life, eating one simple meal a day and sleeping on wooden boards.

senses.def: person who gives up comforts and pleasures, often for religious reasons
senses.ex: The famous ascetic owned nothing but a robe, a bowl, and a few battered books.

origin: From "ascribe" plus the suffix "-able". Latin "ascribere" meant "write down" or "assign to someone".

senses.def: reasonably attributable to a particular cause or source
senses.ex: The sudden improvement was ascribable to a new irrigation system, not an unusually wet summer.

origin: From Latin "ascribere", to add in writing, from "ad", to, plus "scribere", to write.

senses.def: regard something as caused by or belonging to a particular source
senses.ex: The coach ascribed the team's losing streak to injuries rather than poor tactics.

senses.def: credit a work of art or writing to a particular creator
senses.ex: The unsigned painting was long ascribed to a famous Dutch master, but experts now doubt it.

syn: attribute, assign, credit, impute, chalk up

origin: From "a-", without, plus "septic", from Greek "sēptikos", causing rot, so aseptic means free of anything that causes infection.

senses.def: free from bacteria and other germs that cause disease
senses.ex: Surgeons must work in aseptic conditions to keep patients from developing infections.

senses.def: lacking emotion, warmth, or liveliness
senses.ex: The new office building had an aseptic feel, all white walls and humming lights.

origin: From "ash", the gray powder left after burning, plus "-en", made of or like.

senses.def: very pale, especially from shock, fear, or illness
senses.ex: Her father's face turned ashen when the doctor described how serious the injury was.

origin: From Latin "asininus", meaning "of a donkey", from "asinus", donkey. English later used the animal comparison for foolishness.

senses.def: extremely foolish or lacking good judgment
senses.ex: It was asinine to leave the only spare key inside the locked mountain cabin.

origin: Origin unknown; it may be related to older words in English, French, or Italian meaning sideways or aslant.

senses.def: with suspicion, doubt, or disapproval
senses.ex: Longtime residents looked askance at the developer's promise that the new tower would not block their view.

origin: From "a-", on, plus "skew", slanting or turned aside.

senses.def: not straight or level; crooked
senses.ex: After the earthquake, every picture in the hallway hung askew.

senses.def: in a crooked or wrong way; awry
senses.ex: The surprise party went badly askew when the guest of honor arrived an hour early.

origin: From Latin "asperitas", roughness, from "asper", rough, so asperity is a roughness of tone or manner.

senses.def: harshness or sharpness of tone or manner
senses.ex: "That is not what I asked," the professor replied with some asperity, glaring at the unprepared student.

origin: From Latin "aspergere", "to sprinkle", from "ad", toward, and "spargere", to scatter. Accusations came to be imagined as stains.

senses.def: damage someone's reputation by making unfair or false accusations
senses.ex: The columnist tried to asperse the scientist's character with claims he had invented the data.

origin: From Latin "aspersio", a sprinkling, from "aspergere", to sprinkle on, so casting aspersions is like spattering someone's name with mud.

senses.def: damaging or unfair remark attacking someone's reputation
senses.ex: The senator refused to cast aspersions on her rival's character and focused only on his voting record.

origin: Plural of "aspersion", from Latin "aspersio", a sprinkling, from "aspergere", to sprinkle on, as if spattering a person's name with mud.

senses.def: damaging or disparaging remarks, usually in the phrase "cast aspersions"
senses.ex: It is unfair to cast aspersions on the referee's honesty just because a close call went against our team.

origin: Borrowed from French "aspirant", from "aspirer", to strive for, ultimately Latin "aspirare", to breathe toward.

senses.def: a person who seeks a position, achievement, or recognition
senses.ex: Every aspirant for the orchestra's solo chair practiced the passage before sunrise.

senses.def: seeking a particular position or distinction
senses.ex: An aspirant filmmaker borrowed the school camera to shoot her first short documentary.

origin: From "aspire", from Latin "aspirare", to breathe upon or strive toward, from "ad", to, plus "spirare", to breathe.

senses.def: strong hope or ambition to achieve something
senses.ex: Her aspiration to become a surgeon kept her studying long after her friends had gone to bed.

origin: From Old French "asalir", from Latin "ad", at, plus "salire", to leap, so to assail is to leap at someone; "assault" shares the root.

senses.def: attack someone violently and suddenly
senses.ex: The travelers were assailed by bandits as they crossed the mountain pass at dusk.

senses.def: criticize someone harshly and forcefully
senses.ex: The new policy was assailed by teachers, parents, and students alike at the packed board meeting.

senses.def: trouble or overwhelm someone, as doubts or worries do
senses.ex: On the night before her exam, she was assailed by doubts about whether she had studied the right chapters.

syn: attack, assault, set upon, beset, besiege

origin: From Anglo-Norman "assai", a trial or test, from Old French "essai", the same source as "essay", an attempt.

senses.def: test or analysis to find out what a substance contains or how pure it is
senses.ex: The assay showed that the ore contained enough gold to justify reopening the old mine.

senses.def: test a metal, ore, or substance to measure its quality or content
senses.ex: The laboratory assayed blood samples from every volunteer before the trial began.

senses.def: attempt or try something difficult
senses.ex: The young climber assayed the north face alone, against the advice of every guide in town.

origin: From Old French "assentir", from Latin "assentire", to agree, built from "ad", toward, and "sentire", to feel.

senses.def: agree to or approve a proposal or request
senses.ex: The residents would assent to the bridge plan only if it protected the old footpath.

senses.def: agreement or approval, often formally expressed
senses.ex: The committee gave its assent after the engineer explained how the new design would resist floods.

origin: From "assert", from Latin "asserere", to claim or lay hold of, from "ad", to, plus "serere", to join.

senses.def: confident and forceful in stating one's views or claiming one's rights
senses.ex: Her assertive manner in meetings ensured that the junior staff's concerns were finally heard.

origin: From Latin "asseverare", to assert earnestly, from "ad", to, plus "severus", serious.

senses.def: declare something earnestly, solemnly, and positively
senses.ex: Throughout the trial, the defendant continued to asseverate his innocence to anyone who would listen.

origin: From Latin "assiduitas", diligence, built on "assiduus", meaning "constantly present" or "attentive".

senses.def: steady, careful effort devoted to a task
senses.ex: With quiet assiduity, Maya checked every sample twice before submitting the laboratory report.

origin: From Latin "assiduus", constantly present, from "assidere", to sit beside, from "ad", to, plus "sedere", to sit, so an assiduous worker never leaves the desk.

senses.def: showing great care, attention, and persistent effort
senses.ex: Thanks to her assiduous note-taking, the class had a complete record of every lab experiment.

origin: From "assiduous" plus "-ly", from Latin "assiduus", constantly present, from "assidere", to sit beside.

senses.def: with careful, persistent, and diligent effort
senses.ex: The restorers worked assiduously for three years to remove centuries of grime from the chapel frescoes.

origin: From Old French "assignacion", from Latin "assignatio", an assigning or allotting. A scheduled meeting was something assigned.

senses.def: an arranged meeting, especially a secret romantic one
senses.ex: Their assignation beneath the station clock was brief, secret, and charged with anticipation.

origin: From Latin "assimilare", to make like, from "ad", to, plus "similis", like.

senses.def: take in and fully understand information or ideas
senses.ex: It took the new analyst several weeks to assimilate the company's complicated accounting rules.

senses.def: absorb people into a larger group or culture, or become absorbed into it
senses.ex: The immigrant families assimilated quickly, though they kept their language alive at home.

senses.def: absorb nutrients or other substances into the body or a living system
senses.ex: Plants assimilate carbon dioxide from the air and turn it into sugars.

syn: absorb, digest, take in, comprehend, internalize

origin: From French "assonance", rooted in Latin "assonare", "to sound together", from "ad", toward, and "sonare", sound.

senses.def: repetition of similar vowel sounds in nearby words
senses.ex: The assonance of 'glow' and 'stone' gave the poet's short line a slow, open sound.

origin: From Old French "asouagier", to soothe, from Vulgar Latin, based on Latin "ad", to, plus "suavis", sweet, so to assuage a pain is to sweeten it.

senses.def: make an unpleasant feeling such as grief, fear, or guilt less intense
senses.ex: The principal tried to assuage parents' fears by explaining the school's new safety plan in detail.

senses.def: satisfy a need or appetite such as hunger or thirst
senses.ex: After the long hike, nothing assuaged their thirst like the cold water from the spring.

origin: From "astonish", from Old French "estoner", to stun, ultimately from Latin "ex", out, plus "tonare", to thunder, as if struck by thunder.

senses.def: great surprise or amazement
senses.ex: To the astonishment of the crowd, the underdog runner overtook the champion in the final meters.

origin: From Late Latin "astralis", meaning "of the stars", from Latin "astrum", star, itself from Greek "astron".

senses.def: relating to or resembling the stars
senses.ex: In her poem, astral fires flicker above the sleeping city, suggesting stars too distant to name.

senses.def: relating to a supposed nonphysical realm or body
senses.ex: During meditation, he imagined his astral body drifting beyond the walls of his room.

origin: From Old French "estraier", to stray, from Latin "extra", beyond, plus "vagari", to wander.

senses.def: away from the correct path or direction
senses.ex: Several letters went astray when the post office moved to its new building.

senses.def: into error or wrongdoing
senses.ex: His parents worried that older friends would lead him astray during his first year away from home.

syn: off course, lost, amiss, awry, adrift

origin: From "astringent" plus "-cy". "Astringent" traces to Latin "astringere", "to bind tightly", from "ad", toward, and "stringere", draw tight.

senses.def: the quality of producing a dry, puckering feeling in the mouth
senses.ex: The young red wine had enough astringency to leave our mouths dry after each sip.

senses.def: sharp severity in someone's manner, speech, or writing
senses.ex: The astringency of her review startled the cast, though every criticism rested on clear evidence.

origin: From Latin "astringere", to bind fast, from "ad", to, plus "stringere", to draw tight; "stringent" shares the root.

senses.def: sharply critical or severe
senses.ex: The critic's astringent review called the novel's ending lazy and its dialogue painfully stiff.

senses.def: causing a dry, puckering feeling in the mouth, as strong tea or unripe fruit does
senses.ex: The unripe persimmon was so astringent that it left her mouth feeling dry and puckered.

senses.def: causing skin or body tissue to tighten or contract
senses.ex: Witch hazel is an astringent lotion that many people use to shrink pores after shaving.

senses.def: substance that causes body tissue to contract
senses.ex: The pharmacist recommended a mild astringent to help stop the bleeding from the small cut.

origin: From Greek "astronomikos", through Latin and French, built on "astron", star, and "nomos", law or ordering.

senses.def: extremely large in size, amount, or cost
senses.ex: The renovation's astronomical cost forced the museum to postpone its reopening for another year.

senses.def: relating to astronomy or objects in space
senses.ex: Astronomical observations from the desert site helped students track the changing position of Mars.

origin: From Latin "astutus", crafty, from "astus", craft or cunning.

senses.def: quick to notice and understand things and use them to one's advantage
senses.ex: An astute investor, she sold her shares just weeks before the market collapsed.

origin: From Old English "onsundrum", apart, from "on" plus "sundor", separate or alone, the root of "sunder", to split apart.

senses.def: into separate parts or pieces, often violently
senses.ex: The old oak was split asunder by lightning, leaving two blackened halves leaning away from each other.

senses.def: apart from each other in position or relationship
senses.ex: Years of bitter quarrels over the inheritance drove the two brothers asunder, and they stopped speaking entirely.

syn: apart, to pieces, in two, into fragments

origin: From Greek "a-", not, plus "symmetric", which goes back to Greek "symmetria", proportion, from "syn", together, and "metron", measure.

senses.def: not the same on both sides; lacking balanced proportions
senses.ex: The architect's asymmetric facade placed a tall tower on one corner and a low glass wing on the other.

senses.def: unequal between the sides involved, as in power, risk, or information
senses.ex: In asymmetric warfare, a small rebel force avoids open battle and targets the larger army's supply lines instead.

origin: From Greek "ataraxia", calmness, from "a-", not, plus "tarassein", to stir up or disturb: a mind that is "not stirred up".

senses.def: calm, untroubled state of mind free from anxiety or emotional disturbance
senses.ex: After years of anxious striving, the retired judge sought ataraxia in quiet mornings spent tending her garden.

origin: From French "atavisme", from Latin "atavus", a distant ancestor, from "avus", grandfather, so an atavism is a throwback to one's ancestors.

senses.def: reappearance of a trait from remote ancestors after it has been absent for generations
senses.ex: The calf's tiny extra toes were an atavism, a feature its ancestors had lost millions of years ago.

senses.def: return to primitive or ancient behavior, ideas, or attitudes
senses.ex: The historian described the sudden outbreak of mob violence as an atavism from a crueler age.

origin: From "atavism", from French "atavisme", based on Latin "atavus", a remote ancestor (literally a great-great-great-grandfather), from "avus", grandfather.

senses.def: relating to primitive instincts or behavior that seem to return from the distant past
senses.ex: The roar of the stadium crowd awakened an atavistic thrill, as if the fans were tribes cheering warriors into battle.

senses.def: showing a trait that reappears after being absent for several generations
senses.ex: Breeders were puzzled by the atavistic foal, whose faintly striped legs recalled the coats of wild ancestral horses.

origin: From Middle English, "a-", on, plus "thwert", across, borrowed from Old Norse "thvert", across or crosswise.

senses.def: across, from one side to the other, often at a slant
senses.ex: A fallen pine lay athwart the trail, forcing the hikers to scramble over its sticky trunk.

senses.def: in opposition to; contrary to
senses.ex: Her blunt report ran athwart the company's cheerful forecasts, and the board quietly asked her to soften it.

origin: From Middle English "at one", meaning in harmony: to atone is to make yourself "at one" again with someone you have wronged.

senses.def: make amends or repair the harm for a wrong or offense
senses.ex: To atone for missing his sister's graduation, Marcus drove six hours to cook her a celebration dinner.

origin: From Latin "atra bilis", black bile, the body fluid that ancient medicine blamed for gloom and bad temper.

senses.def: gloomy and melancholy by temperament
senses.ex: The atrabilious poet rarely left his rooms in winter, filling notebook after notebook with verses about decay.

senses.def: irritable, sour, and bad-tempered toward others
senses.ex: The atrabilious landlord answered every repair request with a scowl and a complaint about lazy tenants.

origin: From Latin "atrocitas", fierceness, from "atrox", cruel or terrible, which is related to "ater", black.

senses.def: extremely cruel or violent act, especially one committed against civilians in war
senses.ex: Investigators gathered survivors' testimony to document the atrocity committed when soldiers burned the village.

senses.def: something very ugly, badly made, or offensive to good taste
senses.ex: Locals called the neon-green parking garage an atrocity that ruined the view of the historic square.

syn: outrage, abomination, barbarity, horror, war crime

origin: From Greek "atrophia", a wasting away, from "a-", without, plus "trophe", nourishment: tissue that withers when it is not fed or used.

senses.def: wasting away of a body part from disease, injury, or lack of use
senses.ex: After six weeks in a cast, his calf muscles showed visible atrophy, and physical therapy began at once.

senses.def: waste away or weaken, especially through lack of use
senses.ex: Without regular practice, her once fluent Spanish began to atrophy until she struggled to order lunch.

senses.def: gradual decline in the strength or effectiveness of something
senses.ex: Critics blamed the atrophy of local newspapers for the sharp drop in what voters knew about city council races.

origin: From Latin "attenuare", to make thin, from "ad", to, plus "tenuis", thin.

senses.def: reduce the force, effect, or strength of something
senses.ex: Thick curtains attenuated the noise of the traffic outside, letting the baby sleep through the afternoon.

senses.def: make something thin or slender
senses.ex: Years of illness had attenuated his once powerful frame until his coat hung loosely on him.

origin: From Latin "attenuatio", a diminishing, from "attenuare", to make thin, from "tenuis", thin.

senses.def: weakening or reduction in force, effect, value, or amount
senses.ex: After months of bargaining, the attenuation of the treaty's language left almost no binding obligations for either side.

senses.def: loss of strength of a signal, sound, or light as it travels through a medium
senses.ex: Thick concrete walls cause attenuation of the Wi-Fi signal, so the basement office barely gets a connection.

origin: From Latin "attestari", to bear witness, from "ad", to, plus "testis", a witness, the root also found in "testify".

senses.def: show or be clear evidence that something is true or exists
senses.ex: The worn stone steps of the old library attest to centuries of students climbing up to study.

senses.def: declare formally, often as a witness, that something is true or genuine
senses.ex: Two neighbors signed the will to attest that the elderly farmer had made it of his own free will.

syn: confirm, demonstrate, evidence, prove, bear witness to

origin: From Latin "attestatio", from "attestari", to bear witness, from "testis", a witness.

senses.def: formal statement or document confirming that something is true or genuine
senses.ex: Each applicant had to submit an attestation from a doctor confirming that they were fit for deep-sea diving.

senses.def: evidence or proof of something
senses.ex: The packed concert hall was a clear attestation of the young cellist's growing reputation across the region.

origin: From Latin "attritio", a rubbing against, from "atterere", to wear away, from "ad", against, plus "terere", to rub.

senses.def: gradual wearing down of strength or resistance through sustained pressure
senses.ex: The siege became a war of attrition, with both armies slowly running out of food and soldiers.

senses.def: gradual reduction in the number of members or workers as people leave and are not replaced
senses.ex: The company shrank its staff through attrition rather than layoffs, simply not filling jobs when people retired.

senses.def: wearing away of a surface by friction
senses.ex: Centuries of attrition by wind and sand had smoothed the faces of the stone statues.

syn: erosion, wearing down, weakening, depletion, debilitation

origin: From "attune", from "at-", to, plus "tune", so to be attuned is to be tuned in to something.

senses.def: aware of and responsive to something, such as people's feelings or needs
senses.ex: A good teacher is attuned to the moods of the class and knows when students need a break.

syn: responsive, sensitive, alert, in tune, receptive

origin: From Greek "a-", not, plus "typical", which comes through Latin from Greek "typos", a mark, model, or type.

senses.def: not typical; differing from the usual type or pattern
senses.ex: Snow in late May is atypical for the city, so the sudden storm caught gardeners completely off guard.

origin: Borrowed from French "au courant", literally "in the current", from "courant", current or stream: someone moving with the flow of events.

senses.def: fully informed about current events or the latest developments
senses.ex: She reads three newspapers every morning to stay au courant with the negotiations in the capital.

senses.def: fashionable and in line with the latest trends
senses.ex: The cafe's au courant menu featured oat-milk lattes, cardamom buns, and every other food trend of the season.

syn: informed, up to date, abreast, knowledgeable, clued in

origin: From French "aubade", from Old Spanish "albada", a dawn song, from "alba", dawn, from Latin "albus", white, for the pale light of daybreak.

senses.def: poem or song greeting the dawn, often about lovers parting at daybreak
senses.ex: The poet's aubade imagines two lovers at the window, cursing the sunrise that will force them apart.

origin: From Latin "audacia", boldness, from "audax", bold, from "audere", to dare.

senses.def: showing a bold willingness to take surprising risks
senses.ex: The team's audacious plan was to cross the Antarctic ice sheet on skis without any outside support.

senses.def: rudely bold or disrespectful
senses.ex: The audacious intern corrected the CEO's grammar in front of the entire board.

origin: From Medieval Latin "audacitas", from Latin "audax", bold, from "audere", to dare.

senses.def: rude or shameless boldness
senses.ex: After arriving an hour late, he had the audacity to complain that dinner was cold.

senses.def: willingness to take bold and daring risks
senses.ex: The audacity of the rescue, carried out in a blizzard at night, earned the pilots a national award.

origin: From Late Latin "augmentare", to increase, from Latin "augmentum", growth, from "augere", to increase.

senses.def: make something greater by adding to it
senses.ex: She augmented her small salary by tutoring math students on weekends.

origin: From Latin "augur", a Roman priest who read omens such as the flight of birds, a word of uncertain origin.

senses.def: be a sign of a future outcome, good or bad
senses.ex: Record early sales augur well for the new phone, though analysts warn that demand may fade by spring.

senses.def: person who predicts the future from omens, originally a Roman priest who read such signs
senses.ex: In ancient Rome, an augur studied the flight of birds before the senate would approve a war.

origin: From Latin "augurium", the work of an augur, a Roman priest who foretold the future by watching the flight of birds.

senses.def: sign or omen of what will happen in the future
senses.ex: The early spring rains seemed a good augury for the farmers after two years of drought.

senses.def: practice of predicting the future by reading signs such as the flight of birds
senses.ex: Roman generals relied on augury before battle, waiting for priests to read the movements of sacred birds.

origin: From Latin "augustus", venerable or majestic, from "augere", to increase; the first Roman emperor took it as his title, Augustus.

senses.def: respected and impressive, inspiring awe or reverence
senses.ex: The young scientist was nervous about presenting her findings before such an august gathering of Nobel laureates.

origin: From Latin "aura", breeze, from Greek "aura", breath of air: a quality that hangs around someone like a faint breeze.

senses.def: distinctive atmosphere or quality that seems to surround a person, place, or thing
senses.ex: The abandoned lighthouse had an aura of mystery that drew photographers from all along the coast.

senses.def: supposed field of energy surrounding a living being, in spiritual belief
senses.ex: The psychic claimed she could see a pale violet aura glowing around each visitor's head.

senses.def: warning sensation, such as flashing lights, that comes before a migraine or seizure
senses.ex: Before each migraine, he notices an aura of zigzag lights flickering at the edge of his vision.

origin: From Latin "aureatus", decorated with gold, from "aureus", golden, from "aurum", gold: language gilded with fancy words.

senses.def: of writing or speech, elaborately ornate and full of grand, showy words
senses.ex: The senator's aureate eulogy, packed with Latin phrases and soaring metaphors, left mourners more dazed than comforted.

senses.def: golden in color or brilliance
senses.ex: Late afternoon sun turned the wheat fields aureate, and the whole valley seemed dipped in honey.

origin: From Medieval Latin "aureola (corona)", golden (crown), from Latin "aureus", golden.

senses.def: circle of light painted around the head or body of a holy figure; a halo
senses.ex: In the medieval altarpiece, each apostle wears a thin gold aureole that catches the candlelight.

senses.def: ring of light surrounding a bright object such as the sun or moon
senses.ex: Through the thin fog, the streetlamp wore a hazy aureole that softened the empty street.

origin: From Latin "aurora", dawn, also the name of the Roman goddess of dawn, plus "-al", relating to.

senses.def: relating to the dawn; bright and fresh like daybreak
senses.ex: The auroral sky over the harbor shifted from gray to rose as the fishing boats headed out.

senses.def: relating to the northern or southern lights
senses.ex: Satellites recorded intense auroral activity after the solar storm, and green curtains of light appeared over Scotland.

origin: From Latin "auspicium", the reading of omens from birds, from "auspex", bird watcher, from "avis", bird, plus "specere", to look.

senses.def: support, protection, or sponsorship, usually in the phrase "under the auspices of"
senses.ex: The peace talks were held under the auspices of the United Nations, which provided translators and security.

origin: From "auspice", from Latin "auspicium", an omen read from the flight of birds, so an auspicious start is one the birds would bless.

senses.def: suggesting a favorable outcome; promising future success
senses.ex: Winning the first three games was an auspicious start for a team that had finished last the year before.

origin: From Greek "austēros", harsh or bitter, first used of wine and fruit that dry out the tongue.

senses.def: severely plain and simple, without decoration or comfort
senses.ex: The monastery's austere cells held nothing but a narrow bed, a chair, and a small wooden cross.

senses.def: stern, strict, or serious in manner
senses.ex: The austere headmaster rarely smiled and expected students to stand whenever he entered a room.

origin: Through Latin "austeritas" from Greek "austeros", harsh or bitter to the taste, a sense that grew into strict, plain severity.

senses.def: official policy of sharp cuts in public spending to reduce government debt
senses.ex: Years of austerity closed rural clinics and libraries as the government struggled to shrink its deficit.

senses.def: plain, severe simplicity, without comfort or decoration
senses.ex: The monastery's austerity struck visitors at once: bare stone walls, narrow cots, and a single wooden cross.

senses.def: sternness or strict self-discipline in manner or way of life
senses.ex: The coach's austerity, never smiling and rarely praising, made her occasional compliments feel like trophies.

origin: From Greek "autarkeia", self-sufficiency, from "autos", self, plus "arkein", to be enough: a country that is enough for itself.

senses.def: economic self-sufficiency of a nation that relies little on foreign trade
senses.ex: Facing sanctions, the regime pursued autarky, building its own factories rather than importing machinery and fuel.

origin: From Medieval Latin "authenticare", from "authenticus", genuine, from Greek "authentikos", original or carrying first-hand authority.

senses.def: prove or confirm that something is genuine
senses.ex: Experts used X-rays and pigment tests to authenticate the painting as an early work by the artist.

senses.def: verify the identity of a user or device before granting access
senses.ex: The banking app authenticates each user with a fingerprint scan before showing any account details.

origin: From "authority", from Latin "auctoritas", influence or command, from "auctor", originator or master, plus "-arian".

senses.def: demanding strict obedience to authority at the expense of personal freedom
senses.ex: The authoritarian government shut down independent newspapers and jailed anyone who criticized the president.

senses.def: person who demands strict obedience to their authority
senses.ex: Her father was a strict authoritarian who decided what she studied, wore, and read.

origin: From "authority" plus "-ative", from Latin "auctoritas", influence or command, from "auctor", originator or author.

senses.def: reliable and accurate because it comes from an expert or official source
senses.ex: Her history of the Civil War is considered the most authoritative account of the conflict's final year.

senses.def: commanding respect and obedience through confidence
senses.ex: The captain's calm, authoritative voice kept the passengers from panicking as the ship tilted.

origin: From Greek "autochthon", sprung from the land itself, from "autos", self, plus "chthon", earth or soil.

senses.def: native to the place where found; indigenous
senses.ex: Linguists recorded the autochthonous languages of the valley before the last fluent speakers passed away.

origin: From French "autocrate", from Greek "autokrates", ruling by oneself, from "autos", self, plus "kratos", power.

senses.def: ruler who holds absolute power and answers to no one
senses.ex: The autocrat dissolved parliament, jailed opposition leaders, and declared himself president for life.

senses.def: domineering person who insists on having their own way
senses.ex: In the kitchen, the head chef was an autocrat who allowed no one to alter a single recipe.

origin: From "autocrat", from Greek "autokratēs", ruling by oneself, from "autos", self, plus "kratos", power.

senses.def: ruling with absolute power and no checks on authority
senses.ex: The autocratic king dissolved parliament whenever its members questioned his spending.

senses.def: domineering and demanding obedience without consulting others
senses.ex: The autocratic manager made every decision himself and never asked the team for its opinion.

origin: From Greek "autodidaktos", self-taught, from "autos", self, plus "didaskein", to teach.

senses.def: self-taught person who learned without formal schooling or teachers
senses.ex: An autodidact who left school at fourteen, she mastered calculus from library books and later taught engineering.

origin: From "automaton", from Greek "automatos", acting of itself, plus "-ism", for actions that seem to happen by themselves.

senses.def: action performed without conscious thought or control
senses.ex: Sleepwalking is a form of automatism, and the defendant claimed he had no awareness of leaving the house.

senses.def: technique, used especially by surrealist artists, of creating without conscious control
senses.ex: Practicing automatism, the surrealist let her pen wander across the page without planning a single shape.

syn: reflex, involuntary action, automaticity, unconscious action

origin: From Greek "automaton", neuter of "automatos", acting of itself or self-moving.

senses.def: person who acts mechanically, without thought or feeling
senses.ex: After the third night shift in a row, the nurse moved through her rounds like an automaton.

senses.def: machine or mechanical figure that moves by itself, often imitating a person or animal
senses.ex: The museum's eighteenth-century automaton, a brass boy holding a pen, could still write a short poem.

origin: From Greek "autonomos", living by one's own laws, from "autos", self, plus "nomos", law.

senses.def: self-governing and free from outside control
senses.ex: The region became an autonomous province, with its own parliament and police force.

senses.def: able to act or operate independently, without human direction
senses.ex: Engineers tested the autonomous tractor on a small farm before letting it plow larger fields alone.

origin: From "autonomous" plus "-ly", from Greek "autonomos", living by one's own laws, from "autos", self, plus "nomos", law.

senses.def: independently, without outside control or direction
senses.ex: The research teams worked autonomously, choosing their own experiments without approval from headquarters.

origin: From Greek "autonomia", independence, from "autonomos", living by one's own laws, from "autos", self, plus "nomos", law.

senses.def: right of a group or region to govern itself
senses.ex: The island won greater autonomy, though the central government still controlled its foreign policy.

senses.def: freedom of a person to make their own decisions
senses.ex: As teenagers grow older, most want more autonomy over their schedules, friendships, and spending.

origin: From Latin "auxiliarius", helping, from "auxilium", help or aid, which is related to "augere", to increase.

senses.def: giving extra help or support; supplementary or held in reserve
senses.ex: When the storm knocked out city power, the hospital's auxiliary generators kept the operating rooms running.

senses.def: person or group that helps or supports a larger organization
senses.ex: The library's volunteer auxiliary raised enough money at its book sale to fund a new children's reading room.

senses.def: helping verb, such as have, be, or will, used with a main verb
senses.ex: In 'She has finished,' the auxiliary 'has' combines with the main verb to mark a completed action.

origin: From Old French, from Latin "avaritia", greed, from "avarus", greedy, from "avere", to crave.

senses.def: extreme greed for wealth or material gain
senses.ex: In the old fable, the miser's avarice led him to hoard gold while his own family went hungry.

origin: From Old French "avaricieux", from "avarice", from Latin "avaritia", greed, from "avarus", greedy, from "avere", to crave.

senses.def: extremely greedy for money or possessions
senses.ex: The avaricious landlord raised the rent every year while refusing to fix the leaking roof.

origin: From Old French "averer", to confirm as true, from Medieval Latin, based on Latin "ad", to, plus "verus", true.

senses.def: state firmly and positively that something is true
senses.ex: The witness averred that she had seen the defendant leave the building just before midnight.

origin: From Latin "aversus", turned away, past participle of "avertere", to turn away, from "ab", from, plus "vertere", to turn.

senses.def: strongly disliking or opposed to something
senses.ex: Though averse to public speaking, the shy scientist agreed to present her findings to the city council.

origin: From Latin "aversio", a turning away, from "avertere", to turn away, from "ab", from, plus "vertere", to turn.

senses.def: strong dislike or unwillingness
senses.ex: My brother has a lifelong aversion to mushrooms and picks every one out of his pasta.

senses.def: thing or person that one strongly dislikes
senses.ex: Public speaking was her greatest aversion, so she volunteered to do the research instead.

origin: From Old French "avertir", from Latin "avertere", to turn away, from "ab", from, plus "vertere", to turn.

senses.def: prevent something bad from happening
senses.ex: Quick thinking by the engineer averted a collision between the two trains.

senses.def: turn one's eyes or thoughts away from something
senses.ex: She averted her eyes during the gory scenes of the movie.

syn: prevent, forestall, avoid, ward off, preclude

origin: From Latin "avis", bird, plus "-ian", relating to; the same root appears in "aviary" and "aviation".

senses.def: relating to or characteristic of birds
senses.ex: Veterinarians tracked the spread of avian flu after thousands of geese died near the coastal wetlands.

origin: From Latin "aviarium", a place for birds, from "avis", bird.

senses.def: large cage or enclosure where birds are kept
senses.ex: At the zoo's walk-through aviary, bright parrots flew overhead and landed on visitors' shoulders.

origin: From French "avide", from Latin "avidus", eager or greedy, from "avere", to long for.

senses.def: very eager and enthusiastic about something
senses.ex: An avid birdwatcher, he kept a notebook of every species he had spotted since the age of eight.

origin: From Latin "aviditas", eagerness or greed, from "avidus", eager or longing, the source of "avid".

senses.def: intense eagerness or enthusiasm
senses.ex: The children turned the pages with such avidity that the librarian had to order three more copies.

senses.def: greedy desire, especially for wealth or gain
senses.ex: The developer's avidity for profit led him to bulldoze the historic theater before anyone could protest.

origin: From Latin "avocatio", a distraction, from "avocare", to call away: something that calls you away from your main work.

senses.def: hobby or activity pursued for pleasure outside one's regular work
senses.ex: Her vocation is tax law, but her avocation is restoring vintage motorcycles in a garage behind the house.

origin: From Old French "aveir de peis", literally "goods of weight", meaning merchandise sold by weight.

senses.def: weight or heaviness, especially a person's, used humorously
senses.ex: After a winter of holiday feasts, the retired captain joked about his expanding avoirdupois and bought looser trousers.

senses.def: standard system of weights based on a pound of sixteen ounces
senses.ex: In the United States, groceries are weighed in avoirdupois units, so a pound of rice holds sixteen ounces.

origin: From Old French "avouchier", from Latin "advocare", to call to oneself, the same source as "advocate" and "avow".

senses.def: declare or affirm confidently and openly
senses.ex: The elderly witness avouched that she had seen the defendant at the market on the morning of the theft.

senses.def: vouch for or guarantee the truth or worth of
senses.ex: Several colleagues avouched the young researcher's honesty when rumors about faked data began to spread.

origin: From Old French "avouer", to acknowledge, from Latin "advocare", to call upon, from "ad", to, plus "vocare", to call; despite appearances, it is not related to "vow".

senses.def: declare or admit something openly
senses.ex: The candidate avowed her support for the new park, even though it was unpopular with some local businesses.

origin: From "avow", from Old French "avouer", to acknowledge, from Latin "advocare", to call upon, plus "-al".

senses.def: open declaration or admission of something
senses.ex: His public avowal of support for the strike surprised colleagues who assumed he sided with management.

origin: From Latin "avunculus", a mother's brother, an uncle.

senses.def: kind, friendly, and patient toward younger people, like a favorite uncle
senses.ex: The avuncular librarian always had a joke and a book recommendation ready for every child who came in.

origin: From Middle English, "a-", on, plus "wry", twisted: literally "on the twist", turned away from the straight course.

senses.def: away from the planned or expected course; wrong
senses.ex: The surprise party went awry when the guest of honor arrived early and found everyone still hanging balloons.

senses.def: turned or twisted to one side; askew
senses.ex: After the windy walk home, his tie was awry and his hair stood up in stiff tufts.

origin: From Greek "axiōma", that which is thought worthy or fit, from "axios", worthy, so an axiom is a statement worthy of acceptance.

senses.def: statement or principle accepted as obviously true
senses.ex: It is an axiom of good journalism that every important fact should be confirmed by two sources.

senses.def: statement assumed to be true and used as the starting point of a logical or mathematical system
senses.ex: Euclid built his whole geometry on five axioms, including the claim that all right angles are equal.

origin: From Greek "axiōmatikos", from "axiōma", a self-evident principle, from "axios", worthy.

senses.def: so obviously true that it needs no proof
senses.ex: It is axiomatic among gardeners that tomatoes need plenty of sun to ripen.

origin: From Old French "azur", from Arabic "lazaward", lapis lazuli, a blue stone; its first "l" was dropped as if it were the French article.

senses.def: bright blue, like a clear, cloudless sky
senses.ex: The ferry crossed azure water so clear that passengers could see fish darting around the rocks below.

senses.def: clear bright blue color; poetically, the cloudless sky
senses.ex: A single hawk circled in the azure above the canyon, riding the warm afternoon air.

origin: From Middle English "babelen", probably imitating the repeated "ba-ba" sounds a baby makes before it can speak.

senses.def: talk rapidly and foolishly, or in a way others cannot understand
senses.ex: Too nervous to think straight, he babbled about the weather for ten minutes before finally asking her to the dance.

senses.def: make a continuous soft murmuring sound, as flowing water does
senses.ex: We pitched the tent beside a creek that babbled over smooth stones all through the night.

senses.def: foolish or confused talk, or a steady murmur of voices or water
senses.ex: Through the thin hotel wall came a constant babble of voices from the party next door.

origin: From Latin "Bacchanalis", relating to Bacchus, the Roman god of wine, whose festivals were famous for drunken revelry.

senses.def: wild and drunken party or celebration
senses.ex: The quiet graduation dinner turned into a bacchanal that kept the neighbors awake until dawn.

senses.def: person who takes part in drunken revelry
senses.ex: By midnight the last bacchanals were singing on the fountain's edge with their shoes in their hands.

origin: From Latin "Bacchanalia", the riotous festival of Bacchus, the Roman god of wine.

senses.def: marked by wild, drunken, and unrestrained celebration
senses.ex: The rock band's bacchanalian tour left a trail of trashed hotel rooms and furious managers across Europe.

origin: From "back" plus "hand" plus "-ed": first a blow struck with the back of the hand, then a remark that strikes indirectly.

senses.def: seeming to praise but actually expressing criticism or insult in an indirect way
senses.ex: Telling her the cake was "surprisingly edible" was a backhanded compliment she did not soon forget.

senses.def: made with the back of the hand turned forward
senses.ex: The tennis player won the point with a backhanded shot that skimmed just over the net.

origin: The verb comes from the cruel sport of badger-baiting, in which dogs harassed a trapped badger; the animal's name probably comes from "badge", for its white face marking.

senses.def: pester someone repeatedly and annoyingly
senses.ex: The children badgered their parents for a puppy until the family finally visited the animal shelter.

senses.def: burrowing animal with a gray body and a black and white striped face
senses.ex: A badger had dug a tunnel under the garden fence and eaten half the carrots.

origin: From French "badinage", from "badiner", to joke, from "badin", playful.

senses.def: light, playful, witty exchange of remarks
senses.ex: The two old friends kept up an easy badinage about each other's terrible cooking all through dinner.

origin: Of uncertain origin, possibly from Scots "bauchle", to treat with contempt, or French "bafouer", to mock or ridicule.

senses.def: totally bewilder or confuse someone so they cannot understand or explain something
senses.ex: The disappearance of the bees from the orchard baffled scientists for three straight summers.

senses.def: panel or plate that controls or blocks the flow of sound, light, or fluid
senses.ex: Engineers added foam baffles to the concert hall walls so the echoes would not drown out the strings.

origin: From French "bagatelle", from Italian "bagattella", a trifle or small thing of little value.

senses.def: something unimportant or easily dealt with
senses.ex: To a billionaire, the hundred-thousand-dollar fine was a mere bagatelle, paid without a second thought.

senses.def: short, light piece of music, usually for piano
senses.ex: The pianist ended her recital with a playful bagatelle that lasted barely two minutes.

origin: From "bailie", bailiff, plus "wick", dwelling or village, from Old English "wic": first the district a bailiff controlled.

senses.def: person's particular area of activity, authority, skill, or interest
senses.ex: Questions about the budget are not my bailiwick, so you should ask the finance director instead.

origin: Of unknown origin, possibly first a name for a cheap jumbled drink of wine mixed with beer or water.

senses.def: senseless talk or writing; nonsense
senses.ex: The candidate dismissed the reporter's accusation as complete balderdash and walked away from the microphones.

origin: From Old English "bealuful", from "bealu", evil or harm, plus "-ful", so baleful means full of harm.

senses.def: threatening harm in a menacing way
senses.ex: The guard dog fixed the delivery driver with a baleful stare and a low growl.

senses.def: having harmful or destructive effects
senses.ex: Critics warned about the baleful influence of gambling apps on teenagers.

origin: From Old English "balca", a ridge of unplowed land, which came to mean an obstacle, so to balk is to stop short like a horse at a barrier.

senses.def: hesitate or refuse to go ahead with something
senses.ex: Many buyers balked at the price of the new phone and waited for a cheaper model.

syn: hesitate, refuse, recoil, shrink from, demur

origin: From Middle English "bar", bare, plus "last", load: a load carried only for its weight, not as cargo.

senses.def: heavy material placed in a ship or balloon to keep it steady
senses.ex: When the cargo was unloaded, the crew filled the hold with stones as ballast for the return voyage.

senses.def: something that gives steadiness, stability, or seriousness to a person or situation
senses.ex: Her calm older brother provided emotional ballast during the chaotic months after the fire.

senses.def: give stability to something, especially by adding weight
senses.ex: The balloonists ballasted the basket with sandbags before the storm moved in.

origin: From "ballet", from Italian "balletto", a little dance, from "ballo", dance.

senses.def: graceful, light, and precise in movement, like a ballet dancer
senses.ex: The goalkeeper made a balletic leap across the goal and tipped the ball over the crossbar.

origin: From French "balletomane", from "ballet" plus "-mane", a person with a mania for something.

senses.def: devoted enthusiast of ballet
senses.ex: A true balletomane, my aunt has seen every production of "Swan Lake" the city ballet has staged since 1985.

syn: ballet lover, ballet fan, aficionado, devotee

origin: From Italian "pallone", a large ball, from "palla", ball, probably via French "ballon".

senses.def: increase rapidly in amount or size
senses.ex: The cost of the stadium ballooned from two hundred million to nearly a billion dollars.

senses.def: thin rubber bag or large fabric bag that floats when filled with air or gas
senses.ex: Hundreds of colorful hot-air balloons rose above the desert at sunrise.

origin: Of uncertain origin, perhaps from Ballyhooly, an Irish village known for its rowdiness.

senses.def: noisy, extravagant publicity or fuss, often out of proportion to the thing itself
senses.ex: After months of ballyhoo, the new phone turned out to be almost identical to last year's model.

senses.def: promote or praise something with loud, exaggerated publicity
senses.ex: The studio ballyhooed the sequel as the event of the summer, but audiences stayed home.

origin: From Old French "basme", from Latin "balsamum", from Greek "balsamon", a fragrant plant resin used to heal and soothe.

senses.def: fragrant ointment or oil used to heal or soothe the skin
senses.ex: She rubbed a little balm into her cracked hands after a long day of shoveling snow.

senses.def: something that soothes, comforts, or eases pain or distress
senses.ex: After the bitter election, the mayor's generous speech was a balm to her defeated rivals.

origin: From "balm" plus "-y": air that feels as soothing as a fragrant ointment.

senses.def: pleasantly warm and mild, used of weather or air
senses.ex: On balmy summer evenings the whole neighborhood carried chairs out onto the sidewalk to talk.

origin: From French "banal", first used of things like a mill or oven that a feudal lord made all villagers share, so it came to mean commonplace.

senses.def: so lacking in originality as to be boring
senses.ex: The movie's banal dialogue made even its talented actors sound like greeting cards.

origin: From French "banalité", from "banal", first used of feudal services shared by everyone in a village, and so commonplace.

senses.def: quality of being dull, ordinary, and unoriginal
senses.ex: The banality of the office's daily routine drove him to sign up for night classes in painting.

senses.def: trite or boring remark or idea
senses.ex: The graduation speaker offered nothing but banalities about following your dreams.

origin: From Greek "banausikos", of a craftsman, from "banausos", artisan, from a word for a forge. Greek aristocrats looked down on manual work.

senses.def: merely practical or routine, lacking culture, imagination, or higher purpose
senses.ex: He found filling out expense reports so banausic that he did them only at the very last minute.

origin: From French "bander", to hit a tennis ball back and forth, which matches trading words back and forth.

senses.def: pass words, ideas, or names around casually or exchange them in argument
senses.ex: Wild rumors about the layoffs were bandied about the office long before anyone made an announcement.

senses.def: of legs, curving outward at the knees
senses.ex: The old jockey walked with a rolling gait on his short, bandy legs.

syn: exchange, toss about, trade, swap, spread

origin: From Old English "bana", a killer or slayer; it later also meant poison, which survives in plant names like "wolfsbane".

senses.def: cause of great distress, annoyance, or ruin
senses.ex: Potholes are the bane of every cyclist in the city, especially after the spring thaw.

origin: From "bane", a cause of ruin (Old English "bana", killer), plus "-ful", so full of ruin.

senses.def: causing harm, ruin, or destruction
senses.ex: The baneful influence of the gambling ring spread through the small town until few families were untouched.

origin: From Old French "banir", to proclaim or outlaw, of Germanic origin and related to "ban".

senses.def: send someone away from a country or place as an official punishment
senses.ex: The king banished the rebellious duke and seized his castle and lands.

senses.def: drive a thought or feeling out of one's mind
senses.ex: She tried to banish all thoughts of failure as she walked onto the stage.

syn: exile, expel, deport, oust, cast out

origin: Of unknown origin, first recorded in the 1670s, possibly from London street slang.

senses.def: playful and friendly teasing conversation
senses.ex: The radio hosts' easy banter made the long morning commute feel much shorter.

senses.def: talk or exchange remarks in a playful, teasing way
senses.ex: The two coaches bantered with each other about their teams before the charity game.

origin: From Old French "barbe", beard, from Latin "barba". The backward-pointing tip on a fishhook looked like a small beard.

senses.def: deliberately hurtful or cutting remark
senses.ex: The senator ignored her opponent's barbs about her age and kept talking about health care.

senses.def: sharp backward-pointing tip on an arrow or fishhook that makes it hard to pull out
senses.ex: The barb on the hook held fast, so the fisherman had to cut the line to free the turtle.

origin: From Scottish Gaelic "bard", from Old Irish "bard", poet. In Celtic lands bards were professional poets who sang praise and history.

senses.def: poet, especially one who writes or recites epic or heroic verse
senses.ex: The village bard composed a long ballad about the flood, and children could sing every verse of it.

senses.def: the Bard, a common name for William Shakespeare
senses.ex: Our drama club performs a play by the Bard every spring, usually a comedy.

origin: Probably from "bare" plus "faced", showing an uncovered face, hence acting openly and without shame.

senses.def: shameless and undisguised, used especially of lies or wrongdoing
senses.ex: It was a barefaced lie: the security footage clearly showed him leaving the store with the watch.

origin: From Barmecide, a nobleman in "The Thousand and One Nights" who invited a starving beggar to a feast of empty dishes.

senses.def: seeming to offer plenty but actually illusory or disappointing
senses.ex: The company's barmecidal bonus plan promised huge rewards that no employee could ever actually qualify for.

origin: From French "baroque", from Portuguese "barroco", an irregularly shaped pearl; the deeper origin is uncertain.

senses.def: highly ornate, elaborate, or overcomplicated
senses.ex: The tax form's baroque instructions ran to forty pages and confused even the accountants.

senses.def: relating to the ornate style of European art, architecture, and music from about 1600 to 1750
senses.ex: The choir specializes in baroque music, especially the cantatas of Bach and the operas of Handel.

origin: From French "barrage", a barrier, related to "barrier". The heavy gunfire formed a protective barrier in front of advancing troops.

senses.def: overwhelming outpouring of many things at once, such as questions or criticism
senses.ex: The minister faced a barrage of angry questions as soon as she stepped onto the stage.

senses.def: concentrated, continuous firing of artillery over a wide area
senses.ex: The night sky flickered as the barrage pounded the enemy lines for six hours.

senses.def: bombard someone with a great number of things, such as questions or complaints
senses.ex: Fans barraged the radio station with calls after the referee's disputed decision.

origin: From "bar", the rail in a courtroom and hence the legal profession, plus "-ster", one who does something.

senses.def: lawyer, especially in Britain, who is qualified to argue cases in the higher courts
senses.ex: After years of training in London, she became a barrister and argued her first case before the High Court.

origin: From Old French "barater", to trade or haggle, a word that could also mean to cheat.

senses.def: exchange goods or services for other goods or services without using money
senses.ex: The farmer bartered three crates of apples for an afternoon of help repairing his tractor.

senses.def: system or act of trading goods and services directly, without money
senses.ex: In the isolated mountain villages, barter was more common than cash until the new road was built.

origin: The adjective, meaning low, comes through Old French "bas" from Late Latin "bassus", low; the noun and verb come from Greek "basis", a step or foundation.

senses.def: without moral principles; dishonorable or ignoble
senses.ex: The novel's villain is driven by the basest motives, chiefly greed and revenge.

senses.def: lowest part or support on which something stands
senses.ex: The statue's marble base had cracked during the frost, so the museum moved it indoors for repair.

senses.def: main place where a person or organization works or is stationed
senses.ex: The research team used a small village as its base for exploring the glacier.

senses.def: use something as the foundation or starting point for something else
senses.ex: The film is based on a true story about a family who survived a volcanic eruption.

origin: From "base", foundation, plus "-less", without: a claim with nothing to stand on.

senses.def: not supported by evidence or facts
senses.ex: The rumor that the factory would close turned out to be baseless, and the workers were relieved.

origin: From Old Norse "baðask", to bathe oneself, a relative of English "bathe".

senses.def: lie or relax in pleasant warmth or light
senses.ex: A row of turtles basked on the log, soaking up the afternoon sun.

senses.def: take great pleasure in praise, attention, or another good situation
senses.ex: After the championship, the coach basked in the praise of fans who had doubted her all season.

origin: From "bastardize" plus "-ation", from "bastard", a child born outside marriage, hence something impure or not genuine.

senses.def: corrupted, debased, or inferior version of something
senses.ex: Purists called the fast-food chain's taco a bastardization of a dish their grandmothers had perfected.

origin: From French "bastion", from Old French "bastille", fortress.

senses.def: institution, place, or person that strongly protects a principle or way of life
senses.ex: For decades the small newspaper remained a bastion of independent reporting in a heavily censored country.

senses.def: projecting part of a fortress wall that lets defenders fire along the walls
senses.ex: Cannons on each bastion of the old fort covered every approach from the harbor.

origin: From Middle English "baten", a shortened form of "abaten", to abate. "With bated breath" means with breath held back, not "baited".

senses.def: hold back or lessen something, now used mainly in the phrase "with bated breath"
senses.ex: The whole stadium waited with bated breath as the kicker lined up for the last-second field goal.

syn: restrain, hold back, check, lessen, reduce

origin: From "bathos", formed on the pattern of "pathos" and "pathetic".

senses.def: sinking from serious or lofty to trivial or silly, producing an unintended anticlimax
senses.ex: The poem's bathetic ending, which compared eternal love to a favorite sandwich, made the judges laugh.

senses.def: sentimental in an exaggerated, insincere way
senses.ex: The movie's bathetic deathbed scene drew more groans than tears from the audience.

origin: From Greek "bathos", depth. Alexander Pope used it mockingly for the way some writers sink from the sublime to the ridiculous.

senses.def: sudden, unintentionally comic shift from a serious or lofty mood to a trivial one
senses.ex: The speech slid into bathos when the general followed his tribute to fallen soldiers with a joke about parking.

senses.def: exaggerated or insincere sentimentality
senses.ex: The novel's final chapter drowns its tragic heroine in bathos and violins.

origin: The verb "batten on" comes from Old Norse "batna", to improve or grow better. The wooden strip comes from Old French "batent", a beating, from "batre", to beat, and the verb "batten down" comes from that strip.

senses.def: fasten or secure something with strips of wood, used especially in "batten down the hatches"
senses.ex: Before the hurricane hit, the islanders battened down their shutters and moved their boats inland.

senses.def: thrive or grow rich at someone else's expense, followed by "on"
senses.ex: The corrupt officials battened on the aid money meant for the earthquake survivors.

senses.def: long, narrow strip of wood or metal used to strengthen or fasten something
senses.ex: The carpenter nailed a batten across the old door to keep its boards from warping.

syn: secure, fasten, fix, board up, seal

origin: From Old French "baterie", a beating, from "batre", to beat, from Latin "battuere"; a battery of cannons pounded enemies, and Benjamin Franklin borrowed the word for linked electrical jars.

senses.def: extensive series or array of similar things
senses.ex: The patient underwent a battery of tests before the doctors agreed on a diagnosis.

senses.def: device that stores chemical energy and supplies it as electric power
senses.ex: His phone battery died halfway through the hike, leaving him without a map.

senses.def: unlawful physical attack on another person
senses.ex: The man was charged with assault and battery after the fight outside the stadium.

senses.def: group of large guns or cannons operating together
senses.ex: A battery of artillery on the hill fired on the approaching ships.

origin: From Greek "battologia", stammering or babbling speech.

senses.def: needless and tiresome repetition of the same words or ideas in speech or writing
senses.ex: The editor cut the essay in half by removing its battology, especially the five paragraphs saying the same thing.

origin: From Old French "baubel", a child's toy or trinket, probably from Latin "bellus", pretty.

senses.def: small, showy trinket of little value
senses.ex: She ignored the expensive baubles in the jewelry store and chose a simple silver ring.

origin: From "bawd", an old word for a woman who ran a brothel, plus "-y". "Bawd" probably comes from Old French "baud", merry or lively.

senses.def: dealing with sex in a humorous, crude, or indecent way
senses.ex: The sailors sang bawdy songs in the tavern until the landlord told them to keep it down.

origin: From Middle English "baulen", probably from Old Norse "baula", to low like a cow, or Medieval Latin "baulare", to bark.

senses.def: cry or weep loudly and without restraint
senses.ex: The toddler bawled all the way through the grocery store because he could not have the candy.

senses.def: shout something loudly and roughly
senses.ex: The drill sergeant bawled orders at the recruits across the muddy parade ground.

senses.def: scold someone angrily, followed by "out"
senses.ex: My manager bawled me out in front of everyone for missing the delivery deadline.

origin: From "bay", to howl like a hound, from Old French "abaiier", to bark, a word imitating the sound.

senses.def: loudly and angrily demanding something, like hounds chasing prey
senses.ex: The minister left by a back door to avoid the baying crowd of reporters outside the court.

senses.def: howling with long, deep cries, as hunting dogs do
senses.ex: The baying hounds led the searchers through the woods to the lost hiker.

origin: From Latin "beatificus", making blessed, from "beatus", blessed, plus "facere", to make.

senses.def: blissfully happy or serene
senses.ex: The grandmother wore a beatific smile as she held her first great-grandchild.

origin: From French "béatifier", from Latin "beatificare", to make blessed, from "beatus", blessed, plus "facere", to make.

senses.def: in the Roman Catholic Church, officially declare a dead person blessed, a step toward sainthood
senses.ex: The pope beatified the missionary nurse decades after her death, praising her care for lepers.

origin: From Latin "beatitudo", happiness, from "beatus", blessed or happy.

senses.def: supreme blessedness or happiness
senses.ex: The old monk's face wore an expression of perfect beatitude as he listened to the choir.

senses.def: any of the blessings spoken by Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount, beginning "Blessed are"
senses.ex: The children memorized the Beatitudes, starting with "Blessed are the poor in spirit."

origin: From French "beau geste", literally "beautiful gesture".

senses.def: noble or generous gesture, often one made mainly for show
senses.ex: Returning his salary to the struggling team was a beau geste that won the owner admiring headlines.

origin: From "be-", making, plus "calm", so a ship is becalmed when the calm weather holds it still.

senses.def: leave a sailing ship unable to move because there is no wind, usually in the passive
senses.ex: The racing yacht was becalmed for two days in the middle of the ocean.

senses.def: bring an activity or process to a standstill, usually in the passive
senses.ex: Negotiations were becalmed for months while both sides waited for the election results.

origin: From "become" in its older sense of to suit or be fitting, as in "that color becomes you".

senses.def: flattering to one's appearance
senses.ex: The deep green dress was very becoming and brought out the color of her eyes.

senses.def: suitable or proper for a particular person or situation
senses.ex: Gloating over a rival's defeat is hardly becoming behavior for a team captain.

origin: From "be-", thoroughly, plus "deck", to cover or adorn, like Dutch "bedekken", to cover.

senses.def: decorate something or someone lavishly
senses.ex: For the festival the townspeople bedecked every balcony with flowers and strings of paper lanterns.

origin: From "be-" plus "dizen", to dress up, which originally meant to load flax onto a distaff for spinning.

senses.def: dress or decorate someone or something in a gaudy, showy way
senses.ex: For the parade, the horses were bedizened with ribbons, bells, and glittering plastic jewels.

syn: bedeck, festoon, deck out, adorn, trick out

origin: From "Bedlam", the popular name of the Hospital of St Mary of Bethlehem in London, an asylum for the mentally ill known for its noise and disorder.

senses.def: scene of uproar and wild confusion
senses.ex: When the fire alarm went off during the school assembly, the gym turned into bedlam.

origin: From "be-" plus "draggle", to make wet and dirty by dragging through mud, a form of "drag".

senses.def: wet, dirty, and untidy, especially after rain or rough treatment
senses.ex: The bedraggled hikers finally reached the cabin after six hours of walking through a cold downpour.

origin: From "befuddle", from "be-", thoroughly, plus "fuddle", to make drunk or confused.

senses.def: confused and unable to think clearly
senses.ex: The befuddled tourist turned his map upside down twice before asking a police officer for directions.

origin: From Middle English "beggen", a word whose origin is uncertain.

senses.def: ask for something earnestly or humbly
senses.ex: The prisoner's mother begged the judge for mercy, explaining that her son had never been in trouble before.

senses.def: ask people for money or food as charity
senses.ex: During the famine, families walked to the city to beg for bread outside the churches.

senses.def: in "beg the question", assume the very point being argued, or more loosely, invite an obvious question
senses.ex: Saying the book is good because it is well written simply begs the question of what makes writing good.

origin: From Old English "begietan", to get or acquire, from "be-" plus "gietan", to get.

senses.def: cause something to happen or exist
senses.ex: In the cycle of feuding families, violence begets violence, and each revenge invites another.

senses.def: be the father of a child, used mainly in older or biblical writing
senses.ex: According to the old family chronicle, the founder begat seven sons and three daughters.

origin: From Middle English "bigrucchen", to grumble at, from "be-", about, plus "grudge".

senses.def: resent someone for having or enjoying something
senses.ex: Nobody begrudged the retiring nurse her lavish farewell party after forty years of service.

senses.def: give or allow something reluctantly
senses.ex: He begrudged every minute spent in traffic and started taking the train instead.

syn: resent, envy, grudge, mind, object to

origin: From "be-", thoroughly, plus "guile", cunning or deceit.

senses.def: charm or enchant someone, sometimes in a deceptive way
senses.ex: The street magician beguiled the crowd with card tricks while his partner sold tickets to the evening show.

senses.def: trick or mislead someone
senses.ex: The con artist beguiled elderly investors into handing over their savings.

senses.def: make time pass pleasantly
senses.ex: On the long train journey, they beguiled the hours with word games and stories.

origin: From Hebrew "behemoth", probably a plural of "behemah", beast, used in the Book of Job for an enormous creature.

senses.def: something enormous and powerful, especially a large organization
senses.ex: The small bookstore struggled to compete with online retail behemoths that could ship books overnight.

origin: From Old English "behæs", a vow or promise, related to an old verb meaning to command. The final "t" was added later.

senses.def: person's order or urgent request, usually in the phrase "at the behest of"
senses.ex: The museum reopened the closed wing at the behest of local teachers who wanted to bring their classes.

origin: From Middle English "biholden", the old past participle of "behold", though that verb itself did not mean to oblige.

senses.def: owing a debt or favor to someone and therefore under obligation
senses.ex: The mayor refused campaign money from developers because she did not want to be beholden to anyone.

syn: indebted, obligated, obliged, bound, in debt to

origin: From "behoove", from Old English "behōfian", to need, related to "behoof", advantage.

senses.def: is necessary, proper, or advantageous for someone, usually in "it behooves"
senses.ex: It behooves every driver to check the tire pressure before setting out on a long winter trip.

syn: befits, becomes, suits, is incumbent on, is advisable for

origin: From "be-", thoroughly, plus "labor", to work; it first meant to beat someone soundly and later to overwork an argument.

senses.def: argue or explain something in excessive detail
senses.ex: The coach did not belabor the point, saying only that the team had lost because it stopped running.

syn: overdo, overemphasize, harp on, dwell on, labor

origin: From the old verb "belate", to make late, from "be-" plus "late".

senses.def: coming or happening later than it should have
senses.ex: She finally sent a belated birthday card, three weeks after her cousin's party.

origin: From Dutch "belegeren", to besiege, from "be-", around, plus "leger", camp, so to beleaguer a town is to camp around it.

senses.def: trouble someone with many problems or demands
senses.ex: Rising costs and a shortage of workers continued to beleaguer the small family bakery.

senses.def: surround a place with an army; besiege
senses.ex: Enemy troops beleaguered the fortress for six months before its defenders surrendered.

origin: From "beleaguer", from Dutch "belegeren", to besiege, from "be-", around, plus "leger", camp.

senses.def: beset by many difficulties or pressures
senses.ex: The beleaguered mayor faced protests, lawsuits, and a recall petition all in the same week.

senses.def: surrounded and attacked by an army; under siege
senses.ex: Supplies were dropped by parachute to the beleaguered garrison, which had been surrounded for weeks.

origin: From Old French "berfrei", a movable siege tower, of Germanic origin; the spelling with "bel-" came from a mistaken link with "bell".
