senses.def: tower or part of a tower in which bells hang
senses.ex: Pigeons nested in the old church's belfry, scattering whenever the bells rang.

syn: bell tower, campanile, steeple, tower, spire

origin: From Old English "belēogan", to deceive by lying, from "be-", about, plus "lēogan", to lie.

senses.def: give a false impression of something; disguise
senses.ex: Her calm smile belied the panic she felt as the judges studied her sculpture.

senses.def: show something to be false or untrue
senses.ex: The company's soaring profits belie its claim that it cannot afford to raise wages.

origin: Past tense of "belie", from Old English "belēogan", to deceive by lying, from "be-", about, plus "lēogan", to lie.

senses.def: gave a false impression of something; disguised
senses.ex: The old man's quiet voice belied the fierce temper his grandchildren knew all too well.

senses.def: showed something to be false
senses.ex: The team's dismal record belied the owner's boast that they would win the championship.

origin: From "be-", making, plus "little"; Thomas Jefferson is credited with coining it in 1782.

senses.def: make someone or something seem unimportant or worthless
senses.ex: A good mentor never belittles a beginner's questions, no matter how basic they seem.

origin: From German "Belletrist", a word coined by Goethe, from French "belles-lettres", beautiful letters, meaning elegant literature.

senses.def: writer of elegant literary essays and prose valued more for style than for information
senses.ex: A gifted belletrist, he could make an essay about folding laundry read like a short story.

syn: essayist, man of letters, stylist, literary writer, author

origin: From Latin "bellicosus", warlike, from "bellicus", of war, from "bellum", war.

senses.def: eager to fight or start a conflict
senses.ex: The general's bellicose speeches alarmed neighboring countries, which began moving troops to the border.

origin: From Latin "belligerans", waging war, from "bellum", war, plus "gerere", to wage.

senses.def: hostile, aggressive, and eager to fight
senses.ex: The belligerent customer shouted at the cashier and refused to leave until the manager arrived.

senses.def: engaged in a war
senses.ex: The belligerent nations finally agreed to a ceasefire after three years of fighting.

senses.def: nation or group taking part in a war
senses.ex: Both belligerents accused the other of breaking the truce within hours.

origin: From Middle English "belwether", a castrated ram ("wether") wearing a bell that led the rest of the flock.

senses.def: something or someone that leads others or signals future trends
senses.ex: Investors watch the tech giant's earnings as a bellwether for the health of the entire stock market.

origin: From Italian "belvedere", literally "beautiful view", from "bel", beautiful, plus "vedere", to see.

senses.def: building or raised structure, such as a turret or summerhouse, designed to give a fine view
senses.ex: From the belvedere on the hilltop, guests could see the whole valley and the river beyond.

origin: From Old English "bemǣnan", to lament, from "be-", about, plus the verb that became "moan".

senses.def: express sorrow or discontent about something
senses.ex: Veteran teachers bemoan the loss of recess time in many elementary schools.

syn: lament, deplore, bewail, complain about, rue

origin: From "be-" plus "muse", to ponder, so a bemused person is lost in puzzled thought.

senses.def: puzzled or bewildered, often while lost in thought
senses.ex: The tourists looked bemused as the waiter rattled off the specials in rapid local dialect.

origin: From Latin "benedictio", blessing, from "bene", well, plus "dicere", to speak: literally speaking well of someone.

senses.def: spoken blessing, especially at the end of a religious service
senses.ex: The congregation stood with bowed heads as the pastor gave the benediction.

senses.def: approval or good wishes for an undertaking
senses.ex: The founder's benediction helped the new chief executive win over skeptical employees.

origin: From Latin "benefactor", one who does good, from "bene", well, plus "facere", to do or make.

senses.def: person who gives money or other help to a person, cause, or institution
senses.ex: An anonymous benefactor paid for every student in the senior class to visit the capital.

origin: From Latin "beneficentia", kindness, from "bene", well, plus "facere", to do.

senses.def: active kindness and generosity toward others
senses.ex: Thanks to the beneficence of a local donor, every student in the school received a free laptop.

origin: From Latin "bene", well, plus "-ficens", doing, from "facere", to do.

senses.def: doing good or producing good effects; generous
senses.ex: The beneficent foundation paid for clean water wells in more than two hundred villages.

origin: From Latin "beneficiarius", enjoying a favor, from "beneficium", kindness, from "bene", well, plus "facere", to do.

senses.def: person or group that receives money, property, or advantage from something
senses.ex: Small farmers were the main beneficiaries of the new irrigation program.

senses.def: person named to receive money or property under a will, trust, or insurance policy
senses.ex: She named her two nephews as beneficiaries of her life insurance policy.

origin: From Latin "benevolens", wishing well, from "bene", well, plus "volens", wishing.

senses.def: well-meaning, kind, and eager to help others
senses.ex: The benevolent old farmer let neighborhood children pick apples from his orchard every fall.

senses.def: set up to do good rather than to make a profit
senses.ex: The miners formed a benevolent society to support families of workers injured underground.

origin: From "benight", to be overtaken by the darkness of night, from "be-" plus "night", so the benighted are left in the dark.

senses.def: in a state of ignorance or moral darkness
senses.ex: The reformer saw it as her mission to bring modern medicine to what she called benighted villages, a view locals resented.

origin: From Latin "benignus", kind, from "bene", well, plus a root related to "genus", birth or kind, so it first described a good nature.

senses.def: gentle, kindly, and well-meaning
senses.ex: The headmaster gave the nervous new students a benign smile and told them not to worry.

senses.def: not harmful in effect
senses.ex: Most of the insects in the garden are benign, and some even help by eating pests.

senses.def: of a tumor or growth, not cancerous
senses.ex: The family was relieved when the biopsy showed that the lump was benign.

origin: From Old French "beneison", from Latin "benedictio", blessing, so it is a twin of "benediction".

senses.def: blessing, used in literary writing
senses.ex: After the long drought, the farmers greeted the first rain as a benison from heaven.

origin: From "bend", in its old sense of directing the mind toward something, so a bent is the way one's mind naturally leans.

senses.def: natural talent or inclination for something
senses.ex: From an early age, she showed a strong bent for mathematics, solving puzzles meant for older children.

senses.def: determined to do something, usually in "bent on"
senses.ex: The new owner seemed bent on turning the quiet diner into a trendy nightclub.

senses.def: curved or twisted out of a straight shape
senses.ex: He straightened the bent nail with a hammer and used it again.

origin: From "be-", thoroughly, plus "numb".

senses.def: make numb, either physically or in feeling
senses.ex: The icy wind benumbed our fingers until we could no longer work the zipper on the tent.

origin: From Old English "becweþan", to say or declare, from "be-" plus "cweþan", to say, the verb behind "quoth".

senses.def: leave property or money to someone in a will
senses.ex: Her grandfather bequeathed his entire record collection to the local public library.

senses.def: pass something on to people who come later
senses.ex: The architects of the treaty bequeathed a fragile peace to the next generation.

syn: leave, will, hand down, bestow, pass on

origin: From "be-", thoroughly, plus "rate", an old verb meaning to scold.

senses.def: scold or criticize someone angrily
senses.ex: The coach berated the players for missing practice and made them run laps until sunset.

origin: From Old English "berēafian", to deprive or rob, from "be-" plus "rēafian", to rob, the source of the old word "reave".

senses.def: deprive someone of a loved one through death, usually in the passive
senses.ex: The hospital runs a support group for families bereaved by sudden accidents.

origin: From "bereave", from Old English "bereafian", to rob or deprive, plus "-ment".

senses.def: loss of a loved one through death, and the grief that follows
senses.ex: The company gives employees two weeks of paid leave after a bereavement in the family.

origin: Past participle of "bereave", from Old English "berēafian", to rob or deprive, so someone bereft has been robbed of something.

senses.def: deprived of or completely lacking something
senses.ex: After the factory closed, the town was bereft of jobs, shops, and hope.

senses.def: sad and lonely because of a loss
senses.ex: She felt utterly bereft when her best friend moved across the country.

origin: From Old Norse "berserkr", a warrior who fought in a frenzy, probably from "bjorn", bear, plus "serkr", shirt, for their bearskin coats.

senses.def: wildly out of control, especially with rage or excitement, often in "go berserk"
senses.ex: The crowd went berserk when the home team scored the winning goal in the final minute.

syn: frenzied, wild, crazed, amok, out of control

origin: From Middle English "besechen", from "be-", thoroughly, plus "sechen", to seek, so to beseech is to seek urgently.

senses.def: ask someone urgently and fervently to do something
senses.ex: The villagers beseeched the governor to send help before the floodwaters reached their homes.

syn: implore, entreat, beg, plead with, supplicate

origin: From Old English "besettan", to surround, from "be-", around, plus "settan", to set or place.

senses.def: trouble or threaten someone or something persistently
senses.ex: From the start, the bridge project was beset by budget overruns, strikes, and floods.

senses.def: surround and attack from all sides
senses.ex: The travelers were beset by swarms of mosquitoes as soon as the sun went down.

origin: From "be-", around, plus "siege", from Old French "sege", a seat, since an army sits down around the place it attacks.

senses.def: surround a place with armed forces in order to capture it
senses.ex: The army besieged the walled city for months, cutting off its food and water.

senses.def: overwhelm someone with requests, complaints, or questions
senses.ex: After the announcement, the box office was besieged with calls from fans desperate for tickets.

senses.def: crowd around someone or something
senses.ex: Reporters besieged the actor as soon as he stepped out of the car.

syn: surround, lay siege to, blockade, beleaguer, encircle

origin: From "be-", thoroughly, plus "smirch", to stain or soil.

senses.def: damage someone's reputation or good name
senses.ex: The false rumor besmirched the reputation of a doctor who had served the town for thirty years.

senses.def: make something dirty; soil
senses.ex: Muddy boots had besmirched the white carpet in the hallway.

origin: From "besot", from "be-" plus "sot", a fool or drunkard, so being besotted means being made foolish.

senses.def: strongly infatuated with someone or something
senses.ex: The besotted teenager wrote poem after poem about the girl who sat next to him in chemistry.

senses.def: drunk or stupefied with alcohol
senses.ex: By midnight, the besotted guests were singing loudly and off key.

origin: From Late Latin "bestialis", from Latin "bestia", beast, the source of English "beast".

senses.def: savagely cruel or depraved, like a wild animal
senses.ex: The war crimes tribunal heard testimony about the bestial treatment of prisoners in the camp.

senses.def: of or like an animal, especially in lacking human reason or refinement
senses.ex: The mask gave the actor a bestial snout and curling horns.

origin: From Middle English "bistowen", from "be-" plus "stowen", to place, so to place something on someone.

senses.def: give someone an honor, right, or gift
senses.ex: The university bestowed an honorary degree on the nurse who had founded the free clinic.

origin: From Old English "bestridan", from "be-" plus "stride".

senses.def: stand or sit with one leg on each side of something
senses.ex: The rider bestrode a huge black horse that stamped impatiently at the starting line.

senses.def: dominate or tower over something, like a giant
senses.ex: For a decade the champion bestrode the sport, winning nearly every major title.

syn: straddle, dominate, tower over, overshadow, span

origin: From Middle English "bitiden", from "be-" plus "tiden", to happen, from Old English "tidan", related to "tid", time.

senses.def: happen, or happen to someone, used mostly in "woe betide"
senses.ex: Woe betide anyone who interrupts my grandmother while she is watching her favorite quiz show.

syn: befall, happen to, overtake, occur, come to pass

origin: From Old English "betacnian", to signify, from "be-" plus "tacn", token or sign.

senses.def: be a sign or warning of something, often something still to come
senses.ex: The dark clouds gathering over the hills betokened a storm before nightfall.

origin: From "be-" plus Middle English "trayen", to betray, from Old French "trair", from Latin "tradere", to hand over; "traitor" shares the root.

senses.def: be disloyal to a person, group, or cause that trusts you
senses.ex: He betrayed his closest friend by sharing her secrets with the entire class.

senses.def: reveal something without meaning to
senses.ex: Her trembling hands betrayed how nervous she was before the audition.

senses.def: hand someone over to an enemy
senses.ex: The spy betrayed the resistance fighters to the occupying army for a small reward.

syn: double-cross, deceive, sell out, break faith with, stab in the back

origin: From Middle English "bitrouthen", from "be-" plus "trouthe", truth or pledged faith, the same word as "troth".

senses.def: formally promise to marry someone, or promise someone in marriage, usually as "betrothed"
senses.ex: The prince was betrothed to a duchess from a neighboring kingdom when both were still children.

origin: From Middle English "bevey", of uncertain origin, first used for a flock of birds such as quail.

senses.def: large group of people or things of a particular kind
senses.ex: The pop star arrived surrounded by a bevy of photographers, bodyguards, and assistants.

origin: From "bias", from French "biais", a slant or oblique line, so a biased view leans to one side.

senses.def: unfairly favoring or opposing one person, group, or idea
senses.ex: Fans accused the referee of being biased after he called three fouls against the visiting team in two minutes.

senses.def: of data or methods, systematically skewed so the results are not accurate
senses.ex: Because the survey only asked people at the gym, its results on exercise habits were biased.

origin: From French "bibelot", a small trinket. Its earlier origin is uncertain.

senses.def: small decorative object valued for its beauty or rarity
senses.ex: Her shelves were crowded with bibelots: porcelain birds, tiny enamel boxes, and a silver thimble.

origin: From Greek "biblion", book, plus "-mancy", divination, from Greek "manteia", prophecy.

senses.def: attempt to foretell the future by reading a passage chosen at random from a book, especially the Bible
senses.ex: Unsure whether to move abroad, she tried bibliomancy, opening a poetry anthology at random and reading the first line.

origin: From Greek "biblion", book, plus "philos", loving, probably by way of French, first recorded in 1820.

senses.def: person who loves and often collects books
senses.ex: A lifelong bibliophile, he spent every vacation hunting for first editions in dusty secondhand shops.

syn: book lover, booklover, bookworm, bibliomaniac, book collector

origin: From Latin "bibulus", fond of drinking, from "bibere", to drink, the same root as "imbibe" and "beverage".

senses.def: excessively fond of drinking alcohol
senses.ex: The bibulous uncle could always be found near the punch bowl, telling the same fishing story.

origin: From "bi-", two, plus Latin "camera", chamber, plus "-al".

senses.def: having two separate lawmaking chambers or houses
senses.ex: The United States Congress is bicameral, made up of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

origin: From Middle English "bikeren", to attack, from Middle Dutch "bicken", to stab or thrust, plus an "-er" ending for repeated action.

senses.def: argue about small, unimportant matters
senses.ex: The twins bickered for the entire road trip about who got the window seat.

origin: From Latin "biennium", a two-year period, from "bi-", twice, plus "annus", year.

senses.def: happening once every two years
senses.ex: The city hosts a biennial art fair that draws galleries from around the world every other spring.

senses.def: plant that takes two years to complete its life cycle, usually flowering in the second year
senses.ex: Foxglove is a biennial, so the seeds you plant this year will not bloom until next summer.

origin: From Medieval Latin "bifurcatus", from Latin "bifurcus", two-pronged, from "bi-", two, plus "furca", fork.

senses.def: divide into two branches or parts
senses.ex: Just past the bridge, the road bifurcates, with one branch heading to the beach and the other into the hills.

origin: From "bifurcate", from Latin "bifurcus", two-pronged, from "bi-", two, plus "furca", fork.

senses.def: divided into two branches or parts
senses.ex: The country's bifurcated school system sent wealthy children to private academies and everyone else to crowded public schools.

origin: From "bifurcate", from Latin "bifurcus", two-forked, from "bi-", two, plus "furca", fork.

senses.def: division of something into two branches or parts
senses.ex: The bifurcation of the river creates a long island where herons nest each spring.

senses.def: point where something divides into two
senses.ex: The hikers stopped at the bifurcation of the trail, unsure which path led to the lake.

origin: From French "bigot", a religious hypocrite, of disputed origin. A popular theory links it to the oath "by God".

senses.def: person who is intolerant of people with different opinions, beliefs, or backgrounds
senses.ex: The comedian refused to let a single loud bigot in the audience ruin the show for everyone else.

origin: From French "bigoterie", from "bigot", a narrow-minded or hypocritical person.

senses.def: stubborn intolerance of people who hold different opinions or belong to different groups
senses.ex: The school's new program aims to fight bigotry by bringing together students from different faiths.

origin: From French "bijou", jewel, which came from Breton "bizou", a finger ring.

senses.def: small and elegant, used especially of houses, apartments, and shops
senses.ex: They rented a bijou apartment above a bakery, with one room and a tiny balcony full of herbs.

senses.def: jewel or small, finely made trinket
senses.ex: The antique shop's window displayed a single bijou, a gold brooch shaped like a bee.

origin: From German "Bildung", education or formation, plus "Roman", novel.

senses.def: novel that follows a main character's growth and education from youth into adulthood
senses.ex: "Great Expectations" is a classic bildungsroman, tracing Pip from a poor orphan to a wiser young man.

syn: coming-of-age novel, novel of formation, apprenticeship novel

origin: Likely a variant of "bulge", for the rounded bottom of a ship's hull; the foul water that collects there led to the slang sense of worthless talk.

senses.def: nonsense or worthless talk
senses.ex: My grandfather dismissed the horoscope column as utter bilge and turned to the crossword.

senses.def: lowest inner part of a ship's hull, where dirty water collects
senses.ex: The crew spent the morning pumping oily water out of the bilge.

origin: From French "bilieux", from Latin "biliosus", full of bile, from "bilis", bile; too much bile was once thought to make people irritable.

senses.def: bad-tempered, irritable, and quick to find fault
senses.ex: The bilious critic seemed to hate every play he reviewed, no matter how well it was performed.

senses.def: feeling sick to one's stomach; nauseous
senses.ex: The ferry ride across the choppy strait left several passengers pale and bilious.

senses.def: of a sickly, unpleasant yellow-green color
senses.ex: The waiting room was painted a bilious shade of green that made everyone look ill.

origin: Origin uncertain; it may be a variant of "balk", to thwart.

senses.def: cheat or defraud someone, especially out of money
senses.ex: The fake charity bilked thousands of donors out of money meant for hurricane victims.

origin: From French "billet doux", literally "sweet note".

senses.def: love letter
senses.ex: Tucked inside the returned library book was a faded billet-doux signed only with a single initial.

syn: love letter, love note, valentine, mash note

origin: From Billingsgate, the old London fish market, whose traders were famous for their coarse and abusive language.

senses.def: coarse, abusive, and foul language
senses.ex: The two drivers traded a stream of billingsgate after their cars scraped bumpers in the parking lot.

origin: From Old Norse "bylgja", wave, related to "bellow".

senses.def: swell out or roll forward in large waves, used of smoke, cloth, or clouds
senses.ex: Black smoke billowed from the warehouse roof as fire trucks raced down the street.

senses.def: large rolling mass of something, such as smoke, steam, or water
senses.ex: Billows of steam rose from the hot spring into the frosty morning air.

origin: From "bio-", from Greek "bios", life, plus "degradable", able to be broken down, since living organisms do the breaking down.

senses.def: able to be broken down naturally by bacteria or other living things
senses.ex: The festival switched to biodegradable cups made from corn starch instead of plastic.

origin: From Latin "bipes", two-footed, from "bi-", two, plus "pes", foot.

senses.def: animal that walks on two feet
senses.ex: Humans are the only primates that live as true bipeds, walking upright all the time.

origin: From "black" plus "ball", after the black ball dropped into a ballot box to vote against admitting a new member.

senses.def: exclude someone from a group by voting against them or by shutting them out socially
senses.ex: After he reported the safety violations, the engineer found himself blackballed by every firm in the industry.

origin: From French "blague", a joke or tall tale, a word distantly related to English "belly".

senses.def: pretentious nonsense or a joking falsehood that no one is really meant to believe
senses.ex: His story about wrestling a shark was obvious blague, but the children at the campfire loved every word.

origin: From Old French "blanchir", to whiten, from "blanc", white.

senses.def: turn pale suddenly from shock, fear, or embarrassment
senses.ex: The witness blanched when the prosecutor held up the photograph of the missing ring.

senses.def: make something white or pale by removing its color
senses.ex: Years of desert sun had blanched the painted shutters to a ghostly gray.

senses.def: plunge food briefly into boiling water
senses.ex: Blanch the almonds for one minute so their skins slip off easily.

syn: pale, whiten, blench, go white, wince

origin: From Latin "blandus", smooth, flattering, or pleasant. The sense slid from soothing to mild to dull.

senses.def: lacking strong features or interest; dull
senses.ex: The new office building is so bland that visitors drive past it without noticing.

senses.def: of food, mild in flavor and not seasoned or spicy
senses.ex: After the stomach bug, the doctor told him to eat only bland food like rice and toast.

origin: From Old French "blandir", to flatter, from Latin "blandiri", to flatter, from "blandus", smooth-talking or flattering.

senses.def: coax or persuade someone with flattery and pleasant talk
senses.ex: The salesman blandished the elderly couple with compliments until they agreed to the most expensive warranty.

origin: From "blandish", to flatter, from Old French "blandir", from Latin "blandus", smooth or pleasant.

senses.def: flattering or pleasing words or actions used to persuade someone, usually in the plural
senses.ex: Despite the recruiter's blandishments, the star pitcher decided to stay with his hometown team.

origin: From Late Middle English "blaren", to bellow or wail, probably imitating a loud cry, like Dutch "blèren", to bawl.

senses.def: make or cause something to make a loud, harsh sound
senses.ex: Car horns blared as the parade blocked the busiest intersection downtown.

senses.def: loud, harsh sound
senses.ex: The blare of the fire alarm sent students streaming out of the building.

origin: From the Blarney Stone at Blarney Castle in Ireland, said to give the gift of persuasive eloquence to whoever kisses it.

senses.def: charming, flattering talk meant to persuade or amuse
senses.ex: The salesman's blarney about the car's "racing heritage" did not fool my practical grandmother.

syn: flattery, cajolery, sweet talk, blandishment, palaver

origin: From Greek "blasphemia", profane speech, from "blasphemein", to slander or speak evil of.

senses.def: speech or action that shows disrespect for God or sacred things
senses.ex: In some countries, insulting the state religion is still punished as blasphemy.

senses.def: disrespect toward something that people treat as sacred
senses.ex: To my grandfather, putting ketchup on a good steak was pure blasphemy.

origin: From French "blasé", past participle of "blaser", to blunt or dull, so a blasé person has feelings dulled by too much experience.

senses.def: unimpressed or indifferent because something has become too familiar
senses.ex: After ten years of touring, the drummer was blasé about sold-out arenas that would have thrilled him as a teenager.

origin: Coined by the poet Edmund Spenser in 1596 for his noisy "blatant beast", probably from a dialect form of "bleat", so it first meant loudly noisy.

senses.def: done openly and shamelessly, completely obvious
senses.ex: The essay was a blatant copy of a website article, down to the same spelling mistakes.

origin: From "blather", foolish chatter, plus "skite", a vulgar Scots term of contempt. It dates from the 1600s.

senses.def: person who talks at great length without making much sense
senses.ex: The talk show booked a blatherskite who rambled for twenty minutes without answering a single question.

origin: From Old French "blason", shield, later the coat of arms painted on it, and then any showy display.

senses.def: display or announce something prominently and boldly
senses.ex: The team's name was blazoned across every bus shelter in town before the season opener.

senses.def: coat of arms, or a formal description of one
senses.ex: The knight's shield bore the family blazon of a silver lion on a blue field.

origin: From Old English "blǣc" and Old Norse "bleikr", both meaning pale, so a bleak scene is one drained of color and warmth.

senses.def: offering little hope or encouragement, grim and depressing
senses.ex: After the factory closed, the job prospects for young people in the town looked bleak.

senses.def: bare, cold, and exposed to the wind
senses.ex: The hikers crossed a bleak moor where nothing grew taller than their ankles and the wind never stopped.

origin: From Middle English "blery", from "blear", to dim the eyes, plus "-y".

senses.def: of the eyes, dim, watery, and unfocused from tiredness or sleep
senses.ex: After the overnight flight, she stumbled into the meeting with bleary eyes and a large coffee.

origin: Of uncertain origin, possibly linked to Middle English "blichening", mildew or rust on grain, which fits its first use for withering crop diseases.

senses.def: something that spoils, damages, or ruins a place or situation
senses.ex: Rows of boarded-up storefronts had become a blight on the once lively downtown.

senses.def: plant disease that causes leaves, crops, or fruit to wither and die
senses.ex: In the 1840s, potato blight destroyed harvests across Ireland and led to widespread famine.

senses.def: spoil, harm, or ruin something
senses.ex: A string of injuries blighted the striker's final season, and he scored only twice.

origin: From "blinkers", the leather flaps beside a horse's eyes that block its side view, so a blinkered person sees only what lies straight ahead.

senses.def: having a narrow, limited outlook and unwilling to consider other views
senses.ex: The committee's blinkered focus on cutting costs blinded it to the safety problems engineers kept reporting.

origin: From Old English "blīþe", happy or gentle, the older cheerful sense later stretched to cover carefree unconcern.

senses.def: showing casual indifference to something that deserves concern
senses.ex: With blithe disregard for the deadline, he spent the night before the exam watching movies.

senses.def: cheerful and carefree in spirit
senses.ex: Her blithe humming as she weeded the garden made the chore seem almost pleasant to the neighbors.

origin: From "bloat", from Middle English "blout", soft and swollen, probably from Old Norse "blautr", soft or soaked.

senses.def: swollen with liquid or gas
senses.ex: After the huge holiday dinner, everyone lay on the sofa feeling bloated and sleepy.

senses.def: excessively large, costly, or wasteful
senses.ex: Critics called the defense budget bloated and demanded a full review of every program.

origin: Past tense of "bloviate", an American coinage probably built from "blow", in the sense of boasting, with a mock-Latin ending to sound grand.

senses.def: talked at length in a pompous, boastful, or empty way
senses.ex: The candidate bloviated for forty minutes about his vision without answering a single question from the reporters.

origin: From the phrase "blow hard", like someone who talks so much hot air that they seem to be blowing.

senses.def: loud, boastful person who talks too much
senses.ex: The neighborhood blowhard claimed he could have built the new stadium for half the price.

origin: From "blowze", an old word for a red-faced, untidy woman, plus "-y".

senses.def: coarse, red-faced, and untidy in appearance
senses.ex: The innkeeper was a blowsy woman with wild hair and flour on her apron.

senses.def: untidy or overblown, as of flowers past their best
senses.ex: By August the roses were blowsy and drooping, dropping petals at every breeze.

origin: First recorded in 1730 and of uncertain origin, perhaps from Cornish or from Middle French "bougeon", a small club.

senses.def: force or bully someone into doing something
senses.ex: The landlord tried to bludgeon tenants into leaving by cutting off their heat in January.

senses.def: beat someone or something with a heavy club or blunt object
senses.ex: According to the coroner, the victim had been bludgeoned with a heavy wrench.

senses.def: short, heavy club that is thicker or weighted at one end
senses.ex: The museum displayed a carved wooden bludgeon once used by warriors of the island.

origin: From the 18th-century Blue Stockings Society, London literary gatherings that welcomed women. One male guest famously wore casual blue stockings instead of formal black silk.

senses.def: intellectual or literary woman, sometimes used as a dated or mocking label
senses.ex: The novel's heroine is a proud bluestocking who would rather read Greek than attend another ball.

syn: intellectual, scholar, highbrow, egghead, literary woman

origin: The deceiving sense probably comes from Dutch "bluffen", to brag. The cliff and hearty senses come from a separate word for a broad, flat front.

senses.def: try to deceive someone by pretending to be stronger, more confident, or better informed than one is
senses.ex: He had no idea what the answer was, but he bluffed his way through the interview with confident vagueness.

senses.def: attempt to deceive by a false show of strength or confidence
senses.ex: The union's threat to strike was a bluff, and management knew it.

senses.def: steep cliff or bank, especially along a river or coast
senses.ex: Their cabin sat high on a bluff overlooking the Mississippi.

senses.def: good-naturedly frank and blunt in manner
senses.ex: The bluff old sea captain said exactly what he thought and laughed loudly at his own jokes.

origin: From Middle English "blundren", probably from Old Norse "blunda", to shut the eyes, so first to stumble about blindly.

senses.def: stupid or careless mistake
senses.ex: Sending the confidential memo to the whole company was a blunder that cost him his job.

senses.def: make a careless mistake
senses.ex: The general blundered by splitting his forces just before the enemy attacked.

senses.def: move clumsily or as if blind
senses.ex: Half asleep, I blundered into the dark kitchen and knocked over the cat's water bowl.

syn: mistake, error, gaffe, slip, faux pas

origin: Probably imitative of a sudden burst of sound, or possibly from Middle English "blurden", to cry out.

senses.def: say something suddenly and without thinking, usually followed by "out"
senses.ex: Before anyone could stop him, my little brother blurted out the secret about the surprise party.

syn: exclaim, blab, let slip, burst out, babble

origin: From Middle English "blusteren", which picked up its windy sense from Low German "blüstren", to blow violently. It is related to "blow" and "blast".

senses.def: talk in a loud, aggressive, or boastful way that has little real effect
senses.ex: The manager blustered about lawsuits, but everyone knew he would never actually go to court.

senses.def: loud, boastful, or threatening talk with little behind it
senses.ex: Behind all his bluster, the candidate had no real plan for the city's finances.

senses.def: of wind, blow in strong, noisy gusts
senses.ex: An icy wind blustered around the lighthouse all night long.

origin: From Old English "bodian", to announce or foretell, from "boda", messenger.

senses.def: be a sign of a good or bad outcome, usually in "bode well" or "bode ill"
senses.ex: The long line outside the bakery on opening day bodes well for its future.

origin: Probably from "bogle", a Scots word for a ghost or goblin, so the first sense was to shy away as if at a phantom.

senses.def: be overwhelmed or astonished, or overwhelm someone's mind, as in "the mind boggles"
senses.ex: The sheer size of the universe boggles the mind of anyone who looks through a powerful telescope.

senses.def: hesitate or refuse to act because of doubt or fear
senses.ex: Even the bravest climbers boggled at the idea of crossing the glacier at night.

origin: First American criminal slang for a machine that made counterfeit coins, then for the fake coins themselves. Its deeper origin is unknown.

senses.def: not genuine or true, fake or fraudulent
senses.ex: The website sold bogus concert tickets, and hundreds of fans were turned away at the gate.

senses.def: unfair, wrong, or worthless (informal)
senses.ex: Getting detention for something my lab partner did felt totally bogus.

origin: From French "bohémien", a person from Bohemia: Romani travelers were thought to come from there, and the name passed to poor, free-living Paris artists.

senses.def: unconventional and artistic in lifestyle, dress, or attitudes
senses.ex: The couple's bohemian apartment was crowded with easels, thrift-store rugs, and friends who stayed for weeks.

senses.def: person, especially an artist or writer, who lives an unconventional and often impoverished life
senses.ex: As a young bohemian in Paris, he wrote poems in cafes and lived on bread and cheap wine.

origin: From "boiler" plus "plate", the steel sheets used to build boilers. Ready-made newspaper text sent out on metal printing plates took the name, hence stock wording.

senses.def: standard, reusable text, especially in legal documents, used with little or no change
senses.ex: Most of the rental agreement was boilerplate, but one unusual clause banned tenants from owning pianos.

senses.def: standard and formulaic; lacking originality
senses.ex: The company issued a boilerplate apology that could have been written about any data breach in history.

syn: standard text, stock language, template, formula

origin: From Middle English "boistous", rough or crude, of uncertain origin, perhaps from Old French "boitous", limping or uneven.

senses.def: noisy, energetic, and high-spirited
senses.ex: A boisterous group of cousins took over the backyard, shouting and racing each other around the pool.

origin: From Old English "bolster", a long pillow or cushion, so to bolster something is to prop it up as a pillow supports the body.

senses.def: support or strengthen something, such as an argument, morale, or a structure
senses.ex: The lawyer bolstered her case with phone records showing the defendant was across town that night.

senses.def: long, firm pillow or cushion
senses.ex: She propped a striped bolster against the headboard so she could read comfortably in bed.

syn: reinforce, strengthen, shore up, buttress, boost

origin: From "bombard", an early cannon, from French "bombarde", from Latin "bombus", a booming sound, plus "-ment".

senses.def: sustained attack with bombs, shells, or missiles on a place
senses.ex: After three days of bombardment, the old harbor town had no working bridges and barely a single unbroken window.

senses.def: steady, overwhelming flood of questions, criticism, messages, or other things
senses.ex: The new mayor faced a bombardment of angry emails after the city quietly doubled parking fines downtown.

origin: From Old French "bombace", cotton padding, from Late Latin "bombax", cotton, so bombast is speech stuffed with padding.

senses.def: pompous, inflated language meant to impress but with little real meaning
senses.ex: Beneath all the bombast about making history, the mayor's plan offered nothing new for public transit.

syn: grandiloquence, pomposity, bluster, magniloquence, hot air

origin: From "bombast", cotton stuffing once used to pad clothes, plus "-ic", so bombastic speech is padded with grand but empty words.

senses.def: using high-sounding, inflated language with little real meaning
senses.ex: The wrestler's bombastic promises to destroy his rival were part of the show, not a real threat.

origin: From Medieval Latin "bombinare", to buzz or hum, from Greek "bombos", a booming or humming sound, imitating the noise itself.

senses.def: make a low, steady buzzing or humming sound
senses.ex: All afternoon the bees bombinated among the lavender rows while the farmer dozed in the shade of the barn.

origin: From French "bonhomie", good nature, from "bonhomme", good fellow, from "bon", good, and "homme", man.

senses.def: cheerful, easygoing friendliness toward other people
senses.ex: The coach's bonhomie in the locker room hid how worried he was about the playoff game.

origin: From Old Norse "bón", a prayer or request. The sense shifted from a favor asked for to a blessing received, helped by French "bon", good.

senses.def: something helpful or beneficial, a blessing
senses.ex: The free bus service has been a boon to students who cannot afford a car.

origin: Coined in 1929 by scout leader Robert H. Link for a braided cord scouts made. In 1935 critics applied it to New Deal make-work projects, hence wasteful work.

senses.def: project or activity that wastes time and money, especially public money
senses.ex: Critics called the half-built stadium a boondoggle, since taxpayers had spent millions and no team had agreed to play there.

senses.def: waste time or money on pointless work while appearing busy
senses.ex: The auditors concluded that the department had boondoggled for years, holding conferences that produced nothing but expense reports.

syn: waste, white elephant, money pit, fiasco

origin: From Dutch "boer", peasant or farmer. The word slid from meaning a country person to meaning anyone crude and ill-mannered.

senses.def: rude, ill-mannered, and insensitive person
senses.ex: The boor at the next table snapped his fingers at the waiter and complained loudly about every dish.

origin: From "boor", from Dutch "boer", peasant, plus "-ish", so it first meant rustic and now means crude in manners.

senses.def: rough, rude, and ill-mannered
senses.ex: His boorish habit of interrupting guests during dinner made his family dread holiday gatherings.

origin: From Old English "bōtlēas", from "bōt", help or profit (as in "to boot"), plus "-less", so a bootless effort brings no gain.

senses.def: useless and producing no benefit or result (literary)
senses.ex: After hours of bootless searching through the attic, they realized the old letters had been thrown away years ago.

origin: From "boot" plus "licker", picturing someone so eager to please a superior that they would lick the dirt off their boots.

senses.def: person who flatters and obeys powerful people in a servile way to win favor
senses.ex: The new manager surrounded himself with bootlickers who praised every idea and never warned him about the failing budget.

senses.def: someone seen as automatically defending authorities or the powerful
senses.ex: In the online debate about the protest, critics of the police were called radicals, and their defenders were called bootlickers.

origin: From French "boulevardier", one who frequents the boulevards, the broad fashionable avenues of Paris where the stylish went to see and be seen.

senses.def: fashionable, worldly man about town who frequents stylish places
senses.ex: In his silk scarf and polished shoes, the old boulevardier strolled from cafe to gallery, greeting half the neighborhood by name.

syn: man about town, bon vivant, dandy, flaneur, socialite

origin: From "bounty" plus "-ful". "Bounty" comes from Old French "bonte", goodness, from Latin "bonitas", from "bonus", good.

senses.def: large in quantity; plentiful and abundant
senses.ex: After a wet spring, the orchard produced such a bountiful crop of apples that the family gave bushels away to neighbors.

senses.def: giving generously and freely
senses.ex: The bountiful donor paid for new laboratory equipment and asked only that the students invite her to their science fair.

origin: From French "bourgeois", from Old French "burgeis", a town dweller, from a Germanic word for a fortified town, the same root as "borough".

senses.def: typical of the middle class, especially in being conventional, materialistic, or concerned with respectability
senses.ex: My cousin mocks matching furniture sets as hopelessly bourgeois, yet she spent a month choosing her own sofa.

senses.def: member of the middle class, or a person with conventional, materialistic values
senses.ex: In the play, the young painter scorns every bourgeois in town, until he needs one of them to buy his work.

senses.def: in Marxist theory, a member of the capitalist class that owns the means of production
senses.ex: The pamphlet urged factory workers to stop serving the interests of the bourgeois who owned the mills.

origin: From Late Latin "bovinus", relating to cattle, from Latin "bos", ox, a distant relative of the word "beef".

senses.def: of or relating to cattle, oxen, or related animals
senses.ex: The veterinarian specializes in bovine diseases and spends most mornings driving between dairy farms.

senses.def: slow, dull, and placid, like a cow
senses.ex: The guard watched the crowd with a bovine indifference, chewing gum and never once looking up from his stool.

senses.def: animal of the cattle family, such as a cow, buffalo, or bison
senses.ex: The wildlife park keeps several large bovines, including a pair of shaggy bison that tourists love to photograph.

origin: From "bowdlerize", named after Thomas Bowdler, an English editor who in the early 1800s published a family Shakespeare with passages he judged indecent removed.

senses.def: removal of material considered offensive from a text, often weakening or distorting it
senses.ex: The bowdlerization of the novel for school libraries cut so many scenes that the ending no longer made sense.

senses.def: censored version of a work produced by such cutting
senses.ex: The film shown on the airline was a clumsy bowdlerization, with every curse word replaced by a muffled cough.

origin: Named after Thomas Bowdler, who in 1818 published "The Family Shakespeare", an edition with every word he judged improper removed.

senses.def: remove material considered offensive from a text, often weakening it
senses.ex: The television network bowdlerized the film so heavily that several key scenes no longer made sense.

origin: From Scots "brack", from Middle Dutch "brac", salty, plus "-ish", so "somewhat salty".

senses.def: slightly salty, as water is where a river mixes with the sea
senses.ex: The marsh water was too brackish to drink, but the mangroves and crabs along the estuary thrived in it.

origin: Coined by Edmund Spenser as the name of Braggadocchio, a boastful character in The Faerie Queene (1590), made from "brag" with a mock Italian ending.

senses.def: loud, empty boasting or swaggering self-praise
senses.ex: Behind the boxer's braggadocio at the press conference was a fighter who had quietly trained twice a day for months.

origin: From Middle French "bragard", showy or vain, from "braguer", to boast or flaunt.

senses.def: person who constantly boasts about themselves
senses.ex: Nobody at the reunion wanted to sit near the braggart who kept describing his sports car and his stock portfolio.

senses.def: boastful and given to bragging
senses.ex: The play's comic hero is a braggart soldier who flees the moment a real battle begins.

origin: From Old English "braembel", a diminutive of a Germanic word for a thorny shrub, the same root that gave the plant name "broom".

senses.def: prickly, tangled shrub, especially a blackberry bush
senses.ex: The hikers lost the trail and pushed through brambles that tore at their sleeves and left scratches on their arms.

senses.def: blackberry, the fruit of such a shrub (chiefly British)
senses.ex: We filled two jars with brambles picked along the hedgerow and turned them into jam that evening.

origin: From Old French "brandir", to flourish a sword, from Frankish "brand", a sword or firebrand.

senses.def: wave or flourish something, especially a weapon, as a threat or display
senses.ex: The guard brandished his baton at the crowd pressing against the gate, and they slowly backed away.

senses.def: show off something proudly or aggressively to impress others
senses.ex: She walked into the meeting brandishing the sales report that proved her plan had worked.

origin: Of uncertain origin, perhaps from Scots "brash", a sudden attack or assault, which fits its sense of rushing boldness.

senses.def: self-assertive in a rude, tactless, or overly confident way
senses.ex: The brash young lawyer interrupted the judge twice, and the courtroom fell silent in disbelief.

senses.def: loud, bright, or showy in a way that lacks taste
senses.ex: The casino's brash neon signs clashed with the quiet brick storefronts on the rest of the street.

origin: From "brass" plus "-y", having the qualities of brass: its bright yellow color, its hard shine, and the blare of brass instruments.

senses.def: bold, loud, and self-confident, sometimes to the point of rudeness
senses.ex: The brassy talk show host had no trouble asking the senator questions that other reporters only whispered.

senses.def: harsh and blaring in sound, like a trumpet
senses.ex: A brassy fanfare from the marching band announced the start of the parade.

senses.def: bright yellow like brass, often in a cheap or showy way
senses.ex: Her brassy hair dye looked almost orange under the fluorescent lights of the office.

origin: From French "bravade", boasting, from Italian "bravata", from "bravare", to brag, from "bravo", bold.

senses.def: bold, boastful show of confidence meant to impress, often hiding fear
senses.ex: His bravado about skydiving vanished the moment the plane door opened and he saw the ground far below.

origin: From Italian "bravura", skill or spirit, from "bravo", fine or bold. A close cousin of "bravado", but it praises real skill instead of mere show.

senses.def: great technical skill and brilliance shown in a performance or achievement
senses.ex: The pianist played the final movement with such bravura that the audience leapt to its feet before the last chord faded.

senses.def: showing great skill, daring, and flair
senses.ex: The rookie striker scored with a bravura bicycle kick that replayed on every sports channel that night.

origin: From Old French "braon", the fleshy part of the body or a slice of meat, from a Germanic word for roast meat.

senses.def: physical strength and muscle, especially as opposed to intelligence
senses.ex: Moving the piano required more brawn than the two of us had, so we called the neighbors for help.

senses.def: meat from a pig's or calf's head set in jelly; head cheese (chiefly British)
senses.ex: The butcher's window displayed slices of brawn beside the pork pies and sausages.

origin: From "brawn", muscle, plus "-y". "Brawn" comes from Old French "braon", the fleshy part of the body.

senses.def: physically strong and muscular
senses.ex: Two brawny dockworkers lifted the crate onto the truck as if it held feathers instead of engine parts.

origin: From Old English "bræsen", made of brass. A brazen face was pictured as hard as brass, unmoving and showing no shame.

senses.def: bold and shameless, without any embarrassment
senses.ex: In a brazen lie, the student claimed the essay was his own while his friend's name was still on the title page.

senses.def: face an embarrassing situation boldly and without shame, usually with "out"
senses.ex: Caught with the stolen cookies, the boy decided to brazen it out and deny everything.

origin: From Old English "bryce", a breaking or fracture, from the same Germanic root as "break".

senses.def: act of breaking a law, agreement, rule, or relationship
senses.ex: The supplier's late deliveries were a clear breach of contract, so the bakery sued for its lost sales.

senses.def: gap or opening made by breaking through a wall, defense, or security system
senses.ex: The data breach exposed the addresses of two million customers before engineers closed the gap.

senses.def: break through a wall, barrier, or line of defense
senses.ex: The floodwaters breached the levee just after midnight, and the lower streets filled within an hour.

senses.def: break or fail to honor a law, agreement, or promise
senses.ex: By posting the photos online, the employee breached the confidentiality agreement she had signed.

origin: From Latin "breviarium", a summary or abridgment, from "brevis", short, the root of "brief" and "abbreviate".

senses.def: book of the psalms, prayers, and readings a Catholic priest or monk recites each day
senses.ex: Every evening the old monk opened his worn breviary and read the night prayers by candlelight.

origin: From Old French "brieveté", from Latin "brevitas", shortness, from "brevis", short, which also gave English "brief".

senses.def: concise and exact use of words in speech or writing
senses.ex: The editor praised the brevity of the reporter's story, which explained the complex trial in just three paragraphs.

senses.def: shortness of time or duration
senses.ex: The brevity of the cherry blossom season draws huge crowds to the park every spring.

origin: From French "bricolage", built from "bricoler", meaning "to tinker" or "putter about"; the word keeps that improvised, hands-on feel.

senses.def: making something by combining whatever materials or ideas are at hand
senses.ex: With no budget for props, the students relied on bricolage, turning cardboard and old curtains into a castle.

senses.def: work assembled from varied available materials or borrowed elements
senses.ex: The gallery's centerpiece was a bricolage of bicycle parts, family photographs, and broken ceramic tiles.

origin: From Old English "brīdel", the headgear and reins used to control a horse, related to "braid".

senses.def: show resentment or anger, especially by stiffening or drawing back
senses.ex: The veteran nurse bridled when the new doctor suggested she did not know how to take a pulse.

senses.def: restrain or keep under control
senses.ex: He learned to bridle his temper during negotiations, no matter how rude the other side became.

senses.def: headgear with a bit and reins used to guide a horse
senses.ex: The stable hand slipped the bridle over the mare's head and led her out to the ring.

syn: bristle, take umbrage, chafe, take offense

origin: From Old French "brigand", originally a foot soldier, through Italian "briga", meaning trouble or strife. The meaning shifted toward outlaw.

senses.def: an armed robber or outlaw, especially one acting with a gang
senses.ex: Travelers avoided the mountain pass after a brigand robbed two caravans there in one week.

origin: An alteration of "brinded", meaning streaked, probably influenced by similar words such as "speckled" and "grizzled".

senses.def: marked with irregular streaks of contrasting brown, gray, or tawny color
senses.ex: A brindled dog waited outside the bakery, its dark stripes visible even in the evening rain.

origin: From Italian "brio", meaning spirit or talent, itself borrowed from Spanish "brío".

senses.def: spirited energy and confident flair, especially in a performance
senses.ex: She conducted the final movement with brio, giving the weary orchestra a burst of energy.

origin: The origin is uncertain; "brisk" may be related to "brusque", a word associated with abruptness.

senses.def: quick and energetic in movement or manner
senses.ex: We took a brisk walk to the station and still had time to buy coffee.

senses.def: refreshingly cold or sharp, especially of weather or air
senses.ex: A brisk wind swept the heat from the courtyard as the sun went down.

senses.def: active and steady, especially of trade or business
senses.ex: Sales stayed brisk throughout the festival, and the baker ran out of bread by noon.

origin: From Old English "byrst", a stiff hair, plus a diminutive ending. To bristle is to react like an angry animal raising its stiff hairs.

senses.def: react with anger, irritation, or defensiveness
senses.ex: The author bristled when the interviewer suggested that her novel was copied from an older book.

senses.def: be thickly covered or crowded with something, usually with "with"
senses.ex: The harbor bristled with masts as hundreds of sailboats gathered for the regatta.

senses.def: short, stiff hair on an animal or plant, or in a brush
senses.ex: The bristles on his old toothbrush were so worn that they splayed out in every direction.

syn: bridle, take umbrage, chafe, flare up, take offense

origin: From Middle English "britel", from an Old English word meaning prone to break.

senses.def: easily broken or cracked by pressure or bending
senses.ex: The old rubber had grown brittle, so the gasket cracked when Mara tried to remove it.

senses.def: emotionally fragile or easily upset
senses.ex: After weeks of sleepless work, he felt brittle and took a mild correction as an insult.

senses.def: tense and sharp in a way that suggests strain
senses.ex: Her brittle laugh faded quickly when the interviewer asked about the missing funds.

senses.def: hard candy made from caramelized sugar and usually nuts
senses.ex: Grandmother packed peanut brittle in tins so it would survive the long trip to campus.

origin: From Old French "broche", a spike or skewer, from Latin "broccus", projecting. To broach first meant to pierce a cask, then to open a topic.

senses.def: raise a subject, especially a sensitive one, for discussion
senses.ex: He waited until his parents were in a good mood before broaching the idea of taking a gap year.

syn: raise, bring up, introduce, mention, moot

origin: From "broad" plus "side", first the whole side of a ship and then the volley fired by all its guns at once, hence a fierce attack.

senses.def: strongly worded spoken or written attack
senses.ex: The union leader's broadside against management accused the company of hiding profits while cutting wages.

senses.def: simultaneous firing of all the guns on one side of a warship
senses.ex: The frigate turned and fired a broadside that shattered the enemy ship's mast.

senses.def: with the side turned toward something
senses.ex: The truck skidded on the ice and slid broadside into the guardrail.

senses.def: crash into the side of a vehicle
senses.ex: A driver who ran the red light broadsided our car in the middle of the intersection.

origin: From Brobdingnag, the land of giants in Jonathan Swift's "Gulliver's Travels". Its fictional place name became a word for immense size.

senses.def: enormous in size or scale
senses.ex: A brobdingnagian sculpture filled the plaza, forcing pedestrians to walk around its steel legs.

origin: From Italian "broccato", a word for patterned cloth, through other Romance languages. Its older source is Gaulish.

senses.def: heavy fabric with raised patterns woven into it
senses.ex: The tailor lined the coat with red brocade, visible whenever the wearer opened it.

senses.def: decorate fabric with raised patterns woven into its surface
senses.ex: Artisans brocaded the silk with silver threads for the ceremonial robe.

origin: From "bromine" plus "-ide". Bromide salts were used as sedatives, so humorist Gelett Burgess applied the word to dull people and their soothing, stale remarks.

senses.def: trite, unoriginal remark meant to soothe or placate
senses.ex: The principal offered the usual bromides about teamwork but never explained why the art program was cut.

senses.def: chemical compound of bromine with another element
senses.ex: Doctors in the 1800s prescribed potassium bromide to calm patients with nervous disorders.

origin: The verb comes from Old English "brūcan", to use or enjoy, later to put up with. The noun comes from Old English "brōc", a stream.

senses.def: tolerate or allow, usually used with a negative
senses.ex: The conductor brooked no talking during rehearsals, and late players had to wait outside.

senses.def: small natural stream of fresh water
senses.ex: The children spent the afternoon catching tadpoles in the brook behind their grandmother's farm.

origin: Borrowed from French "brouhaha", meaning an uproar. Its deeper origin is disputed.

senses.def: a noisy public fuss or uproar
senses.ex: A minor change to the lunch menu caused a brouhaha at the school board meeting.

origin: From "brow" plus "beat", picturing someone cowing another person with a fierce frown and stern looks.

senses.def: intimidate someone with stern, bullying words or looks
senses.ex: The manager tried to browbeat the staff into working unpaid overtime by hinting at layoffs.

origin: From French "bruit", meaning noise or rumor, ultimately from a Latin verb meaning "to roar".

senses.def: spread widely as a rumor or report
senses.ex: The minister's resignation was bruited about town before any official announcement appeared.

origin: From Latin "brumalis", meaning wintry, from "bruma", the winter solstice or shortest day of the year.

senses.def: related to winter or characteristic of it
senses.ex: A brumal wind rattled the greenhouse panes while seedlings waited under warm lamps.

origin: From a local pronunciation of Birmingham, England, once associated with cheaply made goods that imitated expensive ones.

senses.def: cheaply made and showy, especially in imitation of something valuable
senses.ex: The hotel's brummagem chandeliers glittered above plastic columns painted to look like marble.

origin: From French "brusque", from Italian "brusco", sharp, sour, or abrupt. Its earlier origin is unknown.

senses.def: abrupt or curt in speech or manner
senses.ex: The clerk's brusque answer, a quick "no" without looking up, left the tourist unsure where to go.

origin: From "brusque", from Italian "brusco", sharp or abrupt, plus "-ly".

senses.def: in an abrupt, curt, or offhand way
senses.ex: The coach brusquely waved off reporters' questions and walked straight to the team bus.

origin: From Middle English "bukke", a male goat or deer. The money sense is American, clipped from buckskins used as a unit of trade on the frontier.

senses.def: resist or go against something, such as a trend or rule
senses.ex: The small bookstore bucked the national trend and reported its best sales year ever.

senses.def: dollar, or a unit of money in general (informal)
senses.ex: He sold his old bike to a neighbor for twenty bucks.

senses.def: male deer, rabbit, or similar animal
senses.ex: A young buck with small antlers stepped out of the woods and stared at our car.

senses.def: (of a horse) jump with an arched back, trying to throw its rider
senses.ex: The colt bucked wildly and threw the rider into the dust within three seconds.

syn: resist, defy, oppose, go against, flout

origin: From Latin "bucolicus", from Greek "boukolikos", rustic or pastoral, literally "of cowherds".

senses.def: relating to the pleasant, peaceful side of country life
senses.ex: Tired of traffic, the couple moved to a bucolic village where sheep grazed beside the only road.

origin: From Middle French "buffle", buffalo, through the soft, yellowish leather made from its hide, which was used for polishing.

senses.def: person who is very interested in and knowledgeable about a subject
senses.ex: A true film buff, my aunt can name the director of almost any movie made before 1960.

senses.def: polish a surface by rubbing it with soft material
senses.ex: He buffed the old trophy with a cloth until its silver gleamed again.

senses.def: muscular and physically fit (informal)
senses.ex: After a summer of lifting weights, my brother came back to school looking surprisingly buff.

senses.def: pale yellowish-brown in color
senses.ex: The old envelopes were made of thick buff paper that had faded at the edges.

origin: From an old verb "buff", to make a dull sound when struck, from Old French "buffe", a blow, so a buffer softens a blow.

senses.def: something that lessens a shock or keeps two things apart
senses.ex: A row of tall trees serves as a buffer between the highway and the quiet neighborhood.

senses.def: protect someone or lessen the impact of something harmful
senses.ex: Her savings buffered the family against the sudden loss of her job.

senses.def: (of a device) load data ahead of time so a video or song plays smoothly
senses.ex: The video kept buffering on the slow hotel internet, freezing every few seconds.

origin: From "buffoon", a foolish clown, plus "-ery", which names a kind of behavior or practice.

senses.def: ridiculous clowning or foolish behavior, especially when seriousness is expected
senses.ex: The debate collapsed into buffoonery when two candidates began mocking each other's haircuts.

origin: Its exact origin is uncertain; the word was used for a frightening imaginary creature before it came to mean a persistent worry.

senses.def: a persistent worry or object of exaggerated fear
senses.ex: For the new principal, the school's aging heating system became a bugaboo every winter.

origin: From an old sense of "bug", a frightening thing or goblin (compare "bogey"), plus "bear". It first meant an imaginary monster used to scare children.

senses.def: persistent source of annoyance, dread, or difficulty
senses.ex: Parking downtown has long been the bugbear of shoppers, and many now drive to the mall instead.

syn: bane, pet peeve, bête noire, nuisance, thorn in one's side

origin: From "bulb", a round underground plant structure, plus "-ous", meaning having; the shape suggests a rounded swelling.

senses.def: rounded and swollen like a bulb
senses.ex: The old lamp had a bulbous glass base that barely fit on the narrow shelf.

senses.def: growing from or producing a bulb
senses.ex: She planted bulbous flowers along the path so they would bloom early each spring.

origin: From "bull" and "-headed", likening stubborn resistance to a bull that refuses to turn.

senses.def: unreasonably stubborn and unwilling to change course or accept advice
senses.ex: Despite three warnings about the storm, his bullheaded insistence kept the crew offshore.

origin: From "bull" and "-ish"; the market sense follows "bull market", a market associated with rising prices.

senses.def: confident that something will succeed or improve
senses.ex: The coach sounded bullish about the young team's chances after its strong preseason.

senses.def: expecting the price of an asset or market to rise
senses.ex: Investors turned bullish on the company after its new battery passed independent testing.

senses.def: forcefully assertive in manner or behavior
senses.ex: Her bullish negotiating style won a lower price but irritated the seller.

senses.def: muscular and solidly built like a bull
senses.ex: The bullish porter carried two heavy trunks upstairs without pausing at the landing.

origin: From Middle Dutch "bolwerk", from "bole", tree trunk, plus "werk", work, first a timber rampart. "Boulevard" comes from the same Dutch word.

senses.def: person, idea, or thing that gives strong protection or support
senses.ex: Independent courts are a bulwark against leaders who try to ignore the law.

senses.def: defensive wall or rampart
senses.ex: The villagers built an earthen bulwark around the settlement to keep out raiders.

origin: From "bumble", to blunder or stumble along, probably an imitative word suggesting an aimless buzzing or mumbling sound.

senses.def: acting in a confused, clumsy, or incompetent way
senses.ex: The bumbling intern spilled coffee on the client's contract and then called her by the wrong name.

origin: Probably a playful formation from "bump", on the pattern of words like "fractious", suggesting someone who bumps their way forward.

senses.def: self-assertive or full of self-importance to an irritating degree
senses.ex: The bumptious new member lectured the club's founders on how their own traditions should work.

origin: Of uncertain origin, perhaps imitative like "bumble" and "fumble", or from a Scandinavian source such as Old Swedish "bunga", to strike.

senses.def: carry out a task clumsily or incompetently
senses.ex: The thieves bungled the robbery by locking themselves out of their own getaway car.

senses.def: mistake or task that has been handled clumsily
senses.ex: A clerical bungle sent the graduation invitations to last year's class instead of this one's.

syn: botch, mishandle, fumble, flub, mess up

origin: From "Buncombe", a North Carolina county whose representative gave a showy speech for constituents in 1820. The name became a label for empty talk.

senses.def: nonsense, especially empty public talk meant to impress
senses.ex: The senator's promise of effortless savings sounded like bunkum to the budget analysts.

origin: From "buoy", a floating marker, plus "-ant", so something buoyant stays afloat, whether in water or in spirits.

senses.def: cheerful, optimistic, and resilient
senses.ex: Even after losing the first game, the team stayed in a buoyant mood and joked all the way home.

senses.def: able to float or to keep things afloat
senses.ex: Salt water is more buoyant than fresh water, so swimmers float easily in the Dead Sea.

senses.def: (of an economy or market) strong and rising
senses.ex: A buoyant housing market meant most homes in the area sold within a week.

origin: From "burden", a heavy load to carry, plus "-some", tending to or full of.

senses.def: difficult to carry out or bear, demanding or oppressive
senses.ex: Caring for three younger siblings after school became burdensome when she also took on a part-time job.

origin: From French "bureaucratie", coined by economist Vincent de Gournay from "bureau", desk or office, plus Greek "-kratia", rule, so "rule by desks".

senses.def: system of government or management run by appointed officials following fixed rules
senses.ex: The country's bureaucracy employs thousands of clerks who process pensions, permits, and tax returns.

senses.def: excessive official rules and slow procedures that get in the way
senses.ex: After months of bureaucracy, the charity finally received approval to open its food bank.

origin: From Old French "burjon", a bud or shoot, so to burgeon is to sprout and spread like new growth in spring.

senses.def: grow or expand rapidly
senses.ex: Interest in chess burgeoned after the popular series aired, and the local club doubled its membership.

origin: Present participle of "burgeon", from Old French "burjon", a bud or shoot.

senses.def: growing or expanding rapidly
senses.ex: The burgeoning market for electric bikes has drawn dozens of new companies into the field.

origin: From French "burlesque", borrowed from Italian "burlesco", meaning parodic or joking.

senses.def: comic imitation that mocks a serious work or style
senses.ex: The student troupe staged a burlesque of the school's solemn awards ceremony.

senses.def: stage entertainment featuring comedy, music, and often striptease
senses.ex: The theater reopened with a burlesque that mixed sketches, dance, and a playful striptease.

senses.def: mock by exaggerated comic imitation
senses.ex: The cartoon burlesqued the mayor's grand promises by showing roads paved with gold.

origin: From Middle English "burly", stately or tall, of uncertain origin. The sense slid from "imposing" to "big and sturdy".

senses.def: large, strong, and heavily built
senses.ex: A burly bouncer stood at the club door, arms folded, checking every ID with a small flashlight.

origin: From Old French "burnir", a variant of "brunir", to polish or make brown. Despite the look of it, it is unrelated to "burn".

senses.def: polish something, especially metal, by rubbing until it shines
senses.ex: The silversmith burnished the antique teapot until the engraved flowers stood out clearly.

senses.def: improve or enhance a reputation or image
senses.ex: The senator volunteered at shelters during the campaign, hoping to burnish her image as a friend of the poor.

senses.def: shine or gloss on a polished surface
senses.ex: Years of handling had given the wooden banister a warm burnish.

origin: From "button" plus "hole". The verb, to corner someone for a talk, was reshaped from an older "buttonhold", to hold a person by a coat button.

senses.def: stop someone and keep them in conversation, often against their wishes
senses.ex: A reporter buttonholed the senator in the hallway and refused to let him leave without answering one question.

senses.def: slit in a garment through which a button is pushed to fasten it
senses.ex: The new coat was so stiff that I could barely push the buttons through the buttonholes.

senses.def: flower worn in the buttonhole of a jacket lapel (chiefly British)
senses.ex: Each groomsman wore a white rose buttonhole that matched the bride's bouquet.

origin: From Old French "ars bouterez", supporting arches, from a Frankish word meaning "to push", since a buttress pushes back against a wall.

senses.def: support or strengthen an argument, claim, or structure
senses.ex: The scientist buttressed her theory with data from fifteen years of field observations.

senses.def: structure of stone or brick built against a wall to support it
senses.ex: Massive stone buttresses hold up the walls of the medieval cathedral.

senses.def: anything that supports or strengthens something
senses.ex: Strong friendships served as a buttress against the stress of her first year in college.

syn: bolster, reinforce, shore up, support, strengthen

origin: From Old English "bocsum", pliant or obedient, related to "bow", to bend. The meaning drifted from yielding to cheerful and healthy, then to full-figured.

senses.def: of a woman, having a full, rounded, healthy-looking figure
senses.ex: The painter favored buxom, rosy-cheeked models, in sharp contrast to the slender figures in fashion magazines of his day.

origin: From "by" plus "gone", as in "gone by", describing time that has already passed.

senses.def: belonging to an earlier time
senses.ex: The diner's jukebox and neon sign recall a bygone era of drive-ins and milkshakes.

senses.def: past event or offense, mainly in "let bygones be bygones"
senses.ex: After years of not speaking, the brothers agreed to let bygones be bygones and met for lunch.

origin: From the Byzantine Empire, ruled from Constantinople (old Byzantium), whose court was famous for its complicated rules and scheming politics.

senses.def: excessively complicated and hard to understand
senses.ex: The airline's byzantine refund rules made it nearly impossible to get money back for a canceled flight.

senses.def: involving secret scheming and devious plots
senses.ex: The novel follows the byzantine intrigues of a royal court where every adviser has a hidden agenda.

origin: From French "bête noire", literally "black beast", the creature you most dread or dislike.

senses.def: person or thing that someone especially dislikes, dreads, or keeps clashing with
senses.ex: Long division was my little brother's bête noire, and he would hide under the table whenever worksheets came out.

syn: bane, bugbear, pet peeve, nemesis, anathema

origin: From French "cabale", from Medieval Latin "cabbala", from Hebrew "qabbalah", received tradition, the name for secret mystical lore.

senses.def: small secret group plotting together, especially in politics
senses.ex: Rumors spread that a cabal of board members was planning to force the founder out of the company.

origin: From "cabalist", a student of the Kabbalah, from Medieval Latin "cabbala", from Hebrew "qabbalah", received tradition.

senses.def: having a secret or hidden meaning understood only by insiders
senses.ex: The margins of the old notebook were covered in cabalistic symbols that no one in the family could decode.

senses.def: relating to a cabal, a small secretive group of plotters
senses.ex: The reporter described the cabalistic meetings of the board, where decisions were made long before any public vote.

senses.def: relating to Kabbalah, the Jewish tradition of mystical interpretation
senses.ex: The scholar spent years translating cabalistic commentaries on the opening chapters of Genesis.

origin: From French "cacher", to hide, through French Canadian trappers, who used "cache" for a hidden store of supplies.

senses.def: hidden store of things such as weapons, food, or valuables
senses.ex: Police found a cache of stolen jewelry hidden inside the hollow wall of the garage.

senses.def: temporary computer memory that keeps recently used data for quick access
senses.ex: Clearing the browser's cache fixed the problem, and the website finally loaded its new design.

senses.def: store something away, often in a hidden place
senses.ex: Squirrels cache acorns in dozens of spots each fall and dig them up during the winter.

origin: From French "cachet", a seal stamped on a letter or document. A seal marked something as official, so the word came to mean prestige.

senses.def: prestige or distinction that makes something admired or desirable
senses.ex: Winning the national prize gave the small bakery a cachet that brought customers from three towns away.

origin: From Latin "cachinnare", to laugh aloud, a word that imitates the sound of loud laughter.

senses.def: laugh loudly and without restraint
senses.ex: The friends cachinnated so loudly at the back of the theater that an usher asked them to leave.

origin: From Latin "cacoethes", from Greek "kakoethes", ill-disposed, from "kakos", bad, plus "ethos", disposition or habit: literally a bad habit.

senses.def: irresistible urge or compulsion to do something, often unwise
senses.ex: Her cacoethes for rearranging furniture meant that guests never found the couch in the same place twice.

origin: From Greek "kakos", bad, plus "-graphy", writing, from "graphein", to write. It is the opposite of "calligraphy", beautiful writing.

senses.def: bad handwriting that is messy or hard to read
senses.ex: The pharmacist had to phone the clinic because the doctor's cacography made the dosage on the prescription impossible to read.

senses.def: bad or incorrect spelling
senses.ex: The teacher circled every example of cacography in the essay, from "definately" to "seperate".

origin: From Greek "kakophōnos", from "kakos", bad, and "phōnos", sounding.

senses.def: harsh, jarring, and unpleasant in sound
senses.ex: The cacophonous chorus of car alarms woke the whole street at three in the morning.

origin: From French "cacophonie", from Greek "kakophōnia", from "kakos", bad, and "phōnē", sound.

senses.def: harsh, jarring mixture of sounds
senses.ex: The market was a cacophony of vendors shouting prices, chickens squawking, and scooters honking.

origin: From Latin "cadaver", dead body, probably from "cadere", to fall, picturing a body that has fallen.

senses.def: dead human body, especially one used for medical study or dissection
senses.ex: First-year medical students spend months learning anatomy from a cadaver donated by a generous local family.

origin: From Latin "cadaverosus", corpselike, from "cadaver", a dead body, so a cadaverous face looks like a corpse.

senses.def: very pale, thin, or bony, like a corpse
senses.ex: After weeks lost in the desert, the explorer looked cadaverous, with sunken eyes and hollow cheeks.

origin: From Italian "cadenza", from Latin "cadere", to fall, first describing the fall of the voice or the melody at the end of a phrase.

senses.def: rhythmic rise and fall of a voice or of sounds in speech
senses.ex: The preacher's slow, rolling cadence held the whole congregation still until the final word.

senses.def: regular beat or rhythm of a repeated movement
senses.ex: The soldiers marched to the steady cadence of the drill sergeant's chant across the parade ground.

senses.def: series of chords that brings a musical phrase or piece to a close
senses.ex: The choir paused on the final cadence, letting the last chord ring through the cathedral.

senses.def: regular rate at which something recurring happens
senses.ex: The software team moved to a two-week release cadence so that users received small updates more often.

origin: Of uncertain origin. It is probably linked to "cadger", a traveling peddler, and meant to peddle goods before it meant to beg for them.

senses.def: ask for or get something free by begging or imposing on someone
senses.ex: He spent the whole concert cadging snacks and drinks from strangers sitting nearby.

origin: From French "cadre", frame, from Italian "quadro", from Latin "quadrum", square, from "quattuor", four: a framework that holds a group together.

senses.def: small, trained core group of people at the heart of an organization or movement
senses.ex: The startup began with a cadre of five engineers who had all worked together at the same lab.

senses.def: member of such a group, especially an activist in a Communist party
senses.ex: The village cadre was in charge of organizing the harvest and reporting quotas to the district office.

origin: From Latin "caesura", a cutting, from "caedere", to cut: a cut or break in the flow of a line.

senses.def: pause or break within a line of poetry, often marked by punctuation
senses.ex: In the line "To err is human, to forgive divine," the caesura falls right after the comma.
