senses.def: break or interruption in a process, a piece of music, or the course of history
senses.ex: For many families, the pandemic was a caesura that divided life into a clear before and after.

origin: American slang of unknown origin from the late 1800s. Some link it to the wariness of a caged animal, but that is only a guess.

senses.def: reluctant to give information; deliberately secretive or evasive
senses.ex: When asked about her plans after graduation, my sister got cagey and changed the subject to the weather.

senses.def: shrewd and careful not to be tricked or caught out
senses.ex: The cagey chess veteran refused every pawn his young opponent offered, sensing a trap in each one.

origin: From French "cajoler", probably a blend of "cageoler", to chatter like a jay, and "gaioler", to lure into a cage.

senses.def: persuade someone to do something by flattery, coaxing, or promises
senses.ex: She cajoled her little brother into cleaning the garage by promising him the front seat for a month.

origin: From French "calamiteux", from Latin "calamitosus", disastrous, from "calamitas", disaster or loss.

senses.def: causing great damage, distress, or disaster
senses.ex: Building the dam without testing the soil proved calamitous when the walls cracked after the first heavy rain.

origin: From Middle French "calamite", from Latin "calamitas", loss, damage, or disaster.

senses.def: event that causes great damage, loss, or suffering; a disaster
senses.ex: The collapse of the dam was a calamity that flooded six villages and left thousands without homes.

origin: Past participle of "calculate", from Latin "calculare", to reckon, from "calculus", a small pebble used for counting.

senses.def: done deliberately and with careful planning to achieve a particular effect
senses.ex: Arriving late to the meeting was a calculated insult, meant to show the visitors how little the director valued them.

senses.def: of a risk or move, taken after carefully weighing the likely outcomes
senses.ex: Investing her savings in the family bakery was a calculated risk, since she had studied its accounts for months.

senses.def: likely or intended to have a certain effect, used with "to"
senses.ex: The coach's blunt speech at halftime was calculated to shake the team out of its complacency.

origin: From "calibre" or "caliber", the bore of a gun, plus "-ate". It first meant to measure a gun's bore, then to check any instrument against a standard.

senses.def: check or adjust a measuring instrument against a known standard so it reads accurately
senses.ex: Before each experiment, the lab assistant calibrates the scale with a certified one-gram weight.

senses.def: adjust something carefully so it suits a particular purpose or audience
senses.ex: The teacher calibrates her questions to each student, pushing strong readers and encouraging struggling ones.

origin: From Latin "caliginosus", misty or dark, from "caligo", fog, mist, or gloom, plus "-osus", full of.

senses.def: dark, misty, and gloomy; hard to see through
senses.ex: The ferry crept across the caliginous bay, its foghorn sounding every minute until the harbor lights appeared.

origin: From French "calligraphie", from Greek "kalligraphia", beautiful writing, from "kallos", beauty, plus "graphein", to write.

senses.def: art of producing beautiful, decorative handwriting with a pen or brush
senses.ex: My grandmother practiced Chinese calligraphy every morning, grinding her own ink before painting a single character.

senses.def: decorative handwriting itself, or lettering produced this way
senses.ex: The wedding invitations were addressed in elegant calligraphy that took the designer three full days.

origin: From Greek "kallipygos", from "kallos", beauty, plus "puge", buttocks, the name given to a famous ancient statue of Aphrodite.

senses.def: having beautifully shaped buttocks
senses.ex: The museum guide explained that the callipygian marble figure was one of the most copied statues of the ancient world.

origin: From Latin "callosus", hard-skinned, from "callum", hardened skin, so a callous person's feelings are as toughened as a callus.

senses.def: emotionally hardened and indifferent to other people's suffering
senses.ex: The company's callous decision to fire workers by text message, days before the holidays, drew national outrage.

origin: From Old English "calu", bald or bare. It described young birds without feathers, then anyone young and inexperienced.

senses.def: young, inexperienced, and lacking maturity
senses.ex: As a callow freshman, he believed that charm alone would get him through his chemistry exams.

origin: From Latin "calumniari", to accuse falsely, from "calumnia", a false accusation.

senses.def: make false and damaging statements about someone
senses.ex: Anonymous accounts calumniated the judge online, falsely claiming she had taken bribes from defendants.

origin: From Late Latin "calumniosus", full of false accusation, from "calumnia", slander.

senses.def: containing false and damaging accusations about someone
senses.ex: The coach demanded a public apology for the calumnious rumor that he had fixed the championship game.

origin: From Old French "calomnie" or Latin "calumnia", a false accusation or trick. The word "challenge" comes from the same Latin root.

senses.def: false statement made to damage someone's reputation, or the act of making such statements
senses.ex: The reformer faced years of calumny from officials who accused her of stealing the funds she had exposed.

origin: From French "camaraderie", from "camarade", comrade, which goes back to Spanish "camarada", a group sharing a room.

senses.def: mutual trust and friendship among people who spend time or work together
senses.ex: The camaraderie among the stage crew grew stronger with every late-night rehearsal before opening night.

syn: fellowship, comradeship, companionship, solidarity, esprit de corps

origin: From Spanish "camarilla", literally a little chamber, from "cámara", chamber, plus the diminutive "-illa", suggesting advisers plotting behind a private door.

senses.def: small secret group of advisers who scheme around a ruler or leader
senses.ex: The aging president rarely saw his cabinet, relying instead on a camarilla of relatives and loyal generals who controlled every decision.

origin: Through Middle French from Italian "canaglia", a contemptuous word for the rabble built on Latin "canis", dog, so it likens common people to a pack of dogs.

senses.def: common people viewed with contempt, the rabble
senses.ex: The haughty duke dismissed the striking dockworkers as canaille, unworthy of a single word from anyone of his rank.

origin: From French "canard", duck and also hoax. The hoax sense likely comes from an old French phrase about half-selling a duck, meaning to fool someone.

senses.def: false or unfounded rumor or story, often spread on purpose
senses.ex: The canard that bats are blind keeps spreading, even though most bats see perfectly well.

origin: From Latin "candidus", white or bright, so a candid person is open and clear, with nothing hidden.

senses.def: truthful and straightforward, even when that is uncomfortable
senses.ex: In a candid letter to fans, the singer admitted that she had canceled the tour because of exhaustion.

senses.def: (of a photograph) taken informally, without the subject posing
senses.ex: The best wedding pictures were the candid shots of guests laughing, not the stiff family portraits.

origin: From "candid", from Latin "candidus", white or pure, plus "-ness".

senses.def: quality of being open, honest, and frank
senses.ex: The players respected the new coach's candidness about who would start and why.

origin: From Latin "candor", brightness or whiteness, from "candere", to shine, so candor is speech with nothing dark or hidden.

senses.def: quality of being open, honest, and sincere in speech
senses.ex: The CEO's candor about the company's mistakes won back investors who had expected more excuses.

origin: From Scots and northern English, from "can" in its old sense of "know how to", plus "-y". It is related to "cunning".

senses.def: shrewd and careful, especially in business or politics
senses.ex: The canny shop owner stocked up on umbrellas the week before the rainy season began.

origin: From Latin "canon", from Greek "kanōn", measuring rod or standard, probably related to "kanna", reed. A canon is a yardstick for judging.

senses.def: generally accepted rule, principle, or standard
senses.ex: The new museum wing breaks every canon of classical design, with tilted walls and no straight corridors.

senses.def: body of works accepted as the most important or authoritative in a field
senses.ex: Toni Morrison's novels are now firmly part of the American literary canon.

senses.def: works or story events accepted as genuine or official
senses.ex: Fans debated whether the deleted scene counted as canon or just a director's experiment.

origin: From Medieval Latin "canonicalis", from "canon", rule, from Greek "kanōn", measuring rod or standard.

senses.def: accepted as authoritative, standard, or orthodox
senses.ex: Her paper became the canonical account of the experiment, cited in nearly every textbook since.

senses.def: included in an official list, such as scripture or a story's official version
senses.ex: Only four of the many ancient gospels are considered canonical by most Christian churches.

senses.def: being the most typical or basic example of something
senses.ex: The apple falling on Newton's head is the canonical example teachers use to introduce gravity.

origin: From Medieval Latin "canonizare", to place in the canon, the official list of saints, from Greek "kanōn", rule or standard.

senses.def: treat someone or something as ideal and beyond criticism
senses.ex: Fans canonized the late rock star, refusing to admit that his last two albums were weak.

senses.def: officially declare a dead person to be a saint
senses.ex: The Catholic Church canonized Mother Teresa in 2016, nineteen years after her death.

senses.def: accept a work or artist as part of a field's recognized canon
senses.ex: Critics took decades to canonize the photographer, whose work was once dismissed as mere snapshots.

origin: From Latin "canorus", melodious, from "canere", to sing, the same root behind "chant" and "cantor".

senses.def: pleasantly melodious and resonant in sound
senses.ex: The canorous notes of the cello drifted through the empty cathedral, warm and full enough to silence the last few visitors.

origin: Cant as talk comes from Latin "cantare", to sing, probably via Old Northern French, recalling a whining chant. Cant as tilt comes from Middle Dutch "cant", edge or side.

senses.def: insincere, pious talk, especially moral statements repeated without real belief
senses.ex: Voters grew tired of the mayor's pious cant about honesty once the bribery records became public.

senses.def: special vocabulary or jargon used by a particular group or trade
senses.ex: The old sailors spoke a cant so full of private slang that new deckhands could barely follow the conversation.

senses.def: tilt or set something at an angle
senses.ex: The carpenter canted the shelf slightly backward so that the heavy jars would not slide off during an earthquake.

senses.def: slope or tilt away from a level or upright position
senses.ex: The floor of the old farmhouse had such a cant that a dropped marble rolled straight to the far wall.

origin: Perhaps from an earlier "contenkerous", a blend of "contentious" and "rancorous", which together capture its quarrelsome, bitter mood.

senses.def: bad-tempered, argumentative, and uncooperative
senses.ex: The cantankerous neighbor called the police whenever children's laughter drifted over his fence.

origin: Shortened from "Canterbury pace", the easy gait supposedly used by medieval pilgrims riding to the shrine at Canterbury.

senses.def: horse's easy three-beat gait, between a trot and a gallop
senses.ex: The mare settled into a steady canter along the beach, her hooves throwing up small sprays of wet sand.

senses.def: move or ride at this easy, three-beat pace
senses.ex: We cantered across the meadow at dawn and slowed to a walk only when the trail entered the woods.

origin: From Middle Scots "cantrip" or "cantrap", a magic charm or trick. Its further origin is obscure, though it is probably linked to Latin "cantare", to sing.

senses.def: minor magic spell or charm
senses.ex: In the tabletop campaign, the young wizard used a simple cantrip to light a candle without spending any real magical energy.

senses.def: playful or mischievous trick
senses.ex: Every April the twins pulled some new cantrip on their teachers, this year swapping the labels on all the classroom keys.

origin: From "canvas", coarse hemp cloth, through an old verb meaning to toss someone in a canvas sheet. How that led to seeking votes is unclear.

senses.def: visit people in an area to seek votes, support, or orders
senses.ex: Volunteers canvassed the neighborhood every weekend before the election, knocking on doors and urging residents to vote for the school bond.

senses.def: question people to gather their opinions or information
senses.ex: Detectives canvassed the apartment building, asking each tenant whether they had heard anything unusual on the night of the fire.

senses.def: examine or discuss something thoroughly
senses.ex: The committee canvassed several options for the new library site before settling on the vacant lot downtown.

senses.def: organized survey or campaign to gather votes or opinions, often door to door
senses.ex: A door-to-door canvass of the district showed that most households opposed the proposed highway expansion.

origin: From Latin "capax", able to hold much, from "capere", to take or hold.

senses.def: having a lot of room inside, roomy
senses.ex: The capacious old barn easily held two tractors, a hay wagon, and the family's canoe.

senses.def: (of a mind or memory) able to take in a great deal
senses.ex: Her capacious memory let her recite the names of every student she had taught in thirty years.

origin: From Latin "capacitas", from "capax", able to hold much, from "capere", to hold or take.

senses.def: maximum amount that something can hold or produce
senses.ex: The new reservoir has a capacity of ten billion gallons, enough to supply the city for a year.

senses.def: ability or power to do, feel, or understand something
senses.ex: Children have a remarkable capacity to learn languages simply by hearing them spoken.

senses.def: particular role or position in which someone acts
senses.ex: She attended the conference in her capacity as president of the student council.

origin: Came into English from Middle French "caparasson", which traces back through Old Spanish "caparazón" to Old Occitan "capairon".

senses.def: ornamental cloth covering spread over a horse or elephant
senses.ex: Each elephant in the festival parade wore a caparison of red silk stitched with tiny mirrors.

senses.def: cover a horse with ornamental cloth, or dress someone richly
senses.ex: The stable hands caparisoned the king's horse in blue velvet for the coronation procession.

origin: From "capital" plus "-ize", with "capital" going back to Latin "capitalis", of the head, from "caput", head.

senses.def: take advantage of a situation or opportunity for one's own gain
senses.ex: The small bakery capitalized on the street festival by selling warm pastries to the crowds waiting in line.

senses.def: write or print with a capital letter
senses.ex: Remember to capitalize the names of countries and languages when you proofread your history essay tonight.

senses.def: provide a business with the money it needs to operate
senses.ex: Two local investors agreed to capitalize the startup with enough funding to cover its first three years.

syn: exploit, leverage, cash in on, profit from

origin: From Medieval Latin "capitulare", to draw up under headings, from "capitulum", heading or chapter, from "caput", head. Surrender once meant agreeing to listed terms.

senses.def: stop resisting and surrender or give in to demands
senses.ex: After two days of their daughter's pleading, the parents capitulated and let her adopt the stray kitten.

syn: surrender, yield, submit, give in, relent

origin: From French "capricieux", from Italian "capriccioso", from "capriccio", a sudden whim.

senses.def: given to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood or behavior
senses.ex: Workers never knew what to expect from the capricious manager, who praised a report one day and shredded it the next.

origin: From Latin "captiosus", tricky or quibbling, from "captio", a catching or trick, from "capere", to seize, so a captious critic tries to catch you out.

senses.def: inclined to find fault or raise petty objections
senses.ex: The captious professor marked down an excellent essay because one citation used the wrong punctuation.

origin: From Late Latin "captivare", to capture, from "captivus", prisoner, and "capere", to seize, so something captivating takes your attention prisoner.

senses.def: hold someone's attention completely through charm, beauty, or interest
senses.ex: The young violinist captivated the audience so completely that nobody dared to cough until the final note faded.

origin: From French "carapace", tortoise shell, from Spanish "carapacho", a word of unknown origin.

senses.def: hard upper shell of a turtle, crab, or similar animal
senses.ex: The biologist gently measured the sea turtle's carapace before releasing the animal back into the warm shallow water.

senses.def: protective outer manner that hides a person's feelings
senses.ex: Behind a carapace of sarcasm, the new manager was deeply anxious about disappointing the team.

origin: From "carcino-", cancer, from Greek "karkinos", crab, plus "-genic", producing, so the word literally means producing cancer.

senses.def: causing or tending to cause cancer
senses.ex: Regulators banned the dye after long-term studies showed it was carcinogenic in laboratory animals at surprisingly low doses.

origin: From Latin "cardinalis", from "cardo", hinge, so something cardinal is the point on which everything else turns.

senses.def: of the greatest importance, chief or fundamental
senses.ex: The cardinal rule of the kitchen was simple: never leave a hot pan unattended.

senses.def: senior official of the Roman Catholic Church, ranking just below the pope
senses.ex: The cardinals gathered in the Sistine Chapel to elect a new pope.

senses.def: songbird of North America, the male of which is bright red
senses.ex: A cardinal landed on the snowy fence, its red feathers vivid against the white yard.

origin: From French "carène", keel, from Italian "carena" and Latin "carina", keel of a ship, because careening first meant tipping a ship onto its side.

senses.def: move swiftly and out of control, lurching from side to side
senses.ex: The runaway shopping cart careened down the steep parking lot and crashed into a row of parked bicycles.

senses.def: tilt or lean sharply to one side, as a ship does
senses.ex: Caught by a sudden gust, the small sailboat careened so far that water poured over its low side.

origin: From "career" plus "-ist", a person devoted to something, so a careerist treats getting ahead at work as a creed.

senses.def: person who puts professional advancement above principles or relationships
senses.ex: The new deputy, a ruthless careerist, abandoned every ally and principle that stood in the way of the next promotion.

senses.def: focused on professional advancement above other values
senses.ex: The professor's careerist choice of trendy research topics earned grants but little respect from serious scholars in the field.

origin: From Latin "caret", it lacks, a form of "carere", to lack, because the mark shows where something is missing.

senses.def: mark (‸) used in writing and proofreading to show where something should be inserted
senses.ex: The teacher drew a caret between two words and wrote "not" above it, reversing the sentence's meaning.

senses.def: the symbol ^, used in computing and math, often for raising to a power
senses.ex: On a calculator, typing 2 caret 3 tells it to raise two to the third power.

origin: From "caricature", from Italian "caricatura", from "caricare", to load or exaggerate, so a caricature is an overloaded portrait.

senses.def: portrayed someone with exaggerated features for comic or critical effect
senses.ex: The street artist caricatured tourists for ten dollars, giving each one a giant head and a tiny body.

senses.def: described an idea or person in a crude, distorted, oversimplified way
senses.ex: Her opponents caricatured her climate plan as a ban on cars, though it proposed nothing of the kind.

origin: Borrowed from French "carillon", the name for a tuned set of bells, an instrument that arose in the Low Countries.

senses.def: set of tuned bells in a tower, played from a keyboard
senses.ex: Every evening at six, the university carillon rang out across campus, playing folk melodies from the old stone tower.

senses.def: melody played on such a set of bells
senses.ex: The bell ringer composed a joyful carillon to celebrate the town's bicentennial and performed it from the church tower.

origin: From Middle French "carnage", related to Old French "charnage" and Latin "caro, carnis", flesh, so the word pictures slaughtered bodies.

senses.def: killing of large numbers of people, especially in battle
senses.ex: Reporters who reached the valley after the battle struggled to describe the carnage they found among the burned villages.

senses.def: scene of great destruction or chaos
senses.ex: The overnight storm left carnage along the coast, with boats overturned and beach houses torn from their foundations.

origin: From Old French "charnel" and Late Latin "carnalis", fleshy, from Latin "caro, carnis", flesh, the same root as "carnivore".

senses.def: relating to physical, especially sexual, desires and appetites
senses.ex: The monks renounced carnal pleasures, including rich food and romance, devoting their days to silence, labor, and prayer.

senses.def: worldly or physical rather than spiritual
senses.ex: The sermon warned that carnal ambitions like wealth and status would leave the soul empty in the end.

origin: From "carnival" plus the French-derived suffix "-esque", in the style of, so it describes anything with a carnival's noisy, topsy-turvy spirit.

senses.def: riotously festive and playful, often turning normal rules and hierarchies upside down
senses.ex: The parade had a carnivalesque energy, with students dressed as judges and teachers marching behind them in clown costumes.

origin: From Latin "carnivorus", flesh-eating, from "caro, carnis", flesh, and "vorare", to devour.

senses.def: feeding mainly on the flesh of other animals
senses.ex: Carnivorous animals like wolves have sharp teeth built for tearing meat and short digestive tracts suited to a flesh diet.

senses.def: capturing and digesting insects for nutrients, as certain plants do
senses.ex: The carnivorous sundew traps gnats on its sticky leaves and slowly dissolves them to survive in poor soil.

origin: From "carouse", to drink and party noisily, plus the noun suffix "-al", possibly influenced by a mistaken link with "carousel".

senses.def: noisy, drunken party or bout of merrymaking
senses.ex: After the victory, the sailors' all-night carousal at the harbor tavern woke half the town and ended with a constable's visit.

origin: From "carp", to complain, from Old Norse "karpa", to brag. Its faultfinding sense was probably shaped by Latin "carpere", to pluck or slander.

senses.def: constantly finding fault in a petty, nagging way
senses.ex: The carping customer complained about the napkins, the music, and the temperature before his food even arrived.

senses.def: petty, nagging criticism or complaining
senses.ex: Despite the critics' carping about its length, the film became the year's biggest hit.

origin: From "cartography", from French "carte", map, plus "-graphie", from Greek "graphein", to write or draw.

senses.def: person who draws or produces maps
senses.ex: Early cartographers filled the unknown edges of their maps with sea monsters and blank spaces.

origin: From French "cartographie", from "carte", map, plus "-graphie", from Greek "graphein", to write or draw.

senses.def: science or practice of making maps and charts
senses.ex: Modern cartography relies on satellite data, so even remote mountain trails now appear on phone maps.

origin: From French "cascade" and Italian "cascata", from "cascare", to fall, ultimately from Latin "cadere", to fall, the root of "cadence" and "decay".

senses.def: small waterfall, or a series of them over rocks
senses.ex: Hikers paused beside the cascade, letting the cold spray cool them before climbing the last stretch of the trail.

senses.def: series of events in which each one triggers the next
senses.ex: One failed bank set off a cascade of withdrawals that soon threatened the entire regional financial system.

senses.def: fall or flow downward in large amounts
senses.ex: Long curtains of ivy cascaded down the brick wall and pooled on the courtyard stones below.

origin: Borrowed from Portuguese or Spanish casta, meaning "lineage" or "breed." Its deeper origin is disputed.

senses.def: hereditary social group that shapes a person's status, especially in South Asia
senses.ex: The historian explained how caste shaped access to schooling and marriage in the region.

senses.def: rigid social group whose members have a shared rank or occupation
senses.ex: The novel depicts a ruling caste insulated from the hardships of ordinary citizens.

senses.def: system of dividing people into hereditary social groups
senses.ex: The new constitution sought to end discrimination rooted in caste.

syn: social class, hereditary class, social rank

origin: From Medieval Latin castellatus, meaning "fortified like a castle," ultimately from castellum, "castle." Its battlemented shape is the clue.

senses.def: shaped like a castle, especially with battlements along the top
senses.ex: A castellated tower rose above the station, though no soldiers had ever guarded it.

origin: From Latin "castigare", to correct or punish, from "castus", pure. It shares its root with "chastise" and "chasten".

senses.def: criticize or reprimand someone severely, often in public
senses.ex: The editorial castigated the city council for approving the stadium deal without a public hearing.

origin: From Latin "castigatio", correction or punishment, from "castigare", to correct, from "castus", pure.

senses.def: severe criticism or punishment
senses.ex: The athlete's angry tweets drew a sharp castigation from the league commissioner.

origin: From French casuiste, ultimately from Latin casus, meaning "case." A casuist reasons from individual cases, especially moral ones.

senses.def: person who uses subtle arguments to justify questionable behavior
senses.ex: The manager sounded like a casuist when he claimed that hiding the report was technically honest.

senses.def: person who resolves moral dilemmas by applying principles to particular cases
senses.ex: The hospital consulted a casuist about whether the unusual treatment respected the patient's wishes.

origin: From casuist, ultimately based on Latin casus, meaning "case." It names reasoning through particular moral cases, sometimes too cleverly.

senses.def: clever but strained reasoning used to defend dubious conduct
senses.ex: Her elaborate casuistry could not excuse taking credit for a colleague's work.

senses.def: method of resolving moral questions by examining particular cases
senses.ex: The ethics seminar used casuistry to weigh conflicting duties in a difficult medical decision.

origin: From Greek katakhresis, meaning "misuse," through Latin. The original idea survives in calling a strained expression a misuse of language.

senses.def: misuse of a word or an unusually strained figure of speech
senses.ex: The editor called the phrase a catachresis because its metaphor joined ideas that did not fit.

origin: From Greek "kataklusmos", deluge, from "kata", down, and "kluzein", to wash, so a cataclysm first meant a great flood.

senses.def: sudden, violent event that causes great destruction or upheaval
senses.ex: Historians describe the First World War as a cataclysm that toppled empires across Europe.

origin: From "cataclysm", from Greek "kataklusmos", a great flood, plus "-ic".

senses.def: violently destructive and causing sweeping change
senses.ex: The volcano's cataclysmic eruption buried the ancient town under several meters of ash.

origin: From French catafalque, from Italian catafalco, a funeral platform. Its deeper roots may involve a word for scaffolding.

senses.def: raised platform supporting a coffin during a funeral or public viewing
senses.ex: The casket rested on a flower covered catafalque while mourners filed silently through the hall.

origin: From "catalysis", from Greek "katalusis", dissolving, from "kata", down, and "luein", to loosen.

senses.def: person or event that triggers or speeds up change
senses.ex: A single student's petition became the catalyst for a district-wide ban on plastic lunch trays.

senses.def: substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up
senses.ex: Platinum acts as a catalyst in a car's exhaust system, turning toxic gases into safer ones.

origin: From Greek katapeltes through Latin and French. The Greek parts mean "against" and "swing or throw," recalling a missile launcher.

senses.def: device that hurls objects through the air with sudden force
senses.ex: The museum displayed a wooden catapult that had once launched stones over city walls.

senses.def: hurl or propel something suddenly and forcefully
senses.ex: The collision catapulted the loose suitcase across the train compartment.

senses.def: raise someone or something rapidly to a new level of success
senses.ex: A viral performance catapulted the unknown singer into national attention within a week.

origin: From cat and call, first describing a cry like a cat's yowl. It later came to mean shouted remarks and whistles.

senses.def: unwanted sexual remark or whistle directed at someone in public
senses.ex: A catcall from the passing car made the pedestrian quicken her pace toward the crowded store.

senses.def: shout or whistle expressing public disapproval of a performer or speaker
senses.ex: The speaker paused after a catcall from the back row interrupted her argument.

senses.def: shout or whistle at someone, often with sexual or mocking intent
senses.ex: Several fans catcalled the referee after he reversed the decision.

syn: wolf whistle, lewd remark, street taunt

origin: Formed in English from catch and all. The name suggests a container or category that catches everything left over.

senses.def: broad category or container for many unrelated things
senses.ex: The drawer became a catchall for spare batteries, postcards, and keys nobody recognized.

senses.def: covering many different cases without making fine distinctions
senses.ex: The committee rejected the catchall rule because it treated minor errors like serious misconduct.

origin: Formed from catch and penny. The image is of something flashy enough to catch a buyer's money quickly.

senses.def: made to sell quickly through cheap appeal rather than lasting quality
senses.ex: The critic dismissed the catchpenny thriller for its lurid cover and careless plot.

senses.def: cheap item or publication produced mainly to make quick money
senses.ex: The souvenir looked like a catchpenny, with bright paint already peeling from its handle.

origin: From Greek katecheo, meaning "teach by word of mouth," through Late Latin catechismus. The Greek verb joins ideas of "down" and "sound."

senses.def: set of questions and answers teaching religious beliefs, especially Christian ones
senses.ex: The children studied the catechism before meeting with the pastor on Sunday.

senses.def: series of questions and answers used to teach or test knowledge
senses.ex: The safety manual read like a catechism, with a fixed answer for every possible emergency.

syn: religious primer, doctrinal guide, instruction manual

origin: From Late Latin categoricus, meaning "relating to categories," plus the English ending "-al." The category sense remains in its analytical use.

senses.def: absolute and stated without any exceptions or qualifications
senses.ex: The director gave a categorical denial that the museum planned to sell its collection.

senses.def: relating to categories or the sorting of things into groups
senses.ex: The survey used categorical answers such as yes, no, and unsure.

origin: From Middle English "caterwrawen", from "cater", cat, plus "wrawen", to yowl, imitating the cries of cats at night.

senses.def: make a loud, harsh, wailing cry
senses.ex: Two alley cats caterwauled outside the window, and nobody in the apartment could sleep.

senses.def: loud, harsh, wailing cry
senses.ex: The singer hit a high note that sounded more like a caterwaul than music.

origin: From "caterwaul", from Middle English "cater", cat, plus "wrawen", to yowl, so it names a sound like cats crying at night.

senses.def: shrill, harsh wailing or howling
senses.ex: The baby's caterwauling filled the airplane cabin for most of the six-hour flight.

origin: From Greek katharsis, meaning "cleansing" or "purging," from a verb meaning "cleanse." The emotional sense treats relief as a kind of cleansing.

senses.def: release of strong emotions that brings a sense of relief or renewal
senses.ex: Writing about the accident gave Maya a catharsis she had not found in conversation.

origin: From Greek "kathartikos", cleansing, from "kathairein", to purify, from "katharos", pure.

senses.def: giving emotional relief by releasing strong or pent-up feelings
senses.ex: After the funeral, looking through old photo albums together proved cathartic for the whole family.

origin: From Greek "katholikos", universal, from "kata", according to, and "holos", whole.

senses.def: broad and wide-ranging, including many kinds of things
senses.ex: Her catholic reading habits took her from ancient philosophy to comic books in a single afternoon.

origin: The word arose in colonial American politics, but its ultimate origin is uncertain. Suggested links to Indigenous languages remain unproven.

senses.def: meeting of political party members to choose candidates or decide policy
senses.ex: At the caucus, party members debated the proposal before selecting their preferred candidate.

senses.def: group of lawmakers or party members united by shared political interests
senses.ex: The rural caucus pressed the legislature to protect funding for small schools.

senses.def: meet as members of a political group to plan or make decisions
senses.ex: The delegates caucused privately before announcing their position on the bill.

syn: party meeting, political assembly, party gathering

origin: From Late Latin "causalis", from Latin "causa", cause. Do not confuse it with "casual".

senses.def: relating to or acting as a cause
senses.ex: Researchers found a causal link between the new fertilizer and the algae blooms in the lake.

origin: From Latin causa, meaning "cause," through causalis, "causal," with the ending "-ity." It names the connection between cause and effect.

senses.def: relationship in which one event or condition produces another
senses.ex: The study found a link between sleep and memory, but its design could not establish causality.

syn: cause and effect, causal connection, causal relationship

origin: From Greek "kaustikos", burning, from "kaustos", burnt, so a caustic remark burns like acid.

senses.def: sarcastic in a bitter, scathing way
senses.ex: Her caustic comments about his singing finally convinced him to drop out of the talent show.

senses.def: able to burn or corrode living tissue by chemical action
senses.ex: Wear gloves when using the drain cleaner, because it is caustic enough to burn skin.

origin: From Greek kauter, meaning "branding iron," from a verb meaning "burn," through Latin and French. The root recalls sealing tissue with heat.

senses.def: burn tissue deliberately to seal a wound or stop bleeding
senses.ex: The surgeon used a heated instrument to cauterize the small blood vessel.

origin: From French cavalcade, from Italian cavalcata, a ride on horseback. Behind it lies Latin caballus, meaning "horse."

senses.def: procession of riders, vehicles, or people traveling together
senses.ex: A cavalcade of motorcycles escorted the veterans through the town square.

senses.def: long or striking series of events, things, or people
senses.ex: The documentary offered a cavalcade of failed inventions before revealing the design that worked.

origin: From Middle French "cavalier", horseman, from Late Latin "caballarius", from "caballus", horse. The swagger of gallant horsemen led to its sense of offhand disregard.

senses.def: showing arrogant or careless disregard for others, rules, or risks
senses.ex: His cavalier attitude toward deadlines left his teammates finishing the group project without him.

origin: From Old French "caviller", to mock, from Latin "cavillari", to jeer or quibble, from "cavilla", jeering.

senses.def: raise petty or unnecessary objections
senses.ex: Some readers caviled at the novel's minor historical errors instead of enjoying its story.

senses.def: petty or trivial objection
senses.ex: My only cavil about the hotel was the slow elevator, since everything else was perfect.

syn: quibble, carp, nitpick, niggle, split hairs

origin: Probably an American alteration of vault, meaning "jump," first used of horses. A link to curvet, another horse's leap, is also proposed.

senses.def: move or play about in a lively, carefree way
senses.ex: After the rain stopped, the children cavorted through puddles across the empty playground.

senses.def: behave exuberantly or flirtatiously, often with a hint of disapproval
senses.ex: The tabloid printed photos of the actor cavorting with friends at a beach party.

origin: From French "céder", from Latin "cedere", to yield or go away, the same root found in "concede", "recede", and "secede".

senses.def: give up power, territory, or a right, often unwillingly
senses.ex: After the long chess match, the champion finally ceded her title to a seventeen-year-old challenger.

syn: surrender, relinquish, yield, hand over, concede

origin: From Latin "celeritas", swiftness, from "celer", swift, the same root as "accelerate".

senses.def: swiftness of movement or action
senses.ex: The rescue team moved with such celerity that the stranded climbers were safe before nightfall.

origin: From Old French, from Latin "caelestis", heavenly, from "caelum", sky or heaven.

senses.def: relating to the sky or outer space, as studied in astronomy
senses.ex: The sailors once steered by celestial bodies, fixing their position from the angle of a single bright star.

senses.def: heavenly or divine, or so beautiful it seems not of this world
senses.ex: When the choir reached the final chord, the sound in the old chapel felt almost celestial.

origin: From Latin "caelebs", unmarried or single, so the word first meant someone who stays unwed.

senses.def: abstaining from marriage and sexual relations, often because of a religious vow
senses.ex: The monks remained celibate for life, devoting the time a family would take to prayer and work.

senses.def: person who abstains from marriage and sexual relations
senses.ex: As a lifelong celibate, the elderly priest spoke about loneliness with unusual honesty in his sermon.

origin: From Old French, from Latin "cenaculum", dining room, from "cena", dinner, so a small group gathered around one table.

senses.def: small, close group of writers, artists or thinkers who meet and share ideas
senses.ex: The young poets formed a cenacle that met every Thursday in a cramped apartment above a bakery.

senses.def: the upper room where Jesus and his disciples held the Last Supper
senses.ex: Pilgrims in Jerusalem climb a narrow stair to visit the room traditionally identified as the Cenacle.

origin: From French, from Greek "kenos", empty, and "taphos", tomb: a tomb with no body in it.

senses.def: monument honoring people who are buried elsewhere, especially soldiers killed in war
senses.ex: Every November the town lays wreaths at the cenotaph for the soldiers who never came home from the front.

origin: From Latin "censor", the Roman magistrate who took the census and judged public morals, from "censere", to assess or judge.

senses.def: examine books, films, news, or messages and remove or suppress objectionable parts
senses.ex: The school board censored the student newspaper's article about the cafeteria inspection.

senses.def: official who examines media and suppresses what is considered objectionable
senses.ex: During the war, military censors read every soldier's letter before it was mailed home.

origin: From Latin "censorius", of a censor, severe. Roman censors judged citizens' morals and were known for harshness.

senses.def: severely critical and quick to find fault with others
senses.ex: Her censorious aunt commented on every guest's clothing, manners and choice of career before dessert arrived.

origin: From Latin "censura", the office or judgment of a Roman censor, from "censere", to assess or judge.

senses.def: express severe, often formal disapproval of someone
senses.ex: The medical board censured the surgeon for operating without the patient's full consent.

senses.def: severe, formal expression of disapproval
senses.ex: The senator's remarks earned a rare vote of censure from his own party.

origin: Coined in New Latin by Christiaan Huygens from Latin "centrum", center, and "fugere", to flee: fleeing the center.

senses.def: moving or directed outward, away from a center
senses.ex: As the merry-go-round spun faster, centrifugal force flung the loose hats of the riders into the grass.

senses.def: tending to split a group or system into separate, independent parts
senses.ex: Regional rivalries acted as centrifugal forces, slowly pulling the loose federation toward breakup.

origin: From French "centrifuge", from Latin "centrum", center, and "fugere", to flee, because spinning drives material away from the center.

senses.def: machine that spins rapidly to separate substances of different densities
senses.ex: The technician loaded the test tubes into a centrifuge to separate red blood cells from plasma.

senses.def: spin something in a centrifuge
senses.ex: The students centrifuged the pond water samples to collect the tiny algae at the bottom.

origin: Coined in New Latin by Isaac Newton from Latin "centrum", center, and "petere", to seek: seeking the center.

senses.def: moving or directed inward, toward a center
senses.ex: Centripetal force keeps the satellite curving around the planet instead of shooting off into space.

senses.def: tending to draw parts together toward a single center of power or unity
senses.ex: A shared enemy had a centripetal effect, uniting the quarreling provinces under one government.

origin: From French "cérébral", from Latin "cerebrum", brain, so cerebral things belong to the thinking mind.

senses.def: intellectual and analytical rather than emotional or physical
senses.ex: Chess fans love the game's cerebral drama, though casual viewers just see two people sitting still.

senses.def: relating to the brain
senses.ex: The scan showed reduced cerebral blood flow on the left side of the patient's brain.

origin: From Latin "cerebrum", brain, plus "-ation", so it names the brain at work.

senses.def: the act of thinking, especially careful or deep thought
senses.ex: After hours of solitary cerebration, the mathematician finally saw why her proof had kept failing.

origin: From French or Latin "caerimoniosus", from "caerimonia", sacred rite or ceremony.

senses.def: marked by elaborate formality, ritual or pomp
senses.ex: The ambassador's arrival was ceremonious, with a band, a red carpet and a long exchange of gifts.

senses.def: excessively polite and formal in manner
senses.ex: The butler's ceremonious bows and formal phrases made the young guests giggle nervously.

origin: From French, from Late Latin "certitudo", from Latin "certus", sure or settled.

senses.def: complete confidence that something is true
senses.ex: He spoke with such certitude about the election result that nobody dared mention the uncounted ballots.

senses.def: something regarded as certain or beyond question
senses.ex: The war swept away the old certitudes that her parents had built their lives upon.

origin: From French, from Latin "cessatio", a stopping, from "cessare", to stop or delay. Compare "cease".

senses.def: the ending or stopping of something, whether for a time or for good
senses.ex: The cessation of fighting along the border allowed aid trucks to reach the starving villages at last.

origin: From French, from Latin "cessio", a yielding, from "cedere", to yield. Compare "cede".

senses.def: formal giving up of territory, rights or property, especially by one state to another
senses.ex: The treaty required the cession of two coastal provinces, a loss the defeated nation resented for generations.

origin: From Old French "chaufer", to warm, from Latin "calefacere", to make warm. Friction both heats and irritates.

senses.def: rub against something so as to make it sore or worn
senses.ex: The new hiking boots chafed his heels until both were raw and blistered by the second day.

senses.def: feel irritated or impatient because of a restriction
senses.ex: The ambitious junior lawyer chafed at the firm's rule that only partners could speak to clients.

senses.def: rub skin briskly to make it warm
senses.ex: Coming in from the blizzard, she chafed her numb hands in front of the stove.

origin: From Old English "ceaf", the husks of grain, a native Germanic word.

senses.def: dry husks and other inedible material separated from grain
senses.ex: Farmers once tossed the threshed wheat into the wind so the lighter chaff would blow away.

senses.def: worthless material mixed in with what is valuable
senses.ex: Editing the archive meant separating the few revealing letters from the chaff of routine receipts and memos.

senses.def: tease someone in a light, good-humored way
senses.ex: His teammates chaffed him all week about the own goal, but they bought him dinner afterward.

origin: From French "chagrin", sorrow or vexation. Its earlier origin is uncertain.

senses.def: annoyance or embarrassment at having failed or been humiliated
senses.ex: Much to his chagrin, the magician's rabbit hopped out of his sleeve before the trick began.

senses.def: make someone feel annoyed or embarrassed, usually as "be chagrined"
senses.ex: She was chagrined to learn that her rival had won the scholarship with a weaker essay.

origin: From Old French, from Latin "calix", cup, a word of uncertain earlier origin.

senses.def: large ornate cup with a stem, especially one holding wine in Christian Communion
senses.ex: The priest raised the silver chalice while the congregation knelt in silence.

origin: From Greek "khamaileon", from "khamai", on the ground, and "leon", lion: a "ground lion".

senses.def: person who changes opinions, behavior or appearance to suit each situation
senses.ex: A political chameleon, the senator sounded progressive in the cities and conservative in farm country.

senses.def: small lizard that can change the color of its skin
senses.ex: The chameleon slowly turned from bright green to a mottled brown as it crept along the branch.

origin: From Old French "champion", from Medieval Latin "campio", a fighter in a duel, through a Germanic word that goes back to Latin "campus", field.

senses.def: support or defend a cause or person publicly and vigorously
senses.ex: The young senator championed free school lunches long before the idea became popular.

senses.def: person or team that has won first place in a contest
senses.ex: The reigning spelling bee champion breezed through the first five rounds without hesitation.

senses.def: person who fights for or strongly supports a cause
senses.ex: Rachel Carson became a champion of the environment after writing about the dangers of pesticides.

origin: From "chap", jaw, and "fallen": a disappointed person's jaw drops.

senses.def: dejected and disheartened, especially after a disappointment
senses.ex: The chapfallen candidate thanked his few remaining volunteers and left the hall before the final count.

origin: From Old French "chapelain", from Medieval Latin "cappellanus", priest of a chapel, from "cappella", chapel.

senses.def: member of the clergy attached to an institution such as a hospital, school, prison or army unit
senses.ex: The hospital chaplain sat with the frightened family through the long night of surgery.

origin: From Greek "kharisma", gift of grace, from "kharis", grace or favor. Charisma is a gift that attracts people.

senses.def: compelling personal charm or presence that inspires devotion in others
senses.ex: Her charisma filled the gym, and within minutes the bored students were cheering every line of her speech.

origin: Borrowed from French "charivari", a noisy mock serenade. Its earlier origin is uncertain.

senses.def: noisy mock serenade with banging pots and pans, traditionally for a newly married couple
senses.ex: Neighbors gathered outside the newlyweds' cabin for a charivari, clanging kettles until the couple came out with cider.

senses.def: loud, confused noise or din
senses.ex: The charivari of car horns, sirens and street vendors made it impossible to hear the phone call.

origin: From Italian "ciarlatano", a quack, a blend of "ciarlatore", chatterer, and "cerretano", a person from Cerreto, a village known for its quacks.

senses.def: person who falsely claims special knowledge or skill, especially to make money
senses.ex: The charlatan sold "miracle" bracelets that he claimed could cure arthritis and improve memory.

syn: fraud, quack, impostor, mountebank, con artist

origin: From Old French, from Late Latin "carnale", graveyard, from Latin "carnalis", of the flesh.

senses.def: building or vault where bones or bodies of the dead are kept, also called a charnel house
senses.ex: Beneath the abbey lay a charnel stacked with skulls from centuries of village burials.

senses.def: suggesting death and decay, ghastly
senses.ex: A charnel stench drifted from the abandoned slaughterhouse and hung over the whole street.

origin: From Old English "ċeariġ", careful, anxious, or sorrowful. It is related to "care", so a chary person is full of caution.

senses.def: cautious and wary, reluctant to give or risk something
senses.ex: Burned by a bad roommate before, she was chary of signing a lease with someone she had just met.

origin: From Latin "chasma", from Greek "khasma", a yawning gap or abyss.

senses.def: deep, steep-sided crack or opening in the earth
senses.ex: The rope bridge swayed over a chasm so deep that the river below looked like a silver thread.

senses.def: profound difference between people, groups or views
senses.ex: A chasm of mistrust had opened between the union and management after the secret layoffs.

origin: From Old French "chaste", morally pure, from Latin "castus", pure.

senses.def: abstaining from sex outside marriage, or from sex altogether
senses.ex: Members of the order promised to remain chaste, poor and obedient for the rest of their lives.

senses.def: modest and without sexual suggestion
senses.ex: The old film ended with nothing more than a chaste kiss on the cheek at the train station.

senses.def: simple and restrained in style, without ornament
senses.ex: The architect favored chaste white walls and plain oak floors over carving and gilt.

origin: From Old French "chastier", to punish, from Latin "castigare", to correct. It is related to "chastise", "castigate", and "chaste".

senses.def: make someone humbler or more restrained, especially after a failure or punishment
senses.ex: Chastened by his poor midterm grade, he started going to the professor's office hours every week.

origin: From Old French "chastier", to punish, from Latin "castigare", to correct, the same source as "chasten" and "castigate".

senses.def: scold or criticize someone severely
senses.ex: The coach chastised the players for skipping practice the day before the final.

origin: From Old French "chastiement", from "chastier", to punish, from Latin "castigare", to correct, related to "castus", pure.

senses.def: severe scolding or punishment meant to correct someone
senses.ex: After the public chastisement from the coach, the players never showed up late to practice again.

origin: From French, present participle of "chatoyer", to shine like a cat's eye, from "chat", cat.

senses.def: having a changeable, silky luster that shifts as it moves, like a cat's eye
senses.ex: The jeweler tilted the polished tiger's eye so its chatoyant band of light rippled across the stone.

origin: From Old French "chatel", property, from Medieval Latin "capitale", from Latin "caput", head. The word "cattle" comes from the same source.

senses.def: personal possession that can be moved, as opposed to land or buildings
senses.ex: Under the will, the farm went to the eldest son while the furniture and other chattels were divided among the daughters.

senses.def: person treated as property, especially an enslaved person
senses.ex: Abolitionists argued that no human being could rightfully be bought and sold as a chattel.

origin: Named after Nicolas Chauvin, a legendary French soldier whose fanatical devotion to Napoleon made his name a byword for blind patriotism.

senses.def: prejudiced belief that one's own group or sex is superior, especially men over women
senses.ex: She quit the firm after years of chauvinism, including being asked to take notes at every meeting.

senses.def: excessive, aggressive patriotism and contempt for other nations
senses.ex: The dictator's speeches stirred up a national chauvinism that made neighboring countries nervous.

origin: From "chauvinism", named after Nicolas Chauvin, a legendary French soldier famous for his blind devotion to Napoleon.

senses.def: person who believes their own group or sex is superior to others
senses.ex: The old chauvinist insisted that women could not be good pilots, despite the captain standing beside him.

senses.def: showing prejudiced belief in the superiority of one's own group or sex
senses.ex: The club finally dropped its chauvinist rule that barred women from the main dining room.

origin: From "chauvinist" plus "-ic", after Nicolas Chauvin, a legendary French soldier blindly devoted to Napoleon.

senses.def: showing prejudiced belief in the superiority of one's own group, nation, or sex
senses.ex: The commentator's chauvinistic remarks about the women's team drew complaints from viewers.

origin: From Old French "eschec", check in chess, from Arabic and Persian "shāh", king. Stopping the king in chess gave the sense of restraint.

senses.def: stop, slow, or hold back the progress of something
senses.ex: Firefighters cut a wide trench to check the spread of the wildfire toward the town.

senses.def: something that restrains or limits, a control
senses.ex: A free press acts as a check on officials who might otherwise abuse their power.

senses.def: examine something to make sure it is correct, safe, or working
senses.ex: Always check the tire pressure before driving long distances in the summer heat.

senses.def: written order telling a bank to pay money from an account
senses.ex: Her grandmother still mails her a birthday check every year, even though she could send money online.

syn: restrain, curb, halt, rein in, arrest

origin: From "checker", a chessboard pattern, from Old French "eschequier", chessboard, so a checkered past alternates between light and dark patches.

senses.def: marked by alternating success and failure or by shady episodes
senses.ex: The used car dealer had a checkered history, including two lawsuits and a brief stint in jail.

senses.def: patterned with squares of alternating colors
senses.ex: A red and white checkered tablecloth covered the picnic table in the park.

origin: From "cheek", in the sense of bold, insolent talk, plus "-y".

senses.def: impudent or disrespectful, often in an amusing or endearing way
senses.ex: The cheeky toddler grinned, licked the frosting off the cake, and then pointed at his older sister.

origin: From Old French "cherir", to hold dear, from "cher", dear, from Latin "carus", beloved.

senses.def: hold someone or something dear and protect it lovingly
senses.ex: He cherishes the battered guitar his father played on their road trips across the country.

senses.def: keep a hope, memory, or belief firmly in mind
senses.ex: The exiled writer cherished the hope of one day returning to her hometown.

syn: treasure, value, prize, hold dear, adore

origin: From Italian "chiaro", clear or bright, and "oscuro", dark: light-dark.

senses.def: strong contrast between light and dark used in art to model shapes and create drama
senses.ex: Caravaggio's chiaroscuro makes his figures leap out of black backgrounds as if lit by a single torch.

senses.def: interplay of contrasting qualities, such as light and gloom, in a scene or work
senses.ex: The novel's chiaroscuro of tender family scenes and brutal violence keeps readers off balance.

origin: From Greek "khiasmos", a crossing, from "khiazein", to mark with the letter chi (X), since the phrases cross over.

senses.def: figure of speech in which the second phrase reverses the order of terms in the first
senses.ex: The speechwriter loved chiasmus, as in "we do not live to eat, we eat to live."

origin: From French "chicanerie", trickery, from "chicaner", to quibble, which French borrowed from a Low German verb meaning "to arrange".

senses.def: use of clever trickery to deceive or gain an advantage
senses.ex: The accountant's chicanery, hiding losses in fake companies, fooled investors for nearly a decade.

syn: trickery, deception, subterfuge, skulduggery, sharp practice

origin: From Old English "cīdan", to rebuke, quarrel, or complain.

senses.def: scold or rebuke someone, usually mildly
senses.ex: Her grandmother chided her for wearing sandals in the snow, then handed her a pair of warm socks.

origin: From Greek "Khimaira", a fire-breathing monster of myth with a lion's head, a goat's body, and a serpent's tail. The Greek word meant "she-goat".

senses.def: hope, plan, or idea that is impossible or exists only in the imagination
senses.ex: For the struggling band, a record deal had become a chimera they chased for ten years without success.

senses.def: in Greek myth, a fire-breathing monster made of a lion, a goat, and a serpent
senses.ex: The hero Bellerophon rode the winged horse Pegasus to slay the Chimera.

senses.def: living thing that contains cells with two or more different sets of genes
senses.ex: Scientists created a mouse chimera by injecting cells from one embryo into another.

syn: illusion, fantasy, delusion, pipe dream, mirage

origin: From "chimera", from Greek "khimaira", she-goat, the name of a mythical fire-breathing monster made of mismatched animal parts.

senses.def: existing only in the imagination, wildly fanciful or unrealistic
senses.ex: The founder's chimerical plan to build a city on floating platforms never got past the first investor meeting.

origin: From Old Northern French "chisel", from Late Latin "cisorium", cutting tool, from Latin "caedere", to cut. The word "scissors" shares the source.

senses.def: tool with a flat sharp blade, struck or pushed to cut and shape wood, stone or metal
senses.ex: The carpenter tapped the chisel with a mallet to square the corners of the hinge recess.

senses.def: cut or shape something with a chisel, or carve it as if with one
senses.ex: Over three years the sculptor chiseled the block of marble into a kneeling figure.

origin: From Old French "chevalerous", from "chevalier", knight, from "cheval", horse, so chivalry was the code of honor of mounted knights.

senses.def: courteous, gallant, and considerate, especially toward those who need help
senses.ex: In a chivalrous gesture, the team captain carried the injured opponent's bag off the field.

origin: From Old French "colere", bile or anger, from Greek "khole", bile. Yellow bile was once thought to cause anger.

senses.def: anger or irritability, especially a hot temper
senses.ex: The colonel's choler rose with every delay until he was shouting at the station clerk.

origin: From Old French "colerique", from Greek "kholē", bile. Medieval doctors believed too much yellow bile made people quick to anger.

senses.def: easily angered and quick to lose one's temper
senses.ex: The choleric referee handed out three yellow cards in the first ten minutes of the match.

origin: From French, from Greek "khoreia", dance, and "-graphia", writing: the writing down of dance.

senses.def: art of designing dance movements, or the sequence of steps in a particular work
senses.ex: The choreography for the new ballet asks the dancers to move in silence for the first five minutes.

senses.def: careful planning and coordination of a complex event or series of actions
senses.ex: The summit's choreography was precise, down to which leader would step out of the car first.

origin: Coined by Lewis Carroll in "Through the Looking-Glass" (1871), probably as a blend of "chuckle" and "snort".

senses.def: laugh in a loud, gleeful, chuckling way
senses.ex: The kids chortled as their father tried to assemble the tent and got tangled in the poles.

senses.def: loud, gleeful chuckle, like a laugh mixed with a snort
senses.ex: She let out a chortle when she read the absurd excuse her brother had written for his teacher.

origin: From Greek "khrestomatheia", from "khrestos", useful, and "manthanein", to learn: a book of useful learning.

senses.def: collection of selected passages from one or more authors, especially for learning a language
senses.ex: Her Greek teacher assigned a chrestomathy of short passages from Herodotus, Plato and the poets.

origin: From French, from Latin "chronicus", from Greek "khronikos", of time, from "khronos", time. A chronic problem lasts through time.

senses.def: of an illness or condition, lasting a long time or constantly recurring
senses.ex: Years of chronic back pain made it hard for the mail carrier to finish her route.

senses.def: of a person, having a long-standing habit, inveterate
senses.ex: The chronic latecomer missed the opening of every meeting and blamed traffic each time.

senses.def: of a problem, persistent and difficult to end
senses.ex: The city has struggled with chronic housing shortages for more than two decades.

origin: From Anglo-Norman, from Latin "chronica", from Greek "khronikos", of time, from "khronos", time.

senses.def: factual account of events in the order they happened
senses.ex: A monk kept a chronicle of the abbey, noting floods, famines and visits from the king year by year.

senses.def: record or describe a series of events in detail
senses.ex: The documentary chronicles the team's long climb from last place to the national championship.

origin: From "chronology", from Greek "khronos", time, and "-logia", account or study.

senses.def: arranged in the order in which events happened
senses.ex: The documentary tells the singer's life in chronological order, from childhood to her final concert.

origin: From Greek "khthon", earth or ground, plus "-ic": belonging to what lies beneath the earth.

senses.def: relating to the underworld or to gods and spirits believed to dwell beneath the earth
senses.ex: The ancient Greeks poured offerings into pits in the ground for Hades and other chthonic gods.

senses.def: dark, primitive and elemental, like forces rising from deep below the surface
senses.ex: The critic heard something chthonic in the drumming, a primal force beneath the polished melody.

origin: From Old English "ceorl", a free peasant or common man. Scorn for rustics later turned it into a word for a boor.

senses.def: rude, surly or ill-mannered person
senses.ex: Only a churl would complain about the free dinner while the volunteers were still clearing the tables.

senses.def: in medieval England, a free peasant or commoner of the lowest rank
senses.ex: The history lecture explained how a churl owed labor and rent to his lord but was not a serf.

origin: From Old English "ċeorlisċ", from "ċeorl", a peasant or common man, so churlish manners were once thought typical of rough peasants.

senses.def: rude, mean-spirited, and ungracious
senses.ex: It seemed churlish to complain about the free concert just because the seats were on the grass.

origin: From Italian, from the name of the Roman orator Cicero, perhaps joking that tour guides talk as much as he did.

senses.def: guide who shows visitors around and explains the history and art of a place
senses.ex: Our cicerone in Florence knew a scandalous story about every fresco in the chapel.

origin: From "cinema" plus "-tic". "Cinema" comes from French "cinématographe", built on Greek "kinēma", movement.

senses.def: having the visual qualities, scale, or drama of a film
senses.ex: The video game's cinematic opening, with sweeping shots of a ruined city, felt like a blockbuster movie.

senses.def: relating to films or filmmaking
senses.ex: The festival celebrates the cinematic history of the city, where many silent films were shot.

origin: From Middle English "cifre", via Old French from Arabic "sifr", zero or empty, which explains its sense of a person who counts for nothing.

senses.def: secret system of writing that disguises a message by replacing or rearranging its letters
senses.ex: The spies passed notes in a simple cipher that shifted every letter three places along the alphabet.

senses.def: person or thing of no importance or influence
senses.ex: Overshadowed by his famous father, the young heir was treated as a cipher at every board meeting.

origin: From Latin "circuitus", a going around, from "circum", around, and "ire", to go.

senses.def: (of a route) long and winding rather than direct
senses.ex: Road closures forced the school bus to take a circuitous route that added half an hour to the trip.

senses.def: (of speech or reasoning) indirect and slow to reach the point
senses.ex: After a circuitous explanation about scheduling, the manager finally admitted the event was canceled.

origin: From Latin "circum", around, plus "ambire", to go around, so the word describes whatever surrounds you on every side.

senses.def: surrounding or enveloping something on all sides
senses.ex: The circumambient fog muffled every sound in the harbor, so the ferry crept forward almost by guesswork.

origin: From Latin "circumambulare", to walk around, from "circum", around, plus "ambulare", to walk, the same root as "amble" and "ambulance".

senses.def: walk all the way around something, often as part of a ritual
senses.ex: Pilgrims circumambulate the ancient shrine clockwise, murmuring prayers with each slow lap around its base.

syn: circle, walk around, go around, encircle

origin: From Latin "circumferentia", from "circum", around, plus "ferre", to carry, so it is the line carried all the way around a circle.

senses.def: distance around the edge of a circle or other rounded shape
senses.ex: To fence the circular garden, Maya measured its circumference and bought forty feet of wire to be safe.

senses.def: outer edge or boundary of an area
senses.ex: Guards patrolled the circumference of the camp all night, never stepping inside the ring of tents.

origin: From Latin "circumlocutio", from "circum", around, and "loqui", to speak, so it means talking around a subject.

senses.def: use of many words where fewer would do, especially to avoid saying something directly
senses.ex: Instead of admitting the project had failed, the report relied on circumlocution about "unexpected learning opportunities."

origin: From "circumlocution", from Latin "circum", around, plus "locutio", speaking, so circumlocutory talk goes around its point instead of straight to it.

senses.def: using far more words than needed, talking around the point instead of stating it
senses.ex: The CEO's circumlocutory apology lasted ten minutes without once admitting that the company had made a mistake.

origin: From Latin "circumnavigare", to sail around, from "circum", around, plus "navigare", to sail, from "navis", ship.

senses.def: sail or travel all the way around something, especially the earth
senses.ex: In 1522 the battered survivors of Magellan's fleet became the first crew to circumnavigate the globe.

senses.def: get past an obstacle or difficulty by going around it
senses.ex: The startup circumnavigated the strict office zoning rules by running its whole business from a houseboat.

syn: circle, go around, sail around, orbit

origin: From Latin "circumscribere", from "circum", around, and "scribere", to write or draw, so to circumscribe is to draw a line around something.

senses.def: restrict something within limits
senses.ex: The new rules circumscribe how much money a candidate can accept from a single donor.

senses.def: draw a line around something
senses.ex: The teacher asked us to circumscribe the island on the map with a red marker.

origin: Past participle of "circumscribe", from Latin "circum", around, and "scribere", to write or draw, as if a line were drawn around it.

senses.def: limited or restricted in scope or freedom
senses.ex: Without a car in the rural town, her social life was circumscribed by the bus schedule.

origin: From Latin "circumspectus", careful, from "circumspicere", to look around, from "circum", around, and "specere", to look.

senses.def: careful to consider all risks and consequences before acting or speaking
senses.ex: Knowing the reporters were listening, the coach was circumspect about the injured player's condition.

origin: From Latin "circumstantia", surroundings, from "circumstare", to stand around, so circumstantial things stand around the main fact rather than being it.

senses.def: pointing toward a conclusion by inference without directly proving it, usually said of evidence
senses.ex: With no witness and no confession, the prosecutor built her case on circumstantial evidence like phone records and muddy boots.

senses.def: full of small, precise details
senses.ex: Her circumstantial account of the trip included the price of every coffee and the color of each hotel bedspread.

senses.def: depending on surrounding conditions rather than on anything essential
senses.ex: The drop in sales was circumstantial, caused by a week of storms rather than any flaw in the product.

origin: From Latin "circumvenire", to surround or get around, from "circum", around, and "venire", to come.

senses.def: find a way around a rule, obstacle, or restriction, often cleverly
senses.ex: Some apps circumvent privacy settings by collecting location data through other permissions.

senses.def: go or travel around something that is in the way
senses.ex: The hikers circumvented the flooded valley by following a ridge trail to the north.

syn: bypass, evade, sidestep, get around, skirt

origin: Present tense of "circumvent", from Latin "circumvenire", to get around, from "circum", around, and "venire", to come.

senses.def: finds a way around a rule, obstacle, or restriction, often cleverly
senses.ex: The shipping company circumvents the tax by registering its boats in another country.

syn: bypasses, evades, sidesteps, gets around, skirts

origin: From French "citadelle", from Italian "cittadella", little city, a diminutive of "citta", city, from Latin "civitas".

senses.def: fortress on high ground that protects or commands a city
senses.ex: From the citadel on the hill, soldiers could watch every road leading into the walled town below.

senses.def: place or institution seen as the stronghold of a cause or way of life
senses.ex: For decades the old university was seen as a citadel of classical learning, resisting every educational fad.

origin: From French "clairvoyant", clear-sighted, from "clair", clear, and "voyant", seeing.

senses.def: person who claims to see the future or things beyond the normal senses
senses.ex: The police politely ignored the clairvoyant who called claiming she knew where the missing dog was.

senses.def: having or claiming the power to see the future or hidden things
senses.ex: Her clairvoyant grandmother supposedly predicted every family wedding years in advance.

senses.def: unusually perceptive about what will happen
senses.ex: His clairvoyant warnings about the housing bubble were ignored until prices collapsed.

origin: From Latin "clamans", crying out, from "clamare", to shout, the same root as "clamor" and "claim".

senses.def: demanding attention urgently; pressing
senses.ex: The flooded villages had a clamant need for clean water long before any official relief convoy arrived.

senses.def: noisy and insistent in making demands
senses.ex: The clamant crowd outside the stadium chanted for refunds after the headliner canceled an hour before the show.

origin: From Middle English "clambren", to climb or crawl, probably related to "clamb", an old past tense of "climb".

senses.def: climb or move awkwardly using both hands and feet
senses.ex: The kids clambered over the fallen tree trunk to reach the swimming hole.

senses.def: awkward, difficult climb using hands and feet
senses.ex: After a steep clamber up the rocks, we reached the lookout above the waterfall.

origin: From Old French "clamor", from Latin "clamor", a shout, from "clamare", to cry out, the same root as "claim" and "exclaim".

senses.def: loud, confused noise, especially of many voices
senses.ex: The clamor of the trading floor made it hard for the new broker to hear his own phone.

senses.def: strong public demand or protest
senses.ex: After the bridge collapse, the clamor for safety inspections reached the state capital.

senses.def: demand something loudly and insistently
senses.ex: Fans clamored for an encore, stamping their feet until the band returned to the stage.

origin: From "clamor", from Latin "clamor", a shout, plus "-ous".

senses.def: making a loud, confused noise
senses.ex: A clamorous flock of gulls fought over the scraps behind the fish market.

senses.def: loudly insistent in demanding something
senses.ex: Clamorous shareholders demanded that the board explain why profits had fallen so sharply.

origin: From Latin "clandestinus", secret or concealed, related to "clam", secretly.

senses.def: done secretly, often because it is illegal or forbidden
senses.ex: The resistance printed a clandestine newspaper in a cellar and passed it hand to hand.

origin: From Latin "clangor", a ringing sound, from "clangere", to resound, a word imitating the noise itself.

senses.def: loud, ringing, repeated clanging noise
senses.ex: The clangor of the church bells echoed across the valley on the morning of the festival.

origin: From "clangor", a ringing clang, from Latin "clangere", to resound, plus "-ous".

senses.def: making a loud, harsh, ringing sound
senses.ex: The clangorous fire alarm sent the whole dormitory stumbling outside at two in the morning.

origin: From French "claque", literally a slap or clap, because the first claques were groups hired to applaud at a theater.

senses.def: group of fawning admirers who applaud or agree with someone on cue
senses.ex: The senator arrived with a claque of aides who laughed loudly at every one of his weak jokes.

senses.def: group of people hired to applaud or cheer at a performance
senses.ex: Nineteenth-century Paris opera houses kept a paid claque to start the clapping at exactly the right moments.

origin: From Medieval Latin "clario", a trumpet, from Latin "clarus", clear, so a clarion call rings out loud and clear.

senses.def: loud, clear, and stirring
senses.ex: The coach's clarion voice cut through the rain, urging the exhausted team toward one final push.

senses.def: strong, clear call to action, usually in the phrase clarion call
senses.ex: The report served as a clarion call for cities to plant more trees before summers grow even hotter.

senses.def: shrill, narrow trumpet once used in war
senses.ex: The battle scene opens with a clarion blaring from the castle walls as the knights ride out.

origin: From Latin "claustrum", an enclosed place or cloister, from "claudere", to close, the root shared by "cloister" and "claustrophobia".

senses.def: secluded, shut in, or confining, like a cloister
senses.ex: After years in the city, she found the remote monastery's claustral silence both soothing and slightly unnerving.

senses.def: relating to a cloister or the life lived in one
senses.ex: The guide described the claustral routine of the nuns, from prayers before dawn to meals eaten in silence.

origin: From "claustrophobia", built from Latin "claustrum", enclosed place, plus Greek "phobos", fear, so it means afraid of being shut in.

senses.def: cramped or confining enough to make people feel trapped
senses.ex: The basement apartment felt claustrophobic, with low ceilings, one tiny window, and pipes running overhead.

senses.def: suffering from an intense fear of enclosed spaces
senses.ex: Being claustrophobic, Daniel always took the stairs rather than squeeze into the crowded office elevator.

origin: Two Old English verbs merged into one word: "clēofan", to split, and "clifian", to stick, so "cleave" can mean both to split apart and to cling.

senses.def: split or cut something apart, especially with a sharp blow
senses.ex: With one swing of the axe, he cleaved the frozen log cleanly in two.

senses.def: cling closely or stay faithful to someone or something, usually with "to"
senses.ex: Even after moving abroad, the family cleaved to the traditions of their home village.

senses.def: move forcefully through something, as if cutting it
senses.ex: The icebreaker cleaved a path through the frozen harbor so the cargo ships could follow.

origin: From Old English "geclyft", a split, related to "cleave", to split apart.

senses.def: split, crack, or V-shaped opening
senses.ex: A tiny pine had taken root in a cleft of the granite cliff, its roots gripping the bare rock.

senses.def: split or divided, as in a cleft chin or cleft palate
senses.ex: The actor's cleft chin became so famous that fans mailed him photos of their own dimpled chins.

origin: From Latin "clementia", mildness or mercy, from "clemens", gentle.

senses.def: mercy or leniency, especially toward someone being judged or punished
senses.ex: The judge showed clemency to the teenager, sentencing him to community service instead of jail.

senses.def: official pardon or reduction of a criminal sentence by a governor or president
senses.ex: Her lawyers filed a petition for clemency, asking the governor to commute her death sentence.

origin: From Latin "clemens", mild or merciful, the same root as "clemency".

senses.def: mild and pleasant, said of weather
senses.ex: The clement spring weather let the school hold graduation outdoors for the first time in years.

senses.def: merciful or lenient toward someone who has done wrong
senses.ex: The clement judge reduced the teenager's sentence to community service, noting his sincere remorse.

origin: Coined by the poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge from German "Clerisei", clergy, ultimately from Late Latin "clericus", clergyman, for a class of learned people.

senses.def: educated elite; intellectuals and opinion makers considered as a class
