senses.ex: The sound engineer adjusted dozens of sliders on the mixing console during the live concert.

origin: From Latin "consolidare", to make firm, from "con-", together, plus "solidus", solid.

senses.def: make a position, power, or success stronger and more secure
senses.ex: After winning the election, the new president moved quickly to consolidate her control over the party.

senses.def: combine several things into a single, more effective unit
senses.ex: The district plans to consolidate its three small rural schools into one modern campus.

origin: From Latin "consonantia", harmony, from "consonare", to sound together, from "con-", together, plus "sonare", to sound.

senses.def: agreement or harmony between ideas, actions, or things
senses.ex: The new school policy is in consonance with the principles the founders set out a century ago.

senses.def: repetition of consonant sounds with different vowels, especially in poetry
senses.ex: The poet pairs "blank" with "think" in the closing lines, using consonance where an exact rhyme would sound too neat.

senses.def: pleasing combination of musical tones sounded together
senses.ex: After the jarring chords of the middle section, the symphony settles into a warm, restful consonance.

origin: From Latin "consonans", sounding together, from "con-", with, plus "sonare", to sound, so consonant ideas are in harmony.

senses.def: in agreement or harmony with something
senses.ex: Cutting the arts budget is hardly consonant with the mayor's promise to support local culture.

senses.def: speech sound made by partly blocking the breath, or a letter that stands for it
senses.ex: The word "strengths" packs seven consonants around a single vowel.

syn: consistent, compatible, harmonious, congruent, in keeping

origin: From Latin "consors", partner or one who shares the same lot, from "con-", together, plus "sors", lot or fate.

senses.def: spouse or companion, especially the husband or wife of a reigning monarch
senses.ex: As the queen's consort, he attended every state dinner but held no constitutional power of his own.

senses.def: keep company with someone, often someone others disapprove of (said kun-SORT)
senses.ex: The senator was criticized for consorting with lobbyists at expensive weekend golf retreats.

origin: From Latin "conspicuus", visible or striking, from "conspicere", to catch sight of, from "con-" plus "specere", to look at.

senses.def: easy to see or notice, standing out clearly
senses.ex: In his bright orange jacket, the new student was conspicuous among the rows of navy uniforms.

senses.def: attracting attention because remarkable or unusual
senses.ex: The firefighter received a medal for conspicuous bravery during the warehouse rescue.

origin: From Latin "conspirare", to breathe together, from "con-", together, plus "spirare", to breathe, so plotters whisper close enough to share breath.

senses.def: plan secretly with others to do something harmful or illegal
senses.ex: The two clerks conspired to steal company funds by creating invoices from a fake supplier.

senses.def: of events, combine to produce an unfortunate or striking result
senses.ex: Rain, a flat tire, and a closed bridge conspired to make us miss the wedding ceremony.

origin: From Latin "consternatio", dismay or confusion, from "consternare", to throw into confusion or alarm.

senses.def: feeling of anxiety, alarm, or dismay, usually at something unexpected
senses.ex: To the consternation of the organizers, the keynote speaker canceled two hours before the conference began.

origin: From Latin "constituens", present participle of "constituere", to set up or establish, from "com-", together, plus "statuere", to set or place.

senses.def: voter or resident in an area represented by an elected official
senses.ex: The senator held a town meeting so her constituents could ask questions about the new highway.

senses.def: one of the parts that make up a whole
senses.ex: Nitrogen is the main constituent of the air we breathe, making up about seventy-eight percent of it.

senses.def: forming part of a whole
senses.ex: The federation's constituent states each kept their own courts and police forces.

origin: From Old French "constreinte", from "constreindre", to constrain, from Latin "constringere", to bind tightly, from "con-" plus "stringere", to draw tight.

senses.def: something that limits or restricts what one can do
senses.ex: Budget constraints forced the theater company to stage the play with only four actors and one set.

senses.def: holding back of one's natural feelings or behavior
senses.ex: At first the cousins spoke with constraint, but by dessert they were laughing like old friends.

origin: From Latin "constrictus", past participle of "constringere", to draw or bind together, from "con-" plus "stringere", to draw tight.

senses.def: make or become narrower or tighter, often by squeezing
senses.ex: Cold air can constrict the airways of people with asthma, making it harder to breathe.

senses.def: limit the freedom or development of something
senses.ex: Strict zoning rules constricted the town's growth for decades, keeping new shops and houses out of its historic center.

origin: From Latin "construere", to pile together or build, used in Late Latin to mean to analyze a sentence grammatically.

senses.def: interpret or understand something in a particular way
senses.ex: His silence at the meeting was construed as agreement, although he actually opposed the plan.

origin: From Latin "consummatus", past participle of "consummare", to sum up or finish, from "con-", together, plus "summa", sum.

senses.def: showing great skill and flair, supremely accomplished
senses.ex: A consummate diplomat, she calmed both angry delegations without either side feeling it had lost.

senses.def: complete or perfect in every way, sometimes in a bad sense
senses.ex: The forger was a consummate liar who fooled museum experts for twenty years.

senses.def: complete or finalize something, such as a deal or marriage (said KAHN-suh-mayt)
senses.ex: The two companies consummated the merger after a year of negotiations and government review.

origin: From Latin "consumptio", from "consumere", to use up, from "con-", completely, plus "sumere", to take.

senses.def: using up of a resource such as energy, water, or goods
senses.ex: The new refrigerators cut household electricity consumption by nearly a third.

senses.def: eating or drinking of something
senses.ex: The sign at the pond warns that the fish are not safe for human consumption.

senses.def: old-fashioned name for tuberculosis, a wasting disease of the lungs
senses.ex: In many nineteenth-century novels, a pale young heroine slowly dies of consumption.

origin: From Latin "contagio", a touching or contact, related to "contingere", to touch closely, built on "tangere", to touch.

senses.def: spread of disease from one person to another by close contact
senses.ex: Nurses wore gowns and masks to limit contagion in the crowded children's ward during flu season.

senses.def: harmful spread of an idea, feeling, or problem from one group to another
senses.ex: Economists feared that the bank's collapse would set off a financial contagion across neighboring markets.

origin: From Latin "contaminare", to bring into contact, mix, or defile, probably related to "tangere", to touch.

senses.def: make something impure or unsafe by adding a harmful substance
senses.ex: Runoff from the fertilizer plant contaminated the town's wells, and residents had to drink bottled water for months.

senses.def: corrupt or spoil something nonphysical, such as evidence or judgment
senses.ex: The defense argued that weeks of sensational news coverage had contaminated the entire jury pool.

origin: From Latin "contemnere", to scorn, from "con-", intensive, plus "temnere", to despise, and "contempt" comes from the same verb.

senses.def: treat or regard someone or something with scorn
senses.ex: The proud old aristocrat contemned anyone who earned money through trade.

origin: From Latin "contemporaneus", from "con-", with, plus "tempus", time, so it describes things that share the same time.

senses.def: existing or happening during the same period of time
senses.ex: Historians checked the soldier's diary against contemporaneous newspaper reports to confirm the dates of the battle.

origin: From Latin "contemptus", scorn, from "contemnere", to despise, from "con-", intensive, plus "temnere", to despise.

senses.def: feeling that someone or something is worthless and deserves scorn
senses.ex: The critic made no effort to hide his contempt for the lazy, predictable sequel.

senses.def: open disrespect for or disobedience of a court or lawmaking body
senses.ex: The reporter was held in contempt of court for refusing to name her source.

origin: From Latin "contemptus", scorn, plus the English suffix "-ous", full of.

senses.def: showing scorn or a total lack of respect
senses.ex: The champion gave a contemptuous laugh when the rookie challenged him to a rematch.

origin: From Latin "contendere", to stretch out or strive, from "com-", together, plus "tendere", to stretch.

senses.def: state or argue firmly that something is true
senses.ex: The defense contends that the security camera footage proves its client was elsewhere that night.

senses.def: compete with others to win or gain something
senses.ex: Four teams are still contending for the championship with two weeks left in the season.

senses.def: struggle to deal with a difficulty
senses.ex: Farmers in the valley must contend with drought one year and flooding the next.

origin: From Latin "contentiosus", quarrelsome, from "contentio", a struggle, from "contendere", to strive or contend.

senses.def: causing or likely to cause heated argument
senses.ex: Whether to close the old library branch remains a contentious issue on the city council.

senses.def: inclined to argue or quarrel
senses.ex: The contentious neighbor sued three people on his street over trees, fences, and parking.

origin: From "contextual" plus "-ize", and "context" comes from Latin "contextus", a joining together, from "contexere", to weave together.

senses.def: place something in its surrounding circumstances so it can be properly understood
senses.ex: The museum contextualizes each wartime poster with letters and photographs from the same year.

syn: situate, frame, place in context, put in perspective

origin: From Latin "contiguus", touching or bordering, from "contingere", to touch, built on "tangere", to touch.

senses.def: state of touching or lying next to something, closeness in space or time
senses.ex: The contiguity of the two farms made it easy for the families to share a single irrigation canal.

origin: From Latin "contiguus", touching, from "contingere", to touch, from "con-", together, plus "tangere", to touch.

senses.def: sharing a border or touching, next to each other
senses.ex: Alaska and Hawaii are not part of the contiguous United States, the forty-eight states that touch one another.

senses.def: next in order or sequence, without a break
senses.ex: The hard drive stores the file in contiguous blocks so it can be read quickly.

origin: From Latin "continentia", restraint, from "continere", to hold together or hold back, from "con-", together, plus "tenere", to hold.

senses.def: self-restraint, especially in sexual desire or other appetites
senses.ex: The monks practiced strict continence, eating sparingly, avoiding wine, and remaining celibate all their lives.

senses.def: ability to control the bladder and bowels
senses.ex: After the surgery, the nurse taught him exercises that would help him regain continence within a few weeks.

origin: From Latin "contingens", present participle of "contingere", to touch or befall, from "com-", together, plus "tangere", to touch.

senses.def: depending on something else that may or may not happen
senses.ex: Her admission to the program is contingent on passing the final chemistry exam.

senses.def: group of people forming part of a larger gathering or force
senses.ex: A large contingent of students from Brazil marched together at the opening ceremony.

senses.def: possible but not certain to occur, subject to chance
senses.ex: The insurance plan covers contingent expenses such as emergency travel and lost luggage.

origin: From Latin "contortio", a twisting, from "contorquere", to twist, built on "torquere", to twist, the root of "torque".

senses.def: twisting of something, especially the body, out of its normal shape
senses.ex: The acrobat's contortions, folding her legs behind her head, drew gasps from the circus audience.

senses.def: strained, twisted reasoning or effort used to reach a desired result
senses.ex: The company's legal contortions could not hide the plain fact that its product had failed safety tests.

origin: From Spanish "contrabanda" and Italian "contrabbando", from "contra", against, plus "bando", a ban or decree, so it means goods traded against the law.

senses.def: goods that are illegally imported, exported, or possessed
senses.ex: Guards searched every cell and found contraband ranging from cigarettes to a smuggled cell phone.

senses.def: forbidden by law to be imported, exported, or owned
senses.ex: Customs officers seized several crates of contraband ivory hidden beneath bags of coffee beans.

syn: smuggled goods, bootleg, black-market goods, illicit goods

origin: From Italian "contrappunto", counterpoint, from Medieval Latin "punctus contra punctum", note against note.

senses.def: using counterpoint, with two or more independent melodies played together
senses.ex: In the fugue's final pages, four contrapuntal lines weave around one another without ever colliding.

senses.def: built from contrasting strands that play against each other
senses.ex: The novel's contrapuntal structure alternates chapters between a grieving mother and the son she believes is dead.

origin: Plural of "contrary", from Latin "contrarius", opposite, from "contra", against.

senses.def: things or ideas that are completely opposite to each other
senses.ex: The poet loved to pair contraries such as fire and ice, joy and grief, youth and age.

origin: From Late Latin "contrarietas", from Latin "contrarius", opposite, from "contra", against.

senses.def: state of being opposed or contrary, a clash or inconsistency
senses.ex: The contrariety between the senator's speeches and her voting record finally cost her the union's endorsement.

origin: From Latin "contravenire", to come against, from "contra", against, plus "venire", to come.

senses.def: act against or violate a law, rule, or principle
senses.ex: Dumping the chemicals into the river clearly contravened the state's environmental laws.

senses.def: contradict or deny a statement or claim
senses.ex: New evidence from the excavation contravenes the long-held theory about when the city was founded.

origin: From French "contravention", from Medieval Latin "contravenire", to oppose, from Latin "contra", against, plus "venire", to come.

senses.def: act of breaking a law, rule, treaty, or agreement
senses.ex: Building the dock without a permit was a clear contravention of the county's shoreline protection rules.

origin: From French "contretemps", from "contre", against, plus "temps", time: something happening at the wrong moment, first a fencing term for an ill-timed thrust.

senses.def: minor dispute or disagreement
senses.ex: A brief contretemps over the seating chart nearly delayed the start of the wedding reception.

senses.def: unexpected and embarrassing mishap
senses.ex: The ambassador laughed off the contretemps when his microphone died halfway through the formal toast.

origin: From Latin "contritus", literally ground to pieces, from "conterere", to grind, from "con-" plus "terere", to rub, as if crushed by guilt.

senses.def: feeling or showing sincere regret for having done wrong
senses.ex: The contrite teenager offered to pay for the window he had broken with his baseball.

origin: From Latin "contritio", a grinding, from "conterere", to grind to pieces, so a heart crushed by guilt.

senses.def: sincere regret and sorrow for one's wrongdoing
senses.ex: The judge noted the defendant's obvious contrition and gave him community service instead of jail time.

origin: From Old French "controver", to invent or devise, from "trover", to find.

senses.def: plan or devise something cleverly, often with trickery
senses.ex: The prisoners contrived an escape plan that involved a laundry cart and a forged work order.

senses.def: manage to do something, often despite difficulty or by foolishness
senses.ex: Somehow he contrived to lose both his passport and his phone in the space of one afternoon.

origin: From Medieval Latin "controvertere", from Latin "contro-", against, plus "vertere", to turn, the same roots as "controversy".

senses.def: argue against or deny the truth of a claim
senses.ex: The defense called two engineers to controvert the prosecution's claim that the brakes had been tampered with.

origin: From Latin "contumax", stubborn or insolent, plus the English suffix "-ious".

senses.def: stubbornly disobedient to authority, especially to a court
senses.ex: The contumacious witness refused three direct orders from the judge to answer the question.

origin: From Latin "contumelia", insult, perhaps related to "tumere", to swell, as with pride or anger.

senses.def: scornful, insulting language or treatment
senses.ex: The young reformer endured the contumely of older party members, who mocked her proposals at every meeting.

origin: From Latin "contusio", from "contundere", to beat or bruise, built on "tundere", to beat.

senses.def: bruise, injury in which blood vessels break beneath unbroken skin
senses.ex: The X-ray showed no fracture, only a deep contusion on her shin from colliding with the goalpost.

origin: Origin unknown. It seems to have begun as a joking imitation of scholarly Latin, like "hocus-pocus".

senses.def: confusing and difficult problem or question
senses.ex: Deciding whether to repair the old school or build a new one has become a costly conundrum for the town.

senses.def: riddle whose answer involves a pun or play on words
senses.ex: The magazine's back page featured a conundrum: what has keys but cannot open a single lock?

origin: Coined in 1915 by the Scottish planner Patrick Geddes from Latin "con-", together, plus "urbs", city: towns that have grown together into one.

senses.def: large urban area formed when growing cities and towns merge
senses.ex: The old mill towns along the river have spread into a single conurbation of nearly three million people.

syn: metropolis, megalopolis, metropolitan area, urban sprawl

origin: From Latin "convalescere", to grow strong, from "con-", intensive, plus "valescere", to grow strong, from "valere", to be well.

senses.def: recovering health and strength after an illness
senses.ex: The convalescent soldiers spent their afternoons reading and playing cards on the hospital's sunny porch.

senses.def: person who is recovering from an illness
senses.ex: The seaside home was built for convalescents who needed fresh air after long hospital stays.

origin: From Latin "convenire", to come together, from "con-", together, plus "venire", to come, which also gives "convention" and "convent".

senses.def: come together for a formal meeting
senses.ex: Delegates from forty nations will convene in Geneva next spring to revise the fishing treaty.

senses.def: call people together for a meeting
senses.ex: The principal convened an emergency meeting of teachers after the storm flooded the gym.

origin: From Latin "conventio", a meeting or agreement, from "convenire", to come together, from "con-", together, plus "venire", to come.

senses.def: way of behaving or doing something that is widely accepted as normal
senses.ex: By convention, the bride's family sits on the left side of the aisle at many weddings.

senses.def: large formal meeting of people with a shared interest or profession
senses.ex: Thousands of comic book fans packed the downtown convention center for the annual convention.

senses.def: formal agreement between countries
senses.ex: The Geneva Conventions set rules for the humane treatment of prisoners of war.

origin: From "convention" plus "-al", and "convention" comes from Latin "conventio", an agreement, from "convenire", to come together.

senses.def: following accepted customs and ideas, sometimes to the point of lacking originality
senses.ex: The critic praised the singer's voice but called her songs safe and conventional.

senses.def: of the usual or traditional kind rather than a newer one
senses.ex: The new hybrid car uses far less fuel than a conventional gasoline model.

senses.def: of weapons or war, not nuclear, chemical, or biological
senses.ex: Both nations agreed to reduce their conventional forces along the border.

origin: From Latin "convergere", from "con-", together, plus "vergere", to bend or turn, so lines that converge bend toward one point.

senses.def: come together from different directions toward a single point
senses.ex: Three highways converge just north of the city, which makes the morning traffic notoriously slow.

senses.def: become similar or come to share the same goal
senses.ex: The two parties' plans for health care began to converge after months of negotiation.

syn: meet, merge, unite, join, come together

origin: From Old French "conversant", present participle of "converser", to live among or associate with, from Latin "conversari", to keep company with.

senses.def: familiar with or knowledgeable about a subject
senses.ex: Any lawyer handling the case must be conversant with both American and Japanese patent law.

syn: familiar, knowledgeable, versed, acquainted, au fait

origin: The verb comes from Latin "conversari", to keep company with, while the noun meaning "opposite" comes from "conversus", turned around.

senses.def: talk informally with someone
senses.ex: On the long train ride, she conversed with an elderly farmer about the drought and the price of wheat.

senses.def: the opposite or reverse of a statement or situation (said KAHN-vurs)
senses.ex: Most fast talkers are nervous, but the converse is not true, since plenty of nervous people speak slowly.

senses.def: opposite or reversed in order or relation (said KAHN-vurs)
senses.ex: The two economists drew converse conclusions from exactly the same unemployment figures.

origin: From "converse", reversed, plus "-ly", and "converse" comes from Latin "conversus", turned around, from "convertere", to turn around.

senses.def: in the opposite way, with the relationship reversed
senses.ex: Warm air rises as it expands. Conversely, cool air sinks as it becomes denser.

syn: by contrast, on the other hand, inversely, oppositely

origin: From Latin "conversio", a turning around, from "convertere", to turn around, from "con-" plus "vertere", to turn.

senses.def: change from one form, use, or system to another
senses.ex: The conversion of the old mill into apartments took three years and kept its original brick walls.

senses.def: change of someone's religion, beliefs, or opinions
senses.ex: His conversion to vegetarianism came after he spent a summer working on a dairy farm.

senses.def: in rugby or football, extra points scored after a try or touchdown
senses.ex: The kicker missed the conversion, so the team led by only five points.

origin: From "convey", from Old French "conveier", to escort, from Latin "con-", together, plus "via", way, so to convey was first to go along the way with someone.

senses.def: act or means of carrying people or goods from place to place
senses.ex: Before the railroad arrived, the stagecoach was the only public conveyance between the two mining towns.

senses.def: legal transfer of property ownership, or the document that records it
senses.ex: The lawyer drew up the conveyance that transferred the farm from the elderly brothers to their niece.

senses.def: act of communicating an idea or feeling
senses.ex: For the director, the conveyance of grief through silence mattered more than any line of dialogue.

origin: From Latin "convivium", a feast, from "con-", together, plus "vivere", to live, so a convivial gathering is a shared, lively meal.

senses.def: friendly, lively, and enjoyable, especially with food and drink
senses.ex: The reunion dinner was so convivial that the restaurant had to ask the group to leave at midnight.

origin: From "convivial", from Latin "convivium", a feast, from "con-", together, plus "vivere", to live: living well together at the table.

senses.def: friendly, cheerful, festive enjoyment of good company
senses.ex: The conviviality of the neighborhood potluck, with its music and shared dishes, drew in even the shyest new residents.

origin: From Latin "convocatio", from "convocare", to call together, from "con-", together, plus "vocare", to call.

senses.def: large formal assembly, especially of a college or church
senses.ex: At the opening convocation, the university president welcomed nine hundred first-year students to campus.

senses.def: act of calling people together for a meeting
senses.ex: The king's convocation of parliament after eleven years without one surprised even his fiercest critics.

origin: From Latin "convocare", to call together, from "con-", together, plus "vocare", to call.

senses.def: formally call people together for a meeting or assembly
senses.ex: The king convoked parliament for the first time in eleven years to request money for the war.

origin: From "convolute" plus "-ed", from Latin "convolutus", rolled together, from "con-" plus "volvere", to roll.

senses.def: extremely complex and difficult to follow
senses.ex: The tax form's convoluted instructions sent many confused residents to the help desk.

senses.def: having many coils, twists, or folds
senses.ex: The surface of the human brain is convoluted, with deep folds that pack in more tissue.

origin: Of uncertain origin, first recorded in American English around 1919. Theories link it to Southern African American slang, but none is proven.

senses.def: informal: completely satisfactory, fine and in good order
senses.ex: After the mechanic replaced the belt, he slammed the hood shut and declared everything copacetic.

syn: fine, satisfactory, OK, in order, hunky-dory

origin: From Latin "copiosus", plentiful, from "copia", abundance, the same root found in "cornucopia".

senses.def: abundant in quantity, produced or supplied in large amounts
senses.ex: She took copious notes during the lecture, filling nearly twenty pages in an hour.

origin: From French "coquetterie", from "coquet", a flirt, literally a little rooster, from "coq", rooster, suggesting someone strutting to draw attention.

senses.def: flirtatious behavior meant to win admiration without serious intent
senses.ex: Her coquetry at the dinner party, all fluttering glances and teasing remarks, left two guests sure she was interested.

origin: From French "coquette", feminine of "coquet", a flirt, literally a little rooster, from "coq", rooster, picturing a strutting bird.

senses.def: woman who flirts playfully to win admiration without serious intent
senses.ex: In the comedy, the village coquette keeps three suitors hoping while secretly planning to marry none of them.

origin: From Medieval Latin "cordialis", of the heart, from Latin "cor", heart, so a cordial greeting comes from the heart.

senses.def: warm, friendly, and polite
senses.ex: Although the two candidates disagreed sharply, their conversation after the debate was cordial.

senses.def: sweet, concentrated fruit drink or liqueur
senses.ex: Grandmother served elderflower cordial mixed with sparkling water at the summer picnic.

origin: From "cordial", from Medieval Latin "cordialis", of the heart, from Latin "cor", heart, so cordiality is warmth that comes from the heart.

senses.def: warm, sincere, or politely friendly manner
senses.ex: Despite years of rivalry, the two coaches greeted each other with surprising cordiality at the awards banquet.

origin: From French "cordon", a small cord or ribbon, diminutive of "corde", cord.

senses.def: line of police, soldiers, or barriers surrounding an area to control access
senses.ex: A cordon of police officers kept reporters away from the building where the suspect was hiding.

senses.def: close off an area by surrounding it with guards or barriers
senses.ex: Firefighters cordoned off the street after a gas leak was reported in the bakery.

origin: From Latin "cornu copiae", horn of plenty, from "cornu", horn, plus "copia", abundance.

senses.def: abundant supply of good things
senses.ex: The farmers' market offers a cornucopia of fresh fruit, cheeses, breads, and honey every Saturday.

senses.def: goat's horn overflowing with fruit and grain, used as a symbol of plenty
senses.ex: A wicker cornucopia spilling gourds and apples sat at the center of the Thanksgiving table.

origin: From Late Latin "corollarium", money paid for a garland, hence a gift or extra, from "corolla", small garland, from "corona", crown.

senses.def: natural consequence or result that follows from something else
senses.ex: Higher rents were an almost inevitable corollary of the city's rapid job growth.

senses.def: in logic or math, a statement that follows easily from one already proved
senses.ex: Once the class proved the main theorem about triangles, the corollary about right angles took one line.

origin: From Old French "coronacion", from Latin "coronare", to crown, from "corona", crown or wreath.

senses.def: ceremony of crowning a king or queen
senses.ex: Thousands lined the streets of the capital to glimpse the new monarch's carriage on the morning of the coronation.

senses.def: formal confirmation of someone as leader or winner, often seen as a foregone conclusion
senses.ex: With no serious rival on the ballot, the party convention felt less like a contest than a coronation.

origin: From Latin "corporeus", bodily, from "corpus", body, the same root found in "corpse" and "corporation".

senses.def: having a physical body, material rather than spiritual
senses.ex: The medieval philosopher argued that the soul lives on long after its corporeal home has turned to dust.

origin: From Latin "corpulentus", fleshy or fat, from "corpus", body.

senses.def: large and fat in body
senses.ex: The corpulent innkeeper wheezed as he carried our heavy suitcases up the narrow stairs.

origin: From Latin "corpus", body, so a corpus is the whole "body" of an author's writings or of a collection of texts.

senses.def: complete collection of writings by one author or on one subject
senses.ex: Scholars spent decades editing the full corpus of the poet's letters, notebooks, and unfinished drafts.

senses.def: large body of texts gathered for studying language or training software
senses.ex: The linguists built a corpus of ten million words from online forums to track how slang spreads.

origin: From "cor-", together, plus "relate", so two things that correlate are related to each other.

senses.def: have a mutual relationship in which one thing changes along with another
senses.ex: Researchers found that hours of sleep correlate strongly with students' test scores.

senses.def: show or establish a connection between two or more things
senses.ex: The detective correlated the phone records with the security footage to build a timeline of the night.

origin: From Medieval Latin "corrigibilis", from Latin "corrigere", to correct or set right, from "con-", together, plus "regere", to guide or rule.

senses.def: capable of being corrected or reformed
senses.ex: The judge decided the teenage shoplifter was corrigible and sentenced him to community service instead of detention.

origin: From Latin "corroborare", to strengthen, from "con-", together, plus "roborare", to make strong, from "robur", strength.

senses.def: confirm or support a statement or theory with additional evidence
senses.ex: Two neighbors corroborated the woman's account, saying they also saw a blue van speed away.

origin: From Latin "corrodere", to gnaw to pieces, from "con-", thoroughly, plus "rodere", to gnaw, the root of "rodent".

senses.def: slowly wear away metal or stone by chemical action, such as rust
senses.ex: Salt spray from the ocean had corroded the iron railings until they crumbled at a touch.

senses.def: gradually weaken or destroy something, such as trust or morale
senses.ex: Years of broken promises corroded the voters' trust in the city council.

syn: erode, eat away, rust, wear away, consume

origin: From Late Latin "corrosio", from "corrodere", to gnaw away, from "con-", intensive, plus "rodere", to gnaw, the root of "rodent".

senses.def: gradual destruction of metal or other material by chemical action, such as rust
senses.ex: Years of salt spray caused severe corrosion on the pier's steel supports.

senses.def: gradual weakening or destruction of something
senses.ex: Critics warned that constant scandals were causing a slow corrosion of public trust in the courts.

syn: erosion, rust, deterioration, decay, wearing away

origin: From Old French "corrosif", from Latin "corrodere", to gnaw to pieces, built on "rodere", to gnaw.

senses.def: able to destroy or eat away material by chemical action
senses.ex: Students must wear goggles and gloves when handling corrosive acids in the chemistry lab.

senses.def: gradually harmful or destructive, especially to relationships or morale
senses.ex: The coach warned that locker-room gossip was more corrosive to the team than any losing streak.

origin: From "corrugate", from Latin "corrugare", to wrinkle, from "con-", together, plus "ruga", a wrinkle.

senses.def: shaped into a series of parallel ridges and grooves
senses.ex: The shed's corrugated tin roof rattled loudly whenever the afternoon rain began.

senses.def: wrinkled or furrowed, as a brow in thought or worry
senses.ex: His corrugated brow showed he was still struggling with the last proof on the exam.

origin: From Latin "coruscare", to flash, glitter, or quiver.

senses.def: give off flashes of light, sparkle
senses.ex: Sunlight coruscated across the lake as the wind broke its surface into a thousand ripples.

senses.def: show dazzling brilliance, especially of wit or skill
senses.ex: Her speech coruscated with wit, and even her opponents laughed at the jokes aimed at them.

origin: From Latin "corvinus", ravenlike, from "corvus", raven, the same root as the crow family name "Corvidae".

senses.def: of or like crows or ravens
senses.ex: The old professor had a corvine look, with his black coat, hunched shoulders, and sharp beak of a nose.

origin: From "Corybant", one of the priests of the goddess Cybele in ancient Phrygia, who worshipped her with wild, frenzied dancing.

senses.def: wildly frenzied and unrestrained, especially in dancing or celebration
senses.ex: When the final whistle blew, the fans poured onto the field in a corybantic celebration that lasted past midnight.

origin: From "cosmopolite", citizen of the world, from Greek "kosmos", world, plus "polites", citizen.

senses.def: including people and influences from many different countries
senses.ex: Singapore is a cosmopolitan city where you can hear Malay, Tamil, Mandarin, and English on one bus ride.

senses.def: familiar with many cultures and at ease anywhere in the world
senses.ex: Having lived in six countries, the cosmopolitan diplomat could chat comfortably with almost anyone.

senses.def: of a plant or animal, found in most parts of the world
senses.ex: The house sparrow is a cosmopolitan species found on every continent except Antarctica.

origin: Origin uncertain. It first meant a pet lamb raised by hand, perhaps from Old English "cotsaeta", cottager.

senses.def: care for and protect someone too much, pamper
senses.ex: The billionaire's children were cosseted by nannies, drivers, and private tutors from the day they were born.

origin: Past participle of "cosset", which first meant a pet lamb raised by hand. Its earlier origin is uncertain.

senses.def: pampered and protected, often too much
senses.ex: After a cosseted childhood, he found his first job in a busy restaurant kitchen a shock.

origin: From French "coterie", originally a group of peasants holding land together, related to "cot", a small cottage.

senses.def: small, exclusive group of people with shared interests
senses.ex: The director worked only with a small coterie of actors who had been with her since film school.

syn: clique, circle, set, inner circle, in-crowd

origin: From Latin "conterminus", sharing a boundary, from "con-", with, plus "terminus", boundary or end.

senses.def: having the same boundaries, or the same extent in space or time
senses.ex: The school district is coterminous with the county, so every county resident lives in the same district.

senses.def: sharing a boundary, touching at the edge
senses.ex: The two farms are coterminous along a stone wall that runs for half a mile.

origin: From Old French "contenance", bearing or demeanor, from "contenir", to hold or contain, from Latin "continere", to hold together.

senses.def: person's face or facial expression
senses.ex: The old judge's stern countenance softened into a smile when the child testified.

senses.def: tolerate, approve of, or allow something
senses.ex: The coach would not countenance players skipping practice, no matter how talented they were.

origin: Formed in the twentieth century from "counter-", against, plus "intuitive", from Latin "intueri", to look at or consider.

senses.def: contrary to what common sense or intuition would lead one to expect
senses.ex: It seems counterintuitive, but adding a new road can sometimes make a city's traffic worse.

origin: From Old French "contremander", from Medieval Latin "contramandare", from "contra", against, plus "mandare", to order.

senses.def: cancel an order, usually by giving a new one
senses.ex: The general countermanded the order to retreat once he learned that reinforcements were close.

origin: From Middle English "conterpart", a duplicate copy of a legal document, from "counter-", opposite or matching, plus "part".

senses.def: person or thing with the same role or function as another elsewhere
senses.ex: The French foreign minister flew to Tokyo to discuss the trade agreement with her Japanese counterpart.

senses.def: one of two things that complement or complete each other
senses.ex: The dry, salty cheese is the perfect counterpart to the sweet fig jam on the platter.

syn: equivalent, opposite number, peer, match, analogue

origin: From Medieval Latin "contrapunctum", from "contra", against, plus "punctum", point or note, so one written note set against another.

senses.def: contrasting element that balances or sets off something else
senses.ex: The novel's gentle humor provides a welcome counterpoint to its grim wartime setting.

senses.def: technique of combining two or more independent melodies played together
senses.ex: Bach's fugues are famous for their dazzling counterpoint, with several voices weaving around each other.

senses.def: contrast with or set off something else
senses.ex: In the film, cheerful pop songs counterpoint scenes of quiet suburban despair.

origin: From "counter-", against, plus "productive", from Latin "producere", to bring forth, from "pro-", forward, plus "ducere", to lead.

senses.def: having the opposite of the desired effect
senses.ex: Yelling at a nervous puppy is counterproductive, because it usually makes the puppy more afraid.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "countrevaloir", from Latin "contra valere", to be strong against.

senses.def: offset or counteract something with equal force or effect
senses.ex: Strong exports helped countervail the damage that rising oil prices had done to the economy.

origin: From French "coup", a blow or stroke, from Latin "colaphus", a blow with the fist. A coup is a sudden blow against a government.

senses.def: sudden, illegal seizure of government power, usually by the military
senses.ex: After the army staged a coup, tanks surrounded the presidential palace and the airports were closed.

senses.def: remarkably successful or clever move or achievement
senses.ex: Landing an interview with the reclusive author was a major coup for the student newspaper.

origin: From Old French "covenant", agreement, from Latin "convenire", to come together or agree, the same source as "convene".

senses.def: formal, solemn agreement or promise, often binding
senses.ex: The neighboring villages sealed a covenant never to fish each other's waters during spawning season.

senses.def: clause in a deed or contract that limits how property may be used
senses.ex: A covenant in the deed forbids owners from building any fence taller than four feet.

senses.def: agree or promise formally by a covenant
senses.ex: The two families covenanted to share the well and to repair it together whenever it failed.

origin: From Old French "covert", covered, past participle of "covrir", to cover. Despite the look, it is not formed from "overt".

senses.def: secret, hidden, or not openly acknowledged
senses.ex: The spy agency ran a covert operation to smuggle the scientist and her family out of the country.

senses.def: thicket or patch of dense undergrowth where animals hide
senses.ex: The fox slipped into the covert at the edge of the field, and the hounds lost its scent.

origin: From Old French "coveitier", from "coveitie", desire, probably from Latin "cupiditas", eager desire, the root of "cupidity".

senses.def: strongly desire something, especially something that belongs to someone else
senses.ex: For years the younger chef had coveted the head chef's position and his corner office overlooking the harbor.

syn: crave, desire, envy, hanker after, long for

origin: From Anglo-Norman, from Latin "cupiditas", desire, from "cupere", to long for, the same root as "Cupid" and "cupidity".

senses.def: eagerly wanting something, especially what belongs to someone else
senses.ex: He cast covetous glances at his neighbor's restored sports car every time it rolled out of the garage.

origin: The verb, to intimidate, probably comes from Old Norse "kuga", to oppress. The animal name comes separately from Old English "cu".

senses.def: frighten someone into doing what one wants
senses.ex: The bully tried to cow the younger students with threats, but they reported him to the principal.

senses.def: fully grown female of cattle or of some other large animals, such as elephants or whales
senses.ex: The cow stood patiently in the barn while the farmer's daughter milked her before school.

origin: Past participle of the verb "cow", to intimidate, which probably comes from Old Norse "kuga", to oppress.

senses.def: frightened into submission or silence
senses.ex: The cowed witnesses refused to testify after the gang leader's brother appeared in the courtroom.

origin: From Middle English "couren", probably from Middle Low German "kuren", to lie in wait. Despite the look, it is unrelated to "coward".

senses.def: crouch down or shrink back in fear
senses.ex: The puppy cowered under the bed every time thunder rolled across the valley.

origin: Originally "cock's comb", the red crest of a rooster, then a jester's cap shaped like it, and so a foolish, showy person.

senses.def: vain, conceited man overly proud of his looks or manners
senses.ex: The young coxcomb spent the whole party admiring his reflection in the windows instead of talking to anyone.

origin: From Old French "coi", quiet or still, from Latin "quietus", at rest, the same source as "quiet".

senses.def: pretending to be shy or modest, often in a playful or flirtatious way
senses.ex: She gave a coy smile from behind her menu when the waiter asked whether it was her birthday.

senses.def: reluctant to give details or make a commitment
senses.ex: The company stayed coy about the price of its new headset, promising details at next month's launch.

origin: Origin uncertain. Perhaps from Italian "cozzonare", to cheat, from "cozzone", a broker or horse dealer.

senses.def: trick or deceive someone, especially to gain something from them
senses.ex: The smooth-talking salesman cozened the elderly couple into buying a worthless insurance policy.

origin: From Middle English, from "crab", probably because the creature's sideways, awkward walk suggested something twisted and difficult.

senses.def: of handwriting: cramped and hard to read
senses.ex: The archivist squinted for hours over the sea captain's crabbed handwriting in the faded logbook.

senses.def: bad-tempered, sour, and hard to please
senses.ex: The crabbed old landlord refused to fix anything until a tenant threatened to call the city inspector.

origin: From "crack" plus "pot", slang for the head, probably reshaped from older "crackpate", so a crackpot has a cracked head.

senses.def: eccentric person with strange or foolish ideas
senses.ex: The town dismissed him as a crackpot until his warnings about the old dam proved correct.

senses.def: eccentric, impractical, and unlikely to work
senses.ex: No investor would fund his crackpot scheme to power the city with giant hamster wheels.

origin: From Old English "craeft", strength or skill, related to German "Kraft", strength.

senses.def: activity or trade that requires special skill, especially with the hands
senses.ex: Her grandfather taught her the craft of building wooden boats in his small coastal workshop.

senses.def: make or create something skillfully and with care
senses.ex: The speechwriter spent all night crafting a eulogy that was both funny and deeply moving.

senses.def: boat, ship, aircraft, or spacecraft
senses.ex: Dozens of small craft filled the harbor as the tall ships arrived for the festival.

senses.def: skill in deceiving or outwitting others, cunning
senses.ex: The old fox of a senator used craft rather than force to defeat the bill.

origin: From Old English "craeftig", skillful or strong, from "craeft", skill. Over time the meaning slid from skillful to sly.

senses.def: clever at getting what one wants by indirect or deceitful means
senses.ex: The crafty chess player pretended to blunder a pawn in order to lure her opponent into a trap.

origin: From "crank" plus "-y". A link with Dutch and German "krank", sick, has been suggested.

senses.def: irritable, grumpy, and easily annoyed
senses.ex: The toddler got cranky after skipping his nap and flung his spoon across the kitchen.

senses.def: of a machine: working unreliably or with difficulty
senses.ex: The cabin's cranky old generator took six hard pulls to start on cold mornings.

origin: From Latin "crapulentus", very drunk, from "crapula", excessive drinking or the sickness that follows it.

senses.def: sick or sluggish from drinking or eating too much
senses.ex: The morning after the reunion, a crapulent crowd shuffled into the diner, clutching coffee and avoiding the sunny windows.

origin: From Latin "crassus", thick, dense, or gross, so a crass remark is thick with crude insensitivity.

senses.def: crude and insensitive, lacking taste or refinement
senses.ex: His crass jokes about the layoffs offended coworkers who had just watched friends lose their jobs.

senses.def: of stupidity or ignorance: gross and extreme
senses.ex: Emailing the confidential memo to the entire company was an act of crass carelessness.

origin: From Middle English "cravant", probably from Old French "cravante", defeated, past participle of "cravanter", to crush or overthrow.

senses.def: contemptibly lacking in courage
senses.ex: The captain's craven decision to abandon the sinking ferry before his passengers caused national outrage.

origin: From Medieval Latin "credentia", belief, from Latin "credere", to believe or trust.

senses.def: belief in or acceptance of something as true
senses.ex: Scientists gave little credence to the claim until other labs repeated the experiment.

senses.def: likelihood of being true, believability
senses.ex: The discovery of a second letter lent credence to the theory that the queen had a secret child.

origin: From Medieval Latin "credentialis", giving authority, from Latin "credentia", trust, from "credere", to believe.

senses.def: qualification or achievement that shows someone is suited to something
senses.ex: Her credentials as a former astronaut gave her lectures on spaceflight instant authority.

senses.def: document or digital key that proves identity or authority
senses.ex: The guard checked each reporter's press credential before letting anyone into the courtroom.

origin: From Medieval Latin "credibilitas", from Latin "credibilis", believable, from "credere", to believe.

senses.def: quality of being trusted and believed
senses.ex: The newspaper lost much of its credibility after printing a story based on a forged document.

origin: From Latin "credibilis", worthy of belief, from "credere", to believe.

senses.def: able to be believed, convincing
senses.ex: The witness gave a credible account that matched the security footage in every detail.

senses.def: capable of succeeding or being taken seriously
senses.ex: The small party finally found a credible candidate who could compete in a statewide race.

origin: From "credit" plus "-able", and "credit" comes from Latin "creditum", a loan or thing entrusted, from "credere", to believe or trust.

senses.def: deserving praise or respect, though not outstanding
senses.ex: The rookie gave a creditable performance, scoring ten points in her first professional game.

origin: From Latin "credo", I believe, the opening word of many Christian creeds. It is a twin of the word "creed".

senses.def: statement of the beliefs or principles that guide someone
senses.ex: The chef's credo was simple: cook what is in season and never hide good ingredients under heavy sauce.

origin: From Latin "credulitas", from "credulus", easily believing, from "credere", to believe.

senses.def: tendency to believe things too readily, without good evidence
senses.ex: The scam relied on the credulity of people who believed a stranger would give them a free car.

origin: From Latin "credulus", easily believing, from "credere", to believe.

senses.def: too ready to believe things, and so easily fooled
senses.ex: Only the most credulous tourists believed the guide when he claimed the castle was built by giants.

origin: From Old English "creda", from Latin "credo", I believe, the first word of early Christian creeds. Its ancient root probably meant to place one's heart.

senses.def: set of religious beliefs, or a formal statement of them
senses.ex: The school welcomes students of every creed and requires no religious instruction of anyone.

senses.def: set of principles that guides a person or group
senses.ex: The repair shop's creed was to return every customer's call within one business day.

origin: From Latin "crematio", a burning, from "cremare", to burn up or consume by fire.

senses.def: burning of a dead body to ashes as a funeral practice
senses.ex: Following his wishes, the family chose cremation and scattered his ashes over the mountain lake he loved.

origin: From "crenel", the gap between the raised stones of a battlement, from Old French "crenel", a little notch.

senses.def: having battlements, with regular gaps along the top of a wall
senses.ex: Archers once crouched behind the crenellated walls of the castle, firing through the gaps between the stones.

senses.def: having a notched, square-toothed edge or outline
senses.ex: The cookie cutter gave each piece of shortbread a neat crenellated edge, like a tiny fortress.

origin: From Latin "crepusculum", twilight, plus the English suffix "-ar".

senses.def: relating to or resembling twilight, dim
senses.ex: The forest took on a crepuscular gloom as the storm clouds gathered overhead.

senses.def: of animals, active mainly at dawn and dusk
senses.ex: Deer are crepuscular, so drivers should take extra care on country roads at sunrise and sunset.

origin: From Italian "crescendo", growing, from "crescere", to grow or increase, from Latin "crescere", to grow.

senses.def: gradual increase in loudness in a piece of music
senses.ex: The symphony ends with a thunderous crescendo that brings the entire orchestra to its feet.

senses.def: steady increase in intensity or force, or the peak it reaches
senses.ex: Complaints about the noisy construction rose to a crescendo during the week of final exams.

origin: From "crest" plus "fallen", picturing a defeated bird or horse whose crest or neck hangs down.

senses.def: sad and disappointed after a failure or setback
senses.ex: The crestfallen team sat silently in the locker room after losing the final by a single point.

origin: From Old French "crevace", from "crever", to burst or split, from Latin "crepare", to crack. It is a twin of "crevasse".

senses.def: narrow crack or opening, especially in rock or a wall
senses.ex: A tiny lizard darted into a crevice in the canyon wall before we could photograph it.

origin: From French "cri du coeur", a cry from the heart.

senses.def: passionate appeal, complaint, or protest
senses.ex: The nurse's open letter was a cri de coeur about exhausted staff, empty supply closets, and ignored warnings.

origin: From Middle English "crengen", to bend or bow, related to Old English "cringan", to yield or fall, so cringing first meant shrinking down in fear.

senses.def: shrink back or flinch in fear or pain
senses.ex: The puppy cringed at every clap of thunder and finally hid beneath the porch steps.

senses.def: feel sharp embarrassment or disgust
senses.ex: I still cringe when I remember singing off-key in front of everyone at my sister's wedding.

senses.def: informal: embarrassingly awkward or uncool
senses.ex: My little brother says my old dance videos are so cringe that he has to leave the room.

origin: From Greek "kriterion", a means of judging, from "krites", judge, from "krinein", to decide, the same root as "critic".

senses.def: standard by which something is judged or decided, plural "criteria"
senses.ex: Cost was the main criterion the family used to choose a college, ahead of location or reputation.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "carogne", a term of abuse meaning carrion or carcass. It is a twin of "carrion".

senses.def: old woman, often pictured as ugly or witchlike, often offensive
senses.ex: In the fairy tale, a cackling crone offers the lost children a basket of poisoned sweets.

senses.def: wise older woman as a figure of authority in myth and literature
senses.ex: Some modern novelists recast the crone as a figure of hard-won wisdom rather than menace.

origin: From "crony", a close friend, a 1600s student slang word probably from Greek "khronios", long-lasting, meaning a friend of long standing.

senses.def: unfair practice of giving jobs or favors to friends regardless of merit
senses.ex: Critics accused the mayor of cronyism after she awarded the paving contract to her college roommate's firm.

origin: From "crotchet" in its old sense of an odd whim, from Old French "crochet", a little hook.

senses.def: irritable and cranky, often from age or fixed odd habits
senses.ex: The crotchety old neighbor yelled at anyone whose ball rolled onto his perfectly trimmed lawn.

origin: From Latin "crux", cross, the same root found in "crucial" and "crucify".

senses.def: most important or decisive point of an issue or problem
senses.ex: The crux of the dispute was whether the contract allowed the builder to charge for the weather delays.

origin: From Latin "crypta", vault, from Greek "kryptos", hidden, the same root found in "cryptic" and "cryptography".

senses.def: underground room or vault beneath a church, often used for burials
senses.ex: Candles lit the narrow crypt where the cathedral's early bishops lay in carved stone coffins.

origin: From Late Latin "crypticus", from Greek "kryptikos", from "kryptos", hidden, from "kryptein", to hide, the root of "crypt".

senses.def: having a hidden or mysterious meaning that is hard to understand
senses.ex: Before vanishing, the professor left a cryptic note that read only "Check the third shelf."

senses.def: of animal coloring, serving to camouflage
senses.ex: The moth's cryptic coloring makes it almost invisible against the bark of an oak tree.

origin: From "crystal" plus "-ize", and "crystal" comes from Greek "krystallos", ice or rock crystal.

senses.def: make or become clear, definite, and fixed in form
senses.ex: Her vague interest in medicine crystallized into a firm plan after she volunteered at a rural clinic.

senses.def: form or cause to form crystals
senses.ex: As the salt water evaporated, the salt crystallized into small white cubes at the bottom of the dish.

senses.def: coat fruit or other food with sugar
senses.ex: The pastry chef crystallized strips of ginger to decorate the top of the cake.

syn: clarify, solidify, take shape, materialize, firm up

origin: From Old English "cycgel", a club, from a Germanic word for a knobbed stick, related to "cog".

senses.def: short, thick stick used as a weapon
senses.ex: The night watchman carried a lantern in one hand and a heavy oak cudgel in the other.

senses.def: beat someone with a cudgel or heavy stick
senses.ex: The bandits cudgeled the merchant on the lonely road and fled with his purse.

senses.def: force oneself to think hard, as in "cudgel one's brains"
senses.ex: I cudgeled my brain for an hour but still could not recall the name of my first-grade teacher.

origin: From French "cuisine", cooking or kitchen, from Latin "coquina", kitchen, from "coquere", to cook. It is a twin of "kitchen".

senses.def: style of cooking typical of a country, region, or culture
senses.ex: Ethiopian cuisine is built around injera, a spongy flatbread used to scoop up spiced stews.

senses.def: food prepared by a particular restaurant or cook
senses.ex: The small hotel's cuisine earned glowing reviews for its inventive seafood dishes.

origin: From Latin "culinarius", of the kitchen, from "culina", kitchen.

senses.def: relating to cooking or the kitchen
senses.ex: After two years of culinary school, she could fillet a fish and temper chocolate with equal confidence.

origin: From Old French "cuillir", to gather or pick, from Latin "colligere", to gather together, the same source as "collect".

senses.def: select or gather from a large amount or from many sources
senses.ex: The reporter culled quotes from hundreds of pages of court transcripts for her story.

senses.def: reduce an animal population by selective killing, or remove inferior items
senses.ex: Rangers culled the deer herd after it grew too large for the small island to feed.

senses.def: selective killing of animals to reduce their numbers
senses.ex: The government's planned badger cull drew angry protests from wildlife groups.

origin: From Medieval Latin "culminare", to crown, from Latin "culmen", peak or summit.

senses.def: reach a climax or final point after a gradual build-up
senses.ex: Months of protests culminated in a march of half a million people to the capital.

syn: climax, peak, end, conclude, come to a head

origin: From "culminate", from Medieval Latin "culminare", to crown, from Latin "culmen", summit or peak.

senses.def: highest point or final climax of something that has been developing
senses.ex: The championship was the culmination of six years of early practices and painful losses.

origin: From French "culpabilité", from Latin "culpabilis", blameworthy, from "culpa", fault, the root of "culprit".

senses.def: responsibility for a fault or wrongdoing, the degree of blame deserved
senses.ex: The inquiry examined the culpability of the bridge inspectors who had ignored warnings about rusted cables.

origin: From Latin "culpabilis", blameworthy, from "culpare", to blame, from "culpa", fault.

senses.def: deserving blame for a fault or wrongdoing
senses.ex: The jury found the company culpable for the chemical spill, though not guilty of intentional harm.

syn: blameworthy, guilty, responsible, at fault, liable

origin: From "culture", from Latin "cultura", cultivation or tending, from "colere", to till the soil, so a cultured mind has been cultivated.

senses.def: well educated and refined in taste, especially in the arts
senses.ex: Her cultured grandmother could discuss opera, Russian novels, and Renaissance painting with equal ease.

senses.def: grown or produced under controlled conditions rather than naturally
senses.ex: The necklace was made of cultured pearls grown on a farm in southern Japan.

origin: Of unknown origin. Guesses link it to French "couler", to flow, but none has been confirmed.

senses.def: tunnel or pipe that carries a stream or drain under a road or railway
senses.ex: After the storm, branches clogged the culvert beneath the highway, and water spilled across the asphalt.

origin: From "cumber", a hindrance, the same root as in "encumber", plus the suffix "-some".

senses.def: large, heavy, or awkward and therefore hard to carry or use
senses.ex: The early cell phones were cumbersome devices about the size and weight of a brick.

senses.def: slow and complicated, involving too many steps
senses.ex: Applying for the permit was a cumbersome process that required six forms and three office visits.

origin: From Middle English, from "cumber", trouble or obstruction, plus "-ous", the same root found in "encumber" and "cumbersome".

senses.def: heavy, bulky, and awkward to carry or use, slow and clumsy
senses.ex: Early laptops were cumbrous machines that weighed more than a stack of textbooks.

origin: From Latin "cunctatio", delay, from "cunctari", to hesitate. The Roman general Fabius was nicknamed "Cunctator", the Delayer, for avoiding pitched battles.

senses.def: habit of delaying or putting off action
senses.ex: The committee's endless cunctation over the budget meant the bridge repairs slipped into another winter.

origin: From Latin "cuneus", wedge, plus "forma", shape, describing the wedge-shaped marks pressed into wet clay with a reed.

senses.def: ancient Mesopotamian writing system of wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay
senses.ex: Archaeologists deciphered the cuneiform on the small clay tablet and found it was a receipt for barley.

senses.def: wedge-shaped, or written in cuneiform
senses.ex: The museum displays a cuneiform tablet recording a Babylonian king's canal and temple projects.

origin: From Old English "cunnende", knowing how, present participle of "cunnan", to know or be able, the root of "can". It once meant simply skillful.

senses.def: clever at getting what one wants, especially by deceiving others
senses.ex: The cunning thief disguised himself as a window cleaner to get inside the bank's offices.

senses.def: skill in achieving one's aims by deceit or trickery
senses.ex: With patience and cunning, the fox managed to steal eggs from the farmer's locked henhouse.

senses.def: cleverly designed or made, ingenious
senses.ex: The desk had a cunning hidden drawer that opened only when you pressed a carved rose.

origin: From Latin "cupiditas", strong desire, from "cupidus", eager or desirous, related to "Cupid", the god of desire.

senses.def: excessive greed, especially for money or possessions
senses.ex: The developer's cupidity led him to cut corners on safety in order to squeeze more profit from each building.

origin: From Italian "cupola", from Latin "cupula", little tub, from "cupa", tub or cask, because it looks like an upturned cup.

senses.def: small dome on a roof, often crowning a larger roof or tower
senses.ex: A copper cupola topped with a rooster weathervane crowns the old red barn.

origin: From Latin "curator", caretaker or guardian, from "curare", to take care of, from "cura", care.

senses.def: person in charge of a museum, gallery, or library collection
senses.ex: The curator chose forty photographs from the archive for the exhibition on the city's lost neighborhoods.

senses.def: person who selects and organizes content such as music, art, or articles
senses.ex: As the festival's curator, he picked every band, from the headliners to the morning opening act.

origin: From French "courbe", curved, from Latin "curvus", bent. In English it first named a curved strap or bit used to restrain a horse.

senses.def: restrain or keep something in check
senses.ex: The city passed new rules to curb noise from late-night construction in residential areas.

senses.def: something that restrains or limits
senses.ex: The new law places a curb on how much landlords can raise rent each year.

senses.def: raised edge of a sidewalk along a street
senses.ex: He parked so close to the curb that his tires scraped the concrete.

syn: restrain, check, limit, rein in, control

origin: A shortening of "curiosity", first recorded in the 1850s, for an object that arouses curiosity.

senses.def: small, rare, or unusual object valued as a curiosity
senses.ex: Her grandfather's study was crowded with curios: a narwhal tusk, brass compasses, and a jar of ancient coins.

origin: Origin unknown. The word appears in the late 1500s in many spellings, and the popular stories about its source are folk etymologies.

senses.def: bad-tempered, stubborn person, often an older one, who complains a lot
senses.ex: The neighborhood curmudgeon yelled at children who chased their balls onto his perfectly mowed lawn.

origin: From Latin "cursorius", of running, from "cursor", runner, from "currere", to run, so a cursory look runs over things quickly.

senses.def: hasty and therefore not thorough or detailed
senses.ex: A cursory glance at the contract missed the clause that doubled the fee after the first year.

origin: Altered from "curtal", cut short, from Old French "courtault", from "court", short, from Latin "curtus", short. The spelling was shaped by "tail".

senses.def: reduce, restrict, or cut short
senses.ex: The drought forced the town to curtail water use, banning lawn sprinklers and car washing.

syn: reduce, cut back, limit, restrict, shorten

origin: From Latin "cuspis", a point or spear tip.

senses.def: point of transition between two states, as in "on the cusp of"
senses.ex: At nineteen, the young violinist was on the cusp of an international concert career.

senses.def: pointed end where two curves meet, as on a tooth or crescent moon
senses.ex: The dentist pointed out a small chip on the cusp of my lower left molar.

origin: From Latin "cynicus", from Greek "kynikos", doglike, the nickname of the Cynic philosophers who scorned social conventions.

senses.def: believing that people act only out of self-interest and distrusting their motives
senses.ex: After years covering city politics, the reporter had grown cynical about every promise to fix the potholes.

senses.def: concerned only with one's own interests, without regard for principles
senses.ex: Critics called the company's sudden interest in recycling a cynical attempt to sell more products.

origin: From "cynic", from Greek "kynikos", doglike, a nickname for ancient philosophers who scorned comfort and social convention.

senses.def: distrust of people's motives, believing they act only from self-interest
senses.ex: Years of broken campaign promises had filled the town's voters with cynicism about every new candidate.

origin: From Greek "Kynosoura", dog's tail, the name for the constellation Ursa Minor, whose North Star sailors steered by.

senses.def: person or thing that is the center of attention or admiration
senses.ex: In her sequined gown, the young actress was the cynosure of every camera on the red carpet.

syn: focus, center of attention, focal point, magnet, spotlight

origin: From "dab" plus "-le", a suffix for repeated action, possibly from Middle Dutch "dabbelen", to splash or fumble.

senses.def: take part in an activity casually, without serious commitment
senses.ex: She dabbled in watercolor and pottery before finally committing herself to photography.

senses.def: splash hands or feet gently in water
senses.ex: The children sat at the end of the dock, dabbling their toes in the cool lake.

syn: tinker, toy, trifle, potter, dip into

origin: From Old French "deis", from Latin "discus", disc or dish, later a table. It is a twin of "desk", "dish", and "disc".

senses.def: raised platform at one end of a room for speakers or honored guests
senses.ex: The valedictorian climbed the steps to the dais, adjusted the microphone, and looked out at her classmates.

origin: From Middle English "daliaunce", from "dalien", to chat or flirt, from Old French "dalier". Related to "dally".

senses.def: casual romantic or sexual relationship that is not taken seriously
senses.ex: The tabloids made much of the actor's brief dalliance with a famous tennis player.

senses.def: brief, casual involvement with an activity or interest
senses.ex: After a short dalliance with jazz, the violinist returned to classical music for good.

origin: From Middle English "dalien", from Anglo-Norman, and considered a twin of "delay", which fits its sense of lingering.

senses.def: waste time or move slowly, dawdle
senses.ex: If you dally over breakfast, we will miss the only ferry to the island today.

senses.def: treat a person or idea casually, without serious intent, usually with "with"
senses.ex: The senator dallied with the idea of running for president but never filed the paperwork.

origin: From "damn", from Latin "damnare", to condemn or inflict loss, from "damnum", loss or harm.

senses.def: strongly suggesting guilt, error, or failure
senses.ex: The leaked emails provided damning evidence that executives had known about the defect for years.

origin: From Middle English "dampen", to stifle or choke, related to German "Dampf", vapor or steam.

senses.def: slightly wet but not fully soaked
senses.ex: He wiped the counter with a damp cloth before rolling out the pizza dough.

senses.def: make a feeling, sound, or activity less strong
senses.ex: Reports of a coming recession damped investors' enthusiasm for new technology stocks.

senses.def: moisture in the air or on a surface, often unwelcome
senses.ex: The damp in the old cottage left black mold spreading across the bedroom ceiling.

origin: From "damp", to deaden or check, plus "-er"; "damp" comes from a Germanic word for vapor, as in Middle Low German "damp".

senses.def: something that dulls enthusiasm or enjoyment, as in "put a damper on"
senses.ex: A sudden downpour put a damper on the outdoor graduation party in the park.

senses.def: movable plate in a chimney or flue that controls the air flow
senses.ex: Open the fireplace damper before lighting the logs, or the living room will fill with smoke.

senses.def: device that reduces vibration or sound, such as a felt pad on piano strings
senses.ex: When the pianist lifts her foot from the pedal, the dampers fall back onto the strings and silence them.

syn: dampener, wet blanket, restraint, check, curb

origin: First used in Scotland, of uncertain origin. It may come from "Dandy", a pet form of the name Andrew.

senses.def: man devoted to stylish clothes and an elegant appearance
senses.ex: The dandy strolled through the park in a silk cravat, polished boots, and a silver-tipped cane.

senses.def: informal, often ironic: excellent or fine
senses.ex: Everything was just dandy until the caterer called to say the wedding cake had collapsed.

origin: From Middle English "danke", wet or damp, probably from a Scandinavian source. Compare Swedish "dank", a marshy spot.

senses.def: unpleasantly damp, cold, and musty
senses.ex: The basement apartment was dank and dim, and mildew crept up the walls every spring.

origin: From Middle Dutch "dapper", strong or bold. In English the sense shifted to neat and smart in appearance.

senses.def: neat, trim, and stylishly dressed, usually of a man
senses.ex: Grandpa looked dapper in his pressed gray suit and the bow tie he saved for weddings.

origin: From "dapple", a spot, of uncertain origin, perhaps related to Old Norse "depill", a spot.

senses.def: marked with patches of light and shade or spots of color
senses.ex: We ate our picnic in the dappled shade of an old oak, sunlight flickering across the blanket.

origin: From Old French "danter", to tame, from Latin "domitare", to tame, from "domare", to tame or subdue.

senses.def: make someone feel intimidated or discouraged
senses.ex: The steep, icy trail did not daunt the experienced climbers, who reached the summit before noon.

origin: From "daunt" plus "-ing", and "daunt" comes from Old French "danter", to tame, from Latin "domare", to tame or subdue.

senses.def: seeming so difficult that it causes fear or discouragement
senses.ex: Writing a two-hundred-page thesis can seem daunting, but breaking it into chapters makes it manageable.

origin: From "daunt", to intimidate, from Old French "danter", from Latin "domitare", to tame, plus "-less", so one who cannot be tamed by fear.

senses.def: showing fearless determination in the face of danger
senses.ex: The dauntless rescue team climbed through the blizzard to reach the stranded hikers before nightfall.

origin: Origin uncertain. Perhaps a variant of dialect "daddle" or "doddle", to walk slowly, probably imitative in origin.

senses.def: waste time by moving or acting slowly
senses.ex: If you dawdle at the bookstore again, we will miss the last train home.

origin: From "dead", in the sense of complete or motionless, plus "lock": a situation locked so tightly that nothing can move.

senses.def: situation in which no progress is possible because opposing sides will not yield
senses.ex: After three days of deadlock, the jury told the judge it could not reach a verdict.

senses.def: reach or cause a standstill in which neither side will yield
senses.ex: Talks between the union and the airline deadlocked over pension benefits for retired pilots.

origin: From "dead" plus "pan", American slang for the face, so a deadpan look is a face with no life in it.

senses.def: deliberately expressionless, especially while joking
senses.ex: With a deadpan expression, the comedian announced that he had just been elected king of Canada.

senses.def: style of humor delivered with a blank, serious face
senses.ex: Her perfect deadpan left the audience unsure whether she was joking until the punch line landed.

senses.def: say something, especially something funny, without any expression
senses.ex: "I love Mondays," he deadpanned as the office printer jammed for the third time that morning.

origin: From Middle English "derthe", from "dear" plus the noun suffix "-th", because scarce things become dear, meaning costly.

senses.def: scarcity or lack of something
senses.ex: A dearth of qualified teachers forced the rural district to combine its high school science classes.

origin: From French "débâcle", the breaking up of ice on a river, from "débâcler", to unbar or release.

senses.def: sudden, complete failure that is often embarrassing
senses.ex: The product launch was a debacle: the website crashed and the first batch of phones would not turn on.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "debarrer", from "de-", away, plus "barrer", to bar, so it means to shut someone out as if with a bar.

senses.def: officially exclude someone from a place, activity, or right
senses.ex: The sprinter was debarred from competition for two years after failing a drug test.

syn: bar, exclude, ban, prohibit, shut out

origin: From "de-", down, plus "base", low, from Old French "bas", from Late Latin "bassus", low.

senses.def: lower the quality, value, or character of something
senses.ex: Critics argued that the reality show debased public debate by rewarding insults over ideas.

senses.def: reduce the value of money, especially by lowering the precious metal in coins
senses.ex: Roman emperors repeatedly debased the silver coinage to pay their soldiers.

origin: Past participle of "debase", from "de-", down, plus "base", low, from Old French "bas".

senses.def: reduced in quality, value, or moral character
senses.ex: Collectors avoid the debased coins of that period, which contain more copper than silver.

origin: From French "desbaucher", to lure someone away from work or duty. Where the French word came from is uncertain, possibly from a word for a wooden beam.

senses.def: corrupt someone morally, especially by leading them into excessive drinking or sensual pleasure
senses.ex: In the play, a smooth-talking stranger arrives in the quiet village and sets out to debauch its earnest young students.

senses.def: bout of wild, excessive drinking, eating, or other indulgence
senses.ex: After a three-day debauch in the casinos, the brothers flew home with sore heads and empty wallets.

syn: corrupt, deprave, pervert, seduce, lead astray

origin: From "debauch", from French "débaucher", originally to lure someone away from their work or duty, plus "-ery", a state or practice.

senses.def: excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures such as heavy drinking, drugs, or sex
senses.ex: The novel depicts a young prince whose nights of drinking and debauchery slowly drain the royal treasury.

origin: From Latin "debilitare", to weaken, from "debilis", weak, so a debilitating condition leaves a person feeble.

senses.def: severely weakening, draining energy or strength, or making normal activity difficult
senses.ex: The debilitating illness left the former marathon runner unable to climb a single flight of stairs without resting.

origin: From Latin "debilitas", weakness, from "debilis", weak, from "de-", away from, plus "habilis", able.

senses.def: physical weakness, especially from illness or old age
senses.ex: Months of fever left the sailor in a state of debility, unable to climb the stairs without resting halfway.

origin: From Old French "de bon aire", of good stock or nature, so a debonair person carries the easy charm of good breeding.

senses.def: confident, stylish, and charming in a relaxed, polished way, usually said of a man
senses.ex: The debonair host greeted every guest by name and moved through the crowded ballroom without a hint of strain.

origin: From French "déboucher", from "dé-", out of, plus "bouche", mouth, so to debouch is to come out of the mouth of a narrow place.

senses.def: emerge from a narrow space into a wider, open area
senses.ex: After hours in the dark canyon, the hikers debouched onto a sunlit plain that stretched all the way to the mountains.

syn: emerge, issue, pour out, come out

origin: Coined in 1923 from "de-", away, plus "bunk", nonsense, short for "bunkum", named after Buncombe County, North Carolina, whose congressman gave a famously empty speech.

senses.def: show that a widely held idea, claim, or belief is false or exaggerated
senses.ex: The science teacher debunked the myth that people use only ten percent of their brains with a few simple scans.

origin: From French "débutante", a woman making her first appearance, from "débuter", to make a first move or begin.

senses.def: young woman from a wealthy family making her formal first appearance in society, often at a ball
senses.ex: Each debutante descended the grand staircase on her father's arm while the orchestra played a slow waltz.

senses.def: newcomer making a first public appearance, especially in sport or entertainment
senses.ex: The nineteen-year-old debutante held her nerve on center court and took the first set from the defending champion.

origin: From French "décadence", from Medieval Latin "decadentia", decay, from Latin "de-", down, plus "cadere", to fall.

senses.def: moral or cultural decline marked by excessive indulgence in pleasure and luxury
senses.ex: Critics blamed the empire's fall on the decadence of its rulers, who held lavish banquets while the provinces starved.
