senses.def: luxurious self-indulgence, especially in rich food, used approvingly
senses.ex: The bakery's triple chocolate cake, layered with salted caramel, is pure decadence on a plate.

origin: From French "décadent", from Medieval Latin "decadentia", decay, from Latin "de-", down, plus "cadere", to fall, so a decadent society is falling into decline.

senses.def: marked by moral or cultural decline, especially through love of luxury and pleasure
senses.ex: Historians once blamed the empire's collapse on a decadent ruling class more interested in banquets than in defending its borders.

senses.def: luxuriously and indulgently rich or pleasurable
senses.ex: The bakery's most decadent dessert layers dark chocolate mousse, salted caramel, and whipped cream on a brownie base.

origin: From French "décamper", to break camp, from "dé-", away, plus "camp".

senses.def: leave a place suddenly or secretly, or move away to settle elsewhere
senses.ex: The landlord discovered that the tenants had decamped in the night, leaving three months of unpaid rent behind.

syn: abscond, flee, bolt, run off, take off

origin: From French "décanter", from Medieval Latin "decanthare", from "de-", away, plus "canthus", the lip or spout of a jug.

senses.def: pour a liquid such as wine gently into another container, leaving any sediment behind
senses.ex: The waiter decanted the old red wine slowly by candlelight, stopping just before the dark sediment reached the bottle's neck.

origin: From Late Latin "decapitare", from "de-", off, plus "caput", head, the same root as "capital" and "captain".

senses.def: cut off the head of a person or animal
senses.ex: During the storm a falling branch decapitated the stone statue in the park, and its head rolled into the fountain.

senses.def: remove the leaders of a group or organization, leaving it without direction
senses.ex: The arrests decapitated the smuggling ring, and without its bosses the gang soon fell apart.

origin: From "deci-", one tenth, plus "bel", a unit named after Alexander Graham Bell, so a decibel is one tenth of a bel.

senses.def: unit for measuring how loud a sound is, or the relative strength of a signal
senses.ex: A jet engine at takeoff can exceed 140 decibels, loud enough to cause permanent hearing damage in seconds.

origin: From Latin "deciduus", falling off, from "decidere", to fall down, from "de-", down, plus "cadere", to fall, since the leaves fall each year.

senses.def: of trees and shrubs, shedding their leaves every year, usually in autumn
senses.ex: Maples, oaks, and other deciduous trees turn the hills red and gold before dropping their leaves in November.

origin: From Latin "decimare", to kill one in every ten, from "decimus", tenth, describing a Roman punishment for mutinous legions.

senses.def: kill or destroy a large proportion of a population or group
senses.ex: A fungal disease decimated the region's chestnut trees, leaving only a few scattered survivors in remote valleys.

senses.def: drastically reduce or weaken something, such as an organization or resource
senses.ex: Years of budget cuts decimated the school's arts program until only one part-time music teacher remained.

syn: devastate, annihilate, ravage, wipe out, destroy

origin: From Latin "decimatio", the Roman army punishment of killing every tenth soldier, from "decimus", tenth.

senses.def: destruction or killing of a large part of a population or group
senses.ex: The decimation of the bison herds in the 1800s devastated the Plains peoples who depended on them for food and shelter.

senses.def: Roman military punishment in which every tenth soldier in a unit was executed
senses.ex: Roman generals used decimation sparingly, since executing every tenth soldier also weakened their own fighting force.

origin: From "de-", undoing, plus "cipher", a secret code, modeled on French "déchiffrer". "Cipher" traces back through Medieval Latin "cifra" to Arabic "sifr", zero.

senses.def: convert a coded message into ordinary language
senses.ex: During the war, teams of mathematicians worked around the clock to decipher the enemy's radio messages.

senses.def: succeed in reading or understanding something unclear, such as bad handwriting or someone's motives
senses.ex: The pharmacist squinted for a full minute, trying to decipher the doctor's scrawled prescription.

syn: decode, decrypt, interpret, make out, unravel

origin: From Middle French "décisif", from "decide", which comes from Latin "decidere", to cut off, from "de-", off, plus "caedere", to cut, so a decisive act cuts off debate.

senses.def: settling an issue or contest clearly, with a definite result
senses.ex: The late goal proved decisive, and the underdogs held on to win their first championship in fifty years.

senses.def: able to make choices quickly, firmly, and with confidence
senses.ex: The new captain was calm and decisive, ordering the crew to change course within seconds of spotting the storm.

origin: From Latin "declamare", to practice public speaking, from "de-", thoroughly, plus "clamare", to cry out or shout.

senses.def: speak in a loud, dramatic, or impassioned way, as if addressing an audience
senses.ex: Standing on a park bench, the old activist declaimed against the new highway to anyone who would stop and listen.

senses.def: recite a poem or speech aloud with dramatic expression
senses.ex: For the school assembly, each student had to declaim a famous speech from memory in front of the whole grade.

syn: orate, hold forth, harangue, sermonize, rant

origin: From Latin "declamatio", from "declamare", to speak aloud, from "de-", fully, plus "clamare", to shout.

senses.def: speech or recitation delivered in a loud, dramatic, rhetorical style
senses.ex: The candidate's fiery declamation against the new tax drew cheers from the crowd but offered few concrete facts.

senses.def: practice or art of reciting speeches or poems with expressive delivery
senses.ex: In the nineteenth century, schoolchildren studied declamation and recited famous speeches before the whole town.

origin: From "declaim", from Latin "declamare", to speak loudly, from "clamare", to shout, plus "-atory", relating to.

senses.def: expressed in a loud, dramatic, rhetorical style, often more showy than sincere
senses.ex: The editorial's declamatory tone, full of exclamation points and grand warnings, made readers doubt its claims.

origin: From Latin "declivitas", from "declivis", sloping downward, from "de-", down, plus "clivus", slope.

senses.def: downward slope, especially of land
senses.ex: The hikers slid down the rocky declivity on their heels, grabbing at roots to keep from tumbling into the creek.

origin: From Latin "decorus", fitting or proper, from "decor", grace or beauty, from "decere", to be fitting.

senses.def: in keeping with good taste and propriety, polite and restrained
senses.ex: The usually rowdy fans remained decorous during the memorial ceremony, standing in silence with their caps removed.

origin: From Latin "decorum", that which is proper, the neuter form of "decorus", fitting, from "decere", to be suitable.

senses.def: behavior that is proper, polite, and dignified, in keeping with good taste
senses.ex: The judge banged her gavel and warned the shouting spectators that the courtroom required decorum at all times.

origin: From Latin "decrepitus", very old, from "crepare", to creak, so picture the creaking joints or floorboards of something worn out by age.

senses.def: worn out, weakened, or falling apart from age, long use, or neglect
senses.ex: The decrepit farmhouse had sagging floors, broken windows, and a roof that leaked whenever it rained.

origin: From Middle French "décrépitude", from Latin "decrepitus", very old, from "crepare", to creak.

senses.def: state of being worn out, weak, or falling apart from age or long use
senses.ex: The once grand hotel had sunk into decrepitude, its ballroom ceiling cracked and its carpets eaten by moths.

origin: From French "décrier", to cry down or disparage, from "de-", down, plus "crier", to cry out. It is a doublet of "descry".

senses.def: publicly denounce or criticize something as wrong, harmful, or worthless
senses.ex: Environmental groups decried the decision to open the protected wetlands to oil drilling.

origin: From Latin "deducere", to lead away or bring out, from "de-", from, plus "ducere", to lead, so to deduce is to lead a conclusion out of the facts.

senses.def: reach a conclusion by reasoning from known facts or evidence
senses.ex: From the muddy boots by the door and the wet umbrella, she deduced that her brother had walked home in the rain.

syn: infer, conclude, reason, work out, derive

origin: From Old English "deman", to judge or decide, related to "doom", which originally meant a judgment.

senses.def: regard or judge something in a particular way
senses.ex: The inspector deemed the old bridge unsafe and ordered it closed until engineers could reinforce the supports.

origin: From Old French "desfacier", to disfigure, from "des-", away, plus "face", face, so to deface is to spoil the face of something.

senses.def: spoil the surface or appearance of something, especially by drawing or writing on it
senses.ex: Vandals defaced the newly restored mural overnight, spraying graffiti across the faces of the painted figures.

origin: From Medieval Latin "defalcare", to cut off with a sickle, from Latin "de-", off, plus "falx", sickle, so to lop off money held in trust.

senses.def: misuse or steal money that one has been trusted to manage
senses.ex: Auditors discovered that the club treasurer had defalcated thousands of dollars from the scholarship fund over five years.

origin: From Medieval Latin "defalcatio", a cutting off, from Latin "de-", off, plus "falx", sickle, as if money were lopped off for oneself.

senses.def: misuse or theft of money by someone trusted to manage it
senses.ex: An audit uncovered a defalcation of nearly two million dollars by the charity's treasurer, who had falsified the accounts.

origin: From Latin "diffamatio", from "diffamare", to spread an evil report, from "dis-", apart, plus "fama", report or reputation.

senses.def: damaging someone's good reputation by saying or writing false things about them
senses.ex: The actor sued the magazine for defamation after it falsely reported that he had been arrested for fraud.

syn: slander, libel, calumny, vilification, character assassination

origin: From Latin "diffamare", to spread damaging reports about, from "dis-", apart, plus "fama", reputation or rumor, the root of "fame".

senses.def: damage someone's good reputation by saying or writing false and harmful things
senses.ex: The rival campaign tried to defame the candidate by spreading invented stories about her business dealings.

origin: From Old French "defaute", a failure or lack, ultimately from Latin "de-", away, plus "fallere", to deceive or escape notice.

senses.def: failure to repay a loan or meet some other financial or legal obligation
senses.ex: After months of falling sales, the company's default on its bank loans forced it into bankruptcy.

senses.def: fail to repay a debt or meet an obligation
senses.ex: If the country defaults on its bonds, investors around the world could lose billions of dollars.

senses.def: option or setting that applies automatically unless something else is chosen
senses.ex: The app's default is to share your location, so you must change the setting yourself to keep it private.

senses.def: revert automatically to a standard choice or behavior when no other is made
senses.ex: When the new manager left the meeting undecided, the team simply defaulted to last year's schedule.

origin: From "defeat" plus "-ist", modeled on French "défaitiste", someone who expects or accepts defeat.

senses.def: expecting failure and too ready to give up
senses.ex: Her defeatist attitude before the exam, insisting she would fail anyway, kept her from studying at all.

senses.def: person who expects failure and gives up too easily
senses.ex: Only a defeatist would abandon the fundraiser after one slow morning, when the big donors usually arrive in the afternoon.

origin: From Latin "defectio", a desertion or failing, from "deficere", to desert or fail, from "de-", away, plus "facere", to do.

senses.def: abandonment of one's country, party, or cause in order to join an opposing one
senses.ex: The defection of three senators to the opposition party cost the government its majority overnight.

origin: First recorded in 1904 as a back-formation from "defenestration", built on Latin "de", out of, and "fenestra", window.

senses.def: throw someone or something out of a window
senses.ex: In a fit of rage over the crashed essay, he threatened to defenestrate his old laptop from the dorm.

senses.def: abruptly remove someone from a position of power
senses.ex: The board moved swiftly to defenestrate the chief executive after the accounting scandal reached the national newspapers.

origin: From Old French "defensable", from Latin "defensibilis", able to be defended, related to "defendere", to ward off.

senses.def: able to be justified or supported by reasoned argument
senses.ex: The judge called the agency's decision defensible, since it rested on careful studies and followed the published rules.

senses.def: able to be protected against physical attack
senses.ex: The settlers built their fort on the bluff because it was the most defensible ground for miles along the river.

origin: Two Latin verbs merged: "differre", to carry apart or put off, gave the sense of delay, and "deferre", to carry down or hand over, gave the sense of yielding.

senses.def: put off an action or event until a later time
senses.ex: The university allowed her to defer her admission for a year so she could work at a clinic abroad.

senses.def: yield respectfully to another person's judgment, wishes, or authority
senses.ex: Although the young doctor disagreed, she deferred to the senior surgeon's decision during the operation.

syn: postpone, delay, put off, shelve, suspend

origin: From French "déférence", from "déférer", to yield, from Latin "deferre", to carry down or hand over.

senses.def: polite respect shown by yielding to another's judgment, wishes, or position
senses.ex: Out of deference to his grandmother, Marco kept his phone in his pocket during the entire family dinner.

origin: From "deference", polite yielding, plus "-ial"; the adjective was popularized by Walter Scott. "Deference" goes back to Latin "deferre", to hand over.

senses.def: showing polite respect and a readiness to yield to someone else's judgment or status
senses.ex: The new intern was so deferential that she asked permission before refilling the office coffee pot.

origin: The verb comes from Middle English "defoulen", to trample or pollute, blending "foul" with Old French "defouler", to trample. The noun comes from French "défilé", from "défiler", to march in file.

senses.def: make something dirty, foul, or impure
senses.ex: Runoff from the abandoned mine continues to defile the stream that once supplied the valley with clean drinking water.

senses.def: violate the sacredness or honor of something
senses.ex: Vandals defiled the old cemetery overnight, toppling headstones and spraying slogans across the memorial to the town's veterans.

senses.def: narrow pass or gorge between mountains
senses.ex: The caravan moved single file through the rocky defile, watching the cliffs above for signs of falling stones.

origin: From Middle French "définitif", from Latin "definire", to set limits, based on "finis", end or boundary, so a definitive answer ends the question.

senses.def: settling a matter conclusively and finally
senses.ex: The lab's DNA results gave a definitive answer, ending a decades-old dispute over who had inherited the family farm.

senses.def: most complete and authoritative of its kind
senses.ex: Her three-volume study of Ottoman trade routes is still considered the definitive work on the subject by most historians.

origin: From Latin "deflectere", from "de-", away, plus "flectere", to bend, so to deflect is to bend something away from its path.

senses.def: cause something to change direction, especially after hitting a surface
senses.ex: The goalkeeper's fingertips deflected the shot onto the crossbar, and the ball bounced safely out of play.

senses.def: turn attention, criticism, or a question away from oneself or a topic
senses.ex: Whenever reporters asked about the missing funds, the senator deflected by talking about his record on jobs.

syn: divert, turn aside, redirect, sidetrack, avert

origin: From "de-", meaning removal, and "foliate", from Latin "folium", leaf, so to defoliate is to take the leaves off.

senses.def: strip leaves from plants or trees, especially with chemicals or by pests
senses.ex: Swarms of caterpillars can defoliate an entire oak forest in a few weeks, leaving bare branches in midsummer.

origin: From French "défrayer", from "dé-", out, plus Old French "frai", expense or cost, so to defray is to pay out the cost.

senses.def: pay all or part of the cost of something
senses.ex: The students held a car wash to help defray the cost of their trip to the national robotics competition.

syn: cover, pay for, meet, settle, finance

origin: From French "défroquer", from "dé-", removal, and "froc", a monk's robe, so to defrock someone is to take away the robe of office.

senses.def: formally remove a priest or minister from clerical office
senses.ex: The church council voted to defrock the pastor after an inquiry found he had misused donations for years.

senses.def: strip someone of professional standing or an honored position
senses.ex: The medical board defrocked the surgeon for falsifying records, ending a career that had once seemed beyond reproach.

origin: From Old English "dæfte", gentle or meek, the same source as "daft". Over time the sense shifted from mild and fitting to skillful.

senses.def: quick, neat, and skillful in movement or action
senses.ex: With a few deft strokes of the brush, the calligrapher turned a blank scroll into an elegant line of characters.

origin: From "deft", skillful, plus "-ness", a state or quality. "Deft" comes from Old English "dæfte", gentle or fitting.

senses.def: quickness and skill in movement, handling, or dealing with a situation
senses.ex: The mediator handled the angry neighbors with such deftness that both sides left believing they had won.

origin: From Latin "defunctus", finished or dead, past participle of "defungor", to finish or discharge, so something defunct has completed its course.

senses.def: no longer existing, operating, or in use
senses.ex: The museum displays uniforms and ticket punches from the defunct railway that once linked the mining towns to the coast.

origin: From Latin "degeneratus", past participle of "degenerare", to fall below one's kind, from "de-", away from, and "genus", race or kind.

senses.def: decline gradually to a worse condition
senses.ex: The friendly debate quickly degenerated into a shouting match once someone brought up the disputed election results.

senses.def: morally corrupt or having declined from a former good state
senses.ex: Critics of the emperor blamed a degenerate court for squandering the treasury on banquets while the provinces went hungry.

senses.def: person regarded as immoral or corrupt
senses.ex: The tabloid painted the young heir as a degenerate who gambled away his allowance in casinos across Europe.

origin: From French "dégradation", based on Latin "de-", down, and "gradus", step, so the word pictures a step downward in rank or quality.

senses.def: gradual decline in quality, condition, or strength
senses.ex: Years of overgrazing caused severe soil degradation, turning once productive pastures into dusty, nearly barren land.

senses.def: treatment that humiliates someone and strips away their dignity
senses.ex: The prisoners' memoirs describe the daily degradation of being numbered, shaved, and forced to beg for water.

origin: From Old French "degrader", from Late Latin "degradare", to reduce in rank, from "de-", down, plus "gradus", step or rank.

senses.def: treat someone with disrespect or lower their dignity or status
senses.ex: The coach was fired for degrading players with insults and public humiliation during practice.

senses.def: lower the quality of something or cause it to break down physically or chemically
senses.ex: Sunlight and salt water slowly degrade plastic bags into tiny fragments that fish mistake for food.

origin: From "de-", meaning removal, and "hydrate", which traces back to Greek "hydor", water.

senses.def: remove water from something, often to preserve it
senses.ex: Backpackers often dehydrate fruit and vegetables at home so their food stays light and keeps for the whole trip.

senses.def: lose too much water from the body
senses.ex: Marathon runners can dehydrate quickly on hot days unless they drink regularly at the aid stations along the course.

origin: From Latin "deificatio", from "deus", god, and "-ficare", to make, so the word literally means making someone into a god.

senses.def: act of raising a person or thing to the status of a god
senses.ex: The deification of Roman emperors after death gave their successors a useful claim to sacred authority.

senses.def: excessive admiration that treats someone as beyond criticism
senses.ex: The documentary resists the deification of its rock star subject, showing his cruelty alongside his undeniable genius.

origin: From Latin "deificare", to make into a god, from "deus", god, plus "facere", to make.

senses.def: worship someone as a god or make them into one
senses.ex: Some ancient Egyptians deified their pharaohs, building temples where priests made offerings to the king's spirit.

senses.def: admire or praise someone so much that they are treated as beyond criticism
senses.ex: Fans tend to deify star athletes, then turn on them furiously after a single bad season.

origin: From Old French "deignier", from Latin "dignare", to deem worthy, from "dignus", worthy, the same root as "dignity" and "disdain".

senses.def: do something that one considers beneath one's dignity, often in a condescending way
senses.ex: The famous chef barely deigned to glance at the plates his apprentices had spent all afternoon preparing.

syn: condescend, stoop, lower oneself, vouchsafe, descend

origin: From "Deipnosophistai", a 3rd-century Greek work by Athenaeus, from "deipnon", dinner, and "sophistes", expert, picturing learned guests talking at table.

senses.def: person skilled in the art of dining and learned table conversation
senses.ex: A born deipnosophist, my uncle could carve a roast while explaining Byzantine politics and never lose the table's attention.

origin: From Latin "deicere", to throw down, from "de-", down, plus "iacere", to throw, so a dejected person feels cast down.

senses.def: make someone sad, gloomy, or discouraged, most often used as dejected
senses.ex: The rejection letters dejected him for a week, but by Monday he was polishing his portfolio for the next round.

origin: From Old French "dejection", from Latin "dejectio", a casting down, so a dejected person feels thrown down in spirit.

senses.def: sadness and low spirits, especially after disappointment
senses.ex: After losing the final by one point, the team filed onto the bus in silent dejection and stared out the windows.

origin: From Middle French "délectable", based on Latin "delectare", to delight. It shares its source with the English word "delight".

senses.def: delicious and very pleasing to taste or smell
senses.ex: The bakery's delectable almond pastries usually sell out within an hour of the shop opening on Saturday mornings.

senses.def: delightful or highly attractive
senses.ex: The critic praised the play's delectable wit, which kept the audience chuckling from the first scene to the curtain.

senses.def: delicious food or other delightful thing, usually plural
senses.ex: The holiday market offered a table of delectables, from spiced honey cakes to candied orange peel dipped in chocolate.

origin: From Old French "delectation", enjoyment, from Latin "delectare", to delight or charm, which is also the source of "delight".

senses.def: great pleasure or enjoyment, often used in a lightly formal way
senses.ex: The chef prepared seven tiny courses for the delectation of guests who had waited months for a reservation.

origin: From Latin "delegare", to send away or entrust, from "de-", away, plus "legare", to send as an envoy, the root of "legate".

senses.def: person chosen to represent others, especially at a conference or convention
senses.ex: Each state sent delegates to the convention, where they argued for three days over the party's platform.

senses.def: give a task or responsibility to someone else, usually someone with less authority
senses.ex: A good team captain learns to delegate, trusting teammates to run drills instead of doing everything herself.

senses.def: choose someone to act as one's representative
senses.ex: The union delegated two experienced members to negotiate the new contract with management.

origin: From Greek "deleterios", harmful, from "deleter", a destroyer. Despite the look, it is not related to "delete".

senses.def: causing harm or damage, often in a gradual or unexpected way
senses.ex: Researchers found that the pesticide had a deleterious effect on bee colonies, weakening their ability to navigate home.

origin: From Latin "deliberare", to weigh carefully, from "de-", thoroughly, plus "librare", to weigh, from "libra", a balance or set of scales.

senses.def: done on purpose rather than by accident
senses.ex: The referee ruled that the trip was deliberate and showed the defender a red card.

senses.def: slow, careful, and unhurried in speech or movement
senses.ex: The old carpenter worked in a deliberate rhythm, measuring each board twice before making a single cut.

senses.def: think about or discuss something carefully before reaching a decision
senses.ex: The jury deliberated for two full days before returning a verdict of not guilty.

origin: From French "délimiter", from Late Latin "delimitare", to mark out the limits, from "de-", plus "limitare", to bound, from "limes", boundary.

senses.def: set or mark the limits or boundaries of something
senses.ex: The new policy clearly delimits which areas of the park are open to dogs and which are reserved for nesting birds.

origin: From Latin "delineare", to sketch out, from "de-", plus "linea", line, so to delineate is to trace something in lines.

senses.def: describe or explain something precisely and in detail
senses.ex: The report delineates the steps the city must take to reduce flooding in low-lying neighborhoods.

senses.def: draw or mark the outline or boundary of something
senses.ex: Survey markers delineate the border between the two farms, though the fence has drifted over the years.

origin: From Latin "deliquescere", to melt away, from "de-" and "liquescere", to become liquid, a relative of the word "liquid".

senses.def: become liquid by absorbing moisture from the air
senses.ex: Left uncovered on the humid lab bench, the calcium chloride crystals began to deliquesce into a small clear puddle.

senses.def: melt away or gradually dissolve, often figuratively
senses.ex: Her careful composure seemed to deliquesce the moment she heard her brother's voice on the crackling phone line.

origin: From Latin "delirium", madness, from "delirare", to be deranged, literally to go out of the furrow, from "de", off, and "lira", furrow.

senses.def: acute confused mental state, often with hallucinations, caused by fever, illness, or drugs
senses.ex: In the delirium of a high fever, the patient insisted that the nurses were old classmates visiting from overseas.

senses.def: wild, frenzied excitement or joy
senses.ex: The city erupted in delirium when the home team scored in the last minute to win its first championship.

origin: From Latin "deludere", to mock or deceive, from "de-" and "ludere", to make sport of. The word "ludicrous" comes from the same root.

senses.def: deceive someone, often oneself, into believing something false
senses.ex: Investors deluded themselves into thinking the housing boom would last forever and borrowed far more than they could repay.

origin: From Old French "deluge", from Latin "diluvium", flood, from "diluere", to wash away.

senses.def: severe flood or exceptionally heavy rainfall
senses.ex: The overnight deluge washed out the only bridge into town and left dozens of farms under muddy water.

senses.def: overwhelming quantity of something arriving at once
senses.ex: The senator's office received a deluge of angry letters within days of the controversial vote on water rights.

senses.def: overwhelm with a great quantity of something
senses.ex: After the viral video, the tiny bakery was deluged with orders from customers in three different countries.

senses.def: flood an area with water
senses.ex: Melting snow and spring rain deluged the lower fields, forcing the farmers to move their cattle to higher ground.

origin: From Latin "delusio", a deceiving, from "deludere", to mock or deceive, built on "ludere", to play or make sport.

senses.def: false belief held firmly despite clear evidence against it
senses.ex: He clung to the delusion that his unfinished novel would make him rich, despite forty polite rejection letters.

senses.def: state of being deceived or misled
senses.ex: Years of flattery from his advisers kept the aging dictator living in delusion about how much the public adored him.

origin: From "delude" plus "-ive". "Delude" comes from Latin "deludere", to mock or deceive, from "ludere", to play, so something delusive plays a trick on you.

senses.def: giving a false impression or raising hopes that have no basis in reality
senses.ex: The startup's early sales created a delusive sense of security that vanished when its largest customer canceled the contract.

origin: From Old English "delfan", to dig, a Germanic word, so delving into a subject is digging beneath its surface.

senses.def: search deeply and carefully into a subject, record, or problem
senses.ex: The graduate student delved into decades of shipping ledgers to learn how the port survived the blockade.

senses.def: reach into a bag, pocket, or container to find something
senses.ex: At the toll booth, Marcus delved into his coat pocket, hunting for the last few quarters he owned.

origin: From Greek "demagogos", leader of the people, from "demos", people, plus "agogos", leading. It began as a neutral term in ancient Athens.

senses.def: political leader who gains power by stirring up people's fears, prejudices, and emotions rather than by reasoned argument
senses.ex: The demagogue blamed every local problem on immigrants, and the angry crowd cheered each new accusation.

senses.def: talk about an issue in a way that exploits emotions and prejudice for political gain
senses.ex: Both candidates demagogued the crime statistics, ignoring that rates had actually fallen for a decade.

origin: A back-formation from "demarcation", from Spanish "demarcación", from "marcar", to mark, first used for the line dividing Spanish and Portuguese claims in 1493.

senses.def: set or mark the boundaries or limits of an area
senses.ex: Orange cones demarcated the lane reserved for runners during the city marathon.

senses.def: separate or clearly distinguish one thing from another
senses.ex: The essay carefully demarcates the author's own views from those of the critics she summarizes.

syn: delimit, mark out, bound, define, delineate

origin: From Spanish "demarcación" and Portuguese "demarcação", used for the 1493 line dividing the New World between them, from "marcar", to mark.

senses.def: clear boundary or distinction separating two areas, groups, or ideas
senses.ex: In many small companies, the demarcation between marketing and sales disappears because the same two people handle both jobs.

senses.def: act of officially marking or fixing a boundary
senses.ex: The demarcation of the border took surveyors three years, as they mapped every river bend between the two countries.

origin: From "de-", down, plus "mean", lowly or base, on the model of "debase". An older, unrelated "demean", to conduct oneself, gave us "demeanor".

senses.def: cause someone to lose dignity or the respect of others
senses.ex: She refused to demean herself by answering the anonymous insults posted under her article.

origin: From Middle English "demenen", to handle or manage, from Old French "demener", to guide or conduct, from "mener", to lead. Your demeanor is how you conduct yourself.

senses.def: person's outward manner, shown through expression, posture, and tone of voice
senses.ex: Despite the turbulence, the flight attendant's calm demeanor kept the nervous passengers in the cabin from panicking.

origin: From "dement", from Latin "dementare", to drive mad, built on "de-", away from, and "mens", mind, so it literally means out of one's mind.

senses.def: wildly irrational or crazed, often in a frightening or absurd way
senses.ex: The film's villain hatches a demented scheme to flood the city and hold its drinking water for ransom.

senses.def: affected by dementia, a use now widely considered insensitive
senses.ex: Older medical records often describe patients as demented, a label that most doctors today replace with a specific diagnosis.

origin: From Old French "demeine", from Latin "dominicus", belonging to a lord, from "dominus", master. It is a doublet of "domain", and its silent "s" was never etymological.

senses.def: land attached to a manor and kept for the owner's own use
senses.ex: The medieval lord's demesne included the best wheat fields, which his tenants were obliged to plow before tending their own.

senses.def: region or realm over which someone has control or influence
senses.ex: The head librarian treated the rare book room as a private demesne, admitting only scholars who had earned trust.

origin: From French "demi-monde", literally half-world, from "demi", half, and "monde", world, possibly coined by Alexandre Dumas fils as the title of his 1855 play.

senses.def: group on the fringes of respectable society, often glamorous but of doubtful reputation
senses.ex: The novelist spent his twenties among the demimonde of late-night gamblers, faded actors, and charming swindlers in Havana.

senses.def: class of women in nineteenth-century France supported by wealthy lovers
senses.ex: Courtesans of the Parisian demimonde often hosted salons where bankers, poets, and politicians mingled behind closed doors.

origin: From Middle French "démise", past participle of "démettre", to put down or relinquish. It first meant a legal transfer of property, and "death" grew from that as a euphemism.

senses.def: end or downfall of something, such as a business, institution, or idea
senses.ex: The rise of streaming services hastened the demise of the neighborhood video rental store across most of the country.

senses.def: person's death, especially as described in formal or literary language
senses.ex: After the founder's sudden demise, the family argued for months over who should run the vineyard.

origin: From Greek "demiourgos", public worker or skilled craftsman, from "demos", people, and "ergon", work. Despite its look, it has no link to the prefix "demi-".

senses.def: in Plato's philosophy, the divine craftsman who shapes the physical world from existing matter
senses.ex: In the Timaeus, Plato imagines a demiurge arranging chaotic matter into an ordered cosmos according to eternal patterns.

senses.def: in Gnostic belief, lesser god who created the flawed material world
senses.ex: Gnostic teachers blamed human suffering on a demiurge, an inferior deity who trapped souls inside the material world.

senses.def: person or force with immense creative or controlling power
senses.ex: Critics called the studio head a demiurge of Hollywood, someone who could create a star with a single phone call.

origin: From Greek "demos", people, and "-graphia", writing or description, so demography is literally a written description of the people.

senses.def: statistical study of human populations, including size, age, births, deaths, and migration
senses.ex: Her course in demography showed how falling birth rates reshape housing, schools, and pension systems over several decades.

senses.def: makeup of a particular population by age, origin, income, and similar traits
senses.ex: The demography of the coastal town changed sharply once retirees began buying the old fishing cottages.

origin: From Old French "demolition", from Latin "demolitio", a tearing down, related to "demoliri", to tear down, the source of English "demolish".

senses.def: deliberate tearing down or destruction of a building or other structure
senses.ex: Demolition of the abandoned stadium began at dawn, and by noon only a ring of broken concrete remained.

senses.def: complete defeat or thorough dismantling of an opponent or argument
senses.ex: The debate team's demolition of the opposing case took six minutes and left the judges visibly impressed.

origin: From Latin "demonstrativus", pointing out, from "demonstrare", to show, from "de-", fully, plus "monstrare", to point out or show.

senses.def: serving as clear evidence or proof of something, often used with "of"
senses.ex: Her quick apology was demonstrative of how much the friendship meant to her.

senses.def: openly showing feelings, especially affection
senses.ex: Her family was warm and demonstrative, greeting even distant cousins with long hugs and kisses on both cheeks.

senses.def: in grammar, pointing out a particular person or thing, as "this" or "those" do
senses.ex: In the phrase "that book," the word "that" is a demonstrative adjective identifying which book is meant.

origin: From French "démoraliser", built from "dé-", removing, and "moral", so to demoralize someone is to take away their moral strength and spirit.

senses.def: cause someone to lose confidence, hope, or enthusiasm
senses.ex: Repeated budget cuts demoralized the nursing staff, and several experienced employees left for jobs at other hospitals.

origin: From Greek "demotikos", of the common people, from "demotes", commoner, from "demos", the people.

senses.def: relating to ordinary people, especially their everyday, informal language
senses.ex: The poet mixed demotic street slang with classical allusions, so readers met both rap lyrics and Homer in one stanza.

origin: From Old French "demorer", to delay or linger, from Latin "demorari", from "morari", to delay, from "mora", delay; the sense moved from hesitating to objecting.

senses.def: raise objections or show reluctance to do something
senses.ex: When the committee asked him to chair the event, he demurred, saying he lacked the time to do it well.

senses.def: expression of doubt or objection, often in the phrase "without demur"
senses.ex: The students accepted the extra assignment without demur, which surprised their usually argumentative teacher.

syn: object, protest, balk, hesitate, take exception

origin: From Anglo-Norman "de mure port", of mature bearing, from Old French "meur", mature, from Latin "maturus", ripe, so a demure person looks serious and composed.

senses.def: quiet, modest, and reserved in manner or appearance, sometimes in an affected way
senses.ex: In the photograph she looks demure, hands folded and eyes lowered, though friends remember her as the loudest person in any room.

origin: From "demur" plus "-al". "Demur" comes through Old French "demorer" from Latin "demorari", to linger, from "morari", to delay, so a demurral holds things back for a moment.

senses.def: expression of mild objection, reluctance, or hesitation
senses.ex: Over the treasurer's faint demurral, the committee approved the expensive renovation of the town hall.

origin: From Latin "denigrare", to blacken, from "de-", thoroughly, plus "nigrare", to blacken, from "niger", black, so to denigrate is to blacken a reputation.

senses.def: criticize someone or something unfairly in a way that makes them seem worthless
senses.ex: Instead of answering her arguments, the rival campaign tried to denigrate her by mocking her accent and her hometown.

origin: From Old French "deinzein", one living within, from "deinz", within, from Late Latin "de intus", from inside, so a denizen belongs inside a place.

senses.def: person, animal, or plant that lives in or regularly visits a particular place
senses.ex: Octopuses and anglerfish are among the strange denizens of the deep ocean that scientists are only beginning to study.

origin: From Late Latin "denotatio", from "denotare", to mark out, from "de-", completely, and "notare", to mark, so a denotation is the meaning a word plainly marks.

senses.def: literal, dictionary meaning of a word, apart from its emotional associations
senses.ex: The denotation of "thrifty" and "stingy" is nearly the same, but their connotations differ sharply.

senses.def: act of indicating something by a sign, symbol, or name
senses.ex: Early mapmakers developed a simple denotation of hills and marshes using small symbols that any traveler could read.

origin: From Latin "denotare", to mark out, from "de-", completely, plus "notare", to mark, from "nota", a mark or sign.

senses.def: be a sign of something or indicate it
senses.ex: On the trail map, a black diamond denotes a steep slope suitable only for expert skiers.

senses.def: refer to something directly as a word's literal meaning, apart from its associations
senses.ex: The word "home" denotes a place where one lives, but it often suggests warmth and belonging as well.

origin: From French "dénouement", an untying, from "dénouer", to untie, from Latin "nodus", knot, so the denouement unties the knot of a plot.

senses.def: final part of a story in which the plot's mysteries and conflicts are resolved
senses.ex: In the denouement, the detective gathers everyone in the library and explains exactly how the forged will was made.

senses.def: outcome or resolution of a complicated real-life situation
senses.ex: The long legal battle reached its denouement when the two companies quietly agreed to share the patent.

origin: From Old French "denoncier", from Latin "denuntiare", to announce officially or threaten, from "de-", plus "nuntiare", to announce, from "nuntius", messenger.

senses.def: publicly declare someone or something to be wrong, evil, or harmful
senses.ex: Human rights groups denounced the arrests as an attempt to silence journalists before the election.

senses.def: inform against someone, especially to the authorities
senses.ex: During the purges, frightened neighbors denounced one another to the secret police to protect themselves.

origin: From Latin "denudare", to lay bare, from "de-", completely, plus "nudare", to strip, from "nudus", naked.

senses.def: stripped of a natural covering such as trees, plants, soil, or leaves
senses.ex: After years of logging, the denuded hillsides washed away in the first heavy rains, burying the village road in mud.

senses.def: deprived of something important
senses.ex: The team, denuded of its three best players by injury, struggled to score even a single goal.

origin: From Latin "depictio", from "depingere", to paint or portray, from "de-", fully, plus "pingere", to paint.

senses.def: representation of something in a picture, words, or film
senses.ex: The film's depiction of life aboard a whaling ship was praised for showing the dangers and the boredom alike.

origin: From Latin "deplere", to empty out, from "de-", un-, plus "plere", to fill. It began as a medical term in the 1700s.

senses.def: use up or greatly reduce the supply of something
senses.ex: A week of hot, dry weather depleted the town's reservoir, and officials banned watering lawns.

syn: exhaust, drain, use up, consume, diminish

origin: From Latin "deplorare", to weep over or lament, from "de-", thoroughly, plus "plorare", to wail.

senses.def: strongly disapprove of something and regret it
senses.ex: The editorial deplored the city's decision to tear down the historic theater for a parking garage.

origin: From Middle French "deportement", conduct, linked to Old French "deporter", to behave, and ultimately Latin "portare", to carry, so deportment is how you carry yourself.

senses.def: way a person stands, moves, and carries themselves, especially with trained poise
senses.ex: The ballet academy taught deportment alongside dance, insisting that students walk with straight backs and level shoulders.

senses.def: conduct or behavior judged by standards of politeness and propriety
senses.ex: The old report cards graded each pupil on deportment as well as arithmetic, spelling, and penmanship.

origin: From Latin "depositio", a putting down, from "deponere", to lay down or set aside, from "de-", down, plus "ponere", to place.

senses.def: sworn statement or testimony given outside a courtroom and recorded for later use
senses.ex: During her deposition, the witness described the accident while lawyers from both sides took notes.

senses.def: removal of someone from a position of power, such as a ruler from a throne
senses.ex: The king's deposition by his own generals ended three centuries of rule by his family.

senses.def: natural process of laying down material such as sand, mud, or minerals
senses.ex: The deposition of silt at the river's mouth has built a fertile delta over thousands of years.

origin: From "deprave", from Latin "depravare", to twist or corrupt, from "pravus", crooked, so a depraved person's morals have been bent out of shape.

senses.def: morally corrupt or wicked, especially in a shocking or perverse way
senses.ex: The prosecutor described the poisoning of the village well as a depraved act committed purely for profit.

origin: Linked to "deprave", from Latin "depravare", to distort or corrupt, from "pravus", crooked, so depravity is a moral nature gone crooked.

senses.def: state of extreme moral corruption or wickedness
senses.ex: The documentary exposed the depravity of traffickers who sold forged medicine to desperate families during the epidemic.

senses.def: particular act or habit that is morally corrupt or wicked
senses.ex: The inquiry's final report catalogued the prison guards' depravities in details too disturbing to read aloud at the hearing.

origin: From Latin "deprecari", to pray against or try to ward off, from "de-", away, plus "precari", to pray.

senses.def: express disapproval of something
senses.ex: The principal deprecated the growing habit of students filming fights instead of reporting them.

senses.def: play down the importance or value of something, especially one's own work
senses.ex: She tends to deprecate her own achievements, describing her national science award as a lucky break.

syn: disapprove of, deplore, criticize, condemn, belittle

origin: From "deprecate" plus "-ory". "Deprecate" comes from Latin "deprecari", to ward off by prayer, from "de-", away, and "precari", to pray.

senses.def: expressing disapproval or belittling someone or something
senses.ex: The senior partner's deprecatory remark about the intern's proposal silenced the room before anyone could discuss its merits.

senses.def: apologetic, as if trying to ward off criticism
senses.ex: With a deprecatory shrug, the chef admitted the soufflé had collapsed and offered everyone a second dessert instead.

origin: From Late Latin "depretiare", to lower the price of, from "de-", down, and "pretium", price, the same root found in "appreciate".

senses.def: decrease in value over time, especially through use or market changes
senses.ex: A new car begins to depreciate the moment it leaves the lot, losing thousands of dollars within a year.

senses.def: reduce an asset's recorded value gradually over its useful life
senses.ex: The bakery depreciates its industrial ovens over ten years, which lowers its taxable income each spring.

senses.def: belittle or treat as having little worth
senses.ex: The surgeon tended to depreciate her own achievements, mentioning her medical awards only when someone asked directly.

origin: From Late Latin "depraedari", to plunder, from "de-", thoroughly, plus "praedari", to plunder, from "praeda", booty, the root of "prey".

senses.def: plunder, raid, or lay waste to a place
senses.ex: Bands of pirates depredated the coastal towns each summer, carrying off grain, livestock, and silver.

origin: From Middle French "déprédation", from Latin "depraedatio", plundering, built on "praeda", booty or prey, the same root that gives English "prey".

senses.def: act of plundering, raiding, or causing widespread damage, often used in the plural
senses.ex: Coastal villages built watchtowers to guard against the depredations of pirates who raided their harbors each summer.

senses.def: damage or loss caused to crops or livestock by wild animals
senses.ex: Ranchers in the valley sought compensation for wolf depredation after losing a dozen calves during the winter.

origin: From Middle French "députation", from Late Latin "deputatio", from "deputare", to assign or appoint, the same root that gives us "deputy".

senses.def: group of people chosen to act or speak on behalf of a larger body
senses.ex: A deputation of farmers traveled to the capital to present their complaints about water rights to the minister.

origin: From French "déraciner", to uproot, from "dé-", away, plus "racine", root, from Latin "radix", root.

senses.def: tear someone away from their native culture, home, or social setting
senses.ex: Years of war deracinated whole villages, leaving families scattered across camps with no memory of a settled home.

senses.def: pull up a plant or tree by the roots
senses.ex: The hurricane deracinated ancient oaks along the boulevard and tossed them across the flooded road.

origin: From French "déranger", from Old French "desrengier", to throw out of line, from "des-", apart, plus "reng", line or row, the source of "rank".

senses.def: drive someone insane or make their mind unbalanced, usually used in the passive
senses.ex: The isolation of the long polar winter seemed to derange the stranded explorer, who began talking to the walls.

senses.def: throw something into disorder or stop it from working properly
senses.ex: A sudden power surge deranged the factory's control systems, and the assembly line ground to a halt.

senses.def: upset or disrupt someone's plans or arrangements
senses.ex: The unexpected snowstorm deranged our travel plans, forcing us to spend two nights in a cramped airport hotel.

origin: From Latin "derelictus", completely abandoned, from "derelinquere", from "de-", completely, plus "relinquere", to leave behind.

senses.def: abandoned and left to fall into ruin
senses.ex: The derelict factory, its windows smashed and roof caved in, had become a home for pigeons and stray cats.

senses.def: shamefully neglectful of one's duty
senses.ex: The inspector was found derelict in his duties for approving buildings he had never actually visited.

senses.def: person without a home or job, a term now often considered insulting
senses.ex: The novel follows a once-famous pianist who ends up a derelict sleeping in the train station he used to tour from.

origin: From Latin "deridere", to laugh at or mock, from "de-", down, plus "ridere", to laugh.

senses.def: mock or ridicule someone or something with contempt
senses.ex: Critics derided the inventor's flying machine as a toy, until it carried a passenger across the bay.

syn: ridicule, mock, scorn, jeer at, scoff at

origin: From Latin "derisio", from "deridere", to laugh at, from "de-", down, plus "ridere", to laugh.

senses.def: contemptuous ridicule or mockery
senses.ex: The rookie's claim that he would win the championship was met with derision from the veteran players.

origin: From Latin "derisus", past participle of "deridere", to laugh at, plus "-ive", from "de-", down, plus "ridere", to laugh.

senses.def: expressing contempt or ridicule
senses.ex: When the speaker blamed the weather for the delays, a derisive laugh rippled through the audience.

origin: From Middle French "dérivation", from Latin "derivatio", from "derivare", to draw off water from a stream, from "de-", from, plus "rivus", stream.

senses.def: the source or origin from which something, especially a word, comes
senses.ex: The dictionary gives a Greek derivation for the word, tracing it back to a term for a theater mask.

senses.def: the forming of a new word from an existing word or root, often by adding prefixes or suffixes
senses.ex: In linguistics class we studied derivation, seeing how 'happy' becomes 'unhappiness' through added prefixes and suffixes.

senses.def: step-by-step logical process of reaching a formula or conclusion from basic principles
senses.ex: The professor filled three whiteboards with the derivation of the equation before anyone understood where it came from.

origin: From Latin "derivativus", from "derivare", to draw off or derive, from "de-", away, plus "rivus", stream, so a derivative is drawn from another source.

senses.def: imitating the work of others and lacking originality
senses.ex: Reviewers called the band's second album derivative, little more than a copy of the bands they grew up idolizing.

senses.def: something that comes from or is developed out of another thing
senses.ex: Heroin is a derivative of morphine, which is itself extracted from the opium poppy.

senses.def: in mathematics, the rate at which a function's value changes as its input changes
senses.ex: In calculus class we learned that the derivative of a car's position over time gives its speed.

senses.def: financial contract whose value depends on an underlying asset such as a stock or currency
senses.ex: Banks that traded risky derivatives lost billions when housing prices collapsed in 2008.

origin: From Latin "derivare", to draw off water, from "de-", away, plus "rivus", stream. It is unrelated to "arrive".

senses.def: get something such as pleasure, benefit, or information from a source
senses.ex: My grandfather derives great satisfaction from growing tomatoes that taste better than anything in the store.

senses.def: come or develop from a particular source
senses.ex: The word "salary" derives from the Latin for salt, though historians still debate how a word for salt came to mean wages.

senses.def: work out a result or formula by logical reasoning
senses.ex: Using only basic geometry, the students derived the formula for the area of a circle.

origin: From "derogate", to detract, plus "-ive"; "derogate" comes from Latin "derogare", to repeal part of a law, from "de-", away, plus "rogare", to propose a law.

senses.def: expressing a low opinion of someone or something, disparaging
senses.ex: The coach apologized for the derogative remarks he had made about the opposing team's fans.

origin: From Late Latin "derogatorius", from Latin "derogare", to repeal part of a law or take away from, from "de-", away, plus "rogare", to ask.

senses.def: expressing a low opinion of someone or something in a disrespectful or insulting way
senses.ex: The coach was suspended after making derogatory remarks about the referee's eyesight during a televised interview.

origin: From Middle English "daring do", meaning daring to do, a verb phrase that the poet Edmund Spenser mistook for a noun meaning brave deeds.

senses.def: bold, adventurous action, often with a touch of recklessness or showiness
senses.ex: The film is packed with derring-do, from rooftop chases to a leap across a collapsing bridge.

origin: From Medieval Latin "discantus", a song sung apart, from "dis-", apart, plus "cantus", song, so a descant is a tune set apart above the main one.

senses.def: decorative melody sung or played above the main tune of a piece
senses.ex: On the last verse of the hymn, the sopranos soared into a bright descant above the rest of the choir.

senses.def: talk or write at length about a subject
senses.ex: At dinner my uncle would descant on the history of every wine he poured, whether or not anyone had asked.

origin: From Middle English "descrien", partly from Old French "descrier", to proclaim, a doublet of "decry", and possibly influenced by Old French "descrivre", to describe.

senses.def: catch sight of something, especially something distant or hard to see
senses.ex: From the crow's nest, the sailor could just descry a thin line of smoke rising from the island.

syn: glimpse, spot, discern, espy, make out

origin: Formed from "de-", undoing, plus the stem of "consecrate", which comes from Latin "sacrare", to make holy, from "sacer", sacred.

senses.def: damage or disrespect something sacred or deeply valued
senses.ex: Vandals desecrated the old cemetery, knocking over headstones and spraying slogans on the chapel walls.

senses.def: spoil something beautiful or treasured through careless or destructive change
senses.ex: Locals complained that the new glass tower desecrated the skyline of the medieval town.

origin: From Latin "desiccare", to dry up completely, from "de-", thoroughly, plus "siccare", to dry, from "siccus", dry.

senses.def: remove all the moisture from something, often to preserve it
senses.ex: The museum desiccates wildflowers in trays of silica gel so their colors survive for decades.

syn: dry, dehydrate, parch, dry out, wither

origin: From "desiccate", from Latin "desiccare", to dry up completely, from "de-", thoroughly, plus "siccus", dry.

senses.def: completely dried out, with all moisture removed
senses.ex: Archaeologists found desiccated dates and figs in the tomb, still recognizable after three thousand years in the desert.

senses.def: lacking energy, warmth, or interest
senses.ex: The professor's desiccated lectures, read word for word from yellowed notes, put half the class to sleep.

origin: From Latin "desideratum", something desired, from "desiderare", to long for or miss. The plural is "desiderata".

senses.def: something that is needed or wanted, often regarded as essential
senses.ex: For the search committee, experience with community outreach was the chief desideratum in a new library director.

origin: From Middle French "desister", from Latin "desistere", to stand apart or leave off, from "de-", away, plus "sistere", to stand.

senses.def: stop doing something, especially when ordered or asked to
senses.ex: The company received a letter demanding that it desist from using the rival brand's logo on its packaging.

origin: From Latin "desolatus", past participle of "desolare", to leave alone or lay waste, from "de-", completely, plus "solus", alone.

senses.def: empty of people and life, giving a bleak and dreary impression
senses.ex: The desolate mining town had boarded windows, a silent church, and tumbleweeds drifting down the main street.

senses.def: feeling utterly miserable, lonely, and without hope
senses.ex: After her best friend moved overseas, Maya felt desolate and spent weekends wandering the mall alone.

senses.def: leave someone feeling wretched and forlorn, or lay a place waste
senses.ex: The news of the shipwreck desolated the fishing village, where nearly every family had lost someone at sea.

origin: From Late Latin "despicabilis", from "despicari", to look down on, from "de-", down, plus "specere", to look, so it means fit to be looked down on.

senses.def: so morally bad or cruel that it deserves strong contempt
senses.ex: Stealing donations meant for the flood victims was a despicable act that shocked the entire town.

origin: From Old French "despire", from Latin "despicere", to look down on, from "de-", down, plus "specere", to look.

senses.def: feel intense dislike and contempt for someone or something
senses.ex: He had always despised bullies, so he stepped in when older students cornered the new boy by the lockers.

origin: From "despoil", from Old French "despoillier", from Latin "despoliare", to rob, from "de-", plus "spoliare", to strip, from "spolium", booty, the root of "spoils".

senses.def: robbed of valuable possessions or stripped of natural beauty by force or destruction
senses.ex: The despoiled temple had lost every gold statue and jeweled lamp to the invading army.

senses.def: badly damaged or ruined, especially of land or nature
senses.ex: Miners left behind a despoiled valley of poisoned streams and bare, scarred hillsides.

origin: From "despoil", to strip by force, plus "-er", one who does; "despoil" comes from Latin "despoliare", to rob, from "spolium", booty.

senses.def: person or group that plunders or ruins something valuable, especially land or treasures
senses.ex: Environmental groups branded the logging company a despoiler of the ancient forest.

senses.def: one who robs or loots, especially by force
senses.ex: The museum labels the empty pedestals with the names of the despoilers who carried off each statue.

origin: From Latin "despondere", to give up or lose heart, from "de-", away, plus "spondere", to promise.

senses.def: low spirits caused by loss of hope or courage
senses.ex: After the third rejection letter arrived, a deep despondency settled over the young novelist for weeks.

origin: From Latin "despondens", form of "despondere", to give up or lose heart, from "de-", away, plus "spondere", to promise.

senses.def: in low spirits from loss of hope or courage
senses.ex: The despondent team sat silently in the locker room after losing the championship on a last-second goal.

origin: From Greek "despotes", master or lord of a household, which came to mean any ruler with total power.

senses.def: ruler who holds absolute power, especially one who uses it cruelly
senses.ex: The despot jailed anyone who criticized him and renamed the capital city in his own honor.

syn: tyrant, dictator, autocrat, oppressor, absolute ruler

origin: From Greek "despotikos", of a master, from "despotes", master or lord, via French "despotique".

senses.def: using absolute power in a cruel, unfair, or oppressive way
senses.ex: Under the despotic regime, newspapers printed only what the palace allowed and elections were a sham.

origin: From French "despotisme", from "despote", tyrant, from Greek "despotes", master or lord of a household.

senses.def: rule by a single person with absolute power, usually exercised cruelly or unjustly
senses.ex: The revolutionaries promised to end decades of despotism and hold the country's first free elections.

senses.def: harsh, absolute control exercised by someone over others in any setting
senses.ex: Workers complained about the manager's petty despotism, which included timing their bathroom breaks.

origin: From Latin "destitutus", abandoned, from "destituere", to forsake, from "de-", away, plus "statuere", to set or place, so the destitute are left with nothing.

senses.def: so poor that one lacks food, shelter, or other basic necessities
senses.ex: The flood left hundreds of families destitute, sleeping in school gyms with only the clothes they wore.

senses.def: completely lacking in a particular quality or thing, used with "of"
senses.ex: The final report was destitute of any real evidence, relying entirely on rumors and assumptions.

origin: From Latin "destitutio", abandonment, from "destituere", to forsake, from "de-", away, plus "statuere", to set up or place.

senses.def: extreme poverty in which a person lacks food, shelter, and other basic necessities
senses.ex: The factory closures pushed hundreds of families into destitution, and the food bank's lines stretched around the block.

origin: From Latin "desuetudo", disuse, from "desuescere", to become unaccustomed, from "de-", un-, plus "suescere", to grow used to.

senses.def: state of no longer being used or practiced
senses.ex: The old law against selling goods on Sundays had fallen into desuetude long before the council officially repealed it.

origin: From Latin "desultorius", superficial, from "desultor", a circus rider who leapt from one galloping horse to another, from "de-", down, plus "salire", to jump.

senses.def: lacking a plan, purpose, or enthusiasm, moving randomly from one thing to another
senses.ex: After the exams ended, the class drifted into a desultory conversation about summer jobs, movies, and nothing in particular.

origin: From "detach", from French "détacher", to unfasten, the reverse of "attacher", to attach.

senses.def: emotionally distant and uninvolved
senses.ex: Ever since the accident, he has seemed strangely detached, nodding along without really hearing anything we say.

senses.def: free from bias or personal feeling, impartial
senses.ex: A good referee must stay detached, calling fouls the same way no matter which team the crowd supports.

senses.def: separate and not connected, especially of a house not joined to another
senses.ex: They traded their city apartment for a detached house with a garden and no neighbors on the other side of the wall.

origin: From French "détachement", from "détacher", to unfasten or separate, the reverse of "attacher", to attach.

senses.def: state of being emotionally distant or uninvolved
senses.ex: She watched the chaos at the airport gate with amused detachment, having already decided to take the train.

senses.def: ability to judge fairly without being swayed by personal feelings
senses.ex: Scientists try to examine their own data with detachment, even when the results threaten a favorite theory.

senses.def: group of soldiers or ships sent away from the main force for a special task
senses.ex: A small detachment of engineers was sent ahead to repair the bridge before the army crossed.

origin: From French "détente", a loosening or relaxation, from "détendre", to slacken, as one would slacken a tight bowstring.

senses.def: easing of hostility or strained relations, especially between rival nations
senses.ex: The two governments reached a detente, reopening embassies and resuming trade after years of bitter sanctions.

origin: From Latin "deterrere", to frighten off, from "de-", away, plus "terrere", to frighten, the root of "terror".

senses.def: discourage someone from doing something, especially by making them fear the consequences
senses.ex: Bright lights and a barking dog are often enough to deter burglars from choosing a particular house.

senses.def: prevent something from happening
senses.ex: A coat of special paint helps deter rust on the bridge's steel cables.

syn: discourage, dissuade, put off, daunt, inhibit

origin: From Late Latin "deteriorare", to make worse, from Latin "deterior", worse.

senses.def: become progressively worse in quality, condition, or value
senses.ex: Without regular maintenance, the old wooden pier deteriorated until the city had to fence it off.

origin: From French "déterminant", from "déterminer", to determine, from Latin "determinare", to set limits, from "terminus", boundary.

senses.def: factor that strongly influences or decides the nature or outcome of something
senses.ex: Researchers argue that sleep is a major determinant of how well teenagers perform on exams.

origin: From Latin "determinatus", past participle of "determinare", to set limits, from "de-", completely, plus "terminus", boundary.

senses.def: having exact and fixed limits, form, or value
senses.ex: The judge imposed a determinate sentence of six years, so the defendant knew exactly when he would be released.

origin: From French "déterminisme", from "déterminer", to determine, from Latin "determinare", to set limits, from "terminus", boundary.

senses.def: philosophical view that every event, including human choice, is fully caused by earlier events
senses.ex: In philosophy seminar we debated whether determinism leaves any room for moral responsibility or genuine free will.

senses.def: belief that a single factor, such as genes or geography, decides how people or societies turn out
senses.ex: The historian rejected geographic determinism, arguing that climate alone could not explain why some empires rose.

origin: From Latin "deterrens", frightening off, present participle of "deterrere", from "de-", away, plus "terrere", to frighten.

senses.def: something that discourages people from an action, especially through fear of the consequences
senses.ex: Heavy fines have proved an effective deterrent to drivers who park in spaces reserved for ambulances.

senses.def: serving to discourage or prevent an action
senses.ex: The museum installed cameras mainly for their deterrent effect, since few thieves risk being filmed.

origin: From French "détester", from Latin "detestari", to curse while calling the gods to witness, from "de-" plus "testis", witness.

senses.def: dislike someone or something intensely
senses.ex: My younger brother detests mushrooms and will pick every tiny slice off his pizza before taking a bite.

origin: From French "détonation", from Latin "detonare", to thunder forth, from "de-" plus "tonare", to thunder.

senses.def: act of setting off an explosive, or the violent explosion itself
senses.ex: Engineers cleared the area for a mile before the controlled detonation brought the old stadium crashing down.

origin: From Latin "detractio", a taking away, from "detrahere", to pull down or away, from "de-", down, plus "trahere", to draw or pull.

senses.def: unfair criticism that damages someone's reputation or lessens their worth
senses.ex: The senator dismissed the newspaper's report as mere detraction by political enemies.

senses.def: reduction or taking away of something's value or quality
senses.ex: Lowering the admission standards was seen by alumni as a detraction from the university's prestige.

origin: From Latin "detrimentum", loss or damage, from "deterere", to rub away or wear down, from "de-", away, plus "terere", to rub.

senses.def: causing harm or damage
senses.ex: Doctors warn that staring at screens late at night can be detrimental to a teenager's sleep.

origin: From Latin "detritus", rubbed away, past participle of "deterere", to wear away, from "de-", away, plus "terere", to rub.

senses.def: scattered waste, debris, or leftover fragments after something is used or destroyed
senses.ex: The morning after the festival, volunteers swept up the detritus of paper cups, glow sticks, and trampled flyers.

senses.def: loose fragments of rock, sand, or organic matter worn away by natural processes
senses.ex: Glacial detritus piled up at the foot of the valley, forming long ridges of gravel and boulders.

origin: Latin for "god from the machine", a translation of a Greek phrase for the stage crane that lowered an actor playing a god to sort out the plot.

senses.def: sudden, improbable event or character that conveniently solves a seemingly hopeless problem in a story
senses.ex: Critics called the surprise inheritance a lazy deus ex machina that rescued the hero without any effort on his part.

senses.def: unexpected outside force or person that rescues a real situation at the last moment
senses.ex: The startup was days from bankruptcy when an anonymous investor arrived like a deus ex machina with fresh funding.

senses.def: in ancient Greek and Roman drama, a god lowered onto the stage by machinery to resolve the plot
senses.ex: In the final scene of the tragedy, a deus ex machina descended on a crane and ordered the feuding families to make peace.

syn: contrivance, plot device, gimmick, last-minute rescue

origin: From French "déviance", ultimately from Late Latin "deviare", to turn aside from the road, from "de-", off, plus "via", way.

senses.def: behavior that departs from accepted social rules or norms
senses.ex: The sociology course examines how different societies define deviance, from minor rudeness to serious crime.

origin: From Late Latin "deviare", to turn out of the way, from "de-", off, plus "via", road, so to deviate is to leave the road.

senses.def: move away from a planned course, route, or plan
senses.ex: The pilot had to deviate from the flight path to avoid a line of thunderstorms over the mountains.

senses.def: differ from what is normal, expected, or accepted
senses.ex: Any student whose project deviates from the assigned topic must get the teacher's approval first.

origin: From Medieval Latin "deviatio", from Late Latin "deviare", to turn aside, from "de-", off, plus "via", way.

senses.def: departure from what is normal, expected, planned, or accepted
senses.ex: Any deviation from the recipe, even an extra pinch of salt, would make the chef send the dish back.

senses.def: in statistics, the amount by which a value differs from an average or other reference value
senses.ex: A small standard deviation in the test scores showed that most students performed at about the same level.

origin: From Middle English "develrye", from "devil" plus the suffix "-ry", so it means the doings or behavior of a devil.

senses.def: playful or reckless mischief
senses.ex: There was a glint of devilry in the twins' eyes just before they hid their teacher's chalk inside the piano.

senses.def: cruel or wicked behavior
senses.ex: The villagers spoke in whispers about the devilry of the warlord who burned their fields every harvest.

origin: From Latin "devius", off the main road, from "de", off, plus "via", road, so devious thinking strays from the straight path.

senses.def: using sly, dishonest, or underhanded methods to get what one wants
senses.ex: The devious student forged his parents' signature on the report card and hoped no one would call home.

senses.def: not straight or direct, taking a winding or roundabout course
senses.ex: To avoid the traffic jam, our driver took a devious route through back lanes and farm roads.

origin: From Old French "desvuidier", to empty out, from "des-", out, plus "vuidier", to empty, the source of "void".

senses.def: completely lacking something, used with "of"
senses.ex: The moon's surface is devoid of air and water, so footprints left there decades ago remain perfectly sharp.

origin: From Latin "devolvere", to roll down, from "de-", down, plus "volvere", to roll, so power or duty rolls down to someone else.

senses.def: transfer power or responsibility from a central authority to a lower or local one
senses.ex: The national government agreed to devolve control of schools and hospitals to the regional parliament.

senses.def: pass to someone else as a duty, especially when the original holder cannot act
senses.ex: When the director fell ill, the task of finishing the film devolved on his young assistant.

senses.def: gradually decline or degenerate into a worse state
senses.ex: The town meeting devolved into a shouting match once the subject of parking fees came up.

syn: delegate, transfer, hand down, pass on, entrust

origin: From "devote" plus "-ee", ultimately from Latin "devovere", to vow or dedicate, from "de-" plus "vovere", to vow.

senses.def: person who is extremely enthusiastic about a particular activity, subject, or artist
senses.ex: A devotee of classic jazz, my uncle owns hundreds of vinyl records and can name every session drummer.

senses.def: faithful follower of a particular religion, god, or spiritual leader
senses.ex: Thousands of devotees gathered at the temple before dawn to offer flowers and prayers during the festival.

origin: From Latin "devotus", devoted, past participle of "devovere", to vow, from "de-", fully, plus "vovere", to vow. It is a doublet of "devote".

senses.def: deeply religious and committed to the practices of one's faith
senses.ex: My devout grandmother never missed morning prayers, even when she was in the hospital.

senses.def: sincerely and earnestly committed to a person, cause, or activity
senses.ex: As a devout fan of the team, he has attended every home game for thirty years.

origin: From Latin "dexteritas", skill, from "dexter", on the right, because most people are more skillful with their right hand.

senses.def: skill and ease in using the hands or body
senses.ex: Watchmakers need remarkable dexterity to fit gears smaller than a grain of rice into place.

senses.def: quickness and cleverness in thinking or handling situations
senses.ex: The diplomat showed great dexterity in steering the tense talks away from topics that might end them.

origin: From Latin "dexter", on the right side, skillful, plus "-ous", reflecting the old idea that the right hand is the skilled one.

senses.def: showing skill and quickness with the hands or body
senses.ex: The dexterous pastry chef folded hundreds of delicate dumplings in an hour without tearing a single wrapper.

senses.def: mentally quick and clever, especially in handling difficult situations
senses.ex: The dexterous negotiator found a compromise that let both unions claim victory without losing face.

origin: From French "diablerie", from "diable", devil, so it is a twin of the English word "devilry".

senses.def: black magic or dealings with the devil
senses.ex: The old woman's herbal cures led suspicious neighbors to accuse her of diablerie during the village's witch panic.

senses.def: wild, reckless, or devilish mischief
senses.ex: The comedian's act had a streak of diablerie, mocking every politician in the audience with gleeful abandon.

syn: sorcery, witchcraft, black magic, wizardry, devilry

origin: From Late Latin "diabolicus", from Greek "diabolos", devil or slanderer, from "diaballein", to slander, literally to throw across.

senses.def: extremely wicked or cruel, as if inspired by the devil
senses.ex: The prisoners described a diabolic system of punishments designed to break their spirits.

senses.def: relating to the devil or to devils
senses.ex: Medieval artists filled the margins of manuscripts with diabolic figures sporting horns, tails, and bat wings.

origin: From Late Latin "diabolicus", devilish, from Greek "diabolos", devil or slanderer, from "dia", across, plus "ballein", to throw.

senses.def: extremely wicked or cruel
senses.ex: The villain's diabolical plan was to poison the city's water supply and blame it on his rival.

senses.def: fiendishly clever, cunning, or difficult
senses.ex: The final puzzle in the escape room was diabolical, a locked box with no visible keyhole or seams.

origin: From Old French "diademe", from Latin "diadema", from Greek "diadema", a band worn around the head, from "diadein", to bind around.

senses.def: jeweled crown or headband worn as a sign of royalty
senses.ex: At the coronation, the archbishop placed a gold diadem set with rubies on the young queen's head.

origin: From Greek "dialektike", the art of debate, from "dialegesthai", to converse, from "dia", through, plus "legein", to speak.

senses.def: method of seeking truth by exchanging and testing opposing arguments
senses.ex: Socrates used dialectic to question his students until the weaknesses in their beliefs became obvious to them.

senses.def: tension or interplay between opposing forces or ideas that drives change
senses.ex: The novel explores the dialectic between tradition and progress in a small town divided over a new highway.

origin: From Greek "dia pason", through all, short for a phrase meaning through all the notes, the full span of the octave.

senses.def: the entire range or compass of something, especially of musical tones
senses.ex: The soprano's voice covered an astonishing diapason, from velvety low notes to a crystal-clear high C.

senses.def: rich, full outpouring of harmonious sound
senses.ex: When the cathedral organ began, a great diapason rolled through the nave and seemed to shake the stone floor.

origin: From Medieval Latin "diaphanus", from Greek "diaphanes", transparent, from "dia-", through, plus "phainein", to show or appear.

senses.def: so light, fine, and thin that one can almost see through it
