senses.def: respected senior figure in a profession, field, or group
senses.ex: As the doyen of local journalism, he mentored reporters who had not yet written their first article.

origin: Named after Draco, a lawmaker in ancient Athens whose legal code was famously harsh, punishing even minor crimes with death.

senses.def: excessively harsh and severe, especially of laws, rules, or punishments
senses.ex: Students protested the draconian new policy that suspended anyone caught with a phone in class.

origin: Through French and medieval Greek from Arabic "turjuman", an interpreter; its roots reach older Middle Eastern languages with the same meaning.

senses.def: interpreter or guide, especially in a Middle Eastern historical setting
senses.ex: The visiting envoy relied on a dragoman to interpret the governor's replies during the Ottoman court audience.

origin: From French "dragon", first a firearm and then a mounted soldier who carried one; the verb grew from soldiers' use of force.

senses.def: force or pressure someone into doing something
senses.ex: The director tried to dragoon her assistants into working through the holiday weekend.

senses.def: soldier trained to fight on horseback or on foot
senses.ex: The history museum displayed the helmet of a dragoon who had served in Napoleon's cavalry.

origin: From Old Norse "dregg", sediment; the word later gained a figurative sense for the least desirable remnants.

senses.def: sediment left at the bottom of a drink or other liquid
senses.ex: After the tea cooled, bitter dregs collected at the bottom of the cup.

senses.def: least desirable remnants or lowest part of something
senses.ex: The final chapter salvaged a hopeful insight from the dregs of a miserable year.

origin: From Old English "dreflian", meaning to drool; the idea of uncontrolled saliva became a figure for foolish talk.

senses.def: senseless or foolish speech or writing
senses.ex: The speaker's confident delivery could not disguise the drivel in his argument.

senses.def: speak or write in a foolish, rambling way
senses.ex: He drivelled on about secret plots until the audience began checking their watches.

origin: From French "drôle", funny, a jester, probably from Middle Dutch "drol", a little fat man or goblin.

senses.def: amusing in a dry, odd, or quietly witty way
senses.ex: With a droll smile, the professor remarked that the fire alarm had at least woken up the back row.

origin: From French "drolerie", from "drole", meaning funny or odd; the word names humor expressed through playful oddity.

senses.def: amusingly odd behavior or a playful sense of humor
senses.ex: Her quiet drollery emerged in the deadpan labels she wrote for the museum's strangest exhibits.

senses.def: humorous remark, story, or performance
senses.ex: At dinner, his latest drollery about the failed camping trip had everyone laughing.

origin: The bee sense comes from Old English "dran"; the sound sense developed from a separate Germanic verb for roaring.

senses.def: uncrewed aircraft controlled remotely or flying by itself
senses.ex: With its camera stabilized against the wind, the drone surveyed erosion along the coast.

senses.def: low, steady, monotonous sound
senses.ex: The drone of the refrigerator became impossible to ignore during the silent exam.

senses.def: make a low continuous sound or speak monotonously
senses.ex: The lecturer droned through fifty slides while students silently watched the clock.

senses.def: male bee, or person seen as idle or mechanically obedient
senses.ex: A drone fertilizes a queen bee, while a worker gathers nectar for the hive.

origin: From Old English "dros", dregs, sediment, the waste left behind when something useful is refined.

senses.def: worthless or trivial material, rubbish
senses.ex: The editor sifted through hundreds of dull submissions, discarding the dross to find a few brilliant stories.

senses.def: scum of impurities that forms on the surface of molten metal
senses.ex: The blacksmith skimmed the dross off the melted tin before pouring it into the mold.

origin: From "drudge", a person assigned dull, lowly work, plus "-ery", indicating a practice or condition.

senses.def: tedious, exhausting work that offers little satisfaction
senses.ex: The archive's endless filing felt like drudgery until Maya discovered a missing letter between the folders.

origin: From Latin "dubius", doubtful, wavering, related to "duo", two, the image of a mind torn between two choices.

senses.def: hesitating or doubtful about something
senses.ex: The coach was dubious about the rookie's claim that he could run a mile in under five minutes.

senses.def: probably not true, honest, or valuable, questionable
senses.ex: The website made dubious claims that a single herbal tea could cure the common cold.

origin: From Latin "ductilis", meaning easily led or drawn, through French; it describes both stretchable material and adaptable behavior.

senses.def: able to be drawn into wire or stretched without breaking
senses.ex: The artisan chose ductile copper because it could be pulled into thin strands without snapping.

senses.def: easily shaped, influenced, or adapted
senses.ex: Her ductile imagination turned a failed experiment into the opening scene of a play.

origin: Origin unknown. The word appeared in the late 1500s, and several proposed sources, including a Welsh word for anger, remain unproven.

senses.def: feeling of offended anger or resentment, usually in the phrase "in high dudgeon"
senses.ex: When the restaurant lost his reservation, the critic stormed out in high dudgeon.

origin: Borrowed from Spanish "duende", a goblin or spirit; in English it also names the passionate force felt in art.

senses.def: intense, mysterious emotional power in art or performance
senses.ex: The singer's restrained flamenco performance had duende that held the crowded room completely still.

senses.def: mischievous supernatural creature in Spanish or Portuguese folklore
senses.ex: In the village tale, a duende hid the baker's keys beneath a loose floorboard.

senses.def: captivating personal charm or magnetism
senses.ex: Even in a plain rehearsal room, the young dancer's duende drew every eye.

origin: From Old French "doucet", a diminutive of "douz", sweet, from Latin "dulcis", sweet. Compare Spanish "dulce" and Italian "dolce".

senses.def: sweet and pleasant to hear, especially of a voice or sound
senses.ex: The dulcet tones of the cello drifted through the open window and quieted the noisy courtyard.

origin: From "dull" plus the English suffix "-ard", which can label a person negatively; the result means a slow-witted person.

senses.def: person considered slow to understand or lacking intelligence
senses.ex: The impatient tutor called him a dullard, though he soon solved the puzzle alone.

origin: A blend of "dumb", once meaning speechless, and "confound", meaning bewilder; together they suggest surprise that stops speech.

senses.def: astonish someone so greatly that they are left speechless
senses.ex: The sudden discovery of a working medieval clock dumbfounded the museum's entire restoration team.

origin: From French "dupe", traced to "huppe", the hoopoe, a bird thought to look foolish and easy to catch. The newer sense of a cheap copy is a separate word, short for "duplicate".

senses.def: deceive or trick someone into believing or doing something
senses.ex: The scammers duped hundreds of retirees into buying shares in a gold mine that never existed.

senses.def: person who is easily deceived or used by others
senses.ex: He realized too late that he had been a dupe, carrying packages for a smuggling ring.

senses.def: cheaper copy or imitation of a popular product
senses.ex: She bought a dupe of the designer handbag for a fraction of the price.

origin: From "duplicity", from Late Latin "duplicitas", doubleness, from Latin "duplex", twofold. A duplicitous person shows two faces.

senses.def: deliberately deceptive, saying one thing while doing or meaning another
senses.ex: The duplicitous adviser assured the king of his loyalty while secretly sending letters to the rebels.

origin: From Late Latin "duplicitas", doubleness, from Latin "duplex", twofold. Duplicity is playing a double role to deceive.

senses.def: deliberate deceitfulness in speech or behavior, double-dealing
senses.ex: The spy's duplicity went unnoticed for years because she was so friendly with everyone at the embassy.

origin: From Old French "duresse", hardness, from Latin "duritia", from "durus", hard. Duress is hard pressure applied to force someone.

senses.def: threats, violence, or pressure used to force someone to do something
senses.ex: The defendant claimed he had signed the confession under duress after hours of threats.

origin: From dialect "dwine", to waste away, from Old English "dwinan", plus the ending "-le", which marks a repeated or gradual action.

senses.def: become gradually smaller, fewer, or weaker
senses.ex: As winter dragged on, the family's supply of firewood dwindled to a few damp logs.

origin: Present participle of "dwindle", from Old English "dwinan", to waste away, plus "-le", marking a gradual action.

senses.def: gradually becoming smaller, fewer, or weaker
senses.ex: The dwindling number of bees in the valley worried the orchard owners, who depend on them for pollination.

origin: Short for "dynamo-electric machine", from Greek "dynamis", power, the same root as "dynamic" and "dynamite".

senses.def: extremely energetic, hard-working, and forceful person
senses.ex: The new principal was a dynamo who launched a garden, a robotics club, and a tutoring program in one year.

senses.def: machine that converts mechanical energy into electricity
senses.ex: A small dynamo on the bicycle wheel powered the headlight whenever she pedaled.

syn: powerhouse, live wire, go-getter, ball of fire

origin: Built from "dys-", meaning bad, and the ending of "eulogistic", a word for praise; it reverses praise into censure.

senses.def: expressing blame, disapproval, or a negative judgment
senses.ex: The critic's dyslogistic account of the exhibition named every flaw and ignored its inventive design.

origin: From Greek "dys-", meaning bad, and "pepsis", meaning digestion; the parts literally describe troubled digestion.

senses.def: indigestion or persistent discomfort in the upper stomach
senses.ex: After the rich dinner, his dyspepsia kept him awake with a burning pain below his ribs.

senses.def: habitual irritability or ill temper
senses.ex: The columnist's political dyspepsia colored even her review of the city's cheerful spring festival.

origin: From Greek "dyspeptos", hard to digest, from "dys-", bad, plus "peptein", to digest. Indigestion was thought to sour the temper.

senses.def: irritable, gloomy, and bad-tempered in manner
senses.ex: The dyspeptic critic seemed to dislike every new restaurant in town, no matter how good the food.

senses.def: relating to or suffering from indigestion
senses.ex: The dyspeptic patient was told to avoid spicy food and eat smaller meals.

origin: Borrowed from French "degringolade", a tumble or rapid fall, from "degringoler", meaning to tumble downward.

senses.def: rapid, uncontrolled decline or collapse
senses.ex: The team's dégringolade began with one injury and ended with six straight defeats.

origin: An abbreviation of Latin "exempli gratia", for the sake of an example.

senses.def: for example, used to introduce one or more examples
senses.ex: Pack a few high-energy snacks for the hike, e.g., trail mix, granola bars, or dried apricots.

syn: for example, for instance, such as

origin: From Old English "eornoste", seriousness, zeal, related to German "Ernst", seriousness.

senses.def: sincere and intensely serious in intention or feeling
senses.ex: The earnest young volunteer spent every weekend repairing bicycles for families who could not afford new ones.

senses.def: serious intention, mainly in the phrase "in earnest"
senses.ex: The rain began in earnest just as the marching band took the field.

origin: From Middle English "erthy", simply "earth" plus "-y", having the quality of, so it first described things like soil.

senses.def: frank and uninhibited about the body, coarse but natural
senses.ex: The comedian's earthy humor about farm life and bodily functions delighted the crowd but shocked a few polite guests.

senses.def: direct, practical, and unpretentious
senses.ex: Despite her fame, the chef kept an earthy, practical manner and still greeted every delivery driver by name.

senses.def: resembling soil in smell, taste, or texture
senses.ex: The mushrooms gave the risotto a deep, earthy flavor that reminded us of walking through a damp autumn forest.

origin: From Old English "ebba", the falling tide, from a Germanic root meaning off or away, related to the words "of" and "off".

senses.def: gradually decline or grow weaker
senses.ex: Her enthusiasm for the project began to ebb after the third round of budget cuts and delays.

senses.def: flow back from the shore, as the tide does
senses.ex: As the tide ebbed, children wandered across the wet sand collecting shells and tiny crabs from the pools.

senses.def: flowing back of the tide toward the sea
senses.ex: Fishing boats left the harbor on the ebb, letting the outgoing water carry them past the rocky point.

senses.def: state of decline or low point
senses.ex: By late winter, morale at the struggling newspaper was at a low ebb, and several reporters had quit.

origin: From Latin "ebullire", to boil over, from "e-", out, plus "bullire", to bubble. Ebullience is enthusiasm bubbling over.

senses.def: cheerful, lively, and bubbling enthusiasm
senses.ex: Her ebullience filled the rehearsal room, and soon even the shy cast members were laughing and singing along.

syn: exuberance, enthusiasm, buoyancy, effervescence, high spirits

origin: From Latin "ebullire", to boil over, from "e-", out, plus "bullire", to bubble. An ebullient person bubbles over with enthusiasm.

senses.def: cheerful, lively, and full of overflowing enthusiasm
senses.ex: The ebullient tour guide sang folk songs between stops and had the whole bus clapping along by noon.

origin: From Old French "ebullition" and Latin "ebullitio", from "ebullire", to boil, the same source as "ebullient", bubbling with enthusiasm.

senses.def: sudden outburst of emotion or excitement
senses.ex: The crowd's ebullition of joy at the final whistle spilled from the stadium into the streets for hours.

senses.def: act or state of boiling
senses.ex: The chemist recorded the exact temperature at which ebullition began in each of the sealed glass flasks.

origin: From Medieval Latin "eccentricus", from Greek "ekkentros", off center, from "ek", out of, plus "kentron", center. An eccentric person is off center.

senses.def: unconventional and slightly strange in behavior or appearance
senses.ex: The eccentric inventor wore a different colored sock on each foot and kept a pet tortoise in his lab.

senses.def: person who behaves in an unconventional and slightly strange way
senses.ex: The town's beloved eccentric rode a tricycle to the market every morning wearing a top hat.

senses.def: not centered or not perfectly circular, especially of an orbit
senses.ex: Comets follow highly eccentric orbits that carry them close to the sun and then far out into space.

origin: From Latin "eccentricitas". The base "eccentric" goes back to Greek "ekkentros", out of center, from "ek", out, and "kentron", center.

senses.def: quality of being strange or unconventional in behavior
senses.ex: The inventor's eccentricity was legendary in town, since he wore two watches and ate breakfast only after sunset.

senses.def: odd habit or peculiar personal trait
senses.ex: Among the professor's many eccentricities was a refusal to use any pen that was not bright green.

origin: From Late Latin "ecclesiasticus", of the church, from Greek "ekklesiastikos", based on "ekklesia", an assembly, the early word for a church.

senses.def: priest or other member of the clergy
senses.ex: A senior ecclesiastic from Rome arrived to oversee the restoration of the abbey and its medieval library.

senses.def: relating to the church or its clergy
senses.ex: The bishop's ecclesiastic duties left little time for the gardening and poetry that had filled his younger years.

origin: Coined by H. L. Mencken from "ecdysis", molting, the shedding of an animal's skin, on the model of "enthusiast".

senses.def: striptease performer, a humorously formal term
senses.ex: The burlesque revue featured a comedian, a jazz trio, and a celebrated ecdysiast whose act relied more on wit than on skin.

origin: From French "échelon", rung of a ladder, from "échelle", ladder, from Latin "scala", ladder. Each echelon is one rung up.

senses.def: level or rank in an organization, profession, or society
senses.ex: Only the upper echelons of the company knew about the planned merger before it was announced.

senses.def: formation of troops, ships, or aircraft arranged in staggered diagonal rows
senses.ex: The fighter jets flew past in a tight echelon, each one slightly behind and to the right of the last.

origin: Borrowed from French "éclat", a burst or splinter, and by extension a flash of brilliance, which suits a dazzling public success.

senses.def: conspicuous brilliance or showy success
senses.ex: The young director's first opera opened with great eclat, drawing rave reviews and a standing ovation from the critics.

senses.def: great public acclaim or applause
senses.ex: She retired from the stage amid the eclat of a sold-out farewell tour and tributes from rival performers.

origin: From Greek "eklektikos", selective, from "eklegein", to pick out, from "ek", out, plus "legein", to choose. Related to "elect".

senses.def: drawing ideas, styles, or tastes from a wide and diverse range of sources
senses.ex: Her eclectic music collection ranged from Baroque cello suites to Nigerian Afrobeat and 1980s synth-pop.

origin: From Greek "ekleipsis", a failing, disappearance, from "ekleipein", to leave out, fail, from "ek", out, plus "leipein", to leave.

senses.def: overshadow or surpass someone or something in importance or success
senses.ex: The younger sister's fame as a novelist soon eclipsed her brother's modest career as a poet.

senses.def: blocking of light from one celestial body by another, as when the moon hides the sun
senses.ex: Thousands gathered on the hillside to watch the total eclipse turn noon into an eerie twilight.

senses.def: loss of importance, power, or fame
senses.ex: After the scandal, the once-popular senator's career went into a long eclipse.

origin: From Latin "ecloga" and Greek "ekloge", a selection, from the idea of a short chosen poem, as in Virgil's famous Eclogues.

senses.def: short pastoral poem, often a dialogue between shepherds
senses.ex: For her poetry seminar, she wrote an eclogue in which two shepherds argue about leaving their valley for the city.

origin: From Greek "oikonomikos", skilled in managing a household, from "oikos", house, plus "nemein", to manage or distribute.

senses.def: giving good value or service in relation to the money or resources used
senses.ex: The small hybrid car proved economical, using half the fuel of the family's old van.

senses.def: careful not to waste money, words, or effort
senses.ex: The poet's economical style packs a whole life story into twelve short lines.

origin: From Greek "oikonomia", management of a household, from "oikos", house, plus "nemein", to manage. It first meant careful household management.

senses.def: careful management of resources and avoidance of waste
senses.ex: She wrote with great economy, never using ten words when four would do.

senses.def: system of production, trade, and wealth in a country or region
senses.ex: The island's economy depends heavily on tourism and on fishing for tuna.

origin: From "ecumenic" plus "-al", going back to Greek "oikoumene", the inhabited world, so the word suggests something worldwide and inclusive.

senses.def: promoting unity among Christian churches or among different religions
senses.ex: The ecumenical service brought Catholic, Baptist, and Orthodox congregations together to pray for victims of the flood.

senses.def: broad and inclusive in outlook, welcoming many different views
senses.ex: The editor took an ecumenical approach to the anthology, including poets from rival schools and every political persuasion.

origin: From Latin "edax", greedy, gluttonous, from "edere", to eat, the same root as "edible".

senses.def: having a huge appetite, greedy for food
senses.ex: The edacious teenagers emptied the refrigerator within an hour of arriving at the beach house.

origin: From Latin "edictum", something proclaimed, from "edicere", to declare, from "e-", out, and "dicere", to say.

senses.def: official order or proclamation issued by someone in authority
senses.ex: The emperor issued an edict banning private weapons and ordering every village to surrender its swords within one month.

senses.def: command or rule stated with authority, often an unwelcome one
senses.ex: The new principal's edict against phones in hallways provoked an immediate protest from students and several annoyed parents.

origin: From Old French, from Latin "aedificatio", building, from "aedificare", to build, so edification is the building up of a mind or character.

senses.def: moral or intellectual improvement gained through instruction or good influence
senses.ex: The museum director hoped the free lectures would serve the edification of local students as well as entertain them.

origin: From Old French "edifice", from Latin "aedificium", building, from "aedificare", to build, the same root that gives English "edify".

senses.def: large, imposing building or structure
senses.ex: The marble edifice of the old courthouse towered over the square, dwarfing every shop and restaurant around it.

senses.def: complex system of ideas or institutions built up over time
senses.ex: One falsified study threatened to bring down the whole edifice of theory that the laboratory had constructed over decades.

origin: From Latin "aedificare", to build, from "aedes", dwelling, plus "facere", to make. To edify is to build up someone's mind or character, as in "edifice".

senses.def: instruct or improve someone morally or intellectually
senses.ex: The museum hoped its new exhibit on clean water would both entertain and edify young visitors.

origin: From "edify", from Latin "aedificare", to build, so edifying material builds up the mind or character.

senses.def: providing moral or intellectual instruction or improvement
senses.ex: The lecture on medieval medicine was surprisingly edifying, though a few descriptions made the audience wince.

origin: From Latin "educere", to lead out, from "ex-", out, and "ducere", to lead, so to educe is to draw something out.

senses.def: draw out or bring forth something hidden, latent, or undeveloped
senses.ex: A patient coach can educe remarkable confidence from shy players who never believed they had any talent.

senses.def: work out a conclusion or principle from given facts
senses.ex: From scattered shipping records, the historian educed a clear picture of how the port's trade collapsed.

syn: elicit, draw out, evoke, extract, bring out

origin: Past tense of "efface", from French "effacer", from "es-", out, plus "face", face, so to rub out the face of something.

senses.def: erased or worn away so that little or no trace remains
senses.ex: Centuries of wind and rain had effaced the names carved on the old headstones.

senses.def: made oneself inconspicuous or kept out of the spotlight
senses.ex: The assistant effaced herself at the ceremony, standing quietly at the back while her boss accepted the award.

syn: erased, obliterated, expunged, rubbed out, wiped out

origin: From Old French "effectuel", from Late Latin "effectualis", related to "effect", so something effectual actually produces the effect it was meant to.

senses.def: successful in producing the intended result
senses.ex: Regular handwashing proved the most effectual way to stop the infection from spreading through the crowded hospital ward.

origin: From Renaissance Latin "effectuare", based on Latin "effectus", effect, probably influenced by Middle French "effectuer", so it means to put into effect.

senses.def: cause something to happen or put a plan into effect
senses.ex: The new board moved quickly to effectuate the merger before regulators could raise further objections to the deal.

syn: bring about, effect, accomplish, implement, execute

origin: Borrowed from French "effervescence", built on Latin "ferv-", to boil, with "ef-", out, so it suggests bubbling up and out.

senses.def: bubbly, high-spirited liveliness in a person or mood
senses.ex: Her effervescence lifted the whole rehearsal, and even the tired stagehands began laughing and humming along with the cast.

senses.def: bubbling of gas escaping from a liquid, as in soda
senses.ex: The effervescence of the freshly opened seltzer faded within minutes, leaving the glass of water completely flat.

origin: From Latin "effervescere", to boil up, from "ex-", out, plus "fervescere", to begin to boil, from "fervere", to boil.

senses.def: lively, enthusiastic, and full of high spirits
senses.ex: The effervescent host kept the party lively, introducing strangers and refilling glasses all evening.

senses.def: giving off bubbles, fizzy
senses.ex: She dropped an effervescent tablet into the water and watched it fizz and dissolve.

origin: From Latin "effetus", worn out, exhausted, literally having given birth. The word moved from exhausted to feeble and overrefined.

senses.def: weak, ineffectual, and lacking vitality
senses.ex: The effete aristocracy, absorbed in parties and fashion, failed to see the revolution coming.

senses.def: affected and overrefined, often in a snobbish way
senses.ex: He mocked the effete critics who sniffed at any film that sold too many tickets.

origin: From Latin "efficax", effective, from "efficere", to accomplish, from "ex-", out, plus "facere", to do or make.

senses.def: successful in producing the intended result, effective
senses.ex: Rest, fluids, and patience proved more efficacious than any of the expensive remedies she tried.

origin: From Late Latin "efficacia", from "efficax", effective, from "efficere", to accomplish, from "ex-", out, plus "facere", to do.

senses.def: ability to produce a desired or intended result
senses.ex: Researchers tested the efficacy of the new vaccine in a trial involving thirty thousand volunteers.

origin: From Latin "effigies", likeness, from "effingere", to fashion or portray, from "ex-", out, plus "fingere", to shape.

senses.def: rough model of a hated person, made to be damaged or burned in protest
senses.ex: Angry protesters burned an effigy of the governor outside the state capitol.

senses.def: sculpture or carving of a person, especially on a tomb
senses.ex: A stone effigy of the knight lay on top of his tomb, hands folded in prayer.

origin: From Latin "efflorescere", to blossom out, from "ex-", out, plus "florescere", to begin to bloom, from "flos", flower.

senses.def: period of vigorous growth or flowering, especially in culture or the arts
senses.ex: The 1920s saw an efflorescence of Black art, music, and writing known as the Harlem Renaissance.

senses.def: process of bursting into flower
senses.ex: Each spring the efflorescence of the cherry trees draws crowds to the riverbank.

origin: Plural of "effluvium", from Latin "effluere", to flow out, from "ex-", out, plus "fluere", to flow.

senses.def: unpleasant or harmful vapors, odors, or waste products given off by something
senses.ex: Residents complained about the effluvia drifting from the paper mill on hot summer evenings.

senses.def: unwanted byproducts or leftovers of an activity
senses.ex: The attic was crammed with the effluvia of three generations: broken lamps, old letters, and dusty board games.

origin: From Latin "effluvium", a flowing out, from "effluere", to flow out, from "ex-", out, plus "fluere", to flow.

senses.def: unpleasant or harmful odor or vapor given off by something
senses.ex: A foul effluvium rose from the stagnant pond behind the abandoned factory.

origin: From French "effronterie", from "effronté", shameless. Compare Latin "effrons", barefaced, from "ex-", out, plus "frons", forehead.

senses.def: insolent or shameless boldness
senses.ex: After arriving an hour late, he had the effrontery to complain that dinner was cold.

origin: From Latin "ex-", out of, and "fulgere", to shine, so effulgence is light that seems to pour outward from its source.

senses.def: brilliant, radiant light or splendor
senses.ex: The effulgence of the desert sunrise turned the canyon walls gold and forced the hikers to shield their eyes.

origin: From Latin "effulgens", present participle of "effulgere", to shine forth, from "ex-", out, and "fulgere", to flash or gleam.

senses.def: shining with brilliant, radiant light
senses.ex: An effulgent full moon rose over the frozen lake, bright enough for the skaters to see without lanterns.

origin: Borrowed from Middle French "effusion", from Latin "effusio", an outpouring, so the word pictures feelings or liquid spilling out freely.

senses.def: unrestrained outpouring of words or emotion
senses.ex: After the team's upset victory, the normally stern coach surprised reporters with an effusion of tearful gratitude.

senses.def: flowing out of liquid or gas from a container or source
senses.ex: Engineers traced the slow effusion of gas to a hairline crack in the storage tank's upper valve.

origin: From Medieval Latin "effusivus", from Latin "effundere", to pour out, from "ex-", out, plus "fundere", to pour. Effusive praise pours out.

senses.def: expressing gratitude, praise, or emotion in an unrestrained, gushing way
senses.ex: The effusive host hugged every guest at the door and praised each dish as the best she had ever tasted.

origin: From French "égalitaire", from "égal", equal, from Latin "aequalis", equal.

senses.def: based on the belief that all people deserve equal rights and opportunities
senses.ex: The founders hoped to build an egalitarian community where every member had an equal vote.

senses.def: person who believes in equal rights and opportunities for all people
senses.ex: A committed egalitarian, she refused to let the company give executives a separate dining room.

origin: Formed from "ego-", from the Latin for I, and "-centric", centered on, so an egocentric person treats the self as the center of everything.

senses.def: thinking only of oneself and unable or unwilling to consider others' viewpoints
senses.ex: His egocentric retelling of the group project left out every teammate who had actually written the final report.

origin: From French "égoïsme", built on Latin "ego", I, plus "-ism", so it is literally an outlook centered on the self.

senses.def: habit of acting mainly or only out of concern for one's own interests
senses.ex: Her egoism showed when she took the only lifeboat seat by the window and never offered to trade.

senses.def: ethical theory that people ought to act in their own self-interest
senses.ex: In philosophy class we debated whether ethical egoism can explain why anyone would donate a kidney to a stranger.

origin: From Latin "ego", I, plus "-ism", with an extra "t" probably copied from words like "despotism". It names too much talk about "I".

senses.def: inflated sense of one's own importance, often shown by constant talk about oneself
senses.ex: The candidate's egotism was obvious when every answer in the debate somehow circled back to his own childhood triumphs.

origin: From Latin "ego", I, plus "-ist", with a "t" added for ease of pronunciation, as in "dramatist".

senses.def: person who is conceited and talks or thinks mostly about themselves
senses.ex: The egotist at the dinner table spent two hours describing his own achievements and never asked anyone a question.

origin: From "egotistic" plus "-al", built on "egotism", from Latin "ego", I.

senses.def: excessively conceited and absorbed in oneself, often talking mainly about oneself
senses.ex: The egotistical chef refused to let anyone else's name appear on the menu, even for the desserts they invented.

origin: From Latin "egregius", standing out from the flock, from "e-", out of, plus "grex", flock. Once a compliment, it now means standing out for being bad.

senses.def: outstandingly and shockingly bad
senses.ex: The referee's egregious error, calling a clear goal offside, cost the team the championship.

origin: From Latin "egressus", a going out, from "egredi", to go out, from "e-", out, plus "gradi", to step.

senses.def: way out of a place, or the act of leaving it
senses.ex: Fire codes require that every classroom provide a clear means of egress in case of emergency.

syn: exit, departure, way out, outlet, exodus

origin: From German "eidetisch", from Greek "eidētikos", relating to an image, from "eidos", form or shape.

senses.def: of a mental image so vivid and detailed it seems almost seen
senses.ex: With an eidetic memory, she could close her eyes and read the page number off a book she had skimmed weeks earlier.

origin: From Greek "eidōlon", image or phantom, from "eidos", form or appearance. It is a cousin of "idol" and "idea".

senses.def: phantom or ghostly image of someone or something
senses.ex: Sailors swore an eidolon of the drowned captain walked the deck on foggy nights, silent and translucent.

senses.def: idealized figure or image held up as a perfect model
senses.ex: For the young poet, the reclusive master became an eidolon of artistic purity she could never quite match.

origin: Formed from Greek "eis", into, on the model of "exegesis", whose "ex" means out. Exegesis draws meaning out of a text, eisegesis reads meaning into it.

senses.def: interpretation of a text that reads the interpreter's own ideas into it
senses.ex: The professor warned that calling the medieval poem a feminist manifesto was eisegesis, not careful reading of the evidence.

origin: From Old English "iecan", to increase, add to. To eke out a living is to add little by little until there is just enough.

senses.def: manage to make or obtain something with great difficulty, usually in the phrase "eke out"
senses.ex: The family eked out a living by selling vegetables from their small garden at the weekend market.

senses.def: make a small supply last longer by using it sparingly
senses.ex: The stranded hikers eked out their last loaf of bread over four long days.

origin: From Greek "ekphrasis", description, from "ekphrazein", to describe, from "ek", out, plus "phrazein", to point out or explain.

senses.def: vivid literary description of a work of visual art, often as a poem
senses.ex: Her ekphrasis on a Vermeer painting captured the light on the milk jug so well that readers felt they had seen it.

origin: From Latin "elaboratus", worked out, from "elaborare", to work out fully, from "e-", out, plus "labor", work. Elaborate things show much labor.

senses.def: explain or develop something in more detail
senses.ex: When the teacher asked her to elaborate, she described each step of her experiment in careful detail.

senses.def: involving many carefully arranged parts or details, complicated
senses.ex: The wedding cake was an elaborate tower of six tiers decorated with hand-made sugar roses.

syn: expand, expound, amplify, enlarge, flesh out

origin: From French "élaboration", from Latin "elaborare", to work out with effort, from "e-", out, plus "labor", work.

senses.def: process of developing an idea or plan in greater detail
senses.ex: The committee approved the outline, but the elaboration of the budget took another three months of meetings.

senses.def: added detail or explanation that expands on something
senses.ex: When the teacher asked for elaboration, Marco added two examples and a quotation to support his claim.

origin: From French "élan", a rush or dash, from "élancer", to dart forward, related to "lancer", to throw like a lance.

senses.def: energetic style, confidence, and flair
senses.ex: The young conductor led the orchestra with such elan that the audience was on its feet before the final chord faded.

origin: From Latin "elatus", raised, lifted up, used as the past participle of "efferre", to carry out or raise. Elated spirits are lifted high.

senses.def: extremely happy and excited
senses.ex: The elated students jumped and cheered when they learned their robot had won first prize at the state fair.

origin: From Latin "elatio", a lifting up, from "elatus", raised, the past participle of "efferre", to carry out, from "ex", out, plus "ferre", to carry.

senses.def: great happiness and excitement, often with a sense of triumph
senses.ex: Opening the acceptance letter, she felt such elation that she ran outside and shouted the news to her neighbors.

origin: Of uncertain origin. The ending is usually traced to Old English "rice", realm, and the start to "else" or "elf", suggesting an otherworldly realm.

senses.def: weird, sinister, and unnatural in an eerie way
senses.ex: An eldritch green light flickered among the ruins, and the villagers swore they heard whispering in the wind.

origin: From Medieval Latin "eleemosynarius", from Late Latin "eleemosyna", alms, from Greek "eleēmosynē", pity or alms, from "eleēmōn", merciful. English "alms" comes from the same Greek word.

senses.def: relating to, supported by, or given as charity
senses.ex: The hospital began as an eleemosynary institution, funded entirely by donations from wealthy merchants in the town.

origin: From Latin "elegiacus", from Greek "elegeiakos", from "elegeia", an elegy or mournful song.

senses.def: expressing sorrow or wistful longing, especially for something lost or past
senses.ex: The documentary ends on an elegiac note, with old miners walking past the shuttered pit where they once worked.

origin: From Latin "elegia", from Greek "elegeia", short for "elegeia oide", an elegiac song, a lament.

senses.def: mournful poem or song, especially a lament for someone who has died
senses.ex: At the memorial service, her granddaughter read an elegy she had written about their summers on the lake.

origin: From Latin "elementarius", from "elementum", a first principle or basic part, the same word as "element".

senses.def: relating to the most basic or simple parts of a subject
senses.ex: The tutor began with elementary grammar before moving on to the subtleties of Russian verbs.

senses.def: very simple and easy to understand or solve
senses.ex: Checking the batteries first is an elementary step that many people forget when a remote stops working.

senses.def: relating to the early years of school, roughly ages five to eleven
senses.ex: Her elementary school sat at the end of a quiet street lined with maple trees.

origin: From Latin "elephantinus", of an elephant, from Greek "elephas", elephant. It turns the animal into a byword for huge and clumsy.

senses.def: enormous, heavy, or clumsy, like an elephant
senses.ex: The elephantine wardrobe would not fit through the doorway, so the movers had to take it apart in the hall.

senses.def: of, relating to, or resembling elephants
senses.ex: The fossil skull showed elephantine tusks, suggesting the extinct creature was an early relative of modern elephants.

origin: From Latin "elevare", to lift up, from "e-", out, up, plus "levare", to raise, lighten, from "levis", light.

senses.def: raise something to a higher position or level
senses.ex: Doctors told him to elevate his sprained ankle on a pillow to reduce the swelling.

senses.def: promote someone to a higher rank or status
senses.ex: The board elevated the young editor to chief of the magazine after only three years.

senses.def: improve the quality of something, or raise it morally, intellectually, or culturally
senses.ex: The chef's bold spices elevated a simple bowl of lentils into something memorable.

origin: From Latin "elicere", to draw out, from "e-", out, plus "lacere", to lure or entice.

senses.def: draw out a response, answer, or reaction from someone
senses.ex: The comedian's opening joke elicited only a few awkward coughs from the sleepy audience.

syn: evoke, draw out, extract, provoke, prompt

origin: From Latin "elisio", a striking out, from "elidere", to strike out, from "ex", out, plus "laedere", to strike. It is the noun of "elide".

senses.def: omission of a sound or syllable in speech, as in "can't" for "cannot"
senses.ex: The elision in "fish 'n' chips" drops the vowel and final consonant of "and" so the phrase flows quickly.

senses.def: act of leaving something out or passing over it, often conveniently
senses.ex: The report's elision of the failed safety tests made the new drug look far less risky than it really was.

origin: From "elite", from French "élite", chosen, from "élire", to choose, from Latin "eligere", to pick out.

senses.def: favoring or believing in the superiority and leadership of a small privileged group
senses.ex: Critics called the club's admissions policy elitist because it accepted only students from expensive private schools.

senses.def: person who believes a small privileged group should lead or be favored
senses.ex: He was accused of being an elitist after mocking voters who had not gone to college.

origin: From Medieval Latin, from Arabic "al-iksir", the philosopher's stone, from Greek "xērion", a drying powder for wounds, from "xēros", dry.

senses.def: magical or miraculous potion said to cure all ills or prolong life
senses.ex: The traveling salesman promised his elixir would cure baldness, gout, and heartbreak, all for one silver dollar a bottle.

senses.def: sweetened liquid used to deliver medicine by mouth
senses.ex: The pharmacist mixed the bitter drug into a cherry elixir so the child would swallow it without complaint.

origin: From Latin, from Greek "elleipsis", omission or falling short, from "elleipein", to leave out. The same Greek word gave "ellipse".

senses.def: punctuation mark of three dots showing words left out or a trailing pause
senses.ex: When quoting the long speech, she used an ellipsis to show where she had cut two sentences from the middle.

senses.def: leaving out of words that the reader can still understand from context
senses.ex: In "She ordered tea and he coffee," ellipsis removes the second "ordered" without confusing anyone.

origin: From "elliptic", from Greek "elleiptikos", defective or falling short, from "elleipein", to leave out. It covers both the oval shape and speech with words left out.

senses.def: shaped like an ellipse; oval
senses.ex: The planet follows an elliptical orbit, swinging close to its star and then drifting far away each year.

senses.def: so brief or indirect in speech or writing that the meaning is hard to grasp
senses.ex: The poet's elliptical lines skip so many connecting words that readers argue for hours over what she meant.

senses.def: exercise machine for low-impact stepping in an oval path
senses.ex: With a sore knee, he switched from running to twenty minutes on the elliptical at the gym every morning.

origin: From Latin "elocutio", a speaking out, from "eloqui", to speak out, from "e-", out, plus "loqui", to speak. "Eloquent" shares the root.

senses.def: skill of clear, expressive speaking, especially in distinct pronunciation and delivery
senses.ex: Before her first radio job, she took elocution lessons to slow her speech and sharpen every consonant.

origin: From Latin "eloquentia", from "eloqui", to speak out, from "e-", out, plus "loqui", to speak.

senses.def: fluent, forceful, and persuasive speaking or writing
senses.ex: The young lawyer's eloquence moved several jurors to tears during her closing argument.

origin: From Latin "eloquens", speaking out, from "eloqui", to speak out, from "e-", out, plus "loqui", to speak.

senses.def: fluent and persuasive in speaking or writing
senses.ex: The senator gave an eloquent speech that won over even some of her fiercest opponents.

senses.def: clearly expressing or showing a feeling or fact, even without words
senses.ex: His silence when asked about the missing money was an eloquent admission of guilt.

origin: From Late Latin "elucidare", to make light, from "e-", out, plus "lucidus", bright, clear. To elucidate is to shed light on.

senses.def: make something clear by explaining it
senses.ex: The appendix elucidates the statistical methods that the main chapters only mention in passing.

syn: clarify, explain, illuminate, explicate, clear up

origin: From Latin "eludere", to escape by a trick, from "e-", out, plus "ludere", to play. Eluding a pursuer is outplaying them.

senses.def: escape from or avoid someone or something, often by skill or cunning
senses.ex: The fox eluded the hounds by doubling back along the frozen creek.

senses.def: fail to be understood, remembered, or achieved by someone
senses.ex: The answer to the final riddle eluded her for days, until it came to her in the shower.

syn: evade, escape, dodge, avoid, give the slip

origin: From Latin "elusus", past participle of "eludere", to evade, from "e-", out, plus "ludere", to play.

senses.def: difficult to find, catch, or achieve
senses.ex: The snow leopard is so elusive that researchers spent months in the mountains before photographing one.

senses.def: difficult to define, describe, or remember
senses.ex: The poem has an elusive quality that readers feel strongly but struggle to put into words.

syn: evasive, slippery, fleeting, intangible, hard to pin down

origin: From Latin "Elysius", from Greek "Ēlysion", Elysium, the paradise where heroes lived after death in Greek myth.

senses.def: blissful and heavenly, as if in paradise
senses.ex: After weeks of rain, the elysian afternoon of warm sun and still water made the whole lake feel enchanted.

origin: From Latin "emaciare", to make lean, from "ex-", out, thoroughly, plus "macies", leanness, from "macer", thin, as in "meager".

senses.def: make or become abnormally thin and weak, especially from illness or hunger
senses.ex: Months of illness had emaciated the once-sturdy farmer until his clothes hung loosely from his shoulders.

syn: waste away, starve, shrivel, enfeeble, wither

origin: From Latin "emanare", to flow out, from "e-", out, plus "manare", to flow, so something that emanates flows out from a source.

senses.def: come or spread out from a source, as light, sound, a smell, or a feeling does
senses.ex: A faint smell of cinnamon emanated from the bakery, drawing commuters off the sidewalk before dawn.

senses.def: give out or radiate a quality, mood, or substance
senses.ex: Even in a crowded lecture hall, the visiting chess champion emanated a calm that made the students lower their voices.

origin: From Latin "emancipare", to release from a father's legal power, from "e-", out of, plus "mancipium", ownership, from "manus", hand, plus "capere", to take.

senses.def: set someone free from legal, social, or political restrictions
senses.ex: Many enslaved people were emancipated during the war, though true equality remained a distant goal.

senses.def: free someone from a controlling idea, habit, or influence
senses.ex: Learning to drive emancipated her from depending on her brother for every trip to town.

origin: From Spanish "embargar", to arrest or seize, from Vulgar Latin roots meaning to bar, from "barra", bar or barrier, so an embargo puts up a bar.

senses.def: official ban on trade or other commercial dealings with a particular country
senses.ex: The oil embargo of the 1970s sent fuel prices soaring and left long lines of cars outside gas stations.

senses.def: temporary ban on publishing certain information until a set time
senses.ex: Reporters received the study early but had to honor an embargo until noon on Thursday.

senses.def: officially ban trade in certain goods or the release of information
senses.ex: The government embargoed shipments of advanced chips to the rival nation after the security review.

origin: From Old French "embellir", to make beautiful, from "em-", in, plus "bel", beautiful, from Latin "bellus", pretty.

senses.def: make something more attractive by adding decorations
senses.ex: The bakers embellished the cake with candied violets and thin swirls of gold icing.

senses.def: add exaggerated or invented details to a story to make it more interesting
senses.ex: Each time Grandpa told the fishing story, he embellished it until the trout became the size of a shark.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "embesiler", to steal or make disappear, from Old French "besillier", to destroy, a word of unknown origin.

senses.def: secretly steal money or property that one has been trusted to look after
senses.ex: The club treasurer embezzled nearly ten thousand dollars from the dues account before an audit exposed the missing funds.

origin: From "en-", put on, plus "blazon", a coat of arms, from Old French "blason", shield, so to emblazon is to paint something boldly on a shield.

senses.def: display a design, name, or slogan prominently on something
senses.ex: The team's jerseys were emblazoned with the name of a local pizza shop in bright red letters.

senses.def: depict a coat of arms or heraldic device on something
senses.ex: The craftsman emblazoned the family crest on the heavy oak door of the restored manor.

origin: Borrowed from French "embonpoint", from the phrase "en bon point", in good condition, a polite way of describing a well-fed figure.

senses.def: plumpness of figure, especially a pleasantly full or rounded body
senses.ex: The portrait painter flattered the aging banker, softening his embonpoint into a look of comfortable prosperity.

origin: From Old French "embroder", to embroider, ultimately of Germanic origin, though the exact path is uncertain.

senses.def: add imaginary or exaggerated details to a story to make it more interesting
senses.ex: Every time Grandpa told the story of the blizzard, he embroidered it with taller snowdrifts and a hungrier wolf.

senses.def: sew a decorative design onto cloth with needle and thread
senses.ex: She embroidered tiny blue flowers along the collar of the linen shirt she made for her niece.

origin: From French "embrouiller", to entangle, from "em-", in, plus "brouiller", to mix up or confuse. To embroil someone is to tangle them up in a conflict.

senses.def: involve someone deeply in a conflict or difficult situation
senses.ex: The small town's dispute over a parking lot soon embroiled the mayor, the school board, and two local churches.

origin: Past participle of "embroil", from French "embrouiller", to entangle, from "em-", in, plus "brouiller", to mix up, so being tangled up in a conflict.

senses.def: deeply involved in a conflict, argument, or difficult situation
senses.ex: Embroiled in a bitter lawsuit with his former partner, the inventor had no time left for new projects.

syn: entangled, mired, involved, caught up, enmeshed

origin: From New Latin "embryonicus", from "embryo", from Greek "embryon", from "en", in, plus "bryein", to swell or grow.

senses.def: in a very early stage of development, not yet fully formed
senses.ex: The plan for a student-run radio station was still embryonic, just a few ideas scribbled in a notebook.

senses.def: relating to an embryo
senses.ex: Biologists studied the embryonic development of zebrafish because the eggs are transparent.

origin: From Latin "emendare", to free from faults, from "e-", out, plus "menda", fault or blemish, the same source as "amend".

senses.def: correct and revise a text by removing errors
senses.ex: The editor emended the manuscript, restoring several lines that a careless printer had dropped in the first edition.

origin: From Latin "emendatio", correction, from "emendare", to free from faults, from "menda", fault or blemish.

senses.def: correction or change made to a text, especially by a scholar or editor
senses.ex: Scholars still debate whether the famous line reflects the poet's own words or a later editor's emendation.

senses.def: act of correcting or improving something
senses.ex: The draft treaty underwent careful emendation before the delegates were willing to sign it.

origin: From Greek "emetikos", causing vomiting, from "emetos", vomiting, through French "émétique".

senses.def: substance that causes vomiting
senses.ex: The poison control nurse warned the parents not to give their child an emetic before calling for advice.

senses.def: causing vomiting
senses.ex: The plant's berries have an emetic effect, which protects them from being eaten by most animals.

origin: From Latin "eminentia", prominence, from "eminere", to stand out or project, so eminence is literally standing out above the rest.

senses.def: fame and high standing within a profession or field
senses.ex: The surgeon's eminence in heart transplants drew patients from three continents to her small clinic.

senses.def: important or distinguished person
senses.ex: Several eminences of the art world attended the gallery opening, sipping champagne beside the sculptures.

senses.def: piece of high ground, such as a hill or rise
senses.ex: The general set up his observation post on a grassy eminence overlooking the river valley.

origin: From Latin "eminere", to stand out, project, from "e-", out, plus "minere", to jut. An eminent person stands out above others.

senses.def: famous and highly respected, especially within a particular field
senses.ex: The eminent historian was invited to advise the producers of the new film about ancient Rome.

senses.def: outstanding or remarkable in degree
senses.ex: The judge was praised for her eminent fairness, even in the most emotional cases.

origin: From Latin "emissarius", a scout or agent, from "emittere", to send out, from "e-", out, plus "mittere", to send.

senses.def: person sent on a special mission to represent someone else
senses.ex: The king sent an emissary across the mountains to negotiate a truce with the rebel leaders.

origin: From Latin "emollire", to soften, from "e-", out, thoroughly, plus "mollis", soft.

senses.def: soothing or calming, especially in manner or speech
senses.ex: The manager's emollient words calmed the angry customers who had waited two hours for their flight.

senses.def: cream or lotion that softens and soothes the skin
senses.ex: The pharmacist recommended a thick emollient for the cracked skin on his hands.

origin: From Latin "emolumentum", gain or profit, probably from "emolere", to grind out, perhaps first meaning a miller's fee for grinding grain.

senses.def: salary, fee, or other payment received for work or holding an office
senses.ex: Board members receive no emolument for their service, though the foundation covers their travel to meetings.

origin: A back-formation from "emotion", which comes from Latin "emovere", to move out or stir up.

senses.def: express emotion openly and dramatically, often in an exaggerated way
senses.ex: The young actor emoted so wildly during the death scene that the audience began to giggle instead of weep.

origin: From "empathy", from Greek "en", in, plus "pathos", feeling, with the ending reshaped to match "sympathetic".

senses.def: able to understand and share the feelings of others
senses.ex: The empathetic nurse sat with the frightened boy and explained each step before the procedure began.

origin: From Greek "emphatikos", from "emphainein", to show, from "en", in, plus "phainein", to show. An emphatic statement shows its meaning forcefully.

senses.def: expressed with force and clarity, showing strong conviction
senses.ex: Her answer was an emphatic no, delivered before the salesman could even finish his pitch.

senses.def: clear and decisive, leaving no doubt
senses.ex: The team ended its losing streak with an emphatic six-to-nothing victory.

origin: From Greek "empeirikos", experienced, from "empeiria", experience, from "en", in, plus "peira", trial, attempt.

senses.def: based on observation, measurement, or experiment rather than theory
senses.ex: The researchers gathered empirical evidence by measuring the river's temperature every day for a decade.

origin: From "empiric", from Greek "empeiria", experience, from "en", in, plus "peira", trial, plus "-ism".

senses.def: view that knowledge comes mainly from experience and observation of the senses
senses.ex: Locke's empiricism held that the mind begins as a blank slate filled in by experience.

senses.def: practice of relying on observation and experiment rather than theory
senses.ex: The lab's strict empiricism meant no claim was accepted until it had been tested several times.

origin: From Latin "empyreus", from Greek "empyrios", fiery, from "en", in, plus "pyr", fire, because the highest heaven was thought to be made of pure fire.

senses.def: belonging to the highest heaven or the sky, and so sublime or heavenly
senses.ex: The choir's voices rose into the vaulted ceiling with an empyreal clarity that silenced the restless tourists.

origin: From Latin "empyreus", from Greek "empyrios", fiery, from "en", in, plus "pyr", fire, since ancient thinkers placed a realm of pure fire above the stars.

senses.def: the highest heaven, or the sky seen as a lofty realm
senses.ex: The weather balloon climbed steadily into the empyrean until it shrank to a silver speck and vanished.

senses.def: belonging to the highest heaven, heavenly
senses.ex: From the summit, the hikers watched the empyrean blue of the morning sky deepen above the clouds.

origin: From Latin "aemulari", to rival, try to equal, from "aemulus", rivaling. To emulate is to imitate in order to match.

senses.def: imitate someone you admire, especially in an effort to equal or surpass them
senses.ex: As a young violinist, she tried to emulate the bold, warm tone of her favorite soloist.

syn: imitate, copy, mirror, follow, model oneself on

origin: From Latin "aemulus", striving to equal or excel a rival, the same root as "emulate".

senses.def: eager to equal or surpass someone, driven by rivalry
senses.ex: Emulous of her older brother's science prizes, Maya spent the whole summer building a better solar oven.

origin: From Old French "enamourer", from "en-", in, plus "amour", love, from Latin "amor". To be enamored is to be put in love.

senses.def: fill someone with love or delight, usually in the passive "be enamored of"
senses.ex: The visiting students were so enamored of the little Italian town that several vowed to return.

origin: From "en-", in, plus "capsule", from Latin "capsula", small box, so to encapsulate is to fit something into a little container.

senses.def: express the essential features of something briefly and clearly
senses.ex: Her one-line toast encapsulated twenty years of friendship better than any long speech could have.

senses.def: enclose something completely, as if in a capsule
senses.ex: The fossil record shows insects encapsulated in amber, preserved down to the veins of their wings.

origin: From Old French "enchanter", from Latin "incantare", to chant a spell over, from "in-", on, plus "cantare", to sing.

senses.def: fill someone with great delight, charm
senses.ex: The puppet show enchanted the toddlers, who sat wide-eyed and silent for the entire performance.

senses.def: put someone or something under a magic spell
senses.ex: In the old tale, a jealous sorceress enchants the prince and turns him into a swan.

origin: From Greek "enkheiridion", handbook, from "en", in, plus "kheir", hand, so an enchiridion is literally something held in the hand.

senses.def: handbook or manual, especially a short guide to a subject
senses.ex: The retired captain kept a battered enchiridion of knots and sailing rules in the pocket of his jacket.

syn: handbook, manual, guide, vade mecum, compendium

origin: From "en-", into, plus "cipher", a secret code, from Medieval Latin "cifra", zero, from Arabic "sifr", empty or zero.

senses.def: convert a message into secret code so others cannot read it
senses.ex: During the war, clerks enciphered every radio message before it was transmitted to the fleet.

origin: From French "enclaver", to enclose, from Vulgar Latin "inclavare", to lock in, from Latin "clavis", key.

senses.def: distinct community or group set apart from the larger society around it
senses.ex: The neighborhood grew into a lively Portuguese enclave, with bakeries and social clubs on every block.

senses.def: territory completely surrounded by the territory of another country
senses.ex: The tiny enclave depends on its larger neighbor for water, electricity, and access to the sea.

origin: From Greek "enkomiastes", one who praises, from "enkomion", a song of praise, the source of "encomium".

senses.def: person who praises someone or something in speech or writing, often lavishly
senses.ex: The candidate's official biographer was less a historian than an encomiast, describing every decision as visionary.

origin: From Greek "enkomiastikos", full of praise, from "enkomion", a song of praise sung at a victory celebration.

senses.def: expressing or giving high, often lavish, praise
senses.ex: The retirement dinner featured one encomiastic speech after another, until the honoree begged the guests to stop.

origin: From Greek "enkomion", a song praising a victor, from "komos", a festive celebration or revel.

senses.def: speech or piece of writing that praises someone warmly and formally
senses.ex: At the retirement dinner, colleagues delivered a heartfelt encomium to the teacher who had served for forty years.

origin: From "en-", in, plus "compass", in its old sense of a circle. To encompass is to take in within a circle.

senses.def: include a wide range of things within its scope
senses.ex: The new course encompasses everything from ancient Egyptian art to modern photography.

senses.def: surround or enclose something completely
senses.ex: Thick pine forests encompass the lake, hiding it from the nearby highway.

origin: From "encroach", from Old French "encrochier", to seize, from "croc", hook. Encroaching things hook into space that is not theirs.

senses.def: gradually intruding on another's territory, rights, or time
senses.ex: Farmers worried about the encroaching suburbs that swallowed a few more fields every year.

origin: From Old French "encombrer", to block up, from "en-", in, plus "combrer", to hinder.

senses.def: burden or weigh someone down so as to make movement or action difficult
senses.ex: Encumbered by heavy backpacks and wet boots, the hikers struggled up the last muddy slope.

senses.def: burden property with a debt or legal claim
senses.ex: The house was encumbered with two mortgages, which made it hard to sell.

syn: burden, hamper, impede, saddle, weigh down

origin: From Old French "encombrance", from "encombrer", to block up or hinder, the source of "encumber".

senses.def: something that burdens, hampers, or slows a person down
senses.ex: Hikers on the long trail learn to leave behind every encumbrance, from heavy books to extra cooking pots.

senses.def: legal claim or debt attached to a property, such as a mortgage or lien
senses.ex: Before buying the farm, their lawyer checked the title for any encumbrance that could cloud the sale.

origin: From "encyclopedia", from Greek "enkyklios paideia", all-round education, from "en", in, "kyklos", circle, and "paideia", education.

senses.def: comprehensive in knowledge or information, covering a very wide range
senses.ex: Her encyclopedic knowledge of baseball statistics made her the most valuable player on the trivia team.

origin: From "endear", to make dear or beloved, plus "-ment", so an endearment is something that makes or shows someone is dear.

senses.def: word or phrase that expresses affection, such as darling or sweetheart
senses.ex: My grandmother called every visitor some endearment, from honey to sugar plum, whether she knew them or not.

senses.def: expression of love or affection, in words or gestures
senses.ex: The letters between the soldier and his wife were full of small endearments and worries about the harvest.

syn: pet name, term of affection, affection, fondness, tenderness

origin: From Greek "endemos", native, among one's own people, from "en", in, plus "demos", people.

senses.def: regularly found among a particular people or in a particular place, especially of a disease or problem
senses.ex: Malaria remains endemic in parts of the region, and travelers are urged to take preventive medicine.

senses.def: native to and found only in a certain area, especially of plants and animals
senses.ex: Lemurs are endemic to Madagascar and live naturally nowhere else on Earth.

origin: From Old French "endosser", to put on the back, from Latin "dorsum", back, because a check is endorsed by signing its back.

senses.def: publicly declare support for a person, plan, or product
senses.ex: The teachers' union endorsed the mayor's reelection campaign after she promised smaller class sizes.

senses.def: sign the back of a check or similar document to transfer or cash it
senses.ex: The bank teller asked him to endorse the check before she could deposit it into his savings account.

origin: From Latin "induere", to put on clothes, blended with Old French "enduire", to lead in, so to endue is to clothe someone with a quality.

senses.def: provide someone or something with a quality, power, or ability
senses.ex: The old legend claims the spring endues anyone who drinks from it with uncommon courage and long life.

origin: From "endure", from Latin "indurare", to make hard, from "durus", hard, so what is enduring has hardened enough to last.

senses.def: lasting for a long time without fading or weakening
senses.ex: The two scientists formed an enduring friendship that outlasted their careers, their rivalries, and three changes of country.

origin: From Greek "energoumenos", one worked upon by an outside force, from "energein", to be active, once describing a person possessed by a spirit.

senses.def: wildly enthusiastic fanatic, or a person in a frenzy
senses.ex: At the town meeting, one energumen shouted down every speaker until the moderator finally called security.

senses.def: person believed to be possessed by an evil spirit
senses.ex: Medieval accounts describe priests praying over an energumen who writhed and spoke in strange voices.

origin: From Latin "enervare", to weaken, from "e-", out, plus "nervus", sinew. To enervate is to cut the sinews, not to energize.

senses.def: drain someone of energy or vitality, weaken
senses.ex: The relentless August heat enervated the workers, who moved more slowly with every passing hour.

origin: Past participle of "enervate", from Latin "enervare", to weaken, from "e-", out, plus "nervus", sinew.

senses.def: drained of energy or vitality, weakened
senses.ex: Enervated after the overnight flight, the travelers slept through their first afternoon in Tokyo.

origin: From "enervate", from Latin "enervare", to weaken, from "e-", out, plus "nervus", sinew.

senses.def: causing one to feel drained of energy or strength
senses.ex: After three enervating hours of standardized testing, the students could barely hold their pencils.

origin: From Latin "enervare", to remove the sinews, from "e-", out, plus "nervus", sinew, so enervation is having one's strength cut out.

senses.def: loss of physical, mental, or moral energy, leaving one weak and drained
senses.ex: After weeks of night shifts, the nurses felt a deep enervation that no single day off could cure.

origin: From French "enfiler", to thread on a string, from "fil", thread, because an enfilade runs straight through a line like a thread through beads.

senses.def: gunfire directed along the full length of an enemy's line
senses.ex: Trapped in a straight trench, the soldiers suffered a deadly enfilade from a machine gun at its far end.

senses.def: row of rooms with doorways aligned so one can see straight through them all
senses.ex: The palace's famous enfilade lets visitors gaze through eleven gilded doorways in a single glance.

senses.def: fire along the entire length of an enemy line or position
senses.ex: The defenders placed cannon on the ridge to enfilade any column advancing up the narrow road.

origin: From Old French "enfranchir", to set free, from "en-", in, plus "franc", free, the same root that gives us "frank".

senses.def: give a person or group the right to vote
senses.ex: The amendment enfranchised millions of women, who cast ballots in a national election for the first time.

senses.def: free someone from slavery, servitude, or another restriction
senses.ex: The new law enfranchised the remaining serfs and allowed them to buy the land they had worked.

origin: From "engage", from French "engager", to pledge, from "en-", in, plus "gage", pledge, so engaging things bind your attention.

senses.def: charming and pleasant in a way that attracts people
senses.ex: The tour guide had an engaging smile and a habit of turning dull dates into funny stories.

senses.def: interesting enough to hold one's attention
senses.ex: The museum redesigned its dinosaur hall to be more engaging for children, with touchable bones and sound effects.

origin: From Old French "engendrer", from Latin "ingenerare", to beget, from "in-", in, plus "generare", to beget, produce.

senses.def: cause or give rise to a feeling, situation, or condition
senses.ex: The coach's fairness engendered deep loyalty among players who had never felt respected before.

origin: From French "engorger", to gorge or obstruct, from "en-", in, plus "gorge", throat, so the idea is a throat filled to bursting.

senses.def: swell or fill excessively, especially with blood or another fluid
senses.ex: After the bee sting, her ankle became engorged and turned an alarming shade of purple.

senses.def: eat greedily, gorging oneself
senses.ex: The bears engorged themselves on salmon all autumn to build fat for the long winter.

origin: From "engross", from Old French "en gros", wholesale or in bulk; to engross once meant to buy up a whole supply, hence to absorb completely.

senses.def: so absorbed in something that one ignores everything else
senses.ex: Engrossed in her chemistry homework, Priya did not notice that her tea had gone cold an hour ago.

origin: From "en-", in, plus "gulf", a deep chasm or bay, so to engulf is to swallow something up as if into a gulf.

senses.def: sweep over and completely surround or swallow something
senses.ex: Within minutes, flames engulfed the old barn, and firefighters could only protect the farmhouse nearby.

senses.def: overwhelm someone with a feeling or situation
senses.ex: A wave of homesickness engulfed him the moment the train pulled out of the station.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "enhauncer", to raise, from Latin "in", in, plus "altus", high. To enhance something is to raise its quality.

senses.def: improve the quality, value, or extent of something
senses.ex: A pinch of salt can enhance the sweetness of chocolate desserts and caramel sauces.

origin: From Latin "aenigma", riddle, from Greek "ainigma", a dark saying, a riddle.

senses.def: person or thing that is mysterious or difficult to understand
senses.ex: Even to her closest friends, the quiet painter remained an enigma who never spoke about her past.

origin: From Latin "aenigmaticus", from Greek "ainigmatikos", from "ainigma", a riddle or dark saying.

senses.def: mysterious and difficult to interpret or understand
senses.ex: The detective gave an enigmatic smile and said only that the answer had been in the garden all along.

origin: From French "enjambement", from "enjamber", to stride over, from "jambe", leg, because the sentence steps over the end of the line.

senses.def: in poetry, running a sentence from one line onto the next without a pause
senses.ex: The poet's frequent enjambment pulls readers swiftly down the page, so each line spills into the next.

origin: From Old French "enjoindre", from Latin "iniungere", to fasten on, impose, from "in-", upon, plus "iungere", to join.

senses.def: instruct or urge someone with authority to do something
senses.ex: The doctor enjoined her patient to rest for a full week before returning to the soccer field.

senses.def: legally forbid someone from doing something
senses.ex: The court enjoined the company from dumping waste into the river until the case was decided.

origin: From Old French "enemistie", from Vulgar Latin "inimicitas", from Latin "inimicus", enemy, from "in-", not, plus "amicus", friend.

senses.def: state of deep hostility or mutual hatred
senses.ex: The enmity between the two families began with a dispute over a fence and lasted three generations.

origin: From Old French "ennoblir", from "en-", make, plus "noble", so to ennoble is literally to make noble.

senses.def: give dignity or moral worth to someone or something
senses.ex: The novelist believed that hard, honest labor could ennoble even the most ordinary life.

senses.def: raise someone to the rank of the nobility
senses.ex: The queen ennobled the inventor for his services to the nation, and he became a baron.

origin: From French "ennui", from Old French "enui", annoyance, from Latin "in odio", in hatred. The English word "annoy" shares this source.

senses.def: listless feeling of boredom and dissatisfaction from lack of interest or excitement
senses.ex: By the third week of summer vacation, a heavy ennui had settled over the teenagers, who drifted from couch to couch.

origin: From Latin "enormitas", irregularity, from "enormis", out of the ordinary, from "e-", out of, plus "norma", rule, standard.

senses.def: extreme wickedness or seriousness of a crime or wrong
senses.ex: Only years later did the soldiers grasp the full enormity of the crimes committed in that village.

senses.def: great size or scale, especially of a task or problem
senses.ex: Standing at the foot of the glacier, the climbers finally understood the enormity of their challenge.

origin: From "en-", into, plus "rapture", from Latin "raptus", seized or carried off, so to enrapture is to carry someone away with delight.

senses.def: fill someone with intense delight or wonder
senses.ex: The young pianist's performance enraptured the audience, who sat motionless until the final chord faded.

origin: From "en-", in, plus "sconce", an old word for a small fort, so to ensconce oneself is to settle into a safe, sheltered spot.

senses.def: settle oneself or something comfortably and securely in a place
senses.ex: By noon, Grandpa was ensconced in his favorite armchair with the newspaper and a plate of crackers.

origin: From "en-", in, plus "snare", a trap made of a noose, so to ensnare is to catch something in a trap.

senses.def: catch or trap someone, often by trickery
senses.ex: The undercover detectives ensnared the art forger by posing as wealthy collectors eager to buy a fake.

senses.def: catch an animal in a snare or trap
senses.ex: The trapper set wire loops along the trail to ensnare rabbits during the winter.

origin: Past participle of "ensorcell", from French "ensorceler", to bewitch, from "sorcier", sorcerer.

senses.def: bewitched or enchanted, as if under a spell
senses.ex: Ensorcelled by the music drifting from the old carousel, the child refused to leave the fairground.

origin: From Old French "ensuivre", to follow after, from Latin "insequi", from "in-", upon, plus "sequi", to follow, the root of "sequel".

senses.def: happen afterward, especially as a result of something
senses.ex: When the referee reversed the call, a loud argument ensued between the two coaches.

origin: From Middle English "entanglen", built from "en-", in, plus "tangle", so to be caught inside a knot you cannot easily undo.

senses.def: twist or catch something in a knotted mass that is hard to separate
senses.ex: The young seal had become entangled in a discarded fishing net and could barely lift its head.

senses.def: involve someone in a difficult or compromising situation that is hard to escape
senses.ex: The mayor tried to stay neutral but was soon entangled in a bitter feud between two council members.

origin: From Late Latin, from Greek "entelecheia", a word Aristotle coined from "enteles", complete (from "telos", end), and "echein", to have: having its end within it.

senses.def: the full realization of something's potential, the state of being fully what it was meant to be
senses.ex: For the old sculptor, the finished statue was the entelechy of a shape he had sensed inside the raw marble.

senses.def: in philosophy, an inner force thought to guide a living thing toward its complete form
senses.ex: Some early biologists imagined an entelechy within each seed that steered it toward becoming a particular tree.

origin: From "en-", into, plus "thrall", a slave, from Old Norse "thræll". To enthrall is to make someone a captive of your spell.

senses.def: capture someone's complete attention and interest, captivate
senses.ex: The storyteller enthralled the campers with a ghost story so vivid that no one wanted to walk back to the cabins.

origin: From Old French "enticier", to stir up, set on fire, traced to Latin "titio", a firebrand. Enticing offers kindle desire.

senses.def: attract or tempt someone by offering pleasure or advantage
senses.ex: The bakery enticed passersby with the smell of fresh cinnamon rolls drifting onto the sidewalk.

origin: From "entitle", from Old French "entiteler", from Late Latin "intitulare", to give a title or claim to, from Latin "titulus", title.

senses.def: believing oneself inherently deserving of special privileges or treatment
senses.ex: The entitled guest demanded a free upgrade and shouted at the clerk when the hotel refused.

senses.def: having a legal or rightful claim to something
senses.ex: Full-time employees are entitled to three weeks of paid vacation each year.

senses.def: having a particular title, of a book, film, or other work
senses.ex: Her first novel, entitled "Salt and Smoke", was set in a fishing village in Maine.

origin: From "entitle", to give a right or claim, from Late Latin "intitulare", from Latin "titulus", title, plus "-ment".

senses.def: belief that one deserves special privileges or treatment
senses.ex: His sense of entitlement showed when he expected the team to rearrange practice around his vacation.

senses.def: legal or official right to have or receive something
senses.ex: The new rules reduced workers' entitlement to sick pay during their first six months.

senses.def: government program that guarantees benefits to people who meet certain conditions
senses.ex: Debates over the budget often focus on entitlements such as Social Security and Medicare.

origin: From French "entomologie", from Greek "entomon", insect (literally a thing "cut into", for its segmented body), plus "-logia", study.

senses.def: the scientific study of insects
senses.ex: Her summer job counting beetles in the wetlands convinced her to major in entomology.

origin: Borrowed from French, from "entourer", to surround, so the people who constantly surround an important person.

senses.def: group of assistants, advisers, or followers who accompany an important person
senses.ex: The pop star swept through the airport with an entourage of bodyguards, stylists, and a nervous publicist.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "entraiter", to deal with, negotiate, from "en-", in, plus "traiter", to treat, from Latin "tractare", to handle.

senses.def: ask someone earnestly or anxiously to do something
senses.ex: The villagers entreated the governor to send help before the floodwaters reached their homes.

syn: beg, implore, beseech, plead with, petition
