origin: From "entreat", to plead with, plus the noun ending "-y"; "entreat" came through Old French from "traiter", to treat or deal with someone.

senses.def: earnest, often emotional request or plea
senses.ex: Ignoring the entreaties of her coaches, the injured runner insisted on finishing the final lap.

origin: From "entrench", from "en-", in, plus "trench", first used of soldiers dug into protective trenches and hard to dislodge.

senses.def: firmly established and very difficult to change
senses.ex: Reformers struggled against entrenched habits in a department that had worked the same way for fifty years.

origin: Coined in German as "Entropie" by the physicist Rudolf Clausius in 1865, modeled on "energy" but built on Greek "trope", transformation.

senses.def: gradual decline into disorder, disorganization, or uniformity
senses.ex: Without a manager to keep things running, the once-tidy office slid into a state of cheerful entropy.

senses.def: in physics, a measure of the disorder of a system and of energy no longer available for work
senses.ex: As the ice cube melts in the warm drink, the entropy of the whole system increases.

origin: From Latin "enumerare", to count out, from "e-", out, plus "numerare", to count, from "numerus", number.

senses.def: name or list things one by one
senses.ex: In her letter of complaint, she enumerated every problem with the apartment, from the leaky faucet to the broken heater.

origin: From Latin "enuntiare", to speak out or declare, from "e-", out, plus "nuntiare", to announce.

senses.def: pronounce words clearly and distinctly
senses.ex: The drama teacher made us enunciate every consonant so the back row could follow the dialogue.

senses.def: state an idea or principle clearly and formally
senses.ex: In her first speech, the new principal enunciated three goals she meant to reach by spring.

origin: From Old French "envenimer", to poison, from "en-", in, plus "venim", venom.

senses.def: fill something with bitterness or hostility
senses.ex: Years of petty slights had envenomed the rivalry between the two families beyond any repair.

senses.def: put poison on or into something
senses.ex: The guide explained how hunters once envenomed the tips of their darts with the sap of a forest vine.

origin: From Old French "environner", to encircle, from "environ", around, from "viron", circle; the noun "environment" grew from the same verb.

senses.def: surround or enclose, used mostly in formal or literary writing
senses.ex: The ruined abbey stood alone in the valley, environed by dark pines and a slow river.

origin: From French "envoyé", one who is sent, from "envoyer", to send.

senses.def: messenger or representative sent on a special diplomatic mission
senses.ex: The president sent a special envoy to the region to persuade both sides to resume peace talks.

senses.def: diplomat ranking just below an ambassador
senses.ex: In the nineteenth century, smaller countries often hosted an envoy rather than a full ambassador.

origin: From Latin "aeon", from Greek "aion", age or lifetime, so an age so long it feels endless.

senses.def: extremely long or seemingly endless period of time
senses.ex: The hike back to the car in the freezing rain seemed to last an eon.

senses.def: in geology, the largest division of time, often a billion years or more
senses.ex: Simple bacteria were the only life on Earth for most of the Archean eon.

origin: From Greek "ephemeros", lasting only a day, from "epi", on, plus "hemera", day.

senses.def: lasting for a very short time
senses.ex: Fame on social media is often ephemeral, with yesterday's viral star forgotten by the following week.

origin: From Latin "epicoenus", from Greek "epikoinos", common to many, from "epi-", upon, plus "koinos", common; it first described nouns shared by both sexes.

senses.def: having traits of both sexes or of neither, androgynous
senses.ex: The singer's epicene look, with sharp suits and soft makeup, made critics argue for weeks.

senses.def: in grammar, having one form that refers to either sex
senses.ex: Some writers prefer the epicene pronoun "they" when a person's gender is unknown.

senses.def: lacking vigor or force, effete
senses.ex: The reviewer dismissed the novel's hero as an epicene dreamer who never makes a real decision.

origin: Named after Epicurus, an ancient Greek philosopher who taught that pleasure, wisely pursued, is the chief good in life.

senses.def: person with refined taste who takes special pleasure in fine food and drink
senses.ex: A true epicure, my aunt could tell which region an olive oil came from after a single taste.

syn: gourmet, connoisseur, gastronome, foodie, bon vivant

origin: Named for Epicurus, the Greek philosopher of around 300 BC who taught that a life of calm, well-chosen pleasure is the highest good.

senses.def: devoted to refined pleasure, especially fine food and drink
senses.ex: The chef's epicurean tasting menu included white truffles, aged cheeses, and a rare dessert wine.

senses.def: person who takes great pleasure in fine food and drink
senses.ex: A true epicurean, my uncle will drive two hours for a perfectly made loaf of sourdough.

origin: From French "épigone", from Greek "epigonos", one born after, from "epi-", after, plus "gignesthai", to be born.

senses.def: inferior follower or imitator of a great artist or thinker
senses.ex: After the painter's death, a crowd of epigones copied her bold colors without any of her daring.

origin: From Greek "epigramma", an inscription, from "epi", upon, plus "graphein", to write. Short inscriptions grew into short, witty poems and sayings.

senses.def: brief, clever, and often witty saying or short poem
senses.ex: Oscar Wilde was famous for epigrams such as the claim that he could resist everything except temptation.

syn: aphorism, quip, witticism, maxim, bon mot

origin: Through French and Latin from Greek "epilogos", conclusion, from "epilegein", to say in addition.

senses.def: section at the end of a book, play, or film that comments on or concludes the story
senses.ex: In the epilogue, set twenty years later, we learn that the two rivals became business partners.

senses.def: event or development that follows and rounds off an earlier one
senses.ex: The lawsuit that dragged on after the election was a messy epilogue to an already bitter campaign.

origin: From Greek "epiphaneia", appearance, manifestation, from "epi", upon, plus "phainein", to show or shine. An epiphany is a truth suddenly shining through.

senses.def: sudden and striking realization or insight
senses.ex: Halfway through her run, she had an epiphany: the bug in her code was a single misplaced comma.

senses.def: appearance or revelation of a divine being
senses.ex: The painting depicts an epiphany in which an angel appears in a blaze of light before the frightened shepherds.

origin: From "epi-", on top of, plus "phenomenon", from Greek "phainomenon", a thing that appears, so something riding on top of a deeper process.

senses.def: secondary effect or by-product that accompanies a process but does not cause anything itself
senses.ex: The economist argued that the spike in luxury sales was an epiphenomenon of the boom, not its cause.

origin: From "episode", from Greek "epeisodion", a section added between the choral songs of a Greek play.

senses.def: happening at irregular intervals rather than continuously
senses.ex: His episodic migraines struck without warning, sometimes twice in a week and then not for months.

senses.def: made up of a series of loosely connected parts or events
senses.ex: The novel's episodic structure lets each chapter work almost as a separate short story.

origin: From Greek "episteme", knowledge, plus "-logia", study; the Scottish philosopher James Frederick Ferrier introduced the term into English.

senses.def: branch of philosophy that studies the nature, sources, and limits of knowledge
senses.ex: Our epistemology seminar spent a whole week on whether we can truly know that other minds exist.

syn: theory of knowledge, philosophy of knowledge

origin: From Latin "epistola", letter, from Greek "epistole", a message, from "epistellein", to send to. The same root gives "epistle".

senses.def: relating to or written in the form of letters
senses.ex: "Dracula" is an epistolary novel told through diary entries, letters, and newspaper clippings.

origin: Through Old French and Latin from Greek "epitaphios", of a funeral, from "epi-", over, plus "taphos", tomb: words set over a grave.

senses.def: short inscription on a gravestone in memory of the person buried there
senses.ex: The poet's epitaph, carved in plain letters, read simply: "She loved the sea."

senses.def: short statement or phrase that sums up a person, event, or era after it has ended
senses.ex: The failed product launch became the unofficial epitaph for the company's brief run of success.

origin: Through Latin from Greek "epithalamion", bridal song, from "epi-", upon or at, plus "thalamos", bridal chamber.

senses.def: song or poem written to celebrate a wedding
senses.ex: For her sister's wedding, Maya wrote an epithalamium that drew both laughter and tears from the guests.

syn: wedding song, nuptial poem, marriage hymn, prothalamion

origin: From Greek "epitheton", something added, from "epitithenai", to put on, add, from "epi", on, plus "tithenai", to place.

senses.def: descriptive word or phrase attached to a person's name
senses.ex: King Richard I earned the epithet "the Lionheart" for his courage in battle.

senses.def: insulting or abusive word used to describe a person or group
senses.ex: The player was suspended for shouting a racial epithet at an opponent.

origin: From Greek "epitome", an abridgment, from "epitemnein", to cut short, from "epi", upon, plus "temnein", to cut. A summary cut down to the essential.

senses.def: perfect example of a particular quality or type
senses.ex: With his tailored suit and flawless manners, the butler was the epitome of quiet elegance.

origin: From Greek "epokhe", a pause or fixed point in time, from "epekhein", to hold back, from "epi-", upon, plus "ekhein", to hold.

senses.def: long period of history marked by notable events or a distinctive character
senses.ex: The invention of the printing press opened an epoch in which ideas could spread faster than any ruler could suppress them.

senses.def: division of geologic time that is shorter than a period
senses.ex: Geologists debate whether human activity has pushed Earth into a new epoch called the Anthropocene.

origin: From Greek "eponymos", giving one's name to something, from "epi", upon, plus "onyma", name.

senses.def: person after whom something such as a place, invention, or discovery is named
senses.ex: Louis Pasteur is the eponym of pasteurization, the heating process that makes milk safe to drink.

senses.def: word or name formed from the name of a person
senses.ex: "Sandwich" is an eponym, taken from an English earl who liked to eat meat between slices of bread.

origin: From Greek "eponymos", giving one's name to something, from "epi", upon, plus "onyma", name.

senses.def: named after a particular person, or giving one's name to something
senses.ex: The band's eponymous first album, simply titled "The Lanterns", sold surprisingly well.

origin: From Latin "aequabilis", uniform, from "aequare", to make level, from "aequus", even, level.

senses.def: calm and even-tempered, not easily upset
senses.ex: Her equable temperament made her the perfect person to calm down a room full of angry parents.

senses.def: steady and free from extremes, especially of climate
senses.ex: The island's equable climate rarely drops below sixty degrees or rises above eighty.

origin: From Latin "aequanimitas", from "aequus", even, plus "animus", mind. Equanimity is an even, level mind.

senses.def: mental calm and composure, especially in a difficult situation
senses.ex: The pilot announced the engine failure with remarkable equanimity, and the passengers stayed calm.

origin: From Latin "equester", relating to horsemen, from "equus", horse.

senses.def: relating to horseback riding or to horse riders
senses.ex: The equestrian events at the county fair drew riders who had trained their horses all summer.

senses.def: person who rides horses, especially with skill
senses.ex: A seasoned equestrian, she guided the nervous horse calmly over the final jump.

senses.def: showing a person mounted on a horse, as a statue or portrait
senses.ex: An equestrian statue of the general, sword raised, towers over the town square.

origin: From Latin "aequilibrium", from "aequus", equal, plus "libra", balance or scales, so a state in which the scales hang even.

senses.def: state in which opposing forces or influences are balanced
senses.ex: When supply finally matched demand, prices settled into an equilibrium that lasted for months.

senses.def: calm, steady state of mind
senses.ex: After the shouting match, he took a long walk to recover his equilibrium before rejoining the meeting.

origin: From "equi-", equal, plus "poise", weight or balance. Equipoise is equal weight on both sides of the scale.

senses.def: state of balance between opposing forces or interests
senses.ex: The treaty created a fragile equipoise between the two rival powers that lasted nearly a century.

senses.def: something that balances or offsets something else
senses.ex: Her calm good sense served as an equipoise to her partner's impulsive enthusiasm.

origin: From French "équitable", from "équité", equity, from Latin "aequitas", fairness, from "aequus", even, fair.

senses.def: fair and impartial to everyone involved
senses.ex: The roommates worked out an equitable plan in which each person cleaned the kitchen one week a month.

origin: From Old French "equite", from Latin "aequitas", evenness or fairness, from "aequus", equal or level.

senses.def: quality of being fair and impartial
senses.ex: The new grading policy was designed for equity, so students without home internet would not be penalized.

senses.def: value of a property beyond the amount still owed on it
senses.ex: After ten years of mortgage payments, they had built up enough equity to borrow for the renovation.

senses.def: ownership share in a company, such as stock
senses.ex: Instead of a higher salary, the startup offered its first engineers equity in the company.

origin: From French "equivalence", from Medieval Latin "aequivalentia", from "aequus", equal, plus "valere", to be worth.

senses.def: condition of being equal in value, amount, meaning, or function
senses.ex: Translators argued over whether any English word had true equivalence to the Japanese term for that feeling.

origin: From Late Latin "aequivocus", ambiguous, from "aequus", equal, plus "vocare", to call. An equivocal word calls out two meanings equally.

senses.def: open to more than one interpretation, often deliberately vague
senses.ex: Asked whether he would run for office, the mayor gave an equivocal answer that satisfied no one.

senses.def: uncertain or doubtful in nature or outcome
senses.ex: The results of the drug trial were equivocal, so the company planned a larger study.

origin: From Medieval Latin "aequivocare", to call by the same name, from Late Latin "aequivocus", ambiguous, from "aequus", equal, plus "vocare", to call.

senses.def: use vague or ambiguous language to avoid committing oneself or telling the truth
senses.ex: When reporters pressed her about the missing funds, the treasurer equivocated, saying only that accounts were under review.

syn: prevaricate, hedge, waffle, dodge, hem and haw

origin: From Late Latin "aequivocus", ambiguous, from "aequus", equal, plus "vocare", to call, so calling two different things by one name.

senses.def: use of vague or ambiguous language to avoid committing oneself or to mislead
senses.ex: The senator's equivocation on the tax question frustrated reporters who wanted a simple yes or no.

origin: From Latin "eradicare", to root out, from "e-", out, plus "radix", root, the same root as "radish".

senses.def: destroy something completely or put an end to it
senses.ex: A worldwide vaccination campaign eradicated smallpox, a disease that had killed millions for centuries.

syn: eliminate, exterminate, abolish, uproot, wipe out

origin: From Late Latin "eremita", from Greek "eremites", desert dweller, from "eremos", empty or uninhabited, the same source as "hermit".

senses.def: hermit, especially a religious recluse who lives alone
senses.ex: The eremite had lived in a stone hut on the mountainside for decades, praying and tending a small garden.

origin: From Greek "eristikos", eager for strife, from "eris", strife, also the name of the Greek goddess of discord.

senses.def: given to arguing for its own sake, aiming to win rather than to find the truth
senses.ex: The online debate turned eristic, with each side scoring points instead of trying to understand the other.

senses.def: person who argues mainly for the sake of winning
senses.ex: A practiced eristic, he could defend either side of any question just to provoke his classmates.

origin: From French "eroder", from Latin "erodere", to gnaw away, from "e-", away, plus "rodere", to gnaw, the root of "rodent".

senses.def: wear away gradually, as by wind, water, or ice
senses.ex: Centuries of pounding waves have eroded the cliffs until the old lighthouse now stands at the very edge.

senses.def: gradually weaken or destroy something such as trust or support
senses.ex: Repeated broken promises eroded the voters' trust in the city council.

syn: wear away, wear down, abrade, corrode, undermine

origin: From Old French "errer", from Latin "errare", to wander, stray. To err is to wander from what is right, as in "error".

senses.def: make a mistake or act wrongly
senses.ex: The umpire erred when he called the runner safe, as the replay clearly showed.

syn: blunder, misjudge, slip up, stray, go wrong

origin: From Old French "errant", wandering, traveling, from Latin "iter", journey, influenced by Latin "errare", to stray.

senses.def: straying from the proper course or from accepted standards of behavior
senses.ex: An errant golf ball sailed over the fence and cracked the windshield of a parked car.

senses.def: traveling in search of adventure, as in "knight errant"
senses.ex: The old ballad tells of an errant knight who rides from kingdom to kingdom righting wrongs.

origin: From Latin "erraticus", wandering, from "errare", to wander or stray, the same root as "err" and "error".

senses.def: unpredictable and irregular in movement, behavior, or quality
senses.ex: The old printer's erratic behavior, jamming one day and working perfectly the next, drove the whole office to distraction.

senses.def: departing from what is usual or expected, odd or eccentric
senses.ex: His erratic choices, like wearing a tuxedo to the beach picnic, made his friends wonder what he was thinking.

origin: From Latin "erroneus", straying, from "errare", to wander. An erroneous idea has wandered away from the truth.

senses.def: containing a mistake or based on a false belief, incorrect
senses.ex: The newspaper printed a correction after an erroneous report claimed the mayor had resigned.

origin: Borrowed from German "Ersatz", replacement or substitute, from "ersetzen", to replace. The word spread in English after German wartime substitutes like ersatz coffee.

senses.def: used as an inferior or artificial substitute for the real thing
senses.ex: During the shortage, cafes served an ersatz coffee brewed from roasted chicory and barley.

origin: From "erst", an old word meaning at first or formerly (Old English "ǣrest", earliest), plus "while", so literally "of an earlier time".

senses.def: former, having once been in a role or relationship but no longer
senses.ex: The two erstwhile rivals now run a bakery together and laugh about their old competition.

origin: From Latin "eruditus", educated, past participle of "erudire", to instruct, from "e", out of, and "rudis", rough or untrained: polished out of roughness.

senses.def: having or showing deep knowledge gained from reading and study
senses.ex: The erudite professor could quote Virgil in Latin and then explain the poem's influence on Dante.

senses.def: of writing or speech, full of learned references and scholarship
senses.ex: Her erudite essay on Byzantine coins included footnotes in four languages.

origin: From Latin "eruditio", instruction, from "erudire", to educate, literally to bring out of roughness ("e", out, and "rudis", rough or untrained).

senses.def: deep, wide knowledge acquired through long reading and study
senses.ex: The judge's erudition showed in rulings that drew on Roman law, Shakespeare, and modern economics.

origin: From Latin "erumpens", bursting out, from "erumpere", to break forth, from "e-", out, plus "rumpere", to break, the root of "rupture".

senses.def: bursting forth or breaking through a surface
senses.ex: In the damp spring woods, erumpent mushrooms pushed up through the crust of fallen leaves overnight.

origin: Formed from "escalator", a 1900 trade name blending "escalade", scaling walls with ladders (Latin "scala", ladder), and "elevator". Things that escalate climb step by step.

senses.def: increase or cause to increase rapidly in intensity, size, or seriousness
senses.ex: What began as a dispute over a parking space escalated into a shouting match that brought the police.

senses.def: pass a problem or complaint up to a higher level of authority
senses.ex: When the help desk couldn't fix the outage, they escalated the ticket to the senior engineers.

syn: intensify, heighten, mount, step up, spiral

origin: From French "escapade", from Spanish "escapada", an escape, from "escapar", to escape, so first a breaking loose from the rules.

senses.def: daring, reckless, or mischievous adventure that breaks the usual rules
senses.ex: Their midnight escapade to the abandoned amusement park ended when a security guard's flashlight found them.

origin: From French "escarpement", from "escarpe", a steep slope, originally the steep bank of a fortress ditch.

senses.def: long, steep slope or cliff that separates two levels of land
senses.ex: From the top of the escarpment, the hikers could see the river valley stretching flat for miles below.

origin: From Greek "eskhatos", last, plus "-logy", study, so the study of the last things.

senses.def: branch of theology dealing with death, judgment, and the final destiny of humanity and the world
senses.ex: The seminar compared the eschatology of several religions, from Norse visions of Ragnarok to Christian teachings on the Last Judgment.

syn: doctrine of last things, end-times theology, apocalypticism

origin: From Anglo-Norman "eschiver", to avoid, from a Frankish word meaning to dread or shun. It is distantly related to "skew".

senses.def: deliberately avoid or keep away from something, often on principle
senses.ex: The minimalist architect eschews ornament, preferring bare concrete walls and plain glass.

syn: shun, avoid, forgo, abstain from, renounce

origin: From an older French "escritoire", from "escrire", to write, from Latin "scribere", to write.

senses.def: small writing desk, often with drawers and a hinged writing surface
senses.ex: She kept her grandmother's letters in the pigeonholes of an antique escritoire beside the window.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "escuchon", ultimately from Latin "scutum", shield.

senses.def: shield on which a coat of arms is displayed
senses.ex: The family's escutcheon, a silver lion on a blue field, was carved above the castle gate.

senses.def: reputation or good name, especially in the phrase "a blot on the escutcheon"
senses.ex: The bribery scandal was a blot on the mayor's escutcheon that no later achievement could fully erase.

syn: shield, coat of arms, crest, arms, blazon

origin: Coined by the poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge from Greek "es", into, "hen", one, and "plassein", to mold, so "molding into one".

senses.def: able to shape separate elements into a unified whole, said especially of the imagination
senses.ex: Coleridge praised the esemplastic imagination that fuses scattered images into a single, living poem.

origin: From Greek "esoterikos", belonging to an inner circle, from "eso", within. It first described teachings kept for a philosopher's inner group of students.

senses.def: understood by or meant for only a small group with special knowledge
senses.ex: The conference talk was so esoteric that only a handful of quantum topologists in the room could follow it.

origin: From Old French "espousailles", from Latin "sponsalia", betrothal, from "sponsus", promised in marriage, the same root as "spouse".

senses.def: adoption of or support for a cause, belief, or way of life
senses.ex: Her public espousal of renewable energy surprised colleagues who knew her family had worked in coal mining.

senses.def: marriage or engagement to marry, in formal or literary use
senses.ex: The royal espousal was celebrated with a week of feasts and processions throughout the kingdom.

origin: From Old French "espouser", to marry, from Latin "sponsare", to betroth, from "spondere", to pledge. To espouse a cause is to wed yourself to it.

senses.def: adopt and support a belief, cause, or way of life
senses.ex: After volunteering at the food bank, she began to espouse a policy of free school lunches for every child.

origin: From French "esprit", spirit or mind, from Latin "spiritus", breath or spirit.

senses.def: liveliness of mind and expression; sparkling wit
senses.ex: Her letters sparkled with an esprit that made even descriptions of rainy weekends a pleasure to read.

origin: From French, literally "spirit of the body", meaning the shared spirit of a group.

senses.def: feeling of pride, loyalty, and fellowship shared by the members of a group
senses.ex: Weeks of early-morning practices built an esprit de corps that carried the underdog team to the championship.

syn: camaraderie, morale, solidarity, team spirit, fellowship

origin: From Old French "espier", to watch, from a Frankish word meaning to look or peer. It is a doublet of "spy".

senses.def: catch sight of something, especially something far away or hard to see
senses.ex: From the ridge, the hikers espied a thin plume of smoke rising from the valley below.

origin: From French "essai", a trial or attempt, from Latin "exagium", a weighing. Montaigne called his short prose pieces "essais", meaning attempts.

senses.def: attempt or try something, especially something difficult (formal)
senses.ex: The young pianist essayed a fiendishly hard sonata at her first recital and played it flawlessly.

senses.def: short piece of writing on a single subject, giving the author's view
senses.ex: Her college application essay described learning to cook from her grandmother in Manila.

senses.def: first or tentative attempt at something (formal)
senses.ex: The director's first essay into comedy was clumsy, but critics saw promise in it.

origin: From French "estimer", from Latin "aestimare", to value or appraise, the same source as "estimate".

senses.def: respect and admiration
senses.ex: The retiring nurse was held in such esteem that half the hospital staff came to her farewell party.

senses.def: respect and admire highly
senses.ex: Musicians across the genre esteem her as the finest jazz pianist of her generation.

origin: From Latin "aestimabilis", worthy of value, from "aestimare", to value or appraise, the same root as "esteem" and "estimate".

senses.def: deserving respect and admiration
senses.ex: The retiring nurse was praised as an estimable colleague who never once lost her patience with a frightened patient.

origin: From Old French, from Latin "aestivalis", of summer, from "aestas", summer; also spelled "aestival".

senses.def: relating to or occurring in summer
senses.ex: The village's estival festival fills the square with music on long, warm evenings in July.

origin: From the verb "estrange", from Old French "estranger", from Latin "extraneare", to treat as a stranger, from "extraneus", foreign or outside.

senses.def: no longer close to or on friendly terms with someone once dear
senses.ex: After ten years without speaking, the estranged brothers finally met for coffee at their mother's insistence.

senses.def: of a spouse, separated and no longer living together
senses.ex: His estranged wife still owned half the house while the divorce was being settled.

origin: From Latin "esuriens", hungering, from "esurire", to be hungry, a form of "edere", to eat, that expresses a wish to do the action.

senses.def: hungry or greedy, often in a figurative sense of eager to acquire
senses.ex: The esurient developers circled the old farmland, each hoping to buy it cheaply and build condos.

origin: From Latin "aetherius", of the upper air, from Greek "aither", the bright, pure air the gods were thought to breathe high above the clouds.

senses.def: extremely delicate and light, seeming too fine for this world
senses.ex: The choir's ethereal harmonies seemed to float up into the dark rafters of the cathedral.

senses.def: heavenly or spiritual rather than earthly
senses.ex: Medieval painters gave the angels an ethereal glow to set them apart from the human figures.

origin: Through Old French and Late Latin from Greek "ethikos", moral, from "ethos", character or custom.

senses.def: set of moral principles or values that guides a person or group
senses.ex: Her strong work ethic meant she finished every assignment early, even during basketball season.

senses.def: particular principle of right conduct
senses.ex: The newspaper's guiding ethic was never to print a claim from a single unnamed source.

origin: From Greek "ethnos", nation or people, plus "-logia", study.

senses.def: branch of anthropology that compares different cultures and their customs
senses.ex: His ethnology course compared harvest rituals in villages across Peru, Ghana, and northern India.

origin: From Greek "ethos", character, custom, or habit. The related word "ethikos" gave English "ethics".

senses.def: the characteristic spirit, values, and beliefs of a group, culture, or era
senses.ex: The startup's ethos of openness meant every employee could see the company's finances.

senses.def: in rhetoric, an appeal to the speaker's credibility and character
senses.ex: The doctor used ethos by opening her speech with her twenty years treating heart patients.

origin: From French "étioler", to make pale, from a Norman word for stubble or straw (from Latin "stipula", stalk). A plant kept from light turns pale as straw.

senses.def: of a plant, pale and spindly from growing without enough light
senses.ex: The potatoes forgotten in the dark cellar had sprouted long, etiolated shoots as white as string.

senses.def: pale, weak, and lacking vigor
senses.ex: Critics called the sequel an etiolated copy of the original, with none of its energy or wit.

origin: From Latin "aetiologia", from Greek "aitia", cause, plus "-logia", study; British English spells it "aetiology".

senses.def: cause or set of causes of a disease or condition
senses.ex: Doctors still debate the etiology of the illness, which may involve both genes and diet.

senses.def: study or investigation of the causes of something
senses.ex: The historian's essay offered an etiology of the riot, tracing it to years of unfair rents.

origin: Through Old French and Latin from Greek "etymologia", from "etymon", the true sense of a word, plus "-logia", study.

senses.def: origin and history of a particular word and its meanings
senses.ex: The etymology of "salary" is often traced to the Latin word for salt.

senses.def: study of the origins and development of words
senses.ex: Studying etymology helped him guess the meanings of unfamiliar words on the reading test.

syn: derivation, origin, word history, source, root

origin: Coined by J. R. R. Tolkien in 1944 from "eu-", good, plus "catastrophe", a sudden turn in a story, so a sudden joyful turn.

senses.def: sudden, unexpected turn of events in a story that rescues the hero from seemingly certain doom
senses.ex: Just as the city is about to fall, the arrival of the lost army provides the novel's eucatastrophe.

origin: From Greek "eudaimonia", happiness, from "eu-", good, plus "daimon", guardian spirit: the state of having a good spirit on your side.

senses.def: in Aristotle's ethics, true happiness or flourishing that comes from living a virtuous life
senses.ex: Aristotle argued that eudaemonia comes not from pleasure or wealth but from practicing virtue over a lifetime.

origin: From "eulogy", from Greek "eulogia", praise, from "eu-", well, plus "logos", word, with the adjective ending "-istic".

senses.def: full of high praise, like a eulogy
senses.ex: The coach's eulogistic remarks about the retiring janitor brought the whole gym to its feet.

origin: From "eulogy", from Greek "eulogia", praise, literally good speaking, from "eu-", well, plus "legein", to speak.

senses.def: praise someone highly, especially in a speech at a funeral
senses.ex: At the memorial, her former students eulogized her as a teacher who never gave up on anyone.

senses.def: praise something enthusiastically in speech or writing
senses.ex: Food critics eulogized the tiny noodle shop until the line stretched around the block.

origin: From Medieval Latin "eulogium", from Greek "eulogia", praise, from "eu", well, and "logos", word or speech: literally "good words".

senses.def: speech or piece of writing praising someone who has just died
senses.ex: At the funeral, her granddaughter gave a eulogy full of funny stories about her famously stubborn garden.

senses.def: high praise for a person or thing
senses.ex: The review was less a critique than a eulogy for the restaurant's legendary dumplings.

origin: From "eu-", good, plus "peptic", of digestion, from Greek "peptein", to digest; good digestion was long linked with a cheerful mood.

senses.def: cheerful and optimistic in outlook
senses.ex: Even after the flight was canceled, our eupeptic tour guide kept everyone laughing in the terminal.

senses.def: having or promoting good digestion
senses.ex: The spa promised a eupeptic diet of ginger tea, steamed greens, and plenty of fiber.

origin: From Greek "euphemismos", from "euphemos", speaking well or auspiciously, from "eu", well, and "pheme", speech.

senses.def: mild or indirect word used in place of one that seems harsh, blunt, or embarrassing
senses.ex: The company's memo used "rightsizing" as a euphemism for firing four hundred workers.

origin: From "euphony", from Greek "euphonia", from "eu-", good, plus "phone", sound or voice.

senses.def: pleasing to the ear, sweet-sounding
senses.ex: The parents chose a euphonious name for their daughter that sounded lovely in both Spanish and English.

origin: From Greek "euphonia", from "eu", good or well, and "phone", sound or voice: literally "good sound".

senses.def: pleasing, harmonious quality of sound, especially in words
senses.ex: Poets often choose words for their euphony, favoring soft sounds like "lullaby" and "murmur".

origin: From Greek "euphoria", well-being, from "euphoros", healthy, literally "bearing well", from "eu", well, and "pherein", to bear or carry.

senses.def: intense feeling of happiness, excitement, and well-being
senses.ex: The euphoria in the locker room after the championship win lasted long into the night.

origin: From "euphoria", from Greek "euphoros", healthy, literally "bearing well", from "eu", well, and "pherein", to bear.

senses.def: feeling or showing intense happiness and excitement
senses.ex: The euphoric fans poured onto the field, hugging strangers and waving scarves after the last-minute goal.

origin: Formed from Greek "eurys", wide, and "topos", place: an organism at home in a wide range of places.

senses.def: of a plant or animal, able to live in a wide range of environments
senses.ex: Raccoons are eurytopic animals, thriving equally in forests, farmland, and the alleys of big cities.

origin: From French "évader", from Latin "evadere", to escape, from "e", out, and "vadere", to go: to go out of reach.

senses.def: escape or avoid someone or something, especially by cleverness or trickery
senses.ex: The fox evaded the hounds by doubling back through the creek to hide its scent.

senses.def: avoid dealing with a question, duty, or obligation, often dishonestly
senses.ex: The senator evaded every question about the missing funds by talking about his travel schedule.

origin: From Latin "evanescere", to vanish, from "e", out, and "vanescere", to vanish, from "vanus", empty. The same root gives "vanish" and "vain".

senses.def: quickly fading or disappearing, lasting only a very short time
senses.ex: The evanescent beauty of the cherry blossoms draws crowds to the park for just one week each spring.

origin: From French "évasif", from Latin "evadere", to escape, from "e", out, and "vadere", to go.

senses.def: avoiding direct answers or commitment, especially to hide the truth
senses.ex: When asked where he had been all night, the teenager gave an evasive shrug and mumbled something about a friend.

senses.def: intended to escape or avoid danger
senses.ex: The pilot took evasive action, banking sharply to avoid the flock of geese.

origin: An English compound of "even" and "handed", first recorded around 1600. The image is a judge holding equal weights in each hand.

senses.def: fair and impartial in treating all sides
senses.ex: The moderator's evenhanded approach gave both candidates exactly the same amount of time to respond.

origin: From Old English "æfentid", from "æfen", evening, plus "tid", time.

senses.def: evening, used in poetic or literary writing
senses.ex: At eventide the fishing boats drifted home across the harbor, their lanterns glowing on the water.

origin: An American coinage from Latin "eventus", outcome or happening, plus the verb ending "-ate".

senses.def: result in a particular outcome
senses.ex: The small dispute over a parking space eventuated in a lawsuit that lasted three years.

senses.def: happen or come about as a result
senses.ex: Analysts warned of a market crash, but no such collapse eventuated that year.

syn: result, culminate, ensue, follow, turn out

origin: From Latin "evidentia", clearness or proof, plus the adjective ending "-ary".

senses.def: relating to or serving as evidence, especially in law
senses.ex: The judge held an evidentiary hearing to decide whether the security footage could be shown to the jury.

origin: From Latin "evincere", to overcome or prove decisively, from "e", out, and "vincere", to conquer. Evidence that "conquers" doubt makes something clear.

senses.def: show or reveal clearly a quality, feeling, or fact
senses.ex: Despite her calm words, her trembling hands evinced how nervous she was before the audition.

origin: Past tense of "evince", from Latin "evincere", to overcome or prove decisively, from "e", out, and "vincere", to conquer.

senses.def: showed or revealed clearly a quality, feeling, or fact
senses.ex: The negotiator evinced no surprise when the other side suddenly doubled its demands.

origin: From Latin "evocativus", calling forth, related to "evocare", to call out, from "e-", out, plus "vocare", to call.

senses.def: bringing strong images, memories, or feelings to mind
senses.ex: The smell of woodsmoke was so evocative that she was suddenly back at her grandmother's cabin.

origin: From French "évoquer", from Latin "evocare", to call out or summon, from "e", out, and "vocare", to call, the root of "voice" and "vocal".

senses.def: bring a feeling, memory, or image into someone's mind
senses.ex: The smell of cinnamon rolls always evokes memories of winter mornings in my aunt's kitchen.

senses.def: draw out a particular response or reaction
senses.ex: The minister's blunt remarks evoked an angry response from teachers across the country.

syn: summon, conjure, elicit, call up, arouse

origin: From Latin "exacerbare", to provoke or make harsh, from "ex", thoroughly, and "acerbus", bitter or harsh, the root of "acerbic".

senses.def: make a problem, bad situation, or negative feeling worse
senses.ex: Scratching the mosquito bite only exacerbated the itching and left an angry red welt.

origin: Past tense of "exacerbate", from Latin "exacerbare", to make harsh, from "ex", thoroughly, and "acerbus", bitter or harsh.

senses.def: made a problem, bad situation, or negative feeling worse
senses.ex: The drought was exacerbated by a heat wave that dried out the last reservoirs in the region.

origin: From Latin "exactus", precise, past participle of "exigere", to demand or weigh accurately, from "ex", out, and "agere", to drive.

senses.def: demand and obtain something, such as payment or revenge, often by force
senses.ex: The conquering army exacted a heavy tribute of grain and silver from every village it occupied.

senses.def: completely accurate and correct in every detail
senses.ex: The pharmacist measured the exact dose prescribed, down to a tenth of a milligram.

origin: From "exact", to demand, from Latin "exigere", to demand or weigh accurately, from "ex", out, and "agere", to drive.

senses.def: demanding great effort, care, precision, or skill
senses.ex: Restoring the medieval manuscript was exacting work that required steady hands and months of patience.

senses.def: of a person, having very high standards and difficult to satisfy
senses.ex: Her exacting violin teacher made her replay a single bar fifty times until every note was clean.

origin: Through French from Latin "exactio", a demanding, from "exigere", to drive out or demand, from "ex-", out, plus "agere", to drive.

senses.def: act of demanding something, especially money, forcefully or unfairly
senses.ex: The villagers rebelled against the exaction of heavy tolls by the lord who controlled the bridge.

senses.def: sum of money or payment demanded, such as a harsh tax or fee
senses.ex: The new fees on fishing licenses were an exaction many families simply could not afford.

origin: From French, from "exact", from Latin "exactus", precise, from "exigere", to weigh or measure, from "ex-", out, plus "agere", to drive.

senses.def: quality of being precise and accurate in every detail
senses.ex: The watchmaker assembled each gear with an exactitude that left no room for even a hair's error.

origin: From Latin "exaggerare", to heap up, from "ex", up, and "agger", a heap or pile: to pile a story higher than the facts.

senses.def: describe something as larger, better, or worse than it really is
senses.ex: My brother exaggerates every fishing trip, so his ten-inch trout becomes a monster by dinnertime.

origin: From Old French "exalter", from Latin "exaltare", to lift up, from "ex", up, and "altus", high, the root of "altitude".

senses.def: praise someone or something very highly
senses.ex: The old hymn exalts the beauty of the mountains and the generosity of the harvest.

senses.def: raise someone to a higher rank, power, or status
senses.ex: The new king exalted his loyal cousin to the post of chief adviser.

origin: From Latin "exasperare", to make rough, from "ex", thoroughly, and "asper", rough: to rub someone's patience raw.

senses.def: irritate someone intensely, especially by repeated annoyance
senses.ex: The toddler's endless "why?" questions began to exasperate even his famously patient grandfather.

origin: From "exasperate", from Latin "exasperare", to make rough, from "ex", thoroughly, and "asper", rough.

senses.def: intensely irritated and frustrated, especially after repeated trouble
senses.ex: The exasperated librarian asked the noisy group to leave after warning them for the third time.

syn: infuriated, irritated, frustrated, vexed, fed up

origin: From Latin "excavare", to hollow out, from "ex-", out, plus "cavus", hollow.

senses.def: dig carefully to uncover buried remains, especially in archaeology
senses.ex: Archaeologists spent three summers excavating a Roman villa buried beneath a vineyard.

senses.def: dig out earth to make a hole or channel
senses.ex: Workers excavated a deep pit for the foundation of the new library.

senses.def: uncover or bring to light something hidden, figuratively
senses.ex: In her memoir she excavates family secrets that no one had spoken about for decades.

origin: From "exception", in its old sense of an objection, plus "-able", so open to objection; do not confuse it with "exceptional".

senses.def: likely to cause objection or offense
senses.ex: The principal found nothing exceptionable in the student newspaper's article about the cafeteria.

origin: From Latin "excerptus", picked out, from "excerpere", from "ex-", out, plus "carpere", to pluck.

senses.def: short passage taken from a longer book, speech, film, or piece of music
senses.ex: The magazine printed an excerpt from the novel a month before the book went on sale.

senses.def: take a short passage from a longer work for quotation or use
senses.ex: The documentary excerpted clips from old newscasts to show how the story first unfolded.

origin: The verb is from Latin "excisus", cut out, from "ex", out, and "caedere", to cut. The tax noun is a separate word, from Middle Dutch "excijs".

senses.def: cut out or remove something completely, such as tissue or a passage of text
senses.ex: The editor excised three chapters to bring the sprawling novel under five hundred pages.

senses.def: tax charged on certain goods made or sold within a country (said EK-syz)
senses.ex: The state raised the excise on cigarettes to discourage smoking among teenagers.

origin: From Latin "excisio", a cutting out, from "excidere", to cut out, from "ex", out, and "caedere", to cut.

senses.def: the act of cutting something out, especially tissue or a growth removed in surgery
senses.ex: The surgeon recommended prompt excision of the mole after the biopsy showed abnormal cells.

senses.def: the removal of a passage or section from a text, film, or other work
senses.ex: The editor's excision of two rambling chapters made the memoir far tighter and easier to read.

syn: removal, extraction, cutting out, resection, deletion

origin: From Late Latin "excoriare", to strip off the skin, from "ex", off, and "corium", hide or skin: criticism so harsh it seems to flay.

senses.def: criticize someone or something very severely
senses.ex: The review excoriated the film's lazy script, calling it a two-hour insult to the audience's intelligence.

origin: Past tense of "excoriate", from Late Latin "excoriare", to strip off the skin, from "ex", off, and "corium", hide or skin.

senses.def: criticized someone or something very severely
senses.ex: The auditor's report excoriated the agency for losing track of millions of dollars in disaster aid.

origin: From Latin "excrescentia", abnormal growths, from "excrescere", to grow out, from "ex", out, and "crescere", to grow.

senses.def: abnormal outgrowth on a plant or animal body, such as a wart
senses.ex: The gardener pruned away the knobby excrescence that had swelled on the trunk of the old pear tree.

senses.def: ugly or unwanted addition that spoils the look or quality of something
senses.ex: Residents called the new parking tower a concrete excrescence on the otherwise graceful historic waterfront.

origin: From Latin "excruciare", to torture, from "ex", thoroughly, and "cruciare", to torment or crucify, from "crux", cross.

senses.def: causing intense, almost unbearable physical pain
senses.ex: He fell from the ladder and felt an excruciating pain shoot through his twisted ankle.

senses.def: extremely unpleasant, embarrassing, or tedious to endure
senses.ex: Watching the best man's excruciating toast, the guests stared at their plates and prayed for it to end.

senses.def: of detail, extremely thorough and precise
senses.ex: The lawyer described the contract in excruciating detail, clause by clause, for three hours.

origin: From Medieval Latin "exculpare", from "ex", out of, and "culpa", fault or blame, the root of "culpable" and "culprit": to free from blame.

senses.def: show or declare that someone is not guilty of wrongdoing
senses.ex: Security footage from the gas station exculpated the suspect, proving he was miles away at the time of the robbery.

origin: Past tense of "exculpate", from Medieval Latin "exculpare", from "ex", out of, and "culpa", fault or blame.

senses.def: showed or declared someone not guilty of wrongdoing
senses.ex: The lab results exculpated the restaurant, showing the food poisoning had come from a different source.

origin: From "exculpate", from Medieval Latin "exculpatus", freed from blame, from "ex", out of, and "culpa", fault or blame.

senses.def: tending to clear someone of blame or guilt
senses.ex: The defense argued that prosecutors had hidden exculpatory video showing the accused was miles away that night.

origin: From Latin "excursus", a running out, from "excurrere", to run out, from "ex", out, and "currere", to run. The same root gives "excursion".

senses.def: tending to wander away from the main subject
senses.ex: Her excursive lectures drifted from Roman roads to modern traffic laws, yet students rarely found them dull.

origin: From Latin "exsecrabilis", accursed, from "exsecrari", to curse, from "ex", out, and "sacer", sacred: cast out of the sacred.

senses.def: extremely bad or of very poor quality
senses.ex: The hotel's execrable food, gray eggs and burnt toast, sent most guests out to the diner down the street.

senses.def: deserving to be hated, detestable
senses.ex: The tribunal called the bombing of the hospital an execrable crime against civilians.

origin: From Latin "exsecrari", to curse, from "ex", out, and "sacrare", to declare sacred or accursed (from "sacer", sacred).

senses.def: feel or express intense loathing for
senses.ex: Villagers still execrate the landlord who evicted their grandparents during the famine.

senses.def: denounce publicly as evil or hateful
senses.ex: Editorials across the country execrated the decision to pardon the corrupt officials.

origin: From Greek "exegesis", interpretation, from "exegeisthai", to explain, from "ex", out, and "hegeisthai", to lead: to lead the meaning out of a text.

senses.def: critical explanation or interpretation of a text, especially a religious one
senses.ex: The seminar spent a week on an exegesis of a single paragraph from the Book of Genesis.

origin: From Latin "exemplar", a model or pattern, from "exemplum", example.

senses.def: person or thing serving as an excellent model to be copied
senses.ex: The coach held up the veteran goalie as an exemplar of discipline for the younger players.

senses.def: typical example or specimen of a group or kind
senses.ex: The Parthenon is often studied as the exemplar of classical Greek temple design.

origin: From Latin "exemplaris", serving as a pattern, from "exemplum", an example or model.

senses.def: so good that it serves as a model for others to copy
senses.ex: The volunteer received an award for her exemplary service during the flood, when she worked three nights straight.

senses.def: of a penalty, serving as a warning to deter others
senses.ex: The judge imposed exemplary damages so that other factories would think twice before dumping waste in the river.

origin: From Medieval Latin "exemplificare", from Latin "exemplum", example, and "facere", to make: to make an example of.

senses.def: be a typical or perfect example of something
senses.ex: The tiny, light-filled apartment exemplifies the clever use of space in Tokyo housing.

senses.def: illustrate an idea by giving an example
senses.ex: The teacher exemplified irony by reading a story about a fire station that burned down.

origin: From Latin "exsequiae", a funeral procession, from "exsequi", to follow to the end, from "ex", out, and "sequi", to follow.

senses.def: funeral rites or ceremonies, usually used in the plural
senses.ex: The village gathered in the small chapel for the exequies of the fisherman who had drowned in the storm.

syn: funeral rites, obsequies, funeral, last rites

origin: From "exert", from Latin "exserere", to thrust out or put forth, from "ex", out, and "serere", to join.

senses.def: hard physical or mental effort
senses.ex: After hours of exertion in the summer heat, the movers collapsed onto the couch they had just carried upstairs.

senses.def: the use of power, influence, or a quality to bring something about
senses.ex: The treaty was signed only through the steady exertion of diplomatic pressure from three neighboring countries.

origin: From Latin "exhaustus", drained, from "exhaurire", to draw out completely, from "ex", out, and "haurire", to draw water: covering a topic until nothing is left.

senses.def: complete and thorough, covering every possible detail
senses.ex: After an exhaustive search of the house, they finally found the passports tucked inside a cookbook.

origin: From "exhilarate", from Latin "exhilarare", to gladden, from "ex", thoroughly, and "hilaris", cheerful, the root of "hilarious".

senses.def: making one feel very happy, lively, and excited
senses.ex: The first ride down the steep, snowy slope was exhilarating, and she raced back to the lift for another.

origin: From Latin "exhortari", to encourage, from "ex", thoroughly, and "hortari", to urge or incite.

senses.def: strongly urge or encourage someone to do something
senses.ex: The captain exhorted her exhausted rowers to give one last push as the finish line came into view.

origin: From Latin "exhortatio", encouragement, from "exhortari", to encourage, built on "hortari", to urge.

senses.def: earnest speech or appeal that urges someone to do something
senses.ex: Despite the coach's halftime exhortations to play harder, the exhausted team lost by twenty points.

origin: From Medieval Latin "exhumare", from "ex", out of, and "humare", to bury, from "humus", earth.

senses.def: dig a buried body out of the ground
senses.ex: Investigators received a court order to exhume the body so they could test it for traces of poison.

senses.def: bring something forgotten or hidden back into view
senses.ex: The historian exhumed a forgotten diary from the archive that changed how scholars saw the strike.

origin: From Late Latin "exigentia", urgency, from Latin "exigere", to demand, literally to drive out.

senses.def: pressing need or demand of a situation, often used in the plural
senses.ex: The exigencies of wartime forced the factory to switch from making cars to building aircraft engines.

senses.def: urgent situation that calls for immediate action
senses.ex: In an exigency such as a gas leak, the building manager may enter any apartment without notice.

origin: From Latin "exigens", demanding, from "exigere", to drive out or demand, from "ex", out, and "agere", to drive.

senses.def: pressing, requiring immediate action or attention
senses.ex: The police may enter without a warrant under exigent circumstances, such as hearing screams inside.

senses.def: requiring a great deal of effort or attention, demanding
senses.ex: The exigent schedule of a first-year surgical resident leaves little time for sleep.

origin: From Latin "exiguitas", from "exiguus", scanty or small, the source of "exiguous".

senses.def: the quality of being extremely small, scanty, or meager
senses.ex: The exiguity of the research budget forced the team to share a single microscope among six scientists.

origin: From Latin "exiguus", scanty or strictly measured, from "exigere", to weigh out exactly.

senses.def: very small in amount, scanty
senses.ex: The expedition survived the final week on exiguous rations of rice and dried fish.

origin: From Late Latin "existentialis", relating to existence, from "existere", to stand forth or emerge, from "ex", out, and "sistere", to stand.

senses.def: relating to human existence, especially questions of meaning, freedom, and purpose
senses.ex: Turning forty brought on an existential crisis, and he began asking whether his job meant anything at all.

senses.def: threatening the very survival of something
senses.ex: Many island nations regard rising sea levels as an existential threat to their homes and culture.

senses.def: relating to existence or the fact of being
senses.ex: A philosopher would call the claim that unicorns exist an existential statement, since it asserts that something is real.

origin: From Latin, from Greek "exodos", a going out, from "ex", out, and "hodos", way or road. It names the biblical book of the Israelites leaving Egypt.

senses.def: mass departure of many people from a place
senses.ex: The closing of the steel mill caused an exodus of young families from the town.

origin: From Latin "exonerare", to unload, from "ex", off, and "onus", burden: to lift the burden of blame from someone.

senses.def: officially clear someone of blame or wrongdoing
senses.ex: New DNA evidence exonerated the man after he had spent nineteen years in prison for a crime he did not commit.

origin: From "exorbitant", from Late Latin "exorbitare", to go off the track, from "ex", out of, and "orbita", a wheel rut.

senses.def: the quality of being far beyond what is fair or reasonable, especially in price
senses.ex: Fans complained about the exorbitance of ticket prices, which had tripled since the band's last tour.

origin: From Late Latin "exorbitare", to go out of the track, from "ex", out of, and "orbita", wheel track: prices that have run off the rails.

senses.def: of a price or demand, far higher than is reasonable
senses.ex: The stadium charged an exorbitant twelve dollars for a bottle of water on the hottest day of the summer.

origin: From Greek "exorkizein", to banish an evil spirit by oath, from "ex", out, and "horkos", oath.

senses.def: free oneself of a troubling memory, feeling, or idea
senses.ex: She wrote a novel about the accident partly to exorcise the guilt that had haunted her for years.

senses.def: drive out an evil spirit from a person or place, as by prayer
senses.ex: According to the legend, a monk exorcised the demon that had plagued the village well.

syn: banish, purge, expel, cast out, dispel

origin: Via Late Latin from Greek "exorkizein", to bind by an oath, from "ex", out, and "horkos", oath. The spirit is commanded to leave.

senses.def: the ritual of driving an evil spirit out of a person or place
senses.ex: The old priest refused to perform an exorcism until doctors had examined the frightened girl.

senses.def: the act of getting rid of a painful memory, feeling, or influence
senses.ex: Writing the novel was a kind of exorcism, freeing the author from years of guilt about her brother.

origin: From Latin "exordium", a beginning, from "exordiri", to begin, from "ex", out of, and "ordiri", to begin.

senses.def: the opening part of a speech or written work
senses.ex: In a brief exordium, the lawyer thanked the jury and promised to keep her closing argument short.

origin: From Latin "exoticus", from Greek "exotikos", foreign, literally "from the outside", from "exo", outside.

senses.def: strikingly unusual or colorful, especially because it comes from a faraway place
senses.ex: The market stall sold exotic fruits like rambutan and mangosteen that most shoppers had never tasted.

senses.def: of a plant or animal, not native to the area where it is found
senses.ex: Exotic species such as the cane toad have devastated native wildlife in Australia.

origin: From Latin "expansus", spread out, from "expandere", to spread out, from "ex", out, and "pandere", to spread.

senses.def: covering a wide area or broad range, extensive
senses.ex: From the porch they could see the expansive wheat fields stretching all the way to the horizon.

senses.def: open, talkative, and friendly in manner
senses.ex: After a good dinner, the usually reserved professor became expansive, telling stories about his student days.

origin: From Latin "exspatiari", to wander off course, from "ex", out, and "spatiari", to walk about (from "spatium", space): a speaker who roams over a subject.

senses.def: speak or write at great length and in detail about a subject
senses.ex: Given the chance, my uncle will expatiate for an hour on the merits of his homemade compost.

syn: elaborate, enlarge, expound, dilate, hold forth

origin: From "expatiate", from Latin "exspatiari", to wander or spread out, from "ex", out, and "spatiari", to walk about, from "spatium", space.

senses.def: long and detailed speaking or writing about a subject
senses.ex: The guide's expatiation on every carving in the cathedral kept the tour group inside for two hours.

origin: From Medieval Latin "expatriare", to banish, from "ex", out of, and "patria", native land or fatherland.

senses.def: person who lives outside their native country
senses.ex: The café in Lisbon was a favorite gathering spot for American expatriates working remotely.

senses.def: leave one's own country to live abroad, or force someone to do so
senses.ex: Many writers expatriated to Paris in the 1920s, drawn by cheap rents and artistic freedom.

origin: From Late Latin "expedientia", from Latin "expedire", to free the feet from a snare, hence to help forward, from "ex", out, and "pes", foot.

senses.def: the choice of what is convenient or advantageous, often over what is right
senses.ex: The senator abandoned his principles out of political expedience once the polls turned against him.

senses.def: the quality of being suitable or useful for a particular purpose
senses.ex: The committee debated the expedience of moving the festival indoors before the forecast storm arrived.

origin: From Latin "expediens", useful, from "expedire", to free the feet (from "ex", out, and "pes", foot), and so to get things moving.

senses.def: convenient and practical for a purpose, though possibly unfair or immoral
senses.ex: Blaming the intern was the expedient choice, even though the manager knew the mistake was his own.

senses.def: means of achieving an end, especially one that is quick or improvised
senses.ex: When the ladder broke, they used a stack of crates as a temporary expedient to reach the roof.

origin: From Latin "expeditus", unimpeded, from "expedire", to free the feet (from "ex", out, and "pes", foot): to free a process from what slows it down.

senses.def: make something happen sooner or be done more quickly
senses.ex: For an extra fee, the passport office will expedite your application and mail it within a week.

syn: accelerate, hasten, speed up, quicken, facilitate

origin: From Latin "expeditus", unencumbered or ready, past participle of "expedire", to free the feet, from "ex", out, and "pes", foot.

senses.def: done quickly and efficiently
senses.ex: The airline promised an expeditious refund, and the money appeared in my account within two days.

origin: From Latin "expellere", from "ex", out, and "pellere", to drive or push, the same root as "repel" and "propel".

senses.def: officially force someone to leave a school, organization, or country
senses.ex: The academy expelled two students for hacking into the grading system.

senses.def: force out air, liquid, or another substance from a container or the body
senses.ex: The diver expelled the air from her lungs slowly as she rose toward the surface.

origin: From Medieval Latin "expenditus", from Latin "expendere", to weigh out or pay out, from "ex", out, and "pendere", to weigh.

senses.def: the spending of money, or the amount of money spent
senses.ex: The city cut its expenditure on road repairs and moved the savings into after-school programs.

senses.def: the using up of energy, time, or effort
senses.ex: Climbing the dune required an enormous expenditure of energy for very little forward progress.

origin: From Latin "expiare", to atone, from "ex", thoroughly, and "piare", to appease or purify, related to "pius", devout.

senses.def: make amends for guilt or wrongdoing, atone
senses.ex: He tried to expiate his years of neglect by visiting his elderly father every single weekend.

syn: atone for, redeem, make amends for, redress, compensate for

origin: From Latin "expiatio", atonement, from "expiare", to atone for, built on "piare", to appease, related to "pius", devout.

senses.def: the act of making amends for a wrong or sin
senses.ex: As expiation for the accident, the driver spent every weekend volunteering at the hospital where the victim recovered.

origin: From Late Latin "expletivus", serving to fill out, from "explere", to fill up. An expletive was first a filler word, later a swear word.

senses.def: swear word or profane exclamation, especially one blurted out in anger
senses.ex: When the shelf collapsed onto his foot, my uncle let loose a string of expletives that startled the neighbors.

senses.def: word that fills a grammatical slot without adding meaning, like "it" in "it is raining"
senses.ex: In the sentence "There are three cats," the word "there" is an expletive that carries no meaning of its own.

syn: oath, curse, swear word, profanity, obscenity

origin: From Latin "explicabilis", from "explicare", to unfold or explain, from "ex", out, and "plicare", to fold: what can be unfolded can be understood.

senses.def: able to be explained or accounted for
senses.ex: The strange lights over the lake turned out to be easily explicable: a group of teenagers flying drones.

origin: From Latin "explicare", to unfold, from "ex", out, and "plicare", to fold: to unfold an idea so every part can be seen.

senses.def: analyze and explain an idea or work of literature in detail
senses.ex: For her final paper, she explicated a single Emily Dickinson poem, examining every dash and capital letter.

origin: From "explicate", from Latin "explicare", to unfold, from "ex", out, and "plicare", to fold, plus "-or", one who does.

senses.def: person who explains or interprets something in detail, especially a text
senses.ex: The old professor was a gifted explicator of Shakespeare who made the hardest speeches sound like conversation.

origin: From Latin "explicitus", unfolded or disentangled, from "explicare", to unfold, from "ex", out, and "plicare", to fold.

senses.def: stated clearly and in detail, leaving no room for doubt
senses.ex: The museum's rules were explicit: no flash photography and no touching the paintings.

senses.def: showing or describing sex or violence openly and graphically
senses.ex: The streaming service warns parents when a film contains explicit scenes.

origin: From "exploit", from Old French "esploit", an achievement, ultimately from Latin "explicare", to unfold. Exploiting first meant using something, then using it unfairly.

senses.def: unfairly using people or resources for one's own profit or advantage
senses.ex: The report exposed exploitative factories where workers earned pennies an hour for twelve-hour shifts.

origin: From Latin "exponens", setting forth, from "exponere", to put out or explain, from "ex", out, and "ponere", to place.

senses.def: person who supports and promotes a theory, cause, or method
senses.ex: She became the leading exponent of outdoor classrooms, giving talks to school boards across the state.

senses.def: skilled performer or practitioner of an art or activity
senses.ex: He is the finest living exponent of the Delta blues guitar style.

senses.def: in math, a number showing how many times a base is multiplied by itself
senses.ex: In 2 to the power of 5, the exponent 5 tells you to multiply five twos together.

origin: From Latin "expositio", a setting forth, from "exponere", to put out or explain, from "ex", out, and "ponere", to place.

senses.def: comprehensive explanation or description of an idea or theory
senses.ex: The textbook offers a clear exposition of how vaccines train the immune system.

senses.def: part of a story or play that introduces the background and characters
senses.ex: The novel's exposition drags, but once the heroine reaches the city the plot races ahead.

senses.def: large public exhibition of products, art, or achievements
senses.ex: The 1893 Chicago exposition introduced millions of visitors to the Ferris wheel.

origin: From "exposition" plus "-ory", ultimately from Latin "exponere", to set out or explain, from "ex", out, and "ponere", to put.

senses.def: intended to explain or describe something clearly rather than to tell a story or persuade
senses.ex: Our teacher asked for an expository essay explaining how vaccines train the immune system, not an argument about mandates.

origin: From Latin "expostulare", to demand urgently or complain, from "ex", thoroughly, and "postulare", to demand.

senses.def: express strong disagreement or disapproval, argue earnestly in protest
senses.ex: The tenants expostulated with the landlord for an hour, but he refused to fix the broken heating.

origin: From Old French "espondre", from Latin "exponere", to put forth or explain, from "ex", out, and "ponere", to place.

senses.def: explain or present an idea or theory in detail
senses.ex: At the town meeting, the engineer expounded her plan for a new flood barrier with maps and models.

syn: explain, expatiate, elucidate, set forth, detail

origin: From Medieval Latin "expropriare", to take away property, from "ex", out of, and "proprium", one's own property.

senses.def: take property from its owner, especially by a government for public use
senses.ex: The new regime expropriated the foreign oil companies and promised compensation that never arrived.

senses.def: take something for one's own use without permission
senses.ex: My roommate expropriated my favorite sweater so often that I finally stopped asking for it back.

origin: From Latin "expungere", to prick out, from "ex", out, and "pungere", to prick. Roman scribes marked names for deletion with dots.

senses.def: erase or remove something completely, especially from a record
senses.ex: After five years without another offense, she asked the court to expunge the shoplifting charge from her record.

syn: erase, delete, obliterate, efface, strike out

origin: From Latin "expurgare", to cleanse thoroughly, from "ex", out, and "purgare", to purify, the root of "purge".

senses.def: remove parts of a book or text considered offensive or unsuitable
senses.ex: Victorian editors expurgated Shakespeare's plays so they could be read aloud to families.

syn: censor, bowdlerize, sanitize, cut, clean up

origin: From Latin "exquisitus", carefully sought out, from "exquirere", to search out, from "ex", out, and "quaerere", to seek.

senses.def: extremely beautiful and delicately made or detailed
senses.ex: The museum displayed an exquisite porcelain vase painted with cranes so fine that each feather was visible.

senses.def: intensely felt, whether as pleasure or pain
senses.ex: She felt the exquisite embarrassment of realizing her microphone had been on during the entire complaint.

senses.def: highly sensitive or discriminating in taste or judgment
senses.ex: The chef's exquisite palate could tell which valley the saffron had been grown in.

origin: From Latin "exscindere", to demolish or destroy, from "ex", out, and "scindere", to cut or tear.

senses.def: cut out or remove completely, destroy utterly
senses.ex: The revised constitution exscinded every clause that had once protected the old aristocracy.

syn: excise, extirpate, eradicate, cut out, remove

origin: From Latin "exstans", standing out, from "exstare", to stand out or exist, from "ex", out, and "stare", to stand.

senses.def: still in existence, surviving from the past
senses.ex: Only three copies of the first edition are still extant, and one sits in a locked case in Edinburgh.

origin: From Late Latin "extemporaneus", from the phrase "ex tempore", literally "out of the moment", meaning on the spur of the moment.

senses.def: spoken or done without preparation, improvised
senses.ex: When the teleprompter failed, the mayor gave an extemporaneous speech that many thought was her best.

origin: From Latin "ex tempore", out of the moment, meaning on the spur of the moment.

senses.def: without preparation or notes; on the spur of the moment
senses.ex: When the keynote speaker's flight was canceled, the dean spoke extempore for twenty minutes and charmed everyone.

senses.def: spoken or done without preparation; improvised
senses.ex: His extempore toast at the wedding was funnier than any of the speeches that had been rehearsed for weeks.

syn: impromptu, offhand, ad lib, spontaneously, unrehearsed

origin: From "extempore" plus "-ize", from Latin "ex tempore", out of the moment.

senses.def: speak or perform without preparation; improvise
senses.ex: When the slides failed to load, the professor extemporized a lecture using only a whiteboard and a dry marker.

syn: improvise, ad-lib, wing it, play by ear

origin: From Latin "extendere", to stretch out, from "ex", out, and "tendere", to stretch, the same root as "tension" and "tendon".

senses.def: make something longer, larger, or last for a longer time
senses.ex: The library extended its hours during exam week so students could study until midnight.

senses.def: stretch out or reach over a certain area or distance
senses.ex: The national park extends from the river valley all the way to the snowy peaks.

senses.def: offer or give something, such as help, thanks, or an invitation
senses.ex: The host family extended a warm welcome to the exchange student from Ghana.

origin: From Latin "extenuare", to make thin or lessen, from "ex", out, and "tenuis", thin: such circumstances thin out the blame.

senses.def: making a fault or crime seem less serious or more excusable
senses.ex: Because of extenuating circumstances, a family emergency, the teacher accepted his essay a week late.

origin: From Latin "extenuatio", a thinning or lessening, from "extenuare", to make thin, from "tenuis", thin. It thins out guilt.

senses.def: the partial excusing of a fault or crime by pointing to circumstances that lessen it
senses.ex: In extenuation, the lawyer noted that the teenager had stolen the bread to feed his younger siblings.

origin: From Latin "exstirpare", to uproot, from "ex", out, and "stirps", the stem and roots of a tree: to pull something out by the roots.

senses.def: destroy or remove something completely, as if pulling it up by the roots
senses.ex: The island's rangers worked for a decade to extirpate the rats that were eating seabird eggs.

syn: eradicate, root out, eliminate, exterminate, uproot

origin: From Latin "extollere", to lift up, from "ex", up, and "tollere", to raise: to raise someone high with praise.

senses.def: praise someone or something enthusiastically
senses.ex: The travel article extolled the village's quiet beaches and its fresh grilled sardines.

origin: From Latin "extortus", from "extorquere", to twist out, from "ex", out, and "torquere", to twist, the root of "torture".

senses.def: obtain money or something else by force, threats, or other unfair pressure
senses.ex: The hackers tried to extort two million dollars from the hospital by locking its patient records.

origin: From French "extradition", formed from Latin "ex", out, and "traditio", a handing over.

senses.def: the legal handing over of an accused or convicted person to another country or state
senses.ex: After fleeing to Spain, the embezzler fought extradition for three years before being flown back to face trial.

origin: From Latin "extraneus", from outside or foreign, from "extra", outside. The same word gave English "strange".

senses.def: irrelevant or not essential to the matter at hand
senses.ex: The editor told him to cut the extraneous details about his cat and focus on the election results.

senses.def: coming from outside the thing being considered
senses.ex: The lab filtered the water to remove extraneous particles that could spoil the experiment.

origin: Formed from "extra", outside, and the ending of "interpolate", to estimate between known values: to extrapolate is to reach beyond them.

senses.def: infer or predict something unknown by extending known facts or trends
senses.ex: From one rainy week, it would be foolish to extrapolate that the whole summer will be wet.

senses.def: estimate a value outside a known range from the values inside it
senses.ex: The scientists extrapolated the population curve to estimate how many wolves the park would hold by 2040.

origin: From "extrapolate", coined from "extra", outside, and "interpolate", to insert between. It estimates beyond the known range.

senses.def: estimating unknown values or future trends by extending known data or experience
senses.ex: Simple extrapolation from this year's growth suggests the town will need a new school within a decade.

senses.def: conclusion reached by extending known facts to a new situation
senses.ex: Calling every teenager lazy is a careless extrapolation from one bad experience with a summer employee.

origin: From Medieval Latin "extravagans", wandering beyond bounds, from "extra", beyond, and "vagari", to wander, the root of "vagabond".

senses.def: spending much more money or using far more resources than necessary
senses.ex: Their extravagant wedding featured a string orchestra, fireworks, and a cake taller than the groom.

senses.def: going far beyond what is reasonable or believable
senses.ex: The ad made extravagant claims that the cream could erase twenty years of wrinkles in a week.

origin: From Latin "extremitas", the outermost part or edge, from "extremus", outermost, the root of "extreme".

senses.def: farthest point or limit of something
senses.ex: The lighthouse stands at the western extremity of the peninsula, where the cliffs drop straight into the sea.

senses.def: hand or foot, or any limb of the body
senses.ex: In severe cold, the body pulls blood away from the extremities, which is why fingers and toes freeze first.

senses.def: situation of extreme danger, distress, or need
senses.ex: In their extremity, the stranded climbers rationed a single chocolate bar across four days.

origin: From Latin "extricare", to disentangle, from "ex", out of, and "tricae", tangles or trifles. Compare "intricate".

senses.def: free someone or something from a trap, tangle, or difficult situation
senses.ex: It took firefighters an hour to extricate the driver from the crushed car without injuring her further.

origin: From Latin "extrinsecus", from outside, from a form of "exter", outer, plus "secus", alongside.

senses.def: coming from outside rather than being part of the thing itself
senses.ex: Students who study only for extrinsic rewards like grades often lose interest once the class ends.

origin: From Latin "extrudere", to thrust out, from "ex", out, and "trudere", to push.

senses.def: shape a material such as plastic or metal by forcing it through a shaped opening
senses.ex: The factory extrudes aluminum into long rails that are later cut to size for window frames.

senses.def: push or force something out
senses.ex: The volcano extruded a slow tongue of lava that crept toward the abandoned village.

syn: force out, press out, squeeze out, eject, expel

origin: From Latin "exuberantia", overflowing abundance, from "ex", out, and "uber", udder or fertile. Picture an udder overflowing with milk.

senses.def: the quality of being full of energy, excitement, and cheerfulness
senses.ex: The puppy's exuberance knocked over two lamps and a bowl of soup within its first hour at home.

senses.def: lavish abundance or luxuriance, as in plant growth or ornament
senses.ex: The exuberance of the jungle meant that cleared paths disappeared under new vines within weeks.

syn: ebullience, enthusiasm, zest, vivacity, high spirits
