origin: From Latin "exuberare", to be abundant, from "ex", thoroughly, and "uber", udder or fertile: overflowing like a cow with too much milk.

senses.def: full of energy, excitement, and cheerfulness
senses.ex: The exuberant puppy leapt on every guest, its tail wagging so hard its whole body shook.

senses.def: growing thickly and abundantly
senses.ex: Exuberant vines had climbed over the abandoned house and covered every window.

origin: From Latin "exsudare", to sweat out, from "ex", out, and "sudare", to sweat.

senses.def: display a quality or feeling strongly and obviously
senses.ex: Even before her first serve, the young tennis player exuded a calm confidence that unsettled her opponent.

senses.def: discharge a liquid or smell slowly and steadily
senses.ex: The pine trunks exuded sticky resin that glued pine needles to our hands.

origin: From Latin "exsultare", to leap up, from "ex", out, and "salire", to leap: jumping for joy.

senses.def: feel or show great, triumphant joy
senses.ex: The villagers exulted in the streets when they heard the dam would not be built after all.

origin: From Latin "exsultans", leaping for joy, from "exsultare", to leap up, from "ex", out, and "salire", to leap.

senses.def: triumphantly happy, especially after a success or victory
senses.ex: The exultant fans poured onto the field after their team won its first championship in fifty years.

origin: From Latin "fabricari", to make or build, from "fabrica", a workshop or craft, the source of "fabric" and "forge".

senses.def: invent false information in order to deceive
senses.ex: The reporter was fired after editors discovered he had fabricated quotes from people who did not exist.

senses.def: construct or manufacture something, especially from prepared parts
senses.ex: The small shop fabricates custom steel railings for houses along the coast.

syn: invent, concoct, falsify, forge, make up

origin: From French "fabuliste", from Latin "fabula", story or fable.

senses.def: liar, especially one who invents elaborate false stories
senses.ex: The magazine fired the reporter once editors discovered he was a fabulist who had invented half his sources.

senses.def: writer or teller of fables or fantastical stories
senses.ex: Aesop, the most famous fabulist of the ancient world, used talking animals to teach practical morals.

origin: From French "façade", from Italian "facciata", front of a building, from "faccia", face, from Latin "facies".

senses.def: front of a building, especially a grand or decorative one
senses.ex: The cathedral's limestone facade was cleaned for the first time in a century, revealing carvings hidden under soot.

senses.def: outward appearance meant to hide a less pleasant reality
senses.ex: Behind his facade of cheerful confidence, the new manager was terrified of losing the account.

origin: From French "facétieux", from Latin "facetia", a jest, from "facetus", witty.

senses.def: joking about serious matters in a way that is inappropriate or flippant
senses.ex: When asked how he would pay the rent, he gave a facetious answer about selling his little brother.

origin: From Latin "facilis", easy to do, from "facere", to do or make. The sense "too easy" grew from "easy".

senses.def: too simple, ignoring the real complexity of an issue
senses.ex: The candidate offered a facile solution to poverty that ignored housing, health care, and wages.

senses.def: done or achieved with little effort, fluent and effortless
senses.ex: Her facile command of three languages made her the obvious choice to translate at the summit.

origin: From French "faciliter", to make easy, from Latin "facilis", easy, from "facere", to do or make.

senses.def: make an action or process easier or more likely to happen
senses.ex: The new bridge facilitated trade between the two towns, cutting the trip from two hours to twenty minutes.

senses.def: lead and help along a meeting or discussion without dominating it
senses.ex: A trained mediator facilitated the talks between the union and the company.

origin: From Latin "facilitas", ease, from "facilis", easy to do, from "facere", to do.

senses.def: natural ease or skill in doing something
senses.ex: Her facility with languages let her pick up conversational Portuguese after a single summer in Lisbon.

senses.def: building or place provided for a particular purpose
senses.ex: The county opened a new recycling facility that can sort plastics by type using cameras and air jets.

senses.def: feature or service that makes an action possible
senses.ex: The library's photocopying facility is free for students but charges visitors ten cents a page.

origin: From Latin "fac simile", make it alike, from "facere", to make, and "similis", like. A facsimile is made like the original.

senses.def: exact copy or reproduction, especially of a document, book, or artwork
senses.ex: The museum sells a facsimile of the medieval manuscript, printed so carefully that even the wormholes appear.

senses.def: fax, a document sent electronically over a telephone line
senses.ex: The insurance company still insisted that the signed form arrive by facsimile rather than email.

origin: From Latin "factio", a group acting together, from "facere", to do or make. The same Latin word gave "fashion".

senses.def: small, organized group within a larger one, often in disagreement with the rest
senses.ex: A breakaway faction of the party refused to support the budget and voted with the opposition.

syn: bloc, camp, clique, splinter group, wing

origin: From Latin "factiosus", inclined to form parties, from "factio", a group acting together.

senses.def: inclined to form factions and cause conflict within a group
senses.ex: The factious committee spent so long arguing among themselves that the school festival was canceled.

origin: From Latin "factitius", made by art, artificial, from "facere", to make. Through Portuguese the same Latin word became "fetish".

senses.def: artificial or contrived rather than natural or genuine
senses.ex: The ad campaign stirred up a factitious demand for a toy that nobody had wanted a month earlier.

origin: From Medieval Latin "fac totum", do everything, from "facere", to do, and "totum", the whole.

senses.def: employee or assistant who handles many different kinds of jobs
senses.ex: As the theater's factotum, Marcus sold tickets, repaired the lights, and occasionally played a corpse in the second act.

syn: handyman, jack-of-all-trades, assistant, right hand, dogsbody

origin: From French "fainéant", idler, which French speakers read as "fait néant", does nothing, though it began as Old French "faignant", shirking.

senses.def: idle, lazy person who avoids work or responsibility
senses.ex: The new owner fired the fainéants who had spent years collecting paychecks for jobs they never actually did.

senses.def: idle and lazy; doing nothing useful
senses.ex: Historians often blame the fainéant king for letting his ministers run the country into ruin.

origin: From Latin "fallacia", deceit, from "fallax", deceptive, from "fallere", to deceive, the root of "false" and "fail".

senses.def: based on a mistaken belief or faulty reasoning
senses.ex: The argument that a medicine must be safe because it is natural is fallacious. Many plants are poisonous.

senses.def: tending to mislead, deceptive
senses.ex: The fallacious charts in the brochure made the investment look far safer than it was.

origin: From Latin "fallacia", deceit, from "fallax", deceptive, from "fallere", to deceive.

senses.def: widely held but mistaken belief
senses.ex: It is a common fallacy that we use only ten percent of our brains.

senses.def: error in reasoning that makes an argument invalid
senses.ex: Attacking a speaker's appearance instead of her argument is a classic fallacy called ad hominem.

origin: From "fallible" plus "-ity", from Medieval Latin "fallibilis", from Latin "fallere", to deceive. Our senses and judgment can deceive us.

senses.def: the tendency to make mistakes or be wrong
senses.ex: Good scientists build checks into their experiments because they take their own fallibility seriously.

origin: From Medieval Latin "fallibilis", liable to err, from Latin "fallere", to deceive or fail.

senses.def: capable of making mistakes or being wrong
senses.ex: Even the best referees are fallible, which is why the league now reviews close calls on video.

origin: From Old English "fealh", plowed land. Farmers plowed a field but left it unsown so the soil could rest.

senses.def: of farmland, plowed but left unplanted for a season to restore fertility
senses.ex: The farmer let the north field lie fallow for a year so the tired soil could recover.

senses.def: inactive or unproductive for a period, often before new growth
senses.ex: After two fallow years without a single painting, the artist suddenly produced thirty canvases.

origin: From French "falsifier", from Late Latin "falsificare", to make false, from Latin "falsus", false, and "facere", to make.

senses.def: alter information or a document in order to deceive
senses.ex: The accountant was jailed for falsifying the company's records to hide millions in losses.

senses.def: prove a statement or theory to be false
senses.ex: A single black swan was enough to falsify the old belief that all swans are white.

origin: From Middle English "falteren", to stagger or stammer. Its earlier origin is uncertain, possibly Old Norse "faltrask", to be puzzled or hesitate.

senses.def: lose strength, momentum, or confidence, begin to weaken or waver
senses.ex: The company's sales faltered after a cheaper rival appeared, and by winter it was laying off staff.

senses.def: speak hesitantly, in a weak or broken voice
senses.ex: Her voice faltered when she reached the part of the speech about her late father.

senses.def: move unsteadily or stumble while walking
senses.ex: The exhausted runner faltered on the last hill but kept going.

origin: From French "familial", from Latin "familia", household, from "famulus", servant. A Roman familia included the household's servants.

senses.def: relating to a family or its members
senses.ex: Holiday dinners were tense because of familial grudges that dated back to a disputed will.

senses.def: occurring in or passed down through members of a family
senses.ex: Doctors suspected a familial form of heart disease after three brothers developed the same condition.

origin: From Middle English, from Old French "afamer", to starve, ultimately from Latin "fames", hunger, which also gave English "famine".

senses.def: suffer or cause to suffer extreme hunger, now mostly used as "famished"
senses.ex: After hiking eighteen miles without lunch, we were so famished that we ate the trail mix crumbs from the bag.

origin: From Latin "fanaticus", of a temple, inspired by a god, frenzied, from "fanum", temple. The everyday word "fan" is short for "fanatic".

senses.def: person filled with excessive, uncritical zeal, especially for a religious or political cause
senses.ex: The fanatic refused to listen to any argument and called everyone who disagreed a traitor.

senses.def: person extremely enthusiastic about a hobby or activity
senses.ex: My aunt is a crossword fanatic who finishes the Sunday puzzle in ink before breakfast.

origin: From "fanatic", from Latin "fanaticus", of a temple, divinely inspired or frenzied, from "fanum", temple.

senses.def: filled with excessive, single-minded, often irrational zeal
senses.ex: His fanatical devotion to the team led him to paint his house in its colors and name his son after the coach.

origin: From "fanatic" plus "-ism", from Latin "fanaticus", inspired by a god, from "fanum", temple. Fanatics once seemed possessed by temple frenzy.

senses.def: extreme and unreasoning devotion to a cause, belief, or activity
senses.ex: Political fanaticism made it impossible for either side to admit that the other had any good ideas.

origin: From "fancy" plus "-ful". The word "fancy" is a shortened form of "fantasy", from Greek "phantasia", imagination or appearance.

senses.def: existing only in the imagination, not realistic
senses.ex: The idea that the old mine still hides a fortune in gold is fanciful, but tourists love the story.

senses.def: designed or decorated in a highly imaginative, whimsical way
senses.ex: The bakery's fanciful cakes were shaped like castles, dragons, and teapots.

origin: A shortened form of "fantasy", from Greek "phantasia", appearance or imagination, from "phainein", to show. To fancy something is to picture it in the mind.

senses.def: imagine or believe something, often without being sure
senses.ex: She fancied she heard footsteps on the stairs, but the house was empty.

senses.def: feeling of liking or attraction, often a passing one
senses.ex: The duke took a fancy to the young painter and invited her to live at his estate.

senses.def: elaborate, decorated, or expensive rather than plain
senses.ex: For their anniversary they skipped the fancy restaurant and had a picnic by the lake.

senses.def: want or feel like having something (chiefly British)
senses.ex: Do you fancy a cup of tea before we start the long drive home?

origin: From French "fanfare", a flourish of trumpets, probably imitating the blare of the horns.

senses.def: showy display or publicity surrounding an event or announcement
senses.ex: The phone launched with enormous fanfare, but its battery problems were discovered within a week.

senses.def: short, loud flourish played on trumpets or other brass instruments
senses.ex: A fanfare of trumpets announced the arrival of the queen at the cathedral doors.

origin: From French "fanfaronnade", bragging, from "fanfaron", a braggart. English later linked it with "fanfare" and its noisy show.

senses.def: empty, swaggering boasting or showy display
senses.ex: For all his fanfaronade about crushing the competition, the candidate finished fourth in the primary.

origin: Of unknown origin, first recorded in American English in 1839.

senses.def: state of extreme nervousness, unease, or irritability, usually "the fantods"
senses.ex: Creaking floorboards in the empty farmhouse gave the whole camping group the fantods.

origin: From French "farce", stuffing, from Latin "farcire", to stuff. A comic play, like a stuffing, was a lively mix of varied ingredients.

senses.def: event or situation so badly handled or absurd that it seems a mockery
senses.ex: With no evidence allowed and the verdict decided in advance, the trial was a complete farce.

senses.def: comedy built on ridiculous situations, mistaken identities, and slapstick
senses.ex: The theater's summer farce had actors slamming doors and hiding in closets for two hilarious hours.

origin: From "farce" plus "-ical". "Farce" comes from French "farce", stuffing, because comic scenes were stuffed into serious plays.

senses.def: so absurd or badly handled that it seems ridiculous, like a farce
senses.ex: The trial became farcical when the key witness admitted he had never actually met the defendant.

origin: From Latin "farinaceus", made of flour, from "farina", flour or meal.

senses.def: made of or rich in flour or starch, such as bread, pasta, or potatoes
senses.ex: His doctor advised him to cut back on farinaceous foods like pasta and white bread.

senses.def: having a mealy, floury texture
senses.ex: The old apples had turned soft and farinaceous, crumbling in the mouth like dry sand.

origin: From French "farouche", wild or shy, ultimately from Late Latin "forasticus", living outdoors, from "foras", outside.

senses.def: shy, sullen, and unsociable in a somewhat wild or awkward way
senses.ex: The farouche boy hid behind the barn whenever visitors came, watching them through a gap in the boards.

origin: From Latin "farrago", mixed animal feed, from "far", a kind of grain. A farrago is a jumbled mash.

senses.def: confused, disordered mixture of things, often absurd or worthless
senses.ex: The defendant's alibi was a farrago of contradictions, half-truths, and dates that did not match.

origin: From Latin "fasciculus", little bundle, from "fascis", bundle, the root of "fasces".

senses.def: one installment of a book or reference work published in parts
senses.ex: The dictionary appeared in fascicles over forty years, and subscribers waited eagerly for each new letter.

senses.def: small bundle or cluster, as of leaves, flowers, or fibers
senses.ex: Pine needles grow in fascicles, and counting the needles in each bundle helps identify the species.

origin: From Latin "fastidiosus", disdainful or squeamish, from "fastidium", loathing, perhaps from "fastus", disdain, and "taedium", disgust.

senses.def: very attentive to detail, accuracy, and cleanliness
senses.ex: The fastidious watchmaker cleaned every tiny gear twice before fitting it into the case.

senses.def: hard to please and easily disgusted
senses.ex: The fastidious cat refused any food that had sat in its bowl for more than an hour.

origin: From Old English "fæstnes", firmness or fortress, from "fæst", firm or secure, the older sense of "fast", as in "hold fast".

senses.def: secure, hard-to-reach place such as a fortress or remote wilderness
senses.ex: The rebels retreated to their mountain fastness, where no army had ever managed to follow them.

senses.def: the quality of being firmly fixed or not fading
senses.ex: Before buying the fabric, she tested the dye's fastness by scrubbing a corner in hot water.

origin: From "fatal" plus "-ism", from Latin "fatum", fate, literally what has been spoken, from "fari", to speak.

senses.def: belief that all events are fixed in advance so human effort cannot change them
senses.ex: His fatalism about the climate frustrated his sister, who believed every small reduction in emissions mattered.

origin: From "fatalist" plus "-ic", ultimately from Latin "fatum", fate, literally what has been spoken by the gods.

senses.def: resigned to the belief that events are fixed and cannot be changed
senses.ex: After three failed harvests, the farmers grew fatalistic and stopped repairing the irrigation ditches.

origin: From Old English "fæthm", outstretched arms. A fathom was the span of a sailor's arms used to measure depth, so to fathom became to get to the bottom of something.

senses.def: understand something difficult or puzzling after much thought
senses.ex: I still cannot fathom why anyone would stand in line all night for a new phone.

senses.def: unit for measuring water depth, equal to six feet
senses.ex: The anchor finally caught the rocky seabed at a depth of forty fathoms.

origin: From "fathom" plus "-less". "Fathom" is from Old English "fæthm", outstretched arms, a span later fixed at six feet for measuring depth.

senses.def: too deep to be measured
senses.ex: Sailors once believed the ocean beyond the reef was fathomless because their weighted lines never touched bottom.

senses.def: impossible to understand or fully grasp
senses.ex: The poet's grief seemed fathomless, filling three volumes of verse after his daughter's death.

origin: From Latin "fatidicus", prophetic, from "fatum", fate, and "dicere", to speak. A fatidic voice speaks fate.

senses.def: prophetic; foretelling future events, especially doom
senses.ex: The old sailor's fatidic warning about the storm seemed silly until the sky turned black that afternoon.

origin: From French "fatuité", from Latin "fatuitas", foolishness, from "fatuus", foolish, which also gave English "fatuous".

senses.def: complacent foolishness or silliness
senses.ex: The fatuity of the plan became obvious when someone asked how the elephants would get up the stairs.

senses.def: foolish remark or act
senses.ex: The speech was a string of fatuities about following your passion and never giving up.

origin: From Latin "fatuus", foolish or silly. The same root gives "infatuated", foolishly carried away by love.

senses.def: silly and pointless in a smug, unthinking way
senses.ex: The host kept asking the exhausted astronaut fatuous questions about whether space smelled like cheese.

origin: From New Latin, named after Fauna, a Roman goddess of the countryside and sister of Faunus, the god of forests and herds.

senses.def: the animals living in a particular region, habitat, or period
senses.ex: The island's fauna includes several lizards found nowhere else, because no predators ever reached its shores.

origin: The verb is from Old English "fagnian", to rejoice, as a dog greets its master. The deer noun is from Old French "faon", from Latin "fetus", offspring.

senses.def: try to win favor by flattery and servile behavior
senses.ex: The junior staff fawned over the visiting director, laughing loudly at all of his jokes.

senses.def: young deer in its first year
senses.ex: A spotted fawn stood frozen at the edge of the trail, then bounded into the ferns.

senses.def: light yellowish-brown color, like the coat of a young deer
senses.ex: She chose a fawn coat that matched the autumn leaves.

origin: From "fawn", from Old English "fagnian", to rejoice or be glad, used of a dog showing delight and affection toward its master.

senses.def: seeking favor through servile flattery and excessive attention
senses.ex: The magazine's fawning profile of the billionaire never asked a single hard question.

origin: From dialect English "feeze", to drive off or alarm, from Old English "fesian", to drive away. Do not confuse it with "phase".

senses.def: disturb or unsettle someone, usually used in the negative
senses.ex: The heckling did not faze the comedian, who turned the interruptions into the best jokes of the night.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "feauté", from Latin "fidelitas", faithfulness, from "fidelis", faithful. It is a twin of "fidelity".

senses.def: loyalty owed to a lord or ruler, or deep loyalty in general
senses.ex: Each knight knelt before the king and swore fealty, promising to fight whenever he was called.

origin: From Old French "faisable", doable, from "faire", to do, from Latin "facere", to do or make.

senses.def: possible to do easily or conveniently, practicable
senses.ex: Building a tunnel under the bay is feasible, but the city cannot afford it for another decade.

origin: From Medieval Latin "febrilis", from Latin "febris", fever, the source of English "fever" too.

senses.def: full of nervous, hectic excitement or energy
senses.ex: In the febrile final week of the campaign, rumors spread faster than the staff could deny them.

senses.def: having or caused by a fever
senses.ex: The febrile child was given fluids and medicine until her temperature finally dropped overnight.

origin: From Scots "feck", a shortening of "effect", plus "-less": literally "without effect".

senses.def: lacking initiative, strength of character, or a sense of responsibility
senses.ex: Her feckless brother borrowed money every month and never once paid her back.

senses.def: ineffective, incompetent, and unable to get things done
senses.ex: The feckless committee met for a year and failed to fix a single pothole.

origin: From Latin "fecundus", fertile, related to "fetus", offspring, and "femina", woman.

senses.def: highly fertile, producing many offspring or much growth
senses.ex: The fecund river delta produces three rice harvests a year.

senses.def: intellectually productive and inventive
senses.ex: Her fecund imagination produced twenty novels and countless short stories.

origin: From Latin "fecunditas", fruitfulness, from "fecundus", fruitful or fertile.

senses.def: great productiveness or inventiveness, especially of the mind
senses.ex: The composer's fecundity was astonishing, as he wrote more than six hundred works before turning thirty-five.

senses.def: the ability to produce many offspring or much growth; fertility
senses.ex: Rabbits are famous for their fecundity, and a single pair can produce dozens of young in a year.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "feble", weak, from Latin "flebilis", lamentable, from "flere", to weep. The word "foible" comes from the same source.

senses.def: lacking physical strength, especially from age or illness
senses.ex: After weeks in the hospital, her grandfather was too feeble to climb the stairs alone.

senses.def: lacking force or effectiveness, unconvincing
senses.ex: He offered a feeble excuse about his dog eating the permission slip.

origin: From Old French "feindre", to pretend, from Latin "fingere", to shape or invent, the root of "fiction" and "figment".

senses.def: pretend to feel or have something, such as an emotion, illness, or ignorance
senses.ex: To avoid the math test, he feigned a stomachache, but the nurse saw through it at once.

origin: From French "feinte", from "feindre", to pretend, from Latin "fingere", to shape or invent. It is related to "feign" and "fiction".

senses.def: deceptive move meant to distract an opponent from one's real attack or intention
senses.ex: The boxer's feint toward the body drew his rival's gloves down, leaving his chin open for the punch.

senses.def: make a deceptive movement to mislead an opponent
senses.ex: The striker feinted left, waited for the goalkeeper to dive, and rolled the ball gently to the right.

origin: American, from the 1870s, from "feist", a small, snappy dog, plus "-y". A feisty person shows a small dog's spunk.

senses.def: lively, determined, and spirited, often small but ready to argue or fight
senses.ex: The feisty eighty-year-old marched into city hall and refused to leave until the pothole was fixed.

origin: From Latin "felicitare", to make happy, from "felix", happy or lucky, which also gave "felicity".

senses.def: congratulate someone formally
senses.ex: The ambassador felicitated the newly elected president on behalf of her government.

origin: From "felicity", from Latin "felicitas", happiness or good fortune, from "felix", lucky or happy.

senses.def: well chosen or perfectly suited to the occasion, apt
senses.ex: The speaker's felicitous comparison of the new library to a public living room drew warm applause.

senses.def: pleasing and fortunate in the way it turns out
senses.ex: By a felicitous accident, the two old friends booked seats next to each other on the same flight.

origin: From "felicity", from Latin "felicitas", happiness or good fortune, from "felix", lucky or happy.

senses.def: well chosen or perfectly suited to the occasion, apt
senses.ex: Her felicitous choice of a Mary Oliver poem made the graduation speech unforgettable.

senses.def: pleasing and fortunate in the way it turns out
senses.ex: The felicitous timing of the rainstorm, just after the harvest, delighted every farmer in the valley.

origin: From Old French "felicité", from Latin "felicitas", happiness or good fortune, from "felix", lucky or happy.

senses.def: state of intense, deep happiness
senses.ex: The couple's domestic felicity showed in the way they finished each other's stories.

senses.def: skill in finding the apt, pleasing expression in speech or writing
senses.ex: She writes with such felicity that even her grocery lists are a pleasure to read.

origin: The verb is from Old English "fellan", to make fall, a form of "fall". The adjective is from Old French "fel", cruel or wicked, related to "felon".

senses.def: cut down a tree
senses.ex: The storm damage was so severe that the town had to fell the two-hundred-year-old oak.

senses.def: knock down or kill a person or animal
senses.ex: The boxer felled his opponent with a single punch in the third round.

senses.def: fierce, cruel, or deadly (literary)
senses.ex: In the old ballad, a fell storm sank the king's whole fleet in a single night.

syn: chop down, cut down, hew, level, raze

origin: From Old French "felon", wicked person or traitor, from Medieval Latin "fello", whose further origin is uncertain.

senses.def: person convicted of a serious crime such as murder, robbery, or arson
senses.ex: In some states, a convicted felon loses the right to vote until the full sentence has been served.

origin: From Latin "fermentum", leaven or yeast, probably from "fervere", to boil. Fermenting liquid bubbles as if boiling, like an agitated public.

senses.def: state of widespread excitement, unrest, or agitation
senses.ex: Paris in 1789 was in a ferment, with pamphlets and street speeches calling for the end of the monarchy.

senses.def: undergo or cause a chemical breakdown by yeast or bacteria, as in making wine or bread (said fer-MENT)
senses.ex: The cabbage ferments in salty brine for several weeks before it becomes sauerkraut.

senses.def: slowly build up, as unrest or ideas do, before breaking out (said fer-MENT)
senses.ex: Resentment over unpaid wages fermented among the miners for years before the strike finally began.

origin: From Latin "ferocitas", fierceness, from "ferox", fierce, from "ferus", wild, the root of "feral".

senses.def: the state of being fierce, savage, or extremely intense
senses.ex: The ferocity of the hurricane surprised forecasters, who had expected it to weaken before landfall.

origin: From Old French "furet", from Late Latin "furittus", little thief, from Latin "fur", thief. The animal was used to hunt rabbits out of their burrows.

senses.def: search persistently for something hidden and find it (usually "ferret out")
senses.ex: The investigative reporter spent months ferreting out the names hidden behind the shell companies.

senses.def: small, slender, weasel-like animal often kept as a pet or used for hunting
senses.ex: Our neighbor's pet ferret slipped under the fence and was found asleep in a flowerpot.

syn: unearth, uncover, dig up, root out, track down

origin: From Latin "fervens", boiling or burning, from "fervere", to boil or be hot: feelings at the boiling point.

senses.def: having or showing very strong, sincere, and passionate feeling
senses.ex: She is a fervent believer in public libraries and volunteers at hers every Saturday.

origin: From Latin "fervidus", glowing or boiling, from "fervere", to boil or be hot.

senses.def: intensely enthusiastic or passionate, sometimes to excess
senses.ex: The fervid crowd chanted the singer's name for twenty minutes before she returned for an encore.

origin: From Latin "fervor", boiling heat or passion, from "fervere", to boil or be hot.

senses.def: intense and passionate feeling or enthusiasm
senses.ex: The young volunteers campaigned with such fervor that they knocked on every door in the district.

senses.def: intense heat, as of the sun or a fire (literary)
senses.ex: Under the fervor of the noon sun, even the lizards hid among the rocks.

origin: From Old French "festre", from Latin "fistula", a pipe or a pipe-shaped ulcer. A festering wound is one that will not heal.

senses.def: of a feeling or problem, grow worse because it is neglected or unresolved
senses.ex: Resentment festered between the two neighbors for years after the argument over the fence.

senses.def: of a wound, become infected and fill with pus
senses.ex: Without clean bandages, the small cut on his foot began to fester.

senses.def: rot or decay, often giving off a bad smell
senses.ex: Garbage festered on the sidewalk during the long sanitation strike.

syn: rankle, smolder, worsen, simmer, eat away

origin: From French "feston", from Italian "festone", a festive garland, from "festa", feast or celebration.

senses.def: decorate something with chains, garlands, ribbons, or lights
senses.ex: For the New Year festival, residents festooned the narrow street with red paper lanterns.

senses.def: chain or garland hanging in a curve between two points
senses.ex: Festoons of dried red peppers hung across the farmhouse kitchen, ready for the winter stews.

origin: From French "fête", feast or festival, from Latin "festa", feast days. It is a doublet of "feast" and "fiesta".

senses.def: honor or entertain someone lavishly
senses.ex: The Olympic champion was feted with a parade through her hometown and a dinner at the governor's mansion.

senses.def: celebration or festival, especially an outdoor fair raising money for charity
senses.ex: The village fete featured a pie contest, a tug of war, and pony rides for the children.

origin: From Latin "fetidus" (also "foetidus"), stinking, from "fetere", to stink.

senses.def: smelling extremely unpleasant, as of rot or decay
senses.ex: The fetid water in the abandoned swimming pool had turned green and buzzed with flies.

origin: From French "fétiche", from Portuguese "feitiço", charm or spell, from Latin "facticius", artificial or made by hand.

senses.def: excessive, irrational devotion to one thing or activity
senses.ex: The manager made a fetish of punctuality, locking the door at nine sharp even if a client was on the steps.

senses.def: object believed to hold magical or spiritual power
senses.ex: The museum's exhibit included a carved wooden fetish that villagers once believed protected their crops.

senses.def: unusual object or activity that a person needs or strongly prefers for sexual arousal
senses.ex: The psychology textbook explains how a fetish differs from an ordinary preference in strength and focus.

origin: From Old English "feter", a chain for the feet, related to "foot". Fetters bind the feet, so they restrain.

senses.def: restrict someone's freedom of action or movement
senses.ex: Fettered by outdated regulations, the small airline could not change its routes without a year of paperwork.

senses.def: chain or shackle placed on a prisoner's ankles
senses.ex: Archaeologists found iron fetters still attached to a skeleton in the ruins of the old jail.

senses.def: anything that restrains or holds back, usually "fetters"
senses.ex: She left the corporate world to escape the fetters of meetings, dress codes, and quarterly targets.

origin: From Middle English "fetlen", to make ready, of uncertain origin, possibly from Old English "fetel", a belt, as in girding oneself up.

senses.def: condition or state of health and spirits, usually in "fine fettle"
senses.ex: After a month of rest and physical therapy, the old horse was back in fine fettle and eager to run.

origin: From Old English "fæge", doomed to die. Its otherworldly sense grew from the strange mood once thought to mark someone near death.

senses.def: having a strange, dreamy, otherworldly, or whimsical quality
senses.ex: The singer's fey stage presence, all floating scarves and whispered lyrics, made the concert feel like a dream.

senses.def: seeming to have supernatural insight or the ability to foresee events
senses.ex: My great-aunt was considered fey because she always seemed to know who was calling before the phone rang.

origin: From Italian "fiasco", bottle. Italian theater slang "far fiasco", literally "to make a bottle", meant to fail badly, though why is uncertain.

senses.def: complete and often humiliating failure
senses.ex: The product launch was a fiasco: the demo phone froze on stage in front of three thousand reporters.

origin: From Latin "fiat", let it be done, from "fieri", to be done or become.

senses.def: authoritative or arbitrary order or decree
senses.ex: The new principal banned phones by fiat, without consulting teachers, parents, or the student council.

origin: From Old English "ficol", deceitful or tricky. A fickle person cannot be trusted to stay the same.

senses.def: changing loyalties, interests, or affections often and without warning
senses.ex: Fickle fans who cheered the team in June were booing them by August.

senses.def: of weather or fortune, likely to change suddenly
senses.ex: Pack a raincoat. Mountain weather is fickle, and a sunny morning can end in a storm.

origin: From Latin "ficticius", artificial or invented, from "fingere", to shape or invent, the source of "fiction".

senses.def: invented or false, not real or true
senses.ex: The scammer opened bank accounts under fictitious names and addresses that led to empty lots.

senses.def: existing only in a story or work of fiction
senses.ex: Although the town in the novel is fictitious, readers keep trying to find it on maps of Maine.

origin: From Latin "fidelitas", faithfulness, from "fidelis", faithful, from "fides", faith or trust, the root of "confide".

senses.def: faithfulness and loyalty to a person, cause, or promise
senses.ex: The knight's fidelity to his king never wavered, even when he was offered land to switch sides.

senses.def: accuracy in copying or reproducing something
senses.ex: The translation captures the poem's meaning with remarkable fidelity while keeping its rhythm.

origin: From Latin "fiduciarius", held in trust, from "fiducia", trust, from "fidere", to trust. Compare "fidelity" and "confide".

senses.def: involving a legal duty to act in another person's best interest with money or property
senses.ex: As her grandmother's trustee, Ana had a fiduciary duty to invest the money carefully, not to borrow from it.

senses.def: person or institution trusted to manage money or property for someone else
senses.ex: The court appointed a fiduciary to manage the orphaned children's inheritance until they turned twenty-one.

origin: From Latin "figmentum", something made up, from "fingere", to shape or invent, the root also of "fiction" and "feign".

senses.def: something imagined that does not really exist, usually in "a figment of one's imagination"
senses.ex: The footsteps upstairs turned out to be a figment of his imagination, since the house was completely empty.

origin: From French "figuratif", from Latin "figura", a shape or figure. A figure of speech shapes words beyond their literal meaning.

senses.def: using words in a non-literal way, as in metaphor or simile
senses.ex: When she said her brother had a heart of stone, she was speaking in a figurative sense.

senses.def: of art, representing recognizable people or objects rather than abstract forms
senses.ex: The museum's new wing shows figurative paintings of street life alongside abstract sculpture.

origin: From Middle English "filchen", to steal. Its earlier origin is uncertain, though it may be linked to Old English words for a band of men.

senses.def: steal something small or of little value, usually casually
senses.ex: My little brother filched a handful of cookies from the jar while Mom was on the phone.

origin: From Latin "filialis", from "filius", son, and "filia", daughter.

senses.def: relating to or expected of a son or daughter
senses.ex: Out of filial duty, he moved back home to care for his aging mother after her stroke.

origin: From Spanish "filibustero", pirate, from French "flibustier", from Dutch "vrijbuiter", freebooter (from "vrij", free, and "buit", booty): lawmakers who hijack the floor.

senses.def: very long speech used to delay or block a vote in a legislature
senses.ex: The senator's filibuster lasted over twenty hours, and he read recipes aloud to hold the floor.

senses.def: use long speeches or other delaying tactics to obstruct a vote
senses.ex: The minority party threatened to filibuster any bill that cut school funding.

origin: From French "filigrane", from Italian "filigrana", from Latin "filum", thread, and "granum", grain: fine wire threads set with tiny beads.

senses.def: delicate ornamental work made of fine twisted gold or silver wire
senses.ex: Her grandmother's earrings were made of silver filigree as fine as frost on a window.

senses.def: anything delicate and intricate that resembles such work
senses.ex: The bare winter branches made a black filigree against the pale sky.

origin: From Middle English "filippen", to flick a finger off the thumb, probably imitating the sound. The word "flip" grew from the same word.

senses.def: something that stimulates, boosts, or adds excitement
senses.ex: The new stadium gave a welcome fillip to the restaurants and shops in the struggling neighborhood.

syn: boost, stimulus, spur, impetus, shot in the arm

origin: From French "fin de siècle", literally "end of the century", which came to name a late-century artistic mood.

senses.def: relating to the end of a century, especially the culturally restless late nineteenth century
senses.ex: The museum recreated a fin de siècle salon filled with daring paintings and anxious talk about modern life.

senses.def: the closing years of a century, especially the late nineteenth century
senses.ex: At the fin de siècle, writers challenged inherited ideas about art, morality, and progress.

origin: An Americanism from the 1920s of uncertain origin, perhaps from dialect "fainaigue", to cheat or renege, influenced by "inveigle".

senses.def: obtain or arrange something by clever, indirect, or dishonest means
senses.ex: He managed to finagle two backstage passes by claiming to be the drummer's cousin.

origin: Past tense of "finagle", an Americanism from the 1920s of uncertain origin, perhaps from dialect "fainaigue", to cheat or renege.

senses.def: obtained or arranged something by clever, indirect, or dishonest means
senses.ex: She finagled a corner office by convincing her boss that the plants on her desk needed sunlight.

origin: From Italian "finale", "ending", ultimately from Latin "finis", meaning "end" or "boundary".

senses.def: the concluding part of a performance, often its most impressive moment
senses.ex: The orchestra's finale brought the audience to its feet before the last note faded.

senses.def: the final episode or installment of a continuing story
senses.ex: The season finale resolved the central mystery but left one character's fate uncertain.

origin: From French "finesse", fineness or delicacy, from "fin", fine.

senses.def: refined skill and delicacy in handling a situation or performing a task
senses.ex: The diplomat handled the tense negotiation with such finesse that both sides left believing they had won.

senses.def: handle a difficulty skillfully, sometimes by evading it
senses.ex: The press secretary finessed the awkward question by changing the subject to the economy.

origin: Probably formed in university slang from "fine", suggesting an overly delicate concern with details.

senses.def: excessively particular about small details, appearance, or manners
senses.ex: His finical objections to the invitation's typeface delayed a party that everyone else had already approved.

origin: From "finical", fussy, probably based on "fine" in the sense of overly refined. The exact path is uncertain.

senses.def: overly particular about details and hard to please
senses.ex: My finicky little sister will not eat any food that touches another food on her plate.

senses.def: requiring very careful, precise handling
senses.ex: The old camera is finicky: if you advance the film too fast, it jams.

origin: From Middle English "fyr-brand", a burning stick, from "fire" and "brand", in Old English a flame or torch: someone who sets passions alight.

senses.def: person who passionately stirs up unrest or pushes for radical change
senses.ex: The young firebrand's speeches drew thousands of students into the streets to demand reform.

origin: From Latin "fissura", "a cleft", through Old French, from "findere", meaning "to split".

senses.def: a long, narrow crack in rock, earth, or another solid surface
senses.ex: After the earthquake, a deep fissure ran across the road and swallowed part of the shoulder.

senses.def: a serious division or disagreement within a group or relationship
senses.ex: The budget dispute exposed a fissure between the mayor and her longtime allies.

senses.def: split or crack along a narrow line
senses.ex: Weeks of drought fissured the clay until rainwater could seep deep into the ground.

origin: From "fit", a sudden burst of activity or a seizure, plus "-ful": full of fits and starts.

senses.def: starting and stopping often, not steady or regular
senses.ex: After the scary movie, she drifted into a fitful sleep, waking at every creak of the house.

origin: From "fix" and the verb ending "-ate", drawing on Latin "fixus", meaning "fixed".

senses.def: focus on one thing so intensely that other things are neglected
senses.ex: She began to fixate on one critical comment despite dozens of encouraging responses to her essay.

senses.def: hold one's eyes or attention steadily on a particular point
senses.ex: During the vision test, he had to fixate on a small light without turning his head.

origin: Its origin is uncertain, though it may blend "flabby" or "flap" with "aghast".

senses.def: astonish someone so greatly that they are briefly speechless
senses.ex: The quiet intern flabbergasted the entire lab by solving the problem in a single afternoon.

origin: From Latin "flaccidus", meaning "limp" or "flabby", from "flaccus", "flabby".

senses.def: limp and lacking normal firmness or strength
senses.ex: The neglected plant's flaccid leaves lifted again after a thorough watering.

senses.def: lacking energy, force, or conviction
senses.ex: The candidate's flaccid response failed to address the clear evidence of corruption.

origin: The verb meaning to droop perhaps comes from an old word "flack", to hang loose. The cloth noun is a separate word whose origin is uncertain.

senses.def: become tired, weak, or less enthusiastic
senses.ex: By the tenth mile, the runners' energy began to flag, and the pace slowed noticeably.

senses.def: piece of cloth with a design, used as a symbol or signal
senses.ex: The flag over the town hall flew at half-mast after the mayor's death.

senses.def: mark something for attention, often as a problem
senses.ex: The software flagged three suspicious payments that had been sent at midnight.

origin: From Latin "flagellatus", "whipped", from "flagellare", "to whip", related to "flagellum", "whip".

senses.def: beat someone with a whip, especially as punishment
senses.ex: The cruel overseer threatened to flagellate anyone who stopped working before sunset.

senses.def: criticize or punish oneself harshly for a perceived failure
senses.ex: She refused to flagellate herself over one missed deadline after months of careful work.

origin: From two English uses of "flag" plus "-ing": one meant "droop", while the other named a flat paving stone.

senses.def: becoming weaker, less energetic, or less successful
senses.ex: A short break revived the hikers' flagging spirits before the final climb.

senses.def: flat stones used to pave a path, or the pavement they form
senses.ex: Rain made the old flagging in the courtyard slippery beneath our shoes.

origin: From Old French "flagitieux" or Latin "flagitiosus", both rooted in Latin "flagitium", meaning "shameful crime".

senses.def: shamefully wicked or criminal
senses.ex: The inquiry uncovered a flagitious scheme to steal relief funds from families displaced by the flood.

origin: From Latin "flagrans", blazing, from "flagrare", to burn: wrongdoing so open it blazes for all to see.

senses.def: of wrongdoing, shockingly obvious and done without shame
senses.ex: The referee called a flagrant foul after the player shoved his opponent to the ground from behind.

origin: From Old English "fligel", a hinged threshing tool, through Middle English "flayle". Its older Germanic ancestry is uncertain.

senses.def: swing one's arms or legs wildly, usually while struggling
senses.ex: He began to flail in the deep water until a lifeguard reached him.

senses.def: a farm tool with a swinging stick used to separate grain from stalks
senses.ex: The farmer demonstrated how a flail loosened grain before mechanical threshers existed.

senses.def: a weapon with a striking head attached to its handle by a chain
senses.ex: The actor practiced with a padded flail before filming the battle scene.

senses.def: strike repeatedly with a flail or a similar implement
senses.ex: The workers flailed the dried grain over a canvas sheet to collect the seeds.

origin: From French "flair", "scent", which grew into the idea of having a good nose for something.

senses.def: a natural talent or instinct for doing something well
senses.ex: Her flair for languages let her pick up new expressions after only a few conversations.

senses.def: a distinctive and attractive style in appearance or performance
senses.ex: The chef served a simple soup with flair, adding herbs and a bright swirl of oil.

origin: From "flamboyant" plus "-ance". "Flamboyant" comes from French for "flaming", an image for showy style.

senses.def: striking showiness in style, behavior, or appearance
senses.ex: The designer's flamboyance appeared in every room, from violet ceilings to enormous gold mirrors.

origin: From French "flamboyant", flaming, from "flamboyer", to blaze, from "flambe", flame.

senses.def: showy, bold, and eager to attract attention
senses.ex: The flamboyant pianist wore a sequined cape and played the final chord with his elbow.

senses.def: brightly colored and striking in appearance
senses.ex: The garden's flamboyant dahlias, in orange and magenta, stopped every passerby.

origin: From French "flâneur", "stroller" or "idler", from "flâner", meaning "to stroll or loaf".

senses.def: a person who strolls through a city, observing its streets and people
senses.ex: On his free afternoon, the flaneur wandered through unfamiliar neighborhoods and watched street musicians perform.

origin: The origin is uncertain. It may be a playful coinage built from "flap" and "doodle" to sound silly.

senses.def: empty or foolish talk that makes little sense
senses.ex: The report promised a practical plan, but its final pages were pure flapdoodle.

origin: From Middle French "flatulent", ultimately from Latin "flatus", "a blowing", linking the word to bodily wind.

senses.def: having excessive gas in the digestive tract
senses.ex: After the heavy meal, the flatulent dog drove everyone out of the small room.

senses.def: causing gas to build up in the digestive tract
senses.ex: He avoided flatulent foods before the long bus ride across the desert.

senses.def: pompous, wordy, and empty of real meaning
senses.ex: The editor cut three paragraphs of flatulent praise and asked for specific evidence instead.

origin: Its origin is uncertain, but it may be related to Norwegian "flanta", meaning "to show off".

senses.def: display something openly and ostentatiously to attract attention
senses.ex: He liked to flaunt his wealth by arriving at school in a different luxury car each week.

origin: From Old English "flēan", "to remove the skin", through Middle English "flen". The verbal attack came from the image of skinning.

senses.def: strip the skin from an animal or person
senses.ex: The hunter learned to flay the rabbit carefully so the pelt would remain intact.

senses.def: criticize someone or something with exceptional harshness
senses.ex: Reviewers flayed the film for its careless plot and wooden performances.

origin: From Old Norse "flekkr", meaning "spot", which passed into English through Middle English.

senses.def: a tiny spot or mark that stands out from its surroundings
senses.ex: A fleck of red paint on the white wall revealed where the old poster had hung.

senses.def: mark something with scattered small spots
senses.ex: Early snowflakes flecked the dark coats of people waiting outside the theater.

origin: From "fledge", to grow the feathers needed for flight, plus "-ling", a small or young one.

senses.def: new and inexperienced, just beginning to develop
senses.ex: The fledgling democracy held its first free election amid fears of violence.

senses.def: young bird that has just grown the feathers needed to fly
senses.ex: A fledgling fluttered clumsily from the nest and landed in the hedge below.

senses.def: inexperienced person who is just starting out
senses.ex: The veteran editors took the fledglings in the newsroom out for coffee to share advice.

origin: From Old English "fleos", the wool of a sheep. To fleece someone is to shear them of their money.

senses.def: swindle or overcharge someone, taking their money by trickery
senses.ex: The fake contractor fleeced elderly homeowners, taking deposits for roof repairs he never made.

senses.def: wool coat of a sheep, or the wool sheared from it in one piece
senses.ex: The shearer removed the fleece in a single piece and tossed it onto the sorting table.

senses.def: soft, warm synthetic fabric, or a jacket made from it
senses.ex: She zipped up her fleece before heading out on the cold morning hike.

syn: swindle, cheat, defraud, con, rip off

origin: From "fleet", to pass swiftly, from Old English "fleotan", to float or drift.

senses.def: lasting for a very short time
senses.ex: She caught a fleeting glimpse of the fox before it vanished into the tall grass.

origin: From Latin "flexuosus", "full of bends", from "flexus", "a bending", related to "flectere", "to bend".

senses.def: winding back and forth in a series of curves
senses.ex: A flexuous trail followed the stream around boulders and beneath low branches.

origin: First recorded in 1549 and probably imitating the nonsense chatter of gossips, which matches its meaning of a silly, talkative person.

senses.def: silly, flighty person who chatters constantly
senses.ex: The novel's heroine seems a mere flibbertigibbet at first, gossiping at parties, until she calmly outwits the entire court.

origin: From Middle English "flykke", a light blow or stroke. The movie sense comes from the rapid flickering of early films on screen.

senses.def: move or strike something with a quick, light motion
senses.ex: She flicked the crumbs off the tablecloth and went back to reviewing the seating chart for the wedding.

senses.def: quick, sharp movement, especially of the wrist or finger
senses.ex: With one flick of the wrist, the chef flipped the omelet and landed it neatly back in the pan.

senses.def: informal word for a movie
senses.ex: On rainy Saturdays we rented an old action flick and argued about which car chase was the most ridiculous.

origin: From Middle French "flenchir", to bend, from a Frankish word meaning to bend or twist, which fits a body bending away from pain.

senses.def: pull back suddenly and involuntarily from pain, fear, or surprise
senses.ex: The toddler flinched when the nurse lifted the needle, then giggled as a cartoon bandage covered the spot.

senses.def: shrink from or avoid an unpleasant duty or difficult challenge
senses.ex: The new mayor did not flinch from announcing painful budget cuts, even with the election only months away.

senses.def: sudden, reflexive movement of drawing back
senses.ex: The goalkeeper's slight flinch before the penalty kick told the striker exactly which corner to aim for.

origin: Probably a shortening of "fillip", a flick of the finger, imitating a quick light movement. The adjective is linked to "flippant".

senses.def: casual and lacking proper seriousness or respect, flippant
senses.ex: His flip remark about the flood victims drew angry letters from readers.

senses.def: turn something over quickly, or toss it so it spins in the air
senses.ex: The referee flipped a coin to decide which team would kick off.

origin: Formed from "flippant", meaning lightly disrespectful, plus the noun suffix "-cy", so it names the quality of joking when seriousness is called for.

senses.def: inappropriate lack of seriousness, especially about grave or sensitive matters
senses.ex: The senator's flippancy about the flood damage outraged residents who were still pumping water out of their homes.

origin: From Northern English dialect "flippand", prattling or glib, from "flip", to babble, of Scandinavian origin.

senses.def: treating serious matters with inappropriate lightness or lack of respect
senses.ex: When the judge asked about the damage, the defendant's flippant shrug only made matters worse.

origin: From "flirtation", the act of flirting, plus "-ous", meaning full of, so a flirtatious person is full of playful romantic attention.

senses.def: behaving playfully in a way that suggests romantic attraction
senses.ex: Their flirtatious banter over the coffee counter continued for weeks before either of them finally suggested going to dinner.

origin: From Middle English "flitten", from Old Norse "flytja", to move, which suits a word for quick, light movement from place to place.

senses.def: move lightly and quickly from place to place
senses.ex: Hummingbirds flitted among the feeders all afternoon, never resting on one perch for more than a few seconds.

senses.def: pass briefly through the mind or across the face
senses.ex: A look of doubt flitted across the lawyer's face before she composed herself and addressed the jury.

origin: From Latin "floccus", a tuft or flock of wool, which is why the word describes anything soft, tufted, and woolly.

senses.def: woolly or fluffy, made up of soft tufts or loose clumps
senses.ex: A flocculent white mold had spread across the forgotten loaf, soft and tufted like a patch of raw wool.

origin: From Latin "Flora", the Roman goddess of flowers, whose name came to stand for all the plant life of a place.

senses.def: plants of a particular region, habitat, or period
senses.ex: Botanists cataloged the island's native flora before the new airport construction could destroy its rare coastal orchids.

senses.def: microorganisms living naturally in part of the body, such as the gut
senses.ex: A long course of antibiotics can disturb the intestinal flora and leave patients with weeks of digestive trouble.

origin: From French "floride", from Latin "floridus", flowery or blooming, from "flos", flower. Florida shares the same root.

senses.def: overly elaborate and ornate, especially in language or decoration
senses.ex: The novel's florid prose, with five adjectives for every sunset, exhausted even patient readers.

senses.def: of a complexion, red or flushed
senses.ex: After the long climb, the old man's florid face glowed under his white beard.

origin: From Renaissance Latin "florilegium", a gathering of flowers, modeled on Greek "anthologia", flower-gathering, which is also the source of English "anthology".

senses.def: collection of choice excerpts from literary or religious writings
senses.ex: The medieval monk compiled a florilegium of favorite passages from the church fathers for novices to memorize.

senses.def: illustrated book of detailed flower paintings or drawings
senses.ex: The botanical garden commissioned a florilegium, pairing each painted orchid with notes on where the plant was collected.

origin: From Spanish "flotilla", little fleet, diminutive of "flota", fleet.

senses.def: small fleet of ships or boats
senses.ex: A flotilla of fishing boats escorted the restored tall ship into the harbor.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "floteson", from Old French "flotaison", a floating, from "floter", to float.

senses.def: wreckage or debris floating on the sea or washed ashore
senses.ex: After the storm, the beach was strewn with flotsam: planks, buoys, and a child's plastic sandal.

senses.def: odds and ends, or people, regarded as worthless or cast aside
senses.ex: The attic was crammed with the flotsam of three generations, from broken lamps to old report cards.

origin: The verb is probably Scandinavian, compare Norwegian "flunsa", to hurry, though its origin is uncertain.

senses.def: move or walk away with exaggerated, indignant motions
senses.ex: Furious at the casting decision, the actor flounced out of the theater and slammed the stage door behind him.

senses.def: wide strip of gathered fabric sewn onto a skirt, curtain, or bedspread
senses.ex: The antique dress had a deep lace flounce along its hem that swayed with every step across the ballroom.

origin: The verb is of uncertain origin, probably a blend of "founder" and "blunder". The fish name comes from Old Norse "flyðra".

senses.def: struggle clumsily or be in serious difficulty, confused about what to do
senses.ex: Without his notes, the speaker floundered, repeating himself and losing his place.

senses.def: move clumsily and with great effort, as in water or mud
senses.ex: The calf floundered in the deep snow until the farmer pulled it free.

senses.def: flat-bodied fish that lives on the sea floor
senses.ex: The fishermen brought in a basket of flounder for the evening market.

origin: From Old French "florir", from Latin "florere", to bloom, from "flos", flower: to thrive is to be in bloom.

senses.def: grow or develop vigorously, thrive
senses.ex: Tomatoes flourish in the hot, sunny corner of the garden near the brick wall.

senses.def: wave something about in a bold, dramatic way
senses.ex: The magician flourished his black silk scarf before pulling a dove from beneath it.

senses.def: bold, sweeping gesture or decorative detail meant to impress
senses.ex: She signed the contract with a flourish, finishing her name in a great looping curve.

origin: Of uncertain origin, perhaps from Middle English "flouten", to play the flute, as if mocking a rule with a jeering tune. Do not confuse with "flaunt".

senses.def: openly disregard a rule, law, or convention
senses.ex: Drivers who flout the school-zone speed limit now face doubled fines.

origin: Past tense of "flout", of uncertain origin, perhaps from Middle English "flouten", to play the flute, as if mocking a rule.

senses.def: openly disregarded a rule, law, or convention
senses.ex: The factory flouted pollution laws for years, dumping waste into the river at night.

origin: From Latin "fluctuare", to surge like waves, from "fluctus", a wave, from "fluere", to flow.

senses.def: rise and fall irregularly in number, amount, or level
senses.ex: The price of strawberries fluctuates wildly, doubling in winter and dropping sharply in June.

senses.def: waver between different opinions or feelings
senses.ex: Her mood fluctuated between excitement and dread as the results were announced.

origin: From Late Latin "fluentia", related to Latin "fluere", to flow, so fluent speech streams out easily without stopping.

senses.def: ability to speak or write a language easily and accurately
senses.ex: After two years in Seoul, Priya reached a fluency in Korean that let her negotiate contracts without an interpreter.

senses.def: smooth, effortless skill at a practiced activity such as reading or math
senses.ex: Daily timed drills built the third graders' reading fluency until they could finish a page without stumbling.

origin: The "lucky chance" sense is of unknown origin. It seems first to have meant a lucky shot in billiards.

senses.def: unlikely chance occurrence, especially a lucky one
senses.ex: Their first win was dismissed as a fluke, but they went on to win nine games in a row.

senses.def: either of the two flat lobes of a whale's tail
senses.ex: The humpback raised its flukes high above the water before diving.

syn: chance, accident, coincidence, stroke of luck, freak

origin: Of uncertain origin, probably from English regional dialect. It first appears around 1837 in the writings of Charles Dickens.

senses.def: completely confuse or bewilder someone
senses.ex: The trick question on the last page flummoxed nearly everyone in the class, including the top students.

origin: From the verb "flummox", to baffle, plus "-ed". "Flummox" is of unknown origin, perhaps from English dialect.

senses.def: completely confused and unsure what to do or say
senses.ex: The flummoxed tourist stared at the subway map, unable to work out which line went downtown.

origin: Of uncertain origin, from Middle English "flusshen". It may be linked to "flash", or be a blend of "flow" and "gush".

senses.def: having plenty of money, at least for the moment
senses.ex: After selling her startup, she was flush with cash and finally bought the cabin by the lake.

senses.def: turn red in the face from embarrassment, anger, heat, or emotion
senses.ex: He flushed deeply when the teacher read his anonymous love poem aloud to the class.

senses.def: exactly level or even with an adjoining surface
senses.ex: The carpenter sanded the new shelf until it sat perfectly flush with the wall.

senses.def: clean out with a rush of water, or drive someone out of hiding
senses.ex: The detectives hoped the leaked rumor would flush the real thief out into the open.

origin: Probably from a Scandinavian source, compare Icelandic "flaustra", to bustle, which fits the feeling of being hurried and thrown off balance.

senses.def: make someone nervous, agitated, or confused, especially by rushing them
senses.ex: The interviewer's rapid questions flustered the young engineer, who forgot the name of her own thesis advisor.

senses.def: state of nervous, agitated confusion
senses.ex: Realizing he had left the passports at home, Marcus arrived at the check-in desk in a complete fluster.

origin: From Latin "fluxus", a flowing, from "fluere", to flow. Something in flux keeps flowing and shifting, never settling.

senses.def: continuous change, movement, or instability
senses.ex: The league's rules remained in flux throughout its first season, frustrating coaches and referees alike.

origin: From Middle English "fliting", formed from "flyte", to quarrel or scold, so the word began as plain noisy argument.

senses.def: ritual contest of insults exchanged in verse, especially in early Scottish and Norse poetry
senses.ex: Modern rap battles echo the medieval flyting, in which rival Scottish poets traded inventive insults before an amused royal court.

syn: war of words, slanging match, verbal duel

origin: The noun is from Low German "Fobke" or a similar German word for pocket. The verb, as in "fob off", is from German "foppen", to mock.

senses.def: trick someone into accepting something inferior, or dismiss them with an excuse (usually "fob off")
senses.ex: The contractor tried to fob us off with cheap tiles and a vague promise to return next week.

senses.def: small electronic device, often on a key ring, that unlocks doors or cars remotely
senses.ex: She tapped her key fob against the reader, and the parking garage gate rose with a soft mechanical hum.

senses.def: short chain or ribbon attached to a pocket watch, or the small pocket holding it
senses.ex: The old banker's gold watch hung from a silver fob that glinted against his dark wool waistcoat.

origin: The origin of this word is unknown, and no source root has been established.

senses.def: person with old-fashioned, dull, or overly conservative views and habits
senses.ex: My uncle, a cheerful old fogy, still refuses to own a smartphone and insists that paper maps are superior.

origin: From older French "foible", weak or feeble, a twin of English "feeble". In fencing it named the weaker part of a sword blade.

senses.def: minor weakness or odd habit in someone's character
senses.ex: His habit of alphabetizing the spice rack was a harmless foible his roommates found endearing.

origin: The verb comes from Old French "fouler", to trample. The noun comes from Latin "folium", leaf. A literary foil recalls the metal leaf set behind a gem to make it shine.

senses.def: prevent someone or something from succeeding
senses.ex: An alert bank teller foiled the robbery by quietly pressing the silent alarm under her desk.

senses.def: person or thing that makes another's qualities stand out by contrast
senses.ex: In the novel, the cautious brother serves as a foil to the reckless hero.

senses.def: very thin, flexible sheet of metal, often used for wrapping food
senses.ex: She covered the leftover lasagna with foil before putting it back in the oven.

origin: Probably from archaic Dutch "vuisten", to take into one's hand, from "vuist", fist, which suits the idea of slipping something in by stealth.

senses.def: force someone to accept something unwanted or inferior, often by deception
senses.ex: The dealer tried to foist a rusted, rebuilt engine on the buyer by calling it a rare vintage part.

senses.def: insert something improperly or without authorization into a text or system
senses.ex: A lobbyist managed to foist a tax exemption into the bill during the final hours of late-night negotiations.

syn: impose, palm off, fob off, thrust

origin: Originally a meaningless refrain in old songs, like "fal, al, deral", used to fill out a tune, so it came to mean nonsense.

senses.def: foolish nonsense or needless fuss
senses.ex: The senator dismissed the lengthy ceremony as pure folderol and asked the committee to get back to the budget.

senses.def: showy but worthless ornament or trinket
senses.ex: The souvenir stand overflowed with plastic crowns, glittery wands, and other folderol that nobody would remember buying by evening.

origin: From Middle French "feuillage", from "feuille", leaf, with the spelling later reshaped after Latin "folium", leaf.

senses.def: leaves of plants or trees, taken together
senses.ex: Tourists drive up into the Vermont hills every October to see the red and gold foliage at its peak.

senses.def: carved or painted ornament in the form of leaves
senses.ex: The stone capitals of the old church columns were decorated with delicate foliage that still looked crisp after centuries.

origin: From Old French "folie", madness, from "fol", mad or foolish, the same source as "fool".

senses.def: lack of good sense, or foolish behavior that ignores consequences
senses.ex: Building a new stadium while the city's bridges were crumbling struck most voters as sheer folly.

senses.def: foolish act, idea, or undertaking
senses.ex: His decision to sail alone across the lake in a storm was a youthful folly he never repeated.

senses.def: costly ornamental building with no practical purpose, built for decoration
senses.ex: At the top of the estate's hill stood a folly shaped like a ruined castle, built new in 1790.

origin: From Latin "fomentum", a warm compress, from "fovere", to warm or cherish. To foment trouble is to keep it warm until it grows.

senses.def: stir up or encourage trouble, unrest, or rebellion
senses.ex: The agitators used anonymous leaflets to foment anger against the factory's new owners.

syn: incite, instigate, stir up, provoke, whip up

origin: From Late Latin "fomentatio", from "fomentum", a warm poultice, from "fovere", to warm. It first meant a soothing hot compress, later the stirring up of trouble.

senses.def: act of stirring up trouble, unrest, or rebellion
senses.ex: The government blamed the riots on the fomentation of foreign agents rather than on its own policies.

origin: American slang of uncertain origin, perhaps related to French "fanfaron", a boaster.

senses.def: fuss or commotion over something unimportant
senses.ex: There was a great foofaraw at the office when someone moved the coffee machine to the other end of the hall.

senses.def: excessive or flashy decoration
senses.ex: She stripped the wedding cake of its sugar roses, ribbons, and other foofaraw and served it plain.

origin: From Old French "fol hardi", foolishly bold, from "fol", foolish, and "hardi", bold.

senses.def: recklessly bold in a way that ignores obvious danger
senses.ex: Hiking the ridge in a thunderstorm without a map was a foolhardy decision they nearly regretted.

origin: Probably a variant of British dialect "footer", to idle or trifle, a word that came from French.

senses.def: waste time in aimless or trivial activity, usually with "around" or "about"
senses.ex: Instead of revising for his exams, he footled around in the garage with an old radio all afternoon.

origin: From "fop", a man vain about his clothes (in Middle English, a fool), plus "-ery", conduct.

senses.def: vain, showy fussiness about clothes and appearance
senses.ex: With his silk cravats, scented gloves, and gold-topped cane, the young lord's foppery amused the whole village.

origin: From "fop" plus "-ish". "Fop" once meant a fool, and by the late 1600s a man foolishly vain about his clothes.

senses.def: vain and overly concerned with stylish clothes and appearance
senses.ex: The foppish actor spent an hour adjusting his silk cravat before every scene.

origin: From Old French "fourrage", from "fuerre", fodder, from a Frankish word related to English "fodder" and "food".

senses.def: search widely for food or supplies
senses.ex: Each autumn the squirrels forage across the campus lawn, burying acorns for the winter.

senses.def: search through a place or things to find something
senses.ex: She foraged through the attic boxes looking for her grandfather's old letters.

senses.def: food such as grass or hay for horses and cattle
senses.ex: The drought left farmers scrambling to buy enough forage to feed their herds.

origin: From Middle English "forrayen", to pillage, from Old French "forrier", a forager, from "fuerre", fodder, since raiders went out seizing food.

senses.def: brief attempt at a new activity or field
senses.ex: The novelist's first foray into screenwriting was a modest success, and the studio asked for a second script.

senses.def: sudden raid or attack into enemy territory
senses.ex: Cavalry units made a night foray across the river to burn the enemy's supply wagons.

origin: From Old English "forberan", to hold back or endure, from "for-", away, and "beran", to bear. To forbear is to bear away from acting.

senses.def: politely or patiently refrain from doing or saying something
senses.ex: Though tempted to correct the speaker's error, she forbore from interrupting and waited for questions.

syn: refrain, abstain, desist, hold back, withhold

origin: From "forbear", from Old English "forberan", to hold back or endure, plus "-ance". It names the quality of holding back.

senses.def: patient self-control, restraint, and tolerance
senses.ex: The nurse showed remarkable forbearance with the patient who complained about every meal.

senses.def: lender's agreement to delay enforcing payment of a debt
senses.ex: During the layoffs, the bank granted homeowners six months of forbearance on their mortgage payments.

origin: From Old English "ford", a crossing place. It is related to "fjord" and "firth" and, more distantly, to Latin "portus", harbor.

senses.def: shallow place in a river or stream where people can cross
senses.ex: The wagons rolled across the ford while the river was low in late summer.

senses.def: cross a river or stream by walking or driving through it
senses.ex: The hikers removed their boots to ford the icy creek at the bottom of the canyon.

origin: From "fore", before, plus "bear" in an old sense of "be-er", one who exists, so one who lived before you.

senses.def: ancestor, especially one more distant than a grandparent
senses.ex: Her forebears had farmed the same valley for six generations before the family moved to the city.

origin: From Middle English, from "fore", before, plus "bode", to announce or predict, so a sense that announces trouble in advance.

senses.def: strong feeling that something bad is about to happen
senses.ex: As the phone rang at three in the morning, she was gripped by a sense of foreboding.

senses.def: suggesting that something bad is coming
senses.ex: Foreboding clouds gathered over the harbor, and the fishermen hurried to tie up their boats.

origin: From Old French "forclos", shut out, past participle of "forclore", to exclude, from "clore", to shut.

senses.def: take possession of a mortgaged property because the borrower stopped making payments
senses.ex: After the family missed six mortgage payments, the bank moved to foreclose on their house.

senses.def: rule out or prevent a possibility in advance
senses.ex: The senator's angry speech foreclosed any chance of a compromise before the vote.

origin: From "fore-", front, plus "ground", modeled on Dutch "voorgrond". It began as a painting term for the part of a scene nearest the viewer.

senses.def: part of a scene or picture nearest to the viewer
senses.ex: In the photograph, a red canoe sits in the foreground with misty mountains behind it.

senses.def: most prominent or important position
senses.ex: The debate brought questions of climate policy to the foreground of the campaign.

senses.def: make something the most prominent or important feature
senses.ex: Her documentary foregrounds the voices of nurses rather than hospital executives.

origin: From Latin "forensis", of the forum, from "forum", the public square where Roman courts met and cases were argued.

senses.def: relating to scientific methods used to investigate crimes and produce evidence for court
senses.ex: Forensic analysis of the fibers on the jacket linked the suspect to the stolen car.

senses.def: relating to formal debate or argument, especially in a court of law
senses.ex: Her forensic skill in cross-examination left the witness contradicting his own earlier testimony.

origin: From Middle English, a translation of Latin "praecursor", one who runs ahead, built from "fore", before, plus "runner".

senses.def: person or thing that came before and led the way for a later one
senses.ex: The clunky mobile phones of the 1980s were forerunners of the smartphones we now carry everywhere.

senses.def: sign or warning of something to come
senses.ex: A dry cough was the forerunner of the illness that kept him in bed for two weeks.

origin: From "foresee", Old English "foreseon", to see beforehand, plus "-able". What is foreseeable can be seen before it happens.

senses.def: able to be predicted or anticipated
senses.ex: The library will remain closed for the foreseeable future while engineers repair the damaged roof.

origin: From "fore-", before, plus "shadow" in the sense of a faint outline, so a dim hint of something before it arrives.

senses.def: be a warning or sign of something that will happen later
senses.ex: The broken mirror in the first chapter foreshadows the family's eventual collapse.

origin: From Middle English, a translation of Latin "providentia", seeing ahead, made from "fore", before, plus "sight".

senses.def: ability to anticipate the future and prepare wisely for it
senses.ex: Thanks to her foresight in packing extra water, the hikers made it through the heat wave without trouble.

origin: From Old English "foresteall", an ambush, from "fore-", before, and "steall", position. Forestalling once meant waylaying someone before they arrived.

senses.def: prevent or block something by acting ahead of time
senses.ex: The company raised wages early to forestall a strike by its warehouse workers.

syn: preempt, prevent, avert, head off, obviate

origin: From Old French "forfait", a crime, from "forfaire", to transgress. The meaning later shifted from the crime to the penalty paid for it.

senses.def: lose or give up something as a penalty for wrongdoing
senses.ex: Drivers who flee the scene of an accident may forfeit their licenses for several years.

senses.def: lose a game or contest by failing to appear or play
senses.ex: Too few players showed up, so the team had to forfeit the championship match.

senses.def: something lost or given up as a penalty
senses.ex: Her security deposit was kept as a forfeit for the broken windows.

syn: surrender, relinquish, lose, sacrifice, give up

origin: From Middle English "forfenden", to ward off, from the prefix "for-", away, plus "fend", to defend.

senses.def: prevent or forbid, now mostly used humorously in phrases like "heaven forfend"
senses.ex: My aunt insists the family dinner will start on time, and heaven forfend that anyone arrive with store-bought pie.

origin: From Old French "forge", from Latin "fabrica", workshop, from "faber", smith, the same root as "fabric" and "fabricate".

senses.def: shape metal by heating it and hammering it
senses.ex: The blacksmith forged a new iron hinge for the barn door.

senses.def: create or establish something, such as a bond or agreement, through steady effort
senses.ex: The two coaches forged a lasting friendship during the years they spent rebuilding the league.

senses.def: make a fake copy of a document, signature, or work of art in order to deceive
senses.ex: He was arrested for forging his employer's signature on a stack of company checks.

senses.def: move forward steadily despite difficulty, usually with "ahead"
