senses.ex: Their hybrid music blends traditional Korean drumming with the synthesizers of nineties dance pop.

origin: From "hybrid" plus "-ize". The word "hybrid" comes from Latin "hybrida", the offspring of a tame sow and a wild boar.

senses.def: crossbreed plants or animals of different kinds to produce offspring
senses.ex: The gardener spent a decade trying to hybridize a rose that could survive Minnesota winters.

senses.def: combine different styles, forms, or systems into a mixed whole
senses.ex: The architect hybridized Japanese and Scandinavian design, pairing paper screens with pale birch furniture.

origin: From Greek "hydrophobia", from "hydor", water, plus "phobos", fear, because rabies makes swallowing painful and victims recoil from water.

senses.def: rabies, named for the victim's painful inability to swallow water
senses.ex: Before vaccines, a bite from a mad dog was feared because hydrophobia almost always ended in death.

senses.def: extreme or irrational fear of water
senses.ex: His hydrophobia was so severe that even wading into a shallow pool made his heart pound.

origin: From Medieval Latin "hymnale", from "hymnus", hymn, from Greek "hymnos", a song of praise.

senses.def: book of hymns used in religious services
senses.ex: Each pew held a worn hymnal whose cover had been patched with tape by generations of churchgoers.

origin: From Greek "hyperbole", excess, from "hyper", beyond, plus "ballein", to throw, so hyperbole throws words beyond the truth.

senses.def: deliberate exaggeration used for emphasis and not meant to be taken literally
senses.ex: When Jen said she had a million things to do, her teacher recognized the hyperbole and gave her an extra day.

origin: From Greek "hyperbole", excess, from "hyper", beyond, plus "ballein", to throw, so hyperbole throws words beyond the truth.

senses.def: deliberate exaggeration used for emphasis and not meant to be taken literally
senses.ex: Advertisers rely on hyperbole, calling an ordinary burger the greatest taste experience of your life.

origin: From Greek "hyperboreos", from "hyper", beyond, plus "boreios", northern. The Hyperboreans were a mythical people who lived beyond the north wind.

senses.def: of the far north, or extremely cold and wintry
senses.ex: The hyperborean winds off the lake made waiting for the bus in January feel like an Arctic expedition.

senses.def: person who lives in the far north, often said humorously
senses.ex: Our hosts, cheerful hyperboreans from northern Norway, swam in the fjord while we shivered on the dock.

origin: From Greek "hyper", over or beyond, plus "kritikos", able to judge, from "krinein", to judge, so judging too much.

senses.def: too critical, finding fault with small or unimportant details
senses.ex: Her hypercritical coach pointed out every slightly bent knee, so she stopped enjoying gymnastics altogether.

origin: From Greek "hyper", over or excessive, plus "trophe", nourishment, so growth from too much feeding.

senses.def: enlargement of an organ or tissue because its cells grow larger
senses.ex: Months of heavy lifting caused hypertrophy in his shoulder muscles, which visibly widened his frame.

senses.def: excessive, unhealthy growth or development of something
senses.ex: Critics warned that the hypertrophy of the security agency had left it larger than any threat justified.

origin: From French, from Greek "hypnos", sleep, plus "agogos", leading, so leading into sleep.

senses.def: relating to the drowsy state just before falling asleep
senses.ex: In that hypnagogic haze, she heard her name called so clearly that she sat up and turned on the light.

origin: From Greek "hypnos", sleep, plus "pompe", a sending away, so describing the moment sleep is sent off and waking begins.

senses.def: relating to the half-conscious state just before fully waking up
senses.ex: In a hypnopompic blur, he was sure a stranger stood by the door, until the shape became his coat on a hook.

origin: From Greek "hypochondria", the belly below the ribs, from "hypo", under, plus "chondros", rib cartilage. That region was once thought the seat of gloomy moods.

senses.def: person who constantly and wrongly worries about having a serious illness
senses.ex: A true hypochondriac, my uncle reads about a new disease online and is convinced by dinner that he has it.

senses.def: affected by excessive, unfounded worry about one's health
senses.ex: Her hypochondriac habits included taking her temperature five times a day during flu season.

origin: From Greek "hypokorisma", pet name, from "hypokorizesthai", to call by pet names, related to "koros" and "kore", boy and girl.

senses.def: pet name or affectionate shortened form of a name, such as Lizzie for Elizabeth
senses.ex: Everyone in the family called him Bubba, a hypocorism left over from his toddler sister's attempts to say brother.

syn: pet name, nickname, diminutive, term of endearment

origin: From Greek "hypokrisis", acting on the stage or pretense, from "hypokrinesthai", to play a part, so a hypocrite is literally an actor.

senses.def: pretending to have virtues, beliefs, or standards that one does not actually hold or follow
senses.ex: Voters were angered by the hypocrisy of a senator who preached thrift while billing taxpayers for luxury hotel stays.

origin: From Greek "hypokritikos", from "hypokrites", a stage actor, from "hypo", under, plus "krinein", to judge, so playing a part.

senses.def: claiming standards or beliefs that one's own behavior does not match
senses.ex: It seemed hypocritical for the coach to ban phones at practice while he checked his own every few minutes.

origin: From Greek "hypothetikos", from "hypothesis", a supposition, from "hypo", under, plus "thesis", placing, so an idea set down as a foundation.

senses.def: based on an imagined situation or assumption rather than on known facts
senses.ex: The debate moderator asked a hypothetical question about how each candidate would respond to a sudden stock market crash.

senses.def: imagined situation or example used to explore an idea or argument
senses.ex: The law professor loved hypotheticals, like whether a man who finds a wallet on the moon may keep it.

origin: From Greek "ichor", the fluid that flowed in the veins of the gods. Its earlier origin is unknown.

senses.def: in Greek myth, the ethereal fluid that flows like blood in the veins of gods
senses.ex: In the poem, Aphrodite is wounded in battle, and golden ichor rather than blood runs down her arm.

senses.def: literary term for a blood-like or foul fluid, as from a monster or wound
senses.ex: The fantasy novel described the slain dragon leaking a black, smoking ichor that withered the grass around it.

origin: From Medieval Greek "eikonoklastes", image breaker, from "eikon", image, plus "klan", to break, first used of people who smashed religious images.

senses.def: person who attacks cherished beliefs, traditions, or institutions
senses.ex: An iconoclast in the kitchen, the chef served dessert first and refused to follow any classic French recipe.

senses.def: person who destroys religious images, especially in the Byzantine Empire
senses.ex: Byzantine iconoclasts scraped the faces from church mosaics, believing that sacred images encouraged idol worship.

origin: From "iconoclast", from Greek "eikonoklastes", image breaker, plus "-ic", so it describes breaking cherished images or ideas.

senses.def: attacking or rejecting cherished beliefs and established traditions
senses.ex: The young historian's iconoclastic book argued that the celebrated founder had nearly bankrupted the town.

origin: From Greek "eikon", image, plus "-graphia", writing or drawing, so the description of images.

senses.def: set of traditional images and symbols linked to a subject, person, or movement
senses.ex: The iconography of the civil rights movement includes clasped hands, marching crowds, and the Lincoln Memorial steps.

senses.def: study and interpretation of the symbols and subjects used in art
senses.ex: Her course on medieval iconography explained why saints in paintings carry keys, wheels, or arrows.

origin: From French "idéaliste", from "idéal", ideal, from Latin "idea", from Greek "idea", form or pattern.

senses.def: person guided by high principles or hopes, often more than by practical concerns
senses.ex: An idealist at heart, he quit a well-paid job to start a free tutoring center in his old neighborhood.

senses.def: follower of idealism, the philosophy that reality is fundamentally mental or made of ideas
senses.ex: As an idealist, the philosopher argued that the world we perceive exists only as it appears in minds.

origin: From "ideology", coined in French in the 1790s from Greek "idea", form or notion, plus "-logy", study, plus "-ical".

senses.def: relating to or based on a system of political, social, or economic ideas
senses.ex: The two parties' ideological differences over taxes made any budget compromise seem almost impossible.

origin: From French "idéologue", from "idéologie", ideology, from Greek "idea", idea, plus "logos", word or reasoning.

senses.def: rigid follower of a political or social ideology who resists compromise or contrary evidence
senses.ex: The new budget director was an ideologue who rejected every proposal that did not fit his theory of small government.

syn: zealot, partisan, dogmatist, doctrinaire, true believer

origin: From Greek "idios", one's own or private, plus the ending of "dialect", so a dialect belonging to one person.

senses.def: distinctive way of speaking, including words and habits, unique to one individual
senses.ex: My grandmother's idiolect mixed Cantonese terms of endearment with phrases she picked up from old Hollywood films.

syn: personal speech, vernacular, parlance, speech pattern

origin: From Greek "idiosynkrasia", one's own temperament, from "idios", one's own, "syn", together, and "krasis", mixture, so it is a personal blend of traits.

senses.def: habit or way of behaving that is peculiar to one person
senses.ex: One of the professor's idiosyncrasies was writing every lecture note in green ink on index cards.

senses.def: odd or unusual feature of a thing
senses.ex: An idiosyncrasy of the old elevator is that it skips the third floor unless you press the button twice.

origin: From "idiosyncrasy", from Greek "idiosynkrasia", a peculiar temperament, from "idios", one's own, plus "synkrasis", a mixing together.

senses.def: peculiar to one person or thing, distinctly individual or eccentric
senses.ex: His idiosyncratic filing system, sorted by the color of each folder, baffled everyone else in the office.

origin: From "idolatry", from Greek "eidololatria", from "eidolon", idol, plus "latreia", worship, with the suffix "-ous".

senses.def: showing excessive or uncritical adoration of someone or something
senses.ex: The band's idolatrous fans camped outside the arena for three days just to stand near the stage.

senses.def: worshipping idols or images as gods
senses.ex: The prophet condemned the idolatrous rituals performed before the golden statue in the town square.

origin: From Greek "eidololatria", worship of idols, from "eidolon", image or idol, plus "latreia", worship.

senses.def: extreme admiration, love, or devotion for someone or something
senses.ex: The documentary criticized the media's idolatry of tech founders, who were treated as geniuses beyond question.

senses.def: worship of idols or images as gods
senses.ex: Many ancient religious texts warn against idolatry, forbidding believers to bow before carved statues.

origin: From Latin "idyllium", from Greek "eidyllion", a short descriptive poem, a diminutive of "eidos", form or picture.

senses.def: extremely happy, peaceful, or picturesque scene or period
senses.ex: Their summer on the lake was an idyll of swimming, berry picking, and long evenings on the porch.

senses.def: short poem or prose piece describing a peaceful rural scene
senses.ex: The poet's early idylls celebrate shepherds, orchards, and quiet streams far from the noise of the city.

origin: From "idyll", from Greek "eidyllion", a little picture or short pastoral poem, plus the suffix "-ic".

senses.def: extremely happy, peaceful, and picturesque
senses.ex: The brochure showed an idyllic village of stone cottages, but it left out the highway roaring past the edge of town.

origin: From French, literally "fixed idea", a thought that has become stuck fast in the mind.

senses.def: idea or obsession that dominates someone's mind and resists all argument
senses.ex: Finding the lost treasure of the shipwreck became an idée fixe that consumed his savings and two marriages.

origin: From Latin "igneus", fiery, from "ignis", fire, the same root as "ignite".

senses.def: of rock, formed when molten magma or lava cools and hardens
senses.ex: Granite and basalt are both igneous rocks, formed from melted material that cooled underground or after an eruption.

senses.def: relating to fire, or fiery in nature
senses.ex: The poet described the sunset's igneous glow spreading across the clouds like embers in a stove.

origin: From Modern Latin, literally "foolish fire", for a flickering marsh light that seems to lead travelers astray.

senses.def: illusory hope or goal that misleads those who pursue it
senses.ex: For the struggling inventor, a perpetual motion machine was an ignis fatuus that drained his fortune and his health.

senses.def: faint light seen over marshes at night, likely caused by burning marsh gas
senses.ex: Old villagers warned children not to follow the ignis fatuus that flickered over the bog after dark.

syn: will-o'-the-wisp, chimera, illusion, mirage, pipe dream

origin: From Latin "ignobilis", from "in-", not, plus "gnobilis", an old form of "nobilis", noble or well known.

senses.def: not honorable in character or purpose, base or shameful
senses.ex: Blaming the intern for his own mistake was an ignoble move that cost the manager his team's respect.

senses.def: of humble birth or low social rank
senses.ex: The novel's hero rises from ignoble origins as a stable boy to become an advisor to the king.

origin: From Latin "ignominiosus", from "ignominia", disgrace, from "in-", not, plus "nomen", name, so disgrace means losing one's good name.

senses.def: deserving or causing public disgrace or shame
senses.ex: The favored team suffered an ignominious defeat, losing by forty points to a squad that had not won all season.

origin: From Latin "ignominia", from "in-", not, plus "nomen", name, so ignominy is the loss of one's good name.

senses.def: public shame or disgrace
senses.ex: The senator resigned in ignominy after reporters revealed that he had taken bribes from a construction firm.

origin: From "il-", not, plus "legible", from Latin "legere", to read, so not able to be read.

senses.def: too unclear or messy to be read
senses.ex: The pharmacist called the doctor's office because the handwriting on the prescription was completely illegible.

origin: From Latin "illiberalis", unworthy of a free person, from "in-", not, plus "liberalis", befitting a free man, from "liber", free.

senses.def: opposed to liberal principles such as free speech, fair elections, and individual rights
senses.ex: Critics warned that the new law banning protests near government buildings was a dangerously illiberal measure.

senses.def: narrow-minded and intolerant of other views or ways of life
senses.ex: His illiberal attitude toward anyone who dressed differently made the new students feel unwelcome.

origin: From "illiberal", from Latin "illiberalis", unworthy of a free person, plus the noun suffix "-ity".

senses.def: narrow-minded intolerance, especially toward other people's views or freedoms
senses.ex: The essay attacked the illiberality of a campus culture where unpopular speakers were routinely shouted down.

senses.def: stinginess or lack of generosity
senses.ex: The widow's illiberality became a local legend when she tipped the movers a single quarter each.

origin: From Latin "illicitus", from "in-", not, plus "licitus", allowed, from "licet", it is permitted.

senses.def: forbidden by law, rules, or custom
senses.ex: Customs officers found illicit ivory hidden inside crates labeled as furniture parts.

origin: From "il-", not, plus "limitable", from Latin "limes", boundary, so impossible to fence in.

senses.def: without limits or bounds, too vast to be measured
senses.ex: Lying on the desert sand at night, they felt dwarfed by the illimitable sky crowded with stars.

origin: From Medieval Latin "illusivus", from Latin "illudere", to mock or deceive, from "in", against, plus "ludere", to play.

senses.def: based on illusion, deceptively appearing real but not actually so
senses.ex: The calm of the harbor proved illusive, since a storm was already gathering beyond the headland.

origin: From Latin "illusorius", mocking, related to "illudere", to mock or play with, from "ludere", to play, so an illusory thing plays tricks on you.

senses.def: based on illusion, seeming real or true but not actually so
senses.ex: The company's profits proved illusory once auditors discovered that half the reported sales had never happened.

origin: From Latin "illustris", bright or distinguished, from "illustrare", to light up, so an illustrious person shines with fame.

senses.def: well known and highly respected for past achievements
senses.ex: The orchestra's illustrious history includes premieres of works by several of the century's greatest composers.

origin: From French "imbécile", from Latin "imbecillus", weak or feeble, traditionally explained as "without a staff" to lean on.

senses.def: insulting word for a very stupid or foolish person
senses.ex: The driver called the cyclist an imbecile, though he himself had run the red light.

senses.def: very stupid or foolish
senses.ex: Leaving the campfire burning in such dry weather was an imbecile thing to do.

origin: From French "imbécillité", from Latin "imbecillitas", weakness, from "imbecillus", weak or feeble.

senses.def: great stupidity or foolishness
senses.ex: The editorial mocked the imbecility of building a new stadium in a floodplain that is underwater every spring.

senses.def: foolish act or remark
senses.ex: After a series of public imbecilities, the spokesman was quietly moved to a job without microphones.

origin: From Latin "imbibere", from "in-", in, plus "bibere", to drink, the same root behind "beverage".

senses.def: drink something, especially alcohol
senses.ex: Guests who planned to imbibe at the wedding were asked to leave their car keys with the valet.

senses.def: absorb or take in ideas, knowledge, or influences
senses.ex: Growing up above her parents' bookstore, she imbibed a love of poetry long before she could read it herself.

origin: From Latin "imbricatus", covered with tiles, from "imbrex", a curved roof tile, so overlapping like tiles on a roof.

senses.def: overlap or arrange in an overlapping pattern, often used of ideas or themes
senses.ex: In her novel, the stories of three generations imbricate, each one partly covering and echoing the last.

senses.def: having edges that overlap in a regular pattern, like roof tiles or fish scales
senses.ex: The pine cone's imbricate scales fit so snugly that rain ran off them without reaching the seeds.

origin: From Italian "imbroglio", a tangle or muddle, from "imbrogliare", to tangle, related to French "embrouiller" and English "embroil".

senses.def: complicated, confused, and often embarrassing situation or dispute
senses.ex: What began as a parking dispute between neighbors grew into a legal imbroglio involving the city council and two lawyers.

origin: From Latin "imbuere", to wet or soak, so to imbue something is to soak it thoroughly in a quality or feeling.

senses.def: fill or inspire with a feeling, quality, or idea
senses.ex: The coach imbued her young team with a confidence that carried them all the way to the state finals.

origin: From Latin "immaculatus", unstained, from "in-", not, plus "macula", a spot or blemish.

senses.def: perfectly clean, neat, and tidy
senses.ex: The chef insisted on an immaculate kitchen, so every counter was scrubbed and every pan hung in its place by midnight.

senses.def: free from any flaw or mistake
senses.ex: The pianist gave an immaculate performance, playing the fiendishly difficult sonata without a single wrong note.

origin: From Latin "immanere", to remain in, from "in", in, plus "manere", to stay, so dwelling within something.

senses.def: existing within something as a natural, inherent part of it
senses.ex: The critic argued that a longing for home is immanent in every song the folk singer ever wrote.

senses.def: of God, present throughout the whole of the created universe
senses.ex: Some theologians describe a God immanent in nature, present in every river and stone rather than distant above them.

origin: From Medieval Latin "immaterialis", from "in-", not, plus "materialis", made of matter, so what is immaterial has no substance or weight.

senses.def: unimportant or irrelevant to the matter at hand
senses.ex: Whether the thief was hungry is immaterial, the judge said, because the law makes no exception for motive.

senses.def: spiritual rather than physical, not made of matter
senses.ex: Many traditions describe the soul as an immaterial part of a person that survives the body.

syn: irrelevant, unimportant, inconsequential, extraneous, beside the point

origin: From French "immémorial", from "im-", not, plus "memorial", from Latin "memoria", memory, so older than anyone can remember.

senses.def: so old that it goes back beyond memory or records
senses.ex: Fishermen have launched their boats from this beach since time immemorial, long before the village had a name.

origin: From Latin "immergere", to plunge into, from "in", into, plus "mergere", to dip or sink.

senses.def: involve oneself or someone deeply in an activity or interest
senses.ex: To learn Spanish quickly, she immersed herself in the language by spending a summer with a family in Oaxaca.

senses.def: dip or submerge something completely in a liquid
senses.ex: The baker immersed the doughnuts in hot oil for exactly ninety seconds before flipping them.

origin: From Latin "imminere", to overhang or loom over, so an imminent danger hangs right over you.

senses.def: about to happen very soon
senses.ex: With the hurricane's landfall imminent, officials ordered everyone living near the coast to evacuate by noon.

origin: From French "immobilité", from Latin "immobilis", unmovable, from "in-", not, plus "mobilis", movable.

senses.def: state of not moving or being unable to move
senses.ex: After weeks of immobility in a hospital bed, his leg muscles had grown weak and thin.

origin: From Latin "immoderatus", unrestrained, from "in-", not, plus "moderatus", kept within limits.

senses.def: going beyond reasonable limits, excessive or unrestrained
senses.ex: His immoderate spending on sneakers left him unable to pay for the school trip he had been saving for.

origin: From "im-", not, plus "modest", from Latin "modestus", keeping due measure, from "modus", measure.

senses.def: boastful or conceited about one's own abilities or achievements
senses.ex: At the risk of sounding immodest, the chef admitted that his dumplings were the best in the city.

senses.def: not following accepted standards of decency in dress or behavior
senses.ex: The strict school board once considered knee-length shorts too immodest for students to wear to class.

origin: From Latin "immolare", to sacrifice, originally to sprinkle a victim with "mola", salted grain meal, before sacrifice.

senses.def: kill or offer as a sacrifice, especially by burning
senses.ex: The ancient texts describe priests who immolated a bull on the altar to win the favor of the gods.

senses.def: destroy or give up something for the sake of a cause
senses.ex: He immolated his political career by publicly opposing the war that his own party had championed.

origin: From Latin "immolatio", a sacrifice, from "immolare", to sacrifice, originally to sprinkle a victim with salted meal called "mola".

senses.def: killing or offering of a victim as a sacrifice, especially by burning
senses.ex: The ritual immolation of animals was central to many ancient religions around the Mediterranean.

senses.def: act of sacrificing or destroying oneself or something for a cause
senses.ex: The monk's self-immolation in protest shocked the world and drew attention to the persecution of his faith.

origin: From Latin "immurare", from "in-", in, plus "murus", wall, so to immure someone is literally to wall them in.

senses.def: enclose or imprison someone as if within walls
senses.ex: The reclusive novelist immured herself in a remote farmhouse for two years to finish her final book.

syn: imprison, confine, incarcerate, wall up, shut in

origin: From Latin "immutabilis", unchangeable, from "in-", not, plus "mutabilis", changeable, from "mutare", to change.

senses.def: unchanging over time or impossible to change
senses.ex: For centuries people treated the stars as immutable, until astronomers recorded a brand-new star in 1572.

origin: From Old French "empeirier", from Late Latin "peiorare", to make worse, from "peior", worse, so to impair is to worsen something.

senses.def: weaken or damage something, especially an ability or function
senses.ex: Even mild sleep deprivation can impair a driver's reaction time as much as a couple of drinks.

origin: From French "empaler", from Medieval Latin "impalare", from "in", on, plus "palus", a stake, the same root as the fence "pale".

senses.def: pierce or fix something on a sharp pointed object
senses.ex: The collector impaled each butterfly on a thin steel pin before labeling it for the museum drawer.

origin: From French, from Medieval Latin "impalpabilis", from "in-", not, plus "palpare", to touch gently, so unable to be felt.

senses.def: unable to be felt by touch, having no physical substance
senses.ex: The morning mist was impalpable, yet it soaked through our jackets within minutes.

senses.def: hard for the mind to grasp or perceive, subtle
senses.ex: There was an impalpable tension in the room that no one could name but everyone could sense.

origin: From Latin "impartire", to share, from "in", in, plus "partire", to divide, from "pars", a part, so to give someone a part.

senses.def: communicate or pass on knowledge, information, or a skill
senses.ex: The retiring carpenter was eager to impart everything he knew about joinery to his young apprentice.

senses.def: give a particular quality or feeling to something
senses.ex: A splash of lemon juice imparts a bright, sharp flavor to the otherwise heavy cream sauce.

syn: convey, communicate, pass on, transmit, relay

origin: From "im-", not, plus "partial", favoring one side, from Latin "pars", part, so an impartial judge takes no part or side.

senses.def: treating all sides fairly and equally, without bias
senses.ex: The league hired an impartial referee from another state so neither school could complain about favoritism.

origin: From "im-", not, plus "passable", from French "passer", to pass, from Latin "passus", a step.

senses.def: impossible to travel along or across
senses.ex: After the blizzard, the mountain pass was impassable, and the trucks had to wait three days for the plows.

origin: From French "impasse", dead end, from "im-", not, plus "passer", to pass, so an impasse is a road with no way through.

senses.def: situation in which no progress is possible, especially because of disagreement
senses.ex: Contract talks reached an impasse when neither the union nor management would budge on health benefits.

syn: deadlock, stalemate, standstill, dead end, standoff

origin: From "impassion", to fill with passion, from Italian "impassionare", from "passione", passion, from Latin "pati", to suffer.

senses.def: filled with or expressing strong feeling
senses.ex: Her impassioned speech about the dying reef moved several council members to change their votes.

origin: From "im-", not, plus "passive" in its old sense of able to suffer or feel, from Latin "pati", to suffer.

senses.def: not showing or feeling any emotion
senses.ex: The guard remained impassive as tourists danced, joked, and posed for photos right in front of him.

origin: From Old French "empeechier", to hinder, from Late Latin "impedicare", to fetter, from "pedica", a shackle for the feet.

senses.def: formally charge a public official with serious misconduct in office
senses.ex: The House voted to impeach the governor for misusing disaster relief money, sending the case to the state senate.

senses.def: call into question the truth, honesty, or reliability of something or someone
senses.ex: The defense lawyer tried to impeach the witness by showing that she had changed her story twice.

origin: From Old French "empeechement", hindrance, from "empeechier", to hinder, from Late Latin "impedicare", to fetter the feet.

senses.def: formal charge of serious misconduct brought against a public official
senses.ex: The impeachment of the president dominated the news for months, though the Senate ultimately did not remove him.

senses.def: act of challenging the credibility or validity of something, especially testimony
senses.ex: The impeachment of the expert's testimony came when the lawyer revealed he had been paid by the defendant.

origin: From Latin "impeccabilis", not liable to sin, from "in-", not, plus "peccare", to sin, so it first meant incapable of wrongdoing.

senses.def: flawless and meeting the highest standards
senses.ex: The pianist's technique was impeccable, but some critics felt her performance lacked real emotion.

origin: From "im-", not, plus "pecunious", wealthy, from Latin "pecunia", money, so an impecunious person has no money.

senses.def: having little or no money
senses.ex: As an impecunious graduate student, he lived on rice and beans and biked everywhere to save bus fare.

origin: From Latin "impedire", to shackle the feet, from "in-", in, plus "pes, pedis", foot, so impeding something trips up its progress.

senses.def: slow down or block progress by getting in the way
senses.ex: Fallen trees impeded the ambulance on its way up the mountain road after the storm.

origin: Past participle of "impede", from Latin "impedire", to shackle the feet, from "pes, pedis", foot.

senses.def: slowed, blocked, or obstructed in movement or progress
senses.ex: Impeded by a sprained knee, the runner still managed to limp across the finish line in fifth place.

origin: From Latin "impedimentum", hindrance, from "impedire", to shackle the feet, from "pes, pedis", foot.

senses.def: obstacle that makes progress or action difficult
senses.ex: The high cost of textbooks is a serious impediment for many students trying to finish a degree.

senses.def: physical defect that affects speech, such as a stammer or lisp
senses.ex: Despite a childhood speech impediment, she became one of the most admired radio hosts in the country.

origin: From Latin "impedimenta", baggage, the plural of "impedimentum", hindrance, from "impedire", to shackle the feet, from "pes", foot.

senses.def: baggage or equipment that slows down travel or movement
senses.ex: Loaded with tents, coolers, and a guitar, the family dragged their impedimenta down the long trail to the lake.

origin: From Latin "impellere", to push forward, from "in", on, plus "pellere", to drive or push, the root also of "propel".

senses.def: drive or force someone to do something
senses.ex: Curiosity impelled her to open the old trunk in the attic, even though her aunt had told her not to.

senses.def: drive or push something forward
senses.ex: A steady wind impelled the small sailboat across the bay faster than anyone had expected.

origin: From "impend", from Latin "impendere", to hang over, from "in-", on, plus "pendere", to hang, so impending trouble hangs over you.

senses.def: about to happen, usually describing something unpleasant or threatening
senses.ex: Dark clouds and a sudden drop in temperature warned the sailors of an impending storm.

origin: From Latin "impenetrabilis", from "in-", not, plus "penetrare", to pierce or enter, so nothing can get into it.

senses.def: impossible to pass through or enter
senses.ex: The explorers turned back when the jungle became an impenetrable wall of vines and thorny bushes.

senses.def: impossible or very hard to understand
senses.ex: The insurance contract was written in impenetrable legal jargon that even the agent could not explain.

origin: From Late Latin "impaenitentia", from "in-", not, plus "paenitere", to regret, so a refusal to feel sorry.

senses.def: lack of regret or remorse for one's wrongdoing
senses.ex: The judge cited the defendant's impenitence, noting that he had smirked through the victims' statements.

origin: From Latin "impaenitens", unrepentant, from "in-", not, plus "paenitens", regretting, from "paenitere", to regret.

senses.def: feeling no shame or regret for one's wrongdoing, unrepentant
senses.ex: Even after his third suspension, the impenitent prankster bragged to friends about filling the principal's office with balloons.

origin: From Latin "imperativus", commanded, from "imperare", to command, the same root that gives "emperor".

senses.def: of vital importance, absolutely necessary
senses.ex: It is imperative that patients stop eating twelve hours before surgery to avoid complications.

senses.def: essential or urgent thing that must be done
senses.ex: For the new mayor, fixing the city's crumbling water pipes became a moral imperative.

senses.def: of grammar, expressing a command, as in "Close the door"
senses.ex: In the sentence "Sit down," the verb is in the imperative mood because it gives a direct order.

origin: From Medieval Latin "imperceptibilis", from "in-", not, plus "percipere", to perceive or grasp, so too slight to be noticed.

senses.def: so slight, gradual, or subtle that it cannot be noticed or sensed
senses.ex: The glacier's movement is imperceptible from one day to the next, but over a century it has retreated two miles.

origin: From "im-", in or into, plus "peril", danger, from Latin "periculum", a trial or risk, so to put into danger.

senses.def: put someone or something in danger or at risk
senses.ex: Building the highway through the wetland would imperil the last breeding ground of the rare frog.

origin: From Latin "imperiosus", commanding or powerful, from "imperium", command or rule, so an imperious person acts like a ruler.

senses.def: arrogant and domineering, expecting to be obeyed
senses.ex: With an imperious wave of her hand, the duchess dismissed the servants and demanded a fresh pot of tea.

origin: From "im-", not, plus "permanence", from Latin "permanere", to remain to the end, from "per", through, plus "manere", to stay.

senses.def: state of lasting only for a limited time, not being permanent
senses.ex: The monks spent days on an intricate sand painting and then swept it away to honor the impermanence of all things.

origin: From Latin "impermeabilis", from "in-", not, plus "permeare", to pass through, from "per-", through, plus "meare", to go.

senses.def: not allowing liquid or gas to pass through
senses.ex: The pond is lined with an impermeable clay layer that keeps the water from seeping into the soil.

origin: From "im-", into, plus Latin "persona", a mask or character in a play, so to take on another's role.

senses.def: pretend to be another person, especially to deceive
senses.ex: The scammer impersonated a bank officer over the phone and talked an elderly couple out of their savings.

senses.def: imitate someone's voice and manner to entertain
senses.ex: The comedian can impersonate every recent president, down to their hand gestures and favorite catchphrases.

syn: pose as, masquerade as, pass oneself off as, imitate, mimic

origin: From French, from "impertinent", from Latin "in-", not, plus "pertinere", to relate to, so first irrelevant, then out of place and rude.

senses.def: rude lack of respect, especially toward someone of higher status
senses.ex: The butler was dismissed for the impertinence of correcting his employer's grammar in front of the dinner guests.

origin: From Latin "impertinens", not belonging, from "in-", not, plus "pertinere", to relate to, so it first meant irrelevant, then intrusive and rude.

senses.def: rude and disrespectful, especially toward someone older or in authority
senses.ex: The student's impertinent question about the principal's salary earned him an afternoon of detention.

senses.def: not relevant to the matter being discussed
senses.ex: The lawyer objected that the witness's personal life was impertinent to the question of the contract.

origin: From Late Latin "imperturbabilis", from "in-", not, plus "perturbare", to throw into confusion, from "turba", turmoil.

senses.def: unable to be upset or excited, always calm
senses.ex: The imperturbable pilot calmly announced the engine failure and then landed the plane safely on one engine.

origin: From Latin "impervius", from "in-", not, plus "pervius", passable, so nothing can get through to something impervious.

senses.def: not affected or influenced by something, such as criticism or pressure
senses.ex: The director seemed impervious to bad reviews and went straight to work on an even stranger film.

senses.def: not allowing something such as water to pass through
senses.ex: The hikers wore jackets made of an impervious fabric that kept them dry through hours of rain.

origin: From French "impétuosité", from Latin "impetuosus", from "impetus", an attack or rush, from "impetere", to rush upon.

senses.def: tendency to act suddenly and rashly without careful thought
senses.ex: In a moment of impetuosity, he quit his job by text message and then spent months regretting it.

origin: From Late Latin "impetuosus", violent, from Latin "impetus", attack or rush, so an impetuous person rushes in.

senses.def: acting quickly and without careful thought
senses.ex: In an impetuous moment, Sam quit his job by text message and booked a one-way ticket to Lisbon.

origin: From Latin "impetus", a rushing upon or attack, from "impetere", to rush at, from "in-", upon, plus "petere", to seek or head for.

senses.def: force or motivation that makes something happen or happen faster
senses.ex: The flood of 2011 provided the impetus for the town to finally build a new levee.

senses.def: momentum or energy with which a moving body travels
senses.ex: The boulder gained impetus as it rolled down the slope, smashing through a wooden fence at the bottom.

origin: From Latin "impietas", from "in-", not, plus "pietas", dutiful respect, from "pius", devout.

senses.def: lack of reverence for God, sacred things, or one's duties
senses.ex: The playwright was accused of impiety for portraying the temple priests as greedy fools.

senses.def: act that shows a lack of reverence or respect
senses.ex: Talking loudly during the memorial service struck the elderly mourners as a shocking impiety.

origin: From Latin "impingere", to dash or drive against, from "in-", against, plus "pangere", to fasten, the same verb that gave "impact".

senses.def: have an effect on something, often a limiting or harmful one
senses.ex: Long hours at her part-time job began to impinge on the time she needed for studying.

senses.def: encroach on someone's rights, territory, or freedom
senses.ex: Residents argued that the new surveillance cameras impinged on their right to privacy.

origin: From Latin "impius", from "in-", not, plus "pius", dutiful or devout, so impious means lacking proper reverence.

senses.def: showing a lack of respect for God or for sacred things
senses.ex: The villagers considered it impious to harvest crops on the holy day, so the fields stood empty.

origin: From "imp", a small mischievous demon, plus "-ish". The word "imp" first meant a young shoot of a plant, then a child, then a little devil.

senses.def: playfully mischievous in a way that is amusing rather than harmful
senses.ex: With an impish grin, the toddler dropped her spoon on the floor for the tenth time just to watch her father pick it up.

origin: From Latin "implacabilitas", from "implacabilis", unappeasable, from "in-", not, plus "placare", to calm or soothe.

senses.def: quality of being impossible to calm, satisfy, or turn aside
senses.ex: The implacability of the rival clans meant that even a royal wedding could not end their centuries-old feud.

origin: From Latin "implacabilis", from "in-", not, plus "placabilis", easily calmed, from "placare", to soothe or appease.

senses.def: unable to be calmed, satisfied, or appeased
senses.ex: The two families remained implacable enemies, refusing to speak even at their grandchildren's weddings.

senses.def: relentless and impossible to stop
senses.ex: The army's implacable advance forced villagers to flee ahead of it for weeks.

origin: From "im-", not, plus "plausible", from Latin "plausibilis", deserving applause, from "plaudere", to clap.

senses.def: not seeming reasonable or probable, hard to believe
senses.ex: His excuse that a raccoon had stolen his homework was so implausible that the whole class laughed.

origin: From Latin "implicare", to entangle or fold in, from "in-", in, plus "plicare", to fold, so to implicate someone is to entangle them.

senses.def: show someone to be involved in a crime or wrongdoing
senses.ex: Phone records implicated the mayor's chief of staff in the scheme to rig the city contract.

senses.def: suggest that something is a cause of or is involved in something
senses.ex: Scientists have implicated a single gene mutation in the rare blood disorder.

origin: From Latin "implicatio", an entangling, from "implicare", to fold in, from "plicare", to fold, so an implication is folded inside a statement.

senses.def: conclusion that can be drawn from something even though it is not directly stated
senses.ex: When the coach praised the other goalie so warmly, the implication was that Mia would not start on Saturday.

senses.def: likely consequence or effect of an action or decision
senses.ex: Economists are still studying the long-term implications of the new tariffs for small farmers.

senses.def: act of showing that someone is involved in a crime or wrongdoing
senses.ex: His implication in the bribery scandal ended a political career that had lasted thirty years.

origin: From Latin "implicitus", folded in or entangled, past participle of "implicare", to fold in, so an implicit meaning is folded inside.

senses.def: suggested or understood without being directly stated
senses.ex: Although nobody said so, there was an implicit understanding that the newest employee would make the coffee.

senses.def: complete, absolute, and unquestioning
senses.ex: The climbers had implicit trust in their guide, following her across the glacier without a moment's hesitation.

origin: A back-formation from "implosion", which was modeled on "explosion" with "im-", in, replacing "ex-", out.

senses.def: collapse violently inward on itself
senses.ex: The demolition crew watched as the old stadium imploded and sank into a cloud of dust within seconds.

senses.def: fail or break down suddenly and completely
senses.ex: The startup imploded after its two founders quarreled and investors pulled their money out.

syn: collapse, cave in, fall in, crumple

origin: From "implore", from Latin "implorare", to beg with tears, from "in-", on, plus "plorare", to weep or cry out.

senses.def: begging earnestly or desperately
senses.ex: The puppy gave Jonah an imploring look from beneath the table until he finally dropped a piece of chicken.

origin: From "im-", not, plus "politic", shrewd, from Greek "politikos", of citizens, from "polis", city, so not shrewd in public affairs.

senses.def: unwise or tactless, likely to cause trouble or offense
senses.ex: It was impolitic of the new manager to criticize the founder's old policies during her very first staff meeting.

origin: From "im-", not, plus "ponderable", able to be weighed, from Latin "ponderare", to weigh, from "pondus", weight.

senses.def: something whose effect or importance cannot be measured or predicted
senses.ex: The weather on race day remains the great imponderable that no amount of training can prepare for.

senses.def: difficult or impossible to estimate, measure, or assess
senses.ex: Such imponderable factors as public mood made the election nearly impossible to forecast.

origin: From Latin "importunus", inconvenient or troublesome, the opposite of "opportunus", well timed, the source of "opportune".

senses.def: persistent in making demands or requests, often to the point of annoyance
senses.ex: The importunate reporters camped outside the actor's house and shouted questions every time a curtain moved.

senses.def: urgent and pressing, demanding immediate attention
senses.ex: Her importunate need for a quiet place to study drove her to the library every evening until it closed.

origin: From Latin "importunus", troublesome, originally "without a harbor", the opposite of "opportunus", which gave "opportune".

senses.def: harass someone with persistent, pressing requests
senses.ex: Fans importuned the author for autographs as she tried to eat her lunch in the hotel lobby.

origin: Past tense of "importune", from Latin "importunus", troublesome, a word originally meaning "without a harbor".

senses.def: repeatedly begged or pestered someone with urgent requests
senses.ex: The children importuned their parents for weeks until the family finally adopted a kitten from the shelter.

origin: From Latin "impositio", a laying on, from "imponere", to place upon, from "in", on, plus "ponere", to put.

senses.def: unfair or unwelcome demand or burden placed on someone
senses.ex: Asking a neighbor to feed your cat for a month without paying them is quite an imposition.

senses.def: act of officially introducing something such as a tax, rule, or penalty
senses.ex: The imposition of a curfew after the riots kept the streets empty from dusk until dawn.

origin: From French "imposteur", from Latin "impositor", one who imposes, from "imponere", to place upon, in the sense of to deceive.

senses.def: person who pretends to be someone else in order to deceive others
senses.ex: The man who claimed to be a visiting surgeon turned out to be an impostor with no medical training at all.

origin: From Latin "impotens", powerless, from "in-", not, plus "potens", able or powerful, the root of "potent" and "potential".

senses.def: lacking the power or ability to act or have an effect, helpless
senses.ex: The league proved impotent against the doping scandal, unable to punish the teams that had hired the cheating doctors.

senses.def: of a man, unable to achieve an erection, as a medical condition
senses.ex: The doctor explained that some blood pressure medications can leave patients temporarily impotent.

origin: From "impoverish", from Old French "empovrir", to make poor, from "povre", poor, from Latin "pauper", poor.

senses.def: extremely poor, lacking money and basic necessities
senses.ex: The charity builds wells in impoverished villages where families once walked hours each day to fetch water.

senses.def: drained of richness, quality, or strength, depleted
senses.ex: Decades of planting the same crop had left the soil so impoverished that nothing grew without fertilizer.

origin: From "im-", not, plus "practicable", from French "pratiquer", to practice, from Greek "praktikos", fit for action.

senses.def: impossible to carry out or put into practice
senses.ex: The plan to tow an iceberg to the desert for drinking water proved impracticable once engineers studied the costs.

origin: From Latin "imprecari", to call down upon, from "in", upon, plus "precari", to pray, the root also of "pray" and "precarious".

senses.def: call down a curse or evil upon someone, utter curses
senses.ex: The ruined merchant stood on the dock and imprecated every sailor who had abandoned his sinking ship.

origin: From Latin "imprecatio", a calling down of curses, from "imprecari", to invoke, from "in-", upon, plus "precari", to pray.

senses.def: spoken curse or wish that harm will come to someone
senses.ex: The furious farmer shouted imprecations at the hunters who had trampled his wheat field.

origin: From Old French "imprenable", not able to be taken, from "prendre", to take, and unrelated to "pregnant".

senses.def: unable to be captured, broken into, or entered by force
senses.ex: Built on a sheer cliff above the sea, the fortress was considered impregnable for three hundred years.

senses.def: unable to be challenged, shaken, or defeated
senses.ex: After winning the first eight races, the team held a nearly impregnable lead in the championship.

origin: From Italian "impresario", one who undertakes a project, from "impresa", an undertaking or enterprise.

senses.def: person who organizes and finances concerts, plays, operas, or other entertainments
senses.ex: The jazz impresario booked unknown musicians into his tiny club, and several of them later became legends.

origin: From Latin "imprimatur", let it be printed, the formula a Catholic bishop used to approve a book for publication.

senses.def: official approval or sanction, especially from a respected authority
senses.ex: The new textbook carried the imprimatur of the national science teachers' association on its cover.

senses.def: official license from the Catholic Church allowing a book to be printed
senses.ex: The prayer book was printed only after the bishop granted his imprimatur.

origin: From Latin "improbabilis", from "in-", not, plus "probabilis", likely or provable, from "probare", to test or prove.

senses.def: not likely to be true or to happen
senses.ex: It seemed improbable that the tiny college would beat the national champions, yet they won by a single point.

origin: From French "impromptu", from Latin "in promptu", in readiness, so an impromptu speech comes from whatever is at hand.

senses.def: done without planning or preparation
senses.ex: When the power went out, the guests held an impromptu concert by candlelight with two guitars and a harmonica.

senses.def: short piece of music, often for piano, that sounds improvised
senses.ex: The pianist closed her recital with a lively impromptu that drew a standing ovation.

origin: From French "impropriété", from Latin "improprietas", from "improprius", not one's own, unsuitable, from "in-", not, plus "proprius", one's own.

senses.def: behavior that is improper, dishonest, or not in keeping with accepted standards
senses.ex: The auditor found no financial impropriety, though she criticized the charity for keeping such sloppy records.

senses.def: particular improper act or remark
senses.ex: Accepting free concert tickets from a contractor was a minor impropriety that still cost the official his job.

origin: From Latin "improvidens", not foreseeing, from "in-", not, plus "providens", foreseeing, from "providere", to see ahead.

senses.def: not planning or saving for the future, careless with money or resources
senses.ex: The improvident heir spent his entire inheritance on sports cars within five years and then had to borrow rent money.

origin: From French, from "improviser", to improvise, from Italian "improvviso", unforeseen, from Latin "improvisus", from "in-", not, plus "provisus", foreseen.

senses.def: creation of music, speech, or drama on the spot without preparation
senses.ex: The jazz trio's improvisation lasted twenty minutes, with each player inventing new melodies over the same chords.

senses.def: something made or done quickly with whatever is at hand
senses.ex: With no tent poles, the campers rigged a clever improvisation from branches and a length of rope.

origin: From French "improviser", from Latin "improvisus", unforeseen, from "in-", not, plus "provisus", foreseen, and unrelated to "improve".

senses.def: create or perform something, such as music or a speech, without preparation
senses.ex: When the teleprompter froze, the anchor improvised for five minutes until the technicians fixed it.

senses.def: make or do something using whatever materials happen to be available
senses.ex: Stranded without a tent, the campers improvised a shelter from branches and a plastic tarp.

origin: From Latin "imprudentia", from "in-", not, plus "prudentia", foresight, so imprudence is a failure to look ahead.

senses.def: lack of caution or good judgment
senses.ex: In a moment of imprudence, she posted her vacation dates online, and burglars visited her empty house that week.

origin: From Latin "imprudens", not foreseeing, from "in-", not, plus "prudens", foreseeing or wise.

senses.def: not showing care for the consequences of an action, unwise
senses.ex: It would be imprudent to hike the desert trail at noon without carrying plenty of water.

origin: From Latin "impudentia", shamelessness, from "in-", not, plus "pudere", to feel shame.

senses.def: bold, shameless disrespect toward others
senses.ex: The waiter could hardly believe the impudence of the customer who demanded a refund after eating the entire meal.

origin: From Latin "impudens", shameless, from "in-", not, plus "pudere", to feel shame, so an impudent person shows no shame.

senses.def: boldly and shamelessly disrespectful
senses.ex: The impudent teenager answered every one of the officer's questions with a sarcastic joke.

origin: From Latin "impugnare", to attack, from "in-", against, plus "pugnare", to fight, from "pugnus", fist, as in "pugilist".

senses.def: dispute the truth, validity, or honesty of someone or something
senses.ex: The defense attorney tried to impugn the witness's credibility by pointing out his past convictions for fraud.

origin: From French "impuissance", from "im-", not, plus "puissance", power, from Old French "puissant", powerful.

senses.def: lack of power or strength, helplessness or weakness
senses.ex: The aging king's impuissance was plain to all, as his ministers ignored his orders and ruled in his name.

origin: From French, from "im-", not, plus "puissant", powerful, from Old French "puissant", able, ultimately from Latin "posse", to be able.

senses.def: weak and lacking power, unable to act effectively
senses.ex: The impuissant committee could issue reports but had no authority to make anyone follow its recommendations.

origin: From French "impulsif", from Latin "impulsus", a push, from "impellere", to drive on, so driven by a sudden push.

senses.def: acting suddenly on a feeling or urge without thinking about the consequences
senses.ex: In an impulsive moment at the airport, she bought a ticket to Lisbon instead of flying home.

origin: From Latin "impunitas", from "impunis", unpunished, from "in-", not, plus "poena", punishment.

senses.def: freedom from punishment or harmful consequences
senses.ex: Because the town had no traffic cameras, drivers sped through the school zone with impunity.

origin: From Latin "imputare", to bring into the reckoning or charge to an account, from "in-", in, plus "putare", to reckon.

senses.def: attribute a fault, motive, or quality to someone, often unfairly
senses.ex: It is unfair to impute selfish motives to the volunteers simply because they asked for parking passes.

origin: From Medieval Latin "inadvertens", not paying attention, from "in-", not, plus "advertere", to turn toward, so it happens without turning one's mind to it.

senses.def: not done on purpose, accidental
senses.ex: An inadvertent click on the reply-all button sent his complaint about the boss to the entire department.

origin: From French "inaliénable", from "in-", not, plus "aliénable", able to be transferred to another, from Latin "alienus", belonging to another.

senses.def: unable to be taken away from or given up by its owner
senses.ex: The Declaration of Independence describes life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness as inalienable rights.

origin: From Italian "innamorata", a woman in love or beloved, from "innamorare", to fall in love, from "in" plus "amore", love.

senses.def: woman with whom someone is in love or has a romantic relationship
senses.ex: The aging painter filled his notebooks with sketches of his young inamorata, a cellist he met in Vienna.

origin: From Latin "inanis", empty or vain, a word of unknown origin, so an inane remark is empty of sense.

senses.def: silly and lacking sense or meaning
senses.ex: The talk show host filled the awkward silence with inane chatter about the weather and his favorite cereal.

origin: From Late Latin "inanimatus", lifeless, from "in-", not, plus "animatus", filled with life, from "anima", breath or soul.

senses.def: not alive, especially describing objects as opposed to living things
senses.ex: The toddler talked to inanimate objects as if they were friends, apologizing to the chair whenever she bumped it.

senses.def: showing no sign of life or energy, motionless or dull
senses.ex: He lay inanimate on the couch all Sunday, too exhausted from the marathon even to change the channel.

origin: From Latin "inanitas", emptiness, from "inanis", empty or vain, so inanity is emptiness of thought.

senses.def: lack of sense or meaning, silliness
senses.ex: She left the meeting early, unable to endure another hour of the inanity of arguing over the font on the agenda.

senses.def: silly or pointless remark or act
senses.ex: The reality show was a parade of inanities, with contestants shouting about who had eaten the last yogurt.

origin: From Latin "inarticulatus", indistinct, from "in-", not, plus "articulatus", divided into distinct parts, from "articulus", small joint.

senses.def: unable to express ideas or feelings clearly or fluently
senses.ex: Brilliant in the lab, the chemist became nervous and inarticulate whenever he had to speak at conferences.

senses.def: not expressed in clear words or not clearly spoken
senses.ex: From the next room came an inarticulate cry of frustration as the printer jammed yet again.

origin: A fusion of "in as much", from Middle English "in als mikel", meaning in so great a degree.

senses.def: used in "inasmuch as" to mean since or because
senses.ex: The trip was a success inasmuch as everyone came home safely, even though it rained every single day.

senses.def: used in "inasmuch as" to mean to the extent that
senses.ex: The report is useful inasmuch as it shows where the money went, but it cannot explain why.

syn: since, because, as, seeing that, insofar as

origin: From Latin "inaugurare", to consecrate after reading omens, from "augur", a priest who read the flight of birds before major events.

senses.def: formally install someone in office with a ceremony
senses.ex: The new mayor was inaugurated on the steps of city hall in front of a cheering crowd.

senses.def: begin or introduce a new policy, period, or activity
senses.ex: The invention of the printing press inaugurated an era of cheap books and rapidly spreading ideas.

senses.def: mark the opening of a building or public facility with a ceremony
senses.ex: The governor cut a ribbon to inaugurate the new bridge, and the first cars crossed an hour later.

syn: install, induct, swear in, invest, instate

origin: From "in-", not, plus "auspicious", from Latin "auspicium", reading omens from birds, from "avis", bird, plus "specere", to look.

senses.def: suggesting that the future will be unlucky or unsuccessful
senses.ex: The play had an inauspicious opening night, as the lead actor tripped and the curtain jammed halfway up.

origin: From "in" plus "born", describing a quality that a person is born with rather than one that is learned later.

senses.def: existing from birth, natural rather than learned
senses.ex: Some researchers believe babies have an inborn sense of fairness, reacting with surprise when toys are shared unequally.

origin: From Latin "incandescere", to begin to glow, from "in-", an intensifier, plus "candescere", to become white, related to "candidus", white.

senses.def: glowing or giving off light because of great heat
senses.ex: Old incandescent bulbs waste most of their energy as heat, which is why many cities have phased them out.

senses.def: brilliant, passionate, or dazzling
senses.ex: The young violinist gave an incandescent performance that left the audience silent for a moment before it erupted.

senses.def: extremely angry, almost glowing with rage
senses.ex: The coach was incandescent with rage after the referee disallowed the winning goal.

origin: From Latin "incantare", to chant a spell, from "in", upon, plus "cantare", to sing, the same source as "enchant".

senses.def: series of words spoken or chanted as a magic spell
senses.ex: The fortune teller muttered an incantation over the candle before turning over the first card.

senses.def: words or phrases repeated so often they sound ritual or empty
senses.ex: The coach's pregame incantation of teamwork and hustle no longer inspired players who had heard it all season.

origin: From "incapacity" plus "-ate". The word "capacity" comes from Latin "capax", able to hold, from "capere", to take.

senses.def: prevent someone or something from functioning normally, disable
senses.ex: A severe ankle sprain incapacitated the goalie for six weeks, forcing the team to start an untested backup.

origin: From Medieval Latin "incarcerare", to imprison, from "in", into, plus "carcer", a prison.

senses.def: imprison or confine someone, especially in a jail
senses.ex: The state incarcerated thousands of people for minor drug offenses before reformers changed the sentencing laws.

syn: imprison, jail, confine, detain, lock up

origin: From French "incarnadin", from Italian "incarnatino", flesh-colored, from Latin "incarnatus", made flesh, from "caro, carnis", flesh.

senses.def: having a deep blood-red or crimson color
senses.ex: The sunset turned the snowy peaks an incarnadine shade that faded to violet within minutes.

senses.def: color something blood-red or crimson
senses.ex: The autumn maples incarnadined the hillside, drawing photographers from all over the state.

origin: From Church Latin "incarnatus", made flesh, from "in", into, plus "caro", flesh, the root also of "carnivore".

senses.def: embodied in human form, often placed after a noun to mean the perfect example of a quality
senses.ex: To the frightened villagers, the warlord who burned their crops was evil incarnate.

senses.def: embody or give concrete form to an idea or quality
senses.ex: The architect wanted the new library to incarnate the town's belief that knowledge should be open to everyone.

syn: embodied, personified, in the flesh, in human form

origin: From Latin "incendiarius", setting on fire, from "incendium", fire, from "incendere", to set alight.

senses.def: tending to stir up conflict, anger, or rebellion
senses.ex: The commentator's incendiary remarks about the rival city sparked fights between fans outside the stadium.

senses.def: designed to cause fires
senses.ex: Investigators found the remains of an incendiary device in the burned-out warehouse.

origin: From Latin "incensum", something burned, from "incendere", to set on fire, so to incense someone is to set them ablaze with anger.

senses.def: make someone extremely angry
senses.ex: The decision to cancel the senior trip without explanation incensed students and parents alike.

senses.def: fragrant substance burned for its sweet-smelling smoke, stressed IN-sens as a noun
senses.ex: The scent of sandalwood incense drifted from the temple doors into the busy market street.

origin: Past participle of "incense", from Latin "incendere", to set on fire, so an incensed person is burning with anger.

senses.def: extremely angry, usually because of an offense or injustice
senses.ex: Incensed by the hidden fees on her bill, Rosa spent an hour on the phone demanding a refund.

origin: From Latin "incentivus", setting the tune, from "incinere", to strike up a song, from "in-" plus "canere", to sing, so an incentive calls people to act.

senses.def: something that motivates or encourages someone to act
senses.ex: The company offered a tax-free bonus as an incentive for employees to bike to work.

origin: From Latin "inceptio", a beginning, from "incipere", to begin, from "in", on, plus "capere", to take, so to take something in hand.

senses.def: beginning or establishment of an institution, project, or activity
senses.ex: Since its inception in 1998, the food bank has grown from a church basement to a warehouse serving four counties.

origin: From French "incertitude", from Late Latin "incertitudo", from "in-", not, plus "certus", sure or settled.

senses.def: uncertainty or doubt, especially about what will happen
senses.ex: Months of incertitude about the factory's future left workers unsure whether to sign leases or look for new jobs.

origin: From Late Latin "incessans", unceasing, from "in-", not, plus "cessare", to stop or cease.

senses.def: continuing without pause or interruption, often in an annoying way
senses.ex: The incessant barking of the neighbor's dog kept the whole street awake until dawn.

origin: From Latin "incohatus", begun but unfinished, past participle of "incohare", to begin, so an inchoate plan has only been started.

senses.def: only just begun and not yet fully formed or developed
senses.ex: Her ideas for the novel were still inchoate, a handful of scenes scribbled in a notebook without any plot.

origin: From "incident" plus "-al". The word "incident" comes from Latin "incidere", to fall upon or happen, from "in" plus "cadere", to fall.

senses.def: happening as a minor accompaniment or side effect of something more important
senses.ex: The film's director said the jokes were incidental, since her real goal was to show life in a fishing town.

senses.def: occurring by chance in connection with something else
senses.ex: The incidental discovery of a Roman coin halted construction on the parking garage for months.

senses.def: minor item or expense, usually in the plural
senses.ex: The scholarship covers tuition and housing, but students must pay for incidentals like books and laundry.

origin: From Latin "incipiens", beginning, present participle of "incipere", to begin, from "in-", on, plus "capere", to take.

senses.def: in an early stage, just beginning to develop or appear
senses.ex: The doctor caught the incipient infection early, before it could spread from the cut to the rest of his hand.

origin: From Medieval Latin "incisivus", from "incidere", to cut into, so incisive thinking cuts straight to the heart of a matter.

senses.def: sharply clear and direct, quickly getting to the core of an issue
senses.ex: The judge's incisive questions exposed the flaw in the company's argument within the first ten minutes.

origin: From Latin "incitare", to set in rapid motion or urge on, from "in", on, plus "citare", to set moving or summon.

senses.def: stir up or encourage violent, unlawful, or harmful behavior
senses.ex: The posts were removed because they incited followers to harass the journalist at her home.

senses.def: urge or provoke someone to act
senses.ex: The coach's halftime speech incited the team to play with a fury they had not shown all season.

syn: provoke, instigate, foment, stir up, inflame

origin: From Latin "inclemens", unmerciful, from "in-", not, plus "clemens", mild or merciful, so inclement weather shows no mercy.

senses.def: unpleasantly cold, wet, or stormy, describing weather
senses.ex: Because of inclement weather, the outdoor graduation ceremony was moved into the school gym.

origin: From "incline", from Latin "inclinare", to bend or lean toward, so an inclined person leans toward a choice.

senses.def: disposed or likely to do, think, or feel something
senses.ex: After hearing both speeches, I am inclined to vote for the candidate who promised to fix the bus routes.

senses.def: having a natural talent or interest in a particular area
senses.ex: Mechanically inclined from an early age, Priya rebuilt her first lawn mower engine when she was twelve.

senses.def: sloping or leaning at an angle
senses.ex: Students rolled marbles down an inclined board to measure how the angle affected their speed.

origin: From Italian "incognito", unknown, from Latin "incognitus", from "in-", not, plus "cognitus", known, from "cognoscere", to get to know.

senses.def: with one's real identity hidden or disguised
senses.ex: The famous chef traveled incognito, wearing a cap and glasses to sample rival restaurants without being recognized.

senses.def: having one's real identity concealed
senses.ex: An incognito inspector posed as an ordinary guest and reported every dusty corner of the hotel.

senses.def: assumed or false identity used to avoid being recognized
senses.ex: The prince's incognito as a student lasted only a week before a classmate spotted him in a magazine.

syn: in disguise, anonymously, under an assumed name, secretly, undercover

origin: From "in-", not, plus "coherent", from Latin "cohaerere", to stick together, so incoherent ideas do not hold together.

senses.def: unclear, confused, or lacking logical connection
senses.ex: The memo was so incoherent that no one could tell whether the meeting had been moved or canceled.

senses.def: unable to speak clearly, often because of strong emotion, illness, or exhaustion
senses.ex: Feverish and incoherent, the patient kept mumbling about a train he had to catch.

origin: From "in-", not, plus "commodious", roomy, from Latin "commodus", convenient, from "com-", with, plus "modus", measure, so not fitting one's needs.

senses.def: uncomfortable or inconvenient, especially because of being too small
senses.ex: The band toured in an incommodious van, with five musicians and their drums crammed into seats meant for three.

origin: From French "incompétence", from "in-", not, plus "compétence", from Latin "competere", to be fit or suitable.

senses.def: lack of the skill or ability needed to do something properly
senses.ex: The contractor's incompetence became clear when the newly installed roof leaked during the first light rain.

origin: From "in-", not, plus "conclusive", from Latin "concludere", to shut up or close, from "claudere", to shut, so nothing is closed or settled.

senses.def: not leading to a firm conclusion or result
senses.ex: The first round of tests was inconclusive, so the doctors ordered a second scan the following week.

origin: From Latin "inconditus", unarranged, from "in-", not, plus "conditus", put together, from "condere", to put together or compose.

senses.def: badly composed or put together, crude and unpolished, especially of writing
senses.ex: The judges admired the passion of his incondite first novel but begged him to find an editor for the next one.

origin: From Latin "incongruus", inconsistent, from "in-", not, plus "congruus", agreeing or fitting, so an incongruity is something that does not fit.

senses.def: quality of being strangely out of place or inconsistent with what surrounds it
senses.ex: The incongruity of a tuxedoed waiter serving hot dogs at a muddy campsite made the whole group laugh.

senses.def: something that seems out of place, contradictory, or inconsistent
senses.ex: The auditor flagged several incongruities between the shipping records and the warehouse inventory.

origin: From Latin "incongruus", from "in-", not, plus "congruus", agreeing or fitting, so incongruous things do not fit together.

senses.def: out of place or not in harmony with the surroundings
senses.ex: The bright pink skyscraper looked incongruous among the gray stone churches of the old quarter.

syn: incompatible, discordant, inappropriate, jarring, out of place

origin: From "in-", not, plus "consequence", from Latin "consequi", to follow closely, so it describes what does not follow logically or does not matter.

senses.def: lack of importance or significance
senses.ex: After the storm destroyed their house, the argument about paint colors faded into complete inconsequence.

senses.def: lack of logical connection between ideas or statements
senses.ex: The inconsequence of his speech, jumping from taxes to his childhood dog, left the audience baffled.

origin: From "in-", not, plus "consequential", from Latin "consequi", to follow closely, so something inconsequential has no results that follow from it.

senses.def: not important or significant
senses.ex: The editor cut several inconsequential details from the article, such as the color of the mayor's tie.

origin: From "inconstant", from Latin "inconstans", changeable, from "in-", not, plus "constare", to stand firm.

senses.def: tendency to change one's feelings, opinions, or loyalties, fickleness
senses.ex: Voters punished the senator's inconstancy after he switched positions on the dam project three times in a year.

senses.def: quality of being changeable or irregular
senses.ex: The inconstancy of spring weather in the mountains makes planning a picnic a gamble.

origin: From Latin "inconstans", changeable, from "in-", not, plus "constans", standing firm, from "constare", to stand together.

senses.def: frequently changing in mood, opinion, or behavior; not steady
senses.ex: The inconstant spring weather forced the farmers to cover their seedlings one night and water them the next.

senses.def: unfaithful or disloyal, especially in love
senses.ex: In the opera, the inconstant prince abandons his bride for a new admirer before the second act ends.

origin: From Latin "incontinens", not holding back, from "in-", not, plus "continens", holding together, from "continere", to contain.

senses.def: lacking self-restraint, especially over appetites, emotions, or speech
senses.ex: His incontinent rage at the referee earned him a suspension and a long lecture from his coach.

senses.def: unable to control the bladder or bowels
senses.ex: After the surgery, the elderly patient was briefly incontinent, so the nurses checked on him every hour.

origin: From "in-", not, plus "controvertible", from "controvert", to dispute, from Latin "contra", against, plus "vertere", to turn.

senses.def: impossible to deny or dispute
senses.ex: The security footage provided incontrovertible proof that the delivery driver had left the package on the porch.

origin: From Late Latin "incorporare", to embody, from "in-", into, plus "corpus", body, so to incorporate is to bring something into one body.

senses.def: include something as part of a whole
senses.ex: The architect incorporated solar panels into the roof design so they would blend in with the tiles.

senses.def: form a company or other legal corporation
senses.ex: The two friends incorporated their bakery so that their personal savings would be protected if it failed.

origin: From Latin "incorrigibilis", from "in-", not, plus "corrigere", to correct or set straight.

senses.def: not able to be corrected, reformed, or changed, especially of a bad habit
senses.ex: My incorrigible uncle still tells the same embarrassing stories at every family dinner, no matter how often we protest.

origin: From Latin "incredulus", unbelieving, from "in-", not, plus "credulus", believing, from "credere", to believe.

senses.def: state of being unwilling or unable to believe something
senses.ex: She stared at her test score in incredulity, certain the teacher had mixed up her paper with someone else's.

origin: From Latin "incredulus", unbelieving, from "in-", not, plus "credulus", believing easily, from "credere", to believe.

senses.def: unwilling or unable to believe something, showing disbelief
senses.ex: The incredulous shopper read the price tag twice before asking whether the coat really cost four thousand dollars.

origin: From Latin "incrementum", growth, from "increscere", to grow, from "in-", in, plus "crescere", to grow, the same root as "increase".

senses.def: one of a series of small, regular amounts by which something increases
senses.ex: The physical therapist raised the weight in two-pound increments so her knee could recover safely.

senses.def: increase in amount, especially a scheduled rise in salary
senses.ex: Teachers in the district receive a modest salary increment for every year of service they complete.

origin: From Medieval Latin "incriminare", to accuse, from "in-", in, plus Latin "crimen", charge or crime.

senses.def: make someone appear guilty of a crime or wrongdoing
senses.ex: The muddy boots in his closet seemed to incriminate the gardener, until the detective noticed they were two sizes too small.

origin: From Latin "incubare", to lie upon or hatch, from "in-", on, plus "cubare", to lie down, picturing a bird sitting on its eggs.

senses.def: sit on or keep eggs warm so that they hatch
senses.ex: The penguin father incubates the single egg on his feet for two months through the Antarctic winter.

senses.def: keep cells or microbes under controlled conditions so they grow
senses.ex: The lab technician incubated the bacterial samples overnight at body temperature before counting the colonies.

senses.def: develop an idea or plan slowly, often privately, before it is ready
senses.ex: She incubated the plot of her novel for years before writing a single chapter.

origin: From Latin "incubatio", from "incubare", to lie on, from "in-", on, plus "cubare", to lie down, as a bird lies on its eggs.

senses.def: keeping of eggs warm so that they develop and hatch
senses.ex: During incubation, the penguin father balances the egg on his feet for about two months.

senses.def: period between catching an infection and showing its first symptoms
senses.ex: The virus has an incubation period of up to two weeks, so travelers were asked to monitor their health.

senses.def: slow development of an idea or plan, or early support for a new business
senses.ex: The startup spent a year in the university's incubation program before it found its first investors.

origin: From Late Latin "incubus", nightmare, from "incubare", to lie upon, because the demon was imagined lying on sleeping people.

senses.def: male demon once believed to lie on and attack people in their sleep
senses.ex: Medieval villagers blamed an incubus for the terrifying dreams that troubled the young miller every night.

senses.def: something that weighs on a person like a nightmare; an oppressive burden
senses.ex: The incubus of student debt kept him from taking the low-paying job he really wanted.

origin: From Latin "inculcare", to press in by treading, from "in-", in, plus "calcare", to trample, from "calx", heel, so ideas are stamped in.

senses.def: instill an idea, attitude, or habit through persistent instruction or repetition
senses.ex: The swim coach inculcated a habit of stretching before every practice, and her athletes rarely got injured.

origin: From Late Latin "inculpare", to blame, from "in-", in, plus "culpa", fault or blame, the root also of "culpable".

senses.def: accuse or blame someone, or show that they are guilty
senses.ex: The leaked emails did not inculpate the mayor directly, but they badly damaged the reputation of her chief aide.

origin: From "incumbent", from Latin "incumbere", to lie upon or apply oneself, from "in-", on, plus "-cumbere", to lie down.

senses.def: holding of an official position, or the period during which it is held
senses.ex: During her twelve-year incumbency as principal, the school doubled the number of students taking advanced courses.

senses.def: fact of already holding an office, seen as an advantage in an election
senses.ex: Political scientists argue that incumbency gives sitting senators a huge edge in fundraising and name recognition.

syn: tenure, term, term of office, stint
