senses.ex: Venice grew rich as a mercantile power, its ships carrying spices and silk across the Mediterranean.

origin: From Latin "mercenarius", hired for pay, from "merces", wages or reward.

senses.def: motivated chiefly by money or personal gain rather than principle
senses.ex: Fans called the star's move to a rival team purely mercenary, since he had sworn loyalty only a month earlier.

senses.def: professional soldier hired to fight for a foreign country or group
senses.ex: The rebel army relied on foreign mercenaries who would switch sides for a higher fee.

origin: From Latin "mercurialis", of the god Mercury, the swift messenger. People born under his planet were thought to be quick and changeable.

senses.def: subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood or mind
senses.ex: The mercurial director could praise an actor in the morning and fire him by lunch.

senses.def: lively, quick, and clever
senses.ex: Her mercurial wit kept the dinner guests laughing from the soup to the dessert.

origin: From Latin "meretricius", of a prostitute, from "meretrix", prostitute, from "merere", to earn: flashy charm put on for pay.

senses.def: showily attractive but lacking real value or sincerity
senses.ex: Critics dismissed the novel as meretricious, all glittering plot twists with nothing underneath.

origin: From "merit" plus "-cracy", rule, from Greek "kratos", power: rule by those who have earned it through ability.

senses.def: system in which people advance according to their ability and achievement
senses.ex: The firm claims to be a meritocracy, yet nearly every partner went to the same two universities.

senses.def: ruling or leading class made up of people chosen for their ability
senses.ex: Critics warned that the new meritocracy could become as closed and self-satisfied as the old aristocracy.

origin: From Latin "meritorius", earning money, from "meritus", earned, the past participle of "merere", to earn or deserve. It is related to "merit".

senses.def: deserving praise, reward or honor
senses.ex: The firefighter received a medal for meritorious service after rescuing three children from the flooded basement.

origin: From "mesmerism", the hypnotic healing method of Franz Anton Mesmer, an 18th-century German doctor.

senses.def: hold someone's complete attention, as if by a spell
senses.ex: The toddler was mesmerized by the jellyfish drifting under the aquarium's blue lights.

origin: From French "metamorphoser", from Greek "metamorphosis", from "meta", change, and "morphe", form.

senses.def: change completely in form, nature, or character
senses.ex: Over one summer, the abandoned rail yard metamorphosed into a park with gardens, food stalls, and a skating rink.

origin: From Greek "metamorphosis", from "meta", change, and "morphe", form: a change of form.

senses.def: complete change in form, character, or appearance
senses.ex: The shy freshman's metamorphosis into a confident debate captain surprised everyone who knew her.

senses.def: process by which an insect or amphibian changes from an immature form into an adult
senses.ex: In metamorphosis, a tadpole loses its tail and grows legs to become a frog.

origin: From Greek "metanoia", repentance, literally an afterthought, from "meta", after or beyond, and "noein", to think. It is a change of mind at the deepest level.

senses.def: profound change in one's thinking, outlook or way of life, often spiritual
senses.ex: His year volunteering in the refugee camp brought about a metanoia that redirected his whole career toward public health.

syn: transformation, conversion, change of heart, awakening, repentance

origin: From "metaphor", from Greek "metaphora", a transfer, from "metapherein", to carry over: a meaning carried from one thing to another.

senses.def: expressed through a figure of speech rather than literally
senses.ex: When Dad said the office was a zoo, he meant it in the metaphorical sense, not that there were actual lions.

origin: From Medieval Latin "metaphysicalis", from Greek "ta meta ta physika", the works after the "Physics", Aristotle's books on first principles.

senses.def: relating to abstract questions about the nature of reality, being, and knowledge
senses.ex: Late at night, the roommates drifted into metaphysical debates about whether free will really exists.

senses.def: highly abstract or theoretical, sometimes too much so to be useful
senses.ex: The committee's metaphysical discussion of fairness never produced an actual grading policy.

origin: From Old English "metan", to measure. The same old root gives German "messen", to measure, so to mete out is to measure out a share.

senses.def: give out or allot something, especially punishment or justice, usually with "out"
senses.ex: The coach meted out extra laps to anyone who showed up late to practice.

syn: dispense, allot, deal out, administer, apportion

origin: From "meteor", from Greek "meteoros", raised high in the air: like a meteor, fast, brilliant, and often brief.

senses.def: very rapid and dazzling, especially of a rise to success
senses.ex: The singer's meteoric rise took her from coffee-shop gigs to sold-out arenas in under two years.

senses.def: relating to meteors
senses.ex: Scientists analyzed the meteoric dust collected from the Antarctic ice.

origin: From Greek "meteorologia", study of things high in the air, from "meteoros", lofty, plus "logos", study.

senses.def: relating to the weather and the scientific study of the atmosphere
senses.ex: The meteorological office issued a warning that winds could reach seventy miles an hour by evening.

origin: From Greek "methodikos", systematic, from "methodos", method, a way of pursuing something, from "meta", after, and "hodos", way or road.

senses.def: done in an orderly, step-by-step and systematic way
senses.ex: The detective made a methodical search of the apartment, checking every drawer and shelf in turn.

senses.def: (of a person) careful, orderly and patient in habits and work
senses.ex: A methodical student, she reviewed her notes every evening instead of cramming before tests.

origin: From Latin "meticulosus", fearful or timid, from "metus", fear: so afraid of mistakes that one checks every detail.

senses.def: showing extreme care and precise attention to detail
senses.ex: The meticulous restorer spent months cleaning the painting one square inch at a time.

origin: From Greek "metonymia", change of name, from "meta", change, and "onoma", name. In metonymy one name stands in for another.

senses.def: figure of speech that names something by a thing closely associated with it, as "the crown" for a monarch
senses.ex: Calling the film industry "Hollywood" is an example of metonymy, since a place stands for a whole business.

origin: From Greek "metropolis", mother city, from "meter", mother, and "polis", city. It first meant the parent city of a colony.

senses.def: very large and busy city, often the chief city of a country or region
senses.ex: After growing up on a quiet farm, she found the noise and crowds of the metropolis thrilling at first.

syn: city, megalopolis, conurbation, urban center, capital

origin: Originally a spelling of "metal", used figuratively for what a person is made of. The two spellings split by meaning in the 1700s.

senses.def: courage and strength of spirit in facing difficulty
senses.ex: The rookie firefighter proved her mettle on her first night, carrying a child out of the burning stairwell.

origin: From "mettle", courage, originally a spelling of "metal", plus "-some", full of.

senses.def: full of courage, energy, and spirit
senses.ex: The mettlesome pony refused to turn back at the river and splashed straight across the current.

origin: Perhaps from Middle English "mewen", to whimper, plus "-le", an ending for repeated action. Shakespeare's "mewling" infant in "As You Like It" made it famous.

senses.def: cry weakly and plaintively, as a baby or kitten does
senses.ex: The abandoned kitten mewled under the porch until the neighbors coaxed it out with a saucer of milk.

origin: From Greek "miasma", stain or pollution. People once believed disease spread through foul air.

senses.def: unpleasant or unhealthy smell or vapor
senses.ex: A miasma of rotting fish hung over the docks after the refrigeration failed.

senses.def: oppressive, harmful atmosphere or influence
senses.ex: A miasma of suspicion settled over the office after the leaked emails appeared online.

origin: From Greek "mikros", small, and "kosmos", world or order: a little world that mirrors a larger one.

senses.def: small place, group, or system that has the features of something much larger
senses.ex: With its rivalries, alliances, and gossip, the school cafeteria is a microcosm of national politics.

syn: miniature, epitome, model, reflection, small-scale version

origin: From French "mine", appearance or facial expression, perhaps from Breton "min", the face or muzzle of an animal. Its deeper origin is uncertain.

senses.def: person's look, manner or bearing, especially as a sign of character or mood
senses.ex: Despite the bad news, the ambassador kept a calm and dignified mien throughout the press conference.

origin: From Latin "migratorius", from "migrare", to move from one place to another. It belongs with "migrate", "emigrant" and "immigration".

senses.def: (of animals) moving regularly from one region to another with the seasons
senses.ex: The wetland is a vital resting place for migratory geese flying south each autumn.

senses.def: moving from place to place, not settled in one home
senses.ex: Migratory farm workers follow the harvest from Texas to Michigan over the course of a year.

origin: From French "milieu", middle, from "mi", half or mid, and "lieu", place: the place you live in the middle of.

senses.def: social or cultural environment in which someone lives or works
senses.ex: Raised in the artistic milieu of 1920s Paris, she knew famous painters before she could read.

origin: From Latin "militans", serving as a soldier, from "militare", to serve in the army, from "miles", soldier. A militant fights for a cause.

senses.def: aggressively active and combative in support of a cause
senses.ex: The union's militant leaders called for a strike before negotiations had even begun.

senses.def: person who is aggressively active for a cause, sometimes using force
senses.ex: Government troops clashed with armed militants who had seized the border town.

origin: From Latin "militare", to serve as a soldier, from "miles", soldier: facts that fight for or against an outcome. Do not confuse it with "mitigate".

senses.def: be a powerful factor working against or, less often, in favor of something
senses.ex: The town's remote location and harsh winters militate against attracting new businesses.

syn: weigh against, work against, count against, hinder, impede

origin: From Old English "meolc", milk. The sense of draining every benefit comes from drawing milk from an animal.

senses.def: exploit or take the greatest possible advantage or money from someone or something
senses.ex: The comedian milked the awkward pause for every laugh before finally delivering the punch line.

senses.def: white liquid produced by female mammals to feed their young
senses.ex: She poured warm milk into the kitten's bowl.

senses.def: draw milk from a cow, goat, or other animal
senses.ex: On the farm, the children learned to milk the goats before breakfast.

syn: exploit, squeeze, bleed, drain, capitalize on

origin: From Late Latin "millenarius", containing a thousand, from Latin "mille", thousand, after the belief in a thousand-year reign of peace.

senses.def: relating to the belief that a golden age or total transformation of society is coming soon, often after catastrophe
senses.ex: The millenarian sect sold its property and waited on a hilltop for the world to end.

senses.def: person who believes a coming golden age or end of the world is near
senses.ex: Like many millenarians before him, the preacher kept revising the date of the final judgment.

origin: Named after Caspar Milquetoast, the timid hero of H. T. Webster's 1920s comic strip "The Timid Soul", whose name puns on bland milk toast.

senses.def: timid, meek person who is easily dominated
senses.ex: Critics called the new mayor a milquetoast who would never stand up to the powerful developers.

origin: From Greek "mimesis", imitation, from "mimeisthai", to imitate, from "mimos", mime or imitator. It is a relative of "mimic" and "mime".

senses.def: imitation or representation of the real world in art and literature
senses.ex: Aristotle argued that tragedy is a form of mimesis, imitating human actions to stir pity and fear.

origin: From Greek "mimetikos", imitative, from "mimeisthai", to imitate, from "mimos", mime or imitator.

senses.def: imitating or closely representing the real world, especially in art or literature
senses.ex: The painter rejected mimetic realism and covered her canvases with bold, abstract shapes.

senses.def: relating to mimicry, as when one animal resembles another for protection
senses.ex: The harmless hoverfly's mimetic stripes make birds mistake it for a wasp.

origin: From Latin "mimicus", from Greek "mimikos", of mimes, from "mimos", mime or imitator.

senses.def: imitate someone's voice, gestures, or behavior, often to amuse or mock
senses.ex: My little brother mimics our teacher's accent so well that the whole class laughs.

senses.def: person or animal skilled at imitating others
senses.ex: The mockingbird is a gifted mimic that can copy car alarms as well as other birds.

senses.def: closely resemble or copy the function of something
senses.ex: The new drug mimics a natural hormone that helps the body regulate sleep.

origin: From "mimic", from Greek "mimikos", from "mimos", imitator or mime, plus "-ry", an ending for an activity or skill.

senses.def: action or skill of imitating someone's voice, manner or behavior
senses.ex: Her mimicry of the principal's slow, booming voice had the whole lunch table in tears of laughter.

senses.def: close resemblance of one animal or plant to another, which protects it from predators
senses.ex: The harmless hoverfly survives through mimicry, wearing the yellow and black stripes of a stinging wasp.

origin: From Late Latin "minatorius", from Latin "minari", to threaten, related to "menace".

senses.def: expressing or suggesting a threat
senses.ex: The landlord's minatory letter warned that any tenant who complained to the city would face eviction.

origin: From Middle English "mincen", partly from Old English "minsian", to make smaller, and partly from Old French "mincier", to cut into small pieces, from "mince", slender, from a Frankish word meaning small.

senses.def: soften or moderate words to be polite, usually in the phrase not mince words
senses.ex: The doctor did not mince words, telling him bluntly that he had to stop smoking at once.

senses.def: cut or chop food, especially meat, into very small pieces
senses.ex: Mince the garlic and ginger finely before adding them to the hot oil.

senses.def: walk with short, quick, dainty steps in an affected way
senses.ex: The actor minced across the stage in high heels, drawing roars of laughter.

syn: soften, moderate, temper, euphemize, tone down

origin: From French "mignon", darling or favorite: first a ruler's pampered favorite, then any servile follower.

senses.def: servile follower or subordinate of a powerful person
senses.ex: The tycoon never answered questions himself and sent his minions to deal with reporters.

origin: From French, from Latin "minusculus", rather small, from "minus", less. It first described small lowercase letters, which is why it is spelled with "minus".

senses.def: extremely small
senses.ex: The chef placed a minuscule dot of sauce beside each slice, barely enough to taste.

origin: From Latin "minutus", made small, past participle of "minuere", to lessen. The time word "minute" is a small division of an hour.

senses.def: extremely small
senses.ex: The scientists found minute traces of plastic in every sample of seawater they collected.

senses.def: precise and careful, attending to the smallest details
senses.ex: The detective made a minute examination of the room, checking even the dust on the windowsill.

origin: From Latin "minutiae", trifles, the plural of "minutia", smallness, from "minutus", small. It is a cousin of "minute" in the sense of tiny.

senses.def: small, precise or trivial details of something
senses.ex: The lawyers argued for hours over the minutiae of the contract, down to the placement of a single comma.

syn: details, particulars, fine points, niceties, trivia

origin: From French "mirage", from "se mirer", to be reflected, from Latin "mirari", to wonder at. A mirage is a reflection that makes you wonder.

senses.def: optical illusion caused by hot air, such as seeming water on a desert or road
senses.ex: Across the scorching highway, a shimmering mirage looked exactly like a lake that vanished as we drove closer.

senses.def: hope or goal that seems real or attainable but is not
senses.ex: For the struggling team, a championship turned out to be a mirage that faded by midseason.

origin: From Old Norse "mýrr", bog or swamp. It is related to English "moss", which also grows in wet ground.

senses.def: area of swampy ground or deep, sticky mud
senses.ex: The cart's wheels sank into the mire, and it took four horses to drag it free.

senses.def: difficult or unpleasant situation that is hard to escape
senses.ex: The company spent years trying to climb out of a mire of debt and lawsuits.

senses.def: cause someone or something to be stuck in mud or in difficulties, often as "mired in"
senses.ex: The peace talks were mired in disputes over a few miles of border.

origin: From "mire", deep mud or bog, from Old Norse "myrr", swamp: stuck as if in a bog.

senses.def: stuck in a difficult situation that is hard to escape
senses.ex: The project is mired in legal disputes and will not break ground for at least another year.

senses.def: stuck fast in mud or swampy ground
senses.ex: The farmer used his tractor to pull the mired truck out of the flooded field.

syn: bogged down, entangled, embroiled, stuck, ensnared

origin: From Old English "myrgth", joy, from the same root as "merry".

senses.def: amusement and cheerfulness, especially expressed in laughter
senses.ex: The puppy's clumsy attempt to catch its own tail filled the room with mirth.

origin: From Old French "mesaventure", from "mes-", badly, and "aventure", chance or happening. A misadventure is a happening that goes badly.

senses.def: unlucky accident or mishap
senses.ex: After a series of misadventures, including a flat tire and a lost passport, they finally reached the coast.

origin: From Greek "misanthropos", from "misein", to hate, and "anthropos", human being.

senses.def: person who dislikes and distrusts people in general
senses.ex: The old misanthrope lived alone on the island and fired warning shots at any boat that came too close.

origin: From Greek "misanthropos", from "misein", to hate, and "anthropos", human being. "Misanthropist" simply adds "-ist".

senses.def: person who dislikes, distrusts, and avoids people in general
senses.ex: Years of betrayal in politics turned the once-cheerful senator into a bitter misanthrope who trusted no one.

origin: From "misanthrope", from Greek "misein", to hate, and "anthropos", human being.

senses.def: disliking and distrusting people in general
senses.ex: His misanthropic jokes about the stupidity of the human race wore thin long before dinner ended.

origin: From "mis-", wrongly, and "apprehend", to grasp with the mind, from Latin "apprehendere", to seize. To misapprehend is to grasp an idea wrongly.

senses.def: understand something wrongly; misinterpret
senses.ex: The reporter misapprehended the senator's remark and published it as a promise she never made.

origin: From "mis-", wrongly, and "apprehension", grasping with the mind, from Latin "apprehendere", to seize. It is an idea seized the wrong way.

senses.def: mistaken belief or wrong understanding of something
senses.ex: Many voters were under the misapprehension that the new tax would apply to every household.

origin: From "mis-", wrongly, and "appropriate", to take for oneself, from Latin "appropriare", to make one's own, from "proprius", one's own.

senses.def: dishonestly take something, especially money entrusted to one, for one's own use
senses.ex: The club treasurer misappropriated the dues to pay off her credit cards.

senses.def: use something wrongly or for the wrong purpose
senses.ex: Historians accused the film of misappropriating a civil rights speech to sell sneakers.

origin: From "mis-", wrongly, and "attribute", from Latin "attribuere", to assign, from "tribuere", to give or allot.

senses.def: wrongly credit something, such as a quote, work, or cause, to a particular source
senses.ex: Countless websites misattribute that quote to Einstein, though no record shows he ever said it.

origin: From Latin "miscellanea", a mixture, from "miscellus", mixed, from "miscere", to mix. It shares its root with "miscellaneous" and "mix".

senses.def: mixed collection of different kinds of things
senses.ex: The attic held a miscellany of old trophies, broken lamps, love letters and tax records.

senses.def: book or collection of writings on various subjects or by various authors
senses.ex: The literary magazine's winter issue was a miscellany of poems, recipes and short memoirs.

origin: From Old French "meschance", from "mes-", badly, and "chance", luck or the way things fall out. Mischance is chance going wrong.

senses.def: bad luck, or an unlucky event
senses.ex: By some mischance, the invitation was delivered to the wrong address and she missed the wedding.

syn: misfortune, bad luck, mishap, misadventure, accident

origin: From "mis-", wrongly, and "conception", forming an idea, from Latin "concipere", to take in or conceive. A misconception is an idea conceived wrongly.

senses.def: mistaken belief or idea, often one widely held
senses.ex: A common misconception is that bats are blind, when most species can see quite well.

origin: From "mis-", wrongly, and "construe", to interpret, from Latin "construere", to build or put together: to put a meaning together wrongly.

senses.def: interpret someone's words or actions wrongly
senses.ex: She misconstrued his silence as anger, when in fact he was simply exhausted after the night shift.

origin: From Old French "mescreant", unbeliever, from "mescreire", to disbelieve: first a heretic, later any wrongdoer.

senses.def: person who behaves badly or breaks the law
senses.ex: Security cameras helped police identify the miscreants who spray-painted the war memorial.

origin: From Old English "misdǣd", from "mis-", wrongly, and "dǣd", deed. German "Missetat" is a close cousin built the same way.

senses.def: wrong, wicked or illegal act
senses.ex: The investigation uncovered years of misdeeds by the treasurer, from forged receipts to secret loans.

origin: From "mis-", badly, and "demeanor", conduct or behavior. Literally it is bad behavior, now used for a minor crime.

senses.def: minor crime, less serious than a felony
senses.ex: Shoplifting a candy bar is usually treated as a misdemeanor, punished with a fine rather than prison.

senses.def: minor wrongdoing or bit of misbehavior
senses.ex: Her only misdemeanor at the dinner party was arriving twenty minutes late.

origin: From Latin "miser", wretched or unhappy, the root of "misery": a hoarder was pictured as living a wretched life.

senses.def: person who hoards money and spends as little as possible, even on necessities
senses.ex: The old miser kept his heating off all winter, though he had a fortune stuffed in shoeboxes.

origin: From "miser", a hoarder of money, from Latin "miser", wretched, plus "-ly".

senses.def: extremely unwilling to spend money
senses.ex: Her miserly boss refused to buy new chairs, even after one collapsed during a meeting.

senses.def: of an amount, very small and inadequate
senses.ex: The workers were insulted by the miserly raise of ten cents an hour.

origin: From the older verb "misgive", to make someone feel doubtful, from "mis-", wrongly, and "give". A misgiving is the doubt your mind gives you.

senses.def: feeling of doubt or worry, especially about what will happen
senses.ex: Despite her misgivings about the rickety bridge, she followed the guide across the gorge.

origin: From "mis-", badly, and the old word "hap", luck or chance, which also appears in "happen" and "haphazard".

senses.def: unlucky accident, usually a minor one
senses.ex: Apart from one mishap with a spilled can of paint, the volunteers finished the mural without trouble.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "mesnomer", to misname, from "mes-", wrongly, and "nomer", to name, from Latin "nominare".

senses.def: name or term that is inaccurate or misleading
senses.ex: Calling the koala a bear is a misnomer, since it is actually a marsupial related to the wombat.

origin: From Greek "misogynes", woman-hater, from "misein", to hate, and "gyne", woman.

senses.def: person who hates, distrusts, or is prejudiced against women
senses.ex: The historian showed that the philosopher was a misogynist who argued women were unfit to vote or own property.

senses.def: showing hatred of or prejudice against women
senses.ex: Fans protested the comedian's misogynist jokes and demanded that the network cancel his special.

origin: From Greek "misologia", from "misein", to hate, and "logos", reason or argument. Plato uses the idea in the "Phaedo".

senses.def: hatred or distrust of reasoning and argument
senses.ex: After losing every debate, he slid into a kind of misology, declaring that clever arguments only hide the truth.

origin: From Italian "misoneismo", built from Greek "misein", to hate, and "neos", new. It names a hatred of the new.

senses.def: hatred, fear or distrust of new things, ideas or change
senses.ex: The village's misoneism showed when residents voted down the new library simply because it looked modern.

origin: From Middle French "mespriser", from "mes-", badly, and "priser", to value or prize. To misprize is to value something wrongly.

senses.def: fail to value properly; undervalue or look down on
senses.ex: Critics misprized her early novels, and only after her death were they recognized as masterpieces.

origin: From "mis-", wrongly, and "represent", from Latin "repraesentare", to make present again. To misrepresent is to present something in a false way.

senses.def: give a false or misleading account of someone or something
senses.ex: The advertisement misrepresented the apartment, showing a lake view that was actually from the building next door.

origin: From Medieval Latin "missivus", sent, from Latin "mittere", to send, as in "mission" and "missile".

senses.def: written message, especially a long, formal, or official one
senses.ex: Every December, Aunt Clara sends a ten-page missive describing her year in exhausting detail.

origin: From Old English "mite", a tiny insect. A related Dutch word named a very small coin, which gave English the sense of a tiny amount.

senses.def: tiny animal related to spiders, often living on plants, animals or in dust
senses.ex: Dust mites are too small to see, yet they can trigger allergies in people who sleep on old pillows.

senses.def: very small amount, or a small child
senses.ex: The poor mite had walked all morning and could barely keep his eyes open.

senses.def: slightly or somewhat, used in the phrase "a mite"
senses.ex: I was a mite nervous when the pilot announced we would be landing in heavy fog.

origin: From Latin "mitigare", to soften or tame, from "mitis", gentle or mild: to make something gentler.

senses.def: make something bad less severe, harmful, or painful
senses.ex: The city planted thousands of trees to mitigate the summer heat in its concrete neighborhoods.

origin: From Greek "mnemonikos", relating to memory, from "mnemon", mindful, from "mnasthai", to remember. The silent "m" is a trace of the Greek.

senses.def: device such as a rhyme, phrase or acronym that helps you remember something
senses.ex: Music students learn the mnemonic "Every Good Boy Does Fine" for the lines of the treble staff.

senses.def: intended to help the memory
senses.ex: The teacher used colorful mnemonic charts to help us memorize the order of the planets.

syn: memory aid, memory device, reminder, aide-mémoire

origin: From Old French "mocquer", to deride or jeer, probably from a Dutch or German word meaning to mumble, as if muttering scornfully.

senses.def: make fun of someone or something, often by copying them unkindly
senses.ex: The older boys mocked his accent until the teacher sent them to the principal's office.

senses.def: not real, but made to look like or practice for the real thing
senses.ex: The law students held a mock trial, complete with a jury of volunteers from the community.

syn: ridicule, deride, taunt, tease, jeer at

origin: From Latin "modestus", keeping due measure, from "modus", measure: staying within proper limits.

senses.def: humble and unassuming about one's own abilities or achievements
senses.ex: Though she had won three national awards, the modest scientist credited her students for every discovery.

senses.def: moderate or limited in size, amount, or degree
senses.ex: The bakery made a modest profit in its first year, enough to pay the rent and little else.

senses.def: simple and not showy or expensive
senses.ex: They raised four children in a modest two-bedroom house on the edge of town.

senses.def: avoiding dress or behavior that might be considered improper or revealing
senses.ex: Visitors to the temple are asked to wear modest clothing that covers their shoulders and knees.

origin: From Latin "modicum", a little, from "modicus", moderate, from "modus", measure.

senses.def: small or limited amount of something, usually something desirable
senses.ex: If he had shown even a modicum of remorse, the judge might have reduced his sentence.

syn: small amount, bit, iota, shred, scintilla

origin: From "mode", fashion, from French "mode", from Latin "modus", manner, plus "-ish".

senses.def: fashionable and up to date, sometimes in a superficial way
senses.ex: The café's modish decor of exposed bulbs and reclaimed wood looked exactly like every other café on the street.

origin: From Latin "modulari", to measure or regulate, from "modulus", a small measure. To modulate is to keep something within measure.

senses.def: vary or adjust the pitch, tone or volume of the voice or a sound
senses.ex: The actor modulated his voice from a whisper to a roar as the scene built to its climax.

senses.def: regulate or adjust the strength or degree of something
senses.ex: Certain medications help modulate the body's response to stress.

origin: From Old French "meitié", half, from Late Latin "medietas", middle or half, from Latin "medius", middle.

senses.def: half of something
senses.ex: Under the will, each of the two sisters received a moiety of the family farm.

senses.def: part, portion or share of something, often a small one
senses.ex: Only a moiety of the donated funds ever reached the villages it was meant to help.

origin: From Late Latin "mollificare", to soften, from Latin "mollis", soft: to soften someone's anger.

senses.def: calm the anger or anxiety of someone
senses.ex: The airline tried to mollify the stranded passengers with free meals and hotel vouchers.

senses.def: make demands or harsh feelings less severe
senses.ex: Nothing the company offered could mollify the union's demands for safer working conditions.

origin: From "molly", an old word for a pampered, overly soft man, and "coddle", to treat tenderly. To mollycoddle is to coddle someone far too much.

senses.def: treat someone too indulgently and protectively
senses.ex: His parents mollycoddled him so much that at twenty he still could not cook an egg or do his own laundry.

origin: From Middle English "mouten", from Old English "mutian", to change, from Latin "mutare", to change.

senses.def: shed old feathers, hair, skin, or shell so that new growth can replace them
senses.ex: Every spring, our husky molts so heavily that we sweep up bags of fur.

senses.def: process or period of shedding old feathers, skin, or shell
senses.ex: During its molt, the crab hides under rocks until its new shell hardens.

origin: From Latin "momentum", movement or weight, from "movere", to move: a slight movement that could tip the scales, hence both "an instant" and "importance".

senses.def: importance or significance, as in of great moment
senses.ex: The treaty was a decision of great moment that would shape the region for a century.

senses.def: very brief period of time
senses.ex: Wait a moment while I find my keys.

senses.def: particular point in time, especially one when something important happens
senses.ex: At the moment the lights went out, the crowd fell silent.

origin: From Late Latin "momentarius", of brief duration, from "momentum", an instant.

senses.def: lasting for a very short time
senses.ex: After a momentary hesitation at the edge of the board, the diver launched herself into a perfect double twist.

origin: From "moment" in its older sense of weight or importance, plus "-ous", full of. A momentous event is full of weight.

senses.def: of great importance, especially for what happens in the future
senses.ex: The signing of the treaty was a momentous day that ended forty years of war between the two nations.

origin: From Latin "momentum", movement or moving force, from "movere", to move. It is a doublet of "moment" and "movement".

senses.def: force or speed gained by something in motion or in progress, which makes it hard to stop
senses.ex: After winning three straight primaries, the candidate's campaign gained momentum and donations poured in.

senses.def: in physics, the quantity of motion of a moving body, equal to its mass times its velocity
senses.ex: A loaded freight train has enormous momentum, so it needs more than a mile to stop.

origin: From Late Latin "monasticus", from Greek "monastikos", from "monazein", to live alone, from "monos", alone.

senses.def: relating to monks, nuns, or the life of a monastery
senses.ex: The monastic community rose before dawn each day to pray, farm, and copy manuscripts.

senses.def: resembling a monk's life, austere, simple, and secluded
senses.ex: During exam season, Priya lived a monastic existence of textbooks, rice, and early bedtimes.

origin: Coined in 1954 by writer Sylvia Wright, who as a child misheard the ballad line "laid him on the green" as "Lady Mondegreen".

senses.def: misheard word or phrase, especially from a song lyric, that gives it a new meaning
senses.ex: For years my brother sang "hold me closer, Tony Danza," a classic mondegreen of the real Elton John lyric.

origin: From Latin "monetarius", of a mint, from "moneta", mint or coinage, named after the temple of Juno Moneta in Rome, where coins were made.

senses.def: relating to money or currency, especially a country's supply of money
senses.ex: The central bank adjusted its monetary policy, raising interest rates to slow rising prices.

origin: From Middle English, from "mong", mixture, plus "-rel", a belittling ending. "Mong" goes back to Old English "gemang", mingling, the root of "among".

senses.def: dog of mixed or unknown breed
senses.ex: The shelter's friendliest dog was a scruffy mongrel with one floppy ear and a beagle's howl.

senses.def: of mixed origin, kind or character, sometimes used disparagingly
senses.ex: English is a mongrel language, borrowing freely from Latin, French, Norse and dozens of others.

syn: mutt, crossbreed, mixed breed, hybrid, cur

origin: From Greek "monos", single, and "chroma", color. A monochromatic image uses a single color.

senses.def: having or using only one color, or shades of one color
senses.ex: The designer chose a monochromatic living room in shades of gray, from charcoal sofas to silver curtains.

senses.def: dull and lacking variety
senses.ex: Critics found the novel's monochromatic characters hard to tell apart.

origin: From Greek "monoidia", a solo song, from "monos", alone, and "oide", song. In Greek drama it was a lament sung by a single actor.

senses.def: poem or song of mourning, spoken or sung by one person
senses.ex: The poet wrote a monody for her drowned brother, a single long voice of grief addressed to the sea.

origin: From "monolith", from Greek "monos", single, and "lithos", stone. Something monolithic is like one huge, unbroken block of stone.

senses.def: (of an organization or system) huge, uniform and rigid, hard to change or break apart
senses.ex: Reformers struggled against the monolithic bureaucracy, where every decision passed through the same distant office.

senses.def: formed from a single large block of stone
senses.ex: The temple's monolithic columns were each carved from one piece of granite.

origin: From French "monologue", from Greek "monologos", speaking alone, from "monos", alone, and "logos", speech, on the model of "dialogue".

senses.def: long speech by one actor in a play or film
senses.ex: The play's most famous moment is a five-minute monologue in which the heroine confronts her father.

senses.def: long, uninterrupted talk by one person that keeps others from speaking
senses.ex: Dinner turned into a monologue as my uncle described his fishing trip in exhausting detail.

origin: From Modern Latin "monomania", from Greek "monos", single, and "mania", madness. It is madness about one single thing.

senses.def: obsessive focus on a single subject, idea or goal
senses.ex: Captain Ahab's monomania drives him to chase the white whale at the cost of his ship and crew.

syn: obsession, fixation, fanaticism, compulsion, idée fixe

origin: From Greek "monotonos", from "monos", single, and "tonos", tone: stuck on one unchanging note.

senses.def: dull and tedious because it never varies
senses.ex: The monotonous drive across the flat plains made it hard for him to stay awake.

senses.def: of a sound or voice, staying on one unchanging pitch
senses.ex: The lecturer's monotonous voice put half the hall to sleep within twenty minutes.

origin: From Greek "monotonia", sameness of tone, from "monos", single, and "tonos", tone.

senses.def: tedious lack of variety or change
senses.ex: To break the monotony of the long voyage, the sailors organized chess tournaments and talent shows.

origin: From Late Latin "monumentalis", from Latin "monumentum", a memorial or reminder, from "monere", to remind. Something monumental is worthy of a monument.

senses.def: great in importance, size or extent
senses.ex: Mapping the human genome was a monumental achievement that took thousands of scientists more than a decade.

senses.def: (of something bad) very great; colossal
senses.ex: Selling the company's stock the day before it tripled in value was a monumental blunder.

senses.def: relating to or serving as a monument
senses.ex: The square is lined with monumental statues of the city's founders.

origin: From "moon" and "calf", from an old belief that the moon caused deformed births. It came to mean a foolish, moony person.

senses.def: foolish, absent-minded or dreamy person
senses.ex: He wandered the halls like a mooncalf, staring out windows and forgetting where his classes were.

origin: From "moon" and "struck", from the old belief that the moon could drive people mad. The poet John Milton may have coined it.

senses.def: dreamy, dazed or foolishly romantic, especially from being in love
senses.ex: The moonstruck teenager spent the whole bus ride writing his girlfriend's name in the fogged-up window.

origin: From Old English "mot", a meeting or assembly where disputes were argued: a "moot point" was one fit for debate there.

senses.def: open to argument or debate, not yet settled
senses.ex: Whether the painting is a genuine Rembrandt remains a moot question among experts.

senses.def: having no practical significance because the matter is already decided or no longer relevant
senses.ex: Once the concert was canceled, the argument over who would drive became moot.

senses.def: raise a question or idea for discussion
senses.ex: The idea of a four-day school week was first mooted at a board meeting last spring.

syn: debatable, arguable, disputable, unsettled, open to question

origin: From French "morale", morality or moral spirit, from Latin "moralis", concerning customs and conduct. Do not confuse it with "moral", a lesson.

senses.def: confidence, enthusiasm and spirit of a person or group, especially at a hard time
senses.ex: Morale among the workers sank after the third round of layoffs was announced.

syn: spirit, confidence, esprit de corps, enthusiasm, resolve

origin: From "moral", from Latin "moralis", concerning customs or conduct, plus "-istic". It describes someone who makes a habit of moralizing.

senses.def: narrowly and self-righteously concerned with judging the morals of others
senses.ex: The film's moralistic tone, with every sinner punished in the last scene, felt like a lecture.

origin: From Dutch "moeras", marsh, from Old French "maresc", marsh: a situation as hard to escape as a swamp.

senses.def: complicated or confused situation that is hard to get out of
senses.ex: The new company soon sank into a morass of lawsuits, unpaid bills, and missed deadlines.

senses.def: area of soft, wet, swampy ground
senses.ex: Heavy rain turned the festival field into a morass of mud that swallowed boots.

origin: From Late Latin "moratorius", delaying, from Latin "morari", to delay, from "mora", delay.

senses.def: temporary ban or official suspension of an activity
senses.ex: The state declared a moratorium on new drilling permits until scientists finished studying the earthquakes.

origin: From Latin "morbidus", diseased, from "morbus", sickness.

senses.def: having or showing an unhealthy interest in death or disturbing subjects
senses.ex: His morbid fascination with plane crashes made his friends nervous about flying with him.

senses.def: relating to or caused by disease
senses.ex: The doctor explained that morbid obesity greatly increases the risk of heart disease.

origin: From French "mordant", biting, from Latin "mordere", to bite. A mordant remark bites.

senses.def: sharply sarcastic or bitingly witty in a way that wounds
senses.ex: The critic's mordant review compared the three-hour musical to a long afternoon in a dentist's waiting room.

origin: From Middle English, simply "more" plus "over", meaning beyond what has already been said.

senses.def: in addition to what has already been said, often adding a stronger point
senses.ex: The proposal is too expensive, and moreover, it would take at least five years to finish construction.

syn: furthermore, besides, additionally, what is more

origin: From Latin "mores", customs or character, the plural of "mos", custom, which also gave English "moral".

senses.def: the customs and unwritten moral norms that a community expects its members to follow
senses.ex: The novel satirizes the social mores of Victorian England, where a single unchaperoned dance could ruin a reputation.

origin: From Latin "moribundus", dying, from "mori", to die, the same root as "mortal".

senses.def: in terminal decline and losing vitality, about to come to an end
senses.ex: The once-busy mill town had become moribund, its factories shuttered and its young people long gone to the cities.

senses.def: close to death, about to die
senses.ex: The veterinarian found the moribund seal on the beach and knew it would not survive the night.

origin: From Latin "morosus", peevish or self-willed, from "mos", custom or will. It first meant stubbornly moody, then gloomy.

senses.def: sullen, gloomy, and unwilling to talk or be cheered
senses.ex: After losing the championship, the team sat morose and silent through the long bus ride home.

origin: A shortening of "metamorphose" and "metamorphosis", ultimately from Greek "morphe", form or shape.

senses.def: change gradually and smoothly from one form or character into another
senses.ex: Over three decades, the tiny corner bakery morphed into a national chain with hundreds of locations.

origin: From Old French "morsel", a little bite, from Latin "morsus", a bite, from "mordere", to bite. A morsel is about one bite.

senses.def: small piece or mouthful of food
senses.ex: The hikers shared every last morsel of bread before starting the long walk down the mountain.

senses.def: small amount of something
senses.ex: The detective refused to give reporters even a morsel of information about the suspect.

origin: From Late Latin "mortificare", to put to death, from Latin "mors", death, and "facere", to make. A mortified person feels ready to die of shame.

senses.def: make someone feel deeply embarrassed or humiliated
senses.ex: She was mortified when her phone rang loudly during the silent moment at the funeral.

senses.def: control bodily desires through self-denial or discipline, especially for religious reasons
senses.ex: Some medieval monks mortified the flesh by fasting for days and sleeping on stone floors.

origin: From French "mosaïque", from Italian and Medieval Latin "musaicum", probably meaning work of the Muses.

senses.def: picture or pattern made of small pieces of colored stone, glass, or tile
senses.ex: The bathhouse floor featured a Roman mosaic of dolphins leaping through waves of blue tile.

senses.def: combination of many different elements forming a whole
senses.ex: The city's neighborhoods form a mosaic of cultures, each with its own markets and festivals.

origin: From Old English "mot", meaning "grain of sand" or "speck", through Middle English.

senses.def: tiny speck or particle, especially of dust
senses.ex: A mote of dust drifted through the projector beam while the audience waited for the film.

origin: Borrowed from French "motif", meaning "theme" or "main idea", and related to English "motive".

senses.def: image, idea, or element that recurs throughout an artistic work
senses.ex: A recurring river motif linked the novel's three stories about memory and loss.

senses.def: decorative shape or design repeated within a pattern
senses.ex: The wallpaper carried a leaf motif that matched the embroidered curtains.

senses.def: short musical phrase repeated within a composition
senses.ex: The violin introduced a playful motif that returned whenever the hero appeared onstage.

origin: From Latin "motus", moved, from "movere", to move, plus the suffix "-ile", able to.

senses.def: able to move by itself, used of cells and simple organisms
senses.ex: Under the microscope, the motile bacteria darted across the slide, driven by their whiplike tails.

origin: From Middle English "motlei", multicolored cloth, probably from Old English "mot", speck. Jesters wore motley patchwork costumes.

senses.def: made up of very different and mismatched people or things
senses.ex: A motley crew of retirees, college students, and truck drivers formed the town's surprisingly successful trivia team.

origin: From "mottle", meaning to mark with irregular patches, plus the adjective ending "-ed".

senses.def: marked with irregular patches or spots of different colors
senses.ex: The rescue dog had a mottled coat that blended into the gravel beside the trail.

origin: Borrowed from French "moue", a pout, traced through Old French "moe", a grimace.

senses.def: small pout expressing playful displeasure or flirtation
senses.ex: She answered the teasing with a moue, then laughed and passed the microphone to her brother.

origin: From Italian "montambanco", a quack who climbed onto a bench to sell remedies. Its parts meant "mount" and "bench".

senses.def: person who deceives others with flashy claims, especially while selling supposed cures
senses.ex: The traveling mountebank promised his tonic could restore hair, sharpen memory, and cure every cough.

origin: From New Latin "mucilaginosus", meaning full of mucilage, ultimately related to Latin "mucus".

senses.def: thick, sticky, and slippery, like mucus or plant gum
senses.ex: The soaked seeds released a mucilaginous coating that made the drink unusually thick.

origin: From Middle Dutch "moddelen", meaning to make muddy, through Middle English. Its root "modde" meant "mud".

senses.def: confuse or jumble ideas, facts, or objects
senses.ex: Too many last minute changes muddled the directions, and half the volunteers went to the wrong entrance.

senses.def: crush ingredients gently to release flavor in a drink
senses.ex: Muddle the mint with lime before adding ice, so its oils flavor the lemonade.

senses.def: confused or disordered situation
senses.ex: After three schedule changes, the tournament became a muddle of missed games and empty courts.

senses.def: manage a task despite confusion or limited resources
senses.ex: We muddled through the storm with a flashlight, spare batteries, and a hand drawn map.

origin: From "mud" plus "lark", the bird, as if the scavenger were a bird picking about on muddy riverbanks.

senses.def: person who searches river mud for discarded objects of value
senses.ex: Each weekend, the mudlark searches the exposed riverbank for old coins and pottery fragments.

senses.def: search river mud for objects, especially historical finds
senses.ex: After the tide receded, they mudlarked beneath the bridge and found a clay pipe stem.

origin: From Old French "enmoufler", meaning to wrap up, related to "moufle", a mitten.

senses.def: make a sound quieter or less distinct
senses.ex: Thick curtains muffled the traffic noise while the students rehearsed their lines inside.

senses.def: wrap or cover for warmth or protection
senses.ex: She muffled her face in a wool scarf before stepping into the icy wind.

senses.def: suppress or soften the expression of something
senses.ex: The new rules muffled dissent, but they did not resolve the workers' concerns.

origin: From dialectal English "mug", meaning fog or mist, with "-y", ultimately linked to Old Norse "mugga", drizzle.

senses.def: unpleasantly warm and humid
senses.ex: The muggy afternoon left the runners soaked before they reached the first mile marker.

origin: From Massachusett "mugquomp", meaning war leader, later applied to American politicians who refused party loyalty.

senses.def: person who stays independent of political parties or factions
senses.ex: A self-described mugwump, she backed candidates from both parties when their policies matched her priorities.

origin: From Latin "mulcta" or "multa", a fine or penalty, through French "mulcter", to fine.

senses.def: take money from someone by fraud or trickery
senses.ex: The fake charity mulcted elderly donors out of thousands of dollars with promises of tax refunds.

senses.def: punish someone with a fine or extract money through a penalty
senses.ex: The city mulcted drivers with steep parking penalties to cover its budget shortfall.

origin: From Latin "muliebritas", meaning womanhood, from "muliebris", womanly, which comes from "mulier", woman.

senses.def: womanhood or qualities traditionally associated with women
senses.ex: The essay questioned whether fashion should be treated as a measure of muliebrity.

origin: From "mule" plus "-ish", describing someone as stubborn as the animal.

senses.def: stubbornly unwilling to change one's mind or cooperate
senses.ex: His mulish refusal to check the map cost the group an hour of hiking.

origin: From "multi-", many, plus "facet", from French "facette", little face, like the cut faces of a gem.

senses.def: having many different sides, aspects, or talents
senses.ex: The multifaceted artist designs buildings, composes film scores, and writes award-winning children's books.

origin: From Latin "multifarius", manifold or in many places, built on "multus", many.

senses.def: numerous and of many different kinds
senses.ex: The museum's multifarious collection ranges from Egyptian coffins and Japanese armor to early computer prototypes.

origin: From Latin "multiplicitas", meaning a condition of having many parts or forms.

senses.def: large number or wide variety of things
senses.ex: The committee faced a multiplicity of proposals, each with a different cost and timetable.

senses.def: state of having many parts, forms, or aspects
senses.ex: The painting's multiplicity of viewpoints made the crowded street feel alive and restless.

origin: From Latin "multitudo", meaning a great number, from "multus", meaning many, plus English "-ous".

senses.def: existing in very large numbers
senses.ex: Multitudinous fireflies covered the meadow, turning the dark grass into a shifting field of lights.

origin: A mistaken version of Latin "sumpsimus", meaning "we have taken", kept by a monk who refused correction in a famous story.

senses.def: stubborn insistence on an obvious error after correction
senses.ex: His insistence that the museum opened on Mondays became a mumpsimus, even after staff showed him the schedule.

senses.def: person who clings to an obvious error despite correction
senses.ex: The editor called him a mumpsimus when he restored the same misspelling for the fourth time.

origin: From Latin "mundanus", of the world, from "mundus", world. It first meant earthly as opposed to heavenly, then ordinary.

senses.def: ordinary, routine, and lacking excitement
senses.ex: Astronauts say that even in orbit, mundane chores like cleaning air filters take up much of the day.

senses.def: of this earthly world rather than a spiritual or heavenly one
senses.ex: The monk believed that mundane concerns such as money and status distracted the soul from prayer.

origin: From Latin "munificentia", from "munus", gift, plus "facere", to make. Munificence is gift-making on a grand scale.

senses.def: great and lavish generosity in giving
senses.ex: Thanks to the munificence of an anonymous donor, every student in the graduating class received a full scholarship.

origin: Formed from "munificence", from Latin "munus", gift, plus "facere", to make: literally gift-making.

senses.def: extremely generous, especially in giving large gifts of money
senses.ex: The munificent gift from two alumni funded a new library wing and twenty research fellowships.

origin: From Latin "muralis", meaning "of a wall", from "murus", wall, through French.

senses.def: large painting made directly on a wall or ceiling
senses.ex: The students painted a mural across the library wall to celebrate the town's river.

senses.def: on or related to a wall
senses.ex: The museum preserved a mural inscription carved directly into the wall.

origin: From Middle English "mirky", meaning dark, with relatives in Old Norse. The base is "murk", darkness.

senses.def: dark or cloudy enough to make seeing difficult
senses.ex: The divers stopped when the water grew too murky to see their own hands.

senses.def: unclear, confusing, or hard to understand
senses.ex: The contract's murky language left both teams unsure who would pay for repairs.

senses.def: morally questionable or suspicious
senses.ex: The reporter traced the developer's murky finances through shell companies and unexplained transfers.

origin: From "murmur", a low indistinct sound, plus "-ous", meaning characterized by that sound.

senses.def: making a low, continuous, indistinct sound
senses.ex: A murmurous crowd gathered outside the theater, their voices rising whenever the doors opened.

origin: The noun comes from Greek "Mousa", a goddess of the arts. The verb comes through Old French "muser".

senses.def: person or thing that inspires an artist's work
senses.ex: The city's old train station became her muse for a series of bright, geometric paintings.

senses.def: think deeply or reflect on something
senses.ex: During the long ride home, he mused about whether he should accept the scholarship.

senses.def: one of the Greek goddesses believed to inspire art and learning
senses.ex: In the mural, a Muse carries a lyre beside the poet she inspires.

origin: From French "mostrer", meaning to show, ultimately Latin "monstrare". A muster was a showing of gathered people.

senses.def: gather people or resources for a purpose
senses.ex: Neighbors mustered volunteers to clear the road after the storm blocked the village entrance.

senses.def: summon a feeling or quality with effort
senses.ex: She mustered the courage to challenge the inaccurate figure during the public meeting.

senses.def: assembly or roll call of troops or other members
senses.ex: At the morning muster, the captain checked every name before the crew boarded.

senses.def: inspection or judgment of whether something meets a standard
senses.ex: The proposal passed muster only after the team explained how it would protect patient privacy.

origin: From Latin "mutabilis", meaning liable to change, from "mutare", to change, through Old French.

senses.def: able or likely to change
senses.ex: The company's mutable plans made it difficult for the design team to set a deadline.

origin: From "mute", silent, from Latin "mutus", silent or speechless, through Old French.

senses.def: restrained and not openly or strongly expressed
senses.ex: The proposal received a muted response from investors, who were polite but clearly unconvinced.

senses.def: quiet and softened in sound
senses.ex: Through the hotel wall we could hear the muted voices of the guests arguing next door.

senses.def: soft and subdued in color rather than bright
senses.ex: The designer painted the bedroom in muted greens and grays to make it feel calm.

origin: Related to "mutiny", which came from French "mutiner", meaning "to rebel". The shared root marks defiance of authority.

senses.def: rebellious toward people in command, especially as part of a group
senses.ex: The mutinous crew refused to launch the boat until the captain explained his decision.

origin: From Middle French "mutiner", meaning "to rebel", a verb for collective resistance to authority.

senses.def: organized rebellion against authority, especially by sailors or soldiers against officers
senses.ex: After weeks without pay, the sailors planned a mutiny and seized control of the ship.

senses.def: rebel collectively against people in command
senses.ex: The soldiers mutinied when their officers ordered them to attack unarmed villagers.

origin: The origin of this adjective is uncertain. Its meaning is close to "muddled" or "fuzzy", but no root is established.

senses.def: mentally foggy and unable to think clearly
senses.ex: After the long flight and little sleep, Mara felt muzzy during the morning exam.

senses.def: blurred or lacking clear outlines
senses.ex: The old projector cast a muzzy image that made the map impossible to read.

senses.def: slightly drunk or dazed by alcohol
senses.ex: Two glasses of wine left him muzzy, so he walked home rather than drive.

origin: From "myopia", from Greek "myops", nearsighted, from "myein", to shut, plus "ops", eye: squinting to see.

senses.def: lacking foresight and focused only on the near term or a narrow view
senses.ex: Cutting the research budget to boost one quarter's profits was a myopic decision that crippled the company later.

senses.def: nearsighted, unable to see distant things clearly
senses.ex: The myopic boy squinted at the blackboard until the school nurse suggested he get glasses.

origin: From Greek "myrias", ten thousand, from "myrios", countless. The Greeks used it for the largest number they had a single word for.

senses.def: countless or extremely numerous
senses.ex: On a clear night in the desert, myriad stars shine so brightly that you can see your own shadow.

senses.def: very great number of people or things
senses.ex: The new library offers a myriad of programs, from coding classes to knitting circles for seniors.

origin: From Greek "Myrmidones", the warriors who followed Achilles, through Latin. Their name became a label for unquestioning followers.

senses.def: subordinate who carries out another person's orders without questioning their cruelty
senses.ex: The mayor sent a myrmidon to intimidate the tenants who complained about the unsafe building.

origin: From Greek "mystagogos", a guide to initiates, combining words for "initiate" and "leader".

senses.def: person who introduces others to secret or mystical religious teachings
senses.ex: The self-appointed mystagogue promised his followers access to hidden truths if they obeyed his rituals.

origin: From Greek "mystikos", meaning "connected with secret rites", through Latin and French.

senses.def: relating to direct spiritual experience or hidden religious truths
senses.ex: Her paintings drew on mystic visions that she described as encounters with the divine.

senses.def: strange and difficult to explain
senses.ex: A mystic glow surrounded the ruins, leaving the visitors unsure whether they saw light or mist.

senses.def: person seeking direct experience of spiritual reality
senses.ex: The mystic spent decades in meditation, hoping to know the divine without formal doctrine.

origin: From French "mystifier", built on Greek "mystikos", meaning "secret", and Latin "-ficare", meaning "to make".

senses.def: puzzle deeply by making something hard to understand
senses.ex: The blank page mystified the investigators because every other sheet contained detailed notes.

origin: From Latin "mythicus", meaning "of myths", with the English adjective ending "-al".

senses.def: existing in myths or traditional legends
senses.ex: The mural showed a mythical phoenix rising from the ashes above the town square.

senses.def: imaginary or believed in despite having no real existence
senses.ex: The mythical shortcut through the hills turned out to be an overgrown path ending at a cliff.

origin: Built from Greek-derived "mytho-", meaning "story or myth", and "-mania", meaning "obsessive fixation".

senses.def: compulsive tendency to invent stories and lie
senses.ex: His mythomania turned a routine delay into a tale of kidnappers, spies, and a secret escape.

origin: From Greek "mythopoiia", meaning "the making of myths", with the English ending "-ic".

senses.def: creating myths or giving rise to legendary stories
senses.ex: The novelist's mythopoeic imagination turned a quiet farming valley into a world of gods and monsters.

origin: From "nacre", meaning "mother of pearl", plus "-ous", meaning "having the quality of".

senses.def: having the lustrous, often iridescent appearance of mother of pearl
senses.ex: At dawn, a nacreous light spread across the shells scattered along the wet beach.

origin: From Arabic "nazir as-samt", counterpart of the zenith: the point in the sky directly beneath an observer, and so the lowest point.

senses.def: lowest or worst point of something, such as a career or situation
senses.ex: The nadir of his career came when he was booed off the stage at his own hometown festival.

syn: low point, rock bottom, depths, low-water mark

origin: From French "naive", natural or artless, from Latin "nativus", native or inborn. Doublet of "native".

senses.def: showing a lack of experience, wisdom, or judgment, too ready to trust
senses.ex: It was naive of the young investor to believe that the stock would keep doubling every month.

origin: From French "naivete", from "naif", natural or artless, from Latin "nativus", native or inborn.

senses.def: lack of experience or sophistication, especially a trusting innocence about the world
senses.ex: The scammers exploited the newcomer's naivete, persuading her to pay a deposit on an apartment that did not exist.

origin: From Narcissus, the youth in Greek myth who fell in love with his own reflection in a pool, plus "-ist", one who.

senses.def: person excessively absorbed in admiring themselves and craving the admiration of others
senses.ex: Every group project became a stage for the narcissist, who reframed the team's success as proof of his own brilliance.

origin: From Latin "nascens", being born, the present participle of "nasci", to be born, so a nascent thing is just being born.

senses.def: just beginning to exist or develop and not yet mature
senses.ex: The nascent startup had three employees and a borrowed office, but investors already sensed its potential.

origin: Originally English slang of uncertain origin, possibly connected with "neat", meaning tidy and trim.

senses.def: neat, smart, and fashionable in dress or appearance
senses.ex: My grandfather looked natty in his pressed linen suit and straw hat at the summer wedding.

origin: From Latin "nauseatus", meaning "feeling seasick", linked through "nausea" to Greek "naus", meaning "ship".

senses.def: make someone feel physically sick
senses.ex: The fumes from the open paint cans began to nauseate everyone in the narrow hallway.

senses.def: cause someone to feel strong disgust
senses.ex: The officials' cheerful defense of the scandal continued to nauseate the families they had harmed.

syn: sicken, make queasy, turn the stomach of

origin: From Latin "nauseosus", meaning "causing nausea", from "nausea", originally linked with seasickness.

senses.def: feeling sick to the stomach
senses.ex: After the winding bus ride, Priya felt nauseous and stepped outside for fresh air.

senses.def: causing nausea or intense disgust
senses.ex: A nauseous odor rose from the flooded cellar, sending the workers back upstairs.

syn: queasy, sick, sick to one's stomach

origin: From Latin "navigabilis", meaning "able to be sailed", through Middle French "navigable".

senses.def: deep and wide enough for boats to pass through
senses.ex: After the spring rains, the river became navigable again for cargo barges.

senses.def: possible to travel through or find one's way around
senses.ex: The campus map made the maze of new buildings navigable for first-year students.

origin: Built from "nay", a word of refusal, "say", and "-er" for a person who does something.

senses.def: person who habitually rejects ideas or predicts failure
senses.ex: The naysayers called the garden impossible, but volunteers harvested tomatoes before summer ended.

origin: From French "naïve", the feminine of "naïf", natural or artless, from Latin "nativus", native or inborn.

senses.def: showing a lack of experience or judgment, especially by being too trusting
senses.ex: It was naïve of him to believe the stranger online who promised to double his savings in a week.

origin: From Yiddish "nebish", related to "nebekh", meaning "poor" or "unfortunate".

senses.def: timid, ineffective person who avoids standing up for themselves
senses.ex: The novel's nebbish spent months agreeing to extra work before finally asking for a raise.

origin: From Latin "nebulosus", full of mist or cloudy, from "nebula", mist or cloud, so a nebulous idea is foggy.

senses.def: vague, unclear, or ill-defined in meaning or form
senses.ex: The candidate's nebulous promise to "fix the economy" left voters wondering what she would actually do.

senses.def: cloudy or hazy in appearance, like a mist
senses.ex: Through the telescope the distant galaxy looked like a faint, nebulous smudge of light.

origin: From Medieval Latin "necessito", meaning "to make necessary", itself from "necessitas", meaning "necessity".

senses.def: make something necessary or unavoidable
senses.ex: The bridge closure will necessitate a longer bus route until repairs are complete.

origin: From Greek "nekros", meaning "dead", and "manteia", meaning "divination", through Latin and French.

senses.def: supposed practice of communicating with the dead to gain knowledge
senses.ex: In the fantasy novel, the queen uses necromancy to question a fallen soldier about the invasion.

senses.def: magic associated with raising or controlling the dead
senses.ex: The villagers feared necromancy when they saw empty graves and strange lights above the crypt.

origin: From Greek "nekropolis", city of the dead, from "nekros", dead body, and "polis", city.

senses.def: large cemetery, especially an ancient one with elaborate tombs near a city
senses.ex: Archaeologists mapping the desert necropolis found hundreds of painted tombs carved into the cliffs above the old city.

syn: cemetery, graveyard, burial ground, city of the dead

origin: From Latin "nefarius", wicked, from "nefas", a crime against divine law, from "ne-", not, plus "fas", what the gods allow.

senses.def: extremely wicked or criminal, especially in a scheming way
senses.ex: The hackers had a nefarious plan to lock hospital computers and demand ransom from desperate administrators.

origin: From Latin "negatus", past participle of "negare", to deny or say no.

senses.def: cancel out the effect of something or make it ineffective
senses.ex: Skipping sleep before the exam could negate all the benefits of a week of careful studying.

senses.def: deny the truth or existence of something
senses.ex: The defense lawyer tried to negate the witness's account by showing she had been out of town that night.

origin: From Latin "neglectus", past participle of "neglegere", to disregard, from "nec", not, plus "legere", to pick up.

senses.def: fail to give proper care or attention to someone or something
senses.ex: The landlord neglected the building for years, and the roof finally collapsed after a heavy snowfall.

senses.def: fail to do something, especially through carelessness
senses.ex: She neglected to mention that the concert tickets were nonrefundable until after we had bought them.

senses.def: failure to give proper care, or the state of being uncared for
senses.ex: The abandoned garden had fallen into neglect, its paths buried under weeds and fallen branches.

origin: From Latin "negligens", present participle of "negligere", to disregard, literally "not pick up".

senses.def: failing to take proper care in doing something
senses.ex: The negligent babysitter scrolled on her phone while the toddler wandered toward the pool.

senses.def: failing to take the care the law expects, and so responsible for resulting harm
senses.ex: The court found the trucking company negligent for letting an exhausted driver stay on the road.

origin: From "negligent" plus "-ible", as if from Latin "negligere", to disregard, so a negligible amount can safely be disregarded.

senses.def: so small or unimportant that it is not worth considering
senses.ex: The new filter added a negligible cost to each bottle but made the water taste noticeably cleaner.

origin: Named for Nemesis, the Greek goddess of retribution who punished human arrogance, so a nemesis is the foe you cannot escape.

senses.def: long-standing rival or enemy who seems impossible to defeat
senses.ex: The chess prodigy beat every opponent at the tournament except her old nemesis, who had stopped her three years running.

senses.def: agent or cause of someone's deserved downfall or punishment
senses.ex: The senator's own careless emails became his nemesis when reporters published them a week before the election.

origin: From French "néologisme", from Greek "neos", new, plus "logos", word, so literally a "new word".

senses.def: newly coined word or expression, or a new meaning for an existing word
senses.ex: When "selfie" first appeared, many editors dismissed it as a passing neologism, yet it now fills dictionaries.

origin: A modern coinage from Greek "neos", new, and "philia", love, so literally a love of the new.

senses.def: strong love of novelty and eagerness for new things, ideas, or experiences
senses.ex: His neophilia meant the kitchen was crowded with gadgets he had ordered the week they launched and used only once.

origin: From Greek "neophytos", newly planted, from "neos", new, plus "phyton", plant, first used for new converts in the early Church.

senses.def: person who is new to a subject, skill, or belief
senses.ex: As a neophyte in the kitchen, he burned the rice twice before learning to lower the heat.

origin: From Late Latin "neotericus", from Greek "neoterikos", youthful or new, built on "neos", new.

senses.def: recent in origin; modern or newfangled
senses.ex: The older professors scoffed at the neoteric theories of their younger colleagues, then quietly began citing them.

origin: From Greek "nepenthes", banishing grief, from "ne-", not, and "penthos", sorrow; in Homer it is a drug that erases sorrow.

senses.def: something that brings forgetfulness of pain or sorrow
senses.ex: After the funeral, long walks along the cold beach became her nepenthe, the one thing that quieted her grief.

origin: From Italian "nepotismo", from Latin "nepos", nephew, recalling Renaissance popes who made their nephews cardinals.

senses.def: unfair favoritism shown to relatives or friends, especially in giving jobs or power
senses.ex: Critics accused the mayor of nepotism after he appointed his cousin to run the city's water department.

origin: From Latin "nescientia", ignorance, from "nescire", not to know, from "ne-", not, and "scire", to know, the root of "science".

senses.def: lack of knowledge or awareness; ignorance
senses.ex: The report blamed the outbreak less on malice than on nescience, since few villagers knew the well water was contaminated.

origin: The money sense comes from French "net", clean, from Latin "nitidus", shining, so a net sum is clean of deductions. The mesh sense is Old English "net".

senses.def: remaining after all deductions, costs, or taxes have been subtracted
senses.ex: After rent, supplies, and taxes, the bakery's net profit for the year was smaller than the owner had hoped.

senses.def: gain or earn an amount as clear profit
senses.ex: The charity auction netted nearly fifty thousand dollars for the children's hospital.

senses.def: open mesh of string or cord used for catching things or as a barrier
senses.ex: The fishermen hauled the dripping net onto the deck, silver fish flashing in the morning sun.

senses.def: catch something with a net, or obtain it by skill
senses.ex: The young scientist netted a prestigious research grant on her very first application.

origin: From Old English "netele", the name of the stinging plant, so to nettle someone is to sting them with irritation.

senses.def: irritate or annoy someone, especially in a small but stinging way
senses.ex: His smug comments about my handwriting nettled me more than I wanted to admit.

senses.def: wild plant with leaves covered in stinging hairs
senses.ex: She brushed against a patch of nettles on the hike, and her ankle itched for hours.

origin: From "nettle", the stinging plant, plus "-some", tending to, so something nettlesome stings and irritates.

senses.def: causing irritation or annoyance, or difficult to deal with
senses.ex: The most nettlesome part of the move was untangling a decade of forwarded mail and forgotten subscriptions.

origin: From French "neutraliser", from "neutral", from Latin "neuter", neither one nor the other.

senses.def: make something ineffective by applying an opposite force or effect
senses.ex: The goalkeeper's quick reflexes neutralized the striker's best chances throughout the second half.

senses.def: make a solution chemically neutral, neither acidic nor basic
senses.ex: In the lab we added baking soda drop by drop to neutralize the spilled vinegar.

senses.def: kill, disable, or destroy an enemy or threat
senses.ex: The bomb squad neutralized the device before it could harm anyone in the crowded station.

origin: Both are built from English words: "never" or "none" plus "the less", meaning "not at all the less" despite what was just said.

senses.def: in spite of what has just been said, even so
senses.ex: The forecast called for heavy rain. Nevertheless, thousands of fans showed up for the outdoor concert.

syn: however, still, even so, nonetheless, notwithstanding

origin: From "new" plus "fangled", from an obsolete verb "fangle", to fashion, so literally "newly fashioned".

senses.def: new and unfamiliar, often in a way that seems needlessly complicated
senses.ex: Grandpa refused to use the newfangled smart thermostat and kept adjusting the old dial by hand.

syn: novel, modern, gimmicky, newly devised, trendy

origin: From Latin "nexus", a binding together, from "nectere", to bind or tie.

senses.def: connection or link between things or people
senses.ex: The study explored the nexus between childhood poverty and adult health problems.

senses.def: central point where many things meet or connect
senses.ex: In the nineteenth century, Chicago became the nexus of the nation's railroads and grain trade.

origin: From Old French "nice", foolish, from Latin "nescius", ignorant, from "ne-", not, plus "scire", to know. Its meaning drifted from foolish to fussy to precise to pleasant.

senses.def: requiring or showing fine, precise distinctions, subtle
senses.ex: The lawyers argued over the nice distinction between a promise and a mere statement of intention.

senses.def: pleasant, agreeable, or attractive
senses.ex: It was a nice afternoon for a picnic, warm and breezy with hardly a cloud overhead.

senses.def: kind, friendly, and considerate toward others
senses.ex: The new neighbor was nice enough to carry our groceries up three flights of stairs.

origin: From Old French "nicete", foolishness, from "nice", which once meant simple or silly; as "nice" came to mean precise, "nicety" meant fine detail.

senses.def: fine or subtle detail or distinction
senses.ex: The lawyers spent an hour arguing over the niceties of a single comma in the contract.

senses.def: small point of polite social behavior
senses.ex: Skipping the usual niceties, the new manager opened the meeting by announcing that two departments would merge.

senses.def: precision or exactness, especially in the phrase "to a nicety"
senses.ex: The pastry chef had timed the oven to a nicety, and every croissant came out the same golden shade.

origin: From "niggard", a miser, probably from a Scandinavian word related to Old Norse "hnoggr", stingy. It is unrelated to any racial slur.

senses.def: unwilling to spend or give; stingy
senses.ex: The landlord was so niggardly that he refused to replace the broken heater until the tenants threatened to sue.

senses.def: meager or scanty in amount
senses.ex: The volunteers were grateful for the donation, though the niggardly sum barely covered a week of meals.

origin: First recorded around 1600; its origin is uncertain, but it is probably from a Scandinavian word like Norwegian dialect "nigla", to fuss over trifles.

senses.def: cause slight but persistent worry or annoyance
senses.ex: Something about the stranger's story niggled at the detective long after she had let him leave the station.

senses.def: criticize or fuss over trivial details
senses.ex: Instead of praising the bold design, the committee niggled about the font size on the back cover.

senses.def: small but nagging doubt, complaint, or criticism
senses.ex: My only niggle with the hotel was the noisy ice machine right outside our door.

syn: nag, bother, trouble, irritate, gnaw at

origin: From Latin "nihil", nothing, plus "-ism", so nihilism is literally a belief in nothing.

senses.def: belief that life has no meaning, purpose, or intrinsic value
senses.ex: After his business collapsed, his gloomy nihilism made every plan for the future seem pointless to him.

senses.def: rejection of all moral, religious, or political principles and authority
senses.ex: The novel's young rebel embraces nihilism, mocking every law, custom, and belief his elders hold sacred.

origin: From Old English "naemel", quick to grasp, from "niman", to take; the "b" crept in later. A nimble person is quick to take hold.

senses.def: quick, light, and skillful in movement
