origin: From Portuguese "palavra", word or talk, from Late Latin "parabola", speech, from Greek "parabole", comparison, the same source as "parable".

senses.def: long, idle, or unnecessary talk or fuss
senses.ex: After an hour of palaver about the seating chart, the wedding planners still had not decided anything.

senses.def: talk at length, often idly or to persuade
senses.ex: The salesmen palavered with the customer for an hour before she finally agreed to a test drive.

origin: From French "palette", a little shovel, from Latin "pala", spade; the painter's board was shaped like a flat blade.

senses.def: range of colors used by an artist or in a design
senses.ex: The designer chose a calm palette of sage green, sand, and pale gray for the hospital lobby.

senses.def: thin board on which a painter lays out and mixes paints
senses.ex: She balanced the wooden palette on her thumb and dabbed blue into white to make the sky.

senses.def: range of qualities in another art, such as flavors or sounds
senses.ex: The chef's palette of spices, from smoky paprika to bright sumac, made each dish distinct.

origin: From Greek "palimpsestos", scraped again, because scribes scraped old writing off expensive parchment to reuse it.

senses.def: manuscript page that has been written on again after earlier writing was erased
senses.ex: Using ultraviolet light, scholars recovered a lost work of Archimedes hidden beneath the prayers on a medieval palimpsest.

senses.def: something reused or altered that still shows traces of its earlier forms
senses.ex: The old city is a palimpsest, with Roman walls, medieval churches, and modern shops layered on the same streets.

origin: From Greek "palindromos", running back again, from "palin", back or again, and "dromos", a running.

senses.def: word, phrase, or number that reads the same backward as forward
senses.ex: Her favorite palindrome was "a man, a plan, a canal: Panama," which she wrote on the board every April.

origin: From Greek "palinoidia", a song sung again, from "palin", back or again, and "oide", song; it takes back an earlier poem.

senses.def: poem in which the poet retracts something said in an earlier poem
senses.ex: After his bitter verses about the city, the poet wrote a palinode praising its parks and people.

senses.def: formal retraction of an earlier statement or view
senses.ex: The economist's new essay reads as a palinode, abandoning the theory that made her famous.

origin: The noun comes from Latin "pallium", a cloak or covering. The verb is a shortened form of "appall", first meaning to grow faint or flat.

senses.def: dark cloud or gloomy atmosphere that hangs over something
senses.ex: News of the layoffs cast a pall over the office holiday party.

senses.def: become less appealing or interesting through familiarity
senses.ex: The thrill of living by the beach began to pall after a few months of sand in every room.

senses.def: cloth spread over a coffin
senses.ex: The soldiers carried the coffin, draped in a dark velvet pall, slowly down the cathedral steps.

origin: From Latin "palliatus", cloaked, from "pallium", a cloak, so to palliate is to cloak a pain or a fault without removing it.

senses.def: relieve the symptoms of a disease or problem without curing its cause
senses.ex: The new drug can palliate the pain of arthritis, though it cannot repair the damaged joints.

senses.def: make an offense or wrong seem less serious
senses.ex: No excuse about stress could palliate the cruelty of what he had said to her.

origin: From French "palliatif", from Medieval Latin "palliare", to cloak, from Latin "pallium", a cloak; a palliative cloaks symptoms without curing.

senses.def: relieving pain or symptoms without curing the underlying cause
senses.ex: When the cancer stopped responding to treatment, the family chose palliative care so he could be comfortable at home.

senses.def: something that eases a problem or symptom without solving it
senses.ex: The tax rebate was only a palliative; it did nothing about the real causes of rising rents.

origin: From Latin "pallidus", pale, from "pallere", to be pale. It is a doublet of "pale".

senses.def: pale, especially because of illness or poor health
senses.ex: After weeks in the hospital, his pallid face had lost all its summer color.

senses.def: lacking energy, color, or interest, dull
senses.ex: The sequel was a pallid imitation of the original film, with none of its wit or excitement.

origin: From Latin "pallor", paleness, from "pallere", to be pale.

senses.def: unhealthy paleness of the face, often from illness, fear, or shock
senses.ex: The nurse noticed the patient's sudden pallor and immediately checked his blood pressure.

origin: From Latin "palpabilis", able to be touched, from "palpare", to touch gently, so a palpable feeling is so strong you can almost touch it.

senses.def: so intense or obvious that it can almost be felt
senses.ex: As the judge prepared to read the verdict, the tension in the courtroom was palpable.

senses.def: clear and easily noticed, obvious
senses.ex: The witness's story was a palpable lie, contradicted by every security camera in the building.

senses.def: able to be touched or felt physically
senses.ex: The doctor found a small but palpable lump in the patient's neck and ordered more tests.

origin: From Latin "palpitare", to throb or flutter, a repeated form of "palpare", to touch gently.

senses.def: (of the heart) beat rapidly, strongly, or irregularly
senses.ex: Her heart palpitated as she opened the envelope from her first-choice university.

senses.def: throb, quiver, or tremble
senses.ex: The whole bridge seemed to palpitate as the freight train thundered across it.

origin: From Low German "paltrig", ragged or worthless, from "palte", a rag; something paltry is worth no more than a scrap of cloth.

senses.def: (of an amount) very small or meager
senses.ex: After six months of work on the mural, the artist received a paltry fee that barely covered the paint.

senses.def: petty, trivial, or contemptible
senses.ex: They ended a twenty-year friendship over a paltry argument about a borrowed lawn mower.

origin: From Greek "panakeia", from "pan", all, plus "akos", cure, so literally an "all-cure".

senses.def: solution or remedy thought to cure all problems or diseases
senses.ex: Technology is not a panacea for education, because a tablet cannot replace a patient, skilled teacher.

syn: cure-all, nostrum, elixir, universal remedy, magic bullet

origin: From French "panache", a plume of feathers on a helmet, from Italian "pennacchio", so panache is showy style worn like a plume.

senses.def: confident, stylish, and flamboyant manner
senses.ex: The magician performed each trick with such panache that the audience hardly noticed when one failed.

origin: From Greek "pandemos", of all the people, from "pan", all, plus "demos", people.

senses.def: outbreak of a disease that spreads across many countries or the whole world
senses.ex: During the pandemic, schools around the world closed and classes moved online.

senses.def: of a disease: spread over a very wide area and affecting many people
senses.ex: Health officials feared the new flu strain could become pandemic within months.

origin: Coined by John Milton in "Paradise Lost" as the name of the capital of Hell, from Greek "pan", all, and "daimon", demon.

senses.def: wild, noisy disorder and confusion
senses.ex: Pandemonium broke out in the stadium when the home team scored in the final second of overtime.

origin: From Pandarus, the go-between who helps two lovers meet in Chaucer's poem "Troilus and Criseyde", so a pander serves others' desires.

senses.def: cater to the lower tastes, desires, or prejudices of others to win favor
senses.ex: The talk show began to pander to its audience with shouting matches and staged fights.

senses.def: person who caters to others' base desires, especially a pimp
senses.ex: In the old play, the scheming servant acts as a pander, arranging secret meetings for his master.

syn: cater, indulge, gratify, play up to, toady

origin: From Latin "pandiculari", to stretch oneself, from "pandere", to spread out.

senses.def: act of stretching the body and limbs, often while yawning, as when waking
senses.ex: The cat greeted the morning with a long pandiculation, arching its back and splaying every claw.

origin: From Greek "panegyrikos", fit for a public festival, from "panegyris", a general assembly, where speakers praised famous people.

senses.def: public speech or text that praises someone or something highly
senses.ex: The retiring coach blushed through a long panegyric from his former players at the awards dinner.

origin: Plural of "pang", an English word of uncertain origin for a sudden, sharp pain.

senses.def: sudden sharp feelings of emotional distress
senses.ex: She felt pangs of guilt every time she walked past the friend she had stopped calling.

senses.def: sudden sharp physical pains
senses.ex: By late afternoon, hunger pangs made it hard for the fasting students to concentrate.

origin: Invented as a nonsense word by the English playwright Samuel Foote in the 1700s, in a mock title, "the Grand Panjandrum".

senses.def: person who has or claims great power or importance, often pompously
senses.ex: The corporate panjandrums arrived in a convoy of black cars to announce that the branch office would close.

syn: bigwig, big shot, grandee, mogul, pooh-bah

origin: Past tense of "pan". The criticize sense is American slang of uncertain origin. The camera sense is short for "panorama".

senses.def: criticized harshly, especially in a review
senses.ex: Critics panned the expensive musical, and it closed after only two weeks.

senses.def: swung a camera sideways to follow action or show a wide view
senses.ex: The camera slowly panned across the battlefield, revealing the full scale of the destruction.

senses.def: washed gravel in a pan to separate out gold
senses.ex: Prospectors panned the icy creek for weeks, finding only a few flakes of gold.

origin: From Greek "panoplia", a full suit of armor, from "pan", all, plus "hopla", arms or weapons.

senses.def: impressive or complete range or collection of things
senses.ex: The kitchen store offered a panoply of gadgets, from pasta makers to laser thermometers.

senses.def: splendid display or ceremonial dress
senses.ex: The royal wedding unfolded with the full panoply of horse-drawn carriages, trumpets, and jeweled crowns.

origin: From Greek "pan", all, and "optikos", of sight, so all-seeing.

senses.def: showing or seeing everything at once; all-encompassing
senses.ex: The novel offers a panoptic view of the city, moving from mansions to tenements in a single chapter.

senses.def: relating to constant, total surveillance
senses.ex: Critics warned that cameras on every corner were creating a panoptic society where no one could act unseen.

origin: Coined around 1792 by the painter Robert Barker from Greek "pan", all, and "horama", view, for his huge circular paintings.

senses.def: wide, unbroken view of a whole area
senses.ex: From the summit, hikers enjoyed a panorama of three lakes, the river valley, and distant snowy peaks.

senses.def: complete survey or presentation of a subject or series of events
senses.ex: The exhibition offers a panorama of Japanese printmaking from the seventeenth century to today.

origin: From Greek "pantheion", temple of all the gods, from "pan", all, and "theos", god; the Pantheon in Rome bears the name.

senses.def: all the gods of a particular people or religion
senses.ex: Thor, Odin, and Freya are among the best-known members of the Norse pantheon.

senses.def: group of the most respected or famous people in a field
senses.ex: With her third championship, the sprinter earned a place in the pantheon of track and field.

senses.def: temple dedicated to all the gods
senses.ex: Tourists crane their necks inside the ancient pantheon to see sunlight pouring through its open dome.

origin: From Latin "pantomimus", from Ancient Greek "pantomimos", from "pas", all, and "mimeomai", to mimic, so literally one who imitates everything.

senses.def: wordless performance or communication using only gestures, facial expressions, and movement
senses.ex: Unable to speak the language, the traveler resorted to pantomime, flapping both arms to ask where chickens were sold.

senses.def: family stage show in Britain at Christmas, based on a fairy tale, with songs and slapstick
senses.ex: Every December the village hall stages a pantomime of Cinderella, complete with slapstick villains and loud audience heckling.

senses.def: express or act out something using gestures and no words
senses.ex: From across the noisy gym, the coach pantomimed a timeout by forming a T with both hands.

origin: From Old French "parable", via Late Latin "parabola", from Greek "parabole", comparison, literally a throwing beside, from "para", beside, and "ballein", to throw. A doublet of "parabola".

senses.def: short story that teaches a moral or spiritual lesson through comparison
senses.ex: The minister retold the parable of the lost sheep to show that no member of the community is forgotten.

origin: From Greek "paradeigma", pattern or example, from "paradeiknynai", to show side by side, so a paradigm is a model to compare against.

senses.def: framework of ideas, methods, and assumptions that shapes how a subject is understood
senses.ex: The discovery that continents drift caused a paradigm shift in geology, overturning older theories.

senses.def: typical example or model of something
senses.ex: The tiny village became a paradigm of how renewable energy could power a whole community.

origin: From French "paradigmatique", from Greek "paradeigmatikos", from "paradeigma", pattern or example.

senses.def: serving as a typical example or model of something
senses.ex: Her rise from mailroom clerk to chief executive is a paradigmatic success story.

origin: From Greek "paradoxos", contrary to expectation, from "para-", beyond, plus "doxa", opinion or belief.

senses.def: statement that seems contradictory or absurd but may actually be true
senses.ex: It is a paradox that the more choices people have, the less satisfied they often feel.

senses.def: person, situation, or thing with seemingly contradictory qualities
senses.ex: My grandmother was a paradox: a fierce critic of technology who checked her email every hour.

senses.def: statement that contradicts itself, so it cannot be consistently true or false
senses.ex: "This sentence is false" is a famous paradox that puzzled logicians for centuries.

origin: From "paradox", from Greek "paradoxos", contrary to expectation, plus "-ical".

senses.def: seemingly contradictory or absurd but possibly true
senses.ex: In a paradoxical twist, the medicine meant to calm the patient made him more anxious.

origin: From Old Italian "paragone", a touchstone for testing gold, from "paragonare", to test, so a paragon is the standard others are measured against.

senses.def: model of excellence or perfection, a perfect example
senses.ex: The volunteer firefighter was a paragon of courage, rushing into the burning house to rescue the children.

origin: From Ancient Greek "paraleipsis", omission, from "para", beside, and "leipein", to leave, so a speaker seems to leave something aside.

senses.def: rhetorical device of drawing attention to something by claiming not to mention it
senses.ex: With sly paralipsis, the candidate said, "I won't even bring up my opponent's bankruptcy," and the crowd laughed knowingly.

origin: From "parallel" plus "-ism", and from Late Latin "parallelismus". "Parallel" itself traces to Greek "parallelos", beside one another.

senses.def: repetition of matching grammatical structures in writing or speech for rhythm and emphasis
senses.ex: The speech's parallelism, with each sentence opening on the same three words, gave its closing passage a stirring rhythm.

senses.def: close similarity or correspondence between two things
senses.ex: Historians have noted the striking parallelism between the two empires' collapses, both hastened by inflation and overextended armies.

senses.def: state of lines or surfaces running side by side at equal distance
senses.ex: The carpenter checked the parallelism of the two shelves with a level before fixing the brackets to the wall.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "paramont", above, from Old French "par", by, and "amont", upward, itself from Latin "ad montem", to the mountain.

senses.def: of the highest importance, ranking above all other concerns
senses.ex: For the rescue crew, the safety of the trapped miners was paramount, so every other decision could wait.

senses.def: having the highest rank or authority
senses.ex: The island's paramount chief settled disputes among the villages and spoke for them at the regional council.

origin: From Old French "par amour", by or through love, from "par", by, and "amour", love, from Latin "amor".

senses.def: lover, especially the secret or illicit partner of a married person
senses.ex: The biography reveals that the senator's longtime paramour quietly managed campaign finances for nearly a decade.

origin: From Ancient Greek "paranoia", madness, from "paranoos", demented, from "para", beyond or beside, and "noos", mind, so literally being beside one's mind.

senses.def: extreme, unreasonable suspicion and distrust of other people
senses.ex: Years of office politics left the accountant with a creeping paranoia, certain that every closed door hid colleagues plotting together.

senses.def: mental disorder marked by delusions, especially of being persecuted
senses.ex: Doctors diagnosed the patient with paranoia after she insisted that neighbors were beaming signals through her apartment walls.

origin: From Medieval Latin "paraphernalia", a wife's goods beyond her dowry, from Greek "para", beside, and "pherne", dowry. Her personal items became the word for assorted gear.

senses.def: miscellaneous equipment or articles needed for a particular activity
senses.ex: The garage overflowed with camping paraphernalia, from dented lanterns and tent poles to a leaky inflatable canoe.

senses.def: symbols and trappings associated with an institution or status
senses.ex: The regime surrounded itself with the paraphernalia of power: medals, motorcades, and enormous portraits in every public square.

origin: From Middle French "paraphrase", from Latin "paraphrasis", from Greek "paraphrasis", from "para", beside, and "phrasis", a way of speaking.

senses.def: restate something in different words, often to clarify or simplify it
senses.ex: Rather than quoting the entire report, the journalist paraphrased its main findings in two clear sentences.

senses.def: restatement of a text or speech in other words
senses.ex: Her paraphrase of the dense legal clause finally helped the tenants understand what they had agreed to sign.

origin: From Greek "para", beside or amiss, and "praxis", action, suggesting an act that goes slightly astray.

senses.def: slip of the tongue or memory thought to reveal a hidden thought or motive
senses.ex: When the nervous groom called his bride by his ex's name, the therapist among the guests quietly diagnosed a parapraxis.

syn: Freudian slip, slip of the tongue, lapse

origin: From Greek "parasitos", one who eats at another's table, from "para", beside, and "sitos", food.

senses.def: organism that lives on or inside another and feeds at its expense
senses.ex: The veterinarian found a parasite in the puppy's intestine that had been stealing nutrients from every meal.

senses.def: person who lives off others while giving nothing useful in return
senses.ex: His cousins regarded him as a parasite, since he had lived rent-free in their basement for six years without working.

origin: Past participle of "parch", from Middle English "parchen", to dry or scorch, whose earlier origin is unknown.

senses.def: extremely dry, especially from heat or lack of rain
senses.ex: After three rainless summers, the parched fields cracked open and the farmers sold off most of their cattle.

senses.def: extremely thirsty and badly in need of a drink
senses.ex: The hikers reached the spring completely parched, having emptied their water bottles hours earlier on the exposed ridge.

origin: From Old French "parer", to prepare or trim, from Latin "parare", to prepare or make ready.

senses.def: trim something by cutting away its outer skin or edges
senses.ex: She pared the apples with a small knife, letting the peel fall in one long curl.

senses.def: reduce something gradually, especially by removing what is unnecessary
senses.ex: The council pared the budget down to essentials, cutting parades and new office furniture.

origin: From German "Pareidolie", built from Greek "para", alongside, and "eidolon", image, suggesting a false image seen beside the real one.

senses.def: tendency to perceive familiar shapes, such as faces, in random or vague images or sounds
senses.ex: Thanks to pareidolia, the toddler insisted that the two windows and door of the garage formed a smiling face.

origin: From Medieval Latin "parentheticus", from Greek "parenthesis", a putting in beside, from "para-", beside, plus "en", in, plus "tithenai", to place.

senses.def: added as an extra explanation or aside, not part of the main point
senses.ex: The professor's parenthetical remark about her own college days drew laughter from the class.

senses.def: written inside a pair of parentheses
senses.ex: The author put the dates in a parenthetical note after each historical figure's name.

senses.def: word, phrase, or remark inserted as an aside
senses.ex: Her essay was so full of parentheticals that the main argument kept getting lost.

origin: From Tamil "paraiyar", drummers, a low caste who beat the "parai" drum for public announcements, so the word came to mean an outcast.

senses.def: person who is rejected, despised, or avoided by others
senses.ex: After he leaked the team's playbook to a rival, he became a pariah in the locker room.

senses.def: country or group shunned by the rest of the world
senses.ex: Its repeated attacks on neighbors turned the regime into an international pariah.

syn: outcast, exile, untouchable, persona non grata, leper

origin: From Middle French "parité", from Late Latin "paritas", equality, from Latin "par", equal, the same root as "peer" and "par".

senses.def: state of being equal, especially in pay, status, or power
senses.ex: After years of negotiation, the nurses finally won pay parity with hospital technicians who held similar qualifications.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "parlance", speech, from "parler", to talk, the same root found in "parliament" and "parley".

senses.def: particular way of speaking or vocabulary used by a specific group or field
senses.ex: In Wall Street parlance, a dead cat bounce is a brief rally in a stock that is still falling.

origin: From Old French "parler", to speak, from Late Latin "parabolare", from "parabola", speech. It is related to "palaver" and "parliament".

senses.def: discussion between enemies or opponents to settle a dispute
senses.ex: The two generals met under a white flag for a parley about exchanging prisoners.

senses.def: hold a discussion with an enemy or opponent
senses.ex: The rebels agreed to parley with government officials at a neutral village across the river.

origin: A Middle English contraction of "perilous", from Old French "perillous", from Latin "periculosus", dangerous, from "periculum", danger.

senses.def: full of danger or uncertainty, often describing a bad situation
senses.ex: By winter the charity's finances were in a parlous state, with barely enough cash to keep its shelters heated.

origin: From Late Latin "parochialis", of a parish, from Greek "paroikia", from "para-", near, plus "oikos", house, so parochial views reach only the neighbors' houses.

senses.def: narrow in outlook, concerned only with local matters
senses.ex: The town council's parochial debates over parking ignored the factory closing that threatened every job.

senses.def: relating to a church parish
senses.ex: She attended a parochial school run by the local Catholic church until eighth grade.

origin: From Greek "paroidia", from "para-", beside, plus "oide", song, so a parody is a mocking song sung alongside the original.

senses.def: imitation of a work, style, or person that exaggerates it for comic effect
senses.ex: The comedy troupe's parody of a cooking show had chefs burning everything while praising their own genius.

senses.def: imitate something in an exaggerated way for comic effect
senses.ex: The student newspaper parodied the principal's morning announcements in its April Fools' edition.

senses.def: feeble or absurd imitation of something
senses.ex: The rushed trial, with no defense lawyer present, was a parody of justice.

origin: From Greek "paronomasia", play on similar-sounding words, from "para", beside, and "onomasia", naming.

senses.def: wordplay that exploits similar sounds or multiple meanings of words, or punning
senses.ex: The headline's paronomasia, calling the bakery strike a matter of dough, made even the grumpy editor laugh out loud.

syn: pun, punning, wordplay, play on words

origin: From Greek "paroxysmos", irritation, from "paroxynein", to goad, from "para-" plus "oxynein", to sharpen, from "oxys", sharp.

senses.def: sudden violent outburst of emotion or activity
senses.ex: The comedian's final joke sent the audience into paroxysms of laughter.

senses.def: sudden attack or worsening of a disease's symptoms
senses.ex: A paroxysm of coughing kept the patient awake for most of the night.

origin: From Latin "parricida", killer of a close relative. The first part is of uncertain origin, perhaps from "par", equal.

senses.def: act of killing one's parent or another close relative
senses.ex: The Greek tragedy turns on an act of parricide, as Oedipus unknowingly strikes down his own father at a crossroads.

senses.def: person who kills a parent or another close relative
senses.ex: The jury struggled to see the shy teenager as a parricide, even after prosecutors presented the evidence from the family home.

origin: Probably from French, from "parer", to ward off, from Latin "parare", to prepare or make ready.

senses.def: ward off a weapon or blow by blocking it
senses.ex: The fencer parried her opponent's thrust and struck back in a single swift motion.

senses.def: skillfully avoid answering a question or criticism
senses.ex: The senator parried reporters' questions about the scandal by talking about the weather.

senses.def: act of warding off a blow or deflecting a question
senses.ex: His quick parry of the interviewer's tough question earned admiring nods from the audience.

syn: deflect, evade, sidestep, fend off, ward off

origin: From "parsimony", from Latin "parsimonia", thrift, from "parcere", to spare.

senses.def: extremely unwilling to spend money or use resources, stingy
senses.ex: The parsimonious landlord refused to replace the broken heater, so his tenants shivered all winter.

senses.def: of an explanation: using the fewest possible assumptions
senses.ex: Scientists often prefer the most parsimonious theory, the one that explains the data with the fewest assumptions.

origin: From Latin "parsimonia", thrift, from "parcere", to spare or save. A parsimonious person spares every penny.

senses.def: extreme unwillingness to spend money or use resources, stinginess
senses.ex: The owner's parsimony was legendary, extending even to rationing paper clips and turning off the office heat in January.

senses.def: careful, sparing use of money, words, or other resources
senses.ex: Thanks to the founders' parsimony in the early years, the startup survived the downturn without laying off a single employee.

senses.def: principle of preferring the simplest explanation that fits the evidence
senses.ex: Applying the principle of parsimony, the biologist favored the evolutionary tree that required the fewest separate mutations.

origin: Back-formed from Middle English "part-taking", sharing, modeled on Latin "particeps", participating, and made of "part" plus "take".

senses.def: join in an activity, take part
senses.ex: Few of the older villagers chose to partake in the midsummer dance, preferring to watch from benches along the square.

senses.def: eat or drink something, especially something offered
senses.ex: Guests were invited to partake of the roasted lamb and spiced wine once the wedding toasts had ended.

senses.def: have or show some of a particular quality or character
senses.ex: Her late paintings partake of both realism and dream, so that ordinary kitchens seem faintly haunted.

origin: From Late Latin "partialis", relating to a part, from Latin "pars", part, so partial means involving only part, or taking one part's side.

senses.def: favoring one side in an unfair way, biased
senses.ex: The losing team complained that the referee had been partial to the home side all game.

senses.def: only in part, incomplete
senses.ex: The storm caused a partial collapse of the roof, but the walls stayed standing.

senses.def: having a liking for something, usually followed by "to"
senses.ex: My grandfather is partial to strong black coffee and a slice of apple pie after dinner.

origin: From Medieval Latin "partialitas", from Late Latin "partialis", relating to a part, from Latin "pars", part.

senses.def: unfair bias in favor of one person or side
senses.ex: The judge stepped down from the case to avoid any appearance of partiality toward her former client.

senses.def: particular liking or fondness for something
senses.ex: Her partiality for spicy food meant every family dinner came with a bottle of hot sauce.

origin: From French "partisan", from Italian "partigiano", a supporter of a party, from "parte", part or faction.

senses.def: strongly supporting one party or cause, often with bias
senses.ex: The partisan crowd booed every point the opposing candidate made during the debate.

senses.def: committed supporter of a party, cause, or person
senses.ex: Partisans on both sides flooded social media with angry posts after the vote.

senses.def: member of an armed group fighting secretly against an occupying force
senses.ex: During the war, partisans hid in the forests and sabotaged enemy supply trains.

origin: From French "parvenu", one who has arrived, past participle of "parvenir", to arrive, from Latin "pervenire", to reach.

senses.def: person who has recently gained wealth or status but is seen as lacking refinement
senses.ex: The old families of the town sneered at the parvenu who bought the grandest mansion with his lottery winnings.

syn: upstart, nouveau riche, social climber, arriviste

origin: From Italian "pasquinata", from "Pasquino", the nickname of an ancient statue in Rome on which people posted anonymous satires.

senses.def: satire or lampoon that mocks a person publicly, often posted anonymously
senses.ex: An unsigned pasquinade taped to the town hall door mocked the mayor's vanity and had everyone laughing by noon.

origin: From French "passé", past, the past participle of "passer", to pass, so something whose moment has gone by.

senses.def: no longer fashionable or current, out of date
senses.ex: Flip phones seemed hopelessly passe by 2012, though a few nostalgic teenagers have since revived them as a fashion statement.

syn: outdated, outmoded, unfashionable, old hat, dated

origin: From French "pastiche", from Italian "pasticcio", a pie of mixed ingredients, from Late Latin "pasta", dough.

senses.def: work of art that imitates the style of another artist, work, or period
senses.ex: The new detective novel is a loving pastiche of Victorian mysteries, complete with foggy streets and a brilliant sleuth.

senses.def: jumbled mixture of different elements or styles
senses.ex: The hotel lobby was a pastiche of Greek columns, Japanese lanterns, and neon signs.

origin: From Latin "pastoralis", from "pastor", shepherd, so pastoral scenes show shepherds and fields, and a pastor tends a human flock.

senses.def: relating to the countryside or rural life, especially in an idealized way
senses.ex: The painting showed a pastoral scene of sheep grazing beside a quiet stream at sunset.

senses.def: relating to the spiritual or personal care given by clergy or teachers
senses.ex: The school counselor's pastoral role included checking on students who seemed lonely or stressed.

senses.def: poem, painting, or piece of music depicting idealized country life
senses.ex: The poet's early work was a pastoral about shepherds singing to each other in an imaginary meadow.

origin: From Latin "patens", lying open, from "patere", to be open. A "letter patent" was an open public document granting a right.

senses.def: obvious and clear to everyone
senses.ex: His claim that he had never met the woman was a patent lie, since photos showed them together.

senses.def: legal right granted to an inventor to be the only one to make or sell an invention
senses.ex: The engineer received a patent for her design of a folding bicycle helmet.

senses.def: obtain a patent for an invention
senses.ex: The company rushed to patent the new battery before competitors could copy it.

origin: From Greek "pathos", suffering or disease, plus "-genic", producing, so something pathogenic produces disease.

senses.def: capable of causing disease
senses.ex: Most bacteria in the human gut are harmless, but a few pathogenic strains can cause serious illness.

origin: From "pathology", from Greek "pathos", suffering or disease, plus "-logia", study of.

senses.def: compulsive, extreme, and beyond reason
senses.ex: He was a pathological liar who invented stories even when the truth would have served him better.

senses.def: relating to or caused by disease
senses.ex: The lab confirmed that the swelling was pathological, not just a reaction to the injury.

origin: From Greek "pathos", suffering or experience, the same root as "sympathy" and "empathy".

senses.def: quality in a story, speech, or situation that arouses pity or sadness
senses.ex: The film's final scene, an old man setting a table for his late wife, was full of pathos.

senses.def: in rhetoric, an appeal to the audience's emotions
senses.ex: The charity ad relied on pathos, showing photos of hungry children instead of statistics.

origin: Borrowed from Italian "patina", from Latin "patina", a shallow dish or pan, itself taken from Greek "patane".

senses.def: thin green or brown film that forms on old metal such as bronze or copper
senses.ex: Decades of salt air had given the bronze harbor statue a soft green patina that the town refused to polish away.

senses.def: soft sheen that wood, leather, or similar materials acquire with age and use
senses.ex: The oak banister had developed a warm patina from generations of hands sliding along it on the way downstairs.

senses.def: superficial appearance or impression of a quality, such as respectability or success
senses.ex: The consultant's expensive suit lent a patina of authority to advice that was mostly guesswork.

origin: Borrowed in the 1600s from French "patois", a regional dialect. The French word's own origin is uncertain.

senses.def: regional dialect, often one regarded as nonstandard
senses.ex: My grandmother switched to the local patois whenever she wanted to tell secrets in front of tourists.

senses.def: special jargon or way of speaking of a particular group
senses.ex: The surfers' patois of "gnarly" waves and "barrels" was almost incomprehensible to outsiders.

origin: From Greek "patriarkhes", founder or head of a family, from "patria", family or clan, plus "-arkhes", ruler, the same ending as in "monarch".

senses.def: male head of a family, clan, or tribe
senses.ex: The family patriarch, now ninety, still presided over every holiday dinner and settled every quarrel among his grandchildren.

senses.def: man regarded as the founder or revered elder of a movement, field, or organization
senses.ex: Admirers called him the patriarch of American jazz criticism, since nearly every later critic had studied his early reviews.

senses.def: title of certain high-ranking bishops, especially in the Eastern Orthodox churches
senses.ex: Pilgrims crowded the cathedral steps in Istanbul hoping to receive a blessing from the visiting patriarch.

syn: elder, paterfamilias, head of the family, founder

origin: From Middle French "patricien", from Latin "patricius", of the Roman senators, who were called "patres", meaning fathers.

senses.def: belonging to or typical of the aristocracy, refined and upper-class
senses.ex: Her patrician accent and erect bearing made the new headmistress seem out of place in the noisy public school.

senses.def: person of noble birth or high social rank
senses.ex: Though raised a patrician on a Virginia estate, the senator built her career championing the rights of factory workers.

senses.def: member of the hereditary aristocracy of ancient Rome
senses.ex: In the early Roman Republic, only a patrician could hold the consulship, a privilege that plebeians fought for generations to end.

origin: From Middle French "patrimoine", from Latin "patrimonium", from "pater", father, so property handed down from one's father.

senses.def: property or estate inherited from one's father or ancestors
senses.ex: He gambled away his entire patrimony within three years of his father's funeral, including the family vineyard.

senses.def: heritage or legacy passed down through a group or nation
senses.ex: Italy spends heavily to protect its cultural patrimony, from crumbling Roman arches to Renaissance frescoes in small village churches.

origin: From Old French "patronage", from "patron", a protector or sponsor, plus the noun ending "-age".

senses.def: support, especially financial, given by a patron to an artist, institution, or cause
senses.ex: Without the patronage of wealthy Florentine bankers, many Renaissance painters could never have afforded to pursue their art.

senses.def: power to grant jobs or favors in exchange for political support
senses.ex: The mayor used city patronage to reward loyal precinct captains with comfortable jobs at the water department.

senses.def: regular business given to a store, restaurant, or similar establishment by customers
senses.ex: The bakery thanked the neighborhood for its patronage with free coffee on the anniversary of its opening.

origin: From "patron" plus "-ize". "Patron" comes from Latin "patronus", protector, from "pater", father, so to patronize is to act like a lofty protector.

senses.def: treat someone with an air of kindly superiority, as if they were less capable
senses.ex: Experienced nurses resent doctors who patronize them by explaining procedures they have performed hundreds of times.

senses.def: be a regular customer of a shop, restaurant, or other business
senses.ex: Longtime residents still patronize the corner bakery, even though a chain café opened across the street last year.

senses.def: support an artist, cause, or institution with money or influence
senses.ex: Wealthy merchant families patronized painters and architects, turning Renaissance Florence into a showcase of civic pride.

syn: condescend to, talk down to, look down on, belittle

origin: From "patronize", to treat someone as a lofty protector would treat a dependent, from "patron", from Latin "patronus", protector, from "pater", father.

senses.def: showing condescension, as if the listener were less intelligent or capable
senses.ex: Her patronizing tone, as if she were explaining fractions to a toddler, irritated every engineer in the meeting.

origin: From Latin "paucitas", fewness, from "paucus", few, a distant relative of the English word "few".

senses.def: scarcity, the presence of something in only small or insufficient amounts
senses.ex: The paucity of reliable data from the remote region made the researchers cautious about drawing any firm conclusions.

origin: Borrowed from Latin "pauper", poor, originally as an English legal term, and a doublet of the word "poor" itself.

senses.def: very poor person, especially one dependent on public charity
senses.ex: After the bank collapsed, the once-prosperous merchant died a pauper and was buried at the parish's expense.

origin: From Spanish "pecadillo", little sin, a diminutive of "pecado", sin, from Latin "peccare", to sin, the root of "impeccable".

senses.def: small, relatively harmless fault or offense
senses.ex: Voters forgave the mayor's peccadilloes, such as parking in the fire lane, because the city budget was finally balanced.

origin: From Latin "peculari", to embezzle, linked to "peculium", private property, and "pecu", cattle, once a measure of wealth.

senses.def: steal or misuse money or property entrusted to one's care, especially public funds
senses.ex: The treasurer managed to peculate nearly a million dollars from the pension fund before auditors noticed the missing deposits.

origin: From Latin "peculatio", embezzlement, from "peculari", to defraud the public, tied to "pecu", cattle or money, an early form of wealth.

senses.def: embezzlement of public money or property by someone trusted to look after it
senses.ex: The inquiry uncovered years of peculation at the ministry, where officials had quietly diverted road funds into private accounts.

origin: From Latin "peculiaris", one's own, from "peculium", private property, from "pecus", cattle, since wealth was once counted in livestock.

senses.def: strange or unusual in a way that is unsettling or hard to explain
senses.ex: A peculiar smell drifted from the basement, so the landlord called a plumber before anyone went downstairs.

senses.def: belonging characteristically or exclusively to a particular person, place, or group
senses.ex: The clicking consonants peculiar to several southern African languages fascinated the visiting linguistics students.

origin: From Latin "pecuniarius", from "pecunia", money, which comes from "pecu", cattle, an early form of wealth.

senses.def: relating to or consisting of money
senses.ex: The volunteer insisted she had no pecuniary interest in the land deal, since she would not earn a cent from it.

origin: From "pedagogy", from Greek "paidagogos", the slave who walked a child to school, from "pais", child, and "agein", to lead.

senses.def: relating to teaching, teaching methods, or the theory of education
senses.ex: The workshop covered pedagogical strategies for keeping restless middle schoolers engaged during long science labs.

origin: From Greek "paidagogos", from "pais", child, and "agogos", leader. In ancient Greece, this was a slave who escorted boys to school.

senses.def: teacher, especially one who is strict, dogmatic, or overly concerned with rules
senses.ex: The old pedagogue rapped his ruler on the desk whenever a student misplaced a comma in a Latin translation.

origin: From Greek "paidagogia", from "paidagogos", the slave who led a child to school, from "pais", child, and "agein", to lead.

senses.def: method and practice of teaching, or the study of how best to teach
senses.ex: Her pedagogy relied on small-group debates rather than lectures, and her students' essays grew noticeably sharper.

origin: From French "pedant", from Italian "pedante", schoolmaster. The word's deeper origin is uncertain, but the image of a fussy teacher fits it well.

senses.def: person who is overly concerned with minor details, rules, or displays of learning
senses.ex: Only a pedant would interrupt a moving wedding toast to point out that the best man had misused "literally."

origin: From "pedant" plus "-ic". "Pedant" comes through French from Italian "pedante", schoolmaster, evoking a fussy teacher fixated on petty rules.

senses.def: excessively concerned with minor details or formal rules, often while showing off learning
senses.ex: His pedantic corrections of every comma made the group project drag on for hours longer than necessary.

origin: From Italian "pedanteria", the behavior of a "pedante", or pedant, someone who makes a show of book learning.

senses.def: excessive concern with minor details or rules, especially to display one's learning
senses.ex: His pedantry wore on the book club, since he interrupted every discussion to correct someone's pronunciation of a character's name.

origin: A back-formation from "pedlar" (peddler), a traveling seller, in the same way that "burgle" was formed from "burglar".

senses.def: sell small goods, often by traveling from place to place or door to door
senses.ex: Before opening his hardware store, he spent years peddling pots and brushes from a wagon across rural Ohio.

senses.def: promote an idea, story, or view persistently, often a dubious one
senses.ex: The website kept peddling conspiracy theories about the election long after every recount had confirmed the results.

senses.def: sell illegal drugs, usually in small amounts on the street
senses.ex: Police arrested two men accused of peddling counterfeit pills outside the nightclub on weekend nights.

origin: From Latin "pedester", going on foot, from "pes" (stem "ped-"), foot. Writing that merely plods along on foot came to seem plain and dull.

senses.def: lacking imagination, inspiration, or excitement, dull and ordinary
senses.ex: Critics praised the film's stunning visuals but found its pedestrian dialogue too predictable to hold their interest.

senses.def: person walking rather than traveling in a vehicle
senses.ex: The city widened the crosswalks after several pedestrians were nearly struck by turning delivery trucks.

senses.def: intended for or used by people walking
senses.ex: A new pedestrian bridge now lets commuters cross the river without dodging traffic on the old highway.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "pe de grue", foot of a crane, because the branching lines of a family tree resembled a crane's foot.

senses.def: recorded line of ancestors, especially of a purebred animal
senses.ex: The breeder showed us the spaniel's pedigree, which traced its champion bloodline back through eleven generations of show dogs.

senses.def: person's family background or ancestry, especially when distinguished
senses.ex: Despite her aristocratic pedigree, the young duchess preferred muddy field research to the parties her relatives expected her to attend.

senses.def: history or track record of a person, idea, or thing, showing its quality or origin
senses.ex: The theory has a respectable pedigree, having been refined by economists across three centuries before reaching today's textbooks.

senses.def: descended from a recorded line of purebred ancestors
senses.ex: Their pedigree Labrador cost more than their first car, but the kennel promised a calm temperament and healthy hips.

origin: From Middle English "pereles", from "peer", an equal, plus "-less", so literally having no equal.

senses.def: so excellent that nothing or no one can equal it
senses.ex: Critics praised the pianist's peerless control, noting that even the fastest passages sounded effortless and perfectly clear.

origin: From Middle English "pevish", meaning perverse or willful. Its deeper origin is uncertain.

senses.def: easily irritated or annoyed, especially by unimportant things
senses.ex: After a sleepless night on the train, the travelers grew peevish and snapped at each other over the smallest delays.

origin: From Late Latin "peiorare", to make worse, from Latin "peior", worse. A pejorative word makes its subject sound worse.

senses.def: expressing contempt or disapproval, belittling
senses.ex: In the nineteenth century, "Impressionist" began as a pejorative label before the painters proudly adopted it.

senses.def: word or expression that belittles or insults
senses.ex: The editor removed the pejorative from the article, noting that a neutral description made the point more effectively.

origin: From Latin "pelagicus", from Greek "pelagikos", of the sea, from "pelagos", the sea.

senses.def: relating to or living in the open ocean, away from the coast
senses.ex: Pelagic seabirds such as albatrosses may spend years over the open ocean without once touching solid land.

origin: From Middle English "pelf", stolen goods or riches, possibly from Anglo-Norman "pelfre", booty, and perhaps related to "pilfer". Its earlier history is uncertain.

senses.def: money or wealth, especially when gained dishonestly
senses.ex: The corrupt governor retired to a seaside villa, surrounded by the pelf he had skimmed from two decades of public contracts.

origin: From Latin "pellucidus", from "per", through, and "lucere", to shine. Something pellucid lets light shine right through it.

senses.def: translucently clear, allowing light to pass through
senses.ex: Snorkelers could watch fish darting over the reef through the pellucid water of the sheltered lagoon.

senses.def: expressed so clearly that it is easy to understand
senses.ex: Her pellucid explanation of compound interest finally made the concept click for the confused freshmen.

origin: From Old French "peneance", from Latin "paenitentia", repentance, which also gave English the word "penitence".

senses.def: voluntary suffering or effort undertaken to show sorrow for wrongdoing
senses.ex: As penance for skipping his sister's recital, he spent the whole weekend helping her move into her new apartment.

senses.def: sacrament in some Christian churches in which sins are confessed and forgiven
senses.ex: Catholic children typically receive the sacrament of penance before their first communion, often around the age of seven or eight.

origin: From French "penchant", leaning, from "pencher", to lean, ultimately from Latin "pendere", to hang. A penchant is a leaning toward something.

senses.def: strong liking or habitual tendency toward something
senses.ex: My grandfather had a penchant for terrible puns and would deliver one at every family gathering without fail.

origin: From Anglo-Norman and Middle French "pendant", literally hanging, the present participle of "pendre", to hang.

senses.def: piece of jewelry that hangs from a chain worn around the neck
senses.ex: She wore her grandmother's silver pendant, a tiny locket engraved with initials, to every important exam that year.

senses.def: light fixture that hangs from the ceiling by a cord or rod
senses.ex: Three glass pendants hung over the kitchen island, casting a warm light on the countertop during dinner.

senses.def: artwork or object designed as the matching companion of another
senses.ex: The museum finally reunited the portrait with its pendant, a matching painting of the sitter's wife lost for a century.

origin: From Latin "pendulus", hanging, from "pendere", to hang, the same root found in "pendulum" and "pendant".

senses.def: hanging down loosely, often heavily or with a swaying motion
senses.ex: Pendulous clusters of wisteria drooped from the old pergola, brushing the heads of guests as they passed beneath.

origin: Borrowed from Latin "penetralia", the innermost parts of a place, especially a temple, related to "penetrare", to enter deeply.

senses.def: innermost or most secret parts of a place, such as a building or temple
senses.ex: Only senior monks were admitted to the penetralia of the monastery, where the oldest manuscripts were kept under lock.

senses.def: most private or hidden matters of a person, group, or subject
senses.ex: Her biography probes the penetralia of the composer's mind, drawing on diaries he never meant anyone else to read.

origin: Through Old French from Latin "paenitens", regretting, from "paenitere", to regret or repent, the root also of "penitentiary" and "repent".

senses.def: feeling or showing sorrow and regret for having done wrong
senses.ex: The penitent teenager returned the borrowed car washed and fueled, along with a handwritten apology to his neighbor.

senses.def: person who repents of wrongdoing, especially one seeking religious forgiveness
senses.ex: Each spring, penitents walk barefoot along the mountain path to the shrine as an act of devotion.

origin: From Old French "pensif", thoughtful, from "penser", to think, from Latin "pensare", to weigh or consider.

senses.def: engaged in deep or serious thought, often with a hint of sadness
senses.ex: She grew pensive as the train passed her childhood town, staring silently at the shuttered factory where her father once worked.

origin: From Italian "pentimento", repentance or correction, from "pentirsi", to repent, because the hidden layer shows the painter had a change of heart.

senses.def: trace of an earlier image showing through later paint, revealing the artist's changes
senses.ex: As the varnish aged, a faint pentimento emerged near the duchess's sleeve, showing where the painter had first placed a small dog.

senses.def: trace of an earlier idea or version still visible in a later work
senses.ex: In the revised novel, a pentimento of the abandoned first draft survives in one oddly placed scene about a lighthouse.

origin: From Latin "paenultimus", from "paene", almost, and "ultimus", last. The same "paene" appears in "peninsula", almost an island.

senses.def: second to last in a series or sequence
senses.ex: The penultimate chapter ends on a cliffhanger, so readers rarely put the book down before reaching the final page.

syn: second to last, next to last, second-last

origin: From New Latin, from Latin "paene", almost, and "umbra", shadow. A penumbra is literally an almost-shadow.

senses.def: partly shaded outer region of a shadow, especially during an eclipse
senses.ex: Observers in the penumbra saw the sun only partly covered, while those farther south witnessed total darkness.

senses.def: vague surrounding area of uncertainty, or a fringe around something more definite
senses.ex: The new law left a penumbra of uncertainty about whether small family farms needed the same permits as factories.

origin: From Medieval Latin "penuriosus", from Latin "penuria", want or scarcity, the same source as "penury".

senses.def: extremely unwilling to spend money, stingy
senses.ex: The penurious landlord refused to fix the broken heater until tenants threatened to report him to the city.

senses.def: extremely poor, lacking money or resources
senses.ex: As penurious students, they lived on rice and beans and walked everywhere to save the cost of bus fare.

origin: From Latin "penuria", need or scarcity, possibly related to "paene", almost or barely. The rest of its origin is uncertain.

senses.def: extreme poverty in which basic needs go unmet, destitution
senses.ex: After the mill closed, many families in the valley slid into penury and depended on church food drives to survive.

origin: From Spanish "peón", laborer or foot soldier, from Late Latin "pedo", one who goes on foot, from Latin "pes", foot. "Pawn" comes from the same source.

senses.def: low-ranking workers who do routine drudgery and have little power (informal, often humorous)
senses.ex: The executives flew first class to the conference while the interns and other office peons crammed into coach.

senses.def: laborers, especially in Latin American history, bound to work for a landowner to repay debts
senses.ex: Historians describe how peons on the haciendas could rarely escape the debts their employers kept adding to their accounts.

origin: Directly from Latin "per se", by itself, from "per", by or through, and "se", itself.

senses.def: by itself or in itself, intrinsically, apart from other factors
senses.ex: Owning a pet does not lower blood pressure per se, but the daily walks that come with a dog often do.

senses.def: strictly speaking, exactly as the word is usually meant
senses.ex: The cabin was not a hotel per se, but it had clean sheets, hot water, and a host who cooked breakfast.

syn: intrinsically, in itself, inherently, as such

origin: From Latin "perambulare", to walk through, from "per", through, and "ambulare", to walk, the root of "ambulance" and "amble".

senses.def: walk or stroll through or around a place, usually at a leisurely pace
senses.ex: After dinner the retired professor liked to perambulate the village green, nodding to neighbors and admiring their roses.

origin: From Late Latin "perceptibilis", from Latin "percipere", to grasp or perceive, from "per", thoroughly, + "capere", to take.

senses.def: able to be noticed by the senses or the mind, often only slightly
senses.ex: After the storm passed there was a barely perceptible drop in temperature, so we kept our jackets off.

origin: From Latin "perceptivus", from "percipere", to grasp or perceive, from "per", thoroughly, + "capere", to take: a perceptive person takes in what others miss.

senses.def: quick to notice and understand things, especially feelings or hidden motives
senses.ex: Our perceptive coach sensed that the goalie was nervous long before anyone else noticed the shaking hands.

origin: From Latin "percipiens", perceiving, from "percipere", to seize or perceive, from "per", thoroughly, and "capere", to take. A percipient mind takes everything in.

senses.def: having sharp perception or understanding, quick to notice and grasp things
senses.ex: A percipient reviewer noticed that the novel's cheerful narrator was quietly hiding his own grief.

origin: From Latin "percolare", to strain through, from "per", through, + "colare", to strain, from "colum", a strainer.

senses.def: of a liquid or gas, pass slowly through a porous material; seep
senses.ex: Rainwater percolates through the limestone for years before it reaches the underground river.

senses.def: of ideas or news, spread gradually through a group or develop slowly in the mind
senses.ex: Rumors of the merger percolated through the office for weeks before management made any announcement.

senses.def: make coffee by repeatedly passing boiling water through the grounds
senses.ex: The old camp stove sat by the tent with a battered pot of coffee percolating on it.

origin: From Old French "perdiciun", from Late Latin "perditio", from Latin "perdere", to destroy or lose: perdition is the soul utterly lost.

senses.def: in Christian belief, eternal damnation or punishment in hell
senses.ex: The fiery preacher warned that gamblers and drunkards were sliding toward perdition with every sin.

senses.def: complete and utter ruin from which there is no recovery
senses.ex: Reckless borrowing put the family business on the road to perdition within three years.

origin: From Old French "pardurable", from Latin "perdurare", to last throughout, from "per", throughout, + "durare", to last.

senses.def: lasting a very long time or forever; extremely durable
senses.ex: The poet hoped her verses would prove more perdurable than the bronze statues lining the city square.

origin: From Latin "peregrinari", to travel abroad, from "peregrinus", foreign, from "per", through, and "ager", field or land. "Pilgrim" comes from the same word.

senses.def: travel or wander from place to place, especially on foot or over long distances
senses.ex: After graduating, she peregrinated through the villages of Portugal for a year, sketching churches and sleeping in hostels.

origin: From Latin "peregrinatio", travel abroad, from "peregrinari", to travel, from "peregrinus", foreign, the source also of "pilgrim".

senses.def: long journey or period of wandering, especially from place to place
senses.ex: His peregrinations across Central Asia supplied the material for three travel books and countless dinner-party stories.

origin: From Latin "peremptorius", decisive or deadly, from "perimere", to destroy or cut off. A peremptory command cuts off all discussion.

senses.def: insisting on immediate obedience and allowing no questions or refusal, brusque
senses.ex: With a peremptory wave of her hand, the director ended the debate and ordered everyone back to rehearsal.

origin: From Latin "perennis", lasting through the year, from "per", through, and "annus", year, the root of "annual" and "anniversary".

senses.def: lasting a very long time, or recurring again and again
senses.ex: Parking downtown is a perennial complaint at town meetings, raised every year and never quite solved.

senses.def: of a plant, living for several years rather than one season
senses.ex: Gardeners like perennial herbs such as thyme and mint because they return each spring without replanting.

senses.def: plant that lives for more than two years
senses.ex: She filled the border with hardy perennials so the garden would bloom year after year with little work.

origin: From Late Latin "perfervidus", from "per", thoroughly, + "fervidus", glowing or burning, from "fervere", to boil: passion at a rolling boil.

senses.def: intensely, often excessively, passionate or zealous
senses.ex: The candidate's perfervid supporters chanted for an hour, drowning out every reporter who tried to ask a question.

origin: From Latin "perfidiosus", from "perfidia", treachery, from "perfidus", faithless, built on "fides", faith, the root of "fidelity".

senses.def: deceitful and untrustworthy, guilty of betraying trust
senses.ex: The perfidious adviser sold the king's battle plans to the enemy while swearing loyalty at every council meeting.

origin: From Latin "perfidia", treachery, from "perfidus", faithless, built on "fides", faith, as in "fidelity".

senses.def: deliberate betrayal of trust, treachery
senses.ex: Fans called it perfidy when the star player, after vowing to stay, signed with the team's bitterest rival.

origin: From Latin "perforare", to bore through, from "per", through, + "forare", to bore or pierce.

senses.def: make a hole or holes through something; pierce
senses.ex: A sliver of glass perforated the tire, and we heard the air hissing out within seconds.

senses.def: make a line of small holes in paper or film so it can be torn easily
senses.ex: The printer perforates each ticket so the usher can tear off the stub at the door.

origin: From Old French "par force", by force: what happens perforce happens because circumstances force it.

senses.def: by necessity; because circumstances leave no other choice
senses.ex: With the bridge washed out, the travelers perforce spent the night in the tiny mountain village.

syn: necessarily, inevitably, unavoidably, of necessity, willy-nilly

origin: From Late Latin "perfunctorius", careless, from "perfungi", to discharge or get through a duty, from "per", through, and "fungi", to perform.

senses.def: done routinely and with minimal effort, care, or interest
senses.ex: The guard gave our passports a perfunctory glance and waved us through without asking a single question.

origin: Through French and Latin from Greek "peri", near, and "ge", Earth. Its opposite, "apogee", is the point farthest from Earth.

senses.def: point in the orbit of the moon or a satellite where it is closest to Earth
senses.ex: Because the full moon fell near perigee, it looked noticeably larger and brighter than usual over the harbor.

origin: From Old French "perilleus", from "peril", danger, which goes back to Latin "periculum", danger or trial.

senses.def: full of danger or serious risk
senses.ex: The climbers made a perilous descent along the icy ridge after a sudden storm cut off their planned route.

origin: From Greek "perimetros", from "peri", around, + "metron", measure: the measure all the way around.

senses.def: the outer boundary or edge of an area
senses.ex: Volunteers walked the perimeter of the park, picking up litter along the fence.

senses.def: the total length of the boundary of a closed shape
senses.ex: To find the perimeter of the rectangle, add twice its length to twice its width.

senses.def: guarded or defended boundary around a military position or secure site
senses.ex: Soldiers patrolled the perimeter of the base all night, checking the wire for any breaks.

origin: From Greek "peripatetikos", given to walking about, from "peri", around, and "patein", to walk. Aristotle's followers were called Peripatetics after the walkway where he taught.

senses.def: traveling from place to place, often for work, not settled in one location
senses.ex: Her peripatetic childhood as an army officer's daughter meant attending seven different schools in three countries.

origin: From Greek "peripeteia", a sudden change, from "peri", around, + "piptein", to fall: fortune falls the other way around.

senses.def: sudden reversal of fortune, especially the turning point in a tragedy
senses.ex: The peripeteia comes when Oedipus learns that the killer he has been hunting is himself.

senses.def: any sudden, dramatic change in circumstances
senses.ex: The startup's peripeteia arrived overnight, when its biggest investor pulled out and the bank froze its accounts.

origin: From "periphery", from Greek "periphereia", circumference, from "peri", around, and "pherein", to carry, so the line carried around the edge.

senses.def: of minor or secondary importance, not central to the main issue
senses.ex: The committee spent an hour on peripheral questions about catering and never reached the budget it had met to discuss.

senses.def: located on or near the outer edge of something
senses.ex: A deer appeared in his peripheral vision, and he braked just before it leaped across the dark road.

senses.def: device such as a printer or keyboard connected to a computer
senses.ex: The laptop has only two ports, so she bought a hub to connect her mouse, monitor, and other peripherals.

origin: From Greek "periphereia", circumference, from "peri", around, plus "pherein", to carry: the line carried around the edge.

senses.def: the outer edge or boundary of an area or object
senses.ex: New warehouses are rising on the periphery of the city, where land is cheaper.

senses.def: the less important or influential part of a group, field, or activity
senses.ex: For years she stayed on the periphery of the debate club, attending meetings but never competing.

origin: From Greek "periphrasis", from "peri", around, + "phrazein", to declare or speak: talking around a thing instead of naming it.

senses.def: use of a longer, roundabout expression instead of a shorter, direct one
senses.ex: Calling a lie a terminological inexactitude is a famous example of periphrasis used to soften an insult.

senses.def: a roundabout phrase or expression used in place of a simpler word
senses.ex: The memo was so full of periphrases that nobody realized it was announcing layoffs.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "perjurie", from Latin "periurare", to swear falsely, from "per-", here meaning wrongly, and "iurare", to swear, the root of "jury".

senses.def: crime of deliberately lying while under oath
senses.ex: The witness was charged with perjury after phone records proved she had lied to the jury about her whereabouts.

syn: lying under oath, false testimony, false swearing, forswearing

origin: From Latin "permeabilis", from "permeare", to pass through, from "per", through, + "meare", to go.

senses.def: allowing liquids or gases to pass through
senses.ex: Sandy soil is highly permeable, so the garden needs watering far more often than clay beds do.

senses.def: open to the passage of people, ideas, or influences
senses.ex: The border between the two villages was permeable, and families crossed it daily to trade and visit.

origin: From Latin "permeare", to pass through, from "per", through, and "meare", to go or pass.

senses.def: spread throughout something and fill every part of it
senses.ex: The smell of fresh bread permeated the whole apartment building by the time the tenants woke up.

origin: Past form of "permeate", from Latin "permeare", to pass through, from "per", through, and "meare", to go or pass.

senses.def: spread throughout something and filled every part of it
senses.ex: A sense of dread permeated the newsroom as reporters waited for word about their missing colleague.

senses.def: thoroughly filled or soaked through by a quality, feeling, or substance
senses.ex: The old cabin, permeated with decades of wood smoke, smelled like a campfire even in midsummer.

origin: From French "permissif", from Latin "permittere", to let go through or allow, from "per", through, + "mittere", to send.

senses.def: allowing a great deal of freedom, especially in behavior or morals; lenient
senses.ex: Critics blamed permissive parenting for the children's habit of staying up past midnight on school nights.

senses.def: allowing something but not requiring it
senses.ex: The new zoning rule is permissive, so owners may build backyard cottages but are not obliged to.

origin: From Latin "permutatio", change or exchange, from "permutare", to change thoroughly, from "per", thoroughly, and "mutare", to change, as in "mutation".

senses.def: one of several possible versions, variations, or arrangements of something
senses.ex: The band has gone through so many permutations that only the drummer remains from the original lineup.

senses.def: in mathematics, an ordered arrangement of a set of items
senses.ex: The letters A, B, and C can be lined up in six permutations, from ABC all the way to CBA.

origin: From Latin "perniciosus", destructive, from "pernicies", ruin, from "per", thoroughly, and "nex" (stem "nec-"), violent death.

senses.def: harmful or destructive, especially in a gradual or hidden way
senses.ex: Doctors warned that the pernicious effects of the chemical might not appear until decades after a worker's exposure.

origin: From Latin "peroratio", from "perorare", to speak at length or bring a speech to a close, from "per", through, and "orare", to speak, as in "orator".

senses.def: concluding part of a speech, meant to sum up and stir the audience
senses.ex: In her peroration, the senator urged the graduates to treat public service as a duty rather than a career move.

senses.def: long, grandly worded speech or harangue
senses.ex: The coach's twenty-minute peroration on teamwork left the exhausted players staring at the floor of the locker room.

origin: From Latin "perpetrare", to carry through or accomplish, from "per", through, and "patrare", to bring about.

senses.def: carry out or commit a harmful, illegal, or immoral act
senses.ex: Investigators believe the same small group perpetrated the string of online scams that targeted elderly retirees.

syn: commit, carry out, perform, execute, inflict

origin: From Old French "perpetuel", from Latin "perpetualis", from "perpetuus", continuous, from "per", through, + "petere", to go toward or seek.

senses.def: lasting forever or for an indefinitely long time
senses.ex: The monks kept a perpetual flame burning in the chapel, tending it day and night for centuries.

senses.def: occurring so often or continuously that it seems endless
senses.ex: Living beside the airport meant enduring the perpetual roar of jets taking off.

origin: From Latin "perpetuare", to make permanent, from "perpetuus", continuous or everlasting, the source of "perpetual".

senses.def: cause something, often something bad, to continue indefinitely
senses.ex: Critics argued that the cartoon perpetuated harmful stereotypes about immigrants that schools had spent years trying to undo.

origin: From Latin "perplexus", entangled or confused, from "per", through, + "plexus", woven or braided: a perplexed mind is tangled up.

senses.def: make someone feel completely puzzled or confused
senses.ex: The magician's final trick perplexed even the engineers in the audience, who could not work out how it was done.

origin: From Medieval Latin "perquisitum", something acquired, from Latin "perquirere", to seek out thoroughly. The casual word "perk" is a shortening of it.

senses.def: benefit or privilege that comes with a job in addition to the salary
senses.ex: A company car was the perquisite she valued most, since it saved her thousands of dollars every year.

senses.def: right or privilege regarded as belonging to a particular person or group
senses.ex: In that office, choosing the music during lunch was considered the perquisite of whoever had worked there longest.

syn: perk, benefit, fringe benefit, bonus, extra

origin: Plural of "perquisite", from Medieval Latin "perquisitum", something acquired, from Latin "perquirere", to seek out thoroughly. "Perks" is the everyday short form.

senses.def: benefits or privileges that come with a job in addition to the salary
senses.ex: The perquisites of the ambassador's post included a furnished residence, a driver, and free schooling for her children.

senses.def: rights or privileges regarded as belonging to a particular person or group
senses.ex: Front-row seats and early access to new menus were among the perquisites the club reserved for founding members.

syn: perks, benefits, fringe benefits, bonuses, extras

origin: From Latin "perseverantia", from "perseverare", to persist, from "per", thoroughly, and "severus", strict or serious.

senses.def: continued effort to do or achieve something despite difficulty, failure, or delay
senses.ex: After forty rejection letters, the novelist's perseverance paid off when a small press agreed to publish her first book.

origin: From French "persiflage", from "persifler", to tease or mock, from "per", through, + "siffler", to whistle, from Latin "sibilare", to hiss.

senses.def: light, teasing talk or good-natured banter
senses.ex: The two old friends kept up a stream of persiflage about each other's cooking throughout the dinner party.

origin: An American form of Scots "pernickety", fussy about small details, a word of uncertain origin.

senses.def: overly fussy about small details; hard to please
senses.ex: The persnickety editor sent the article back twice because of a single misplaced comma.

senses.def: of a task or device, requiring very precise care to get right
senses.ex: Tuning the antique clock is persnickety work, since a tiny turn of the screw throws off the timing.

origin: From Latin "persona", the mask worn by an actor, then a character, of uncertain origin, possibly from Etruscan "phersu", masked figure.

senses.def: the image or personality a person presents to others, often different from the private self
senses.ex: On stage the comedian had a brash, loud persona, but friends knew him as shy and thoughtful.

senses.def: character or speaking voice adopted by a writer or performer in a work
senses.ex: The poet writes in the persona of an aging lighthouse keeper looking back on his lonely life.

origin: From Middle English, formed from "person" plus "-able". It first meant having a pleasing appearance, then came to mean having a pleasant manner.

senses.def: pleasant in manner and appearance, easy to like
senses.ex: The personable new receptionist learned every patient's name within a week, and the waiting room felt warmer for it.

origin: Past form of "personify", based on French "personnifier", from "person" plus "-fy", to make. To personify is to make something into a person.

senses.def: embodied a quality perfectly, was a typical example of it
senses.ex: For many fans, the quiet goalkeeper personified the team's values of patience, discipline, and loyalty.

senses.def: represented an idea or thing as a person or gave it human qualities
senses.ex: Ancient sculptors personified Justice as a woman holding scales, an image still seen outside many courthouses.

senses.def: after a noun, in human form, as a perfect embodiment of that quality
senses.ex: Our grandmother was patience personified, calmly teaching six restless cousins to knit on a rainy afternoon.

origin: From Latin "perspicax", sharp-sighted, from "perspicere", to see through, from "per", through, and "specere", to look, the root also of "perspective".

senses.def: having keen insight and understanding, quick to notice what others miss
senses.ex: A perspicacious investor, she sold her shares months before the company's accounting problems became public.

origin: From Latin "perspicacitas", sharpness of sight, from "perspicax", sharp-sighted, from "perspicere", to see through, from "per", through, and "specere", to look.

senses.def: keen insight, the ability to understand things quickly and clearly
senses.ex: The detective's perspicacity let her spot the single inconsistent detail in a suspect's otherwise flawless alibi.

origin: From Latin "perspicuus", transparent or clear, from "perspicere", to see through, from "per", through, + "specere", to look.

senses.def: clearly expressed and easy to understand; lucid
senses.ex: Her perspicuous explanation of the tax changes made sense even to readers with no background in finance.

origin: From Middle English "pert", shortened from "apert", open, from Old French "apert" and Latin "apertus", open, suggesting someone unusually forward.

senses.def: boldly cheeky or playfully disrespectful, especially in speech or manner
senses.ex: When the teacher asked for her homework, the girl gave a pert reply that made the whole class giggle.

senses.def: small, neat, and attractively perky in shape or style
senses.ex: The sculptor gave the marble fox a pert nose and upright ears, so it seemed ready to dart away.

senses.def: lively and cheerful in a bright, alert way
senses.ex: Despite the early hour, the pert host of the morning radio show joked with callers about the terrible weather.

origin: From Latin "pertinax", very tenacious, from "per", thoroughly, and "tenax", holding fast, the source of "tenacious".

senses.def: stubbornly persistent in holding to a purpose, opinion, or course of action
senses.ex: The pertinacious reporter called the agency every morning for six months until it finally released the records.

origin: From Latin "pertinens", from "pertinere", to reach or relate to, from "per", through, and "tenere", to hold. "Pertain" comes from the same verb.

senses.def: directly relevant to the matter being considered
senses.ex: The judge allowed only pertinent evidence, so the lawyer's stories about the defendant's childhood were struck from the record.

origin: From Latin "perturbare", to throw into confusion, from "per", thoroughly, and "turbare", to disturb, a relative of "turbulent".

senses.def: make someone anxious, worried, or unsettled
senses.ex: News that the only bridge into town might close for a year perturbed commuters who had no other route to work.

origin: From Middle English, probably from "per-", thoroughly, plus "use". It first meant to use up, then to go through something in detail.

senses.def: read or examine something carefully and in detail
senses.ex: Before signing the lease, she perused every clause and found a hidden fee for using the building's laundry room.

senses.def: look over or browse casually (a common use some careful writers avoid)
senses.ex: We perused the menu while waiting for our friends, though we already knew we would order the dumplings.

origin: From Latin "pervadere", to go through, from "per", through, and "vadere", to go, so something that pervades passes through everything.

senses.def: spread through and be present in every part of something
senses.ex: The smell of fresh bread pervaded the old apartment building, drawing sleepy tenants down to the bakery at dawn.

origin: From Latin "pervasus", from "pervadere", to spread through, from "per", through, and "vadere", to go. Something pervasive goes everywhere.

senses.def: spreading widely through an area, group, or system and present everywhere
senses.ex: Smartphones have become so pervasive that many teenagers cannot remember a time before constant texting.

origin: From Latin "perversus", turned the wrong way, from "pervertere", to overturn, from "per", thoroughly, and "vertere", to turn.

senses.def: deliberately and unreasonably doing the opposite of what is expected or wanted
senses.ex: With perverse delight, my little brother wore his loudest shirt to the formal dinner precisely because Mom had banned it.
