senses.def: of a result or effect, contrary to what was intended or sensible
senses.ex: In a perverse twist, the new parking fines brought so much traffic to side streets that congestion actually worsened.

senses.def: morally wrong or unnatural in a disturbing way
senses.ex: The jury was shocked by the perverse pleasure the con artist seemed to take in ruining his victims.

origin: From French "pessimisme", built on Latin "pessimus", worst, the superlative of "malus", bad, so a pessimist expects the worst.

senses.def: tendency to expect the worst and focus on the bad side of things
senses.ex: Her pessimism about the science fair vanished when the judges praised the water filter she had spent months building.

senses.def: philosophical view that suffering and evil outweigh good in the world
senses.ex: Schopenhauer's pessimism holds that life is driven by restless desire and that suffering outweighs any happiness we achieve.

origin: From Latin "pestifer", bearing plague, from "pestis", plague, and "-fer", carrying.

senses.def: annoying in a persistent, troublesome way
senses.ex: A pestiferous mosquito whined around the tent all night, keeping the exhausted hikers awake until the sky turned gray.

senses.def: carrying or spreading infectious disease
senses.ex: Trading ships unknowingly carried pestiferous rats from port to port, helping spread plague along the medieval sea routes.

origin: From Latin "pestilentialis", from "pestilentia", plague, the source of "pestilence", so the word still carries the idea of spreading disease.

senses.def: causing or spreading a deadly infectious disease
senses.ex: Cholera thrived in the pestilential slums of the nineteenth-century city, where sewage seeped into the drinking wells.

senses.def: morally harmful and likely to corrupt others
senses.ex: The reformer denounced gambling dens as a pestilential influence that was ruining young workers and their families.

senses.def: extremely annoying or unpleasant
senses.ex: We spent the whole afternoon stuck behind a pestilential tour bus that crawled along the narrow mountain road.

origin: Coined in 1964 by Australian scientist Richard Thomas, in a paper with Isabel Bear, from Greek "petra", rock, and "ichor", the fluid in the veins of the gods.

senses.def: pleasant earthy smell that rises when rain falls after a long dry spell
senses.ex: When the first storm broke the August drought, she opened every window to breathe in the petrichor rising from the fields.

origin: From Middle French "pétrifier", from Medieval Latin "petrificare", from Greek "petra", rock, and Latin "facere", to make, so literally to make into rock.

senses.def: frighten someone so badly that they cannot move or think
senses.ex: The thought of speaking before the entire school petrified him, and his hands shook for an hour beforehand.

senses.def: change organic material into stone by slowly replacing it with minerals
senses.ex: Over millions of years, groundwater rich in silica petrified the fallen trees, preserving their growth rings in stone.

senses.def: make or become rigid, lifeless, and unable to change
senses.ex: Decades without new leadership had petrified the agency, whose managers rejected every reform as a threat to tradition.

origin: From Latin "petrosus", rocky, from "petra", rock, borrowed from Greek "petra", the root also of "petrify" and "petroleum".

senses.def: hard like stone, rocky or stony
senses.ex: The hikers' boots clattered across the petrous slope, where not a single blade of grass could take root.

origin: From "petty", small or trivial, plus "fogger", an old word of uncertain origin. The "petty" half is the memory hook: someone fussing over small things.

senses.def: someone who quibbles over trivial details and raises petty objections
senses.ex: The committee's resident pettifogger delayed the vote for an hour by disputing the placement of a single comma.

senses.def: lawyer of little skill or scruple who handles minor cases with shady tricks
senses.ex: Cheated by a small-town pettifogger, the farmer paid twice for a deed that the court later declared worthless.

origin: From Middle English "pety", small or minor, from Old French "petit", little. English "petite" comes from the same French word.

senses.def: of little importance or value, trivial
senses.ex: Don't let petty complaints about parking distract the council from the real budget crisis facing the town this year.

senses.def: small-minded and spiteful about minor things
senses.ex: It was petty of him to unfollow his friend simply because she forgot to like his vacation photos.

senses.def: minor in scale or rank, especially of crimes or officials
senses.ex: He began with petty theft, pocketing candy from corner stores, before the police finally caught him stealing a bicycle.

origin: From Latin "petulans", bold or impudent, related to "petere", to seek or attack. The modern sense of sulky, childish bad temper developed later.

senses.def: childishly sulky, impatient, or bad-tempered
senses.ex: When the referee denied his appeal, the petulant tennis star smashed his racket and refused to shake hands.

origin: From Greek "phalanx", line of battle. The ancient Greek phalanx was a tight block of soldiers with overlapping shields and long spears.

senses.def: closely packed group of people or things, often united in a common purpose
senses.ex: A phalanx of photographers blocked the courthouse doors as the famous defendant stepped out of her car.

senses.def: ancient Greek battle formation of infantry standing in close, deep ranks
senses.ex: The Macedonian phalanx, bristling with eighteen-foot spears, was nearly impossible to break with a frontal charge.

origin: From Old French "fantasme", through Latin, from Greek "phantasma", an apparition, from "phantazein", to make visible. It is a doublet of "phantom".

senses.def: ghostly figure or image that seems real but has no physical existence
senses.ex: Alone in the foggy graveyard, the traveler mistook a swaying willow for a phantasm drifting between the headstones.

senses.def: illusion or mental image produced by the imagination
senses.ex: In his fever he was tormented by phantasms of old enemies, who vanished whenever the nurse turned on the lamp.

origin: From "phantasmagoria", the name of a popular early 1800s show of ghostly projected images, built on Greek "phantasma", apparition.

senses.def: dreamlike and bizarre, with strange images that shift and change rapidly
senses.ex: The parade's phantasmagorical floats, with glowing dragons and melting clocks, drew gasps from children lining the street.

origin: From Greek "phatos", spoken, from "phemi", I say, plus "-ic". Phatic speech is spoken for the sake of contact rather than content.

senses.def: of speech used to maintain social contact rather than convey information
senses.ex: When a neighbor asks how you are, the question is usually phatic, a friendly gesture rather than a request for medical news.

origin: Plural of "phenomenon", from Greek "phainomenon", thing that appears, from "phainein", to show. It keeps the Greek plural ending "-a".

senses.def: facts, events, or situations that can be observed, especially remarkable or puzzling ones
senses.ex: Ball lightning and other rare weather phenomena are hard to study because they vanish within seconds.

origin: From Philander, a stock name for a lover in 18th-century stories and poems, taken from a Greek name built from "philos", loving, and "andr-", man.

senses.def: of a man, have casual love affairs with women, especially while married or committed
senses.ex: The biography revealed that the beloved actor had philandered for years while his wife managed his career.

syn: womanize, have affairs, play around, flirt

origin: From "philanthropy", from Greek "philanthropia", love of humankind, from "philos", loving, and "anthropos", human being.

senses.def: person who gives money or time generously to improve the welfare of others
senses.ex: A local philanthropist paid for the new library wing, asking only that it stay open late for working parents.

origin: From Greek "philanthropia", love of humankind, from "philos", loving, and "anthropos", human being, as in "anthropology".

senses.def: generous giving of money or effort to promote the welfare of others
senses.ex: Her philanthropy focused on rural clinics, and over two decades she funded more than forty of them.

senses.def: organization or foundation that distributes charitable gifts
senses.ex: Several large philanthropies joined forces to pay for clean water projects across the drought-stricken region.

origin: From French "philatélie", coined in 1864 from Greek "philein", to love, and "ateleia", freedom from tax, since a stamp showed delivery was already paid.

senses.def: someone who collects and studies postage stamps
senses.ex: A devoted philatelist, my uncle spent weekends cataloging rare airmail stamps from countries that no longer exist.

origin: From Greek "philippikos", concerning Philip, after the fiery speeches Demosthenes delivered against Philip II of Macedon, whose name means "lover of horses".

senses.def: bitter, impassioned speech or written attack denouncing someone
senses.ex: The senator's twenty-minute philippic against the governor left the chamber silent and dominated the next morning's headlines.

origin: From the biblical Philistines, enemies of the Israelites. German university students later called townspeople "Philister", and the word came to mean an uncultured person.

senses.def: person who is hostile or indifferent to art, culture, and learning
senses.ex: The new owner, a self-declared philistine, wanted to paint over the historic mural to make room for an advertisement.

senses.def: hostile or indifferent to art, culture, and learning
senses.ex: Critics attacked the council's philistine decision to cut all funding for the city orchestra and the public art program.

origin: From Latin "philologia", from Greek "philologia", love of learning and literature, from "philos", loving, and "logos", word or reason.

senses.def: study of language in historical texts, especially ancient and classical ones
senses.ex: Her training in philology let her date the medieval manuscript by studying its spelling, grammar, and scribal habits.

senses.def: historical and comparative study of how languages develop and relate
senses.ex: Nineteenth-century philology traced the kinship of Sanskrit, Greek, and Latin by comparing their sound changes and grammar.

origin: From Latin "philtrum", love potion, from Greek "philtron", love charm and also the dimple in the upper lip. It shares its source with "philter".

senses.def: shallow vertical groove between the base of the nose and the upper lip
senses.ex: The makeup artist dabbed a little highlighter on the actor's philtrum to give his upper lip more definition.

origin: From Greek "phlegmatikos", from "phlegma", phlegm, one of the four bodily humors that ancient doctors believed made a person calm and sluggish.

senses.def: calm, unemotional, and not easily excited or upset
senses.ex: Even when the stage lights failed mid-performance, the phlegmatic pianist kept playing as if nothing had happened.

origin: First recorded around 1790, taken from words ending in "-phobia", which goes back to Greek "phobos", fear.

senses.def: intense, irrational fear of a particular thing or situation
senses.ex: Her phobia of elevators was so severe that she climbed fourteen flights of stairs to her office every morning.

senses.def: strong dislike or aversion toward something
senses.ex: My brother has a real phobia about paperwork and will let tax forms pile up unopened for months.

origin: Of uncertain origin, perhaps from "fawney", a fake gilt ring used by swindlers, from Irish "fáinne", ring.

senses.def: not genuine, fake, fraudulent, or insincere
senses.ex: The caller claimed to be from the bank, but his phony account number gave the scam away immediately.

senses.def: person who pretends to be something they are not, or who fakes their beliefs
senses.ex: Classmates called him a phony for preaching about the environment while driving his huge truck to school every day.

origin: From French "phosphène", from Greek "phos", light, and "phainein", to appear or shine, describing light that appears without any real source.

senses.def: spot or flash of light seen without light entering the eye, as when rubbing closed eyes
senses.ex: Pressing his palms against his tired eyes, he watched phosphenes bloom and drift across the darkness like tiny green fireworks.

origin: From Late Latin "physiognomia", from Greek "physis", nature or appearance, and "gnome", a means of knowing, suggesting a person's nature can be read from their looks.

senses.def: person's facial features, especially when seen as revealing character
senses.ex: The portrait captured the general's stern physiognomy, from his heavy brow to the hard, unsmiling line of his mouth.

senses.def: discredited practice of judging someone's character from their face
senses.ex: Some nineteenth-century criminologists leaned on physiognomy, wrongly claiming that a sloping forehead or large jaw marked a born criminal.

senses.def: general outward form or character of a place or thing
senses.ex: New highways and glass towers have altered the physiognomy of the old port city beyond recognition.

origin: From "physiology", from Greek "physis", nature, and "-logia", study, so the study of how living bodies naturally work.

senses.def: relating to the normal functions and processes of living bodies
senses.ex: Fear triggers physiological changes such as a racing heart, faster breathing, and a sudden rush of adrenaline.

origin: From Spanish "picaresco", from "pícaro", rogue. Spanish picaresque novels followed a lovable rascal through a string of adventures.

senses.def: relating to episodic fiction about the adventures of a roguish but appealing hero
senses.ex: The picaresque novel follows a teenage con artist as he tricks his way from one Mississippi river town to the next.

senses.def: involving rambling, roguish adventures loosely strung together
senses.ex: His picaresque year abroad included busking in Lisbon, picking grapes in Burgundy, and sleeping on a Greek ferry.

origin: From Louisiana French "picaillon", a small coin of little value, from Occitan "picalhon", a cheap coin. Something picayune is worth only small change.

senses.def: petty or trivial, of very little value or importance
senses.ex: The two neighbors spent years in court over a picayune dispute about a fence that stood six inches too far left.

senses.def: small-minded and fussy about unimportant details
senses.ex: Her picayune editor rejected the article over comma placement while ignoring the factual error in the headline.

origin: From "picture" plus "-esque", in the manner of, modeled on French "pittoresque". A picturesque scene looks as if it belongs in a painting.

senses.def: visually charming or quaint, like a scene in a painting
senses.ex: Tourists crowded the picturesque fishing village to photograph its pastel houses and bobbing wooden boats.

senses.def: of language, vivid and colorful
senses.ex: Her grandfather had a picturesque way of speaking, describing a cold morning as colder than a banker's handshake.

origin: From "pie", an old name for the black-and-white magpie, and "bald", having white patches, as in the bald eagle.

senses.def: having irregular patches of two colors, especially black and white
senses.ex: The piebald pony, black with bold white splotches, was the easiest horse to spot in the crowded pasture.

senses.def: horse or other animal with black and white patches
senses.ex: At the county fair, the young rider led her gentle piebald around the ring and won a blue ribbon.

origin: From Middle English "pecemele", from "pece", piece, and Old English "mælum", at a time, so it literally means one piece at a time.

senses.def: done gradually in separate stages, often without an overall plan
senses.ex: The city's piecemeal approach to road repair left drivers dodging fresh potholes a block from newly paved streets.

senses.def: bit by bit, in small separate stages
senses.ex: Unable to afford a full renovation, they rebuilt the old farmhouse piecemeal over the course of ten years.

origin: From "pie", an old word for the magpie, from Latin "pica". The Pied Piper of the legend wore a patchwork coat of many colors.

senses.def: having two or more colors in patches or blotches
senses.ex: A pied wagtail, its feathers neatly split into black and white, bobbed along the edge of the pond.

origin: From Middle French "pieté", from Latin "pietas", dutiful devotion, from "pius", dutiful. The word "pity" comes from the same Latin source.

senses.def: deep devotion and reverence toward God or religion
senses.ex: Known for her piety, the elderly widow attended the dawn service every day and quietly fed the parish's poor.

senses.def: dutiful respect and loyalty toward parents, family, or country
senses.ex: In Confucian tradition, filial piety requires children to honor their parents and care for them in old age.

senses.def: conventional moral statement that sounds virtuous but may be insincere
senses.ex: Voters grew tired of the candidate's empty pieties about family values after reports of his many broken promises.

origin: From Latin "pigmentum", coloring matter, from "pingere", to paint, the same verb that gave English "picture".

senses.def: powdered substance mixed into paint, ink, or dye to give it color
senses.ex: The restorers analyzed the blue pigment and found it was ground lapis lazuli, an expensive mineral imported from Afghanistan.

senses.def: natural substance that gives color to skin, hair, leaves, or other tissue
senses.ex: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that lets plant leaves capture sunlight and turn it into chemical energy.

senses.def: color something with pigment, usually used in the form pigmented
senses.ex: Her heavily pigmented skin protected her from sunburn during the long summer fieldwork in the desert.

origin: From Old French "pelfre", plunder or booty, of unknown origin. It is related to "pelf", money gained dishonestly.

senses.def: steal small items or small amounts, often repeatedly
senses.ex: The night clerk was fired after cameras caught him pilfering candy bars and cigarettes from the store's shelves.

origin: From Old French "piller", to plunder, probably from Latin "pilare", to strip of hair, so pillagers strip a place bare.

senses.def: rob a place violently of its goods, especially during war
senses.ex: After the city fell, the invading soldiers pillaged the churches and carried off gold candlesticks and jeweled altar cloths.

senses.def: violent robbery of a place, especially by soldiers in wartime
senses.ex: The museum's oldest manuscripts survived the pillage only because a monk had buried them beneath the cellar floor.

origin: From Old French "pilori", a wooden frame with holes for the head and hands, where offenders were locked up for public mockery. Its earlier origin is uncertain.

senses.def: attack or ridicule someone publicly and harshly
senses.ex: Late-night comedians pilloried the senator for days after he admitted he had never read the bill he sponsored.

senses.def: wooden frame with holes for the head and hands, used in the past for public punishment
senses.ex: In colonial Boston, a man caught cheating customers might spend an afternoon in the pillory while neighbors jeered.

origin: Named after Christopher Pinchbeck, an 18th-century London watchmaker who developed this cheap alloy that imitated gold.

senses.def: cheap and showy but fake, an inferior imitation of something better
senses.ex: Critics dismissed the senator's speech as pinchbeck patriotism, all flag-waving slogans with no real policy behind them.

senses.def: alloy of copper and zinc once used as imitation gold in cheap jewelry
senses.ex: The antique dealer tested the locket and sadly told her it was only pinchbeck, not the gold she had hoped.

origin: The verb comes from Middle English "pinen", to suffer or torment, from an old word for pain, probably from Latin "poena", punishment. The tree name comes separately from Latin "pinus".

senses.def: long intensely for something or someone that is lost or out of reach
senses.ex: Living in a cramped city apartment, she pined for the open fields and quiet nights of her family's farm.

senses.def: waste away or lose strength from grief or longing, usually with "away"
senses.ex: According to the legend, the faithful dog pined away at the train station after its owner never returned.

senses.def: evergreen cone-bearing tree with clusters of long needles, or the wood from it
senses.ex: The cabin's walls were built from local pine, and the whole room smelled faintly of resin on warm days.

origin: The wing sense comes from Old French "pignon", from Latin "penna", feather, while the gear sense is a separate borrowing of French "pignon".

senses.def: hold or tie someone's arms so they cannot move or resist
senses.ex: Two security guards pinioned the intruder's arms behind his back until the police arrived at the gallery.

senses.def: literary word for a bird's wing, especially its outer part
senses.ex: The hawk spread its broad pinions and rose effortlessly on the warm air above the canyon.

senses.def: small gear whose teeth mesh with a larger gear or a toothed bar
senses.ex: In a rack-and-pinion steering system, turning the wheel rotates a pinion that slides the toothed rack sideways.

origin: From Late Latin "pinnaculum", peak, a diminutive of Latin "pinna", a pointed battlement or feather.

senses.def: highest point of achievement, success, or development
senses.ex: Winning the national championship was the pinnacle of her coaching career, and she retired the following spring.

senses.def: tall, pointed peak of rock or mountain
senses.ex: Climbers spent two days reaching the granite pinnacle that towered above the rest of the ridge.

senses.def: small pointed turret on a roof or buttress, common in Gothic buildings
senses.ex: Stone pinnacles rose from every corner of the cathedral, making its outline look like a row of spears.

origin: From "pioneer", from French "pionnier", originally a foot soldier who went ahead of an army to dig and clear the way.

senses.def: introducing new ideas or methods, among the first to do something
senses.ex: Her pioneering research on bee communication changed how scientists understand insect intelligence.

senses.def: being the first to develop, explore, or use something
senses.ex: The small startup is pioneering a method for turning food waste into cheap fertilizer for local farms.

origin: From Latin "pius", dutiful or devout. In Rome the word praised faithful duty to the gods, to one's family, and to one's country.

senses.def: deeply religious and devoted to worship and religious duties
senses.ex: Her pious grandmother attended Mass every morning and kept a small shrine beside the kitchen window.

senses.def: making a hypocritical show of virtue, sanctimonious
senses.ex: The executive's pious speech about honesty rang hollow after reporters uncovered his falsified expense reports.

senses.def: of a hope or wish, sincere but unlikely to come true
senses.ex: The treaty expressed the pious hope that both armies would withdraw, but neither side moved a single tank.

origin: From French "piquant", pricking or stinging, from "piquer", to prick. A piquant flavor pricks the tongue in a pleasant way.

senses.def: having a pleasantly sharp, tangy, or spicy taste
senses.ex: The chef added capers and lemon to give the mild fish a piquant sauce that woke up every bite.

senses.def: pleasantly stimulating, intriguing, or provocative
senses.ex: The memoir's most piquant detail was that the strict headmaster had once played drums in a punk band.

origin: From French "piquer", to prick or sting. To pique someone's curiosity is to prick it awake, and a fit of pique is the sting of hurt pride.

senses.def: stimulate or arouse interest or curiosity
senses.ex: A mysterious locked trunk in the attic piqued the children's curiosity, and they spent all afternoon hunting for the key.

senses.def: feeling of irritation or resentment caused by wounded pride
senses.ex: In a fit of pique after losing the election, the club president quit and took the trophy case keys with him.

senses.def: irritate someone or hurt their pride
senses.ex: She was piqued that nobody at the party had noticed the haircut she had spent all afternoon getting.

origin: From Latin "piscis", fish, the same root found in "Pisces", the zodiac sign of the fish.

senses.def: relating to fish or resembling a fish
senses.ex: The creature in the old woodcut had a human face but piscine scales, fins, and a forked tail.

origin: From "pit" plus "fall" in an old sense of trap, from Old English "fealle", trap. A pitfall was originally a hidden pit for catching animals.

senses.def: hidden or unexpected danger or difficulty that is easy to run into
senses.ex: The guide warns first-time home buyers about common pitfalls, such as skipping the inspection to save money.

senses.def: concealed pit used as a trap for animals or people
senses.ex: The hunters covered the pitfall with branches and leaves so the wild boar would not notice it.

origin: From Old English "pitha", the soft inner part of a plant. Its deeper origin is unknown. It is related to "pit", the stone of a fruit.

senses.def: essential or most important part of an argument, idea, or matter
senses.ex: The professor skipped the background details and went straight to the pith of the debate over free will.

senses.def: spongy tissue in plant stems, or the white layer under the peel of citrus fruit
senses.ex: He carefully scraped the bitter white pith from the orange peel before candying the strips for dessert.

origin: From "pith", the essential core of something, plus "-y". A pithy remark is all core and no padding.

senses.def: brief but full of meaning and force
senses.ex: Instead of a long lecture, the coach offered a pithy reminder before the final: play hard, play smart, play together.

origin: From Old French "pitance", from Medieval Latin "pietantia", from Latin "pietas", piety. It first named a small charitable allowance of food.

senses.def: very small or inadequate amount of money, especially as wages
senses.ex: Farmworkers picked strawberries for a pittance while the grocery chain sold the berries at triple the price.

syn: trifle, peanuts, chicken feed, mite, modicum

origin: From "pivot", the pin or point on which something turns, plus "-al". "Pivot" comes from French, and its earlier origin is uncertain.

senses.def: of crucial importance in deciding how something develops or turns out
senses.ex: The pivotal moment in the trial came when a surprise witness produced a receipt that destroyed the defendant's alibi.

origin: From Latin "placare", to calm or soothe, related to "placere", to please, the root of "placid" and "please".

senses.def: make someone less angry or hostile, often by giving them something
senses.ex: To placate the furious passengers, the airline handed out meal vouchers and promised seats on the next flight.

origin: From Latin "placebo", I will please, from "placere", to please. A placebo pleases the patient without containing any active drug.

senses.def: harmless substance with no active ingredients, given as if it were medicine or to test a drug
senses.ex: Half the volunteers received the new drug and half received a placebo, and nobody knew which they had taken.

senses.def: measure taken mainly to soothe or satisfy people rather than to have a real effect
senses.ex: Critics dismissed the new committee as a political placebo meant to calm voters without changing any policy.

syn: sugar pill, dummy pill, inactive treatment, sham treatment

origin: From French "placide", from Latin "placidus", calm or gentle, from "placere", to please.

senses.def: calm and not easily upset or excited
senses.ex: The placid old horse stood perfectly still while a crowd of shrieking children took turns patting its nose.

senses.def: of water or a place, calm, still, and peaceful
senses.ex: At dawn the lake was so placid that the pine trees on the far shore appeared perfectly mirrored in the water.

origin: From "plagiary", from Latin "plagiarius", kidnapper, from "plagium", kidnapping, so someone who plagiarizes kidnaps another person's words.

senses.def: present someone else's writing, ideas, or work as one's own
senses.ex: The professor discovered that the student had plagiarized three paragraphs of his essay from an online encyclopedia.

origin: From Old French "plaintif", lamenting, from "plainte", lament or complaint, the same source that gave English "plaintiff".

senses.def: sounding sad, mournful, and full of longing
senses.ex: The plaintive cry of a loon echoed across the dark lake as the campers banked their fire for the night.

origin: From Latin "plangens", from "plangere", to strike or beat, especially to beat the breast in mourning.

senses.def: loud, deep, and resonant, often with a mournful tone
senses.ex: The plangent tolling of the cathedral bells carried across the city on the morning of the queen's funeral.

origin: From Latin "plasticus", from Greek "plastikos", fit for molding, from "plassein", to mold or shape. The synthetic material is named for its moldability.

senses.def: easily shaped or molded, or able to change and adapt
senses.ex: Children's brains are remarkably plastic, which is why young kids can pick up a second language so quickly.

senses.def: synthetic material that can be molded into shape while soft and then set
senses.ex: The town banned single-use plastic bags after volunteers pulled thousands of them out of the river.

senses.def: artificial, fake, or insincere in manner
senses.ex: The host's plastic smile never wavered, even when the guest insulted her cooking on live television.

origin: From "plastic", from Greek "plastikos", fit for molding, from "plassein", to mold, plus "-ity", the state of being.

senses.def: quality of being easily shaped, molded, or adapted
senses.ex: Potters prize this local clay for its plasticity, since it can be stretched into thin walls without cracking.

senses.def: ability of the brain or a living thing to change in response to experience
senses.ex: Studies of brain plasticity show that adults who learn to juggle develop measurable changes in visual areas.

origin: From French "platitude", flatness, from "plat", flat. A platitude is a flat, stale remark.

senses.def: remark used so often that it has become dull and almost meaningless
senses.ex: The principal's speech was full of platitudes like "follow your dreams," and the seniors were checking their phones within minutes.

origin: From "platitude", from French "platitude", flatness, from "plat", flat, and was shaped to match adjectives like "multitudinous".

senses.def: full of dull, overused remarks presented as if they were wise or new
senses.ex: The commencement speaker offered platitudinous advice about following your dreams, and half the graduates were checking their phones.

origin: From the Greek philosopher Plato, whose writings describe a love that rises above physical desire. That idea gave English the phrase "platonic love".

senses.def: close and affectionate but not romantic or sexual
senses.ex: Their friendship stayed strictly platonic for twenty years, even though everyone at school assumed they would marry.

senses.def: usually capitalized, relating to Plato or his philosophy
senses.ex: The seminar compared Platonic ideas about perfect forms with Aristotle's focus on observing the physical world.

origin: From Latin "plaudite", applaud!, the request Roman actors made at the end of a play, from "plaudere", to clap.

senses.def: praise, applause, or enthusiastic approval
senses.ex: The young architect won plaudits from critics for a library that let natural light reach every reading table.

origin: From Latin "plausibilis", deserving applause, from "plaudere", to clap. Its meaning shifted from praiseworthy to seemingly acceptable.

senses.def: seeming reasonable or likely to be true
senses.ex: A dead phone battery was a plausible excuse for missing the call, so her mother let the matter drop.

senses.def: of a person or argument, convincing on the surface but possibly deceptive
senses.ex: The plausible salesman answered every question smoothly, yet the warranty he promised never appeared in the contract.

origin: From Latin "plebeius", of the common people, from "plebs", the ordinary citizens of ancient Rome, as opposed to the aristocratic patricians.

senses.def: belonging to the common people or the lower social classes
senses.ex: Though born into a plebeian family of dockworkers, she rose to become the city's first elected woman mayor.

senses.def: lacking refinement, ordinary or crude in taste
senses.ex: The food critic sniffed at the diner's plebeian menu, then quietly ordered a second plate of chili fries.

senses.def: member of the common people, originally in ancient Rome
senses.ex: In the early Roman Republic, plebeians fought for years to win the right to hold high public office.

origin: A variant spelling of "plebeian", often treated as a misspelling. It comes from Latin "plebs", the common people of ancient Rome.

senses.def: belonging to the common people or the lower social classes
senses.ex: The novel contrasts the duke's glittering ballroom with the plebian taverns where his servants spent their evenings.

senses.def: lacking refinement, ordinary or crude in taste
senses.ex: He considered karaoke a plebian pastime until his colleagues dragged him onstage and he discovered he loved it.

senses.def: member of the common people, originally in ancient Rome
senses.ex: The tribune promised the plebians cheaper grain if they would support his law in the assembly.

origin: From Latin "plebiscitum", a decree of the common people, from "plebs", the common people, plus "scitum", decree.

senses.def: direct vote by all citizens on an important public question
senses.ex: In the plebiscite, a clear majority of voters chose independence over remaining part of the larger federation.

origin: From Late Latin "plenarius", from Latin "plenus", full, the root of "plenty" and "replenish".

senses.def: attended by all members of a group, not just a committee or section
senses.ex: After a week of small workshops, the delegates gathered for a plenary session to vote on the final climate agreement.

senses.def: complete and without limits, absolute
senses.ex: During the emergency, the governor was granted plenary powers to close roads and order evacuations.

senses.def: meeting or session attended by all participants of a conference
senses.ex: The keynote speaker's talk at the morning plenary drew more than two thousand scientists into the main hall.

origin: From Medieval Latin "plenipotentiarius", having full power, from Latin "plenus", full, and "potens", powerful.

senses.def: diplomat or envoy given full power to act and sign agreements for a government
senses.ex: The plenipotentiaries of both nations signed the peace treaty without waiting for further instructions from their capitals.

senses.def: having full power to act on behalf of a government or ruler
senses.ex: She was appointed ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary, with authority to negotiate the trade deal on her own.

origin: From Latin "plenitudo", fullness, from "plenus", full, the same root found in "plenty" and "plenary".

senses.def: great abundance, more than enough of something
senses.ex: The farmers' market offered a plenitude of autumn produce, from heirloom squash to six kinds of apples.

senses.def: condition of being full or complete
senses.ex: In the plenitude of her powers, the aging pianist played the concerto with a depth younger performers could not match.

origin: From Greek "pleonasmos", from "pleonazein", to be more than enough, from "pleion", more.

senses.def: use of more words than needed to express an idea
senses.ex: The editor trimmed the report's pleonasm, cutting phrases like "past history" and "end result" down to single words.

senses.def: redundant expression in which a word repeats a meaning already present
senses.ex: "Free gift" is a familiar pleonasm, since every gift is free by definition.

origin: From Greek "plethore", fullness, from "plethein", to be full. It first named an excess of blood, then any oversupply.

senses.def: excessive amount of something, or loosely, a very large amount
senses.ex: Faced with a plethora of cereal brands, the exhausted shopper grabbed the nearest box and headed for checkout.

origin: From Old French "ploier", to fold or bend, from Latin "plicare", to fold, the root shared with "pliant" and "ply".

senses.def: easily bent or shaped without breaking
senses.ex: The basket weaver soaked the willow branches overnight to keep them pliable enough to bend into tight curves.

senses.def: easily influenced or persuaded by others
senses.ex: The board wanted a pliable chief executive who would approve their plans without asking difficult questions.

origin: From Old French "ploiant", bending, from "ploier", to fold or bend, which goes back to Latin "plicare", to fold.

senses.def: bending easily without breaking, flexible
senses.ex: Basket weavers soak the willow branches overnight so they become pliant enough to twist into tight patterns.

senses.def: easily influenced or controlled by others, compliant
senses.ex: The dictator replaced independent judges with pliant loyalists who approved every decree he issued.

origin: From Middle English "plit", condition or fold, from Old French "pleit", blended with Old English "pliht", danger or risk.

senses.def: dangerous, difficult, or unhappy situation
senses.ex: The documentary drew national attention to the plight of families left homeless after the river flooded their town.

origin: From Middle English, probably first meaning to splash through mud, linked to an old word "plodde", puddle. Its exact origin is uncertain.

senses.def: walk slowly and heavily, as if tired or burdened
senses.ex: The soaked hikers plodded up the muddy trail, too exhausted to talk as the rain kept falling.

senses.def: work slowly and steadily at a dull or difficult task
senses.ex: She plodded through three hundred pages of tax regulations before finding the rule that saved her business.

origin: From "plod", to walk slowly and heavily, a Middle English word probably first meaning to splash through mud.

senses.def: slow, steady, and laborious
senses.ex: The plodding pace of the negotiations frustrated reporters, who waited outside the hotel for eleven straight days.

senses.def: dull and lacking inspiration or energy
senses.ex: Despite a gripping premise, the thriller's plodding prose made every chapter feel twice as long as it was.

origin: Of uncertain origin, possibly a shortening of "employ" or "deploy".

senses.def: clever tactic or scheme designed to gain an advantage, often by deception
senses.ex: The free trial was a ploy to collect credit card numbers, and most users were charged before they could cancel.

origin: From Old English "pluccian", to pull off or pick. The sense of courage comes from "pluck" meaning an animal's heart and innards, much like "guts".

senses.def: courage and determination in the face of difficulty
senses.ex: It took real pluck for the shy freshman to stand up at the board meeting and challenge the new dress code.

senses.def: pull or pick something off or out with a quick tug
senses.ex: Grandma plucked a ripe tomato from the vine and handed it to me still warm from the sun.

senses.def: sound a string of a musical instrument by pulling and releasing it
senses.ex: He plucked the cello strings softly while the rest of the orchestra held a long, quiet chord.

origin: From "pluck", courage, plus "-y". "Pluck" once meant an animal's heart and innards, so plucky is close to "gutsy".

senses.def: brave and determined, especially when facing a stronger opponent
senses.ex: The plucky underdogs from the tiny rural school pushed the state champions into double overtime.

origin: From Old French "plumage", from "plume", feather, from Latin "pluma", feather.

senses.def: feathers covering a bird's body, considered as a whole
senses.ex: In spring the male cardinal's plumage turns a brilliant red that stands out against the bare branches.

senses.def: fine or showy clothing worn by a person
senses.ex: The guests arrived at the gala in full plumage, with sequined gowns, silk scarves, and towering feathered hats.

origin: From Latin "plumbum", lead, because sounding lines and builders' plumb lines used a lead weight. Plumbers got their name from early lead pipes.

senses.def: explore or examine something very deeply in order to understand it
senses.ex: The documentary plumbs the depths of the singer's grief after the deaths of her two brothers.

senses.def: exactly vertical, as checked with a weighted line
senses.ex: The carpenter checked that the doorframe was plumb before nailing it, so the door would not swing open on its own.

senses.def: lead weight on a line, used to find a true vertical or to measure water depth
senses.ex: Sailors dropped a plumb over the side every few minutes to make sure the ship was not drifting toward the reef.

syn: fathom, probe, explore, delve into, penetrate

origin: From Old French "plommet", small lead weight, from Latin "plumbum", lead. A plummet was a weight dropped on a line, so the verb means to drop straight down.

senses.def: fall or drop suddenly and steeply
senses.ex: Ticket sales plummeted after the lead actor left the show, and the theater closed within a month.

origin: From Greek "ploutokratia", rule of the wealthy, from "ploutos", wealth, and "kratos", power or rule, as in "democracy".

senses.def: government by the wealthy, or a society ruled by its richest members
senses.ex: Critics warned that unlimited campaign donations were turning the republic into a plutocracy run by a few billionaires.

senses.def: wealthy class that controls a country or society
senses.ex: The city's plutocracy decided every major question at private dinners long before the council ever voted.

origin: From Latin "pluvialis", of rain, from "pluvia", rain.

senses.def: relating to rain or caused by heavy rainfall
senses.ex: Geologists believe the dry lakebed was filled by pluvial floods during a much wetter period thousands of years ago.

origin: From Italian "poco curante", caring little, made famous by Pococurante, a bored, indifferent Venetian nobleman in Voltaire's "Candide".

senses.def: casually indifferent or unconcerned about things others care about
senses.ex: His pococurante attitude toward deadlines amused his friends but infuriated the editors waiting for his overdue manuscript.

senses.def: person who is casually indifferent to everything
senses.ex: Surrounded by eager volunteers, the pococurante in the corner shrugged and said the election would change nothing.

origin: From Latin "podium", raised platform, from Greek "podion", a small foot or base, from "pous", foot.

senses.def: small raised platform on which a speaker or conductor stands
senses.ex: The conductor stepped onto the podium, raised her baton, and the restless audience fell silent.

senses.def: upright stand with a slanted top for holding a speaker's notes
senses.ex: Nervous before her first debate, the candidate gripped the edges of the podium so tightly her knuckles whitened.

senses.def: platform where the top three finishers stand to receive medals
senses.ex: The three sprinters stood on the podium as the anthem played and the crowd waved flags.

senses.def: finish among the top three in a sports competition
senses.ex: The young skier podiumed in her first World Cup race, finishing third behind two former Olympic champions.

origin: From New Latin "poetaster", from "poeta", poet, plus "-aster", a suffix meaning a poor imitation, so a would-be poet.

senses.def: writer of inferior or trivial poetry
senses.ex: Every week the local paper printed sentimental verses by some poetaster who rhymed "heart" with "apart" without fail.

origin: From Old French "poignant", pricking, from "poindre", to prick, from Latin "pungere", to prick, the root also of "pungent".

senses.def: deeply moving, causing a sharp feeling of sadness, regret, or tenderness
senses.ex: The most poignant moment of the reunion came when the veteran recognized the nurse who had saved his life.

origin: From Old French "pois", weight, from Latin "pendere", to weigh, so poise first meant evenly balanced weight.

senses.def: calm, graceful self-control, especially under pressure
senses.ex: Despite the hostile questions from reporters, the young mayor answered each one with remarkable poise and good humor.

senses.def: graceful and balanced way of holding or moving the body
senses.ex: Years of ballet training gave her a poise that made her stand out even when she was simply walking.

senses.def: hold something balanced, steady, or ready in a position
senses.ex: The cat poised itself on the fence rail, tail twitching, ready to leap at the sparrow below.

origin: From "polar", from Latin "polus", the end of an axis, from Greek "polos", pivot or axis.

senses.def: state of having two sharply opposed sides, views, or tendencies
senses.ex: The growing polarity between rural and urban voters made it hard for either party to win a lasting majority.

senses.def: condition of being positive or negative in electric charge or magnetism
senses.ex: If you insert the batteries with the wrong polarity, the flashlight will not turn on.

origin: From French "polariser", from "polar", relating to the poles, plus "-ize". To polarize people is to push them toward opposite poles.

senses.def: divide a group into two sharply opposed sides
senses.ex: The proposal to close the old high school polarized the town, splitting neighbors into angry rival camps.

senses.def: in physics, filter light so its waves vibrate in only one direction
senses.ex: Fishing sunglasses polarize the light reflected off the water, so anglers can see fish beneath the glare.

origin: From "polarize", from French "polariser", based on "polar", relating to the poles. A polarized group has drifted to opposite poles.

senses.def: sharply divided into two opposing groups or extremes
senses.ex: In such a polarized climate, even a simple question about road repairs turned into a shouting match online.

senses.def: of lenses or light, filtered so the light waves vibrate in one direction
senses.ex: Polarized lenses cut the glare from the snow, so the skiers could spot icy patches on the slope.

origin: From French "polémique", from Greek "polemikos", warlike, from "polemos", war. A polemic wages war with words.

senses.def: strong written or spoken attack on an opinion, policy, or person
senses.ex: Her pamphlet was a fierce polemic against factory farming, and it sold out within a week of publication.

senses.def: usually plural, the art or practice of heated argument and dispute
senses.ex: Tired of the polemics on cable news, he started reading long, carefully sourced articles instead.

origin: From "polemic" plus "-al". "Polemic" comes from Greek "polemikos", warlike, from "polemos", war.

senses.def: strongly critical or argumentative, attacking an opinion or position
senses.ex: The essay's polemical tone won applause from her allies but persuaded none of the readers who disagreed with her.

origin: From French "politesse", politeness, from Italian "politezza", from Latin "polire", to polish. Polite manners are polished manners.

senses.def: formal politeness and courtesy, often elaborate or ceremonial
senses.ex: Behind the diplomatic politesse of toasts and handshakes, the two delegations were furious with each other.

origin: From Middle French "politique", from Greek "politikos", relating to citizens, from "polites", citizen.

senses.def: wise and shrewd in a practical way, especially in avoiding offense
senses.ex: It seemed politic to praise the host's cooking, even though the casserole was barely warm in the middle.

origin: From Greek "politeia", meaning "citizenship" or "government", through Latin and French.

senses.def: politically organized community, such as a nation or state
senses.ex: The island polity wrote a constitution after gaining independence from its former colonial ruler.

senses.def: system by which a political or religious group is governed
senses.ex: The church revised its polity to give local congregations a greater voice in decisions.

origin: From Pollyanna, the relentlessly cheerful heroine of Eleanor H. Porter's 1913 novel "Pollyanna", who finds something to be glad about in every misfortune, plus "-ish".

senses.def: naively or excessively optimistic, refusing to see real problems
senses.ex: His Pollyannaish forecast that the failing store would double its profits by summer made the bank nervous.

syn: naively optimistic, rose-tinted, starry-eyed, unrealistic, sanguine

origin: From Italian "poltrone", meaning "coward", through French "poltron". The insult still suggests shameful fear.

senses.def: person who shows contemptible cowardice when courage is needed
senses.ex: He called the guard a poltroon for abandoning the villagers as the fire approached.

senses.def: shamefully cowardly when courage is needed
senses.ex: The council's poltroon refusal to confront the corrupt official angered the entire town.

origin: From Greek "polyglottos", many-tongued, from "polys", many, and "glotta", tongue or language, as in "glossary".

senses.def: person who knows and uses many languages
senses.ex: A true polyglot, the tour guide switched effortlessly between Italian, Japanese, and Arabic as new groups arrived.

senses.def: speaking, written in, or made up of many languages
senses.ex: The polyglot neighborhood had street signs in four languages and markets selling spices from three continents.

origin: From Greek "polymathes", having learned much, from "polys", much, and "manthanein", to learn, the same root as "mathematics".

senses.def: person with wide and deep knowledge across many different fields
senses.ex: Leonardo da Vinci, the classic polymath, filled notebooks with studies of anatomy, engineering, botany, and painting.

syn: Renaissance person, universal genius, polyhistor, savant

origin: From Latin "pompa", procession, from Greek "pompe", a solemn procession or sending, from "pempein", to send.

senses.def: grand, showy display and ceremony, especially on official occasions
senses.ex: The coronation unfolded with great pomp, including golden carriages, trumpeters, and soldiers in scarlet uniforms.

origin: From Late Latin "pomposus", from Latin "pompa", a solemn procession, from Greek "pompe". A pompous person acts like a one-man parade.

senses.def: self-important and acting with an inflated sense of one's own dignity
senses.ex: The pompous professor insisted that students stand whenever he entered the room and address him by his full title.

senses.def: of language or style, overly grand and solemn
senses.ex: The brochure's pompous prose described a simple roadside motel as a sanctuary of unparalleled refinement.

origin: From Latin "ponderosus", weighty, from "pondus", weight, the same root as "ponder", to weigh something in the mind.

senses.def: slow and clumsy because of great weight or size
senses.ex: The ponderous elephant seal hauled itself across the beach, pausing every few yards to catch its breath.

senses.def: dull, labored, and overly solemn in style
senses.ex: The report's ponderous language buried its one important finding under forty pages of jargon.

origin: From Latin "pontifex", high priest, literally bridge-maker, from "pons", bridge, and "facere", to make. To pontificate is to speak as if with a pope's authority.

senses.def: express opinions in a pompous, dogmatic way, as if they were beyond question
senses.ex: Uncle Ray loves to pontificate about the economy at Thanksgiving, though he has never read a single economics book.

syn: sermonize, lecture, preach, moralize, hold forth

origin: From Anglo-Norman papegai, "parrot," probably through Old Occitan from Arabic babgha, also meaning "parrot." The bird's showy image shaped the insult.

senses.def: a vain, showy person who takes excessive pride in appearance
senses.ex: The new courtier strutted through the reception like a popinjay, admiring his jeweled cuffs more than the guests.

origin: From Latin "populus", the people, plus "-ist". The word grew popular with the American People's Party of the 1890s.

senses.def: claiming to represent ordinary people against a powerful or corrupt elite
senses.ex: The candidate's populist message about greedy bankers drew huge crowds in towns hit hardest by foreclosures.

senses.def: politician or activist who claims to champion ordinary people against elites
senses.ex: Historians still debate whether the governor was a genuine populist or a wealthy man borrowing working-class slogans.

origin: From Middle French porcin and Latin porcinus, both meaning "of a pig," from Latin porcus, "pig."

senses.def: relating to pigs or their characteristics
senses.ex: The veterinarian studied the porcine virus before visiting farms where several pigs had fallen ill.

senses.def: resembling a pig in appearance, appetite, or behavior
senses.ex: His porcine appetite astonished the hikers when he finished the entire stew and asked for dessert.

origin: From Old French "poros", from Latin "porus", an opening or pore. Something porous is full of tiny openings.

senses.def: full of tiny holes that let liquid or air pass through
senses.ex: Unglazed clay pots are porous, so water slowly seeps through their walls and keeps plant roots moist.

senses.def: easily crossed, penetrated, or gotten around
senses.ex: Smugglers took advantage of the porous border, crossing at night through unguarded stretches of desert.

origin: From Latin "portendere", to foretell, from "por-", forward, and "tendere", to stretch, as if a sign stretches toward the future.

senses.def: be a sign or warning that something, usually bad, is going to happen
senses.ex: Dark clouds gathering over the mountains portended a storm, so the shepherds drove their flocks down early.

origin: From Latin portentum, "omen," related to portendere, "to foretell." Its older sense points to a sign of what is coming.

senses.def: a sign that something important, often bad, is about to happen
senses.ex: The sudden silence among the birds seemed a portent of the storm gathering beyond the ridge.

origin: A nonstandard form of "portentous", probably shaped by "pretentious". The standard word comes from Latin "portentum", omen.

senses.def: nonstandard spelling of portentous: ominous, or pompously solemn
senses.ex: Editors changed the reviewer's "portentious" to "portentous" before printing her complaint about the film's grim, heavy narration.

origin: From Latin "portentosus", monstrous or marvelous, from "portentum", omen, from "portendere", to foretell.

senses.def: ominous, warning that something important or bad is about to happen
senses.ex: A portentous silence fell over the courtroom as the jury filed back in with its verdict.

senses.def: pompously solemn or self-important, trying too hard to seem significant
senses.ex: The documentary's portentous narration made a simple story about a bakery sound like the fall of Rome.

origin: From port, an older word for "bearing" or "carriage," plus -ly. It first suggested an imposing presence before describing a stout build.

senses.def: somewhat heavy and round in build, often with a dignified appearance
senses.ex: The portly mayor climbed the courthouse steps slowly, then greeted the waiting crowd with a broad smile.

origin: From French portemanteau, literally "carries coat," from porter, "carry," and manteau, "coat." The suitcase image later inspired the word-blending sense.

senses.def: a word formed by blending the sounds and meanings of two words
senses.ex: She called the weekend retreat a workation, a portmanteau that combined work with vacation.

senses.def: a large traveling case that opens into two sections
senses.ex: In the attic, Mara found a leather portmanteau packed with her grandfather's travel clothes.

senses.def: combining several distinct elements into a single whole
senses.ex: The council passed a portmanteau bill covering parks, buses, and public libraries.

senses.def: combine words to form a new blended expression
senses.ex: The students portmanteaued two animal names to invent a playful title for their mascot.

origin: From French "poseur", one who poses, from "poser", to put in place or strike a pose.

senses.def: person who behaves affectedly or pretends to be something they are not to impress others
senses.ex: The other musicians dismissed him as a poseur who owned vintage guitars but could barely play three chords.

origin: From Latin "positus", placed, past participle of "ponere", to put or place. To posit an idea is to put it forward.

senses.def: put forward an idea as a fact or as the basis for an argument
senses.ex: Some astronomers posit a ninth planet far beyond Neptune to explain the strange orbits of distant icy objects.

origin: From French posterite and Latin posteritas, "future generations," from posterus, "coming after," itself related to post, "after."

senses.def: people of future generations, especially those who will remember the present
senses.ex: The archivist saved the protest signs for posterity, knowing future students would ask how the movement began.

senses.def: the descendants of a particular person or group
senses.ex: The family planted cedar trees so that their posterity could enjoy shade on the old farm.

origin: From Latin "postumus", last-born, the superlative of "posterus", coming after. The "h" was added through a mistaken link with "humus", earth, as in burial.

senses.def: happening, awarded, or appearing after a person's death
senses.ex: The firefighter received a posthumous medal for bravery, accepted by his daughter at a ceremony downtown.

senses.def: of a book or work, published after its creator's death
senses.ex: Her posthumous novel, found in a drawer by her nephew, became a surprise bestseller decades after she died.

senses.def: of a child, born after the father's death
senses.ex: The posthumous son never met his father, who had been killed in a mining accident two months before the birth.

origin: From Latin post, "after," and prandium, "meal." The parts place an activity after eating.

senses.def: happening or done after a meal
senses.ex: A postprandial walk around the block helped us stay awake after the heavy Sunday lunch.

origin: From Latin postulare, "to demand or request." A postulate began as something an argument asks its audience to grant.

senses.def: assume something as a starting point without first proving it
senses.ex: The physicist postulated an unseen planet to explain the strange movement of the known ones.

senses.def: a basic assumption accepted as the foundation for reasoning
senses.ex: The proof depended on a postulate that every student in the class had already learned.

origin: From Latin positura, "position," through Italian postura and French posture. The physical position later became a metaphor for attitudes.

senses.def: the way someone holds or positions their body
senses.ex: After hours at the desk, her posture slumped and her shoulders began to ache.

senses.def: a person's stated attitude or position toward an issue
senses.ex: The governor's cautious posture on the proposal disappointed supporters who wanted a clear commitment.

senses.def: arrange or hold the body in a particular pose
senses.ex: The dancers postured beneath the lights while the photographer adjusted the camera.

senses.def: pretend to hold a belief or attitude to impress others
senses.ex: Some candidates posture as reformers but avoid naming any policy they would actually change.

origin: From French potable and Latin potabilis, "drinkable," based on Latin potare, "to drink."

senses.def: safe and suitable to drink
senses.ex: After the flood, volunteers delivered potable water because the town's wells were contaminated.

senses.def: a drinkable liquid, especially a beverage served to guests
senses.ex: The host offered several potables, including tea, lemonade, and chilled mineral water.

origin: From pot and boiler, suggesting work done to keep the cooking pot boiling and earn a living.

senses.def: a book or other creative work made chiefly to earn money
senses.ex: The novelist wrote a quick potboiler between serious books to pay the rent on her studio.

origin: From Latin potens, "powerful" or "able," related to posse, "to be able."

senses.def: having great power, influence, or effect
senses.ex: Her quiet account of the fire was more potent than any dramatic speech at the hearing.

senses.def: having a strong physical or chemical effect
senses.ex: The medicine was so potent that the doctor prescribed only a small dose.

origin: From Late Latin "potentatus", power or rule, from Latin "potens", powerful, from "posse", to be able, the root of "potent".

senses.def: ruler with great power, especially one who rules without limits
senses.ex: The oil-rich potentate built himself a palace with three hundred rooms while his subjects lacked clean water.

origin: From French pot-pourri, literally "rotten pot," once a stew of mixed ingredients. The name later shifted to mixed scents and assortments.

senses.def: a mixture of dried fragrant flowers and herbs used to scent a room
senses.ex: Grandmother filled a ceramic bowl with potpourri, and the bedroom smelled faintly of lavender.

senses.def: a varied mixture or collection of unrelated things
senses.ex: The festival offered a potpourri of crafts, regional foods, street games, and outdoor performances.

senses.def: a medley of different tunes or musical pieces
senses.ex: The orchestra closed with a potpourri of film themes that the audience recognized immediately.

origin: From an Eastern Algonquian word, probably Narragansett or Massachusett, for a spiritual healer or shaman, going back to a root meaning one who dreams.

senses.def: traditional Native American gathering with dancing, singing, and celebration
senses.ex: Dancers from dozens of tribes competed at the summer powwow, their regalia flashing as the drums kept time.

senses.def: informal meeting or discussion (a casual use some people consider disrespectful)
senses.ex: The coaches held a quick powwow on the sideline before deciding to go for the two-point conversion.

origin: From Latin practicabilis, "capable of being put into practice," with influence from French praticable.

senses.def: possible to carry out successfully in real conditions
senses.ex: The first design looked elegant, but only the simpler bridge was practicable within the budget.

origin: From French practicien, based on Latin practicus, "concerned with action." A practitioner applies a craft rather than only studying it.

senses.def: someone who works in a profession or regularly practices a skill
senses.ex: The clinic hired an experienced practitioner who could treat routine injuries and explain each treatment clearly.

senses.def: someone who actively follows a practice, belief, or discipline
senses.ex: As a longtime practitioner of meditation, he set aside twenty quiet minutes every morning.

origin: From Greek "pragmatikos", skilled in affairs, from "pragma", a deed or thing done, from "prassein", to do. A pragmatic person cares about what actually works.

senses.def: dealing with problems in a practical, realistic way rather than by theory or ideals
senses.ex: Rather than wait for a perfect solution, the pragmatic mayor fixed the worst potholes first and planned the rest later.

origin: From Middle English "praten", related to Middle Dutch and Low German "praten", to chatter, from an old Germanic word for idle or boastful talk.

senses.def: talk foolishly and at tiresome length about unimportant things
senses.ex: He prated on about his golf scores for an hour while the other guests stared longingly at the door.

senses.def: foolish, idle, or boastful talk
senses.ex: The old sailor ignored the young recruits' prate about adventure and handed them mops for the deck.

origin: From "prate", to chatter idly, plus the "-le" ending that marks a repeated action, as in "sparkle" from "spark".

senses.def: talk at length in a foolish, childish, or trivial way
senses.ex: The toddler prattled happily to her stuffed rabbit all through the long drive to her grandparents' house.

senses.def: silly, childish, or empty talk
senses.ex: The senator dismissed his opponent's warnings as mere prattle, but voters took them seriously.

origin: From Medieval Latin "praeambulum", from "praeambulare", to walk before, from "prae", before, and "ambulare", to walk. A preamble walks in ahead of the main text.

senses.def: introductory statement, especially at the start of a formal document, law, or speech
senses.ex: Students memorized the preamble to the Constitution, which explains the purposes the new government was meant to serve.

origin: From Latin "precarius", obtained by begging, from "prex", prayer. Whatever you hold only by someone else's favor could be taken away at any moment.

senses.def: dangerously unstable, insecure, or likely to collapse
senses.ex: The stack of dishes in the sink reached a precarious height, wobbling every time someone walked past.

origin: Past form of "precede", from Latin "praecedere", to go before, from "prae", before, and "cedere", to go.

senses.def: came before something in time, order, or rank
senses.ex: A week of unusual tremors preceded the volcanic eruption, giving villagers just enough time to evacuate.

senses.def: went in front of someone or something
senses.ex: A marching band preceded the floats down Main Street, clearing a path through the cheering crowd.

senses.def: introduced something by saying or doing something first
senses.ex: She preceded her toast with a funny story about the night the couple first met at a bowling alley.

syn: came before, predated, antedated, led up to, ushered in

origin: From Middle French precedence, "the state of coming before," related to English precede. The sense of arriving first became priority.

senses.def: priority in importance, rank, or order
senses.ex: During the evacuation, medical need took precedence over the order in which people had arrived.

origin: From Latin "praecedens", going before, from "praecedere", to precede, from "prae", before, and "cedere", to go.

senses.def: earlier event or action that serves as an example or guide for later ones
senses.ex: Letting one student retake the exam would set a precedent, and soon every student would demand the same chance.

senses.def: earlier court ruling that guides how judges decide similar later cases
senses.ex: The lawyer cited a 1954 precedent to argue that the school district's policy was unconstitutional.

origin: From Latin "praeceptum", a rule or teaching, from "praecipere", to instruct, from "prae", before, and "capere", to take.

senses.def: general rule or principle meant to guide behavior or thought
senses.ex: Her grandfather lived by one simple precept: never borrow money you cannot repay within a year.

origin: From Latin praecipitium, "steep place," related to praeceps, "headfirst," from prae, "before," and caput, "head."

senses.def: a very steep cliff or rock face
senses.ex: The trail ended at a precipice above the sea, so the hikers turned back carefully.

senses.def: the point just before a dangerous or disastrous event
senses.ex: After months of missed payments, the theater stood on the precipice of closing.

origin: From Latin "praecipitare", to throw headlong, from "praeceps", headfirst, from "prae", before, and "caput", head.

senses.def: cause something, usually bad, to happen suddenly or sooner than expected
senses.ex: The assassination of the archduke precipitated a crisis that dragged most of Europe into war within weeks.

senses.def: plunge someone or something suddenly into a particular state
senses.ex: The factory's closure precipitated the small town into a decade of unemployment and decline.

senses.def: done suddenly and hastily, without enough thought
senses.ex: Selling all his shares in a panic was a precipitate decision he regretted when prices recovered a week later.

syn: trigger, bring on, spark, hasten, provoke

origin: From obsolete French, based on Latin "praeceps", headlong or steep, from "prae", before, and "caput", head. Compare "precipice".

senses.def: dangerously high or steep
senses.ex: The goat path wound along a precipitous cliff, with a sheer drop of three hundred feet to the sea below.

senses.def: of a change, sudden and dramatic, especially a decline
senses.ex: The company suffered a precipitous drop in sales after news of the product recall spread online.

senses.def: done hastily and without careful thought
senses.ex: Critics called the coach's firing precipitous, since the team had lost only two games of the new season.

origin: From French "précis", precise or exact, from Latin "praecisus", cut short, from "praecidere", to cut off in front.

senses.def: short summary of the main points of a text or speech
senses.ex: Before the board meeting, the assistant prepared a one-page precis of the hundred-page consultant's report.

senses.def: write a short summary of a text
senses.ex: For homework, each student had to precis a newspaper editorial in no more than one hundred words.

origin: From Latin "praecludere", to shut off, from "prae", before, and "claudere", to close. To preclude something is to close the door on it in advance.

senses.def: make something impossible in advance, prevent it from happening
senses.ex: His knee injury precluded any chance of playing in the championship, so he coached from the bench instead.

syn: prevent, rule out, prohibit, exclude, forestall

origin: From Latin "praecox", ripe before its time, from "prae", before, and "coquere", to cook or ripen. "Apricot", an early-ripening fruit, comes from the same word.

senses.def: showing abilities or maturity unusually early, especially as a child
senses.ex: The precocious eight-year-old corrected her teacher's math and then asked for a harder workbook.

origin: From Latin "praecursor", forerunner, from "praecurrere", to run ahead, from "prae", before, and "currere", to run.

senses.def: something that comes before and leads to or signals a later development
senses.ex: The telegraph was a precursor of the telephone, proving that messages could travel instantly along wires.

origin: From Latin praedatorius, "of a plunderer," based on praedator, someone who seizes prey.

senses.def: exploiting vulnerable people for selfish gain
senses.ex: The city banned predatory loan terms that trapped borrowers in years of growing debt.

senses.def: hunting or feeding on other animals
senses.ex: The island's predatory birds keep the mouse population from growing too quickly.

origin: From Late Latin praedecessor, built from prae, "before," and decessor, "one who leaves office."

senses.def: a person who held a position before someone else
senses.ex: The new principal kept the reading program that her predecessor had started.

senses.def: an earlier version of something that a newer one replaces
senses.ex: This camera is lighter than its predecessor and can record much clearer video.

origin: From Late Latin "praedicamentum", something asserted or a category in logic, from "praedicare", to declare. It came to mean a state or condition, then an unpleasant one.

senses.def: difficult, unpleasant, or embarrassing situation that is hard to get out of
senses.ex: Locked out of the car with the engine running, she faced an awkward predicament on the busy highway shoulder.

origin: From Latin praedicare, "declare publicly," formed from prae, "before," and dicare, "proclaim." In grammar, a predicate says something about a subject.

senses.def: base a claim, action, or decision on something
senses.ex: The board predicated its funding decision on proof that the program had helped local students.

senses.def: the part of a sentence that says something about its subject
senses.ex: In the sentence about the fox, the predicate tells us that the animal crossed the road.

senses.def: state that a quality or action belongs to a subject
senses.ex: The philosopher predicated kindness of the stranger after hearing how she had helped the child.

origin: From Medieval Latin "praedilectio", from Latin "prae", before, and "diligere", to choose or love. A predilection is something chosen ahead of others.

senses.def: strong preference or special liking for something
senses.ex: The novelist's predilection for gloomy coastal settings shows in nearly every book, from Maine to the Scottish islands.

origin: From "pre-", before, and "disposed", inclined, from Latin "disponere", to arrange. Someone predisposed is inclined in a certain direction ahead of time.

senses.def: inclined in advance to think, feel, or act in a certain way
senses.ex: Having grown up near the ocean, she was predisposed to like any job that involved boats and fresh air.

senses.def: more likely than usual to suffer from a particular condition
senses.ex: People with a family history of diabetes are predisposed to the disease and should get regular blood tests.

origin: From Medieval Latin "praedominans", ruling over, from "prae", before or above, plus "dominari", to rule, from "dominus", lord.

senses.def: present as the main or strongest element, most common or noticeable
senses.ex: Gray was the predominant color in the old factory town, from the sky to the brick walls.

senses.def: having the most power or influence over others
senses.ex: For decades a single family held the predominant position in the island's sugar trade.

origin: From Latin "praeeminens", standing out above others, from "prae", before, plus "eminere", to stand out or project.

senses.def: surpassing all others, the most distinguished in a field
senses.ex: She was the preeminent violinist of her generation, and concert halls sold out within hours of announcing her.

origin: A back-formation from "preemption", the right to buy before others, from Latin "prae", before, and "emere", to buy.

senses.def: act in advance to prevent something expected from happening
senses.ex: The company cut its prices early to preempt a rival that was about to launch a cheaper version of the phone.

senses.def: take something for oneself before anyone else can
senses.ex: Early arrivals preempted the best picnic tables, leaving latecomers to spread blankets on the damp grass.

senses.def: replace or interrupt a scheduled program or plan by taking precedence over it
senses.ex: The evening news was preempted by live coverage of the hurricane as it made landfall near the coast.

syn: forestall, anticipate, head off, prevent, preclude

origin: From "preempt", to act first, from "preemption", the right to buy before others, from Latin "prae", before, and "emere", to buy.

senses.def: done in advance to prevent an expected attack, danger, or action
senses.ex: The city made a preemptive decision to close schools the night before the blizzard, keeping buses off icy roads.

origin: From Middle English, probably an altered form of "proinen", to trim, influenced by "prene", pin. Its exact origin is uncertain.

senses.def: spend time grooming oneself and admiring one's appearance
senses.ex: He preened in front of the hallway mirror for twenty minutes, adjusting his tie before the school dance.

senses.def: congratulate oneself smugly or show off one's achievements
senses.ex: The winning candidate preened before the cameras, boasting that his victory had never been in doubt.

senses.def: of a bird, clean and arrange its feathers with its beak
senses.ex: A pair of swans preened on the riverbank, carefully smoothing their white feathers after a swim.

syn: primp, groom, prink, spruce up, titivate

origin: Formed from Latin "praefatio", a saying beforehand, the source of "preface", from "prae", before, plus "fari", to speak.

senses.def: serving as an introduction to a book, speech or event
senses.ex: After a few prefatory remarks thanking the hosts, the senator turned to the real subject of her speech.

origin: From Latin "praefigurare", to show by a figure beforehand, from "prae", before, plus "figurare", to shape or picture.

senses.def: be an early sign or version of something that comes later
senses.ex: The clumsy early flying machines prefigured the jet age, though few people at the time could imagine it.

origin: From French "préhensile", from Latin "prehensus", grasped, from "prehendere", to seize or grasp.

senses.def: able to grasp or hold things by wrapping around them, as some tails and limbs do
senses.ex: The spider monkey swung from branch to branch, using its prehensile tail like a fifth hand.

origin: From "pre-", before, plus Latin "lapsus", a fall: the time before the Fall of Adam and Eve, when humans were innocent.

senses.def: belonging to an imagined time of innocence before things were spoiled or corrupted
senses.ex: The film paints the town before the highway arrived as a prelapsarian paradise of orchards and open doors.

origin: From Medieval Latin "praelatus", one set above others, past participle of "praeferre", to carry before, the same verb behind "prefer".

senses.def: high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop or abbot
senses.ex: The visiting prelate, dressed in purple robes, blessed the new cathedral bells before they were raised into the tower.

origin: From Medieval Latin "praeludium", from Latin "praeludere", to play beforehand, from "prae", before, plus "ludere", to play.

senses.def: event or action that comes before and leads into something larger or more important
senses.ex: The border skirmishes turned out to be a prelude to a long and devastating war.

senses.def: short piece of music that introduces a longer work, or a short independent piano piece
senses.ex: The pianist opened the recital with a quiet Chopin prelude before launching into the thunderous sonata.

origin: From Latin "praemeditari", to consider beforehand, from "prae", before, and "meditari", to think over, the source of "meditate".

senses.def: think out or plan an action, especially a crime, in advance
senses.ex: Prosecutors argued that the thief had premeditated the robbery, since he had studied the guards' schedule for weeks.

origin: From Medieval Latin "praemissa", a proposition set before, from Latin "praemittere", to send ahead, from "prae", before, plus "mittere", to send.

senses.def: statement or idea assumed to be true and used as the basis of an argument
senses.ex: The whole plan rested on the premise that customers would pay more for faster delivery.

senses.def: house or building together with its land, used in the plural
senses.ex: Smoking is not permitted anywhere on the premises, including the parking lot behind the restaurant.

senses.def: base an argument, theory or plan on a particular assumption
senses.ex: The detective show is premised on the idea that one sharp observer can outthink an entire police force.

origin: From Late Latin "praemonitio", forewarning, from "prae", before, and "monere", to warn, the root of "monitor".

senses.def: strong feeling that something, usually unpleasant, is about to happen
senses.ex: Seized by a premonition of disaster, she canceled her flight, and the next morning heard the airport had flooded.

origin: From "pre-", before, plus "ordain", to decree, from Latin "ordinare", to put in order: to decree something before it happens.
