senses.def: eggs of fish, frogs, or other water animals
senses.ex: Children crouched by the pond to look at clumps of frog spawn floating near the reeds.

syn: generate, produce, breed, give rise to, engender

origin: From "spear" + "head": the sharp point that strikes first, so the person or group that leads an attack or campaign.

senses.def: lead an attack, campaign, or movement
senses.ex: Two high school students spearheaded the campaign to ban plastic bags in their town.

senses.def: person or group that leads an attack, campaign, or movement
senses.ex: The armored division served as the spearhead of the advance across the plains.

senses.def: pointed tip of a spear
senses.ex: Archaeologists found a flint spearhead buried beside the remains of the ancient campfire.

origin: From Latin "speciosus", good-looking or showy, from "species", appearance: a specious argument looks good but falls apart.

senses.def: seeming reasonable or true at first but actually wrong or misleading
senses.ex: The ad's specious claim that the drink "boosts brainpower" was based on a study of only twelve people.

origin: From Latin "spectaculum", a public show, from "spectare", to look at, the root of "spectator" and "inspect".

senses.def: visually impressive show or display
senses.ex: The fireworks over the harbor were a spectacle that drew thousands of people to the waterfront.

senses.def: embarrassing or unusual sight that attracts attention
senses.ex: He made a spectacle of himself by arguing loudly with the referee in front of the whole crowd.

senses.def: in the plural, an old-fashioned word for eyeglasses
senses.ex: Grandpa peered over his wire-rimmed spectacles and asked who had eaten the last slice of pie.

origin: From French "spectre", from Latin "spectrum", an appearance or apparition, from "specere", to look, also the source of "spectrum".

senses.def: ghost or phantom
senses.ex: Visitors swore that a pale specter drifted through the abandoned hotel's ballroom every night at midnight.

senses.def: threatening possibility that causes fear or dread
senses.ex: The specter of layoffs hung over the factory as orders kept falling month after month.

origin: From Latin "spectrum", appearance or apparition, from "specere", to look at. Isaac Newton applied it to the band of colors made by a prism.

senses.def: broad range of related qualities, ideas, or activities
senses.ex: The town hall drew voters from across the political spectrum, from staunch conservatives to democratic socialists.

senses.def: band of colors produced when light is split, as by a prism or raindrops
senses.ex: Sunlight passing through the prism spread across the wall in a spectrum from red to violet.

origin: From Latin "speculari", to watch or spy out, from "specula", a watchtower, from "specere", to look.

senses.def: form a theory or opinion without firm evidence
senses.ex: Fans speculated for months about who would play the lead role before the studio finally announced it.

senses.def: invest in something risky in the hope of a large, quick profit
senses.ex: During the boom, many people speculated in land, buying lots they had never even seen.

origin: From "spend" + "thrift" in its old sense of savings or wealth: a spendthrift spends what others have saved.

senses.def: person who spends money recklessly or wastefully
senses.ex: The heir was a notorious spendthrift who burned through his inheritance on yachts and racehorses.

senses.def: spending money recklessly or wastefully
senses.ex: Critics accused the spendthrift council of buying luxury cars while the schools needed new roofs.

syn: wastrel, squanderer, prodigal, profligate, big spender

origin: From Scots "spindrift", probably a variant of the older "spoondrift", from "spoon", to scud before the wind, plus "drift".

senses.def: spray blown from the tops of waves, or snow whipped up by the wind
senses.ex: Spindrift stung the sailors' faces as the gale tore the white crests off the waves.

origin: From Greek "splen", the spleen. Medieval medicine treated this organ as the seat of bad temper, so "venting spleen" means pouring out anger.

senses.def: bad temper or spiteful, irritable anger
senses.ex: In his letter to the editor, the retired colonel vented his spleen about the new parking rules.

senses.def: organ near the stomach that filters the blood
senses.ex: The doctor warned that a hard tackle could rupture the patient's enlarged spleen.

origin: From Late Latin "spleneticus", from "splen", spleen. Anger and bad temper were once believed to come from the spleen.

senses.def: bad-tempered, irritable, and spiteful
senses.ex: The splenetic columnist attacked every new restaurant in town, rarely finding anything to praise.

origin: From Latin "spontaneus", voluntary, from "sponte", of one's own accord, plus "-ity".

senses.def: quality of acting on sudden impulse, naturally and without planning
senses.ex: Her friends loved her spontaneity, like the time she suggested a midnight drive to watch the sunrise.

origin: Named after William Archibald Spooner (1844 to 1930), an Oxford clergyman and scholar said to swap the first sounds of words by accident.

senses.def: slip of the tongue that swaps the first sounds of two words
senses.ex: The best man's spoonerism turned 'loving shepherd' into 'shoving leopard', and the wedding guests roared.

syn: slip of the tongue, transposition, verbal slip

origin: From Afrikaans "spoor", from Dutch "spoor", track, related to Old English "spor", a footprint or trace.

senses.def: track, trail, droppings, or scent left by an animal
senses.ex: The guide knelt to study the lion's spoor in the dust and announced that the pride had passed at dawn.

origin: From Greek "sporadikos", scattered, from "spora", a sowing of seed: events scattered like seeds tossed across a field.

senses.def: occurring at irregular intervals or in scattered places
senses.ex: Despite the ceasefire, sporadic gunfire could still be heard in the hills at night.

origin: From "sport" + "-ive". "Sport" is short for "disport", from Old French "desporter", to carry away, that is, to divert from serious things.

senses.def: playful, lighthearted, and fond of fun
senses.ex: The sportive puppies tumbled over each other in the grass while their mother watched calmly.

origin: From Italian "sprezzatura", nonchalance, coined by Baldassare Castiglione in 1528 for the courtier's art of making hard things look effortless.

senses.def: studied carelessness, the art of making difficult things look effortless
senses.ex: The pianist played the fiendish passage with such sprezzatura that she seemed to be improvising for fun.

origin: From "spright", an old spelling of "sprite", a spirit or elf, plus "-ly", so lively as a sprite.

senses.def: lively and energetic, especially for someone older
senses.ex: The sprightly eighty-year-old led the hiking group up the steep trail without stopping to rest.

origin: From British dialect "sprey", probably of Scandinavian origin; compare Old Norse "sprækr", nimble or lively.

senses.def: active and nimble, especially in old age
senses.ex: Though nearly ninety, Mrs. Ortiz was spry enough to tend her vegetable garden every morning.

origin: From Old French "espume", from Latin "spuma", foam or froth.

senses.def: foam or froth, especially on breaking waves
senses.ex: White spume flew from the breakers as the storm drove the waves against the seawall.

origin: From Late Latin "spurius", illegitimate, used of a child born outside marriage. Its deeper origin is uncertain.

senses.def: false or fake, not genuine
senses.ex: The museum withdrew the letter after experts showed that its spurious signature was a modern forgery.

senses.def: based on faulty reasoning, though appearing valid
senses.ex: The study's link between ice cream sales and drowning was a spurious correlation, since both rise in summer.

origin: From Old English "spurnan", to kick or strike against, then to reject: to spurn an offer is to kick it away.

senses.def: reject someone or something with contempt
senses.ex: The young artist spurned a lucrative advertising job, insisting she would paint only what she chose.

origin: Probably of Scandinavian origin and imitative of noisy chatter; compare Swedish dialect "skvabbel", a quarrel.

senses.def: noisy argument over something unimportant
senses.ex: A squabble over who got the front seat delayed the family's road trip by twenty minutes.

senses.def: argue noisily about trivial things
senses.ex: The roommates squabbled every week about whose turn it was to take out the trash.

origin: From Latin "squalidus", filthy, from "squalere", to be rough or dirty.

senses.def: extremely dirty and unpleasant, especially from poverty or neglect
senses.ex: Reporters exposed the squalid conditions in the factory dormitories, where twelve workers shared one filthy room.

senses.def: morally degraded or shameful
senses.ex: The scandal began as a squalid dispute over expense claims and ended with two resignations.

origin: From Latin "squalor", filthiness or roughness, from "squalere", to be stiff with dirt.

senses.def: filthy, wretched conditions, especially from poverty or neglect
senses.ex: Reporters described the squalor of the overcrowded shelter, where families slept beside overflowing garbage bins.

origin: First recorded in the late 1500s and of unknown origin. It may be a blend of "scatter" and "wander".

senses.def: waste money, time, or an opportunity carelessly or foolishly
senses.ex: The team squandered a twenty-point lead in the fourth quarter and lost by three.

syn: waste, fritter away, dissipate, misspend, blow

origin: Origin obscure, probably from Anglo-Norman "escoymous", of unknown origin, perhaps blended with the dialect word "sweamish", faint or queasy.

senses.def: easily made sick, faint, or disgusted, especially by blood
senses.ex: Too squeamish to watch the surgery video, Jordan covered his eyes until biology class ended.

senses.def: having strong scruples, unwilling to do something unpleasant or questionable
senses.ex: The senator was not squeamish about attacking rivals in public, however personal the insults became.

origin: Of unknown origin, perhaps a blend of "squash", "quell", and "quench", or an imitation of a sucking sound.

senses.def: forcefully silence or suppress something
senses.ex: The regime squelched every protest within hours, arresting organizers before crowds could gather.

senses.def: make a soft sucking sound, as when walking through mud
senses.ex: Our boots squelched through the marsh as we searched for the heron's nest.

origin: From Latin "stagnans", forming a pool, from "stagnare", from "stagnum", a pond of standing water.

senses.def: not flowing, and often stale or foul as a result
senses.ex: Mosquitoes bred in the stagnant water that collected in old tires behind the garage.

senses.def: showing no growth, development, or activity
senses.ex: With wages stagnant for a decade, many families struggled to keep up with rising rents.

origin: An old spelling of "stayed", the past participle of "stay": someone staid has stayed fixed, steady, and settled.

senses.def: sedate, respectable, and unadventurous
senses.ex: The staid old bank surprised everyone by hiring a twenty-five-year-old designer to redo its logo.

origin: From "stale", an older chess word for a position with no legal move, plus "mate", as in "checkmate".

senses.def: situation in which neither side can make progress, a deadlock
senses.ex: Talks between the union and the company reached a stalemate, and neither side would offer anything new.

senses.def: chess position where the player to move has no legal move, ending in a draw
senses.ex: Down to a lone king, the young player escaped defeat by forcing a clever stalemate.

origin: From Old English "stælwierthe", serviceable or able to stand firm. The Scots form "stalwart" spread through the novels of Walter Scott.

senses.def: loyal, reliable, and hardworking
senses.ex: Her stalwart support during the long recall campaign earned her a seat on the mayor's cabinet.

senses.def: loyal, reliable supporter of an organization or cause
senses.ex: Party stalwarts who had knocked on doors for thirty years felt ignored by the new leadership.

senses.def: strongly and sturdily built
senses.ex: Two stalwart oak beams held up the roof of the old barn.

origin: From Latin "stamina", threads, the plural of "stamen". The threads of life spun by the Fates suggested inborn strength and staying power.

senses.def: ability to keep up physical or mental effort over a long time
senses.ex: Marathon training built up her stamina until she could run for three hours without tiring.

syn: endurance, staying power, energy, resilience, fortitude

origin: From Middle English "staunchen", to stop a flow of blood, from Old French "estanchier", to stop a flow or make watertight.

senses.def: stop the flow of a liquid, especially blood from a wound
senses.ex: The medic pressed gauze firmly against the cut to stanch the bleeding until the ambulance arrived.

senses.def: stop or check something harmful from continuing
senses.ex: The company cut prices to stanch the loss of customers to its cheaper rivals.

origin: From "stand" + "-ing", from Old English "standan", to stand: your standing is where you stand in others' eyes.

senses.def: status, rank, or reputation within a group or society
senses.ex: The scandal damaged the senator's standing with voters in her home state.

senses.def: permanent and continuing, not formed for a single occasion
senses.ex: The legislature has a standing committee on education that meets every month.

senses.def: length of time something has existed, often in the phrase of long standing
senses.ex: The two families have a feud of long standing that began over a disputed fence.

origin: From Italian "stanza", a stopping place or room, from Latin "stare", to stand: each stanza is a room in the house of the poem.

senses.def: group of lines forming a unit in a poem or song
senses.ex: The ballad has twelve stanzas, each ending with the same haunting refrain.

origin: The "main item" sense comes from Old French "estaple", a market, from a Germanic word for a post. The wire fastener comes from Old English "stapol", a post.

senses.def: basic item or main element that is used or eaten regularly
senses.ex: Rice is a staple of the diet in much of Asia, served at nearly every meal.

senses.def: main, basic, or standard
senses.ex: Wheat and soybeans are the staple crops on most farms in the region.

senses.def: small bent wire used to fasten papers or other materials together
senses.ex: The report fell apart because someone had forgotten to put a staple in the corner.

origin: From Old English "stearc", stiff, strong, or severe. German "stark", strong, is a cousin.

senses.def: severe or bare in appearance, without softening details
senses.ex: The stark white walls of the gallery made the colorful paintings stand out vividly.

senses.def: sharply clear and impossible to ignore, often unpleasantly so
senses.ex: The report painted a stark picture of the drought, with reservoirs at their lowest level in a century.

senses.def: completely or utterly, as in stark naked
senses.ex: The toddler ran stark naked through the backyard sprinkler while his parents laughed.

origin: From Middle English "sterten", to leap up suddenly, from Old English "styrtan", to leap up. The jump of surprise is the older meaning.

senses.def: begin doing something, or set something in motion
senses.ex: The orchestra will start rehearsing the new symphony next Monday.

senses.def: jump or jerk suddenly from surprise or alarm
senses.ex: She started when the door slammed behind her in the empty house.

senses.def: sudden jerk or movement of surprise
senses.ex: He woke with a start, convinced he had heard footsteps in the hallway.

origin: From Greek "stasis", a standing or standstill, related to "histanai", to make stand.

senses.def: state of inactivity or balance in which nothing changes or develops
senses.ex: After years of political stasis, the new government passed three major reforms in its first month.

origin: From "state", in its old sense of rank or grandeur, plus "-ly", so having the dignity of high rank.

senses.def: dignified, impressive, and grand in size or manner
senses.ex: The stately old mansion stood at the end of a long avenue lined with towering oak trees.

senses.def: slow, measured, and dignified in movement
senses.ex: The bride walked down the aisle at a stately pace while the organ played softly.

origin: From Greek "statikos", causing to stand, from "histanai", to make stand.

senses.def: lacking movement, action, or change
senses.ex: Population in the rural county has remained static for decades, neither growing nor shrinking.

senses.def: crackling noise or interference on a radio, television, or phone
senses.ex: The storm filled the radio broadcast with static, so we could barely hear the score.

senses.def: electric charge that builds up on a surface, often causing small shocks
senses.ex: Dry winter air creates static that makes your hair stand up when you pull off a sweater.

origin: From French "statuesque", from "statue" + "-esque", like: tall and dignified like a statue.

senses.def: tall, dignified, and graceful, like a classical statue
senses.ex: The statuesque actress swept down the staircase in a long silver gown as photographers crowded the entrance.

origin: Latin, literally "the state in which", from "status", state, + "quo", in which: the state in which things already are.

senses.def: existing state of affairs, especially in social or political matters
senses.ex: The young reformers challenged the status quo by proposing that students sit on the school board.

syn: existing order, current state, norm, prevailing conditions

origin: From Old French "estanche", firm or watertight: a staunch ally holds firm, like a hull that lets in no water.

senses.def: loyal, committed, and firm in support of a person or cause
senses.ex: A staunch environmentalist, she has biked to work every day for twenty years.

senses.def: stop the flow of something, especially blood (a variant of stanch)
senses.ex: The coach used a towel to staunch the player's bloody nose on the sideline.

origin: From Old English "stedefæst", from "stede", place, + "fæst", firm: fixed firmly in one place.

senses.def: firmly loyal and unwavering in purpose or belief
senses.ex: Despite years of criticism, the scientist remained steadfast in her support for the controversial theory.

senses.def: fixed and steady, not moving or changing
senses.ex: The sailor kept a steadfast gaze on the lighthouse as the storm tossed the small boat.

origin: From Middle English "stelthe", theft, from "steal" plus the noun ending "-th", so first the act of stealing, then of moving secretly.

senses.def: quiet, careful, secret action meant to avoid being noticed
senses.ex: The cat crept toward the pigeon with perfect stealth, placing each paw silently on the gravel.

senses.def: secret or hidden, designed to avoid notice or detection
senses.ex: Critics called the new parking fee a stealth tax, since few drivers realized they were paying it.

origin: The "soak" sense is probably of Scandinavian origin. The "sharply sloping" sense is a separate word, from Old English "steap", high or lofty.

senses.def: soak something in liquid to soften it or draw out its flavor
senses.ex: Steep the tea leaves in hot water for three minutes, then remove them before serving.

senses.def: fill or surround thoroughly with a quality or influence, usually in the passive
senses.ex: The old university town is steeped in history, with buildings dating back to the 1400s.

senses.def: rising or falling sharply, nearly vertical
senses.ex: The hikers paused often on the steep trail, gasping for breath in the thin mountain air.

senses.def: excessively high, especially of a price or demand (informal)
senses.ex: Five dollars for a bottle of water seemed steep, but the thirsty tourists paid it anyway.

origin: Past participle of "steep", to soak, probably of Scandinavian origin: something steeped in a quality is soaked through with it.

senses.def: thoroughly filled with or deeply influenced by a quality or tradition
senses.ex: Raised in a family steeped in music, she could read sheet music before she could read books.

senses.def: soaked in liquid for a period of time
senses.ex: The cook steeped the dried mushrooms in warm broth until they softened.

origin: The "stop the flow" verb comes from Old Norse "stemma", to dam up. The noun, a plant stalk, comes from Old English "stemn", a trunk or stalk.

senses.def: stop or restrict the flow or spread of something
senses.ex: The city built sandbag walls to stem the rising floodwaters before they reached downtown.

senses.def: originate from or be caused by, followed by from
senses.ex: Many of the patient's health problems stem from years of poor sleep.

senses.def: main stalk of a plant, or the slender part supporting a leaf or flower
senses.ex: She trimmed the rose stems at an angle so the flowers would last longer in the vase.

origin: From Stentor, the herald of the Greek army in Homer's "Iliad", whose voice was said to be as loud as fifty men's.

senses.def: extremely loud and powerful, especially of a voice
senses.ex: The drill sergeant's stentorian voice carried across the entire parade ground without a megaphone.

origin: From Latin "sterilis", barren or unproductive.

senses.def: free from germs and bacteria
senses.ex: The surgeon unwrapped a sterile scalpel just before making the first incision.

senses.def: unable to produce offspring, crops, or fruit
senses.ex: Years of overfarming left the soil so sterile that nothing would grow without heavy fertilizer.

senses.def: lacking imagination, life, or useful results
senses.ex: The debate became a sterile exchange of slogans that persuaded nobody in the audience.

origin: The adjective comes from Old English "styrne", severe or strict. The noun for a ship's rear is a separate word, probably from Old Norse "stjórn", steering.

senses.def: serious, strict, and severe in manner or attitude
senses.ex: The judge gave the young offender a stern warning that a second arrest would mean jail time.

senses.def: rear part of a ship or boat
senses.ex: The fisherman sat in the stern of the rowboat, steering with a single oar.

origin: From Latin "stertere", to snore, plus "-ous".

senses.def: noisy and harsh, like heavy snoring
senses.ex: Through the thin wall she could hear her uncle's stertorous breathing rattling like an old engine all night.

origin: From Spanish "estibador", a loader, from "estibar", to stow cargo, from Latin "stipare", to cram or pack tightly.

senses.def: person employed at a port to load and unload ships
senses.ex: The stevedores worked through the night to unload the container ship before the morning tide.

origin: From Middle English "stuflen", to choke from heat or lack of air, perhaps linked to Old French "estouffer", to smother, but the origin is uncertain.

senses.def: suppress, restrain, or prevent something from developing or being expressed
senses.ex: Strict rules about uniforms and silence stifled the students' creativity, their art teacher complained.

senses.def: make someone unable to breathe properly, smother or suffocate
senses.ex: The stifling heat in the attic forced the movers to take a break every twenty minutes.

syn: suppress, smother, repress, stamp out, muffle

origin: From Greek "stigma", a mark made by a pointed tool, such as the brand on a slave, from "stizein", to prick or mark.

senses.def: mark of disgrace or shame associated with a circumstance, quality, or person
senses.ex: Campaigns to fight the stigma of mental illness encourage people to talk openly about therapy.

senses.def: part of a flower's pistil that receives pollen
senses.ex: Bees brush pollen onto the sticky stigma as they move from blossom to blossom.

origin: Plural of "stigma", from Greek "stigma", a mark or brand, from "stizein", to prick or mark.

senses.def: marks of disgrace or shame associated with particular circumstances or groups
senses.ex: Older stigmas around divorce have faded, and few people now judge a coworker for ending a marriage.

senses.def: parts of flowers' pistils that receive pollen
senses.ex: Under the microscope, the students could see pollen grains stuck to the lily's three stigmas.

origin: From Medieval Latin "stigmatizare", to brand, from Greek "stigmatizein", from "stigma", a mark or brand.

senses.def: describe or regard someone as worthy of disgrace or shame
senses.ex: Doctors worry that harsh public warnings may stigmatize patients and discourage them from seeking treatment.

origin: From "stilt" + "-ed": stilted speech moves as stiffly and awkwardly as someone walking on stilts.

senses.def: stiff, artificially formal, and unnatural in speech or writing
senses.ex: The translation was accurate but stilted, full of phrases no native speaker would ever use.

origin: Of uncertain origin, possibly from "stinge", a dialect form of "sting".

senses.def: unwilling to give, spend, or share
senses.ex: The stingy landlord refused to fix the broken heater until the tenants threatened to call the city.

senses.def: small in amount, meager or scanty
senses.ex: The restaurant's stingy portions left us ordering pizza on the way home.

origin: From Old English "styntan", to blunt or dull, from a Germanic root meaning to make short: a stint is a limited stretch of time.

senses.def: fixed or limited period spent doing a particular job or activity
senses.ex: After a two-year stint teaching English in Seoul, he returned home to attend law school.

senses.def: be sparing or frugal with something, often used in the negative
senses.ex: The hosts did not stint on the food, serving six courses and three kinds of dessert.

origin: From "stint", to limit or hold back, + "-ing". "Stint" comes from Old English "styntan", to blunt or dull.

senses.def: sparing or restrained in giving or spending
senses.ex: The committee was stinting in its praise, offering only a brief nod to the volunteers who had organized the event.

origin: From Latin "stipendium", soldiers' pay, from "stips", a small coin or gift, + "pendere", to weigh out or pay.

senses.def: fixed, regular sum paid as a salary or allowance, especially to students, interns, or clergy
senses.ex: The research fellowship provides a modest monthly stipend that covers rent and groceries.

origin: From Latin "stipulari", to demand a formal promise, as when making a binding contract.

senses.def: demand or specify something as a condition of an agreement
senses.ex: The will stipulated that the house could not be sold until the youngest grandchild turned twenty-one.

syn: specify, require, prescribe, set down, insist on

origin: From Greek "Stōikos", from the "Stoa Poikile", the painted porch in Athens where Zeno taught that wisdom means accepting fate calmly.

senses.def: enduring pain or hardship without complaining or showing emotion
senses.ex: The stoic farmer said little after the hailstorm destroyed his crop and simply began replanting.

senses.def: person who endures hardship calmly without complaint
senses.ex: A true stoic, my grandmother never mentioned her arthritis, even on the coldest mornings.

senses.def: follower of Stoicism, the ancient Greek and Roman philosophy (usually capitalized)
senses.ex: The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius, a devoted Stoic, wrote private reflections on duty and self-control.

origin: Both forms come from Greek "Stōikos", after the "Stoa Poikile", the painted porch in Athens where Zeno taught calm acceptance of fate.

senses.def: enduring pain or hardship calmly without complaint
senses.ex: The injured hiker remained stoical during the six-hour rescue, joking with the paramedics to keep everyone calm.

origin: From Middle Dutch or Middle Low German "stoken", to poke or thrust, as in poking a fire to keep it burning.

senses.def: add fuel to a fire or furnace and stir it to burn hotter
senses.ex: Every hour the blacksmith stoked the forge with coal until the iron glowed bright orange.

senses.def: encourage or intensify a feeling or situation
senses.ex: Rumors spreading online stoked fears that the bank would collapse by the end of the week.

origin: From Latin "stolidus", dull, slow, or foolish. In English it softened to mean calm and unemotional.

senses.def: calm and dependable, showing little emotion or animation
senses.ex: The stolid security guard watched the screaming fans without a flicker of expression.

origin: From "story" + "-ed": celebrated in many stories. "Story" came through Old French "estorie" from Latin "historia", history.

senses.def: celebrated in history, legend, or many stories
senses.ex: The storied football program has won more national titles than any other college in the conference.

senses.def: having a stated number of floors, as in two-storied
senses.ex: A three-storied brick warehouse stood at the end of the dock.

origin: From Greek "stratēgēma", the act of a general, from "stratēgos", a general: a clever move, first in war and then anywhere.

senses.def: plan or trick designed to outwit an opponent or achieve a goal
senses.ex: The general's stratagem of lighting hundreds of campfires convinced the enemy that his small army was enormous.

origin: From Latin "stratum", something spread out, such as a bed covering, from "sternere", to spread. "Street" comes from the same Latin root.

senses.def: layer of rock, soil, or other material, usually one of several
senses.ex: Geologists found fossils of ancient fish in a stratum of limestone halfway up the canyon wall.

senses.def: level or class of society
senses.ex: The new tax would fall most heavily on the lowest economic stratum of the population.

origin: From "streamline", the path of smooth flow in a moving fluid, + "-ed": shaped so air or water flows smoothly past.

senses.def: made simpler and more efficient
senses.ex: The streamlined application now takes ten minutes to complete instead of an hour.

senses.def: shaped to move easily through air or water with little resistance
senses.ex: The streamlined body of the bullet train lets it reach speeds of nearly two hundred miles per hour.

origin: From Latin "strenuus", brisk, vigorous, or active, so strenuous work calls for vigorous effort.

senses.def: requiring great effort or physical exertion
senses.ex: Doctors advised him to avoid strenuous exercise, such as running or heavy lifting, for six weeks after surgery.

senses.def: showing great energy, determination, or force
senses.ex: Despite strenuous objections from residents, the council approved the new highway ramp.

origin: From Old English "streowian", to scatter, related to "straw", which was once scattered over floors.

senses.def: scatter things untidily over a surface or area
senses.ex: After the storm, branches and shingles were strewn across every lawn on the street.

origin: From Latin "striatus", grooved, from "stria", a furrow or channel.

senses.def: marked with parallel lines, grooves, or bands
senses.ex: The striated cliffs showed layers of red, tan, and gray rock laid down over millions of years.

origin: From Late Latin "strictura", a tightening, from Latin "strictus", drawn tight: a stricture tightens limits or delivers a sharp rebuke.

senses.def: rule or limit that restricts behavior or action
senses.ex: The monastery's strictures included silence at meals and no visitors during the winter months.

senses.def: severe criticism or disapproval
senses.ex: Despite the critics' strictures, the experimental novel became a surprise bestseller.

origin: From Latin "stridens", making a harsh noise, from "stridere", to creak or grate, so a strident voice grates on the ear.

senses.def: loud, harsh, and grating in sound
senses.ex: The strident whine of the leaf blower next door made it impossible to concentrate on her calculus homework.

senses.def: forcefully and aggressively assertive in expressing views or demands
senses.ex: His strident op-ed demanding the coach's firing alienated even readers who agreed the team needed changes.

origin: From Old French "estrif", a quarrel, from "estriver", to strive or contend, a word of Germanic origin; "strife" and "strive" are relatives.

senses.def: angry or bitter disagreement or conflict, sometimes violent
senses.ex: Decades of ethnic strife had left the border towns divided, with neighbors refusing to shop at each other's markets.

origin: From Latin "stringens", drawing tight, from "stringere", to bind or draw tight, so stringent rules pull everything tight.

senses.def: strict, demanding, and exactly enforced
senses.ex: The lab's stringent safety rules required goggles, gloves, and a signed checklist before anyone touched a chemical.

origin: From Old English "strutian", to stand out stiffly, from a Germanic root meaning to swell or puff up, like a bird strutting with chest out.

senses.def: walk in a stiff, upright, self-important way
senses.ex: After winning the spelling bee, Marcus strutted down the hallway as if he owned the entire school.

senses.def: proud, swaggering way of walking
senses.ex: The rooster crossed the barnyard with a confident strut, scattering the hens in his path.

senses.def: rod or bar that braces or supports part of a structure
senses.ex: Engineers added steel struts beneath the old pier to keep it from sagging into the harbor.

origin: From "study", from Latin "studium", eager effort. Something studied has been carefully thought out in advance rather than felt naturally.

senses.def: carefully planned or deliberate, often not genuine or spontaneous
senses.ex: She answered with studied indifference, though everyone could see how much the award meant to her.

origin: From Late Latin "stultificare", to make foolish, from Latin "stultus", foolish: it first meant, in law, to declare someone of unsound mind, then to make someone look foolish, and later to make dull and useless.

senses.def: make dull, sluggish, or ineffective, especially through tedious routine or rigid rules
senses.ex: Years of copying worksheets had stultified the students' curiosity until a new teacher let them design their own experiments.

origin: Past participle of "stupefy", from Latin "stupefacere", to strike senseless, from "stupere", to be stunned, and "facere", to make.

senses.def: so astonished or shocked that one cannot think or react
senses.ex: The audience sat stupefied as the magician's assistant reappeared at the back of the theater seconds after vanishing.

senses.def: dazed and dull-witted, as from drugs, alcohol, heat, or exhaustion
senses.ex: Stupefied by the sweltering afternoon, the tourists slumped on the benches and barely noticed the parade.

origin: From Latin "stupefacere", to make senseless, from "stupere", to be stunned (as in "stupor"), and "facere", to make, via French.

senses.def: astonish or shock someone so much that they cannot think clearly
senses.ex: The sheer size of the blue whale's skeleton stupefied the visiting second graders into total silence.

senses.def: dull the senses or mind, as a drug, heat, or fatigue does
senses.ex: The cough syrup stupefied him so thoroughly that he slept through the entire thunderstorm.

origin: From Late Latin "stupendus", amazing, from "stupere", to be stunned, the same root as "stupor" and "stupid".

senses.def: astonishingly great in size, degree, or quality
senses.ex: From the summit they enjoyed a stupendous view stretching across three states and a glittering lake.

origin: From Latin "stupor", numbness or dullness, from "stupere", to be stunned.

senses.def: state of near-unconsciousness or greatly dulled senses
senses.ex: After forty hours without sleep, the exhausted pilot sat in a stupor, staring blankly at the controls.

origin: From Greek "Stygios", of the Styx, the river of the underworld in Greek myth, so the word carries the darkness of the land of the dead.

senses.def: extremely dark, gloomy, and forbidding
senses.ex: When the power failed, the cave tour was plunged into stygian blackness, and everyone grabbed the person in front of them.

senses.def: hellish or infernal, like the underworld of Greek myth
senses.ex: The novel describes the factory's furnace room as a stygian pit of smoke, noise, and endless heat.

origin: From golf, where a "stymie" was a ball blocking another ball's path to the hole; the term may come from Scots, but its origin is uncertain.

senses.def: block or obstruct the progress of someone or something
senses.ex: A shortage of computer chips stymied the carmaker's plans to double production this year.

origin: From golf, where a "stymie" was a ball lying between an opponent's ball and the hole; the term may come from Scots, but its origin is uncertain.

senses.def: block or obstruct the progress of someone or something
senses.ex: Heavy snow stymied the search party, forcing them to wait two days before climbing to the stranded hikers.

origin: From Latin "suasio", advice or persuasion, from "suadere", to urge, the root of "persuade" and "dissuade".

senses.def: act of persuading or urging, especially by argument rather than force
senses.ex: The principal relied on gentle suasion rather than punishment to convince students to stop vaping.

origin: From Latin "suavis", sweet or pleasant, a distant relative of English "sweet".

senses.def: charming, confident, and polished in manner, sometimes insincerely so
senses.ex: The suave salesman complimented every customer and somehow made the overpriced cars seem like bargains.

origin: From Late Latin "subalternus", from "sub", under, plus "alternus", alternate, from "alter", other, so one ranked under another.

senses.def: person of lower rank, a subordinate
senses.ex: The manager treated every subaltern on his staff like a servant, never once asking for their opinions.

senses.def: junior officer, especially in the British army, ranking below captain
senses.ex: As a young subaltern in India, he commanded a platoon of soldiers older than himself.

senses.def: of lower rank, status, or power
senses.ex: The historian gave subaltern groups, such as peasants and servants, a voice in her account of the revolution.

origin: From Old French "souduire", from Latin "subducere", to draw away, probably influenced by "subdere", to put under or subject.

senses.def: overcome and bring under control, by force or effort
senses.ex: It took four officers to subdue the struggling suspect and get him into the patrol car.

senses.def: make quieter, softer, or less intense
senses.ex: She subdued her excitement until the judges had officially announced the winner of the contest.

origin: From Latin "subjectivus", from "subjectum", subject, literally "thrown under", from "sub", under, and "jacere", to throw.

senses.def: based on personal feelings, tastes, or opinions rather than on facts
senses.ex: Whether a painting is beautiful is subjective, but whether it is a forgery can be settled by scientific tests.

senses.def: existing in the mind of the person perceiving rather than in the outside world
senses.ex: Psychologists study how pain is a subjective experience that two patients with identical injuries may feel very differently.

origin: From Latin "subiugare", to bring under the yoke, from "sub", under, plus "iugum", yoke. Defeated Roman enemies were made to pass under a yoke.

senses.def: bring under complete control, especially by conquest
senses.ex: The empire subjugated the neighboring tribes, forcing them to pay tribute and abandon their own laws.

senses.def: treat something as less important than something else
senses.ex: She refused to subjugate her own ambitions to her family's expectations about a safe career.

origin: From Latin sublimare, "raise" or "elevate," through its past participle sublimatus, suggesting an impulse lifted into another form.

senses.def: redirect an unacceptable impulse into a socially valued activity
senses.ex: He sublimated his anger into marathon training, running each morning before work.

senses.def: change directly from a solid to a gas
senses.ex: In the demonstration, dry ice sublimated into gas without forming a puddle.

origin: From Latin "sublimis", lofty or raised high; the deeper origin of the Latin word is uncertain.

senses.def: so beautiful, grand, or excellent that it inspires awe
senses.ex: Watching the sunrise from the summit of Mount Fuji was a sublime experience she never forgot.

senses.def: something of awe-inspiring grandeur, usually as "the sublime"
senses.ex: The lecture traced how Romantic painters tried to capture the sublime in storms, glaciers, and towering waterfalls.

senses.def: extreme or complete, often of a careless or foolish attitude
senses.ex: He walked into the final exam with sublime confidence, having never opened the textbook.

origin: From Latin "sub", below, and "limen", threshold: a subliminal signal stays below the threshold of conscious awareness.

senses.def: below the threshold of conscious awareness but still able to influence the mind
senses.ex: The study tested whether subliminal images of food, flashed too quickly to see, made viewers feel hungry.

origin: From Latin sub, "below," and lunaris, "of the moon," from luna, "moon."

senses.def: belonging to the earthly world rather than the heavens
senses.ex: The astronomer called storms and tides sublunary events, unlike the distant movements of stars.

senses.def: ordinary, mundane, or concerned with material life
senses.ex: Her speech returned from lofty ideals to sublunary concerns such as rent and groceries.

origin: From "submit", from Latin "submittere", to lower or put under, from "sub", under, and "mittere", to send or put.

senses.def: quick to obey others and accept their authority without resisting
senses.ex: The trainer warned that a dog rolling onto its back is showing submissive behavior toward the larger dog.

origin: From Medieval Latin "subordinatus", placed lower in order, from "sub", under, and "ordinare", to arrange in order.

senses.def: lower in rank, position, or importance
senses.ex: In the army, a lieutenant is subordinate to a captain and must follow the captain's orders.

senses.def: person who works under the authority of another
senses.ex: A good manager gives subordinates credit for their ideas instead of presenting them as her own.

senses.def: treat or regard as less important than something else
senses.ex: The council voted to subordinate short-term profits to the long-term health of the river.

origin: From Latin "sub poena", under penalty, the opening words of the writ, warning that anyone who ignored it would be punished.

senses.def: legal order requiring someone to appear in court or hand over evidence
senses.ex: The accountant received a subpoena ordering her to testify about the company's missing funds.

senses.def: summon someone or demand documents with such a legal order
senses.ex: The committee subpoenaed the bank's emails after executives refused to share them voluntarily.

origin: From Latin "subsequens", following closely, from "subsequi", from "sub", close after, and "sequi", to follow.

senses.def: coming after something in time or order
senses.ex: The first chapter introduces the family, and subsequent chapters follow each sibling into adulthood.

origin: From Latin "subserviens", from "subservire", to serve under, from "sub", under, and "servire", to serve.

senses.def: too eager to obey or please others
senses.ex: The new assistant was so subservient that he agreed with every opinion his boss expressed, even contradictory ones.

senses.def: less important than something else and serving its purposes
senses.ex: In the director's view, the music should stay subservient to the story rather than overwhelm it.

origin: From Latin "subsidere", to settle or sink down, from "sub", down, and "sidere", to settle.

senses.def: become less intense, loud, or violent
senses.ex: Once the laughter subsided, the teacher calmly asked who had put the rubber snake in her desk.

senses.def: sink or settle to a lower level, as ground or floodwater does
senses.ex: Residents returned to their homes only after the floodwaters had subsided below the doorsteps.

origin: From Latin "subsidiarius", belonging to the reserve troops, from "subsidium", reserve or help, from "sub", behind, and "sedere", to sit.

senses.def: secondary or supporting, less important than the main thing
senses.ex: The committee spent so long on subsidiary questions that it never voted on the main budget proposal.

senses.def: company controlled by a larger parent company
senses.ex: The streaming service is a subsidiary of a giant media group that also owns two film studios.

origin: From Latin "subsidium", support or aid, from "sub", under, and "sedere", to sit, via French; the Latin word first meant troops held in reserve.

senses.def: money granted by a government to support an industry, cause, or price
senses.ex: A federal subsidy lowered the price of solar panels enough that many farmers installed them on their barns.

origin: From Late Latin "subsistentia", from Latin "subsistere", to stand firm or hold out, from "sub", under, and "sistere", to stand.

senses.def: state of having just enough food and money to stay alive
senses.ex: The families in the valley lived at subsistence level, growing barely enough corn and beans to last the winter.

senses.def: means of supporting life, such as food and shelter
senses.ex: The fishermen depended on the river for their subsistence, so the new dam threatened their whole way of life.

origin: From Medieval Latin "substantiare", to give substance to, from Latin "substantia", substance or essence.

senses.def: provide evidence to support or prove a claim
senses.ex: The reporter refused to publish the rumor until she could substantiate it with documents and two independent sources.

origin: From Old French "substantif", from Late Latin "substantivus", having substance, from "substantia", substance, from "sub", under, and "stare", to stand.

senses.def: dealing with real, important matters rather than appearances or details
senses.ex: The two leaders posed for photographs, but aides admitted no substantive agreement had been reached on trade.

senses.def: solid and considerable in amount or effect
senses.ex: After the review, the board made substantive changes to the safety rules instead of merely rewording them.

origin: From Medieval Latin "subsumere", from "sub", under, and "sumere", to take: to subsume is to take something in under a larger heading.

senses.def: include or absorb something into a larger category, group, or system
senses.ex: After the merger, the small design studio was subsumed into the corporation's marketing department and lost its name.

origin: From Latin "subterfugere", to flee secretly, from "subter", beneath or in secret, and "fugere", to flee: a subterfuge is a sneaky escape.

senses.def: trickery or deception used to achieve a goal or avoid something
senses.ex: The spy relied on subterfuge, posing as a wine merchant to gain entry to the embassy party.

origin: From Latin "subterraneus", underground, from "sub", under, and "terra", earth.

senses.def: existing or happening under the surface of the earth
senses.ex: Explorers mapped a subterranean river that flowed for miles through limestone caves beneath the desert.

senses.def: hidden or secret, operating out of public view
senses.ex: A subterranean network of collectors traded the banned books in back rooms and basements.

origin: From Latin "subtilis", fine, thin, or delicate, through Old French; the "b" was put back into the spelling to match Latin but is never pronounced.

senses.def: so delicate or slight that it is hard to notice or describe
senses.ex: The chef added a subtle hint of cardamom that most diners tasted but could not quite name.

senses.def: clever and indirect, or skilled at noticing fine distinctions
senses.ex: Rather than scolding her brother, she made a subtle remark about the empty cookie jar and let him confess.

origin: From "subvert", from Latin "subvertere", to overturn, from "sub", from below, and "vertere", to turn.

senses.def: seeking or tending to undermine an established system or authority
senses.ex: The regime banned the poet's books as subversive after students began reciting them at protests.

senses.def: person who works secretly to undermine a government or system
senses.ex: During the Cold War, government agencies kept files on writers they suspected of being subversives.

origin: From Latin "subvertere", to overturn, literally "to turn from below", from "sub", under, and "vertere", to turn.

senses.def: undermine the power or authority of an established system or institution
senses.ex: The general was accused of plotting to subvert the election by intimidating poll workers.

senses.def: overturn usual expectations or conventions in a surprising way
senses.ex: The film subverts the fairy-tale formula when the princess rescues the knight from the dragon's tower.

origin: From "succeed", from Latin "succedere", to come after, from "sub", next to or after, and "cedere", to go.

senses.def: coming after or following in order
senses.ex: The first season of the show was modest, but each succeeding season drew millions more viewers.

origin: From Latin "successio", a following after, from "succedere", to come after, from "sub", next to, and "cedere", to go.

senses.def: number of people or things following one another in order
senses.ex: A succession of storms battered the coast that winter, giving crews no time to repair the damaged pier.

senses.def: process by which someone inherits a title, office or position
senses.ex: The old king's death without an heir set off a bitter fight over the succession to the throne.

origin: From Latin "succinctus", tucked up with a belt, from "succingere", to gird up: a succinct statement is tightly belted, with nothing loose.

senses.def: expressed briefly and clearly, without wasted words
senses.ex: Her succinct summary of the hundred-page report fit on a single index card.

origin: From Old French "socours", from Latin "succurrere", to run to help, from "sub", up to, and "currere", to run.

senses.def: help and comfort given in a time of hardship or distress
senses.ex: After the earthquake, the monastery offered food, blankets, and succor to hundreds of homeless families.

senses.def: give help or comfort to someone in distress
senses.ex: Volunteers worked through the night to succor the stranded passengers at the snowbound airport.

origin: From Latin "succulentus", full of juice, from "sucus", juice or sap.

senses.def: full of juice and delicious to eat
senses.ex: The chef served succulent slices of roast pork that dripped with juice the moment they were cut.

senses.def: plant with thick fleshy leaves or stems that store water
senses.ex: She filled her sunny windowsill with succulents because they need watering only once every few weeks.

senses.def: of a plant, having thick fleshy parts that store water
senses.ex: Aloe and jade are succulent plants that survive long dry spells by storing water in their leaves.

origin: From Latin "succumbere", to sink down or yield, from "sub", under, and "-cumbere", to lie down, via French.

senses.def: give in to a stronger force, pressure, or temptation
senses.ex: After resisting for weeks, Jamal finally succumbed to his sister's pleading and bought her a puppy.

senses.def: die from an illness, injury, or other harmful condition
senses.ex: The ancient oak survived three hurricanes but eventually succumbed to a fungal disease.

syn: yield, surrender, submit, give in, capitulate

origin: From Latin "sufficiens", from "sufficere", to be enough or to supply, from "sub", under, and "facere", to make.

senses.def: enough to meet a particular need or purpose
senses.ex: The judge ruled that the blurry photograph was not sufficient evidence to convict the driver.

origin: From Latin "suffragium", support or a vote. Despite the look, it is not related to "suffer".

senses.def: right to vote in political elections
senses.ex: The campaign for women's suffrage in Britain lasted decades before women finally won the vote in 1918.

origin: From Latin "suffusus", past participle of "suffundere", to pour beneath or spread over, from "sub", under, and "fundere", to pour.

senses.def: spread gradually through or over something, as light, color or feeling does
senses.ex: As the sun rose, a soft pink glow suffused the sky above the harbor, and the gulls began to call.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "soleyn", alone, from Latin "solus", alone: in Middle English the meaning shifted from solitary to gloomy and withdrawn.

senses.def: bad-tempered and silently resentful
senses.ex: Grounded for the weekend, the sullen teenager refused to say a word during dinner.

senses.def: dark, dull, and gloomy, especially of sky or weather
senses.ex: A sullen gray sky hung over the harbor all week, and the fishing boats stayed tied up.

origin: From Old English "sylian", to soil or make dirty, perhaps also influenced by Old French "souiller", to soil.

senses.def: damage the purity, reputation, or integrity of something
senses.ex: The senator worried that his aide's bribery scandal would sully his own reputation for honesty.

senses.def: make something dirty or stained
senses.ex: She refused to let the muddy dog sully her freshly washed white couch.

origin: From the obsolete verb "sulter", a variant of "swelter", plus "-y", so sultry weather makes you swelter.

senses.def: hot and humid, making people uncomfortable
senses.ex: On sultry August nights the whole street sat on their porches, waiting for any breeze off the river.

senses.def: attractive in a sensual, smoldering way
senses.ex: The jazz singer's sultry voice filled the dim club, low and slow over the soft piano.

origin: From "sum" plus "-ation". "Sum" comes from Latin "summa", the total, from "summus", highest.

senses.def: summing up of the main points, especially a lawyer's closing argument
senses.ex: In her summation, the defense attorney reminded the jury that no witness had placed her client at the scene.

senses.def: process of adding things together, or the total that results
senses.ex: The final grade is the summation of scores from homework, quizzes and the end-of-term exam.

origin: From Old French "somet", a little top, from "som", top, from Latin "summum", highest point.

senses.def: highest point of a mountain or hill
senses.ex: The climbers reached the summit just after dawn and could see three countries below them.

senses.def: meeting between heads of government or other top leaders
senses.ex: The two presidents met at a summit in Geneva to discuss reducing nuclear weapons.

senses.def: highest level of achievement or success
senses.ex: Winning the Nobel Prize marked the summit of her long scientific career.

senses.def: climb to the top of a mountain
senses.ex: Only a handful of climbers have summited the peak in winter, when the winds exceed a hundred miles an hour.

origin: From Latin "sumptuarius", relating to expense, from "sumptus", cost, from "sumere", to take or spend.

senses.def: relating to laws that limit private spending on luxuries such as clothing and food
senses.ex: Medieval sumptuary laws forbade merchants from wearing the silk and fur reserved for the nobility.

origin: From Latin "sumptuosus", costly, from "sumptus", expense, from "sumere", to take or spend.

senses.def: splendid, lavish and expensive-looking
senses.ex: The wedding guests gasped at the sumptuous banquet of roast duck, oysters and towering cakes laid out under chandeliers.

origin: From Old English "sundrian", to separate, from "sundor", apart. The same root gives "asunder" and "sundry".

senses.def: split or tear apart, often violently
senses.ex: The earthquake sundered the highway, leaving a gap wide enough to swallow a truck.

senses.def: separate people or groups who belonged together
senses.ex: The bitter quarrel over the inheritance sundered the family for nearly twenty years.

origin: From Old English "syndrig", separate or special, from "sundor", apart, the same root found in "asunder".

senses.def: of various kinds; several and assorted
senses.ex: The junk drawer held sundry objects: rubber bands, dead batteries, a key to nothing, and a single chopstick.

senses.def: various small items not worth listing separately, usually as "sundries"
senses.ex: The camp store sold sundries like toothpaste, sunscreen, and bug spray at twice the normal price.

origin: From Medieval Latin "superannuatus", more than a year old, from "super", beyond, and "annus", year.

senses.def: too old to be useful, outdated or obsolete
senses.ex: The office still ran its payroll on a superannuated computer that nobody under fifty knew how to repair.

senses.def: retired from work because of age, often with a pension
senses.ex: The club was full of superannuated teachers and civil servants who spent their afternoons playing bridge.

origin: From "superb", from Latin "superbus", proud or splendid, a word related to "super", above, plus "-ly".

senses.def: extremely well; excellently
senses.ex: The understudy performed superbly on opening night, and few in the audience missed the injured star.

origin: From Latin "superciliosus", haughty, from "supercilium", eyebrow: a supercilious person looks down on others with a raised eyebrow.

senses.def: behaving as though one is superior to others; disdainful
senses.ex: The supercilious waiter smirked when we asked whether the restaurant had a children's menu.

origin: From Latin "supererogare", to pay out beyond what is owed, from "super", above, and "erogare", to pay out.

senses.def: going beyond what duty or need requires
senses.ex: Returning the lost wallet was her duty, but driving two hours to deliver it in person was supererogatory kindness.

senses.def: more than is needed, and so superfluous
senses.ex: The editor cut the supererogatory final paragraph, since the essay had already made its point.

syn: superfluous, gratuitous, unnecessary, excessive, beyond the call of duty

origin: From Late Latin "superficialis", of the surface, from "superficies", surface, from "super", above, and "facies", face.

senses.def: not thorough or deep; concerned only with the obvious
senses.ex: The committee's superficial review missed the cracks hidden behind the bridge's fresh coat of paint.

senses.def: existing or occurring only at the surface
senses.ex: The cyclist's fall left only superficial scrapes on his elbows, and he finished the race.

senses.def: appearing real or significant only until examined more closely
senses.ex: Despite a superficial resemblance, the two mushrooms differ sharply, and one of them is deadly.

origin: From Latin "superfluus", overflowing, from "super", over, and "fluere", to flow: what is superfluous spills over beyond what is needed.

senses.def: more than is needed or wanted; unnecessary
senses.ex: The editor cut every superfluous adjective until the essay was half its original length.

origin: From Late Latin "superlativus", from "superlatus", carried beyond or exaggerated, from "super", above, and "ferre", to carry.

senses.def: of the highest quality, excellent
senses.ex: Critics praised the young violinist's superlative performance, calling it the finest of the whole festival.

senses.def: form of an adjective or adverb showing the highest degree, such as "fastest"
senses.ex: The teacher asked us to list the superlatives of good, bad and far, which turned out to be irregular.

senses.def: exaggerated word or expression of praise
senses.ex: The travel brochure was full of superlatives, calling every beach the most beautiful on earth.

origin: From Old French "supernel", from Latin "supernus", above or on high, from "super", above.

senses.def: heavenly or divine, belonging to the realm above
senses.ex: The poet described the sunrise over the mountains as a supernal light pouring down from another world.

senses.def: of exceptional, almost otherworldly excellence
senses.ex: Even the bored teenagers fell silent at the supernal beauty of the choir's final chord.

origin: From Latin "supersedere", to sit above, from "super", above, and "sedere", to sit; the meaning "replace" arose in the 1600s.

senses.def: take the place of something older, weaker, or less effective
senses.ex: Streaming services have largely superseded the video rental stores that were common in the 1990s.

origin: From Latin "supinus", lying on the back or turned upward, a word related to "sub", under, that pictures a body laid flat with its face up.

senses.def: lying flat on one's back, face upward
senses.ex: The physical therapist asked him to lie supine on the mat and slowly raise one leg.

senses.def: failing to act or resist, out of laziness, weakness, or indifference
senses.ex: Critics accused the supine legislature of approving every one of the governor's demands without debate.

origin: From Latin "supplantare", to trip up, from "sub", under, and "planta", sole of the foot: to supplant someone is to trip them and take their place.

senses.def: take the place of someone or something, often by force, scheming, or superiority
senses.ex: Digital cameras quickly supplanted film, and within a decade most photo labs had closed.

origin: From Old French "souple", soft or yielding, from Latin "supplex", kneeling or submissive, of uncertain formation.

senses.def: bending and moving easily, flexible and graceful
senses.ex: Years of yoga had kept her supple enough to touch her toes at eighty.

senses.def: soft and pliable rather than stiff
senses.ex: The saddle maker rubbed oil into the leather until it was supple enough to fold without cracking.

senses.def: quick to adapt to new situations or ideas
senses.ex: Her supple mind let her switch from debating philosophy to fixing an engine in the same afternoon.

origin: From French "suppliant", begging, from "supplier", to beg, from Latin "supplicare", to kneel in plea.

senses.def: person who humbly asks for something, especially from someone powerful
senses.ex: Suppliants lined the palace steps each morning, hoping the queen would hear their petitions.

senses.def: asking humbly and earnestly
senses.ex: He raised his hands in a suppliant gesture and begged the referee to reconsider the penalty.

origin: From Latin "supplicans", from "supplicare", to bow down in plea, from "sub", under, and "plicare", to fold or bend: a supplicant bends low to beg.

senses.def: person who humbly asks or pleads for something
senses.ex: Treated as a supplicant rather than a partner, the small nation had to beg for every loan.

senses.def: humbly pleading or begging
senses.ex: The dog fixed its supplicant eyes on the last slice of pizza.

origin: From Latin "supplicare", to beg humbly, from "sub", under, and "plicare", to fold or bend, picturing someone bowed low in plea.

senses.def: ask or beg humbly and earnestly, especially of someone in authority or a god
senses.ex: The villagers gathered at the temple to supplicate the gods for rain after months of drought.

origin: From Latin "suppositio", a placing under, from "sub", under, and "ponere", to put: a supposition is an idea placed under an argument as its base.

senses.def: belief or idea assumed to be true without proof
senses.ex: The detective warned that the theory was pure supposition until the lab confirmed whose fingerprints were on the glass.

origin: From Old French "sorfait", excess, from "sorfaire", to overdo, from "sur", over, and "faire", to do.

senses.def: excessive amount of something
senses.ex: The town had a surfeit of coffee shops but not a single place to buy a hammer.

senses.def: supply or fill someone with too much of something
senses.ex: Surfeited with holiday sweets, the children could not face another cookie by New Year's Day.

origin: A 16th-century respelling of "sirly", from "sir" plus "-ly": it first meant lordly or haughty, then rude and gruff.

senses.def: bad-tempered, rude, and unfriendly
senses.ex: The surly ticket clerk grunted at every question and slid our change back without looking up.

origin: From Old French "surmis", from "surmettre", to accuse, from "sur", upon, and "mettre", to put: to surmise is to put an idea onto thin evidence.

senses.def: suppose that something is true without solid evidence
senses.ex: Seeing the empty food bowl and the guilty-looking cat, she surmised that the fish had not died of natural causes.

senses.def: guess or idea based on little evidence
senses.ex: The historian admitted that her account of the queen's last days was largely surmise.

origin: From Old French "surmonter", to rise above, from "sur", over, and "monter", to climb.

senses.def: overcome a difficulty or obstacle
senses.ex: The team surmounted a shoestring budget and a broken robot to win the regional engineering competition.

senses.def: stand or be placed on top of something
senses.ex: The old courthouse dome is surmounted by a bronze statue of Justice holding her scales.

syn: overcome, conquer, defeat, master, get over

origin: From "surpass", from French "surpasser", to go beyond, from "sur", over, and "passer", to pass.

senses.def: exceptionally great; exceeding all others
senses.ex: Visitors to the gardens praised their surpassing beauty, especially when the cherry trees bloomed.

origin: From Latin "surrepticius", furtive, from "surrepere", to creep up stealthily, from "sub", under, and "repere", to creep.

senses.def: done secretly or stealthily to avoid being noticed
senses.ex: During the long sermon, Leo cast surreptitious glances at the football score on his phone.

origin: From Latin "surrogatus", chosen as a substitute, from "surrogare", from "sub", in place of, and "rogare", to ask.

senses.def: substitute, especially a person who acts or speaks in another's place
senses.ex: The candidate was ill, so a surrogate delivered the campaign speech in her place.

senses.def: woman who carries and gives birth to a baby for another person or couple
senses.ex: After years of trying, the couple worked with a surrogate who gave birth to their twins in March.

senses.def: serving as a substitute for someone or something
senses.ex: The older brother became a surrogate father to his siblings after their parents died.

origin: From French "surveiller", to watch over, from "sur-", over, plus "veiller", to watch, from Latin "vigilare", to stay awake, as in "vigil".

senses.def: close, continued watching of a person, group, or place, often secretly
senses.ex: Detectives kept the warehouse under surveillance for three weeks before they finally caught the smugglers unloading stolen goods.

senses.def: systematic monitoring of something, such as the spread of a disease
senses.ex: Health officials stepped up surveillance of local hospitals after several patients showed symptoms of a new strain of flu.

origin: From Late Latin "susceptibilis", from Latin "suscipere", to take up or receive, from "sub", up from under, and "capere", to take.

senses.def: likely to be harmed, influenced, or affected by something
senses.ex: Young seedlings are highly susceptible to frost, so the gardener covers them on cold nights.

senses.def: easily moved by emotion or easily persuaded
senses.ex: Scammers target lonely, susceptible people who are eager to trust a friendly voice.

origin: From Old French "sustenance", from Latin "sustinere", to hold up, from "sub-", from below, plus "tenere", to hold.

senses.def: food and drink that keep a person or animal alive
senses.ex: Stranded on the mountain for two days, the hikers relied on a few granola bars and melted snow for sustenance.

senses.def: something that supports or strengthens the mind, spirit, or an effort
senses.ex: During her long illness, letters from old friends gave her more sustenance than any medicine.

origin: From Latin "susurrus", a whispering or humming, a word that imitates the soft sound it names.

senses.def: soft whispering, rustling, or murmuring sound
senses.ex: Lying in the tent, she listened to the susurrus of wind through the pines until she drifted off to sleep.

origin: From French "svelte", from Italian "svelto", stretched out or slender, from "svellere", to pluck out.

senses.def: slender and graceful in a way that is attractive
senses.ex: The svelte dancer moved across the stage so lightly that she seemed to weigh nothing at all.

senses.def: sleek and elegant in design or style
senses.ex: The company replaced its bulky old laptop with a svelte aluminum model barely thicker than a magazine.

origin: Formed from "swag", to sway, plus a suffix for repeated action, first recorded in Shakespeare's "A Midsummer Night's Dream".

senses.def: walk or behave in a very confident, arrogant, or showy way
senses.ex: Fresh from his championship win, the boxer swaggered into the press conference wearing sunglasses and a gold belt.

senses.def: very confident, often arrogant manner of walking or behaving
senses.ex: The new quarterback played with a swagger that thrilled the fans and irritated his opponents.

origin: From Old English "sweard", skin or rind, which by Middle English also meant turf, the grassy skin of the ground.

senses.def: stretch of short, thick grass
senses.ex: Children ran barefoot across the green sward in front of the old manor house while their parents spread out picnic blankets.

origin: An alteration of "swarty", from "swart", dark, from Old English "sweart", black.

senses.def: having a dark complexion, often from sun or weather
senses.ex: The swarthy fisherman, his face weathered by forty years at sea, mended his nets on the dock each morning.

origin: From "swashbuckler", a swaggering fighter, from "swash", to strike noisily, plus "buckler", a small shield, like a brawler banging sword on shield.

senses.def: full of daring, romantic adventure, especially involving sword fights
senses.ex: The swashbuckling film follows a pirate captain who duels his way across the decks of three different ships.

senses.def: boldly adventurous and flamboyant in style or behavior
senses.ex: The swashbuckling investor made and lost several fortunes before he turned forty, always chasing the next risky deal.

origin: From Old English words for wrapping and bandages, a family that also gave us "swaddle"; the "broad strip" sense comes from the variant "swath".

senses.def: wrap someone or something in several layers of fabric
senses.ex: The nurse swathed the newborn in a soft blanket before handing her to her father.

senses.def: broad strip or large area of something
senses.ex: The wildfire burned a swathe of forest ten miles long through the national park.

origin: From German "Schwindler", a cheat or reckless schemer, from "schwindeln", to be dizzy, and later to cheat.

senses.def: person who cheats others out of money or property by deception
senses.ex: The swindler persuaded dozens of retirees to invest their savings in a gold mine that never existed.

syn: fraudster, con artist, cheat, charlatan, scammer

origin: From Greek "Sybarites", a citizen of Sybaris, an ancient Greek city in southern Italy famous for its luxury and pleasure-seeking.

senses.def: person devoted to luxury and sensual pleasure
senses.ex: A true sybarite, he spent his vacation moving between the spa, the hot tub, and the five-course dinner.

origin: From Greek "sykophantes", informer, from "sykon", fig, and "phainein", to show; why figs were involved is disputed, and the meaning later shifted to flatterer.

senses.def: person who flatters powerful people to win their favor
senses.ex: Surrounded by sycophants who praised every idea, the CEO never heard that his product was failing.

origin: From Greek "syllogismos", inference or conclusion, built from "syn-", together, and "logos", reason, so reasons put together.

senses.def: argument in which a conclusion follows from two connected premises
senses.ex: The classic syllogism runs: all humans are mortal, Socrates is human, therefore Socrates is mortal.

senses.def: subtle or misleading argument that only seems logical
senses.ex: The lawyer's closing was a clever syllogism that sounded airtight until the jury noticed its first premise was false.

origin: From New Latin "sylphes", coined by the 16th-century writer Paracelsus for spirits of the air, possibly from "sylvestris", of the woods, and "nympha", nymph.

senses.def: slender, graceful woman or girl
senses.ex: In the ballet's opening scene, a sylph in pale silk seemed to float across the moonlit stage.

senses.def: imaginary spirit of the air in folklore and fantasy
senses.ex: The old tale tells of a sylph who lived in the clouds and guided lost travelers home with gentle breezes.

origin: From Latin "silvanus", of the woods, from "silva", forest, and Silvanus was also the Roman god who guarded woodlands.

senses.def: relating to or set among woods and forests
senses.ex: The poet retreated to a sylvan cottage where the only sounds were birdsong and a stream running over stones.

senses.def: full of trees, wooded
senses.ex: Developers promised to preserve the sylvan hillsides, but within a decade most of the oaks had been cleared.

origin: From Greek "symbiosis", living together, from "syn", together, and "bios", life.

senses.def: close, long-term relationship between two different species, often benefiting both
senses.ex: Clownfish and sea anemones live in symbiosis: the fish gets shelter and the anemone gets cleaned.

senses.def: mutually beneficial relationship between people, groups, or things
senses.ex: The bookstore and the café next door developed a happy symbiosis, sharing customers and a back patio.

origin: From Greek "symmetria", from "syn-", together, plus "metron", measure, so parts that measure up to each other.

senses.def: exact match of shape and size on opposite sides of a dividing line
senses.ex: A butterfly's wings show near-perfect symmetry, with each spot on the left matched by one on the right.

senses.def: pleasing balance and proportion among the parts of a whole
senses.ex: Architects praise the building's symmetry, with its central dome flanked by identical wings and matching rows of columns.

senses.def: close similarity or correspondence between two things or events
senses.ex: Historians have noted the odd symmetry between the two presidents' careers, each rising and falling within a decade.

origin: From Greek "symposion", drinking party, from "syn-", together, plus "pinein", to drink, and such parties often featured serious conversation.

senses.def: conference where experts present and discuss views on one subject
senses.ex: The university hosted a two-day symposium on artificial intelligence, with speakers from law, medicine, and philosophy.

senses.def: collection of essays by different writers on a single topic
senses.ex: The journal's spring issue is a symposium on free speech, with twelve contributors arguing very different positions.

senses.def: drinking party in ancient Greece with music and intellectual talk
senses.ex: In Plato's dialogue, the guests at a symposium take turns giving speeches in praise of love.

origin: From Greek "symptomatikos", from "symptoma", a chance happening or symptom, from "sympiptein", to fall together or happen.

senses.def: serving as a sign or indication of a larger problem or condition
senses.ex: The constant staff turnover was symptomatic of deeper problems with the company's management and pay.

senses.def: showing the physical signs of a disease
senses.ex: Only patients who were symptomatic, with fever or coughing, were sent for further testing at the clinic.

origin: From Greek "synchronos", happening at the same time, from "syn", together, and "chronos", time.

senses.def: existing or happening at exactly the same time or rate
senses.ex: The dancers' synchronous movements made the twenty of them look like a single flowing body.

senses.def: happening live, with all participants present at the same time
senses.ex: The online course mixes recorded lectures with synchronous discussions every Thursday evening.

origin: From "syncopate", from Late Latin "syncopare", to cut short, from Greek "synkope", a cutting off, from "syn", together, and "koptein", to cut.

senses.def: having a rhythm in which normally weak beats or off-beats are stressed
senses.ex: The pianist's syncopated left hand gave the old hymn an unexpected ragtime swing.

origin: From Greek "synkretismos", a union of Cretan cities against a common enemy, from "syn-", together, plus "Krētes", Cretans.

senses.def: blending of different religions, cultures, or schools of thought into one
senses.ex: The festival is a striking example of syncretism, mixing Catholic saints with older Indigenous harvest rituals.

origin: From Greek "synekdoche", understanding one thing along with another, from "syn-", with, "ek", out of, and "dechesthai", to receive.

senses.def: figure of speech using a part for the whole or the whole for a part
senses.ex: Calling workers "hired hands" is a synecdoche, since the hands stand for the whole person doing the labor.

syn: pars pro toto, trope, figure of speech

origin: From Greek "synergia", cooperation, from "syn", together, and "ergon", work.

senses.def: combined effect of people or things working together that exceeds their separate effects
senses.ex: The synergy between the quiet coder and the outgoing designer produced an app neither could have built alone.

origin: From Greek "syn-", together, plus "aisthesis", sensation, so two senses perceived together.

senses.def: condition in which one sense triggers another, such as hearing colors
senses.ex: Because of her synesthesia, the composer saw each musical key as a different color, with D major glowing yellow.

senses.def: describing one sense in terms of another in writing
senses.ex: The poet's line about a "loud yellow" is a vivid use of synesthesia, giving sound to a color.

origin: From Greek "synonymos", having the same name, from "syn-", together, plus "onoma", name.

senses.def: having the same or nearly the same meaning as another word
senses.ex: In everyday speech "big" and "large" are synonymous, but writers often choose one for its sound.

senses.def: so closely linked with something that one suggests the other
senses.ex: For many travelers, the brand has become synonymous with reliability, comfort, and on-time flights.

origin: From Greek "synopsis", a general view, from "syn-", together, plus "opsis", sight, so seeing the whole at once.

senses.def: brief summary of the main points of a book, film, or argument
senses.ex: Before pitching her novel to agents, the author wrote a one-page synopsis covering the plot from beginning to end.

origin: From Greek "synoptikos", seeing all together, from "syn", together, and "opsis", view, the same roots as "synopsis".

senses.def: giving a broad summary or general view of a whole subject
senses.ex: The professor's synoptic lecture covered three centuries of European history in a single hour.

senses.def: relating to the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, which tell the story in similar ways
senses.ex: Scholars compare the synoptic Gospels side by side to see which stories each writer added or left out.

origin: From Greek "syntaxis", arrangement, from "syn", together, and "tassein", to arrange, the same root as "tactics".

senses.def: arrangement of words and phrases to form well-formed sentences
senses.ex: Yoda's odd syntax, putting the verb at the end, makes his sentences instantly recognizable.

senses.def: set of rules for how statements must be written in a programming language
senses.ex: The program would not run because of a single syntax error: a missing semicolon on line forty.

syn: grammar, sentence structure, word order, structure
