senses.def: remaining from an earlier stage after losing most of its original function
senses.ex: The cave fish has vestigial eyes that detect light but cannot form useful images.

senses.def: remaining from an older system after most of its purpose has disappeared
senses.ex: A vestigial signature line still appeared on the digital form years after approvals moved online.

origin: From Latin "veto", "I forbid", a word Roman officials used when blocking a measure.

senses.def: act of formally rejecting or blocking a proposal
senses.ex: The governor's veto stopped the bill despite its strong support in both chambers.

senses.def: the official power to reject a proposed decision or law
senses.ex: Each permanent council member holds a veto over resolutions, allowing one objection to stop adoption.

senses.def: reject or block a proposal by exercising authority
senses.ex: The board vetoed the expansion after residents raised concerns about traffic near the school.

origin: From Old French "vexer", from Latin "vexare", to shake, disturb, or harass.

senses.def: annoy, frustrate, or worry someone
senses.ex: The constant beeping of the smoke alarm vexed the whole household until someone finally changed the battery.

origin: From Latin "vexatio", distress or harassment, from "vexare", to shake or disturb.

senses.def: state of being annoyed, frustrated, or worried
senses.ex: To her vexation, the train sat motionless outside the station for forty minutes without any announcement.

senses.def: something that causes annoyance or worry
senses.ex: Slow internet was the chief vexation of working from the remote mountain cabin.

origin: From Latin "via", road or way, used in the form meaning "by way of".

senses.def: traveling through a place on the way to somewhere else
senses.ex: We flew from Boston to Tokyo via Seattle, stretching our legs during a short layover.

senses.def: by means of or using
senses.ex: Students submit their essays via the school's website instead of handing in paper copies.

syn: through, by way of, by means of

origin: From French "viable", able to live, from "vie", life, from Latin "vita", life.

senses.def: capable of working successfully, feasible
senses.ex: Engineers concluded that a tunnel was not viable, so the city decided to build a bridge instead.

senses.def: able to survive, grow, or develop
senses.ex: Only about half of the seeds collected from the old plants were still viable after ten years in storage.

origin: From Latin "vicarius", substitute, from "vicis", turn or change, the same root as "vicar", someone who acts in another's place.

senses.def: experienced in imagination through the actions or feelings of another person
senses.ex: Grandpa got vicarious thrills from watching his granddaughter's skydiving videos again and again.

origin: From Latin "vicissitudo", change, from "vicissim", in turn, from "vicis", turn or change.

senses.def: change in circumstances, usually unwelcome or unpredictable
senses.ex: The family business survived the vicissitudes of war, recession, and three changes of ownership.

syn: change, fluctuation, shift, reversal, ups and downs

origin: Shortened from Middle English "envien", to challenge, from Old French "envier", to invite or challenge, from Latin "invitare", to invite.

senses.def: compete eagerly with others to achieve or obtain something
senses.ex: Three restaurants vie for customers on the same busy corner, each offering a cheaper lunch special.

origin: From Latin "vigilans", staying awake, from "vigilare", to keep watch, from "vigil", awake.

senses.def: keeping careful watch for possible danger or trouble
senses.ex: Lifeguards must stay vigilant even on calm days, since swimmers can get into trouble within seconds.

origin: From French "vignette", a little vine design, from "vigne", "vine", ultimately linked to Latin "vinum", "wine".

senses.def: brief scene or description that vividly captures a person, place, or moment
senses.ex: Each chapter ends with a vignette of one neighbor, letting the town emerge through small encounters.

senses.def: small illustration or photograph with edges that fade into its background
senses.ex: The cookbook opens with a vignette of rosemary sprigs fading into the cream-colored page.

senses.def: make the edges of an image fade toward the background
senses.ex: The designer vignetted the portrait so the viewer's eye settled on the musician's face.

origin: From Old French "vigour", from Latin "vigor", liveliness, from "vigere", to be lively or thrive.

senses.def: physical strength, energy, and good health
senses.ex: At seventy, the farmer still worked the fields with the vigor of a much younger man.

senses.def: force and enthusiasm in effort or expression
senses.ex: The senator defended the bill with such vigor that several opponents changed their votes.

origin: From Late Latin "vilificare", to make vile, from Latin "vilis", cheap or worthless, plus "facere", to make.

senses.def: speak or write about someone in an abusive, disparaging way
senses.ex: Tabloids vilified the referee for weeks after his disputed call cost the home team the championship.

origin: Possibly from Latin "vim", a form of "vis", force or strength, though it may instead be a playful modern invention.

senses.def: lively energy and enthusiasm
senses.ex: The new coach brought fresh vim to the team, running drills with music blasting and jokes flying.

origin: From Latin "vindicare", to claim, set free, or avenge, probably from "vim", force, plus "dicere", to say.

senses.def: clear someone of blame or suspicion
senses.ex: DNA evidence vindicated the man, who had spent eleven years in prison for a robbery he did not commit.

senses.def: show to be right, reasonable, or justified
senses.ex: The company's huge profits vindicated the founder's risky decision to drop its oldest product line.

origin: From Latin "vindicta", vengeance, related to "vindicare", to avenge, plus the suffix "-ive".

senses.def: having or showing a strong desire for revenge
senses.ex: After losing the election, the vindictive councilman tried to cut funding for every project his rival supported.

origin: From Old French "vendange", from Latin "vindemia", grape harvest, from "vinum", wine, plus "demere", to take off.

senses.def: of high quality and lasting value, especially from the past
senses.ex: He restores vintage motorcycles from the 1950s and sells them to collectors around the world.

senses.def: typical of someone's best or most characteristic work or behavior
senses.ex: The witty, rambling toast was vintage Grandpa, full of puns and stories about his navy days.

senses.def: wine from a particular year's grape harvest, or the year it was made
senses.ex: The 2015 vintage from that valley is prized for its rich, balanced flavor.

origin: From Latin "virago", a warlike or heroic woman, literally "manlike", from "vir", man.

senses.def: domineering, aggressive, or bad-tempered woman
senses.ex: In the old comedy, the innkeeper's wife is played as a virago who chases customers out with a broom.

origin: From Latin "virilis", "of a man", through French "viril", based on Latin "vir", "man".

senses.def: showing strength or energy traditionally associated with adult men
senses.ex: His virile stage presence came from a powerful voice and unhurried, confident movements.

senses.def: marked by vigor, force, or creative energy
senses.ex: The quartet gave a virile performance that made the familiar piece sound urgent.

senses.def: sexually potent or capable of fathering children
senses.ex: The novel's aging king boasts that he remains virile and can still father an heir.

origin: From Medieval Latin "virtualis", having power or effect, from Latin "virtus", excellence or power, so something virtual has the effect of a thing without being it.

senses.def: almost or nearly as described, but not completely or officially
senses.ex: Heavy snow brought the city to a virtual standstill, with only snowplows moving on the main roads.

senses.def: existing or happening online or in a computer simulation rather than physically
senses.ex: The school held a virtual open house, letting families tour classrooms by video from home.

origin: From Italian "virtuoso", skilled or learned, from Late Latin "virtuosus", virtuous, from Latin "virtus", excellence.

senses.def: person highly skilled in music or another art
senses.ex: The twelve-year-old violin virtuoso performed a concerto that many adult professionals find daunting.

senses.def: showing exceptional skill or technique
senses.ex: The striker's virtuoso performance included two goals and an assist in the championship final.

origin: From Late Latin "virtuosus", "full of virtue", through French, ultimately from Latin "virtus", "excellence of character".

senses.def: showing strong moral principles and a commitment to doing what is right
senses.ex: The mayor's virtuous reputation survived because she disclosed the mistake before anyone else found it.

senses.def: producing beneficial effects that help create further benefits
senses.ex: By saving energy, the school cut costs and funded more upgrades, creating a virtuous cycle.

origin: From Latin "virulentus", full of poison, from "virus", poison or slimy liquid, the word scientists later borrowed for viruses.

senses.def: extremely severe, harmful, or fast-spreading, of a disease or poison
senses.ex: A virulent strain of flu swept through the dormitory, sending dozens of students to the clinic.

senses.def: bitterly hostile or hateful
senses.ex: The candidate faced a virulent online campaign full of insults and false rumors.

origin: From French "visage", "face", ultimately from Latin "visus", "appearance" or "sight", related to "videre", "to see".

senses.def: person's face or facial expression
senses.ex: Under the harsh stage lights, her tired visage appeared older than it had at rehearsal.

senses.def: the visible appearance or character of a place or thing
senses.ex: The city's visage changed as warehouses became galleries and cafes.

origin: From French "viscéral", "of the internal organs", based on Latin "viscera", "internal organs".

senses.def: arising from deep feeling rather than conscious reasoning
senses.ex: The film's sudden silence produced a visceral fear that no dialogue could have created.

senses.def: relating to the internal organs of the body
senses.ex: The surgeon checked for visceral injuries after the cyclist fell onto the handlebars.

origin: Both come from Late Latin words built on "viscum", birdlime, a sticky paste made from mistletoe berries for trapping birds.

senses.def: thick, sticky, and slow to flow
senses.ex: Cold honey is so viscid that it barely drips from the spoon until you warm the jar in hot water.

origin: From Late Latin "viscosus", sticky, from Latin "viscum", birdlime, a sticky paste once spread on branches to trap birds.

senses.def: thick and sticky, resisting flow
senses.ex: Motor oil becomes more viscous in freezing weather, which is one reason cars can be hard to start in winter.

origin: From "vision", from Latin "visio", sight, from "videre", to see, plus the suffix "-ary".

senses.def: thinking about the future with imagination, foresight, and wisdom
senses.ex: The visionary mayor planted thousands of trees decades before anyone talked about urban heat islands.

senses.def: person with original, inspired ideas about what the future could be
senses.ex: Many early computer visionaries predicted that families would one day carry tiny machines in their pockets.

senses.def: idealistic in an impractical or unrealistic way
senses.ex: Critics called the floating city plan visionary in the worst sense, beautiful but impossible to fund.

origin: From Italian "vista", "view", from "visto", "seen", related to Latin "videre", "to see".

senses.def: broad, distant view, often seen through an opening
senses.ex: At the trail's final bend, a vista of snow-covered peaks opened beyond the pines.

senses.def: broad prospect of future possibilities
senses.ex: The scholarship opened a vista of choices that had seemed impossible a year earlier.

origin: From Latin "vitalitas", vital force, from "vitalis", of life, from "vita", life.

senses.def: state of being strong, active, and full of energy
senses.ex: Regular exercise and good sleep restored the vitality she had lost during months of overwork.

senses.def: capacity of a place, group, or culture to stay active and thriving
senses.ex: New cafes and galleries have brought vitality back to the once-empty downtown.

origin: From Latin "vitiare", to spoil or damage, from "vitium", fault or vice.

senses.def: spoil or weaken the quality or effectiveness of something
senses.ex: One careless error in the data vitiated the entire study, and the journal withdrew the paper.

senses.def: make something legally invalid
senses.ex: The judge ruled that the missing signature vitiated the contract, so neither party was bound by it.

origin: From Latin "vitreus", "glassy", from "vitrum", "glass", the root behind descriptions of glasslike surfaces.

senses.def: having the appearance or physical qualities of glass
senses.ex: The kiln transformed the clay coating into a smooth, vitreous surface that reflected the studio lights.

senses.def: relating to the clear gel filling most of the eyeball
senses.ex: The textbook diagram showed the vitreous body filling the space behind the lens.

origin: From Medieval Latin "vitriolum", from "vitrum", glass, a name for glassy-looking sulfates and the burning acid made from them, hence cruel, corrosive words.

senses.def: cruel and bitter criticism or hostility
senses.ex: The online vitriol aimed at the young referee was so intense that she deleted her social media accounts.

origin: From "vitriol", an old name for sulfuric acid, plus "-ic", so vitriolic words burn like acid.

senses.def: filled with bitter criticism or malice
senses.ex: The critic's vitriolic review called the play an insult to anyone who had paid for a ticket.

origin: From Latin "vituperare", to blame or scold, from "vitium", fault, plus "parare", to prepare, literally to find fault.

senses.def: criticize or abuse someone harshly with insulting language
senses.ex: The angry customer vituperated the manager for ten minutes while the whole store fell silent.

origin: From Latin "vituperare", to blame or scold, from "vitium", fault, plus "parare", to prepare.

senses.def: criticize or abuse someone harshly with insulting language
senses.ex: Rather than vituperate the umpire, the veteran pitcher calmly asked him to explain the call.

origin: Past tense of "vituperate", from Latin "vituperare", to blame or scold, from "vitium", fault, plus "parare", to prepare.

senses.def: criticized or abused someone harshly with insulting language
senses.ex: The coach vituperated his players at halftime, calling their effort the worst he had seen in years.

origin: From Latin "vituperatus", "blamed", based on "vituperare", "to blame or censure", plus the adjective ending "-ive".

senses.def: marked by harsh, insulting criticism or verbal abuse
senses.ex: The columnist's vituperative review attacked the chef's character instead of discussing the food.

origin: From Latin "vivax", lively or long-lived, from "vivere", to live, plus the suffix "-acious".

senses.def: attractively lively and animated
senses.ex: The vivacious tour guide kept the tired group laughing all the way up the four hundred steps of the tower.

origin: From Old French "vivifier", "to give life", from Late Latin "vivificare", "to make alive".

senses.def: make something more lively, vivid, or animated
senses.ex: The teacher used a family diary to vivify the bare dates in the history lesson.

senses.def: bring to life or restore life to something
senses.ex: In the tale, a spring storm vivifies the carved birds, and they fly from the temple roof.

origin: From Latin "vocatio", a calling, from "vocare", to call, because a vocation was first a divine call to religious life.

senses.def: strong feeling of being suited to a particular career or way of life
senses.ex: After volunteering at the animal shelter, she discovered her vocation and enrolled in veterinary school.

senses.def: person's occupation or profession
senses.ex: His official vocation was accounting, but his real passion was building furniture on weekends.

origin: From Latin "vocifer", shouting, from "vox", voice, plus "ferre", to carry, so vociferous people carry their voices far.

senses.def: expressing opinions or feelings loudly and forcefully
senses.ex: Vociferous fans booed the referee's decision so loudly that the stadium announcer could not be heard.

origin: From French "vogue", a wave or course of success, from "voguer", to row or sail, so something in vogue is carried along on the current.

senses.def: the prevailing fashion or style at a particular time
senses.ex: Wide-legged trousers came back into vogue last spring, and every shop window on the avenue suddenly displayed them.

senses.def: general popularity or acceptance, especially a passing craze
senses.ex: Meditation apps enjoyed a brief vogue among the office staff before most people quietly stopped opening them.

origin: From Latin "volatilis", flying or fleeting, from "volare", to fly, so volatile things can fly off or change in an instant.

senses.def: likely to change suddenly and unpredictably, especially for the worse
senses.ex: Oil prices were so volatile that spring that airlines changed their ticket prices almost daily.

senses.def: quick to become angry or violent
senses.ex: His volatile temper made coworkers afraid to bring him even small problems.

senses.def: evaporating easily at normal temperatures
senses.ex: Gasoline is highly volatile, so its fumes can fill a closed garage within minutes.

origin: From Medieval Latin "volitio", will, from Latin "volo", I wish or want.

senses.def: power of using one's own will to choose or decide
senses.ex: No one forced him to resign, since he left the company of his own volition to start a bakery.

syn: will, choice, free will, choosing, determination

origin: From French "volte-face", literally "turn face", borrowed from Italian "voltafaccia", the act of turning around to face the other way.

senses.def: a sudden, complete reversal of opinion, policy, or attitude
senses.ex: After months of defending the tax, the senator performed a stunning volte-face and voted to repeal it.

origin: From Latin "volubilitas", from "volubilis", rolling, from "volvere", to roll, so words roll easily from a voluble speaker.

senses.def: quality of talking fluently, readily, and at length
senses.ex: The host's volubility filled every awkward pause, though guests sometimes struggled to get a word in.

origin: From Latin "volubilis", rolling or turning easily, from "volvere", to roll, so a voluble talker's words roll out freely.

senses.def: speaking easily, readily, and at length
senses.ex: Usually voluble at dinner, my uncle grew strangely quiet when someone asked about his new job.

origin: From Late Latin "voluminosus", from "volumen", a roll of writing or scroll, from "volvere", to roll.

senses.def: very large in size, amount, or extent
senses.ex: Investigators sifted through voluminous financial records, thousands of pages long, before finding the hidden payments.

senses.def: of clothing, loose and full, using much fabric
senses.ex: The singer swept onstage in a voluminous red gown that trailed several feet behind her.

senses.def: writing or speaking a great deal
senses.ex: A voluminous letter writer, the poet sent thousands of letters to friends during her lifetime.

origin: From Latin "voluptarius", devoted to pleasure, from "voluptas", pleasure or delight.

senses.def: a person devoted to luxury and sensual pleasure
senses.ex: The retired banker became a cheerful voluptuary, spending his days on fine wines, silk robes, and long lunches.

senses.def: concerned with or devoted to sensual pleasure and luxury
senses.ex: Critics mocked the novel's voluptuary heroine, whose only ambition seemed to be the next lavish banquet.

origin: From Latin "voluptuosus", full of delight, from "voluptas", pleasure.

senses.def: rich in sensual pleasure, luxury, or delight to the senses
senses.ex: The dessert was voluptuous: dark chocolate, warm cherries, and cream so thick it barely moved on the spoon.

senses.def: of a woman, having a full, curvy, and attractive figure
senses.ex: The painter favored voluptuous figures, filling his canvases with women whose curves echoed the rolling hills behind them.

origin: From Latin "vorax", greedy for food, from "vorare", to devour, the same root found in "devour" and "carnivore".

senses.def: wanting or devouring great quantities of food
senses.ex: Caterpillars are voracious eaters, and a few dozen can strip a young tree of its leaves in a week.

senses.def: very eager for an activity, especially reading or learning
senses.ex: A voracious reader, she finished every book in the small library before her twelfth birthday.

origin: From Latin "vortex", a whirlpool or eddy, a variant of "vertex", from "vertere" (or "vortere"), to turn.

senses.def: a mass of whirling fluid or air, such as a whirlpool or whirlwind
senses.ex: The draining bathtub formed a tiny vortex that swirled a stray leaf around before swallowing it.

senses.def: a situation or force that draws people irresistibly in and is hard to escape
senses.ex: Within weeks of taking the job, she was pulled into a vortex of meetings, deadlines, and late-night emails.

origin: From Latin "votus", vowed, past participle of "vovere", to vow or devote, so a votary is someone bound to a cause as if by a vow.

senses.def: a devoted follower, enthusiast, or advocate of a cause, pursuit, or person
senses.ex: A lifelong votary of jazz, he had traveled to New Orleans every spring for forty years to hear the bands.

senses.def: a person, such as a monk or nun, bound by religious vows
senses.ex: The temple's votaries rose before dawn to chant, sweep the courtyard, and tend the sacred flame.

origin: From Old French "vocher", to summon or call upon, from Latin "vocare", to call, as when calling on someone to stand as witness.

senses.def: to assert or confirm from personal knowledge that someone or something is reliable
senses.ex: I can vouch for Mira; she has watered my plants and fed my cat every summer without a single mishap.

origin: From Middle English "vouchen sauf", literally to vouch as safe, meaning to guarantee or grant something, often from a position of superiority.

senses.def: to grant or give something graciously, often as if from a superior position
senses.ex: The reclusive author rarely vouchsafed interviews, so the student was thrilled when he agreed to answer three questions.

senses.def: to reveal or disclose information, usually reluctantly or sparingly
senses.ex: Pressed about the merger, the spokesperson vouchsafed only that talks were continuing and refused to say more.

origin: Borrowed from French "voyeur", one who watches, from "voir", to see.

senses.def: person who gets pleasure, often sexual, from secretly watching others
senses.ex: Police arrested a voyeur who had been peering into apartment windows from the parking garage across the street.

senses.def: person who enjoys watching other people's private troubles or misfortunes
senses.ex: Reality television turns viewers into voyeurs, peering into strangers' family fights from the comfort of the couch.

syn: peeping Tom, spy, watcher, onlooker, observer

origin: From Latin "vulgaris", belonging to the common people, from "vulgus", the crowd or common folk.

senses.def: lacking refinement or good taste, especially in a showy or crude way
senses.ex: Their mansion was decorated with gold-plated faucets and life-size statues of themselves, which even their friends found vulgar.

senses.def: rude or obscene, especially referring to sex or bodily functions
senses.ex: The comedian's vulgar jokes drew groans from the parents and got his set cut short by the organizers.

senses.def: characteristic of or used by ordinary people rather than scholars
senses.ex: Dante chose to write in the vulgar tongue of Florence instead of Latin, so ordinary readers could follow him.

origin: From Late Latin "vulnerabilis", wounding, from Latin "vulnerare", to wound, from "vulnus", a wound.

senses.def: exposed to the risk of being attacked, harmed, or damaged
senses.ex: The seedlings are most vulnerable in their first week, when a single frost or hungry slug can wipe them out.

senses.def: emotionally open, willing to reveal feelings despite the risk of being hurt
senses.ex: In her speech she let herself be vulnerable, admitting that she had nearly quit the team after her injury.

syn: exposed, defenseless, susceptible, unprotected, at risk

origin: From Latin "vulpinus", foxlike, from "vulpes", fox.

senses.def: cunning, sly, or crafty like a fox
senses.ex: The negotiator's vulpine smile suggested he had already found a loophole the rest of us had missed.

senses.def: of, relating to, or resembling a fox
senses.ex: The dog had vulpine features, with a narrow muzzle, pointed ears, and a thick reddish tail.

origin: The verb comes from Scots "waff", to wave or flap, while the breakfast food comes from Dutch "wafel", a separate word.

senses.def: speak or write at length without saying anything clear or useful
senses.ex: Asked a simple yes or no question, the official waffled for five minutes about context and nuance.

senses.def: be unable to make a decision, keep changing one's mind
senses.ex: The committee waffled for months over the new logo before finally keeping the old one.

senses.def: crisp batter cake cooked in a hinged iron with a grid pattern
senses.ex: On Sunday mornings he makes waffles topped with strawberries and a spoonful of whipped cream.

origin: Of uncertain origin, possibly linked to Old English "wafian", to wave, so a scent that wafts seems to wave through the air.

senses.def: drift or carry gently through the air
senses.ex: The smell of fresh bread wafted from the bakery and drew a line of customers before it even opened.

senses.def: faint smell or gentle puff of air carried on a breeze
senses.ex: A waft of sea air through the open window reminded her how close the beach was.

origin: The verb comes from Middle English "waggen", to shake or sway, probably from Old English "wagian", while the sense of a joker is of less certain origin.

senses.def: person who habitually makes witty or playful jokes
senses.ex: Some wag in the office stuck googly eyes on the broken copier and labeled it the new intern.

senses.def: move quickly back and forth or up and down
senses.ex: The puppy wagged its tail so hard that its whole back half swayed from side to side.

origin: From "wag", a joker or mischievous fellow, plus "-ish".

senses.def: humorous in a playful, teasing, or mischievous way
senses.ex: My waggish uncle swapped the salt and sugar at every family dinner, and somehow we fell for it each year.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "weyver", to abandon or give up, related to "waif", something abandoned.

senses.def: to give up or refrain from insisting on a right, claim, or requirement
senses.ex: The museum waives its entrance fee on the first Sunday of each month, so the galleries are packed.

senses.def: to set aside a rule or requirement for someone in a particular case
senses.ex: Because of her strong portfolio, the college waived the usual prerequisite and let her enroll in the advanced course.

syn: forgo, relinquish, renounce, surrender, set aside

origin: From Old English "wealwian", to roll about, related to Latin "volvere", to roll.

senses.def: to indulge without restraint in an unpleasant emotion, especially self-pity
senses.ex: After the breakup he spent a week wallowing in misery, playing sad songs and refusing to leave the apartment.

senses.def: to roll about or lie relaxed in mud, water, or another substance
senses.ex: On hot afternoons the hippos wallow in the shallow river, with only their eyes and nostrils above the surface.

senses.def: to luxuriate or revel in something pleasurable
senses.ex: For one glorious weekend we wallowed in idleness, reading novels and eating breakfast at noon.

syn: indulge, revel, bask, luxuriate, steep oneself

origin: From Old English "wann", dark or dusky, a word whose meaning shifted over the centuries from gloomy to pale and gray.

senses.def: pale and looking sick or exhausted
senses.ex: After a week in the hospital, his face was wan and thin, though his eyes were still bright.

senses.def: weak or faint, especially of a smile or light
senses.ex: She gave a wan smile and said she was fine, but no one at the table believed her.

origin: From German "Wanderlust", from "wandern", to wander or hike, and "Lust", desire.

senses.def: a strong, restless desire to travel and explore the world
senses.ex: Her wanderlust began with a childhood atlas and eventually took her to forty countries before she turned thirty.

syn: restlessness, itchy feet, urge to travel, travel bug

origin: From Old English "wanian", to lessen or decrease, related to "want" in its old sense of lack.

senses.def: decrease gradually in size, strength, power, or importance
senses.ex: Interest in the fad waned after a few months, and stores slashed prices on the leftover toys.

senses.def: of the moon, show a smaller lit portion each night after the full moon
senses.ex: As the moon waned through the week, the stars over the desert grew brighter and brighter.

senses.def: gradual decline in size, strength, power, or importance, usually in the phrase "on the wane"
senses.ex: By the end of the decade, support for the old policy was clearly on the wane.

origin: From "want" in its older sense of lack, plus "-ing", so something found wanting lacks what it needs.

senses.def: lacking a required quality, not good enough
senses.ex: The judges found the bridge design wanting, since it could not support even half the required weight.

senses.def: absent or missing
senses.ex: Several pages were wanting from the old diary, torn out long before the family found it in the attic.

origin: From Middle English "wantoun", undisciplined, from "wan-", not, plus "towen", trained or brought up, so the wanton were once simply badly raised.

senses.def: deliberate, cruel, and without cause or provocation
senses.ex: The wanton destruction of the ancient statues shocked archaeologists around the world.

senses.def: sexually immodest or unrestrained, an old-fashioned sense
senses.ex: Victorian novels often punished wanton characters, while their modest heroines were rewarded with happy marriages.

origin: From "war" plus "monger", a dealer or trader, so a warmonger is someone who peddles war.

senses.def: a person who eagerly advocates or tries to stir up war
senses.ex: Opponents branded the minister a warmonger after he called for airstrikes before diplomats had even met.

origin: From "warrant", to justify or guarantee, from Old North French "warant", a protector or guarantee, a word of Germanic origin.

senses.def: justified or deserved by the circumstances
senses.ex: Given the icy roads and falling snow, the principal's decision to close school was fully warranted.

origin: From "ware", an old word for watchful or aware, plus "-y", the same root found in "beware" and "aware".

senses.def: feeling or showing caution about possible dangers or problems
senses.ex: Wary of strangers, the stray cat watched from under the porch for days before accepting any food.

origin: From "wasp" plus "-ish", comparing a sharp-tongued person to the stinging insect.

senses.def: quick to show irritation and make sharp, spiteful remarks
senses.ex: The waspish critic dismissed the new restaurant in one line, saying the soup was cold and so was the welcome.

origin: From "waste" plus the belittling suffix "-rel", as in "scoundrel", first recorded in the nineteenth century.

senses.def: a person who wastes money, time, or opportunities, especially an idle spendthrift
senses.ex: Her grandfather built the company from nothing, but his wastrel son gambled most of it away within a decade.

origin: From "water" plus "shed", modeled on German "Wasserscheide", a ridge that divides waters flowing toward different rivers, hence a turning point.

senses.def: event or period marking a major turning point
senses.ex: The invention of the printing press was a watershed in the spread of knowledge across Europe.

senses.def: ridge of high land dividing areas drained by different rivers
senses.ex: Rain falling east of the watershed flows to the Atlantic, while rain to the west reaches the Pacific.

senses.def: area of land that drains into a particular river, lake, or bay
senses.ex: Farm runoff from across the watershed carries fertilizer into the bay every spring.

syn: turning point, milestone, landmark, crossroads, threshold

origin: From Middle English "waveren", to move to and fro, related to "wave", so wavering thoughts sway back and forth.

senses.def: be undecided between two opinions or courses of action
senses.ex: He never wavered in his support for the project, even when its budget tripled.

senses.def: move unsteadily or flicker, of a light, voice, or flame
senses.ex: Her voice wavered as she read the farewell letter aloud to the crowded room.

origin: The verb meaning grow comes from Old English "weaxan", to grow, while the substance comes from Old English "weax", beeswax, a separate word.

senses.def: grow gradually larger, stronger, or fuller, especially of the moon
senses.ex: As the moon waxed toward full, the night hikers no longer needed their flashlights.

senses.def: speak or write in a specified manner, as in "wax poetic"
senses.ex: Grandma waxes nostalgic whenever she drives past the diner where she first met Grandpa.

senses.def: soft, oily substance that melts easily, used for candles and polish
senses.ex: She dripped red wax onto the envelope and pressed her grandfather's old seal into it.

senses.def: coat or polish something with wax
senses.ex: Every fall they wax their skis in the garage before the first trip to the mountains.

origin: From Middle English "weyfarere", from "way" plus "farer", one who fares or travels.

senses.def: a traveler, especially one who goes on foot
senses.ex: The old inn at the mountain pass once offered wayfarers bread, a fire, and a straw mattress for a few coins.

origin: From "way" plus "lay", probably modeled on Middle Dutch "wegelagen", lying in wait along the roads to rob travelers.

senses.def: to stop or interrupt someone unexpectedly, delaying them
senses.ex: A chatty neighbor waylaid me in the parking lot, and I arrived twenty minutes late for my dentist appointment.

senses.def: to lie in wait for and attack someone by surprise
senses.ex: In the old ballad, highwaymen waylay a merchant on the forest road and make off with his gold.

origin: Shortened from "awayward", turned away, from "away" plus "-ward", so the wayward turn away from the right path.

senses.def: difficult to control or predict because of willful or wrong behavior
senses.ex: The counselor helped wayward teenagers find jobs and finish school instead of skipping class.

senses.def: going off course or in an unexpected direction
senses.ex: A wayward golf ball crashed through the clubhouse window during the final round.

origin: From Old English "wela", well-being or wealth, the same root as "well" and "wealth". The welt sense is a separate word, an altered form of "wale".

senses.def: well-being, prosperity, or welfare, especially of a whole community
senses.ex: The founders insisted that laws should serve the public weal rather than the interests of a few wealthy families.

senses.def: a raised red mark on the skin, such as one left by a blow
senses.ex: The nettles left an angry weal across her ankle that itched for the rest of the hike.

origin: From Old English "wenian", to accustom or train, related to "wont", habit, so weaning gets a child used to a new kind of food.

senses.def: to gradually get someone to stop depending on or wanting something
senses.ex: The doctor slowly weaned him off the painkillers, lowering the dose a little each week.

senses.def: to accustom a young child or animal to food other than its mother's milk
senses.ex: Farmers usually wean lambs at about three months, once they are grazing well on their own.

senses.def: to be strongly shaped by something from an early age, used as "weaned on"
senses.ex: Weaned on old science-fiction films, she now designs robots for a living.

syn: withdraw, detach, disengage, break, ease off

origin: From Old English "werig", tired, a word with close relatives in other Germanic languages.

senses.def: very tired, especially after long effort
senses.ex: Weary after a twelve-hour shift, the firefighters slept on cots at the station.

senses.def: having lost patience or interest, usually "weary of"
senses.ex: Voters grew weary of the endless campaign ads that interrupted every television show.

senses.def: make or become tired or bored
senses.ex: The long lecture on tax law soon wearied even the most dedicated students in the hall.

syn: tired, exhausted, fatigued, drained, worn out

origin: From Old English "weder", the condition of the air, and the verb grew from things enduring exposure to wind, rain, and sun.

senses.def: come safely through a difficulty or crisis
senses.ex: The small bookstore weathered the recession by hosting readings and opening a cafe in the back.

senses.def: wear away or change through long exposure to wind, rain, and sun
senses.ex: Decades of salt spray had weathered the fence posts to a soft silver gray.

senses.def: state of the atmosphere at a place and time, such as heat, rain, or wind
senses.ex: The weather turned so stormy that the ferry to the island was cancelled for two days.

syn: survive, withstand, endure, ride out, overcome

origin: From Middle English "welteren", to roll or toss about, related to "wallow" and to Latin "volvere", to roll, so a welter tumbles together in confusion.

senses.def: large, confused, or disordered mass or jumble
senses.ex: Lost in a welter of conflicting reports, journalists struggled to confirm how many people had been rescued.

origin: From German "Weltschmerz", from "Welt", world, and "Schmerz", pain, literally "world pain".

senses.def: a melancholy weariness or sadness about the state of the world
senses.ex: Reading the news every morning filled him with a weltschmerz that no amount of coffee could lift.

origin: From Old English "wendan", to turn, the same verb whose past tense "went" became the past tense of "go".

senses.def: go slowly or by an indirect route, usually in the phrase "wend one's way"
senses.ex: The parade wended its way through the old town, stopping at every square for music and dancing.

syn: meander, wind, make one's way, journey, travel

origin: Of uncertain origin, perhaps from Old English "wædlian", to beg, or from German "wedeln", to wag the tail, as a fawning dog does.

senses.def: use flattery or coaxing to persuade someone to do something
senses.ex: The children wheedled their father into buying ice cream by promising to clean the garage afterward.

senses.def: obtain something by flattery or coaxing
senses.ex: She wheedled the secret recipe out of the chef by praising his cooking all evening.

origin: From "where" plus "as", in the old sense of "that", first used in English in the 1300s.

senses.def: in contrast with the fact that
senses.ex: My brother loves crowded cities, whereas I would rather live on a quiet farm far from any highway.

senses.def: considering the fact that, used to begin formal or legal statements
senses.ex: The council's resolution states that, whereas the bridge is unsafe, it shall stay closed until repairs are finished.

origin: From "where" plus "withal", meaning with which, originally an adverb asking with what something could be done, used as a noun since about 1800.

senses.def: the money, means, or resources needed to do something
senses.ex: The tiny bakery lacked the wherewithal to open a second shop, so the owners began crowdfunding.

origin: From Old English "hwettan", to sharpen, which also gives us "whetstone", a stone for sharpening blades.

senses.def: sharpen or stimulate an appetite, interest, or desire
senses.ex: The trailer whetted fans' appetite for the sequel without giving away any of the plot.

senses.def: sharpen a blade by rubbing it on a stone
senses.ex: Before the harvest, he whetted the scythe until its edge gleamed in the morning sun.

origin: Probably imitative, echoing the sound of a quick puff of air, and partly from Middle English "weffe", a smell or vapor.

senses.def: a faint or brief smell carried in the air
senses.ex: As I passed the bakery, a whiff of warm cinnamon drifted through the open door and made me stop.

senses.def: a slight hint or trace of something
senses.ex: Investors pulled out at the first whiff of scandal, long before any wrongdoing had been proven.

senses.def: to swing and miss completely, especially in baseball or golf
senses.ex: With the bases loaded, the rookie whiffed on three straight fastballs and walked back to the dugout.

origin: From "whimsy", a playful notion, plus "-ical", and "whimsy" is related to "whim", a sudden fancy whose deeper origin is uncertain.

senses.def: playfully quaint or fanciful, especially in an appealing way
senses.ex: The children's book is full of whimsical drawings of teapots with legs and umbrellas that fly.

senses.def: acting on sudden, unpredictable impulses
senses.ex: The rules changed so often under the whimsical manager that no one knew what to expect each Monday.

origin: Probably from "whim" plus "-sy", related to the older "whim-wham", a fanciful trifle.

senses.def: playful, fanciful, or quaintly odd humor or behavior
senses.ex: The children's library is full of whimsy, with bookshelves shaped like trees and a reading nook inside a giant teacup.

senses.def: a sudden fanciful idea or impulse; a whim
senses.ex: On a whimsy, they drove three hours to the coast just to watch the sunrise over the water.

origin: From Old English "wiht", a thing or creature, the same word as "wight", so "not a whit" means not a single thing.

senses.def: the smallest amount, used mostly with negatives such as "not a whit"
senses.ex: Despite the scolding, the puppy seemed not a whit sorry and immediately went back to chewing the shoe.

origin: From "white" plus "wash", first the name of a lime and water paint for walls, later used for covering up faults.

senses.def: hide or play down mistakes or wrongdoing to protect someone's reputation
senses.ex: Critics accused the board of whitewashing the scandal by releasing only a short, vague summary of the investigation.

senses.def: deliberate attempt to cover up wrongdoing
senses.ex: Families of the victims called the official report a whitewash that blamed no one at all.

senses.def: paint a wall or building with a white mixture of lime and water
senses.ex: Every spring the farmers whitewashed the barn walls to brighten them and keep insects away.

senses.def: cast white actors in roles meant for people of color, or downplay their part in history
senses.ex: Viewers complained that the studio had whitewashed the story by casting white actors as the Japanese heroes.

syn: cover up, gloss over, conceal, hush up, sugarcoat

origin: From "whole" plus "sale", originally selling goods "by whole", in large lots rather than piece by piece.

senses.def: done on a large scale, extensively and often without discrimination
senses.ex: The new manager's wholesale firing of the staff left the restaurant with no one who knew the recipes.

senses.def: the selling of goods in large quantities to retailers rather than to consumers
senses.ex: The farm sells most of its apples at wholesale to supermarkets and keeps only a few for its roadside stand.

senses.def: in large quantities or on a large scale, often indiscriminately
senses.ex: The committee rejected the proposal wholesale instead of considering any of its individual suggestions.

origin: From Middle English "holsum", from "whole" in its old sense "healthy" (or "hale") plus "-some".

senses.def: good for health and physical well-being
senses.ex: After weeks of fast food, she craved a wholesome meal of soup, fresh bread, and roasted vegetables.

senses.def: morally good, decent, and free of anything offensive
senses.ex: The town's summer festival offers wholesome fun such as pie contests, sack races, and a puppet show.

origin: An altered form of "whirl", describing a shape that seems to spin around a center.

senses.def: a pattern of spirals or concentric circles
senses.ex: Under the magnifying glass, every whorl of the fingerprint stood out as clearly as rings on a tree stump.

senses.def: a ring of leaves, petals, or other parts around a single point on a stem
senses.ex: The lily's leaves grow in neat whorls, each ring spaced evenly up the tall green stalk.

origin: From Middle Low German "weddersinnes", from "wedder", against, and "sin", direction, so literally "against the way".

senses.def: in a counterclockwise direction, or against the apparent course of the sun
senses.ex: According to the folktale, walking widdershins around the church three times would summon the fairies.

senses.def: in the wrong or opposite direction
senses.ex: The plan went widdershins from the start, with every step taking the project further from its goal.

origin: From Old English "wealdan" and "wieldan", to rule or control.

senses.def: to have and use power, authority, or influence
senses.ex: Though she holds no official title, the founder still wields enormous influence over every hiring decision.

senses.def: to hold and use a weapon or tool skillfully
senses.ex: The chef wielded a cleaver with such speed that the onions seemed to fall apart on their own.

origin: From "will", one's wishes or determination, plus "-ful", so a willful act is full of will rather than accidental.

senses.def: done deliberately and on purpose, often in a harmful way
senses.ex: The court ruled that the company's failure to warn customers was willful, not an honest mistake.

senses.def: stubbornly determined to have one's own way
senses.ex: The willful toddler refused to wear anything but her rain boots, even on sunny days.

origin: From "willow" plus "-y", comparing a person to the tall, slender, gracefully bending willow tree.

senses.def: tall, slender, and graceful
senses.ex: The willowy dancer seemed to float across the stage, her long arms rising like branches in a breeze.

senses.def: bordered by or full of willow trees
senses.ex: We paddled down a willowy stream where the branches hung so low they brushed our shoulders.

origin: Probably an altered form of the older "welk", to wither, from Dutch or Low German, first recorded in the late 1600s.

senses.def: of a plant, to droop and become limp from heat, lack of water, or disease
senses.ex: The basil wilted within hours of being left on the sunny windowsill without water.

senses.def: of a person, to lose energy, confidence, or strength
senses.ex: By the final mile, the runners were wilting under the afternoon sun and slowed to a walk.

senses.def: a plant disease that causes the leaves and stems to droop
senses.ex: The farmer lost half his tomato crop to a fungal wilt that spread through the field in July.

origin: From "wile", a trick or cunning plan, plus "-y", so a wily person is full of tricks.

senses.def: skilled at gaining an advantage, especially through cleverness or deceit
senses.ex: The wily fox learned to open the henhouse latch, so the farmer finally had to install a padlock.

origin: From Anglo-Norman "winchir", from a Frankish word meaning to bend or turn aside, like a body flinching away.

senses.def: to make a slight involuntary grimace or flinch in pain, embarrassment, or distress
senses.ex: She winced as the nurse cleaned the cut, then laughed at herself for making such a fuss.

senses.def: a brief grimace or flinching movement caused by pain or discomfort
senses.ex: He gave a small wince when the teacher read his clumsy opening line aloud to the class.

origin: From Middle English "wyndbagge", from "wind" plus "bag", a bag full of nothing but air.

senses.def: a person who talks at length but says little of value
senses.ex: The council meeting ran three hours because one windbag insisted on repeating every point he had already made.

origin: From Middle English "windfal", from "wind" plus "fall", originally fruit or timber blown down by the wind, a free gift to whoever found it.

senses.def: an unexpected sum of money or piece of good fortune
senses.ex: When her great-aunt left her a small inheritance, she used the windfall to pay off her student loans.

senses.def: a fruit that has been blown down from a tree by the wind
senses.ex: The orchard floor was covered in windfalls after the storm, and we gathered baskets of them for cider.

syn: bonanza, godsend, boon, jackpot, stroke of luck

origin: From Old English "windwian", to fan or toss grain, done so the breeze blows away the light chaff and leaves the heavy kernels.

senses.def: narrow down a group by removing the least wanted or weakest members
senses.ex: The committee winnowed two hundred applications down to a shortlist of five finalists.

senses.def: separate grain from chaff by tossing it in the air or blowing air through it
senses.ex: Villagers still winnow rice by hand, tossing it from wide baskets so the wind carries off the husks.

syn: sift, sort, screen, separate, narrow down

origin: From Old English "wynsum", pleasant or joyful, from "wynn", joy, plus "-sum", the ancestor of the suffix "-some".

senses.def: charming and appealing, often in an innocent way
senses.ex: The puppy's winsome expression persuaded the whole family to adopt him on the spot.

origin: From Middle Dutch "wijssegger", a soothsayer or wise man, later used mockingly for someone who only pretends to be wise.

senses.def: a person who irritatingly pretends to know everything or makes smart remarks
senses.ex: Some wiseacre in the back row kept correcting the guide's dates, and he was wrong every time.

syn: know-it-all, smart aleck, wisenheimer, wise guy

origin: Probably from "whist", silent, plus "-ful", with its sense of longing shaped by the similar word "wishful".

senses.def: having or showing a gentle, longing sadness or regret
senses.ex: She gave a wistful look at the old photos of the beach house her family had sold years ago.

origin: From Middle English "wydderen", to dry up, probably related to "weather", as if exposed to the weather until it shrivels.

senses.def: of a plant, to become dry, shrunken, and faded
senses.ex: Without rain all summer, the corn withered in the fields and the stalks turned brown by August.

senses.def: to grow weak or fade away over time
senses.ex: Her interest in the violin withered once her favorite teacher moved away.

senses.def: to make someone feel scorned or humiliated, often with a look or remark
senses.ex: The coach withered the chatty players with a single glance, and the gym fell silent.

syn: shrivel, dry up, wilt, fade, droop

origin: From Middle English "withholden", from "with" in its old sense "back" or "away" plus "hold", so to hold something back.

senses.def: to refuse to give, grant, or reveal something
senses.ex: The witness withheld crucial details from the police until her lawyer arrived.

senses.def: to deduct an amount, such as tax, from pay before it is received
senses.ex: My employer withholds a portion of every paycheck for federal and state income taxes.

syn: hold back, keep back, retain, conceal, suppress

origin: From Old English "withstandan", from "with", against, plus "stand", literally to stand against.

senses.def: to resist or endure something successfully without being damaged or defeated
senses.ex: The new seawall is designed to withstand waves twice as high as those of the last great storm.

origin: Coined by the poet John Dryden in the 1670s from "witty", modeled on "criticism".

senses.def: a clever and amusing remark
senses.ex: The host's witticisms kept the long awards ceremony lively, and even the losing nominees were laughing.

syn: quip, bon mot, jest, wisecrack, epigram

origin: From "wizen", to shrivel, from Old English "wisnian", to wither or dry up.

senses.def: shriveled or wrinkled with age
senses.ex: A wizened old fisherman sat mending nets on the dock, his hands as weathered as the planks beneath him.

origin: From Middle English "wo begon", from "woe" plus "begone", overtaken or beset, so literally overwhelmed by woe.

senses.def: looking sad, miserable, or sorrowful
senses.ex: The woebegone puppy sat by the door all afternoon, waiting for the children to come home from school.

senses.def: in a sorry, neglected, or run-down condition
senses.ex: The woebegone little theater, with its peeling paint and broken seats, was finally restored by volunteers.

origin: From "woe", great sorrow, plus "-ful", so it first meant full of grief before also meaning deplorably bad.

senses.def: very bad or deplorable
senses.ex: The team's woeful defense allowed thirty points in the first half alone.

senses.def: full of sorrow or misery
senses.ex: The lost child's woeful sobs drew a crowd of worried shoppers to the store entrance.

origin: From Old English "gewunod", accustomed, past participle of "gewunian", to be used to something or to dwell.

senses.def: person's customary behavior or habit, as in "as is her wont"
senses.ex: As was his wont, the professor arrived ten minutes late with a cup of coffee in each hand.

senses.def: accustomed or likely to do something
senses.ex: Teenagers, as they are wont to do, rolled their eyes all the way through the safety video.

origin: From Old English "wogian", to court or woo, a word whose deeper origin is uncertain.

senses.def: try to gain the support, favor, or business of someone
senses.ex: Both candidates spent the final week wooing undecided voters in the suburbs.

senses.def: try to win someone's love, especially in hope of marriage
senses.ex: In the old story, the young farmer wooed the baker's daughter with poems left under her door.

syn: court, pursue, cultivate, win over, seek

origin: From "wool" plus "gathering", picturing someone wandering aimlessly to collect stray tufts of wool caught on hedges and bushes.

senses.def: idle daydreaming or absent-minded indulgence in fanciful thoughts
senses.ex: His woolgathering during the lecture cost him, because he missed the professor's hint about the exam.

origin: From Middle English "werkedei", a working day, influenced by Old Norse "virkr dagr", used as an adjective since the 1500s.

senses.def: ordinary and everyday rather than special or interesting
senses.ex: She longed to escape her workaday routine of commuting, filing reports, and microwaving the same lunch.

senses.def: suitable for everyday work or use rather than for show
senses.ex: He kept his good suit for weddings and wore workaday boots and overalls the rest of the week.

origin: From "workman", a skilled manual worker, plus "-like", so it describes the steady competence of a good laborer rather than artistic flair.

senses.def: competent and efficient but not especially inspired
senses.ex: Critics praised the director's workmanlike handling of the sequel but missed the daring style of the original.

origin: From Old English "woruldlic", of this world, from "woruld", world, plus "-lic", like.

senses.def: experienced and sophisticated in the ways of the world
senses.ex: Her worldly older cousin, who had lived in four countries, seemed to know the best cafe in every city.

senses.def: concerned with material or earthly things rather than spiritual ones
senses.ex: The monks gave up all worldly possessions, keeping only a robe, a bowl, and a few books.

origin: The sense of ruin, as in "wrack and ruin", comes from Old English "wræc", misery or punishment, related to "wreak". The sense of seaweed and debris washed ashore comes from Middle Dutch "wrak", wreckage, related to "wreck". As a verb it is often a variant spelling of "rack", to torment.

senses.def: destruction or ruin, mostly in the phrase "wrack and ruin"
senses.ex: After the owner died, the old estate fell to wrack and ruin, its gardens choked with weeds.

senses.def: to cause great physical or mental suffering to someone (a variant of "rack")
senses.ex: Wracked with guilt over the lie, she finally called her friend and confessed everything.

senses.def: seaweed or other debris washed up on the shore
senses.ex: After the storm, the beach was strewn with wrack, tangled nets, and broken driftwood.

origin: From Scots "wraith", first recorded in 1513, of uncertain origin, possibly connected to "wrath" or to Old Norse "vörðr", guardian.

senses.def: ghost or ghostlike image of a person, often seen just before or after death
senses.ex: Villagers claimed a pale wraith drifted along the cliff path on foggy nights.

senses.def: pale, extremely thin person
senses.ex: After months of illness he was a wraith of his former self, barely able to climb the stairs.

origin: From Middle English "wranglen", from a Low German or Dutch word meaning to struggle or wrestle, related to "wring".

senses.def: to argue or dispute noisily, angrily, or at length
senses.ex: The two families wrangled for years over who owned the strip of land between their farms.

senses.def: a long, complicated, or bitter dispute
senses.ex: The contract wrangle between the players and the league delayed the start of the season by a month.

senses.def: to round up, herd, or take charge of animals or people
senses.ex: It took three counselors to wrangle the excited campers onto the bus after the field trip.

origin: From Old English "wraeththu", anger, formed from "wroth", angry, from a root meaning to twist, related to "writhe".

senses.def: extreme anger, especially anger that seeks punishment or revenge
senses.ex: The players feared the coach's wrath more than losing, so no one admitted to breaking the window.

origin: From Old English "wrecan", to drive out or avenge, related to Latin "urgere", to press, and distantly to "wreck".

senses.def: to cause a great amount of damage or harm, as in "wreak havoc"
senses.ex: The flash flood wreaked havoc on the valley, washing out roads and filling basements with mud.

senses.def: to inflict revenge or punishment on someone
senses.ex: The novel's hero spends twenty years plotting to wreak vengeance on the men who betrayed him.

syn: inflict, cause, unleash, bring about, create

origin: From Old English "wraestan", to twist or wrench, related to "writhe" and "wry".

senses.def: to take something, such as power or control, through force or great effort
senses.ex: The rebels wrested control of the capital from the army after weeks of fighting.

senses.def: to pull something away from someone with a violent twisting movement
senses.ex: The goalie wrested the ball from the striker's feet just before he could shoot.

origin: From Middle English "wrecched", from "wrecche", a miserable person, from Old English "wrecca", an exile or outcast.

senses.def: deeply unhappy, miserable, or unfortunate
senses.ex: After two sleepless nights with the flu, she felt utterly wretched and could barely lift her head.

senses.def: of very poor quality or in a terrible condition
senses.ex: The refugees lived in wretched shelters made of plastic sheeting and scraps of metal.

senses.def: contemptible or annoying, often used to express irritation
senses.ex: That wretched printer jammed again just as I was trying to print my essay.

origin: From Old English "writhan", to twist or turn, related to "wreath", "wrest", and "wry".

senses.def: to twist or squirm the body, as from pain, discomfort, or strong emotion
senses.ex: The injured player writhed on the grass until the medics arrived with a stretcher.

senses.def: to suffer greatly from embarrassment or another painful emotion
senses.ex: He writhed with embarrassment as his mother showed his baby photos to his new girlfriend.

origin: From "wrong" plus "headed", describing someone whose head is set in the wrong direction and stays there.

senses.def: having or showing bad judgment, stubbornly misguided
senses.ex: The plan to cut the library budget to pay for a new stadium struck most parents as wrongheaded.

origin: From Old English "wrigian", to turn or twist, so a wry smile is literally a twisted one, a sense kept in "awry".

senses.def: using or showing dry, mocking, or ironic humor
senses.ex: Stuck in traffic for the third hour, she made a wry joke about finally having time to learn Italian.

senses.def: twisted to one side, of the face, in disgust or displeasure
senses.ex: He made a wry face after tasting the bitter cough medicine his mother handed him.

origin: From German "Wunderkind", from "Wunder", wonder, and "Kind", child, literally "wonder child".

senses.def: a person who achieves great success or shows remarkable talent at a young age
senses.ex: The tech wunderkind founded her first company at nineteen and sold it for millions before graduating.

syn: prodigy, whiz kid, genius, phenom, virtuoso

origin: From Greek "xenia", hospitality, from "xenos", stranger or guest, the bond of friendship between host and visitor.

senses.def: hospitable, especially toward guests, strangers, or foreigners
senses.ex: The xenial villagers invited the stranded hikers into their homes and fed them until the pass reopened.

origin: From Greek "xenos", stranger or foreigner, plus "-phile", lover, from "philos", loving.

senses.def: a person who is attracted to foreign peoples, cultures, and customs
senses.ex: A true xenophile, he learned four languages and spent every vacation eating at markets in unfamiliar cities.

origin: From Greek "xenos", stranger or foreigner, plus "phobos", fear, so it literally means fear of strangers.

senses.def: dislike, fear, or prejudice against people from other countries or cultures
senses.ex: During the economic crisis, politicians who stirred up xenophobia blamed immigrants for every lost job.

origin: The noun comes from Jonathan Swift's "Gulliver's Travels" (1726), where the Yahoos are a race of brutish creatures in human form. The cry of joy is probably separate and imitative.

senses.def: a rude, coarse, or loutish person
senses.ex: A few yahoos in the parking lot spent the whole concert honking horns and shouting at passersby.

senses.def: used to express great joy or excitement
senses.ex: When the acceptance letter arrived, my sister ran around the kitchen yelling "Yahoo!" at the top of her lungs.

origin: From Middle English "yolpen", to yelp, of imitative origin, a word meant to sound like a harsh cry.

senses.def: a loud, harsh cry or yell
senses.ex: From the top of the mountain, she let out a joyful yawp that echoed across the empty valley.

senses.def: to shout or cry out loudly and harshly
senses.ex: The gulls yawped over the fishing boats, diving for scraps as the crew sorted the catch.

senses.def: to talk loudly and foolishly or complain noisily
senses.ex: Pundits yawped on every channel about the scandal, but few had read the actual report.

origin: From "yeast" plus "-y", borrowing the idea of yeast making dough bubble and rise.

senses.def: full of exuberant energy, ferment, or creative excitement
senses.ex: The city's yeasty music scene of the early 1990s produced dozens of bands that later became famous.

senses.def: tasting or smelling of yeast, or frothy like fermenting yeast
senses.ex: The kitchen was filled with the warm, yeasty smell of bread dough rising under a cloth.

origin: The craving sense probably comes from Cantonese "yan", a craving, first used for an opium addict's longing. The currency is a separate word from Japanese "en", round.

senses.def: a strong longing or desire for something
senses.ex: After a month of cafeteria food, I had a real yen for my grandmother's spicy noodle soup.

senses.def: the basic monetary unit of Japan
senses.ex: The souvenir shop priced the paper fans at five hundred yen, about the cost of a sandwich.

origin: Coined by the poet Dante Gabriel Rossetti in 1870 from "yester-", as in "yesterday", plus "year", to translate a line of François Villon.

senses.def: the past, especially a past time remembered with nostalgia
senses.ex: The diner's jukebox and chrome stools are a loving tribute to the soda fountains of yesteryear.

syn: the past, bygone days, yore, olden days, days gone by

origin: From Old English "geoc", yoke, related to Latin "iugum" and Sanskrit "yoga", all from an ancient root meaning to join.

senses.def: join or link together, often as a burden
senses.ex: The two towns were yoked together by a single school district, though they rarely agreed on anything.

senses.def: fasten a yoke on animals so they can pull together
senses.ex: The farmer yoked the oxen to the plow before sunrise.

senses.def: wooden crosspiece fastened over the necks of two animals so they can pull a load
senses.ex: The pair of oxen strained against the heavy yoke as the wagon climbed the hill.

senses.def: heavy burden or oppressive control
senses.ex: The colony finally threw off the yoke of foreign rule after a long struggle.

origin: First recorded around 1812, of uncertain origin, possibly from a dialect word for the green woodpecker or from German "Jokel", a nickname for Jakob.

senses.def: an unsophisticated person from the countryside, used as an insult
senses.ex: The city reporters treated the farmers like yokels, until one calmly corrected their statistics on crop yields.

origin: From Italian "zanni", a clown character in Italian comedy, a Venetian form of "Giovanni", John.

senses.def: amusingly unconventional, wacky, and eccentric
senses.ex: The zany science teacher arrived dressed as Isaac Newton and dropped apples from the ceiling to explain gravity.

senses.def: a clownish or eccentric person who acts the fool to amuse others
senses.ex: Every office has its zany, and ours wore a different novelty tie to work every single day.

origin: From Late Latin "zelus", from Greek "zelos", zeal or jealousy, which is also the source of the English word "jealous".

senses.def: great energy or enthusiasm in pursuit of a cause or goal
senses.ex: The new volunteers cleaned the riverbank with such zeal that they filled forty bags of trash by noon.

origin: From Greek "zelotes", an eager follower, from "zelos", zeal or jealousy. The Zealots were ancient Jewish rebels against Rome.

senses.def: a person who is fanatical and uncompromising in pursuing their beliefs or goals
senses.ex: The fitness zealot refused to let anyone at the party eat cake without lecturing them about sugar.

origin: From Latin "zelosus", full of zeal, from Greek "zelos", zeal or jealousy, and the word is a twin of "jealous".

senses.def: having or showing great energy or enthusiasm for a cause or goal
senses.ex: A zealous fact-checker, she called every source in the article before allowing it to run.

origin: Borrowed from German "Zeitgeist", from "Zeit", time, plus "Geist", spirit, literally "the spirit of the time".

senses.def: defining spirit, mood, or set of ideas of a particular period in history
senses.ex: The protest songs of the late 1960s captured the zeitgeist of a generation questioning authority.

syn: spirit of the age, ethos, climate, mood, temper

origin: From Medieval Latin "cenit", from Arabic "samt ar-ras", direction of the head, the "n" possibly coming from a copyist misreading "m".

senses.def: time when something is most powerful or successful, its highest point
senses.ex: At the zenith of its power, the empire controlled trade routes from the Mediterranean to India.

senses.def: point in the sky directly above an observer
senses.ex: At noon on the equinox, the sun stands almost at the zenith for people living on the equator.

origin: From Latin "zephyrus", from Greek "Zephyros", the god of the west wind.

senses.def: soft, gentle breeze, originally the west wind
senses.ex: A warm zephyr drifted through the open windows, carrying the scent of cut grass into the classroom.

syn: breeze, gentle wind, puff, draft, waft

origin: From French "zeste", the peel of a citrus fruit, whose sharp flavor led to the sense of keen enjoyment. Its earlier origin is unknown.

senses.def: great enthusiasm and energy, or keen enjoyment
senses.ex: At ninety, my grandfather still tackled every new hobby with the zest of a teenager.

senses.def: the outer colored skin of a citrus fruit, used as flavoring
senses.ex: Grate the lemon zest over the cake while it is still warm so the oils soak into the sponge.

senses.def: a quality of excitement, piquancy, or interest
senses.ex: A surprise twist in the final chapter added zest to an otherwise predictable mystery.

origin: From Greek "zeugma", a yoking or bond, from "zeugnynai", to yoke, because one word is yoked to two others.

senses.def: a figure of speech in which one word applies to two others in different senses
senses.ex: "She lost her keys and her temper" is a zeugma, since "lost" applies differently to the keys and the temper.

origin: From Greek "zoion", animal, and "morphe", form or shape.

senses.def: having the shape or form of an animal
senses.ex: The museum displays zoomorphic clay jars shaped like owls, turtles, and jaguars from ancient Mexico.

senses.def: attributing animal forms or qualities to gods, people, or things
senses.ex: Many early religions had zoomorphic gods, portrayed with the heads of hawks, cats, or jackals.
